There is no Science that teaches man such great, weighty, and necessary truths. The Mysteries of which it speaks are mysteries of Godliness <note>original: "Godzaligheid," referring to the practice of a devout and holy life</note>, and it gives him a foretaste of infinite joy. The pleasure that Theology <term>God-Geleertheid: The formal study of divine things or divinity</term> provides to those who practice it as is proper, is pure and Spiritual; one enjoys it without remorse, and it leaves no distaste behind; the source is inexhaustible, and there is abundance to satisfy all mortals.

<margin>The little care one has for practicing Theology.</margin>
It seems, therefore, that one should show all earnestness to acquire this science; but one must acknowledge that it is neglected to the extreme. There is nothing that men care for less than knowing Religion <term>Godsdienst: Literally "service to God," the standard Dutch term for religion</term>. Everyone believes, or at least wants to believe, that the one they profess is the best, and yet there is almost no one who takes the trouble to investigate the same. Some remain in it because they were born into it, as if one were bound to follow the path that leads to Hell, under the pretext that one happened upon it by birth.

*Others persevere in it because, by leaving the same, they would lose their fortune, as if there were any advantage in the world that can outweigh the loss of the Soul.*

*Others stay with it because they find Men of an outstanding learning in it, as if one had never seen great Men err.* There are few who investigate whether their religion has the marks of the true religion. Of so many people who bear the name of Christians <note>original: "Cristenen" and "Christenen" are used interchangeably in the text</note>, the fewest are so through knowledge. One would embarrass several of them if one asked them why they are Christians, since they have never let their thoughts dwell upon it. One sweats and toils to acquire sciences that most of the time are not certain, so that those who practice them most find that they have progressed the least, doubting things that previously appeared certain to them. But one miserably neglects the knowledge of Salvation <term>Zaligheid: The state of being saved or eternal blessedness</term>, which enlightens and satisfies the spirit, which satisfies the conscience, and fills the Soul with joy; which cleanses and comforts the heart. One applies oneself to learn all kinds of languages, to understand the diversity of the course of the Heavenly lights <note>original: "Hemelsche ligten," referring to the sun, moon, and stars</note>, to measure the body of the Sun and Stars, to discover a new constellation in the heavens, to know the future; and one shows no desire to strive for the truths that God has revealed to men; to ask for the path that leads to heaven; to know what we shall become after our death. One thinks only of gathering treasures, of climbing to honorable offices, of taking pleasure. But there are few who search for that which can make them attain lasting goods, eternal glory, and steadfast joy.

Few make this wholesome observation: that no true satisfaction is to be obtained in the world; that earthly goods leave us, or that we must leave them; that Honorable offices are but wind, and pleasures but vanity; and that finally death, which threatens to overtake us at any moment, will strike them down into the grave in a few years and possibly in a few days, into a state of eternal Salvation, if they...

they have embraced the true Religion <term>Godsdienst: Literally "service to God," the standard Dutch term for religion</term>, and directed their lives according to its commands, or pass into a state of eternal misery, if the Religion in which they have practiced is false. One thinks only of being pleasing to the Great Ones of the world, who are nevertheless inconstancy itself, and can do nothing for us after our soul is separated from our body; and one does not deign to investigate even once how one shall please the King of Kings, upon whom the happiness or misfortune of worldlings absolutely depends, who can cast our soul and our body into hell, and who has eternal crowns to reward those who love him and apply themselves to please him. One cannot sufficiently despise such conduct, and one has difficulty believing that men, who possess reason, make such evil use of it. Is it possible that one employs so much labor to preserve the body, which in spite of all our care must return to dust, and that one concerns oneself so little with caring for the soul, which is immortal? Is it to be understood that one undertakes everything to satisfy one's lusts, which under the hope of an imagined pleasure make us suffer a thousand substantial inconveniences, and that one does nothing toward the attainment of eternal Salvation <term>Zaligheid: The state of being saved or blessedness</term> and immortality? There must have occurred a wondrous reversal in the nature of men, for them not to even deign to inquire whether the path they take leads to Heaven or to Hell.

<margin>Reasons of those who do not wish to learn the matters of Theology.</margin>
One must not say, then, that it is enough that a certain order of Persons in the world apply themselves to Theology <term>God-Geleertheid: The formal study of divinity</term>. For there is no one who is not bound to practice it. One can entrust one's legal cases to Pleaders and Lawyers, and one's health to Physicians; but one must not leave the care for one's soul and Salvation to the judgment and discretion of others. One must also not say that Theological exercises are burdensome, and that there are great obscurities in the knowledge of Salvation: do not other Sciences <term>Wetenschappen: Systematic branches of knowledge or study</term> have their obscurities and their depths as well? Does this prevent one from practicing them diligently? Why does one not have the same passion for the mysteries of God in grace, as one has for the secrets of God in nature? How is it that one finds less pleasure in treating Theological matters than in investigating Nature and Astronomy? If there are obscure things in the knowledge of Salvation, are there not also those that are clear? Even if one had to take much trouble to know the true Religion, should one regret one's diligence and labor when it comes to obtaining the most excellent of all Sciences, which discovers to us the most sublime objects: a God, a Savior, an eternal Happiness? Is it not a sign of a corrupt heart that one exerts all one's strength to know a thousand things that are useless, and that one does not allow oneself to be instructed in the only knowledge that is absolutely necessary to us? But it is far from the case that the labor is as great as one imagines. An upright man, who fervently seeks to know the truth, does not seek it long in vain. <margin>John 7:17</margin> *If any man will do the will of him that sent me,* said Christ, *he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God, or whether I speak of myself.* <margin>1 Thess. 5:21 <note>The original text cites verse 22, but the quote "Prove all things" is verse 21.</note></margin> *Prove all things,* said Paul to all the believers, *and hold fast that which is good.*

# PREFACE

become worthy, if they fulfill the commands of God, and the misery they have to fear if they remain in their corruption.

There is no Science that teaches man such great, weighty, and necessary truths. The Mysteries of which it speaks are mysteries of Godliness <note>original: "Godzaligheid"</note>, and it gives him a foretaste of infinite joy. The pleasure that Theology <note>original: "God-Geleertheid"</note> provides to those who practice it as is fitting is pure and Spiritual; one enjoys it without remorse, and it leaves no distaste behind; its source is inexhaustible, and there is abundance enough to satisfy all mortals.

<margin>The little care that is taken to practice Theology.</margin>
It seems, therefore, that one should show all earnestness to acquire this science; but one must acknowledge that it is neglected to the extreme. There is nothing that men care for less than knowing Religion <note>original: "Godsdienſt"</note>. Everyone believes, or at least wants to believe, that the one they profess is the best, and yet there is almost no one who takes the trouble to investigate the same. Some remain in it because they were born into it, as if one were bound to follow the path that leads to Hell under the pretext that one happened upon it by birth.

*Others persevere in it because, by leaving the same, they would lose their fortune, as if there were any advantage in the world that could outweigh the loss of the Soul.*

*Others remain with it because they find Men of an outstanding learning therein,* as if one had never seen great Men err. There are few who investigate whether their Religion has the marks of the true Religion. Of so many people who bear the name of Christians <note>original: "Criſtenen"</note>, the fewest are so through knowledge. One would embarrass several of them if one asked why they are Christians, since they have never let their thoughts dwell upon it. One sweats and toils to acquire sciences that most of the time are not firm, so that those who practice them most find that they have progressed the least, doubting things that previously appeared certain to them. But one miserably neglects the knowledge of Salvation <note>original: "Zaligheid"</note>, which enlightens and satisfies the spirit, which contents the conscience, and fills the Soul with joy; which purifies and comforts the heart. One applies oneself to learn all kinds of languages, to understand the variety of the course of the Heavenly lights <note>original: "Hemelſche ligten," referring to the planets and stars</note>, to measure the body of the Sun and Stars, to discover a new constellation in heaven, to know the future; and one shows no desire to strive for the truths that God has revealed to men; to ask after the way that leads to heaven; to know what we shall become after our death. One thinks only of gathering treasures, of climbing to honorable offices <note>original: "eer-ampten"</note>, of taking pleasure. But there are few who search for that which can make them attain lasting goods, eternal glory, and steadfast joy.

Few make this salutary observation: that there is no true contentment to be obtained in the world; that earthly goods leave us, or that we must leave them; that Honorable offices are but wind, and pleasures but vanity; and that finally death, which threatens to overtake us at every moment, will strike them down into the grave in a few years and possibly in a few days, into a state of eternal Blessedness, if they

whether they have embraced the true Religion <note>original: "Godsdienst"</note> and directed their lives according to its commands, or whether they shall pass into a state of eternal misery if the Religion they have practiced is false. One thinks only of being pleasing to the Great Ones of the world, who are nevertheless inconstancy itself and can do nothing for us after our soul is separated from our body; yet one does not deign to investigate even once how one shall please the King of Kings, upon whom the happiness or misery of worldly people absolutely depends—He who can cast our soul and body into hell, and who holds eternal crowns to reward those who love Him and apply themselves to pleasing Him. One cannot sufficiently despise such conduct, and it is difficult to believe that men, who possess reason, make such evil use of it. Is it possible that one employs so much labor to preserve the body, which despite all our care must return to dust, and that one concerns oneself so little with caring for the soul, which is immortal? Is it conceivable that one undertakes everything to satisfy one's lusts, which under the hope of an imagined pleasure make us suffer a thousand real inconveniences, and that one does nothing toward the attainment of eternal Salvation <note>original: "Zaligheid"</note> and immortality? There must have occurred a wondrous reversal in the nature of men, for them not to deign even once to inquire whether the path they take leads to Heaven or to Hell.

<margin>Reasons for those who teach the matters of Theology.</margin>
<margin>John 7:17; 1 Thessalonians 5:21.</margin>
One must not say, then, that it is enough that a certain order of Persons in the world apply themselves to Theology <note>original: "God-Geleertheid"</note>. For there is no one who is not bound to exercise himself therein. One can entrust one's legal cases to Pleaders and Lawyers, and one's health to Physicians, but one must not leave the care of one's soul and Salvation to the judgment and discretion of others. Nor should one say that Theological exercises are burdensome, or that there are great obscurities in the knowledge of Salvation: do not other Sciences have their obscurities and their depths as well? Does this prevent one from diligently practicing them? Why does one not have the same passion for the mysteries of God in grace as one has for the secrets of God in nature? How is it that one finds less pleasure in treating Theological Matters than in investigating Nature and Astronomy <note>original: "Sterrekunde"</note>? If there are obscure things in the knowledge of Salvation, are there not also those that are clear? Even if one had to take great pains to know the true Religion, should one regret one's diligence and labor when it comes to obtaining the most excellent of all Sciences, which discovers to us the most sublime objects: a God, a Savior <note>original: "Zaligmaaker"</note>, an eternal Blessedness? Is it not a sign of a corrupt heart that one exerts all one's strength to know thousands of things that are useless, and that one does not allow oneself to be instructed in the only knowledge that is absolutely necessary to us? But it is far from the case that the labor is as great as one imagines. An upright man, who fervently seeks to know the truth, does not seek it long in vain. *If any man will do his will, said Christ, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God, or whether I speak of myself. Prove all things, said Paul to all the believers, and hold fast that which is good.*

The idea that we have of God as a being who is perfectly good does not allow us to believe that He [withholds] the knowledge of Salvation...

nor to that of the pious, because the experience of all times teaches that the wisest Teachers and the most pious people have, on various occasions, deceived themselves.

7. It is better to mistrust oneself than to be stubborn in one's opinions: but one must also not mistrust one's own knowledge so much that one lets one's faith depend entirely upon that of another.

8. One must never be captivated by the outward appearance of beauty in a Religion; that is only to be forgiven in children.

9. It is permitted to consult the senses in matters that are within their reach; but when it comes to things that do not fall under the senses, such as spiritual matters, one must listen to reason and the Scripture <note>original: "Schrift"</note> alone.

10. In the matter of Religion <note>original: "Godsdienst"</note> one must never take counsel with our passions <note>original: "hartstogten"</note> and our personal interests, for those are evil Counselors.

11. One must also not reject the truths presented to us because they are common, or even if we cannot reconcile them with others.

12. One must likewise not demand a mathematical demonstration for that which cannot be proven in a mathematical manner, such as all Historical events. We must content ourselves with the proofs that can be given to us regarding the subjects presented.

13. To seek the truth, and not to desire to be regarded as a high-flying spirit <note>A "high-flying spirit" refers to someone who is intellectually arrogant or overly speculative.</note>, must be our primary goal.

14. We must always take good note that God has not given us the understanding we possess to waste it on thousands of idle speculations, but to apply it to the use for which He has intended it.

15. We must be on our guard not to be misled by the foundations of a vain Philosophy <note>original: "Filosofie"</note>, although we may use the principles of the true kind to our advantage.

16. One must avoid all company which, by corrupting our heart, can distract our spirit from the pursuit of truth.

17. On the contrary, we must seek the fellowship of those who can be helpful to us in dispelling the darkness of our understanding and in fighting our passions.

18. One must show as much zeal to know the truth and the true Religion as worldly people have to make themselves great.

19. One must diligently and with fervor read the Holy Scriptures <note>original: "Heilige Schriften"</note>, in which God has made Himself known to us and deigned to instruct us.

20. Finally, since we can do nothing without God's spirit, we must constantly call upon Him and pray that He humbles our pride <note>original: "hoogmoet"</note>, which is the cause of most of our errors. For it is pride <note>original: "hovaardy"</note> that makes us have an aversion to a doctrine presented to us before we know whether it comes from God or from men. When our heart, as has been very well noted, has taken on this inclination, it communicates the same to our understanding. It makes the doctrine appear hateful from every angle that can make it hateful.

It applies itself to magnifying all the difficulties that accompany the doctrine, and to diminishing the reason by which one can overcome them, in order to...

-># OF THE AUTHOR.<-

... to be more affected by it, and to submit with honor. Through such a seduction of the heart, the Spirit turns its gaze away from the true reasons that confirm the truth, so that they—far from making the spirit lean toward the good side—can barely keep it in balance to outweigh the counter-arguments, however weak and vain they may be.

After giving these counsels, which I judge necessary in order not to fall into error, nothing remains for me but to say something beforehand about the work that I am bringing to light.

<margin>
The method that has been followed in this work.
</margin>
I present here a system of Christian Theology <note>original: "Chriſtelyke God-Geleertheid"</note>, and an explanation of the truths that God has revealed to men in the Holy Scripture.

I have endeavored to explain the same as clearly as I can, and to adapt myself to the understanding and the reach of the simplest people. But, for the service of the more advanced, I have added several observations, and unfolded the most powerful as well as the most difficult passages of Scripture.

After I have presented the truth through the strongest and most convincing reasons, I answer the objections that are brought forward. Those that fall away of their own accord, I have only touched with a finger; and those that have some obscurity, I have endeavored to clear up.

Alongside the reasons that I bring forward to present the truth, and which are mostly drawn from the Scripture, I have added several remarkable passages from the Ancient Fathers <note>The "Ancient Fathers" refers to the early Christian theologians and bishops of the first few centuries, often called the Church Fathers.</note> regarding each subject; I have enriched these with a historical account of the sentiments of the Church, in order to know, according to a proper chronological chain, what was taught and believed in the preceding centuries that have passed from the death of the Apostles until this time.

To this end, I have made use of the labor of the Learned, whose writings I have been able to obtain, and I am not ashamed to have frequently made their expressions my own.

I do not cite the names of all the contemporary writers, although I hold their merits in high esteem. I have nevertheless done so sometimes in this new edition, when I have been able to recall who those are from whom I have transcribed entire passages; I make it a point of honor to confess that I have drawn and scooped from the springs of good books, of whatever denomination <note>original: "gezintheid"</note> the writers may be.

I also do not always cite the Teachers and the Sects <note>original: "Gezintheden"</note> that I oppose. I do that sometimes in the margin.

I treat the subjects simply, and I answer the difficulties, and if it is found that I solve them well, it must be enough for the Reader to enter into an opinion with me.

It serves no purpose to know who the author of the proof is that I, to clarify the truth, propose. If it is good, one must abide by it, even if it came from the pen of the most ignorant man; and, if it does not prove anything, one has only to set it aside, even if it were produced by the wisest. I have acted thus so that one might judge without prejudice, and to be briefer, because I would otherwise have been obliged to expand much more to unravel <note>original: "ontzwagtelen," literally to unswaddle or unwrap.</note> the state of the questions and the sentiments that the writers have regarding them.

Regarding the order that I have followed, I have kept to that which appeared most natural to me.

<meta>This page continues the author's preface, specifically outlining the systematic structure and theological sequence of the book, transitioning from the methodology mentioned on the previous page to a detailed table of contents in narrative form.</meta>

# P R E F A C E

1. I investigate immediately whether there is a God, and how he has made himself known.
2. I subsequently bring forward the reasons that prove that what we call Holy Scripture is truly God's work, and I give a small understanding of the Books contained therein.
3. I investigate whether the Scripture is perfect, or whether one must take refuge in tradition; whether it is clear enough to be understood, and whether one must read it. I treat of its authority, and I consider whether it is the rule of our faith and morals. I go through the translations that have been made of it, and I raise the further points of dispute that are commonly proposed and researched concerning this matter.
4. I further investigate what the Scripture tells us of the Nature and Perfections of the Divinity, of the Divine Persons, of the Trinity, and of God's Decrees.
5. From there I pass over to God's works, and I begin with the *creation of the world, of the Angels, and of Mankind*.
6. I show in what state God created Man, and how he fell into sin, of which I describe the deadly consequences.
7. After the *Creation*, I treat of Providence, and of what it does regarding *Sin*.
8. From the *Fall of Man* into Sin with its sorrowful consequences, I ascend to the decree of God, who did not will that all men should be eternally miserable, as they had deserved through their sins. And I treat in this place of the Decree of *Election*, through which God has destined some to salvation, while he leaves the others in their corruption.
9. Just as God could not make men blessed without satisfaction to his justice, so I treat of the Decree that God made to send his Son to redeem us, and of the manner in which this Decree was carried out. I speak there of the *Incarnation* of the Son of God, of what preceded his coming, of his Offices, of the various States through which he passed, and of the *Covenant of Grace*, which God established with men through his mediation.
10. I then come to the fruits of the death of the Mediator *Jesus Christ*, which are *Calling*, *Justification*, *Sanctification*, and on this occasion I explain the *Ten Commandments*, and after that I step over to *Glorification*.
11. Just as all these fruits and goods are only for the church, so I treat here of the *Church*, and I investigate what is taught of the Nature of the Church, of its Visibility, Infallibility, Holiness, Head, Members, Ministers, and what further concerns it.
12. I end with the *signs* <note>The author refers here to the Sacraments, viewed as outward signs and seals of God's promises.</note>, which are the seals of the Covenant of Grace.
I have not sought the Ornaments of eloquence of this century; I have kept myself in all my treatises to the simplest and clearest method of teaching.
I request that all who shall read my work may please to excuse my failings; God give to them all the spirit of *truth* and the *anointing* <note>A reference to 1 John 2:27, implying spiritual insight granted by the Holy Spirit.</note> that teaches us all things. Amen.

He emphasizes a simple teaching style intended for spiritual edification rather than academic display.</summary>

# N O T I C E.
### R E G A R D I N G
## THE LATEST EDITION.

This is the third edition of my <term>Christian Theology<note>original: "Christelyke God-Geleertheid"</note></term>.
I have added nothing to the two volumes that were previously printed: But I have incorporated most of the notes that stood in the margin into the text, because several people, whose advice I highly esteem, requested this of me, since it is inconvenient to leave the text and search for the marginal notes.

As the insertion of the notes into the text causes the volumes to expand, I have omitted three things from them.
1. The <term>Index of the Fathers and Teachers<note>original: "Register der Vaders en Leeraars"; referring to the Early Church Fathers and influential theologians.</note></term>, which was in Volume I.
2. The Index of the <term>Councils<note>original: "Koncilien"</note></term>.
3. And a short summary of general history, both contained in Volume II.

But I have added a third volume to these two, which contains:
1. The Index of the Fathers, which was in Volume I, but greatly increased with remarks about every Father and Teacher, and continued up to and including the 18th Century.
2. An Index of the <term>Popes<note>original: "Pauzen"</note></term>.
3. --- Of the <term>Heretics<note>original: "Ketters"</note></term>.
4. --- Of the <term>Church Assemblies<note>original: "Kerkvergaderingen"</note></term>, much broader than in Volume II.
5. A General History, which is also more extensive than that which stands in Volume II.
6. The <term>Jewish Antiquities<note>original: "Joodsche Oudheden"</note></term>.

THE STATES OF HOLLAND AND WEST FRIESLAND <note>The governing body of the most influential provinces in the Dutch Republic</note>; make it known; That whereas it has been shown to us by Daniel vander Vecht, Citizen and Bookseller within the City of Leiden, that he was busily engaged in having printed *The Christian Theology and Knowledge of Salvation*, or the presentation of the Truths which God has revealed to Men in the Holy Scripture, with the Refutation of Errors against these truths, the origin of most of these Errors, the sentiments of the Church Fathers; and a short discourse on all the most remarkable things in Sacred and Secular Histories, written in French by Mr. *Benedictus Pictet*, in his life Professor at the Academy, and Minister in the Church of Geneva, and now translated into the Dutch Language; but since such a Patent and Privilege could not be granted without our consent and permission: So he, the Petitioner, therefore humbly turned with this request before us, to obtain such a request: SO IT IS, that we, having considered the matters and the aforementioned request, and being inclined to the prayer of the Petitioner, out of our certain knowledge, Sovereign power and authority have consented, accorded, and granted to the same Petitioner; do consent, accord, and grant to him by these presents, that he during the time of the first fifteen consecutive years may alone print, have printed, publish, and sell the aforementioned Book in such manner as requested by the Petitioner and expressed hereinbefore, within our aforementioned Lands, forbidding therefore any and everyone to print, counterfeit, have counterfeited, trade or sell the aforementioned Book in whole or in part, or to bring into our same Lands, publish, or trade and sell it if counterfeited elsewhere, upon forfeiture of all the counterfeited, imported, traded, or sold copies, and a fine of three thousand guilders to be forfeited in addition, to be applied one third part for the Officer who shall make the accusation <term>calange: a legal challenge or prosecution of a crime</term>, one third part for the poor of the place where the case shall occur, and the remaining third part for the Petitioner, and this each time as often as the same shall be caught; all this being understood, that we, wishing only to gratify the Petitioner with this our Patent, for the prevention of his damage through the counterfeiting of the aforementioned Book, do not intend in any way to authorize or endorse the contents thereof, and much less to give the same any greater credit, standing, or reputation under our protection and defense, but rather, the Petitioner in case anything improper [is found] therein...

Therefore, one can distinguish and divide the rise and continuation of Scholastic Theology <term>School-God-geleertheid: the medieval method of theology based on logic and dialectic</term> into three periods.

<margin>
The 3 periods of Scholastic Theology.
</margin>
The 1st runs from the time of Abelard to Albertus Magnus, teacher of the famous Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> in the year 1260. The most renowned proponents of Scholastic Theology in this era are Peter Lombard, Hugh of St. Victor, Raymond of Penyafort, William of Paris, Peter of Poitiers, etc.

The first.
</margin>
The 2nd period extends from Albertus Magnus to Durandus of Saint-Pourçain, who died in the year 1333. During this time flourished Alexander of Hales, Thomas, and Scotus <note>Duns Scotus</note>.

<margin>
The second.
</margin>
The 3rd period begins with Durandus and goes until Gabriel Biel, who died in the year 1495.

<margin>
The third.
</margin>
This Scholastic Theology is so confused and entangled with so many obscure terms, useless and vain arguments, and extravagant questions, that it has been disapproved of and rejected by several great men. Among these are Stephen of Tournai, in his 251st Letter; Gerson in his Lessons on Mark in the year 1389; The Theological Faculty of Paris in the year 1530; Nicolaus Clemanges in his book on the practice of Theology; Melchior Cano in his Theological treatises Book VIII, Chapter I. Lord de Godeau says plainly that the Scholastics have darkened and blackened the Truths which they claimed to clarify, and have miserably violated and dragged down the knowledge of Holy Scripture, the

On this matter, Father Mabillon may be further consulted in his learned work on monastic studies.

III. As for Pagan Theology <note>original: "Heidensche God-geleertheid"</note>, it can conveniently be divided into three types or parts, as appears from a passage by Varro, whom Augustine cited in his book written on the *City of God*, Book VI, Chapter 5.

<margin>
Pagan Theology divided into three types.
</margin>
The 1st is called Mythical <note>original: "Fabulosa"</note>. The Poets made use of this, and in it were attributed to the Gods not only all the deeds of mortals, but of the softest and most wicked mortals. Such is the theology found in Homer, Hesiod, etc.

<margin>
Mythical.
</margin>
The 2nd bears the name of Natural <note>original: "Physica"</note>. In this, the Philosophers exercised themselves, having written and left behind several books on the subject. Therein one finds who are to be considered Gods, where they are and from what they have their origin, what their essence is, and from what time they came forth: one also investigates therein whether they have been from eternity, or whether they were brought forth by fire, as Heraclitus <note>The text reads "Heraclius," likely referring to the philosopher Heraclitus</note> believed, or by the union of certain numbers, as Pythagoras asserted, or from indivisible particles <note>atoms</note>, as Epicurus taught. It was not permitted at all to speak of these Gods before the common people.

<margin>
Natural.
</margin>
The 3rd type of Scholastic Theology <note>The author likely means "Pagan Theology" here in context of the three types</note> was nothing other than a Political or Civil <note>original: "Politica, Civilis"</note> knowledge, which every inhabitant and especially the Priests had to understand and observe; therein one saw which Gods were kept and worshipped, and what offerings one had to religiously sacrifice to them, etc.

<margin>
Political.
</margin>

## I. CHAPTER.

->In which it is proven that there<-
->is a God.<-

<margin>
Reasons why one must prove that there is a God.
</margin>
THAT there is a God—that is, a Supreme Being who is infinite, most perfect, independent, the cause and origin of all other beings and Creatures—is a truth so certain and so clear that one cannot deny nor gainsay it without bidding farewell to the light of reason. Therefore, it seems at first glance that one might well spare the effort of constructing a proof for it. However, we are of the opinion that at the beginning of our discourses this fundamental principle must be established for several reasons. I. Because this truth is the first upon which all other truths depend. II. Because there are many Free-Thinkers <note>original: "Vry-Geesten"; refers to deists or atheists who rejected traditional dogma</note> who attempt to persuade themselves that there is no God. III. Because there are many who, notwithstanding the confession they make of believing that there is a God, nevertheless can give no reasons for their faith.

<margin>
Proofs brought forward by Philosophers etc. to demonstrate God's existence.
</margin>
The proofs for laying this foundation are easily found; many present themselves immediately. Renowned Philosophers and Theologians have demonstrated the existence of the Deity through the idea that one has by nature of a most perfect being. One can—so they reason—affirm of a thing everything that is clearly and distinctly contained within its concept. Now, it is certain that one could not have a concept of a most perfect being without the concept of the actual existence of such a supreme being; so that actual existence is included in the concept of a most most perfect being. Therefore, one can, upon

<column-break/>

a firm ground, affirm that the most perfect supreme being actually exists.

<insert>
It is true that there are those among the Learned who nowadays consider this proof, which is from Descartes, to be a pseudo-proof; but there are many among them who give it their assent.
</insert>

<margin>
In *Proslogion* Chapter 23, regarding the 3rd Chapter of Exodus 3:2.
</margin>
The reasoning of Anselm <note>Saint Anselm of Canterbury, known for the Ontological Argument</note> is nearly the same as that of Descartes, and Tostatus <note>Alonso Tostado, a prolific 15th-century Spanish theologian</note> did nothing other than follow Anselm. They also draw a proof for the Deity from this: that the idea one has of a most perfect being can neither be placed nor produced in man except by the most perfect supreme being himself. Others are intent on proving this truth through the necessity of positing a first cause of all things, otherwise all created things would run into infinity, which would be absurd. Those who make use of this proof demonstrate that if one could not ascend to a first cause, one could also never, in descending, arrive at the final effect; for, they add to this, to ascend from the effect to the cause, or to descend from the cause to the effect, are two things as closely linked as a mountain to a valley. If it is objected to them that one can begin to draw a line from the place where one is and extend it unto the indefinite, or begin a number and increase the same unto infinity, in such a way that there can be a first number and a first point without one finding the last of it, they give as an answer that it does not depend here on a line that one can draw or a number that one can increase, but that it depends on a completed line and on a finished number. Now it is evident that every line that one ends after the beginning, and every number that one stops increasing, is necessarily finite. Others prove the existence of a God—

Others bring forward the sensations of pleasure and of sadness / which we perceive in ourselves / through the intervention of the body / as proof that it is God alone / who can work and impress them upon us. Others reason in this way / either / they say / one must maintain / that there has been a time / in which no being existed / or one must recognize that there has been one before all times and from eternity / which has existed highly and above all beings and of itself. Others prove the existence of the most perfect Supreme Being from this / that the idea that one has of the Supreme Being / contains and concludes no contradiction within itself / and therefore they say / it is possible just as it is / that there is a Supreme Being / so it follows necessarily from that that it has always been. There would be almost no end to be found for such reasonings / if one wished to bring them all to the table; one must confess that there are many / which have more ingenuity than conciseness.

Since then these proofs are not all equally comprehensible to all men / I shall keep myself only to the proofs / which are the simplest and the easiest to understand / firmly trusting that they will satisfy those / who wish to give place to reason / and that one cannot contradict them without doing force and violence / (as they say /) to oneself.

<margin>
I. Proof of the existence of the Deity taken from the constitution of our body.
</margin>
I. Man has but to consider himself to be convinced that there is a God.

Indeed, one cannot give the slightest attention to the human body / that amazing masterpiece of which all the members are equally admirable / without concluding that it is an incomparable Master-builder who has made it / and that this Maker is God / since no being / but the Divine / which possesses the highest Wisdom and Omnipotence / is capable / of producing such a work of Art / as the body is. Behold the parts of it / and you shall stand amazed by it. A heart that is the center of heat and life. The brain which is like the Palace of the Soul. See the great number of veins and arteries, nerves and muscles, bones and cartilages, ligaments, fibers and glands, of which all the wondrous workings are not yet all discovered. The eyes, serving to behold all objects that present themselves;

<column-break/>

The ears which stand open to hear and distinguish all kinds of sound; what a construction is the palate of the mouth / <margin>Galatians 4 <note>The marginal reference to Galatians 4 likely refers to the physical nature of man or the "elements of the world."</note></margin> that tastes and tests all foods / the hands to do all kinds of work / and the feet to walk? If you further consider what the parts of the body / which we / to be brief / pass over / are suited for / you shall find yourself persuaded / that God alone is the Master-builder of such a masterpiece.

If one will not confess that God is the Maker of it / then one must posit one of three things / either that man made himself / or that he owes the production of our bodies only to our parents / or that they were produced by chance. Yet without absurdity one cannot maintain these propositions.

How is it to be made good / that man made himself / since he cannot add a single cubit <note>original: "elle"; an old unit of measurement, here referencing Matthew 6:27</note> to his stature / and cannot keep himself in life for a single moment. It is impossible that one and the same thing should be and not be at the same time. Now if man himself had made himself / he would have been and not been at one time; he would have existed / since it is presupposed that he would have been active. Now it is certain / that he could not have been active / without existing beforehand. He would not have existed / since he could not be in being / before he was made. How could one say that our bodies are entirely the work of our parents / since they do not know in what manner all these parts are formed / and who contribute so little to it? Finally, how can it be said that our bodies are an effect of chance / since such happens every day in the same manner?

<margin>
II. Proof from the consideration of the soul to the consideration of the King of [the Soul].
</margin>
II. If we pass from the contemplation of our bodies to the consideration of our Soul / we shall be even more convinced / that there is a God / who is the Maker of it. For one must say / either that our soul has always been / or that it is produced from some matter / or that it made itself / or that it is created by some creature / or that it has God as its cause.

There is no one who would dare to maintain that the soul has always been / that it exists necessarily, and that all souls are eternal, as Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, Roman philosopher who argued for the immortality and pre-existence of the soul.</note> wished / because one must propose nothing without some proof. Now one can bring no proof / that the soul has always been present / it has all too many imperfections / to [ascribe] to it the

# THEOLOGY. BOOK I. Chapter I.

to attribute the greatest perfection to the Deity who exists in eternity.

Also, one can say with no basis that the soul made itself; for it would have made itself more perfect, not to mention that it is contradictory for a thing to bring itself forth.

To say that it was brought forth by matter is the greatest of all absurdities. For who could understand that from a coarse matter can come a Spirit that thinks, that reasons, that raises itself above all the senses, that contains sublime truths, that corrects the defects of our imagination, that meditates upon its own thoughts, that brings the past to mind, penetrates into the future, discovers the greatest secrets, unwinds the most difficult hardships, that measures the heavenly bodies, traverses the vastness of the world, remembers many languages, and can perform those wonderful things?

I truly have difficulty understanding that there are people foolish enough to believe that a Spirit, such as I have described it, can come forth from a coarse and rough matter. No being can bring forth any being unless it is at least as perfect as it is itself. How is it to be understood that matter gives perfections which it does not have?

One cannot even conceive how motion, which is the action of matter, could bring forth a thought, because one does not understand that motion has any other immediate effect than to arrange, to displace, and to prepare matter differently than it was before. One will possibly say that we have various thoughts according to the variety of the movements that arise in our brains, and that a little matter overturned in our constitution causes a strange confusion in our ideas, at least in our imagination. But this reasoning proves nothing other than that the movements which happen in our bodies give our souls occasion to form certain thoughts, since God has united our bodies with our souls so closely that when the one moves in a certain way, the other thinks certain things that are related to it. That in no way proves that the movement of matter brings forth the thought. It must then be another being that has created our soul. But since this can be no creature, because an infinite power is required to make something out of nothing, so one is forced to con-

<column-break/>

fess that our soul is brought forth by an infinite Being whom we call GOD.

There is also nothing but a GOD who could have united a Spirit with a body so closely, that upon certain movements of the body, certain thoughts arise in the soul, and that upon certain thoughts of the soul, certain movements arise in the body.

<margin>
III. Considered from the knowledge of God accepted from the gnawings of the conscience.
</margin>
III. If we, having considered the soul in general, enter into the soul and take into consideration some of its thoughts, we shall be even more convinced of this truth: that there is a God. For if there were no God, no Supreme Judge nor Lawgiver, from where would the gnawings of the conscience <note>The "gnawings of conscience" refers to the "remorse" or "stings" of guilt felt after a perceived sin.</note> and those hidden disturbances come, which strike such terror into those who have committed some crime, even in secret, and which make them tremble at the witness of a leaf, at the movement of a shadow, at a clap of thunder, and at the mere name of God and of death? From where would those movements come that accompany the memory of our deeds? From where does it come that someone who has done a praiseworthy deed feels a hidden joy and an unspeakable satisfaction within himself, whereas he cannot bring to mind manslaughter, perjury, adultery, or any other crying injustice without condemning himself and passing his own sentence? It is beyond dispute that one can find no other cause for these various emotions than the knowledge we have of a God who sees our most hidden deeds and who must punish them.

<margin>
Whether the terrors come from upbringing or from the conscience, from the punishment.
</margin>
One cannot say that these terrors come from the upbringing <note>The author is arguing against the idea that morality is merely a social construct or "nurture" rather than "nature."</note> which we have received from our parents, who have not neglected to instill in us the fear of a Deity; for, besides the fact that these terrors are found in men who are raised in evil, from where does it come that so many other things which our parents taught us are so easily forgotten, and these are not? And how does it happen that all men together are not capable of stilling the disturbances of the conscience that is unsettled by the reflection on its crimes? The errors of upbringing can be corrected by reason and by experience, especially if they are errors that cause so much unrest that one wishes to be freed from them.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument for the existence of God, transitioning from the complexity of the human soul and intellect to the internal witness of conscience and the external evidence of the cosmos.</meta>

# THE CHRISTIAN <note>original: "DE CHRISTELYKE" - likely part of a larger title like "The Christian Religion"</note>

<columns>
If it is then true that these terrors are merely the effects of our upbringing, how is it that reason does not make them disappear? One cannot say that these terrors are only found in small children, or in some weak minds; for it is certain that those who are called great spirits are not free from them. One must also not say that the fear of punishments established by laws causes these anxieties. The greatest *Absolute Monarchs* <note>original: "Alleen-Heerschers"</note> who believe themselves to be above human laws, feel this fear no less than their subjects. A *Tiberius*, a *Caligula*, and a *Nero* were seized by this, even though the flatterers sought to make them believe that they themselves were *Gods*. Finally, one must not say that those who have smothered themselves in excess have been free from these anxieties; for 1. even if it were true that some are freed from them, one would nonetheless have reason to ask: from whence does it come that so many people of every station are troubled in their conscience, if there is no *God* whom they must fear? 2. I cannot believe that there has ever been any man who has never felt these terrors after committing some crime. 3. Finally, it can happen that sinners harden themselves for a time, as happens when those guilty of death make themselves drunk in their dungeon. But their conscience wakes up sooner or later.

<margin>IV. Proof of the existence of the Deity taken from the Universe.</margin>
IV. If, after having considered ourselves, we let our eye pass over all the *Creatures* that are around us, we shall discover new proofs of the existence of a *Deity*. One cannot regard the *universe* <note>original: "geheel al"</note>, the arrangement of its parts which exist through the mutual help they give one another, the order of nature which never fails, the immeasurable extent of the *Heavens*, the innumerable multitude of the *Stars*, their movements and various positions, the depth of the *Seas*, the heights of the mountains, the variety of stones, metals, plants, fruits, and animals, the alternation of days and nights, and the orderly returns of the *Seasons of the Year*, with any attention, without acknowledging an all-wise and almighty *Being*, and consequently concluding that there is a *God* who made them.

<margin>Whether matter is eternal.</margin>
One must not say that the matter of these bodies is eternal, as *Hermogenes* <note>A 2nd-century heretic who argued that God created the world out of pre-existing eternal matter.</note> believed in the 2nd *Century*, both because it is the greatest of all absurdities to attribute to

<column-break/>

an imperfect being, as matter is, the greatest and first of all perfections, consisting in this: that it has been necessary from all times; as also because one can give no reason why matter should have the greatest of all perfections without possessing the other perfections linked thereto: for who could determine its perfections, since one would equally have to suppose that it had no beginning of its existence? One will say that the eternity of *God* is as incomprehensible as that of matter, but this is an error. One cannot conceive of a *God* who had a beginning of existence, because, as we shall see in another place, one can form no idea of *God* without thinking of a being that has all perfections. Now one knows that it is a perfection to exist necessarily and eternally. Eternity does not in any way fall into the idea that we have of matter. It is incomprehensible that there are people who will believe neither the eternity of an all-wise and all-knowing *Being*, nor the *Creation* of the *Universe* by the omnipotence of that *Being*, yet attribute to matter this same eternity and *Creation* which causes them so much trouble when one ascribes them to an immaterial *Being*. And even if one supposed that the matter of all the bodies that surround us were eternal, one would have to ask: Who impressed upon it the motion that it has? Who divided all its parts? Who gave them such various forms? Who brought forth from one and the same matter so many *Creatures* whose variety is incomprehensible? Who arranged the course of the *Heavenly Lights*, who the *Ebb* and *Flow* of the *Sea* so orderly? Who made it so that the *Heavenly Lights* are necessary for the earth? That the earth serves for the production of plants, that the plants serve for the maintenance of animals, and that the plants and animals serve as food for man? Who made the variety of the sexes for the maintenance of the particular species? In short, who brought forth that innumerable variety of animals, and provided them with all that accords with their nature and is necessary? Matter is no more determined to move in one way than in another; and assuming that it moves, who is it that impressed the motion upon it that was most necessary to make the world, and to...

# DIVINE THEOLOGY. BOOK I. CHAPTER I.
### Page 7

maintained? Who has given to the parts of matter these particular determinations?

<margin>That motion is not essential to matter.</margin>
One must admit either that someone gave motion to matter, or that motion is inherent to matter itself. One would not dare to maintain the latter. One can equally conceive of these two things: that matter can move without ceasing to be what it is, and that it can exist even when it is not in actual motion. If it were inherent to matter to move, then it would always move, and all its parts would be in constant motion, which is nonetheless not the case. One must therefore conclude that there is a Being who has given motion to matter. This Being can be none other than God, since there is nothing but God who can produce such well-ordered motions and, through them, cause such perfect Creatures to appear.

<margin>That the world is not an effect of chance.</margin>
One must not say that all this is an effect of chance, as has been maintained by some Pagan Philosophers, claiming that the Universe owes its beginning to a fortuitous clumping of indivisible atoms <note>original: "bezeltjes" - literally "little fibers" or "particles," here referring to the atoms of Epicurean philosophy</note>. For that is the greatest absurdity that has ever been brought forth. I would just as soon have someone say: throw from the top of a mountain a mixture of Marble, Jasper, Fir and Cedar trees, gold, sky-blue pigment, and precious stones, and from that will by chance arise a magnificent Palace of admirable Architecture, where the Pillars will be of Marble, and the Cedars, sky-blue, and gold will adorn the paneling; or that a Printer, scattering all the letters together into the air, has by accident composed an excellent work, a well-followed History, and a Poem as beautiful as that of Virgil; or that a Painter, by throwing his brush and colors onto a panel all at once, has produced a perfect portrait. One must then confess that the world was made by an all-wise and almighty Being, and consequently posit that there is a God. One cannot deny that it is much more difficult to understand that matter moves of itself, and that by chance it brought forth the world as it is—or that some unknown principle of life inherent to bodies made all that we see and made us ourselves, without knowing what it made and without the intention to make it—than to conceive that an infinite Intelligence placed motion into

<column-break/>

matter and made everything with a purpose, and for reasons worthy of His wisdom. It is told that someone once countered the Epicureans <note>Followers of Epicurus who believed the world formed by the random collision of atoms</note> by saying he would join their sect if chance could produce even the smallest part of the human body within a hundred years.

<margin>Proof from the Creatures, though the end is not always known.</margin>
V. One will be confirmed in these thoughts when one observes that of all the Creatures, there is not one that does not lead to a certain end, although that end is not always known to us. Who is it that has designated to each Creature the end toward which it must strive? And who has arranged it for that purpose with as much wisdom as God?

<margin>Of the wonderful composition of our body.</margin>
One will be convinced of this when one takes the trouble to examine only the composition of our body. Is it not a wonderful thing that our eyes, which must serve us to see objects, are placed in our head, the most elevated part of our body; that our mouth has communication with our stomach; that at the same time there is a heart that receives the blood, there are veins through which the blood flows into the heart, where it is warmed and thinned; that there are arteries which distribute the thinned blood; that there are nerves to carry the Spirits <note>original: "Geesten" - referring to 'animal spirits,' a historical medical concept thought to transmit sensation and movement</note> from the brain into the muscles, which like small gears move our body? Is it not a wonderful thing that since our eyes are made to see, the air brings light to us, without which our eyes would be of no use; that our ears being made to hear, the air brings sound to us, and that the same air creates our breathing and the movement of the lungs, to say nothing of its other uses? Certainly, he who does not recognize a God in all these things is more than blind, and he is more ridiculous than a man who, hearing the various strings of a sweet lute make a harmony, would say there is no hand touching them; or who, seeing a well-ordered State or a well-regulated household, would say that this State and this household have no governor.

<margin>Whether there are things that serve no end.</margin>
One will say that there are many things that seem to have no end; for example, why does the thunder roll in uninhabited deserts, and why does the hail fall on rocks? To what purpose do so many Creatures serve that seem only suited to disturb the order of the world? Why so many wild beasts that live by prey? Why so many animals that the air...

# DIVINITY. BOOK I. Chapter I.
## Volume 1. Part B.

to the learned—or appeared to all the learned—it was very acceptable; that which is believed by most men, both learned and unlearned, was even more probable; but that in which all men agree was as certain as it could possibly be.

One cannot pay heed to this universal consent without acknowledging that this truth (there is a God) is a **Natural light**, or that we have by nature a disposition of mind to embrace this truth as soon as it is presented to us—just as our eyes are naturally disposed to behold the light as soon as it shines—or that a powerful reason, which presents itself spontaneously to the understanding of all men, has produced this agreement. It follows then that this proposition (there is a God) is so certain that, to deny it, one must renounce the light of Nature and go directly against the dispositions and inclinations that we have by nature.

<margin>Statius book III. *Thebaid*. "Fear first created gods in the world" <note>original Latin: *Primus in orbe Deos fecit timor*</note>, that is, Fear brought the first Gods into the world.</margin>
It is said that the natural weakness of men keeps them in a constant anxiety regarding the future; and that this state of soul causes them to imagine not only an invisible Being that rules the world, but even terrifying phantoms. It is added that ignorance of the causes of what happens makes people attribute to the Divinity everything for which they cannot provide a reason.

But one answers: I. That it is true that those who believe there is a God fear Him; but it does not follow that the belief in a Deity arose from the fear that men have for the future. Also, no one is less anxious about the future than those who have the true fear of God.

II. The **Atheists** <note>original: *Ongodisten*, literally "un-godists"</note> are wrong to claim that the Divinity, according to the opinion of most men, is nothing other than a terrifying idea: on the contrary, since one calls upon God in times of need and trusts in Him, it is proof that one forms an idea of Him as an infinitely good being.

III. It is so far from the truth that ignorance of the causes of things caused men to believe in a Deity; on the contrary, it is the knowledge of causes that leads directly to God, and **Atheism**

<column-break/>

is itself the ignorance of those causes.

The Atheists can explain neither the origin of the world nor that of their own souls. Perhaps one will say that this knowledge came to men through an ancient tradition <note>original: *overlevering*</note>.

But one will ask: how was it introduced into the world and spread among men? Did those who first said there is a God invent it out of their own heads? If so, how is it that this opinion is so uniformly accepted everywhere, and that it could never be erased from the souls of men, whereas all other opinions are easily erased and forgotten as soon as their falsehood is discovered? Is that not proof that this tradition has its foundation in nature itself, since it would otherwise be impossible to understand how it has maintained itself until now?

<margin>Whether the belief in a Deity is the invention of the first Lawgivers.</margin>
There have been such bold men who have argued that the belief in a Deity is the invention of the first **Lawgivers**, who, in order to keep the people in subjection and fear, made them believe that there is an Invisible Spirit, a God Creator and sustainer of all things, Avenger of the perjured and the rebellious. But those who reason thus do not notice that one must distinguish between the *use* of the belief to keep the people in check, and the *invention* of a doctrine to terrify men. We agree that **Politicians** <note>original: *staat-kundige*, those skilled in statecraft</note> have made a useful application of the belief in a Deity; but we deny that they forged this opinion (that there is a God) out of their own brains. Is it believable that they would have so easily convinced the entire world of what they had invented merely to make themselves formidable? Is it probable that they would have made so many enlightened and penetrating minds, as have been found in all ages, acknowledge this? Statecraft <note>original: *Staat-kunde*</note> sets forth as a fundamental principle that there is a God, and it builds upon that. But it is false that the politicians invented it. They may well have made people believe that the Deity desired to be served with ceremony, but they always presupposed that the world was convinced that there is a God. If the belief in a Deity were the opinion of certain nations alone, then one might...

If there have been any Philosophers who must be regarded as Atheists, they were without doubt Democritus and Epicurus, who sought the principle of all the excellences of the Universe, and of all that is in it, in the accidental coincidence of some small bodies <note>original: "kleine lighaamtjes" - referring to the theory of atoms</note>; that is to say, in the most imperfect and least of all beings, which is the highest peak of God-denial. <margin>That our proofs are taken from what we know; and most of those of the ungodly from that of which we are ignorant.</margin> The first is that all proofs that we bring against the ungodly are proofs taken from what we see, feel, and know; but that the proofs they bring against us are for the most part taken from what is unknown to us, where what one does not know can never serve as a proof in reasoning. Someone seeing a beautiful order and excellent things, which are well understood and well expressed in a book, would say that book was made by a capable Writer, and would reason well: but he who would want to maintain that it is not the work of a learned Writer because he finds something in it that he cannot understand, would reason poorly.

This must be well observed against those who say that it is our ignorance that makes us recognize a first cause. That is false; all our arguments are taken from what we see, feel, and know. # DIVINE THEOLOGY. BOOK I. Chapter I.
<sig>B 3</sig>

against those who do not expect it. It is said that atheism <note>original: "ongodistery" - literally "un-godliness" or the practice of being an atheist</note> is an art that cannot be acquired except after a considerable time; that there are few capable of learning it, and it is very probable that no one understands it perfectly.

<margin>That atheism naturally leads to crimes.</margin>
The third observation is that this sentiment naturally leads to all kinds of crimes. As soon as one does not believe that there is a God, one recognizes no law other than one's own interest; one holds to nothing but one's own lust; one makes no difficulty of committing villainous acts; one only seeks to hide them from the eyes of men; whereas the thought of a Deity brings us to the practice of all virtues: to justice, honor and virtue, humility, moderation, faithfulness, benevolence, wisdom; and to everything that elevates man and distinguishes him from the animals.

<margin>Whether all atheists are evildoers?</margin>
I do not mean to say by this that it does not happen that an atheist lives other than as a faithless person, if he has a fortunate temperament that does not carry him toward atrocious crimes; but I want it understood that such a person has nothing but his own interest to prevent him from committing crying sins, and that one must not trust any man who knows no holier law than that of his own advantage.

It seems to me that this is enough to show that there is a God; which was the thing to be proven.

<margin>Objections of the God-deniers.</margin>
I shall only add here some *Objections* <note>original: "Tegenwerpen"</note> that the God-deniers make. One finds many kinds. There are those who combat Providence: these take up the disorder that one observes in the world, and the sins committed therein. We postpone the examination of these objections until we have come to the treatise on Providence and the permission of sin. There are others taken from our ignorance regarding the cause of many things that happen on the earth. But we have shown that these propositions prove nothing. The other objections are so weak that one is ashamed to present them. "One does not see God," they say; "therefore there is none"; fine reasoning! as if there were nothing in the world except what falls within the reach of the senses: by this reasoning I could prove that we have no Soul. Yet we are assured of the existence of our Souls by the internal feeling that we have of their thoughts, and because

<column-break/>

nothingness cannot act. 2. It is said that if there were a God, one would be able to form a proportionate idea of Him, but that one does not have this. This is false; for one has only to consult reason, and one will find that one has the idea of God as an all-perfect being. It is true that we cannot perfectly understand His essence, since it is incomprehensible; but we clearly understand that it is a Spiritual being that possesses all perfection. It is said that the infinity <note>original: "oneindigheid"</note> which one includes in the idea of God is an incomprehensible thing. I answer that one cannot perfectly understand the infinite, but that one can comprehend that there is a being whose perfections have no end. 3. It is said that it appears we have no right idea of God, since there are as many ideas that correspond with the name of God as there are various imaginations. I answer that there is in truth so great an inequality between our Spirit and the essence of God, that one should not be surprised if we strive to improve all the imaginations one uses to represent Him to us. Indeed, when we understand God as a being who has all perfections, we can have a right idea of Him that we do not need to improve. 4. It is said that if there were a God, He would have to hear all the Prayers of Men, and that their Prayers being almost always contradictory, He cannot hear them without going against Himself. I answer that it is false that if there were a God, He would have to hear all the Prayers of Men. When one has the idea of God, one has the idea of an almighty and all-just being, who consequently is not obliged to grant the prayers of all men, much less to satisfy the unjust desires of Creatures. 5. It is said, if there were a God, He would be able to do all things, and that He would therefore be able to kill Himself. Can one produce anything more absurd! ## CHAPTER II.

->Of the knowledge which Men<-
->Naturally have of God.<-

**I**t appears from what I have said in the preceding Chapter, that all men naturally have some knowledge of the Deity; such that as soon as they begin to make use of their reason, they cannot fail to frequently think of a God; it is impossible for them to entirely banish these thoughts, although they often attempt to extinguish them.

<margin>Of the idea of God.</margin>
Although we say that the idea of God is natural to all men, one must nevertheless observe that, as it is a spiritual idea, one does not perceive it except when one makes use of reason; and the more we make use of it, the more we have a correct idea of God. One must not be surprised that men do not have the same idea of God; that happens because they add to this another idea, which their imagination or their senses produce; and because they do not all make an equal use of their reason, as they indeed ought to do.

<margin>Locke's human understanding.</margin>
There are Scholars <note>A reference to John Locke and his "An Essay Concerning Human Understanding" (1689), which famously argued against innate ideas.</note> who deny the ideas that are called innate <term>ingeschapen - literally "in-created" or innate</term>; but there is reason to believe that they

<column-break/>

do not well understand the sentiment of those who are in favor of them. They imagine that one believes these ideas must be known by their own light, without instruction, without labor, without investigation, or any use of reason; without external help that makes them perceived; and that they consequently must be understood as perfectly, indeed better, by children, by the ignorant, and by savages—since they are without prejudice—as by scholars; but that is not the thought of those who maintain these innate ideas.

It is said that if children and the ignorant had these innate ideas and natural impressions, they would necessarily perceive them and give their consent to them, because one cannot say that the understanding has ideas that one never discovers; and that to imprint something in the understanding is the same as making him understand it.

<margin>Sherlock.</margin>
One answers that one must know the human understanding very little to maintain that it actually perceives everything that is imprinted there. One discovers nothing except that which one is actually thinking about; are there then no more impressions in the soul when one has fallen into a deep sleep? One can add to this that children and the ignorant perceive these ideas as soon as they begin to make use of their reason: it is enough to make them understand what one means by God, by virtue, and vice; they understand it without difficulty.

Sherlock <note>William Sherlock (c. 1640–1707), an English divine who defended the concept of innate ideas against Locke.</note>, an English Teacher who defended innate ideas, observes that it is indeed possible that one has impressions that one will never perceive, since one has those that one does not actually notice. That a child can just as well have ideas that he will never perceive, as a grown man has those that he does not actually notice; that there is no distinction between a child who has no grasp of his ideas, and an old man who, having learned all sciences, has so declined through the years that it is impossible for him to perceive any of his ideas; and just as one cannot say that the Soul of this old man has become an erased Tablet <term>tabula rasa - a blank slate</term> on which nothing more is written, so one also cannot say of the Soul of the child that it is an erased Tablet.

# THEOLOGY. Book I. Chapter II.

It is inconceivable that God would have given to man a soul that reasons without having imprinted the idea of some matter therein: But one must admit that it is difficult to explain how this impression occurs: one cannot understand that the soul has the capacity to know that which is presented to her without allowing for innate ideas <note>original: "ingeschape denkbeelden"</note>.

Sherlock <note>William Sherlock (c. 1640–1707), an English divine whose works on providence and the soul were widely translated.</note> remarks that if we have no innate ideas, neither of the Deity, nor of Virtue, nor of vice, the atheists <note>original: "Godverzaakers" - literally 'God-deniers'</note> will not fail to say that all ideas we possess spring from a false upbringing; and that these ideas have been imprinted in the minds of children for the well-being of society, and to keep them in fear.

It also appears that we cannot behold the Heaven, the Earth, and all that is in them, without concluding that God has made all these things.

And even if we had no other knowledge of God than that which we obtain through the contemplation of His works, we would still call that a Natural knowledge. These are the truths that Paul presents to the Romans, Romans 2 verse 15, where he says that the Heathens show the work of the Law written in their hearts; their Conscience also bearing witness; and their thoughts accusing or else excusing one another.

<margin>
Against Smalcius <note>Valentin Smalcius (1572–1622), a prominent Socinian theologian.</note> Disputation 8. Against Frantzius: on free will <note>Latin: "de lib arb." (de libero arbitrio)</note> page 419.
</margin>
One must well observe, 1. that in this passage the Heathens are dealt with such as they were before the Gospel was proclaimed to them; for they are here set in opposition to the Jews, who under the New Testament are united in one body with the Heathens. 2. That it deals with a Law which teaches man to know what is honorable and what is not, and which compels him to do the one and leave the other. One does not doubt that by these "works of the Law," one must understand the idea of good and evil, and that this idea is joined to that of God: for one cannot think of a Law without thinking of a Lawgiver. The Apostle says that the work of the Law is written, not on tables of stone like the Law of Moses, nor in the spirits of men or in their memory alone, like a history or a Philosophical truth; but in their hearts. And this causes it so that, as soon as they have committed some crime, their thoughts accuse them

<column-break/>

whereas when they have acted according to their reason, their thoughts excuse them.

It would be poorly reasoned if one wished to prove by this expression of "written Law" that it refers to the Heathens to whom the Gospel has been proclaimed, because God promises in the Covenant of Grace to write His Law in our hearts, Jeremiah 31 verse 33. For it is clear that in the passage of Jeremiah, a different Law than the Natural one is being discussed, of which Paul in Romans 2 verse 15 speaks exclusively.

This great Teacher of the Heathens also says in Romans 1 verses 18, 19, 20, that what is known of God is manifest in them; where he adds: For the invisible things of God, namely His Eternal power and Divinity, are seen as if before the eye, being understood by His works. To well understand the thoughts of the Apostle, one must observe what he had said before. He had accused the Heathens of holding the truth in unrighteousness; he subsequently shows what this truth is which they unjustly held captive, namely the knowledge of God, whereupon he proves that God has indeed made Himself known to them through His works.

God being a Spirit, is by Himself invisible; as are all His perfections: But this Spirit, who was invisible in His essence, has as it were assumed a body to make Himself seen before our eyes: He has produced works which elevate those who see them to the knowledge of the perfections of Him who made them, in such a way that they are more visible than the works themselves. Paul mentions God's power in this place before he speaks of the Deity, to teach us the manner in which that which we see in the World makes us know a God. When we behold the Heaven, the Earth, etc., it is not possible, unless we immediately judge, that it is an Almighty being who created them; so that the power of the Master-worker <note>original: "Werk-meester"</note>, or cause of all these creatures, is the first perfection that strikes us with amazement: from that we draw this conclusion, that this Maker must be a God, for one cannot find this Omnipotence except in the infinite being that one calls God.

By the **power of God**, one should understand this virtue which is in God, which we call His power, and not His promises, of which no mention is made in this passage. Nor is the Gospel being discussed there, for the dispute concerns the Heathens <note>Non-Christians or those outside the biblical tradition.</note>, as they were before their conversion; and although Paul in this Chapter calls the Gospel "the power of God," nevertheless this word "the power of God," when used on its own, never signifies the Gospel.

By the **Godhead**, one must understand the Divine Essence, along with the perfections that have shone forth in the Creation of the World and in the governance of Providence; such as Wisdom, Justice, and Goodness. It is as if Paul said that the Works of Nature have made it known that He who made them is almighty, Wise, and Good; and that this Almighty, Good, and Wise Being is God. For I see no reason why one should explain this word "Godhead" only as the love of God, nor why Paul would have made more use of the word "Godhead" than that of "love" or "beneficence." I also could not believe that by "Godhead" one must understand "that which God wants us to do"; and one cannot produce a single passage where this word is taken in that sense. To explain Colossians 2:9 and Ephesians 3:19 in such a way is to willfully deceive oneself.

The Prophet wishes to teach us in these words that the Heavens and the Firmament are like the Heralds of God’s perfections; and that they give those who behold them to know not only that they did not make themselves, or are not the product of chance, but that they are the work of God’s hands; this is the true

By **the whole earth**, one must not only understand the whole of Judea, as some have believed, but the entire earth in general, since the Heavens can be seen everywhere. Paul applies this passage to the proclamation of the Gospel by the Apostles in Romans 10. 1. Those who dispute this Truth argue that the feelings one has regarding right and wrong arise from the prejudices held since one's childhood.

2. That our **passions** fight against these principles, since they often incline us to do harm to others for the sake of our own well-being.

3. That our duties are only grounded in the **contract** <note>Referring to the "Social Contract," the idea that moral obligations depend on an agreement between people to form a society.</note> that we have made among one another, and for our own advantage.

4. That if all laws were natural, all people would observe them, whereas many violate them without any remorse.

5. That if laws were Natural, one could give no reason why one thing is good and the other is evil.

6. That God could never change these laws, yet he commanded Abraham to sacrifice his Son; and that the Gospel opposes these laws, wanting us to give up our lives, "hate" our parents, etc. etc.

But it is easy to answer:

1. If these natural laws were mere prejudices, one could easily rid oneself of them; whereas, the more one thinks upon them, the more one is convinced of the Truth of these Laws.

2. It is true that our passions fight against these principles, but **conscience** convinces us of the injustice of these passions.

3. Even if there were no contract whatsoever among men, they would still be convinced that failing to forgive someone who has done them much good is a great crime.

4. That which prevents people from following these laws is not a lack of conviction regarding their justice, but that they only listen to their passions; if there are those who violate these laws without remorse, it is because their conscience has fallen into a deep sleep by constantly being refused a hearing.

5. Just as one can give reasons for mathematical demonstrations, one can also do so for these natural laws.

6. God does not change these laws, since—

<column-break/>

—the first law, by which one is bound under the same, commands that one obey all that God wills, and says that we owe Him everything.
