For, it is added, it would follow from this that all men are pleasing to God, since they all believe in a Godhead. Enoch did not only believe that there is a God, but he knew the true God and placed his trust in Him. One does not pay enough attention to the purpose of the Apostle; he had said that Enoch was taken away through faith without seeing death. To prove that he had faith, he says that he pleased God, which he would not have done if he had not believed; for without faith it is impossible to please God, he adds, and he who comes to God must believe that He is, and that He is a rewarder of those who seek Him. Since it is absolutely necessary that the practice of piety has an object, those who practice it must know this object, as well as His essence and perfections, and they must be certain that this object not only exists, but that He is truly God—that He is almighty, wise, and good, that He has promised to be our God, and that by serving Him according to His command and seeking Him as He wishes to be sought, one is pleasing to Him. Such was the faith of Enoch; certainly, then, it was no Natural faith. III. ...the nature of the Gods has written, bringing forward the various opinions of the Philosophers on this matter without daring to make any choice. <margin>Rom. 1:19</margin> One might possibly object here with the passage from Romans 1:19, where it is said that what may be known of God is manifest to the Heathens <note>original: "Heidenen" — typically referring to non-Christians or Gentiles in a biblical context.</note>. But this passage proves nothing other than that everything that can be known of God through Nature was revealed and made known to the Heathens; which Paul defines in the following verse as the Power of God, and His Divinity, that is to say, the knowledge of God’s existence and perfections, which shine forth in the works of Creation and preservation. But there are many things in God that Nature does not discover to us, and which one must nonetheless know.

2. Nature and reason cannot teach man how God can be appeased, and consequently, they could not quiet a conscience troubled by the feeling of its misdeeds.

This is the true cause for which the Heathens offered such a multitude of sacrifices, even to the point of human sacrifice, seeking all kinds of means to reconcile the Deity without being able to find them, so that their conscience always remained in movement and unrest. <margin>Rom. 2:14, 15</margin> One might possibly object with a passage from Romans 2:14, 15, where mention is made of thoughts that excuse men; from which one will draw the conclusion that since the Heathens had such thoughts, their conscience enjoyed some peace. But one confuses two things here: having thoughts that excuse us, and enjoying a sweet peace in one's conscience. When the Heathens kept themselves from high-handed crimes and compared themselves with others worse than themselves, they had thoughts that excused them, to speak with Paul; but when they considered their committed sins, by which they had angered the Deity, they were in great unrest, since they did not know how to appease the Deity whom they had offended.

3. Nature and reason do not teach us what we shall be after this life, or whether our Soul, which is immortal by its nature, will not be destroyed by Him who created it at the same time when our body returns to dust.

Nothing is more lamentable than what most

<column-break/>

Poets and Philosophers of the Heathens have said about this matter; and if some have been more reasonable than others, it is <margin>Eph. 2:12</margin> likely that they had other Teachers besides nature and reason. Paul, speaking of the Heathens, also says that they were without hope in the world, Ephesians 2:12.

4. Nature and reason do not teach man what the origin of his corruption is, nor how great it may be. This knowledge is nonetheless necessary to him; how could he recognize the justice of God in His Judgments poured out over the Human race if he did not know that he himself is the cause of his misfortune? How could he cherish God’s goodness in the Preservation of the Universe if he did not know that he, through his conduct, has deserved to be entirely destroyed?

5. Nature and reason provide us with not the slightest comfort against the terrors of death and the miseries of life.

Reason tells us that one must submit to what one cannot avoid. But this is a small comfort, for the saddest thing in the evils one suffers is when one has no help or outcome to expect. Reason also tells us that one should not grieve over what happens to everyone, and that there is no one who is not subject to some adversities and who must not die. Another small comfort: is one any less miserable because one has companions in one's misery? Does someone who suffers severely from Gout <note>original: "Jigt" — a common and painful inflammatory arthritis.</note> or the Stone <note>original: "Graveel" — kidney or bladder stones, a frequent ailment in the 17th and 18th centuries.</note> suffer any less because he knows that many have the same pains? Most Heathens comfort themselves with the hope that death will be the end of all things. But how could they know whether death would end all their miseries, since they did not know what they would become after their death?

6. Finally, nature and reason do not teach us the resurrection of our bodies.

It is true, there have been Heathens <margin>Diog. Laertius</margin> who said that men must one day revive from the dust and become immortal. This opinion is attributed to Aeneas <margin>Aeneas Gazaeus</margin> (an Ancient Poet and Philosopher named Gazaeus), Phocylides, and some others. But St. Paul does not mean to say that it is simply enough to believe in the existence of a God who rewards honest people; to believe that God *is*, is not only to believe that there is a God, but also that He is *our* God; that is, to know Him as He made Himself known to the Patriarchs, and to believe in Him as Enoch did. 2. One stands amazed at all the absurdities perceived in Paganism; one often finds oneself forced to give no credit to what one reads about it.

Most understood the Deity as finite, corporeal, weak, wretched, and tainted with a thousand defects. What an idea! Furthermore, one cannot deny that there were some Early Church Fathers who had good hope for the Salvation of the Heathens, such as Clement of Alexandria, Justin <note>Justin Martyr (c. 100–165 AD), an early Christian apologist.</note>, Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), Archbishop of Constantinople.</note>, etc.; but this is not the only matter in which they have erred.

<margin>à Costa. *Exemplar of Human Life*. <note>original: "Exemp. vitæ hum." — referring to Uriel d'Acosta (c. 1585–1640), a philosopher who criticized organized religion and championed "Natural Law."</note></margin>
Some arguments are raised to prove the sufficiency of natural religion.

It is said that the Law of Nature is common to all men, that it is innate in us, that it unites and binds all mortals together; that people only become divided when they deviate from it; that if Revelation adds some laws to those of nature, they are either already included within it, or else they are impossible to perform—such as loving one's enemies—or they merely serve to promote division.

<column-break/>

I answer that the Law of Nature is indeed common to all men, but I deny that what is added to the Law of Nature creates division. There are things that the Law of Nature does not teach us, and which it cannot discover, but which we marvel at when they are unfolded to us. The Law of Nature does not teach us to love our enemies; but it also does not condemn those who love them and who pray for their persecutors; on the contrary, it causes us to hold them in high esteem. To be reconciled with one's enemies and to love them is seen by reason as a heroic deed—proof that the Christian Religion leads us to greater perfection and that it is more perfect than the Law of Nature. Furthermore, it is not true that loving one's enemies is an impossible thing, since there are many people who do love them. Beyond that, what seems impossible to us becomes possible through God’s Grace. The Christian Religion provides us with strong evidence and powerful motives to bring us to the practice of this duty and to oblige us to it; it sets before us excellent examples, outstanding promises, and terrible threats.

# IV. CHAPTER.

## That God has made Himself known to Men in another way than through the works of Creation, etc., namely through His Word.

<margin>The Heathens have recognized the necessity of a supernatural revelation.</margin>
It is easy to conclude from what has been said that it was necessary for God to make Himself known to men in a way other than through the works of Nature and Providence. Even the Heathens recognized the necessity of a supernatural revelation. It is for this reason that those who wished to invent a new ceremony or religion made the people believe that they had a special communion with some deity, and that this deity had taught them what they were making known to the people. Thus, even if one explained these words of Paul as some do, one could not conclude from them that natural religion is enough to make us Saved. It is even certain that the light of nature is greatly darkened by sin, and it very rarely happens that men consult their reason as they ought to do; for this reason it is also said that, although reason teaches man that there is only one God, the Pagans nevertheless worshipped many gods, among which they counted not only the Sun and other Heavenly lights, but even the lowliest animals; they even deified their own Passions. One stands amazed at all the absurdities perceived in Heathendom; one often finds oneself forced to give no credit to what one reads about it.

Most conceived of the Deity as finite, physical, weak, miserable, and tainted with a thousand defects. What a concept! Furthermore, it cannot be denied that there have been some early Church Fathers who held good hope for the Salvation of the Pagans, such as Clement of Alexandria, Justin Martyr, Chrysostom, etc.; but this is not the only matter in which they have erred. <note>The author is referring to the "Virtuous Pagan" debate—whether good people who lived before Christ or without the Gospel could be saved. <margin>
à Costa. *Examples of human life.* <note>Original: "Exemp. vitæ hum." likely referring to Uriel d'Acosta, a philosopher who questioned revealed religion in favor of natural law.</note>

It is said that the Law of Nature is common to all men, that it is innate within us, and that it unites and binds all mortals together; that people only become divided when they deviate from it; and that if Revelation adds any laws to those of nature, they are either already included within it or else impossible to perform, thereby perpetuating division.

<column-break/>

I answer that the Law of Nature is indeed common to all men, but I deny that what is added by the Law of Nature <insert>meaning Revelation</insert> creates division. There are things that the Law of Nature does not teach us, and which it cannot discover, but which we marvel at when they are unfolded to us. The Law of Nature does not teach us to love our enemies; but neither does it condemn those who love them and who pray for their persecutors. On the contrary, it causes us to hold them in high esteem; it views reconciling with and loving one's enemies as a heroic deed—proof that the Christian Religion leads us to greater perfection and that it is more perfect than the Law of Nature.

Furthermore, it is not true that loving one’s enemies is an impossible thing, since there are many people who do love them. Beyond that, what seems impossible to us becomes possible through God's Grace. The Christian Religion provides us with strong proofs and powerful motives to bring us to the practice of this duty and to oblige us to it; it presents us with excellent examples, eminent promises, and terrifying threats.

<margin>Why God's word was not written from the beginning.</margin>
God did not immediately have His word written down, since in the beginning it was not necessary: there were few people on Earth who lived for a very long time, and who could instruct their descendants in what they had seen and experienced; moreover, God honored men with many appearances to make His will known to them. **Methuselah** lived with **Adam** for more than 200 years, and he died only shortly before the Deluge; **Shem**, **Noah's** son, lived about 98 years with **Methuselah**; **Isaac** lived 50 years with **Shem**, and died only 10 years before **Jacob's** journey to **Egypt**. Thus these four persons—**Adam, Methuselah, Shem**, and **Isaac**—could sufficiently prevent the truths that God had revealed from being lost. It has been noted that although more than 25 centuries passed between **Adam** and **Moses**, one could nevertheless know the account of the creation of the world through eight persons: **Methuselah, Shem, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Levi, Amram**, and **Moses**.

# DIVINE THEOLOGY. Book I, Chapter V.
B
<meta>catchword: clear</meta>

<margin>Why God willed that His word should be written down.</margin>
As people multiplied upon the earth, God willed that His word should be written down, so that the Divine instructions He had given to humanity would not be lost through their negligence, or corrupted by the malice and artifices <note>The word "kunstenaryen" refers to the clever tricks or deceptive schemes attributed to the Devil in early modern theology.</note> of the Devil, or mixed with worldly customs and principles—just as water loses its purity and is spoiled as it flows through various pipes. He no longer wished to leave His truth solely to the memory of men, knowing how fickle and unstable the human mind is, and the tendency it has to follow its own thoughts more than those of God. He therefore had His word written down: 1. so that it would be preserved in its purity and serve humanity as a certain rule of faith and good works. It is for this same reason that laws are sometimes engraved on marble and copper. 2. so that it would be protected from the cunning and deceits of Satan; for this enemy of our Salvation would not have failed to pass off his errors and lies as the utterances of God. 3. so that it could be handed down to posterity, which could not have happened as effectively without the Scripture.

<margin>The benefits we obtain from the writing down of God’s word.</margin>
One must not doubt, however, that if God had always wished to instruct His Church with the tongue and voice, He could easily have done so; but it was consistent with His wisdom to have His word written. Those who wish to conclude that the Christian Church could presently do without the Scripture, because the Church formerly existed before God’s word was recorded, reason as poorly as if I said that it is just as easy to teach millions of people as it is two or three thousand; or that one can do without food because God sustained some people for many days without eating or drinking; or that it is useless to practice the knowledge of Heavenly truths because the Apostles came to them without prior practice. One must always distinguish the times. One cannot sufficiently express the great benefits that people have enjoyed, and continue to enjoy, from the Scripture. 1. The Church has therein a perfect rule for what she must do and believe. 2. Those who have been the cruelest enemies of the truth taught in the Scripture have

<column-break/>

been able to read it, and therein come to know the certainty of that which they once opposed because they did not know it, and have been converted by this reading—which would not have happened if this truth had not been set down in writing. 3. When we read the Books of the Old Testament, they contribute not a little to proving the Christian Religion to us; we find therein strong weapons to combat the arguments of the Jews. Now, it is certain that one could not have read them if they had not been written down. 4. The Jews and Heathens <note>The term "Heidenen" refers to non-Christians, specifically practitioners of Greco-Roman or other polytheistic religions.</note> accused the Christian Religion of many things which were falsely charged against it. It was necessary that the Christian Church be relieved of these false slanders by making known the records of her doctrine and discipline. And we shall see in the following that the harmony between the Old and New Testament is a proof of their Divinity. One could point out many other advantages that come to us from the fact that God had His word written down.

<margin>Whether there was any other Scripture before Moses’ time.</margin>
Before the time of Moses, there were no books of Divine inspiration; but I do not doubt that there were many other writings, and that the use of letters had been invented long before. It appears that in the time of Job people were already writing, not to mention what Josephus says <note>original: "Antiquit. l. 1. Cap. 3." referring to Flavius Josephus's *Antiquities of the Jews*.</note> regarding the pillars of the children of Seth; it is very probable that every Father of a household wrote down the most important things that had happened to him; at least, there were those who did so, especially those to whom God revealed Himself in a special way.

<margin>That God’s word began to be written by Moses.</margin>
It was only from Moses’ time that God began to have His word written. For what the Jews and Muslims <note>original: "Mahometanen"</note> say about the Books of Adam, Seth, Enoch, and Abraham must be regarded as stories meant for a laugh.

<margin>Regarding the Books of Adam, Enoch, and Abraham.</margin>
The Jews claim that Adam wrote books about the Creation of the World and about the Divinity. Some Rabbis attribute the 92nd Psalm to him. They also speak much of a book of Enoch: but one has only to read it to be convinced that it is a forged book, made by a man who did not have much sense. It contains the absurdities <note>original: "mummeryen," literally mummery or farcical performances.</note> of twenty Angels with the Daughters of men; and possibly it is from there that some have said that by the "Sons of God" in Genesis 6:2 one must understand the Angels, which is absurd, since it is clear...

## CHAPTER VI.
### Of the Books of Holy Scripture, and in particular those of the Old Testament.

<margin>On the number of the Books of the O.T.</margin>
I proceed to the second question, which concerns the Books of Scripture. We shall begin with those of the Old Testament.

They are counted as thirty-nine; though some count only twenty-two, others twenty-four, and others twenty-seven. Those who say there are thirty-nine precisely mark the number of the individual Books. Those who say there are only twenty-two count them according to the number of letters in the Hebrew Alphabet; these, and the others who set the number at twenty-four or twenty-seven, join many Books together—for example, they recognize the twelve Minor Prophets as a single Book. However, it comes to the same thing. The Jews divided the Holy Scripture into three parts: the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and those called the <term>Hagiographa</term> <note>original: "Hagiographische"; from the Greek *hagios* (holy) and *graphē* (writing).</note>—a Greek word meaning "Holy Writings"—which corresponds to the word used by the Jews when they speak of the two Books of Chronicles, the Book of Esther, Ezra, and Nehemiah, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs, Job, Lamentations of Jeremiah, and the Prophecy of Daniel.

This division corresponds with that which we find in Luke 24:44, where, to all appearances, Jesus Christ intends to divide the entire Scripture of the O.T. into three parts: the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms.

To now give an idea of all these Books, we shall follow the order of our Bibles and begin with the five Books of Moses.

<margin>Whether Moses wrote the five books?</margin>
We call these the "Books of Moses," as we are assured that God made use of him to write them; although we believe that Joshua, Ezra, or some other Prophet added certain things to them that could not have flowed from Moses’ own pen, and changed some words to make the histories brought forth by this great Lawgiver more understandable for those who would live in the following centuries. Thus, we do not doubt that Joshua, or some other Holy Man, added the account of the Death of Moses; some

<column-break/>

old names of cities were also changed to those they held afterward, because otherwise people would not have known them.

A Jewish Teacher named Aben Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a famous Spanish-Jewish scholar known for his grammatical and philosophical commentaries on the Bible.</note> wished to suggest that Moses was not the writer of the five books; for although some think he did not actually hold this view, it is certain that he brought forward the strongest objections against the common opinion, to which he did not provide answers. This has given the Learned reason to think that he at least had great doubts about this matter. We shall not exert much effort to know exactly what he believed: it is certain that many in this century have been of the opinion that Moses did not write the five books. But their reasons appear all too weak to be set against the opinion of so many Jewish and Christian Teachers, who highly testify that Moses was the writer whom God used to write the five books that bear his name. One cannot deny that Moses wrote the Laws contained in Exodus and elsewhere, just as God had commanded him, Exodus 34:27; Deuteronomy 31:9; as well as all the words of the Lord, Exodus 24:4. And one cannot doubt that he wrote the Song, Deuteronomy 32 and 33. One also cannot deny that he wrote many things regarding what happened to the Jewish people, such as the battle against Amalek, Exodus 17:14, and the various journeys and covenants of the Israelites, spoken of in the Book of Numbers, Numbers 33:2. One cannot notice that these things were of more consequence than others contained in the Book of Genesis and elsewhere. That which is drawn from the five books in the New Testament is always brought forward under the name of Moses. Peter says in Acts 15:21 that Moses was read in all the synagogues of the Jews; see also 2 Chronicles 34:18 <note>The Dutch text says 2 Chron XXII. 18, but 34:18 is the standard reference for finding the book of the Law.</note> and Ezra 6:18. Christ says that Moses wrote of Him, John 5:45-46. Objection I: that if Moses had written them, he would have spoken of himself in the first person instead of the third. That he does not do it without necessity. 4. That holy men have done this, such as Paul and John. 5. Finally, that he also did not hide his own failings. III. It is also likely that the Prophets and men inspired by God’s Spirit added some words there for clarification of the history, such as Genesis 14:14 and 13:18; 23:19; 35:27; 37:14; Exodus 16:35; Deuteronomy 3:14. <margin>Of Genesis.</margin>
The first book of Moses is called **Genesis**, from a Greek word meaning birth, beginning, origin, or production, since it encompasses the origin of the world and the first beginnings of the Church.

<margin>About Exodus.</margin>
The second book of Moses is called **Exodus**, from a word that signifies *departure* <note>Derived from the Greek *exodos*.</note>, because its principal subject is the departure of the people of Israel from Egypt. One finds in this book the terrible persecution by **Pharaoh Rameses II** against the children of Israel: the manner in which Moses was exposed as a foundling in the Nile, miraculously preserved, and raised by the King’s daughter. (d) How he killed the Egyptian and took flight to Midian; how he was called by God and sent to **Pharaoh Amenophis II**. One finds here the wonders that God performed through him and Aaron; the plagues with which He struck Egypt; the institution of the Passover, the departure of the people from Egypt, and their passage through the **Red Sea**. (e) The Law that God gave him on Mount Sinai, and the construction of the **Tabernacle** <note>The portable sanctuary used by the Israelites in the wilderness.</note>. One also finds here the constant rebellions and murmurings of the Israelites against God, as well as their idolatry.

The purpose of God’s Spirit in this book is to teach us what the fate of the Church in this world is; the care that God takes for it, and His judgments upon its persecutors.

# THE CHRISTIAN [THEOLOGY]

One also finds there the Song <note>The "Song of Moses" from Deuteronomy 32.</note> that this great Lawgiver pronounced, with his blessings over the 12 Tribes, and his death. This Book <note>Deuteronomy.</note> covers the history of two months, or of one month and a few days.

Those who wish to prove that the five books <note>The Pentateuch: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.</note> are a summary of many books say that there are repetitions in them, that no chronological order is observed, and that the writing style is not consistent. But these reasons have no power of conviction. Repetitions are not defects of writers who describe histories in brief. They are very common among the Ancients. They correspond with the nature of the Hebrews; many of these repetitions explain the events that occurred. The Holy Writers did not observe the order of time too scrupulously, and regarding the writing style, one does not notice that it is as varied in the five books as is often claimed.

<margin>About the Book of Joshua.</margin>
The book of Joshua immediately follows the five books of Moses. It is so named because it contains a historical account of the deeds of *Joshua*, the son of *Nun*, who succeeded *Moses* around the Year of the World <term>Year of the World (Anno Mundi)</term> 2550 or 2554. In this book, one sees the manner in which God put the Israelites in possession of the land that He had promised their fathers: making them go through the **Jordan** on dry feet and giving the Kings of the Canaanites with their lands into their hands. The taking of **Jericho** at the sound of the Trumpets, and the standing still of the Sun and Moon at the command of *Joshua*, are two of the greatest events that occur in this History.

One also finds there the division of the land of Canaan that was made among the 12 Tribes.

Some believe that this book covers a narrative of only 17 years; others maintain that the narrative covers 27 years.

It is not known exactly who the compiler of this Book is; the common thought is that it is *Joshua* himself. One cannot doubt that he wrote what we read in the 24th Chapter, as this is clearly proven from verse 26. But one must also admit that there are many things

<column-break/>

that Joshua could not have written. In this category, one places what is found in *Joshua* 4:9 and in *Joshua* 15:13-19, compared with *Judges* 1:10-15, and even *Joshua* 15 and 16:10 compared with *Judges* 1:20; see also *Joshua* 19:47 compared with *Judges* 18:29. The same thing that happened regarding the Books of Moses could have occurred with respect to the Book of Joshua <note>Meaning that later editors likely added clarifying details or finished the account after the author's death.</note>. Whatever the case may be, it is certain that if this book was not written by Joshua, it was nonetheless written by some Prophet. Some have believed that *Eleazar* <note>The High Priest and son of Aaron.</note> had written it; it is at least probable that Joshua had made a daily record of what God performed through him. **Masius** <note>Andreas Masius (1514–1573), a Flemish Catholic priest and scholar.</note> was of the opinion that **Ezra** <note>original: "Esdras"</note> had written this book, and that it is an excerpt from the ancient annals of the Hebrews. Those who believe that this book was written a long time after the death of *Joshua* prove this by these words, which are often found: *unto this day*, such as in *Joshua* 5:9 and 9:27. But this is not a convincing reason: these words could have been added by writers of the same era after the passage of a few years, just as in *Matthew* 27:8 and 28:15. One also wishes to take an argument from the cities and lands which are claimed not to have existed in the time of Joshua, but others believe it is not certain that these cities would have been unknown in Joshua's time.

These Judges were extraordinary authorities, almost like the **Dictators** <note>In the Roman Republic, a Dictator was a temporary magistrate with absolute power granted during a national emergency.</note> in Rome.

<margin>Of the Book of Ruth.</margin>
The Book of Ruth is like a sequel to that of the Judges; many have even made but one book out of these two. It is clear that this book was made solely to follow and link together the genealogy of Jesus Christ.

<margin>Of the 1st Book of Kings.</margin>
The two books of Kings, which the Greeks and Latins call the 3rd and 4th book of Kings, contain the histories under the Kings who ruled the people of God after the death of David.
One finds in the 1st book the history of Solomon, who reigned 40 years, and of four Kings of Judah; namely Rehoboam, who reigned over the tribe of Judah for 17 years; Abijah <note>original: "Abia"</note>, who reigned 3 years; Asa, who reigned 41 years; and Jehoshaphat <note>original: "Jozafat"</note>, whose first 17 years are described; which makes 118 years. One also finds there the events under eight Kings of Israel: Jeroboam, Nadab, Baasha, Elah, Zimri, Tibni, Omri <note>original: "Homri"</note>, and Ahab.
One sees in the 2nd book the continuation of what Jehoshaphat, King of Judah, did, who reigned 25 years, along with the things that happened under 16 more Kings who succeeded him: Joram, Ahaziah <note>original: "Achafia"</note>, Athaliah, Joash, Amaziah, Uzziah (or Azariah), Jotham, Ahaz, Hezekiah <note>original: "Hiskia"</note>, Manasseh, Amon, Josiah, Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, and Zedekiah, under whom Jerusalem was taken by Nebuchadnezzar.
One also sees a narrative of the reign of 12 Kings of Israel: Ahaziah, Joram, Jehu, Jehoahaz, Joash, Jeroboam II, Zechariah, Shallum, Menahem, Pekahiah, Pekah, and Hoshea. Under this last King, the ten tribes were taken into captivity.
It is held then that the 2nd book of Kings contains a narrative of 320 years; others say more, others less. (g)

# DIVINITY. BOOK I. CHAPTER VII.

There are scholars who claim that this book was written by one of Job's friends. I would gladly follow the opinion of those who think that, Job having written to his friends about what had befallen him—and indeed in Arabic—one or another Prophet led by God's Spirit gave it the style and form which is presently seen in the book of Job. But it is very difficult to know when this writer lived. Some believe in the time of David, or of Solomon, because of the similarity they find between the writings of these two Kings and Job's book. Others think that it was written a long time after that; some maintain that Isaiah is the author of it.

<margin>Who Job was.</margin> Many have believed that Job was the same as Jobab, spoken of in Genesis 36:33, one of the descendants of Esau. This opinion rests on an ancient addition found in the Greek translation <note>The Septuagint</note> at the end of the book of Job, where it is said that he had the name of Jobab. But this is improbable: 1. It is not to be believed that Moses would have said nothing to make Job known and to distinguish him from the other children of Esau. 2. One does not see why he is always named Job and never Jobab, neither before nor after his adversity. 3. Jobab is shown as a King, which is never said of Job. Some believe that he was much more likely a descendant of Abraham, through one of the children of Kethura; or from the lineage of Nahor, Abraham's brother. Those who hold this view say that one must look for Uz, which is the name of Job's homeland, in desert Arabia, and that Job lived while the people of Israel were in Egypt. Some believe that he was a contemporary of Abraham and Isaac, and even lived before them. This they wish to prove: 1. By the length of his life, which was longer than that of Abraham. 2. By the offerings which he himself sacrificed, which shows that he lived before Moses <note>The Law of Moses restricted animal sacrifices to the formal priesthood; before this, the heads of families acted as priests</note>. 3. By the constant revelations, etc. It appears that Job lived before the Law

Some mean that Job was a son of Huz, son of Nahor; and that, if he had lived during the servitude of Egypt, he would have made mention of Abraham etc. in his book.

This book contains the account of the adversities of this Holy Man and of his patience; the judgment that his friends passed on his state, and his happy restoration. ## CHAPTER VIII.
### Continuation of the Books of the Old Testament.

I now move on to the Prophets. There are the Major and the twelve Minor Prophets.

The four that are called the Major Prophets are *Isaiah* <note>original: "Ezaias"</note>, *Jeremiah*, *Ezekiel*, and *Daniel*.

<margin>
The Book of Isaiah.
</margin>
*Isaiah*, son of *Amoz*, of royal lineage, has—if one believes the Jews—prophesied under *Uzziah* <note>original: "Ozias"</note>, *Jotham*, *Ahaz* <note>original: "Achas"</note>, and *Hezekiah* <note>original: "Hiskias"</note>, and even, according to the opinion of some, under *Manasseh*, by whose command it is said he was sawn asunder; to which it is thought that *Paul* alludes in Hebrews 11:37. But that tradition is very uncertain.

<margin>
Why Manasseh.
</margin>
The Jews say that the reason why *Manasseh* had *Isaiah* sawn asunder was the god-

<column-break/>

lessness and cruelty of this King; and they give the pretext he used to put this Prophet to death: namely, because he had said, "I have seen the Lord," while it is written in the Law, *Man shall not see my face and live* (Exodus 33:20). But this is quite uncertain. The Jews have also said that *Isaiah* was hidden in the trunk of a tree, and that *Manasseh* had both the tree and the Prophet sawn through.

<margin>
Isaiah sawn asunder?
</margin>
There are those who say that the Book of *Isaiah* which we have is but a collection drawn from the works of *Isaiah*, but this is without foundation, and their reasons are weak. One objects: I. That the prophecy begins with Chapter 6, because it is noted that he was only then appointed as a prophet. Answer: He was only confirmed there; for although the prophet says there that God appeared to him, he does not say it was the first time; God could also have appeared to him in another manner. Furthermore, if this were the beginning of his prophecy, it would not follow that his book is merely a compilation, but only that this chapter was not placed in its proper sequence. II. One objects: That what he says in Chapter 2 concerning the destruction of Judea does not correspond with the reign of *Uzziah*. Answer: Could he not have predicted a future destruction? III. One objects: That one does not find the life and deeds of *Uzziah* in this book. Answer: But the book of the deeds of *Uzziah* <note>Likely referring to the historical records mentioned in 2 Chronicles 26:22.</note> was distinct from the Book of the prophecies of *Isaiah*. IV. One objects: That there is nothing in it concerning the reign of *Manasseh*. Answer: It is uncertain whether *Isaiah* wrote under *Manasseh*. V. One objects: That the order of matters is reversed. Answer: One must not seek a chronological order in the Prophets as in other books.

It is believed that *Isaiah* began to prophesy in the Year of the World <note>original: "Jaar der wereld"; referring to Anno Mundi, a calendar system dating from the creation.</note> 3220 or 3224.

He has been called the fifth Evangelist because he speaks of *Jesus Christ* almost as clearly as the Evangelists, as can be seen in *Isaiah* 7, 9, and 53.

One can distinguish his entire prophecy into four parts.

# THEOLOGY. Book I. Chapter VIII.

The prophecies concerning the destruction of Jerusalem, the Babylonian captivity, the deliverance from this captivity, and the history of Hezekiah are found from the 29th to the 40th chapter.

The prophecies concerning the Messiah—his suffering, kingdom, and our redemption, which is described to us under the symbol <note>The author uses the term "Zinnebeeld," suggesting an allegorical or typological relationship between the historical exile and spiritual salvation.</note> of the Jewish people's deliverance from the Babylonian captivity—comprise the 40th chapter until the end of the book.

<margin>On the Book of Jeremiah.</margin>
Jeremiah, of priestly descent, prophesied under Josiah in the Year of the World <note>original: "Jaar der wereld"; this refers to *Anno Mundi*, a calendar based on the biblical creation date.</note> 3350 or 3375, according to other chronologists, and subsequently under Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah. Unlike the other Jews, he was not carried away to Babylon; instead, having remained in his land to mourn its destruction, he was later taken captive to Egypt with Baruch, where, according to the account of Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymus"</note>, he was stoned to death.

This book contains not only many exhortations to repentance and appropriate rebukes against the Jews and other nations, but also excellent promises regarding the Messiah and the New Covenant (Jeremiah 23:5, 6; 31:33, 34, 35, 36).

This is not the only book that Jeremiah composed. To him are attributed Psalms 46 and 147, as well as the First and Second Books of Kings.

He also composed one that bears the name **Lamentations** <note>original: "Klaag-Liederen"</note>, in which he depicts with very vivid strokes the destruction and overthrow of Jerusalem and tender-heartedly expresses the sorrow he felt over it.

There have been teachers who believed that this book is merely a mourning lament over the death of Josiah; however, one only has to read it to be convinced that those who hold this opinion are mistaken.

There are many things that do not correspond with the time of Josiah. The Greek <note>The Septuagint</note> and common Latin translators <note>The Vulgate</note> have a preface that is found neither in the Hebrew source language nor in the Chaldean paraphrase <note>The Targum</note>, and which was likely added to serve as a summary of the book.

<margin>On the Book of Ezekiel.</margin>
The prophecy of Ezekiel follows that of Jeremiah. Ezekiel, having been carried away to Babylon under Jeconiah, prophesied, according to some chronologists, in the year 3400; according to others, 3410 or 3414. It is thought

<column-break/>

that he prophesied for about 20 years, and some have said that he was killed by a Jewish prince.

He was the son of the priest Buzi. There is no prophet about whom so many fables have been invented. It is said that he was buried in the tomb of Shem <note>The son of Noah</note> and that a great concourse of people flocked to this grave; that the Chaldeans decided one day to kill all these false worshippers, but that the prophet held back the waters of the river, ensuring that when the Israelites had reached the other bank, the Chaldeans pursuing them were drowned. I shall not recount here all the dreams <note>The author uses "dromeryen" to mean fantasies or legends.</note> spread by a Rabbi of the 12th century, whose travels were published in Hebrew and Latin in the year 1687, named Rabbi Pethahiah <note>original: "Rabbi Petechias"</note>. Some have said that Pythagoras was a disciple of Ezekiel, but it is without foundation. There is a treatise in the **Talmud** <note>The central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note> in which it is told that many Rabbis, wishing to remove the prophecy of Ezekiel from the number of the Canonical Books <note>original: "Regelmatige Boeken"</note>, were dissuaded from doing so by a certain Ananias. The Jews did not permit the reading of the beginning and the end of Ezekiel’s book except to those who had reached the age of 30.

This book is filled with wonderful Visions, some of which are very difficult to understand and very obscure.

There are Visions concerning God’s people; there are those concerning other nations; and there are those concerning the Temple of Jerusalem.

The last two chapters of this book are extraordinarily obscure. The Jews understand this Temple of Ezekiel to be a third, holy, and eternal Temple that will be built, they say, when God delivers them from their third captivity—that is to say, according to their thoughts, from the state they are now in under the Christians—and when they shall return to Canaan. Many Christian teachers have believed that there are nothing but pure mysteries in the visions of this prophet. Others believe it is the same temple as that of Solomon.

### CHAPTER VIII.

#### Continuation of the Books of the Old Testament.

I now move on to the Prophets. There are the four Great and the twelve Minor Prophets.

The four who are called Great Prophets are Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel.

<margin>The Book of Isaiah</margin>
Isaiah, son of Amoz, of royal lineage, prophesied—if the Jews are to be believed—under Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah; and even, according to the opinion of some, under Manasseh, by whose command it is said he was sawn asunder; a point to which some believe Paul alludes in Hebrews 11:37. But that tradition is very uncertain.

<margin>Why Manasseh had Isaiah sawn asunder</margin>
The Jews say that the reason why Manasseh had Isaiah sawn asunder was the god-

<column-break/>

lessness and cruelty of this King; and they provide the pretext he used to put this Prophet to death: <margin>Isaiah sawn asunder?</margin> namely, because Isaiah had said, *I saw the Lord*, whereas it is written in the Law, *no man shall see my face and live.* Exod. 33:20. But this is quite uncertain. The Jews have also said that Isaiah was hidden in the trunk of a tree, and that Manasseh had both the tree and the Prophet sawn through. There are those who say that the Book of Isaiah which we possess is only a collection drawn from the works of Isaiah, but this is without foundation, and their reasons are weak. It is objected: I. That the prophecy begins with the 6th Chapter, because it is assumed he was only then appointed as a prophet. Answer: He was merely confirmed there; for although the Prophet says God appeared to him there, he does not say it was the first time; God could also have appeared to him in another manner. Furthermore, if this were the beginning of his predictions, it would not follow that his book is a mere compilation, but only that this chapter was not placed in its chronological order. II. It is objected that what he says in the 1st Chapter regarding the destruction of Judea does not match the reign of Uzziah. Answer: Could he not have predicted a future destruction? III. It is objected that the life and deeds of Uzziah are not found in this book. Answer: But the *Book of the Acts of Uzziah* was distinct from the *Book of the Prophecies of Isaiah*. IV. It is objected that there is nothing in it concerning the reign of Manasseh. Answer: It is uncertain whether Isaiah wrote under Manasseh. V. It is objected that the order of subjects is inverted. Answer: One should not look for a sequential order in the Prophets as one does in other books.

It is believed that Isaiah began to prophesy in the Year of the World 3220 or 3224. <note>This refers to the "Anno Mundi" calendar, dating from the creation of the world.</note>

He has been called the "Fifth Evangelist" because he speaks almost as clearly of Jesus Christ as the Evangelists do, as can be seen in Isaiah 7, 9, and 53.

His entire prophecy can be distinguished into four parts.

The Prophecies that specifically concern the Jewish people are found from Chapter 1 to Chapter 13.

->DIVINITY. BOOK I. CHAPTER VIII.<-

...concerning God’s people are recorded from the 13th to the 29th [chapters].

The Prophecies concerning the destruction of Jerusalem, the captivity of Babylon, the deliverance from this captivity, and the history of Hezekiah, are found from the 29th to the 40th Chapter.

The Prophecies which look toward the Messiah—his suffering, kingdom, and our redemption, which is described to us under the symbol of the deliverance of the Jewish people from the Babylonian captivity—comprise from the 40th Chapter until the end of the Book.

<margin>Concerning the Book of Jeremiah.</margin>
Jeremiah, of priestly descent, prophesied under Josiah, in the year of the world 3350, or 3375 according to other chronologists, and subsequently under Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah. He was not brought over to Babylon with the other Jews, but having remained in his land to mourn its destruction, he was later led captive into Egypt with Baruch, where, according to the account of Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymus"; a prominent early Christian scholar known for his Latin translation of the Bible</note>, he was stoned.

This Book contains not only many exhortations to repentance and terrible threats against the Jews and other nations, but also excellent promises regarding the Messiah and the New Covenant. Jer. 23:5, 6; 31:13, 14, 15, 16.

This is not the only Book that Jeremiah composed. To him are attributed Psalms 46 and 147, and the 1st and 2nd Books of Kings. <note>While Jeremiah is traditionally credited by some ancient sources with writing the Books of Kings, modern scholars usually view them as part of a larger historical work by various authors.</note>

He composed one that bears the name of **Lamentations** <note>original: "Klaag Liederen"</note>, in which he depicts the destruction and overthrow of Jerusalem with very vivid strokes, tenderly expressing the grief he felt over it.

There have been teachers who believed that this book is merely a mourning lament over the death of Josiah; however, one only has to read it to be convinced that those who hold this opinion are mistaken.

There are many things that do not correspond with the time of Josiah. The Greek and common Latin translators have a preface that is found neither in the Hebrew original nor in the Chaldean <note>The author refers to the Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> interpreter, and which was likely added to serve as a short summary of the Book.

<margin>Concerning the Book of Ezekiel.</margin>
The Prophecy of Ezekiel follows that of Jeremiah. Ezekiel, having been carried away to Babylon under Jeconiah, prophesied, according to some chronologists, in the year 3400; according to others, 3410 or 3414. It is believed /

<column-break/>

that he prophesied for about 20 years, and some have said that he was killed by a Jewish prince.

He was the son of the priest Buzi. There is no prophet about whom so many fables have been invented. It is said that he was buried in the tomb of Shem <note>The son of Noah</note>; it is also said that the Chaldeans resolved one day to kill all these false worshippers <note>referring to the exiled Israelites</note>, but that the Prophet held back the waters of the river and ensured that, once the Israelites had gained the other shore, the Chaldeans who pursued them were drowned. I will not recount all the daydreams here that a Rabbi of the 12th century scattered, whose travels were published in Hebrew and Latin in the year 1687, named Rabbi Petachiah. <note>Rabbi Petachiah of Ratisbon was a medieval traveler whose accounts mixed geography with folklore.</note> Some have said that Pythagoras was a disciple of Ezekiel, but it is without foundation. There is a treatise in the Talmud in which it is related that many Rabbis, wishing to remove the prophecy of Ezekiel from the number of canonical books, were dissuaded by a certain Ananias. The Jews did not allow the reading of the beginning and the end of the book of Ezekiel except to those who had reached 30 years of age. <note>Ancient scholars restricted access to these sections because they contained complex mystical descriptions of God’s "Chariot" (the Merkabah).</note>

This book is filled with wonderful Visions, some of which are very difficult to understand and very obscure.

There are Visions concerning God’s people; there are those concerning other nations; and there are those concerning the Temple of Jerusalem.

The last two chapters of this Book are exceptionally obscure. By this Temple of Ezekiel, the Jews understand a third, holy, and eternal Temple, which will be built, they say, when God shall deliver them from their third captivity—that is to say, in their view, from the state they are now in under the Christians—and when they shall return to Canaan. Many Christian teachers have believed that there are nothing but pure mysteries in the visions of this Prophet. Others believe that it is the same Temple as that of Solomon.

<margin>The Book of Daniel.</margin>
Daniel is placed after Ezekiel; it is believed that he was of the lineage of the princes of Judah. He was led into captivity in his young years, and it is not known whether he ever returned. The Jews do not place him among the rank of the Prophets; but one

<header>THE CHRISTIAN</header>

<margin>Whether Daniel was a Prophet.</margin>
one has only to read his book to be certain that they are grossly and foolishly mistaken.
The reasons for which the Jews do not wish to place Daniel in the number of the Prophets <note>In the Hebrew Bible, Daniel is traditionally placed in the *Ketuvim* (Writings) rather than the *Nevi'im* (Prophets).</note> are: 1. He lived as a great Lord; as if that prevented him from being a Prophet. 2. They say that the Spirit of Prophecy was not given outside the Holy Land: as if Ezekiel and Jeremiah had not prophesied outside the land of Canaan. Their other reasons are no better.
The Rabbis say that there are eleven degrees of Prophecy, and that to possess the quality of a Prophet, one must have three of them; and to have those, it must be said that the word of the Lord came to the Prophet, and that the revelation given to him in a dream is no longer called a dream. Both the one and the other, they say, are lacking in Daniel. But these are imaginary rules. Christ and Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a first-century Jewish historian.</note> call Daniel a Prophet. Some Jews are of the same opinion; and one of them admits that Daniel reached the highest degree of Prophecy. The godless Celsus, and before him Porphyry <note>Ancient critics of Christianity who argued that Daniel’s prophecies were written after the events occurred.</note>, falsely alleged that this Book was not made by Daniel, but by someone who lived in the time of Antiochus Epiphanes <note>A Seleucid king who persecuted the Jews in the 2nd century BC.</note>. Methodius, Eusebius, and Apollinaris have refuted this error.
Daniel describes in this book what happened to him under Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar, and Darius; and gives us at the same time a concise history of these Kings.
He subsequently describes the wonderful visions that he had. One sees there an excellent prediction of the time of the coming of the Messiah, Daniel 9:24 etc., and of the cruel persecution of Antiochus Epiphanes, Daniel 11.
The **Twelve Minor Prophets** made up but one Book among the Hebrews. One can observe some diversity among these Prophets. Some prophesied against the Kingdom of the Ten Tribes <note>The Northern Kingdom of Israel.</note>, such as Hosea, Amos, and Micah. Others against the Kingdom of Judah and against Jerusalem, such as Joel, Zephaniah, and in part Habakkuk. Others against the Ninevites, such as Jonah and Nahum. Habakkuk prophesies against Babylon; Obadiah against the Edomites.
The others turn themselves to the people who returned from captivity; such as Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi. They almost all speak of Jesus Christ.
<margin>Hosea.</margin>
Hosea, who is placed first, prophe-

<column-break/>

sied under the Kings Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, and under the reign of Jeroboam II and his successors; so that it is maintained that he prophesied for about 60 years.
It is believed that he lived in the Year 3215, or according to others 3220 <note>These dates refer to *Anno Mundi*, or years since the creation of the world.</note>. The book of this Prophet can be split into two parts.
In the first, Hosea very vividly uncovers, rebukes, and condemns the general corruption that had taken the upper hand among the ten tribes, to whom he proclaims their final downfall.
In the second, he promises God’s Grace and Salvation to the true Believers, and the conversion of the whole people in the latter times. These threats and promises are mixed throughout the entire book, and sometimes presented in obscure, sometimes in clear words.
Joel follows Hosea; one could not precisely determine the time in which he wrote. Some maintain that he prophesied before the famine under Joram, son of Ahab, came (2 Kings 8:1). Others say that he wrote under Manasseh, after the captivity of the ten tribes; based on what is said in Chapter 3:2, that they have scattered the people of Israel among the nations. Others place him in the time of Josiah, under whom there was also a great famine <margin>Jeremiah 14:4. 1 Kings 23:26.</margin> in the Year 3350.
Whatever the case may be, one can distinguish this Prophecy in three parts.
In the first, the Prophet threatens Judah with an extraordinary famine and exhorts the people to an earnest repentance.
In the second, he promises to the Church, in the last days, a great abundance of the gifts of the Holy Spirit.
Finally, in the third, he proclaims God’s Judgments to the enemies of his Church.
Amos, the Tekoite, prophesied in the days of Uzziah, King of Judah; and in the days of Jeroboam, son of Joash, King of Israel, two years before the earthquake spoken of in Zechariah 14:5, around the Year 3218 or 3220.
His Prophecy contains three things.
1. Threats of God’s judgments against six nations.
2. Threats of God’s judgments against the tribe of Judah, and against the ten tribes of Israel.
3. Finally, promises of Grace.

# THE CHRISTIAN

He [Zephaniah] foretells Jerusalem’s destruction by the Chaldeans, and threatens the Sinners with a complete downfall.

He then exhorts the believers to repentance / to prayer / and perseverance in Godliness; assuring them / that God would one day restore his church.

Finally / after having powerfully rebuked the sins of the Inhabitants of Jerusalem / he comforts the believers through the hope / which he gives them of the redemption and peace of the Church / which was to be gathered from all nations of the world.

<margin>Haggai.</margin>
Haggai Prophesied after the return from captivity / in the second Year of King Darius : But there is no agreement / regarding this Darius. Some believe / that it is Darius the Son of Hystaspes. Others take him for Darius the Bastard <note>original: "Darius den Bastaart," referring to Darius II Nothus.</note>.

<margin>Under which Darius Haggai lived.</margin>
Everyone agrees / that it is not Darius the Mede; Those who believe that it is Darius Nothus or the Bastard / and not Darius, Son of Hystaspes, note / that Zechariah and Haggai prophesied in the same time / and that Zechariah says in Chapter 1:12 and 7:5 / that there were 70 Years / in which God was angry against his people. But they say / the second Year of Darius, Son of Hystaspes, is not the 70th Year of the captivity. Those who believe it is Darius Son of Hystaspes / and not Darius the Bastard, say / that if it were Darius the Bastard / those / of whom it is said in the Prophecy of Haggai / that they had seen the first Temple / must have been around 176 Years old.

The Prophet strongly stirs the people / in his book / to rebuild the Temple / and assures them of God's Grace.

He promises them that the Glory of the second House would be greater / than that of the first / and foretells the calling of the Heathen <note>original: "Heidenen," a term used here for the non-Jewish nations or Gentiles.</note>.

He rebukes the Hypocritical and Godless Jews / and makes an exceptional promise to Zerubbabel.

<column-break/>

Siege of this great City followed. # THEOLOGY. BOOK I. CHAPTER IX.

<margin>Malachi.</margin>
Malachi (x) appears to have been the last of the Prophets: at the least, one cannot deny that he wrote after the rebuilding of the Temple. He rebukes many flaws that prevailed among the Jews: their impiety, polygamy <note>The practice of having multiple wives.</note>, divorce, negligence in paying tithes, their marriages with foreign women, and many other sins.

He clearly promises the coming of the Messiah, his entry into the Temple, and his forerunner <note>Referring to John the Baptist.</note>.

There you have it—those are the Books of the Old Testament; let us now pass over to those of the New.

I shall only add that these Books were written in Hebrew; except for some chapters in Daniel and Ezra, as well as the eleventh verse of Jeremiah X, which were written in Chaldean <note>term: Chaldean (Aramaic), a language closely related to Hebrew used by the Jews after the Babylonian exile.</note>. (y)

---

### CHAPTER IX.

->Of the Books of the New Testament.<-

---

<margin>Regarding the number of Books of the N.T.</margin>
One counts 27 Books of the New Testament: 5 which are called Historical; 14 Letters of Paul; 7 Letters of the other Apostles; and one Prophetic Book, the Revelation.

They were written in Greek for the most part; for there are many Scholars who believe that some of them were written in Hebrew.

It is certain that the Greek language was the most well-known and common in the time of the Apostles; much more so than Hebrew, and even more so than Latin.

The first four Books are the IV Evangelists <note>The authors of the Gospels.</note>: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. In these, we find the account of the Birth, Life, Miracles, Death, Resurrection, and Ascension of Jesus Christ.

<margin>Matthew.</margin>
The first Evangelist is Matthew, who from being a Tax Collector <note>original: "Tollenaar," often called a Publican in older English Bibles.</note> became an Apostle of Jesus Christ.

<column-break/>

<margin>Why is he called an Evangelist?</margin>
When I call Matthew an Evangelist, why do I not take this word in the sense in which it is sometimes used, to signify a distinct Order from that of the Apostles? <note>The author is distinguishing between the office of "evangelist" as a traveling preacher and the specific title given to the four Gospel writers.</note>

He was also called Levi; since he was a Jew, Tertullian <note>An early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155–220 AD).</note> is wrong to claim that all Tax Collectors were Heathens and not Jews. Pope Gelasius condemned a book regarding the Birth of Jesus Christ under the name of Matthew, from which it is claimed the Valentinians <note>A group of Gnostics, followers of Valentinus, who held unorthodox spiritual beliefs.</note> drew some narratives. Some attribute an Ethiopian Liturgy to him, which has been found to be false.

One cannot precisely determine the time in which he wrote; there are those who believe he wrote 6 years, others 8 (which is the most common opinion), and others 15 years after the Ascension of Christ; there are others who place this much later.

It is asked on what occasion he wrote? The Church Fathers <note>The influential early teachers and bishops of the Christian Church.</note> say that Matthew, having taught for some time in Judea and being on the point of leaving it to go and preach elsewhere, wrote his Gospel while he was still in Judea and at Jerusalem, so that this Book might fill the void of his presence.

<margin>In which language he wrote?</margin>
<margin>In Irenaeus; in Eusebius, Eccl. Hist. Book 5, Ch. 8. Origen in Eusebius, Eccl. Hist. Book 6, Ch. 25.</margin>
It is asked in what Language he wrote? Opinions are divided: there are those who believe that he wrote in Hebrew, or at least in a language mixed with Chaldean and Syrian, which the Jews in Palestine used at that time. Those of this opinion point to many Church Fathers who believed it, such as Papias, cited by Eusebius (Eccl. Hist. Book 3, Ch. 39), Irenaeus, Origen, the author of the work on Matthew attributed to Chrysostom, Epiphanius, the author of the summary of Scripture attributed to Athanasius, Jerome, etc. They also cite what is found at the end of Matthew's Gospel in the Syriac and Arabic translations; they say that in the time of Jerome, this Gospel was found in Hebrew. Those who believe that Matthew wrote in Greek say: 1. that the Apostles wrote not only for the Jews, but also for the Heathens; that the truth—

---

(x) Some have believed that he was an Angel, as did some Church Fathers. Others, that he was Melchia <note>Malchijah</note>, of whom is spoken in Ezra X:25, 31, Nehemiah III:2, and VIII:4. Others Ezra, others Zechariah; all these opinions have little probability.

<margin>Hottinger, Eccl. Hist. Vol. III. p. 347-348. Bale, Century III.</margin>

Others attribute it to an Englishman named Langton <note>Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury (c. 1150–1228).</note>, who flourished in the year 1200.

THE CHRISTIAN <note>Likely "THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION," continued from the previous page's header.</note>

it is more likely that Matthew wrote in Greek than in Hebrew, especially since the Jews of that time understood Greek. 2. They <note>The scholars arguing for a Greek original.</note> add that it is surprising that, if Matthew had written in Hebrew, this Gospel was not preserved in that language; for all voices agree that the Hebrew Gospels currently in existence are not very old. They say the original Hebrew text was lost because the Jews of Jerusalem and Judea, having converted to Christianity, soon stopped speaking the Chaldean language <note>term: Chaldean; here referring to Aramaic, the common tongue of Judea at the time.</note>. This is not a complete explanation, for if the original Hebrew of the Old Testament was well-preserved, why would it not be possible to keep the original Hebrew of the New Testament? 3. Against the authority of the Church Fathers <note>Early influential Christian theologians and writers.</note>, they argue that this is not the only error they have attempted to establish as fact. 4. They note that the Syriac and Arabic subscriptions <note>Notes added to the end of manuscript copies by later scribes.</note> are not authentic; that the Syriac subscription only states that Matthew *preached* in Hebrew, not that he wrote in that language; and that nothing of the sort is found in the Arabic subscription read in the Polyglot Bibles <note>term: Polyglot Bibles; Bibles printed with the text in several languages side-by-side, such as Hebrew, Greek, Latin, and Syriac.</note>. 5. That the Hebrew Gospel used by the Nazarenes <note>A group of early Jewish Christians who maintained Jewish Law.</note> is not the same as the Gospel of Matthew, as is evident from many fables found in the Gospel of the Nazarenes. 6. That while Jerome <note>The scholar famous for translating the Bible into the Latin Vulgate.</note> may have possessed a Hebrew Gospel, one should not conclude from this that Matthew wrote it. 7. That it is unlikely that anyone translating Matthew’s Hebrew Gospel into Greek would have interpreted a word as clear as <term>Holy</term> <note>original: "קדוש" (Qadosh)</note>—which they claim signifies "of the morning"—using the word <term>Holy</term> <note>original: "Ἅγιος" (Hagios)</note>, which is so obscure and is translated by us as "daily" in the Lord’s Prayer. <note>This refers to a complex historical debate regarding the Greek word *epiousios* in the Lord's Prayer ("daily bread"). Some scholars tried to trace it back to a Hebrew root meaning "of the morrow."</note>

Whatever the case may be, some suggest that if this Gospel which we have in Greek was not written by Matthew, it was written by James or some other Apostle or Evangelist, such as John, Barnabas, or Luke. There are those who claim that Matthew wrote it in Hebrew for the Jews and in Greek for the Gentiles <note>Non-Jewish people.</note>. A historian (Theodorus Lector, Book 2) relates that when the body of

<column-break/>

Barnabas was found around the year 488, he had the Gospel of Matthew lying on his chest, which Barnabas had written with his own hand. This copy was in Greek and written on wood (called *Thie*), which was very rare and brought from the East. The Emperor Zeno desired to have that copy, adorned it with gold, and ordered it to be kept in the Palace. There is also no agreement on where and how Matthew died.

<margin>Matthew's death.</margin>
Some believe it was in Persia, or at Warliane in Carmania (then subject to the Parthians); others say in Hierapolis, others in the city of Nadaver in Ethiopia. Some maintain he died a natural death, others that he suffered a violent death as a martyr. The Greek Church celebrates the Feast of Matthew on November 16; the Latin Church on September 21.

The Ebionites and the Nazarenes <note>Two early Jewish-Christian sects.</note> accepted no other Gospel but this one, and even then, they had corrupted it greatly. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a famous Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> points out many such instances in his remarks on Matthew I. Two fragments of it can be found in two treatises by Origen: the 8th on Matthew and the 2nd on John.

<margin>Mark.</margin>
The second Evangelist is Mark. There is a dispute as to whether he is the same person who was called John, mentioned in Acts 12:12. Jerome was of this opinion.

There is reason to doubt whether they are the same. The Church Fathers always call this Evangelist Mark, and never John; and they always give him Peter as a companion. The Roman Martyrology <note>A directory of martyrs and saints arranged by their feast days.</note>, which sets the Feast of John Mark (mentioned in Acts 12) on September 27, places that of Mark the Evangelist on April 25. It is not known what Mark was before he became an Evangelist; some have said he was a priest. There is also no agreement regarding the time in which he wrote.

The most common opinion is that it was in the year 40 or 43. Others say in the year 45 after Christ’s birth. The claim that Mark wrote in Latin and that his manuscript is found in Venice is a fiction. Henschenius, in his *Acts of the Saints* for April 25, relates that Charles IV, having found the Gospel of Mark in Aquileia on seven sheets, received the last two as a gift, which he sent to Prague along with 2,000 guilders to be placed together in a precious chest.

### THEOLOGY. BOOK I. CHAPTER IX.

<note>original: "GOD-GELEERTHEID"</note>

the Republic of Venice boasts of having the other part of this Latin Gospel. But the learned Mabillon, in his *Italian Journey* <note>original: "Iter: Ital: p: 32"</note>, to whom the chest in which this rare monument is kept was shown, says that it is closed to all people for fear that the matter might be investigated. Grand, a famous physician of Venice, says, according to the account of Burnet, that he saw the book and that the letters are so decayed that one does not know whether it is Greek or Latin; and that one only perceives that it is written in capital letters. Misson, in his travel descriptions of Italy, says that he noticed the word "According to" <note>original Greek: "KATA"</note> in it. Those who believe that Mark wrote in Latin say that it is because he wrote for the Romans: But 1. this is based solely on the testimony of Papias, a credulous man. 2. It is certain that the Romans for the most part understood the Greek language, and there were Jews among them who were more proficient in Greek than in Latin. 3. It is surprising that the Romans had not preserved a copy of this Latin Gospel: for it is agreed that the one we have is a translation from the Greek.

<margin>Where Mark wrote: Clement of Alexandria in the *Hypotyposes* <note>term: Hypotyposes; a lost work by Clement of Alexandria known as "Outlines" or "Sketches."</note></margin>
Some Church Fathers have believed that Mark wrote in Rome; they have said that those who had heard Peter preach wished to have in writing what he had taught them, and that they requested Mark to do them this favor. Some scholars believe, however, that this is not so certain that one may not doubt it; and prefer to believe that Mark wrote his Gospel in Egypt rather than in Rome.

It is not known for certain in what manner Mark died.

There are those who have said that the pagans in Alexandria attacked him on a Sunday and, having thrown a rope around his neck, dragged him for two days and tore his body to pieces, after which they burned it; however, this account is doubted.

<margin>Luke: Colossians 4:14, 2 Timothy 4:11, Philemon 1:24, 2 Corinthians 8:18.</margin>
Luke, who is the third Evangelist, was from Antioch, the capital of Syria: he was a physician and accompanied Paul in his travels. It is believed that Paul speaks of him when he mentions a brother whose praise, in respect to the Gospel, was spread throughout all the churches.

<column-break/>

There are those who believe that he speaks of Silas instead.

<margin>Whether he was a painter?</margin>
It is not true that he is or was a painter, and that he painted the image of the Blessed Virgin; although some have said so (Nicephorus, book 11, chapter 43).

It is claimed that he not only made the likeness of the Virgin but had also painted the Lord Jesus: but these are mere fictions. A historian of the 6th century says that the supposed likeness which Luke had made of the Virgin was sent from Jerusalem to Pulcheria <note>Empress Pulcheria (399–453 AD) was known for her religious influence in the Byzantine Empire.</note>.

<margin>When he wrote.</margin>
Scholars do not agree regarding the time in which Luke wrote his Gospel. Some say in the year 53; others 56; others 58; others earlier, others later. It is asked whether he wrote before or after Matthew? The beginning of his Gospel leads some to believe that he wrote before the other Evangelists: others draw an opposite conclusion from it. The ancient ecclesiastical writers say that he wrote after Matthew, and many maintain that he wrote to stem the tide of some false gospels that were being circulated. Marcion and his followers accepted none but the Gospel of Luke, from which they had omitted many passages.

He dedicated it to Theophilus, who was possibly a prominent man of Rome or of Antioch.

<margin>Who Theophilus was.</margin>
Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century bishop and theologian known for his defense of orthodoxy.</note> will not make a judgment whether this Theophilus was an ordinary person, or whether one should understand by it every man who loves God <note>The name Theophilus literally means "Lover of God" or "Friend of God" in Greek.</note>. Others mean that it was a distinguished man from the government of Achaia. The author of the *Recognitions* <note>term: Recognitions; an early Christian romance or novel attributed to Clement of Rome.</note> speaks of a Theophilus who was rich and powerful in Antioch. Luke recounts many things that were skipped by Matthew and Mark.

There are various accounts of his death. It is claimed that he lived to be 84 years old and that he is buried in Constantinople: others assert that he suffered martyrdom in Bithynia; others in Rome; others that he died in Ephesus. Nicephorus says that he was hanged from an olive tree.

John, who is the fourth Evangelist, son of Zebedee and brother of James (whom Herod put to death), was one of the Apostles of the Lord Jesus and the disciple whom he loved, and to whom, while dying, he entrusted the care of his mother.

He powerfully proves the Divinity of Jesus Christ, his incarnation, and our union with him.

One finds in this Gospel the final discourses that our Savior had with his Disciples before his death, as well as the sublime Prayer that he offered to his Father before Judas delivered him to the Jews. The Book of the Acts of the Apostles is placed after the four Evangelists. Luke is the writer of it: it is believed that he wrote it in the fourth year of Nero, or a little later. One finds there the account of what happened since the Ascension of Christ, over a period of 28 years.

This book contains, then, not only the Ascension of our Savior, but also the outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles, their miracles, and sermons. The election of Matthias to fill the place of the traitor Judas, and that of the first Deacons; the martyrdom of Stephen; the conversion of Saul, and his experiences until he was sent to Rome by Festus.

It also contains the imprisonment of Peter and John, and their miraculous deliverance; the sudden and terrible death of Ananias and Sapphira, by a righteous judgment of God; the conversion of the Chamberlain of Queen Candace of Ethiopia by Philip, and of Cornelius by Peter; the death of the Apostle James, and of Herod his persecutor.

# DIVINITY. I. B. X. Chapter.

**Column 1**

...[Bar]nabas <note>likely referring to the Epistle of Barnabas</note> did not cite any Gospels, or that they did so so obscurely that one does not know whether they borrowed what they say from Matthew or from any other writer, citing profane authors alongside the sacred ones. 4. That Justin Martyr and Irenaeus are the first who truly made the Gospels known to us. 5. That the Rule <note>The "Rule" or Canon refers to the officially accepted list of books in the New Testament.</note> of the N. Testament was established through the tradition of certain elders who testified that these were the works of the Apostles, and that this Canon was compiled during the reign of Trajan.

But see how other scholars, and particularly Mr. Basnage <note>Jacques Basnage (1653–1723), a celebrated French Protestant theologian and historian.</note>, in his *Ecclesiastical History* Vol. I. p. 426, refute this proposition. Basnage notes that the Gospels could not have remained hidden for so long unless the Apostles had secretly commanded them to be hidden; which would breed some suspicion against their faithfulness, as if they had feared that their account would be judged false. For otherwise, he adds, why did they not share the same fate as other books, which become public as soon as they fall into the hands of the people? Curiosity impels everyone to know them, and the early Christians were obligated to investigate them diligently. 2. The opinion of Dodwell <note>Henry Dodwell (1641–1711), an Anglo-Irish scholar who questioned the early date of the New Testament canon.</note> deprives us of a strong proof of the truth of the Gospel histories, namely, that the Apostles proclaimed these histories in the presence of those who could have contradicted them. 3. Basnage believes that the Christians read the Gospel in public assemblies, just as the Jews read the Law, and he proves it from Justin Martyr who, making mention of this reading, does not record it as a new church custom. 4. It is not probable that the believers for whom Matthew wrote the Gospel, being scattered, did not take this Gospel with them. 5. One does not see why it is believed that Luke had only seen fabricated Gospels. The Ebionites <note>A Jewish Christian sect that followed a different version of the Gospel.</note> are the first who (to all appearances) fabricated false books, such as the *Travels of Peter*, and other works under the name of James and the other Apostles. But these fabrications are later than Luke. 6. Luke does not say that he had seen false Gospels; but he could have seen the writings of certain believers who, not being the primary witnesses of the Church's events, wished to hand down the other Gospels to posterity. 7. One cannot believe that John—

<column-break/>

—had not seen them. Eusebius says explicitly (*book 3. chap. 24.*) <note>original: "lib. 3. c. 24."</note> that the three Gospels were brought to John, who approved them and confirmed them by his testimony. 8. One finds, in the letters of Ignatius, indications from the Gospels of John, of Matthew, and from the Acts of the Apostles (*Ignatius, Letter to the Smyrnaeans, to the Philadelphians, to the Philippians*) <note>original: "Ignat. Ep. ad Smyr. ad Philad. ad Philip:"</note> 9. One finds in the writings of Barnabas passages from Matthew. 10. Polycarp relates a portion of Christ's sermon on the Mount, and other passages from Matthew and Luke. (*Polycarp, Letter to the Philippians*) <note>original: "Polyc: Epist. ad Philipp:"</note> 11. Clement of Rome, in his Letter to the Corinthians, cites extensive passages from Matthew and Luke. 12. Those who wrote before the time of Trajan did not make use of the irregular <note>meaning apocryphal or uncanonical</note> books any more than those who followed the time of Trajan. 13. There is no true contradiction in the Gospels. 14. Finally, it is said without foundation that the Canon was made in the time of Trajan. It is much more probable to say that the Gospels were released as soon as they were finished, and they were known to the heretics. Cerinthus <note>A Gnostic leader who was a contemporary of the Apostle John.</note> relied on the genealogy in Matthew to prove that Jesus Christ was but a mere man. Ebion accepted three Gospels and rejected that of John. In the following centuries, Faustus the Manichean rejected the first chapter of Matthew because he could not reconcile its genealogy with that of Luke; he called the orthodox "Matthew-ists" because they followed Matthew too simple-heartedly <note>The original "stzoom-hartig" likely means credulously or blindly.</note>, he said, and the Manicheans believed that Jesus Christ was called David's son.
