THE CHRISTIAN <note>The header "DE CHRISTELYKE" likely continues to "RELIGIE" (Religion) or "KERK" (Church).</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>
*Ezekiel Spanheim, The Roman World,* p. 141. <note>Spanheim (1629–1710) was a prominent diplomat and scholar of ancient history and numismatics.</note>
</margin>
...believe that he was a Citizen of **Rome** by birth, since **Augustus** had granted the people of **Tarsus** the right of a free colony and Roman citizenship. However, many doubt this, and not without reason.

The renowned **Spanheim** clearly proves that after the city of **Tarsus** had suffered much from **Cassius**, its inhabitants only received some exemption from tribute, but no citizenship. Others believe that **Paul** was a citizen of **Rome** because one of his ancestors had earned this citizenship in the Civil Wars that took place between **Caesar Augustus** and **Brutus and Cassius**, or between **Caesar** and **Antony**.

One counts 14 Letters. Some were written while **Paul** was not in bonds <note>Meaning he was not yet imprisoned.</note>, such as the two letters to the **Thessalonians**; the letter to the **Galatians**; the letter to the **Romans**; and the two letters to the **Corinthians**. The others were written during his first imprisonment; such as the letters to the **Philippians**, to **Philemon**, to the **Ephesians**, the **Hebrews**, and the **Colossians**, though some believe that the letter to the **Colossians** and the one to **Titus** were written during the final imprisonment of **Paul**, when **Paul** was in prison for the second time and shortly before his death.

<margin>
Letter to the Romans.
</margin>
The letter to the **Romans** is placed first in order, not because it was the first one written, nor solely because of the excellence of the subject matter discussed within it: but because it was sent to the inhabitants of **Rome**, which was regarded as the Capital of the World.

This letter was written from **Corinth**, during the journey that **Paul** made there for the second time, to collect the support <note>A collection of funds or alms.</note> that this Church had arranged for the church in **Jerusalem**. It was written <note>Scribed</note> by **Tertius**, and carried by **Phoebe** (a) a Deaconess at **Cenchreae**, a harbor of **Corinth**.

<margin>
*Romans 15:25, 26.* Who was **Phoebe**?
</margin>
One cannot precisely determine the time when **Paul** wrote this Letter. Some fix it to the year 57, others to the 58th, and others to the 60th year. Whatever the case may be, it is held to be of a later date than the two Letters to the **Thessalonians** and the two Letters to the **Corinthians**. This Letter has two general parts: one contains the Doctrines, which extend to Chapter 12.

<margin>
When was the Letter to the Romans written?
</margin>
(a) It is believed that **Paul** lodged with her. The Martyrologies <note>Historical records of Christian martyrs and saints.</note> speak of this woman on the third of September.

<column-break/>

The other part contains the Moral Lessons from Chapter 12 to the end of the Letter.

<margin>
What **Paul** speaks of in this Letter?
</margin>
**Paul** discusses in the first 11 Chapters two great points of inquiry over which the Jews and the Christians were in dispute with one another: namely, that of our **Justification** <term>Regtvaardigmaking: a theological term for being declared righteous before God</term> before God, and that of the Calling of the Gentiles. The Jews believed that man is justified through the Legal Covenant <note>The Old Testament Law given at Sinai.</note>; and they could not tolerate that the Apostles called the Gentiles to the knowledge of the true God and the hope of Salvation.

To understand this Letter well, it is necessary to know what those whom **Paul** intends to oppose believed. It is certain that the Apostle writes to such persons who had been either Gentiles or Jews, and that his purpose is to remove the prejudices that both held.

<margin>
Sentiments of the Gentiles regarding the subject Paul discusses.
</margin>
Most Gentiles, living in a thick ignorance, concerned themselves little with the forgiveness of their sins and the Salvation of their Souls. Others believed that their virtues earned the favor of the Gods, either in this life or in the future one, if there was anything to be expected after death: they thought that their faults were wiped out by their virtues, especially if they had a true sorrow over their crimes; for they declared a man innocent who repented of his evil.

To atone for the most terrible sins, they had their Purifications and Sacrifices; sometimes they sacrificed humans, sometimes they imposed punishments upon themselves, sometimes they took their refuge in Kings, to whom they attributed the power to atone for another's sins; but the wisest among them asserted that nothing was more fitting to appease the Deity than a change of life. This was the sentiment of the Gentiles.

<margin>
Sentiments of the Jews on the same. *Maimonides, On Repentance, chapter 3.* <note>Original: "Maimon de poeni. c. 3." referring to Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the medieval Jewish philosopher.</note>
</margin>
With respect to the Jews, they divided men into three orders, the first of which was composed of the **Righteous**, whose righteousness outweighed their sins; the second of evildoers, whose sins were greater in number than their good deeds; the third, of those whose acts of righteousness equaled their sins. They believed, however, that no one was so righteous that he did not need forgiveness of sins: but they believed at the same time that this was obtainable through repentance, through the help <note>Atonement or remission</note> of sins...

# THEOLOGY. Book I. Chapter X.

...through alms, through prayer, through the adversities that God sent to them, through punishments they took upon themselves, through purifications, sacrifices, and changes in lifestyle; above all through the sacrifices they offered on the great Day of Atonement. And if anything remained to be forgiven, they say that everything was wiped away by death.

But they claimed that they obtained eternal life through the merits of their works, and said that God had given them a great number of commands so that they would have more opportunity to merit and obtain various degrees of glory. The Pharisees themselves did many things that the Law had not commanded in order to have more merit.

The Pagans and Jews then agreed in this: that they believed they obtained the forgiveness of their sins and salvation through their works; but they did not think of the righteousness of the Messiah. Some Jews who had embraced Christianity wanted to combine the righteousness of Jesus Christ with their own righteousness, as if they were justified by both.

It is against all these errors that Paul wrote his Letter to the Romans. He proves therein that there is no Pagan nor Jew who can obtain the forgiveness of sins, or the right to life, either in whole or in part, through his works, and that we must seek our righteousness nowhere else but in that of Jesus Christ, which we must apply to ourselves through Faith.

The whole of Theology is contained in the first eleven chapters of this Letter. There, mention is made of Natural Revelation; of the necessity and severity of the last Judgment; of the corruption of the entire human race; of our justification through faith in the blood of Jesus Christ; of the imputation <note>The theological concept of "counting" or "crediting" Christ's merit to a believer.</note> of the righteousness of Christ, and of the imputation of the sin of Adam; of the two principal effects of our justification, namely peace of mind and the certainty of salvation, even in the midst of adversity; of the connection between our justification and Sanctification <note>The process of becoming holy through God's grace.</note>; of election and rejection; of the calling of the Pagans, the rejection of the Jews, and of their re-integration into God's true fellowship.

<sig>Part I</sig>

<column-break/>

In the final chapters, beginning with the 12th, Paul gives not only general rules of doctrine for the conduct of the faithful, but also specific lessons on how one must behave in civil society and in the ecclesiastical community.

<margin>About the Letters to the Corinthians.</margin>
After the Letter to the Romans, those which Paul wrote to the believers of **Corinth** are placed—the capital of **Achaia**—where he had converted **Crispus** and **Sosthenes**, stayed for 18 months, and laid the foundations of an excellent congregation.

<margin>About the first [letter], and where it was written.</margin>
The first letter was not written from **Philippi**, as the subscription added to it and the Syriac and Arabic translations suggest, but from **Ephesus**, as seems to be inferred from Chapter 16:8, compared with Acts 19:22, or from some place near **Ephesus**. It is believed that Paul wrote it in the year 59 according to the Christian era, or according to others, in the year 56 or 57. The disorders and schisms that existed in the congregation of **Corinth** caused Paul to write this letter. He also begins it with powerful rebukes which he presents to the **Corinthians** for their divisions, and he exhorts them to Unity. He then shows the excellence and dignity of his ministry, of which some had spoken with contempt, and he justifies his conduct; he accuses them of having so neglected Church Discipline that they failed to exercise it regarding a shameful incestuous person.

He rebukes them for their disputes, for which they made the Pagans judges. Furthermore, he shows them the abominable nature of fornication. He speaks of Marriage, and of things sacrificed to Idols; of the consideration one must have for weak brothers; of Idolatry, for which he gives a righteous dread; of the disorders that were among them, especially in the observance of the Holy Supper <note>Commonly known as the Eucharist or Communion.</note>, the first institution of which he points out; of the gifts of miracles of God's Spirit; of charity which he highly praises; and of the Resurrection of the Dead, which he proves against some heretics who denied it then; he exhorts them to help the brothers of the congregation of **Jerusalem**, and he ends his Letter with these words, which all Christians must contemplate: <margin>1 Cor. 16:22.</margin> If any man love not the Lord Jesus, let him be anathema <note>original: "vervlockinge," meaning accursed or excommunicated.</note>, Maranatha <note>Aramaic: "Our Lord comes."</note>.

# THE CHRISTIAN <note>Likely "The Christian Religion" or "The Christian Way," continuing the header from previous pages.</note>

<margin>On the second Letter.</margin>
The second Letter to the Corinthians was written a short time thereafter, possibly at the beginning of the year 60. It is believed that Paul wrote it from Philippi, a city in Macedonia, as the subscription implies; and from Chapter 7, verse 5, it is clear that it was written from Macedonia; others, however, believe it was sent from Nicopolis.

The contents of this Letter are as follows:
Paul, having learned that many false teachers spoke of him with contempt, recounts to them his labor, struggles, and the dangers in which he had found himself. He exhorts them to receive back the <term>incestuous man</term> <note>referring to the man mentioned in 1 Corinthians 5 who had been expelled from the church</note>, whose repentance he had heard of. He highly defends his ministry and that of the other Apostles; he exalts the ministry of the Gospel above that of Moses; he shows how God's power is made perfect in weakness, and the hope that believers have for an Eternal Glory. He exhorts Christians to separate themselves from Unbelievers and Idolaters; he speaks of his <term>rapture</term> <note>original: "verrukking," a state of being carried away into a divine vision</note> into the third Heaven (a) and of a thorn in his flesh (b). Throughout this entire Letter, he scatters excellent moral lessons which serve for the instruction and comfort of those who read them.

<margin>The Letter to the Galatians.</margin>
The Letter to the Galatians was, according to the opinion of many scholars, written in the year 58 or 59. Others place it earlier, in the year 56 or 54.

<margin>Galatia.</margin>
Galatia is a province of Asia Minor. It is said to be named after the <term>Gauls</term> <note>A Celtic people who migrated to central Anatolia in the 3rd century BCE</note>, who, after burning Rome and

<column-break/>

having devastated Italy, came to settle there.

There is little probability that it was written from Rome; the opinion of those who think it was much likely from Ephesus or Antioch is more probable.

<margin>One may compare Acts 18:23.</margin>
The Apostle strongly rebukes the Galatians in this Letter for having allowed themselves to be turned away from the Gospel that he had preached to them; and he pronounces a curse upon anyone who preached another doctrine than the one he had taught them. He demonstrates the authority of his ministry: that he was in no way inferior to the other Apostles, and that he had even rebuked Peter. He clearly sets forth our justification through Faith, without the works of the Law, and proves that one must not mix the two covenants together. He describes the advantages for believers under the New Dispensation over those of the Old, and treats of <term>Christian Liberty</term>. He makes it understood that the Gospel, which has freed Christians from the Yoke of the Law, allows for no <term>licentiousness</term> <note>original: "ongebondentheid," meaning a lack of moral restraint</note>, and that everyone is obliged to live for God, to crucify his flesh, and to renounce his lusts.

<margin>Galatians 1:6.</margin>
<margin>The Letter to the Ephesians.</margin>
The Letter to the Ephesians was written by Paul during his first imprisonment, in the year 60. This Holy Teacher, having foreseen that "ravenous wolves" who would not spare the flock would arise in the Church he had founded at Ephesus—a famous city in Asia Minor—thought it was his duty to write to these believers from his prison to strengthen them.

<meta>catchword: In</meta>

---

<margin>When was Paul caught up into Heaven?</margin>
(a) It is not possible to know when Paul was caught up in ecstasy. If Paul wrote this second Letter in the year 60, then this rapture occurred in the year 46 or 45. *I know a man,* says Paul in 2 Corinthians 12:2, *fourteen years ago, etc.* It is true that another interpretation can be given to these words. I cannot believe that this rapture happened, as some claim, during the three days he was in Damascus, without sight, and without eating or drinking. <term>Lucian</term> <note>referring to a dialogue titled *Philopatris*, once attributed to the satirist Lucian of Samosata</note> in his *Philopatris* (if it is true that this work is by Lucian) had heard of this rapture, for he has a Christian named Tryphon say that he was renewed in the water by this "Galilean" who had been caught up into the air, into the third heaven, and had there learned wonderful things. <term>Epiphanius</term> <note>a 4th-century Church Father known for cataloging heresies</note> speaks of certain heretics called <term>Cainites</term> who compiled a book that they attributed to Paul, and called the

<column-break/>

*Ascension of Paul* <note>original: "Verheffing van Paulus"</note>. And in <term>Augustine</term> mention is made of a fictional book under the title of the *Apocalypse of Paul*, in which they undertook to recount the things that the Apostle says are inexpressible. I do not know if it is the same book that, according to the account of <term>Sozomen</term> <note>a 5th-century historian of the Christian Church</note>, was highly esteemed by many monks in the 5th century, and which is falsely said to have been found under <term>Theodosius I</term> in the house of Paul in <term>Tarsus</term> <note>The OCR reads "Tarfis," an archaic or mistaken rendering of Tarsus, Paul's birthplace</note>.

<margin>What is the thorn?</margin>
(b) There is no one who knows what this "Thorn" is; everyone guesses at it, but these are only riddles. Some say it was a False Teacher; others, that it was some physical ailment; some that it was a temptation and lust of the flesh; others that it was the stings of conscience; some that it was the persecutions inflicted upon him; many, that it was the Devil who struck him. The 1st, 2nd, and last opinions are the three most probable.

### DIVINE THEOLOGY. BOOK I. CHAPTER X.

In this Letter, he first thanks God that he has chosen us, prepared us, and adopted us as his children in Jesus Christ; and that he has blessed us with all Spiritual Blessings in this Divine Savior. He then prays to God for the Ephesians, that he might pour out upon them his Spirit of knowledge and revelation. Following this, he describes the <term>natural state</term> <note>the state of humanity inherited from Adam, before receiving divine grace</note> of all people, alongside the state into which Grace has restored us; the excellent fruits of the death of the Lord Jesus; and the length, height, width, and depth of his love. Then from there, he transitions to moral lessons and exhorts the Ephesians to arrange their lives in a manner worthy of their calling; he exhorts them to meekness, unity, charity, truth, and righteousness, so as to use the gifts they had received from the Spirit for the building up of the body of Jesus Christ, and to be imitators of God. He shows what the duty of Wives and Husbands is, of Fathers and Children, of Servants and Masters. Finally, he describes the spiritual struggle that Believers have with the Devil and the World, and the armor they must put on to carry away the victory.

<margin>The Letter to the Philippians.</margin>
The Letter to the Philippians was also written from Rome at the same time as the one to the Ephesians.

<margin>What Philippi was.</margin>
Philippi was a city of Macedonia, built and enlarged by Philip, the Father of Alexander the Great. That which moved Paul to write to the Believers of this city was not only the love he bore for all the congregations he had planted; but in particular, the assistance that the Philippians had sent to the Apostle in his prison through Epaphroditus, and the favorable report that this Evangelical envoy had given him concerning the steadfastness of this Church; and concerning the bad faith of many false brothers who sought to instill in the congregations the necessity of maintaining the <term>Mosaic ceremonies</term> <note>referring to Jewish laws and rituals, such as circumcision, which some early Christians believed were still mandatory</note>.

Some Scholars draw from Chapter II, verse 24, a proof that this Letter was written during Paul's first imprisonment.

The Apostle thanks God in this Letter for the Faith and the perseverance of the Philippians; he speaks to them of his suffering, and of the fruit that his bonds produced; he makes known to them his faith and entire submission to God's

<column-break/>

will, whether he should live or whether he should die.

<margin>Philippians II. 6. 7.</margin>
He exhorts them to unity and humility through the example of Jesus Christ, who, <note>original: "geen roof hebbende geagt Gode evengelyk te zyn," a reference to the Greek 'harpagmos,' meaning he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized or clung to</note> did not consider it robbery to be equal to God, yet nevertheless emptied himself, having become obedient to his Father unto the Death of the Cross. He also exhorts them to rejoice in the Lord and to watch out for false Teachers, to value Jesus Christ and his Righteousness above all things, to strive for perfection, and to live as Citizens of Heaven; to remain steadfast, and to practice all things in which there is any virtue and praise; he ends his letter with Thanksgivings for their charity.

<margin>Of the Letter to the Colossians.</margin>
The letter to the Colossians was not written at the same time as the letter to the Philippians, but some time thereafter; although one cannot know the exact Year, it nonetheless appears that it was written from Rome.

<margin>What Colossae was.</margin>
Colossae was an Ancient City of Greater Phrygia, in Asia Minor, on the borders of Caria; it was later called <term>Konus</term> <note>now known as Chonae</note>, and it is to this city that <term>Nicetas Coniatus</term> <note>Nicetas Choniates, a famous 12th-century Byzantine historian</note>, one of the most renowned writers of the later times of Greece, owes his birth; he also boasts in one of his works that the Apostle had honored the inhabitants of the City of Konus with one of his letters.

The Congregation of Colossae was not founded by Paul: for it seems one can infer from Chapter II, verse 1, that he had never seen the Colossians: but rather by Archippus, Onesimus, Tychicus, and primarily by Epaphroditus and Epaphras.

That which prompted Paul to write this letter was that Epaphras, having come to Rome, made known to the Apostle the state in which this congregation then was, and as it stood exposed to the deception of many false Teachers, it needed instruction to remain standing.

He thanks God in this Letter for the faith and love of the Colossians, and prays to the Lord that he might pour out new Blessings upon them, and that he might strengthen them through his power. He then presents to them Jesus Christ, the dignity of his Person, and that which he has obtained for us through his death and through the preaching of the Gospel. After which he exhorts them to watch out for those who wished to seduce them and urged them to give some Religious Honor to the Angels

### DIVINITY. Book I. Chapter X.

...of Righteousness, which the Lord, the Righteous Judge, shall give me on that day: and not to me only, but also to all those who have loved his appearing. <note>original: "zyne verschyninge", referring to the Second Coming of Christ.</note>

<margin>The Letter to *Titus*.</margin>
Scholars do not agree on the time and the place where this letter was written. Some maintain that it was before, and others after, his arrival at his first imprisonment, around the same time as when he wrote the first letter to *Timothy*.

From Chapter III:12, it appears that it was written from *Nicopolis*; so says the subscription. <note>The "subscription" is a postscript found in some ancient manuscripts identifying the location of writing.</note> But one might possibly give another interpretation to this passage, and furthermore, there are several cities that have carried the name of *Nicopolis*.

Arguments are made to determine whether this refers to the City of *Nicopolis* located in the Empire—famous everywhere for the great naval battle in which *Augustus* achieved victory over *Mark Antony*—or one of those *Nicopolises* that were in *Thrace*. <note>The Battle of Actium (31 BCE) was fought near Nicopolis in Epirus.</note>

For the rest, this letter has much in common with the 1st to *Timothy*. *Paul*, having left *Titus* in *Crete*, wrote to him how he was to arrange his conduct and teaching there.

<margin>The Letter to *Philemon*.</margin>
The letter to *Philemon* was written by *Paul* during his first imprisonment. If one believes *Jerome* <note>original: "Hieronymus"</note>, *Philemon* was a man of distinction in the City of *Colossae*. The conversion of *Onesimus*, who was one of *Philemon's* slaves, gave the Apostle the occasion to write this letter. *Onesimus* had robbed his Master, but having embraced the Christian faith, he took refuge with *Paul*, who therefore requested *Philemon* to receive *Onesimus* and to forgive the crime.

<margin>The Letter to the *Hebrews*.</margin>
Among the letters of *Paul*, the one written to the *Hebrews* is also commonly placed under the Apostle’s Name, and it is also most probable that he is the Author of it, although by some it is attributed to *Luke*, by others to *Barnabas*, by others to *Clement*, by others to *Apollos*, and by some even to *Tertullian*.

<margin>Whether *Paul* wrote this Letter.</margin>
The *Greek* Fathers are of this opinion: *Justin*, *Clement of Alexandria*, the Fathers of the Council of *Laodicea*, *Eusebius* Bishop of *Alexandria*, *Athanasius*, *Ephrem*, *Didymus of Alexandria*, *Cyril of Jerusalem*,

<column-break/>

*Gregory of Nyssa*, *Basil*, *Gregory of Nazianzus*, *Antiochus*, *Epiphanius*, *Theophilus of Alexandria*, *Chrysostom*, etc. *Origen* <note>original: "Origines"</note> says that the thoughts are *Paul's*, but the manner of writing is someone else's. The *Arians* <note>A group of early Christians who held a non-traditional view of the nature of Christ.</note> rejected this letter with all stubbornness because it was entirely contrary to their new doctrine.

*Theodoret*, speaking of these Heretics, says that they should at least have respected the antiquity of this letter and noted that it had always been read in the Church; and against their opinion, he sets the testimony of *Eusebius of Caesarea*, whom they regarded as one of their heads.

The *Latin* Fathers, such as *Jerome*—as can be seen from many places in his writings—*Hilary*, *Ambrose*, *Augustine*, *Optatus*, etc. etc., agree in this matter with the *Greek* Fathers.

1. This opinion can be proven from 2 *Pet.* III:15, 16, where *Peter* mentions a certain letter written by *Paul* to those to whom he himself had written, who were none other than the scattered *Hebrews*, and in which letter he testifies that many things were hard to understand.

2. From the spirit and style of *Paul*, as well as from the mark by which he desired his Letters to be known: 2 *Thessal.* III:17, 18.

3. From the subscription of this Letter, as being written from *Italy*, where *Paul* stayed for a long time and died.

4. From what he mentions in *Hebr.* X:34 of his bonds, of which he also speaks many times elsewhere: *Philip.* I:13.

5. From the testimony that the Writer of this letter gives to *Timothy*, whom he recognizes as his Brother and traveling companion, in which one certainly discovers the Apostle *Paul*.

6. Finally, it is certain that one can attribute this Letter to no one with more probability than to *Paul*. Against this opinion, some objections are made, which are of no importance and can easily be refuted.

1. It is said that the Writer of this Letter cites the passages of the Old *Testament* not from the original *Hebrew Text*, but from the *Greek* translation of the *LXX* <note>The Septuagint, a Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible produced in the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE.</note>. This objection would have some force if this Letter had first been written in *Hebrew*, but as it was...

<margin>The first Letter to the Thessalonians.</margin>
The first letter to the Thessalonians is in all probability the first / that Paul wrote / in the Year 49, 52, or 54, from Athens, as the subscription indicates / or from Corinth.

It was written when Silvanus and Timothy were with Paul; as can be gathered from 1 Thess. 3:6 compared with Acts 18:5.

<margin>Thessalonica.</margin>
Thessalonica, which is now called Salonika <note>modern-day Thessaloniki, Greece</note> / was a City of Macedonia. Paul converted some Jews there / and many Heathens; But the persecution / that was raised against him there / forced him to depart quickly.

Having subsequently heard from Timothy the state of this fledgling congregation / he wrote this letter / and sent it with this dear disciple.

He praises in this letter the readiness / with which the Thessalonians had received the Gospel. He exalts their faith / their love / and their patience. He comforts them in their tribulations by the example of the Lord Christ, of the suffering Churches in Judea / and of himself. He exhorts them to the practice of holiness / charity / peace / and similar virtues / as well as to the moderation of the all too great sorrow / to which some gave themselves over the passing of their friends.

<margin>The second Letter to the Thessalonians.</margin>
The 2nd letter to the Thessalonians follows the first. Paul had two reasons (c) to write it. 1. Having understood / that they were being harshly persecuted / he found it necessary to comfort them. 2. And because the deceivers, taking occasion from what he had told them in his 1st letter (4:15), *We who will remain alive until the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who have fallen asleep*, had led them...

<column-break/>

...to take heart / that the day of the Lord was near / he exhorts them / not to give ear to these men. One finds in this letter an excellent description of the Antichrist.

<margin>First Letter to Timothy.</margin>
It is believed / that the 1st letter to Timothy was written by Paul / after his first imprisonment / when the Apostle passed into Phrygia; from the signature one also sees / that it was written from Laodicea; many doubt that, however.

To confirm this congregation / which Paul had founded / he had left Timothy in Ephesus; meanwhile the Apostle wrote him this letter / in which he exhorts him: 1. To oppose the course of the false teachings of some Jews / who wanted to be regarded as Teachers of the Law / though they did not understand the true use of it. 2. To establish Public Prayers for all kinds of Persons and States. 3. He describes the qualities / which are required / in an Overseer <note>original: "Opziender," often translated as Bishop</note> and Deacon. 4. He predicts the great apostasy / that would happen in the last times / of those who would forbid Marriage / and command the abstinence from foods / which God created for man. He warns him / that he must arm himself against all kinds of evil teachings / and prescribes him several useful rules of duty.

Two passages are found in this letter / which one should always reflect upon. The first is contained in the 16th verse of the 3rd Chapter: *Beyond all doubt the mystery of Godliness is great: God is revealed in the Flesh, is justified in the Spirit, is seen by the Angels, is Preached among the Gentiles, is believed in the World, is taken up into Glory.* The second in Chapter 6, verse 6: *Godliness is a great gain with contentment.*

<margin>The second Letter to Timothy.</margin>
There is much probability / that Paul wrote the second letter to Timothy a short time before his death in the Year of our Lord 66, 67, or 68.

This is gathered from his last words in 2 Tim. 4:6-8: *For I am now offered as a drink offering, and the time of my dissolution is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith, henceforth there is laid up for me the Crown...*

***

<margin>Whether it was written under Caligula.</margin>
(c) One must be willfully blind to dare to maintain that it was written under Caligula <note>original: "Kaligula"</note>, before the first Letter, since Paul in this second [letter] argues against those who had misunderstood the meaning of what he had written in the first.

### THEOLOGY. Book I. Chapter X.
G 3

> of righteousness, which the Lord,
> the righteous Judge, shall give me
> on that day: and not only to me, but also
> to all those who have loved His appearing.
<note>This is the conclusion of 2 Timothy 4:8, where Paul expresses his confidence in his heavenly reward as his life nears its end.</note>

<margin>The Epistle to Titus.</margin>
Scholars do not agree on the time and the place where this letter was written. Some believe it was before, and others after his first imprisonment in Rome, around the same time that he wrote the first letter to Timothy.

From Chapter III, verse 12, it appears that it was written from Nicopolis; so says the subscription <note>The "subscription" refers to the brief note at the end of many New Testament manuscripts indicating the letter's origin; these were added by later scribes and are not always historically accurate.</note>. But one could possibly give another interpretation to this passage; and furthermore, there are several cities that have borne the name of Nicopolis.

There is a dispute to know whether the city of Nicopolis mentioned here is the one located in the Empire—famous for the great naval battle in which Augustus achieved victory over Mark Antony <note>The Battle of Actium in 31 BCE, which led to the founding of Nicopolis in Epirus, Greece.</note>—or one of those Nicopolises that were in Thrace.

For the rest, this letter has much in common with the 1st to Timothy. Paul, having left Titus in Crete, wrote to him how he was to conduct himself and organize his teaching there.

<margin>The Epistle to Philemon.</margin>
The letter to Philemon was written by Paul during his first imprisonment. If one believes Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the scholar responsible for the Vulgate Latin Bible.</note>, Philemon was a man of distinction in the city of Colossae. The conversion of Onesimus, who was one of Philemon's slaves, gave the Apostle the opportunity to write this letter. Onesimus had robbed his Master, but having embraced the Christian faith, he took refuge with Paul, who therefore requested Philemon to receive Onesimus and forgive the crime.

<margin>The Epistle to the Hebrews.</margin>
Among the letters of Paul, the one written to the Hebrews is also commonly placed under the Apostle’s name, and it is also most probable that he is the author of it, although it is attributed by some to Luke, by others to Barnabas, by others to Clement, by others to Apollos, and by some even to Tertullian.

<margin>Whether Paul wrote this Letter.</margin>
The Greek Fathers are of this opinion: Justin, Clement of Alexandria, the Fathers of the Council of Laodicea, Eusebius Bishop of Alexandria, Athanasius, Ephrem, Didymus of Alexandria, Cyril of Jerusalem,

<column-break/>

Gregory of Nyssa, Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, Antiochus, Epiphanius, Theophilus of Alexandria, Chrysostom, etc. Origen says that the thoughts are Paul's, but the manner of writing is by another. The Arians <note>A group of early Christians who followed the teachings of Arius, who argued that Jesus Christ was a created being and not co-eternal with God the Father.</note> rejected this letter with all obstinacy because it was entirely contrary to their new doctrine.

Theodoret, speaking of these heretics, says that they should at least have respected the antiquity of this letter and noted that it had always been read in the Church; and against their opinion, he sets the testimony of Eusebius of Caesarea, whom they regarded as one of their leaders.

The Latin Fathers—such as Jerome (as can be seen from many places in his writings), Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, Optatus, etc., etc.—agree on this point with the Greek Fathers.

1. This opinion can be proven from 2 Peter III, verses 15 and 16, where Peter mentions a certain letter written by Paul to those to whom he himself had written—who were none other than the scattered Hebrews—and in which letter he testifies that many things were hard to understand.

2. From the spirit and style of Paul, as well as from the mark by which he desired his Letters to be recognized in 2 Thessalonians III, verses 17 and 18.

3. From the subscription of this Letter, as being written from Italy, where Paul stayed for a long time and died.

4. From what he mentions in Hebrews X, verse 34, regarding his bonds, which he also speaks of many times elsewhere, such as in Philippians I, verse 13.

5. From the testimony that the writer of this letter gives to Timothy, whom he acknowledges as his Brother and traveling companion, in which one certainly discovers the Apostle Paul.

6. Finally, it is certain that one can attribute this Letter to no one with more probability than to Paul. Against this opinion, some objections are made, which are of no importance and can be easily refuted.

1. It is said that the writer of this Letter quotes the passages of the Old Testament not from the original Hebrew Text, but from the Greek translation of the LXX <note>original: "LXX" / The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures.</note>. This objection would have some force if this Letter had first been written in Hebrew; but if it was...

<column-break/>

was—that it cannot be proven—one could answer that the Greek translator placed the passages of the Old Testament in his translation according to the version of the **Septuagint** <note>original: "LXX"; the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>, which was then in use. **II.** It is said that there is a great difference regarding the style of writing between this and the other Epistles of Paul, but one can prove the opposite with many reasons. Those who wish for **Luke** to be the author attempt to show this through the similarity of expressions found in **Acts 3:15, 5:31** and **Hebrews 2:10, 12:2**; **Acts 14:12, 15:22** and **Hebrews 13:7, 17, 24**; **Acts 15:20, 21:25** and **Hebrews 13:22**. But who does not know that various writers can use the same expressions, and that one finds such a similarity in writing among all the Holy Writers? **III.** It is said that Paul would not have hidden his name if this Letter were his; but, rather than saying with **Theodoret** <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–458 AD), an influential theologian and bishop</note> that Paul, writing to the Hebrews, did not express his name because he was sent only to the Gentiles, it seems to me that one can answer that he did not mention his name because he knew he was hated among the Hebrews. **IV.** It is said that the author of this Letter seems to support the opinion of the **Novatians** <note>A rigorist sect that believed those who committed serious sins after baptism could not be readmitted to the Church</note> in the 6th Chapter, verses 4 and 6; at least it is certain that these heretics used this passage to support their errors. But those who throw this against us do not understand this passage.

<margin>Simon, Critical History of the N.T. ch. 16.</margin>
We shall explain this elsewhere and show that the error of the Novatians by no means appears there. It is not necessary here to bring up the solution of a modern critical researcher who cites an old translation of this passage, made before the time of **Jerome** <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the translator of the Latin Vulgate</note>, in which, instead of what the Text says, "*it is impossible*", one reads "*it is difficult*" to be renewed again unto repentance; for however old this translation may be, it does not have enough authority to override all the Greek manuscripts.

<column-break/>

<margin>When this Letter was written.</margin>
The time in which this letter was written cannot be well determined. Some are of the opinion that it was during his first imprisonment, others after he was set on his feet <note>meaning after his release or during his travels</note>. Paul's intention therein is to prove that **Christ** is the end, the foundation, the body, and the truth of all the shadows of the Law.

He exalts the Lord Christ above the Angels, above **Moses**, and above the Priests of the old dispensation.

He deals extensively with the Priesthood of our Savior, and clearly shows that the old covenant had to make way for another that is eternal; likewise, that all the ceremonies of the law had to be abolished by the coming of Christ.

One also finds in this Letter excellent exhortations to charity and good works, to perseverance and faith, the nature and wonderful effects of which he describes. He exhorts everyone to follow all the holy Men who lived before the coming of the Messiah—principally the Lord Christ himself, who is the author and finisher of faith—in order to thus practice patience, holiness, brotherly love, charity, steadfastness, and all other virtues.

For the rest, it is not necessary that I mention the conversion of Paul, his life, and his death. One finds the account of it in the Book of the **Acts of the Apostles**, and one can look up further circumstances in his Epistles. Everyone knows that he was beheaded under the reign of the Godless **Nero** (d).

We can [respond] to the thoughts (k) of those who wish...

---

The common opinion is that he was crucified with his head downward, just as he himself had requested. Many fictions have been brought forward regarding this, which are too long to be recounted. One cannot say with certainty that he was crucified.

(i) Many understand **Rome** by this, which is named thus in the **Revelation** <note>The Book of Revelation/Apocalypse</note>. But others do not see for what reason Peter would not have expressed the name of Rome, since Paul explicitly names that city in all his Letters. It is true that John gives this Great City the name of **Babel** in the Revelation, but he did this because it is a Prophetic Book, in which it is necessary to speak with hidden words.

(k) **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian</note> was of this opinion, because in this Letter the total destruction of the world, which was expected by the Christians of that time, is spoken of. Now it is certain, he says, that no Christian expected this destruction except after the devastation of the **Jewish Commonwealth**. But this opinion has no basis, and the reason brought for it does not hold up. The first Christians expected the downfall of the Jewish state and believed that it would be followed by the general destruction of the world.

<margin>How we know</margin>
One asks, how do we know that the New Testament is the work of the Apostles?

We shall in the following bring forth the proofs we have for the Divine authority of the Books of the Old and New Testaments, and here only say that there is no Book in the World whose authors one cannot put in doubt or question, if one can doubt that the Books of the Old and New Testaments are by those to whom they are attributed according to a steadfast tradition. When the Manichaeans <note>A dualistic religious movement</note> asked the Christians how one knew that the New Testament was the work of the Apostles and their Disciples, *Augustine* asked them (*Augustine against Faustus, book 33, ch. 6*) how one knew that the Books said to be by *Homer*, *Virgil*, and *Cicero* were truly by these Writers? and by what did they themselves know that the *Letter of the Foundation* was the work of *Mani*?

Furthermore, the writers who wrote shortly thereafter cited them under those same names. The Christian Churches spread everywhere have recognized most of these Books to be written by those whose names they bear; and these Books do not have the slightest sign of forgery. In the beginning, one had the original writings of the Apostles, which the congregations carefully preserved, and to which one could have recourse. *Tertullian*, even in his time, sent those who doubted to the Congregations of Rome, Corinth, etc., because there one found the copies <note>likely referring to the original manuscripts or direct transcripts</note> of Paul.

## CHAPTER XII.

->Of the Divinity of the Books of Holy Scripture.<-

We have seen which are the Books of the Old and New Testament; but because one might doubt their Divinity <note>In this context, "Divinity" refers to the divine origin or inspired authority of the texts</note>, it is necessary to provide proof for them.

In order to lay out this matter clearly, there are only two things to do. 1. We must see what the marks are that must be found in Books of divine inspiration to distinguish them from human books. 2. We must then examine whether these marks are found in the Books we spoke of in the previous Chapter.

<margin>By what can one recognize a Divine Book?</margin>Certainly, the more I reflect on this matter, the more I find that one cannot keep oneself from recognizing them as Divine Books.

1. Books that contain nothing but truth, for God is truth itself.
2. Books that, in all they teach, lift us up toward God.
3. Books *whose commandments are all Holy, and which stir us up to love God in the highest degree, and to forsake all that can displease Him.*
4. Books that teach us everything we must know to be happy.
5. Books whose parts all harmonize wonderfully, such that one notices no contradiction in them.
6. Books that teach us all that can quiet the stirrings of our soul, all that could comfort her, make her terrors disappear, and all that is capable of Sanctifying her.

<column-break/>

7. Books that agree very well with the light of the conscience.
8. Books in which one finds mysteries that no man could ever have invented, and which are above, but not against, reason; which also harmonize with the other truths we understand, even with the most certain principles of natural religion.
9. Books that contain a great number of Prophecies and predictions that have had their fulfillment.
10. Books that have been wonderfully preserved, even though nothing was spared in the effort to destroy them.
11. Books that are confirmed by many miracles, and sealed by many martyrs <note>original: "bloedgetuigen," literally "blood-witnesses"</note>.
12. Books that, in a short time, converted almost the entire world.
13. Books written in such a way that one perceives no artificial ornamentation in them: but rather a Noble Simplicity, joined with a great Majesty.
14. Books, finally, that are highly esteemed even by those who have most opposed them.

Let one now gather all these marks together; if the book in which one finds them all is not Divine, I do not know what one shall call Divine. I confess that there are some among these marks that can be found in human books: but there are those that one will not find therein, far from discovering them all there together.

Let us now examine whether the books of the Old and New Testament have these aforementioned marks. But, before we proceed to this examination, it is necessary to make this observation: that we view all these books, which we have dealt with in the preceding Chapters, as one book that was written at various intervals, by various persons, in various times. I note this so that one does not look for all the mentioned marks of Divinity in every single part of this great work: one must not think that one will find the same loftiness in the books that are purely Historical as in the books containing Doctrines; for example, in the History of Ruth as in the letters of Paul. All heavenly lights do not shine with the same brilliance in the firmament.

After having made this general observation, I request all Christians to take note.

# XII. CHAPTER.
## Of the Divinity of the Books of the Holy Scripture.

We have seen which are the Books of the Old and New Testament; but because one might doubt their Divinity, it must be proven.

To lay out this subject clearly, there are only two things to do. 1. One must see what the marks are that must be found in books of divine inspiration to distinguish them from human books. 2. One must then examine whether these marks are found in the Books we spoke of in the preceding Chapter.

<margin>By what can one recognize a Divine Book?</margin>
1. Books that contain nothing but truth, for God is truth itself.
2. Books that, in all they teach, lead us up to God.
3. Books whose commandments are all Holy, and which stir us up to love God in the highest degree and to forsake all that can displease Him.
4. Books that teach us everything we must know to be happy <note>In this context, "happy" refers to eternal blessedness or salvation.</note>.
5. Books whose parts all wonderfully agree, such that one notices no contradiction in them.
6. Books that teach us everything that can quiet the stirrings of our soul, or what could comfort her, make her terrors disappear, and everything capable of Sanctifying her.

<column-break/>

7. Books that agree very well with the light of the conscience.
8. Books in which one finds mysteries that no man could ever have invented, and which are above, but not against, reason; which also harmonize with the other truths we understand, even with the surest principles of natural Religion.
9. Books that contain a great number of Prophecies and predictions that have had their fulfillment.
10. Books that have been wonderfully preserved, although nothing was left undone in the attempt to destroy them.
11. Books that are confirmed by many miracles and sealed by many martyrs <note>The original Dutch uses "bloedgetuigen," literally "blood-witnesses."</note>.
12. Books that, in a short time, converted almost the entire world.
13. Books written in such a way that one perceives no artificial adornment in them, but rather a Noble Simplicity joined with a great Majesty.
14. Finally, books that are highly esteemed even by those who have most contested them.

Let one now gather all these marks together; if the book in which one finds them all is not Divine, I do not know what one shall call Divine. I confess that there are some among these marks that can be found in human books: but there are those that one will not find therein, far from discovering them all together.

Let us now examine whether the books of the Old and New Testament have these aforementioned marks. But before we proceed to this examination, it is necessary to make this observation: that we view all these books, of which we have treated in the preceding Chapters, as one book that was written at various intervals, by various persons, in various times. I note this so that one does not seek all the mentioned marks of Divinity in every single part of this great work: one must not think that one will find the same loftiness in the books that are purely Historical as in the books containing the Doctrines—for example, in the History of Ruth as in the Epistles of Paul. All heavenly lights do not shine with the same radiance in the firmament.

After having made this general observation, I request all Christians to take note.

## CHAPTER XII.

->On the Divinity of the Books of Holy Scripture.<-

We have seen which are the Books of the Old and New Testament, but because their Divinity could be doubted, one must prove them.

To clearly explain this subject, there are only two things to do. 1. One must see what signs must be found in Books of Divine inspiration to distinguish them from human Books. 2. One must then examine whether these signs are found in the Books we spoke of in the preceding Chapter.

<margin>How can one recognize a Divine Book?</margin>
Certainly, the more I reflect on this matter, the more I find that one cannot help but recognize them as Divine Books.
1. Books that contain nothing but truth, for God is truth itself.
2. Books that, in all they teach, lead us up to God.
3. Books whose commandments are all Holy, and which stir us to love God most highly and to forsake all that may displease Him.
4. Books that teach us everything we must know to be happy <note>In this context, "happy" refers to eternal blessedness or salvation.</note>.
5. Books whose parts all match wonderfully, so that one notices no contradiction in them.
6. Books that teach us everything that can quiet the stirrings of our soul, everything that could comfort her, make her terrors disappear, and everything capable of Sanctifying her.

<column-break/>

7. Books that agree very well with the light of conscience.
8. Books in which one finds mysteries that no man could ever have invented, and which are above, but not against reason; which also connect with the other truths we understand, even with the surest principles of natural Religion <note>Natural religion refers to truths about God that can be discovered through reason and nature without supernatural revelation.</note>.
9. Books containing a great number of Prophecies and predictions that have had their fulfillment.
10. Books that have been wonderfully preserved, though nothing was left undone to destroy them.
11. Books confirmed by many miracles and sealed by many martyrs <note>Original: "bloedgetuigen," literally "blood-witnesses."</note>.
12. Books that, in a short time, converted nearly the whole world.
13. Books written in such a way that no artificiality <note>Original: "opgesmuktheid," meaning overly ornate or deceptive rhetorical flourishes.</note> is perceived in them: but a Noble Simplicity joined with a great Majesty.
14. Finally, Books that are highly esteemed even by those who have most opposed them.

Now gather all these signs together; if the book in which one finds them all is not Divine, I do not know what one shall call Divine. I confess that there are signs among these that can be found in human Books: but there are some that one will not find therein, far from discovering them all there together.

Let us now examine if the books of the Old and New Testament have these aforementioned signs. But, before we proceed to this examination, it is necessary to make this observation: that we view all these books, which we have treated in the preceding Chapters, as one book written at various intervals, by various persons, in various times. I note this so that one does not seek all the mentioned signs of Divinity in every part of this great work: one must not think that one will find the same loftiness in books that are purely Historical as in the books containing the Doctrines—for example, in the History of Ruth as in the letters of Paul. Not all heavenly lights shine with the same radiance in the firmament.

After having made this general observation, I request all Christians to take note.

<header>THE CHRISTIAN [RELIGION]</header>

<margin>
That all which is contained in the Holy Books is true. And 1. that which is contained in the Books of *Moses*.
</margin>

Firstly, there are countless reasons that convince us of the truth of all things contained in the Holy Books.

One could not suspect the things that *Moses* relates in the five books that bear his name of any falsehood without accusing this great Lawgiver of being the greatest deceiver who has ever been in the world. But one will not be able to hold these unjust thoughts of this excellent man if one makes the following observations:

1. It is incredible that *Moses*, if he had been such a great deceiver, would have given such a perfect and Holy law to men—a law that does not permit the slightest <unclear>sin</unclear>, and which condemns all evil thoughts and guilty desires. One must at least admit that a deceiver has never been seen making such excellent laws.

2. It is even more incredible that *Moses* would have dared to spread stories among the people of *Israel* of whose falsehood he could have been convicted and put to shame. Is it possible that he would have told them that he had turned his staff into a snake before *Pharaoh* in *Egypt*; that the rivers turned to blood; that frogs entered the houses; that the *Egyptian* fields were devastated by hail and locusts; that darkness covered the whole land except for *Goshen*; that the firstborn of the *Egyptians* were killed in one night, but the *Israelites* were miraculously preserved; that the waters of the *Red Sea* were divided and made a double wall to let the *Israelites* pass through, and that they had lured *Pharaoh* with his army into it; that they had lived for forty years on food descended from Heaven; that he, with one strike of his staff, had made a spring gush from a rock, sufficient to quench the thirst of more than six hundred thousand people; that *God* had given them His Law on a mountain in the midst of lightning and fire; that the Earth had swallowed people before their eyes, and fire consumed those who had tried to oppose his ministry, and other such wonderful things? Is it possible that *Moses* would have related such things if they had been false, and that he would have used them as motives

<column-break/>

to urge the people of *Israel* to love and fear *God*? Is it possible that he would have proposed fictions as the foundation of his laws and Religion? Would he have brought forth lies and chosen as his judges the eyes and ears of more than six hundred thousand people? And would he have taken them as witnesses in things where the contrary could so easily have been shown?

3. One has no less difficulty understanding why, among such a large population, no one was found who contradicted the deceits and false miracles of *Moses*. If *Moses* had indeed been a deceiver and what he proposed was false—can one believe that a people who so often rose up against him, and whom he reproached for their failings and ingratitude, would not have put him to shame on account of so many fabricated tales?

4. One does not see to what end or with what purpose *Moses* would have invented all these things. Was it to obtain honor or wealth? It does not appear that he sought honor or profit. One does not see that he tried to promote his friends or give them dominion. Too much sincerity and boldness shines through in his actions and writing; he does not hide his own faults, nor his neglect in circumcising his son, nor his lack of faith <note>original: "ongeloovigheid"</note> for which *God* cast him out of the promised land. He even brings up the crime of *Levi*, the head of his tribe <note>This refers to the violent episode involving the Shechemites in Genesis 34, which Moses recorded despite Levi being his own ancestor.</note>.

5. If what *Moses* says is but a fiction, where does it come from that for such a long time among the *Jewish* people the memorials of the things *Moses* describes were seen? Such as *Aaron's* staff, which had blossomed in one night; the *Manna*, which was kept in a golden jar; the bronze serpent, which remained until the time of *Hezekiah* <note>King Hezekiah eventually destroyed the bronze serpent because the people began to worship it as an idol.</note>; the stone Tables on which the law was written; the ceremony of the *Passover*, which reminded the *Israelites* of their departure from *Egypt* and the wonders *God* had done to pull them out of their slavery; the *Pentecost* <note>The Feast of Weeks, celebrating the giving of the Law at Sinai.</note>, which made them think of the manner in which *God* had given them His Law on Mount *Sinai*; the Feast of Tabernacles <note>original: "loverhutten-feest"</note>, by which they kept a memory of their stay in the wilderness; and the separation *God* made of the tribe of *Levi* to hallow them for Himself instead of—

# DIVINE THEOLOGY. Book I. Chapter XII.

...of Israel’s firstborn, whom he had preserved in Egypt, and many other such things.

<margin>Memorials in the writings of the Pagans concerning the histories told by Moses.</margin>
5 Not only are these memorials found among the Jewish people, but also among other nations. Scholars note that the history of Adam and Noah gave rise to the fable of Saturn <note>The Roman god of agriculture and time, often identified with the Greek Cronus</note>. The poets say that Saturn was a son of Heaven and Earth; that under his reign the Golden Age flourished, and all men were free. Who does not perceive Adam in this, created from the Earth by the God of Heaven, and the state of uprightness <note>the "Status Integritatis" or state before the Fall</note> in which he found himself? The Pagan writers relate that Saturn taught the use of wine and the cultivation of vineyards; that the feast of Saturnalia was given to excess and drunkenness; that one cannot view the deities naked without being punished; that Saturn and his wife Rhea were descended from Oceanus and Thetis; and that the symbol of Saturn’s arrival was a ship; that Saturn had devoured all his children except three: who does not see in this, through a disguise, the history of Noah? The testimonies of Alexander Polyhistor and those of Abydenus <note>Ancient historians whose works survive only in fragments quoted by others</note> can be added to this, as brought forward by Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria</note> writing against Julian the Apostate; these say that Xisutrus <note>A hero in Mesopotamian mythology similar to Noah</note>, King of Assyria, escaped the Flood that Saturn had predicted to him by throwing himself, according to his counsel, into an Ark with all sorts of beasts; that he sailed to Armenia and released some birds to know if the waters had subsided from above the Ark. It is also believed that the Wrath of the Aloadae <note>In Greek myth, giants who tried to storm heaven by piling mountains</note>, of which Homer speaks, is taken from the Tower of Babel.

<margin>Homer, *Odyssey*, book 11, verse 306. Origen, *Against Celsus*, Cambridge edition, 174.</margin>
Scholars also find wonderful similarities between the history of Noah and the fable of Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto, the three sons of Saturn. Others have believed that the Janus of the Pagans, and their Prometheus, as well as their Bacchus, was actually Noah.

As for the history of Moses, it is claimed that it is disguised under the story of Bacchus, to whom Orpheus gave the name of Mizes <note>A name likely derived from the Greek word for "Moses"</note> and of Lawgiver, and whom he said was born from the waters; to whom was attributed the power of having struck a rock and caused water to come forth from it, and even of having dried up the river Hydaspes. Others believe, however, that 

<column-break/>

Nimrod is the Bacchus and Mars of the Pagans. If we believe Epiphanius (Heresies, XVIII), then the memory of the deliverance from the bondage of Egypt was preserved among the Egyptians until the coming of Christ; for on the eve of Passover, they marked their sheep, trees, fields, and houses with vermilion red <note>This likely refers to a pagan echo of the blood smeared on the lintels during the original Passover</note>.

6 Finally, it is certain that even the Pagans have given excellent praises to Moses.

<margin>Praise given by the Pagans to Moses.</margin>
Diodorus Siculus says that he had learned from the Egyptians that Moses was the first and most excellent of all lawmakers, and that he was a man full of courage and of a praiseworthy life. Porphyry, one of the greatest enemies the Jews and Christians ever had, says in one of his books that Moses wrote the histories of the Jewish people very faithfully, and that he had discovered this by comparing his writings with those of Sanchoniathon of Berytus <note>Beirut</note>, who was a historian of Phoenicia and who, in the judgment of some scholars, lived in the time of Gideon. Many things are also found in the writings of the Pagans that are similar to what the Holy History of Moses relates to us.

<margin>Book 4, Cambridge edition, page 184.</margin>
Origen, arguing against Celsus (a great enemy of the Jews and Christians), confronts him with the fact that the Egyptians used these words in their exorcisms: *the God of Israel, the God of the Hebrews, the God who caused the Egyptians and their King to drown in the Red Sea.* This shows that the truth of this historical account was not doubted. Eusebius says (*Preparation for the Gospel*, Book IX) that the Egyptians had consecrated a staff in their temples because of the staff that Moses used, to which they paid the same divine worship as they did to Isis. Numenius, a Pythagorean philosopher, speaks explicitly of Jannes and Jambres, the Egyptian Sages <note>the magicians</note> who opposed Moses (whom he calls Musaeus). It would be easy to add other testimonies to these.

But some will say: perhaps the Jews assisted in the trickery of Moses to attract the admiration of other nations? But this is absurd. 1. Who can imagine that a people so difficult to govern would subject themselves to a Law brought forth by a single man, and allow themselves to be punished with death for its violation? 2. Who can believe that five or six hundred thousand people could agree in such a way, without any one of them...

or if their descendants' accounts contradicted one another. 
3. Was that not the way to make themselves ridiculous before other nations, instead of making them respected? For what would the Egyptians have said of all the plagues with which God struck them, according to Moses’ account; of the death of all their firstborn; of the drowning of Pharaoh’s army in the waters of the Red Sea, if this entire story was trivial <note>original: "beuzelachtig," meaning frivolous or nonsensical</note>? Finally, can one believe that if the people of Israel had consented to Moses’ deception in order to be respected by other nations, they would have allowed Moses to describe their rebellions, mutinies, ingratitude, and God’s judgments poured out over them?

What I have said of Moses’ books can very well be applied to the other historical books, and one can use some of the same arguments already brought forward. I will now be satisfied with adding these two things to them.

1. That all these books have a wonderful connection with one another: the events that preceded are very well joined with those that follow.

<margin>The book of Ruth.</margin>
The book of Ruth, which seems to have nothing remarkable except the conversion of Ruth the Moabitess, nevertheless contains two significant matters. 1. A precise observance of the Law which Moses had proclaimed regarding the necessity of marrying the widow of a relative who died without children <note>This refers to the "Levirate law" (from the Latin 'levir,' meaning brother-in-law), where a man was obligated to provide an heir for a deceased kinsman</note>.

2. The genealogy of David, whom the author of this story shows to be born from a Moabite woman; which certainly does not give much honor to a King of Israel, but establishes the truth of the events contained in this book.

2. The second matter which I add is that although the people of God lived separated from other nations, such that their neighbors had very little knowledge of their history, one nevertheless finds among the Pagan historians and poets several stories which show that many incidents mentioned by the Holy Writers were known to them.

<margin>Memorials of Joshua's history etc. in the writings of the Pagans.</margin>
The memory of Joshua and his victories was famous among the Pagans, as appears from what Procopius relates <note>Procopius, *History of the Vandalic War*, book 2, chapter 10. He mentions an ancient inscription in North Africa regarding those fleeing from the face of "Joshua the Robber"</note>; and it is very probable that the fiction of the Phoenician Hercules, the destruction of the giants, and the famous Typhon, owes its 

<column-break/>

origin to the History of Joshua, to the destruction of Og, King of Bashan, and the Anakim <note>A race of giants mentioned in the Old Testament</note>, who bore the name of giants. The memory of the deeds of Gideon is preserved by Sanchoniathon <note>A Phoenician author whose works are known through later fragments</note>. The history of Iphigenia <note>A daughter of King Agamemnon in Greek myth, sacrificed or nearly sacrificed to Artemis</note> is probably taken from Jephthah’s daughter. The story of Samson, which had passed into Italy by means of the Phoenicians, was possibly the origin of the Feast celebrated at Rome in the month of April. This was the time of the harvest in Judea, but not in Italy; in this Feast, they let foxes loose with lit torches tied to them <note>The Cerealia festival, where foxes with torches were released in the Circus Maximus, mirroring Samson's actions against the Philistines in Judges 15</note>. The Pagans have appropriated many things said of Samson for their own Hercules: the Delilah of Samson is not poorly imitated by the Omphale of Hercules.

Nicolaus of Damascus <note>A friend of Herod the Great and a prolific historian</note> (as cited in Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, book VII, chapter 6) brings forward the account of the Kings of Syria in almost the same way as the Holy Historians relate it; as also the reign of Tiglath-Pileser, who is believed to have been Ninus the younger. There is much agreement in the manner in which the Pagans relate the history of Sennacherib, the capture of Nineveh and Babylon, and the death of Belshazzar, with that which has been provided by the Holy Writers.

This similarity shows the accuracy and faithfulness with which these Divine Writers have written. I shall say no more to prove the truth of the books of the Old Testament. I proceed to those of the New.

III. Finally, that, even if they had wanted to deceive, they would not have been able to do so.

<margin>That the Apostles could not have been deceived.</margin>
I. One will be convinced that they were not deceived if one makes the following observations. 1. There is no reason to think that their imagination was confused: for one sees in all their behavior, and especially in their writings, a wonderful wisdom shining through. 2. They gave testimony of things that fall under the senses <note>The author is using an empirical argument: the events were physical and observable, not merely spiritual "feelings."</note>, and in which one cannot understand how one could be deceived, such as of healed sick people, of raised dead, and above all of the resurrection of their Master, with whom they had associated for several years. 3. They testified to what they had seen, not from afar, but from nearby and at a proper distance. 4. They used not just one of their senses to judge that which they testify, but many—indeed, the senses by which a living person can be judged, such as eyes, ears, and hands. 5. Finally, they used these senses many times; having interacted with Jesus Christ for 40 days after his resurrection, during which time they saw this Divine Savior move, speak, and live; they observed the features of his face, placed their hands in his pierced side, saw the signs of his wounds, and heard him speak with them, as before, of the mysteries of the Kingdom of Heaven.

One cannot say that they were misled by illusions <note>original: "beguichelingen," referring to conjuring or sleight of hand</note>, by enchantments, or that it was the Devil who deceived their senses and caused them to make a false judgment through his seductions; for it is absolutely ridiculous in this case to bring in the Devil, since the entire dispensation of the Gospel of Christ, which is grounded on the truth of his resurrection, serves to destroy the kingdom of the Devil; not to mention that those who make objections about these matters seem little convinced of the existence or presence of Devils. Moreover, how could one suppose that the Apostles could have deceived themselves regarding the gifts of the Spirit which they testified to have received? Did they not perceive that they spoke foreign languages, that they understood them, and that they performed true miracles?

<column-break/>

It would be impious to say that God or the good Angels misled the senses of the Apostles; for that conflicts with God's wisdom, Holiness, and truth, and with the purity, faithfulness, and sincerity of the good Angels.

II. One will be convinced that the Apostles did not artfully and maliciously intend to deceive other people, if one observes:

<margin>That the Apostles did not intend to deceive.</margin>
1. That the Apostles were people who had an aversion to the craftiness and trickery of the world; poor Fishermen, Tax Collectors, Tentmakers—people of a low birth. What likelihood is there that such as these would have been capable of forging the design of maliciously deceiving the entire world?

2. No one among the enemies of the Christians has denounced them as corrupt people; on the contrary, one sees much sincerity, love toward their neighbors, and piety toward God shining through in their writings. What likelihood is there, then, that they had such a foul intention of deceiving the whole human race?

3. One could not bring forward a single reason that could have incited the Apostles to lie. As humans are natured, they undertake nothing except toward a certain end: for, to deceive solely for the pleasure of deceiving, one must be the foulest rogue in the highest degree. What objective could the Apostles then have had? Is it for Wealth, Honor, or status—three great motivators that set men in motion? But the Apostles knew that their teaching would cause them a thousand difficulties, persecutions, insults, punishment, and a shameful death.

4. On the contrary, there are many reasons that should have restrained them from lying; the preservation of their peace and life strongly obligated them to that. That a deceived man is taken with a lie in such a way—which he powerfully believes to be a truth—that he even maintains it at the risk of his life and contempt for all sorts of pains, can easily be understood: but that a man, who knows in his conscience that he is deceiving the world, loves his knavery and deception more than his life, is perhaps a matter without precedent.

5. Is it to be believed that the Apostles would have wanted to die for Jesus Christ if he had not in fact risen? For he would have miserably deceived them; and

6. How can it be that none of the Apostles or Disciples betrayed the secret, being challenged by their conscience, by the innate respect one has for the truth, by the dignity of the tribunals <note>The "tribunals" refers to the Roman and Jewish courts where the Apostles were tried.</note> before which they appeared, and by the terrifying thought of bringing the hatred of the whole world upon themselves?

7. How is it possible that they testify in such a consistent manner?

8. If they were deceivers, how did they—with such foul and treacherous souls—establish such a pure and Holy Religion, which so powerfully condemns lies?

9. If their testimony is false, where does it come from that the old prophecies agree so well with their deception, and that one even finds records in the writings of the Heathens <note>The author uses "Heathen" to refer to non-Christian Greek and Roman historians like Tacitus or Josephus.</note> that confirm what the Apostles said?

10. The Apostles do not write in such a way that one could judge from it that they intended to deceive. They include things that immediately give offense to worldly people, and which ungodly men use to attack the Christian Religion: they do not hide the humility <note>In this context, "humility" refers to the lowly status and perceived weakness of Jesus's earthly life and crucifixion.</note> of their Master, nor their own flaws; their birth; the dispute that arose among them to know who would be the greatest in the Kingdom of the Messiah; their ignorance in many things; their cowardice which made them flee when men came to capture their Master; their unbelief, etc. They do not adapt themselves to the inclinations of the nations; they powerfully oppose the traditions of the Jews and the Religion of the Heathens, and will not suffer the Gospel to be mixed with the Law <term>Law: The Mosaic Law or Torah</term>, or that the Mosaic ceremonies be maintained; they do not spare the corruption of Men; they do not seek the formal arguments of the eloquence of the time. They do not think to tickle the ears of their listeners, nor to satisfy their passions. Is it in such a way that people who had set out to mislead the world would have gone to work?

<margin>
That they could not have deceived.
</margin>

III. But the Apostles not only did not *want* to deceive us, it is also certain that, even had they wanted to, they would not have been *able* to do so; for they relate things that had many witnesses, and which were done in the presence of countless people. How would they have dared to bring forward things of which it was easy to convict them and cause them to be seen as dishonorable deceivers?

<margin>
Objections against the truth of the history of the N. T.
</margin>

It appears then that the Histories of the Old and New Testament are true: for I do not see what weighty matter one can bring against all our proofs. Will it be said that one can have no certainty of a matter that is so far from our time? But it is certain that one can give very clear proofs of things that happened many centuries before, matters that will not allow us to deny them; and that there is much less reason to doubt the account of the Holy Scripture than all those we have from the Greeks and Romans; so that one must either doubt everything or accept the Holy Books. Will it be said that these books were written in a time in which they could be refuted? But 1. it clearly appears that they were written in a time in which there were many thousands of people who could have convicted those who wrote them of falsehood. 2. One could suppose no time in which these books were written where they could not have been refuted, if all the accounts they contain were false. Will it be said that, if everything these books teach were true, the foreign writers would have confirmed the testimony of the Apostles with their own testimony? But can it be denied that the Heathen writers spoke of the Christians, even though they said false things about them? And is it not certain that they confirmed many accounts found in the writings of the Apostles?

The truth of the Holy books cannot then be contradicted. And this is the first mark that one must find in the Divine Scriptures. Let us proceed to the second.
