# DIVINITY <note>original: "GOD-GELEERTHEID"</note>. I. B. XIV. CHAPTER.

## CHAPTER XIV.

### Continuation of the Proofs of the Divinity of the Books of the Old and New Testaments.

<margin>Second proof of the Divinity of the Holy Scriptures, taken from the fact that they lead us to God in everything they teach.</margin>
I 1. **I** take my Second proof for the Divinity of the Books of the Old and New Testament from this: that in everything they teach, they lead us to God.

To be convinced of this truth, one has only to read them. It is evident that all they contain is written to make us highly esteem God’s greatness, His infinite power, incomprehensible wisdom, unwavering goodness, terrifying justice, all His perfections, and the wonders of His providence; to obligate us to love Him most highly and above all things, to submit our will entirely to Him, never to murmur against His commands, to give Him all our desires and affections, to even sacrifice ourselves to Him, to contribute everything to His Glory, to give the Honor and service worthy of Him and which He commands; to place all our trust in Him, to fear His judgments, to take our refuge in Him through our prayers; and finally, to glorify Him through our words, thoughts, works, and through all the movements of our bodies and faculties of our souls.

They represent God to us as the most perfect of all Beings, as the supreme Ruler of the world, as the first truth, as our great Lawgiver, the almighty commander of all outcomes, the beginning and cause of all good; as the Judge of Angels and Men, as the ultimate end of all things, and as our highest good: in a word, exactly as one would suppose God would have presented Himself, had He wished to make Himself known.

One cannot read these Books without noticing that they not only erase from our minds everything that is against God’s Glory—as we shall see in the following—but that they also contain everything that can exalt this Glory. God does everything there, and Man does nothing that is good except through the help of God. If there is talk of any victory by the Israelites, it is God who makes them conquer; if they lose any battle, it is God
<sig>Part I.</sig>

<column-break/>

who chastens them: if Sennacherib was forced to break off the siege of Jerusalem, it is because the Angel of the Lord defeated the army of this impious Prince. Everything that is great, excellent, and useful is entirely attributed to God; I do not see how one can hide from seeing therein a second mark of the Divinity of the Books of the Old and N. Testament.

<margin>Holiness of the commandments.</margin>
III. The Holiness of the commandments found in these books, and the excellence of the Ethics <term>Ethics: "Zedeleer" refers to the moral framework and rules for living</term> which they present to us, is a third proof of their Divinity: for who will not call Divine that which shows God’s image on all sides, which consists in Holiness? Everything in these Books works together to combat sins, without excluding a single one, and to make us like the Angels, and like God Himself. They make us aware of the most secret flaws within us, such as vanity, the desire for revenge, and the seeds of unbelief and ungodliness. They condemn the slightest failings that were unknown even to the strictest followers of the philosophers.

They do not permit even the smallest unbecoming desire. They are not satisfied with prescribing an outward Holiness for us: they want soul and body to be pure. It is not enough that they combat and forbid our flaws; they want us to extinguish all the impulses that lead to sin and to pull the root of it out of our hearts. It is not enough to encourage us toward Christian virtues, but they command us to possess them in the most perfect degree that a creature can attain. They are not satisfied with commanding us not to love ourselves too much, but they command us to deny ourselves and not to spare our lives if God’s Glory requires it. They are not satisfied with commanding us to love our friends, but they demand that we love our enemies. They are not satisfied with urging us to love our brothers <note>In this context, "brothers" refers to fellow believers or neighbors in a Christian sense.</note>, to the extent that they obligate us to share our goods with them when they are poor, to protect them when they are attacked, and to do them all kinds of good; but they want us to give our lives for them. They prescribe each person’s duty: to fathers and children, to wives and husbands, to servants and masters, to Princes and subjects; to old and young people. All these moral rules are supported

Can one, after all this, fail to recognize that God is the author <note>original: "ingeeber," meaning the one who gave or inspired the text</note> of these books? If they had come solely from men, would they not have flattered human passions? Would they have forbidden mere desire <note>in the sense of internal lust or covetousness</note>, of which Paul said in Romans 7:7, that he *would never have known it was sin, if the law had not said, you shall not covet.*?

One may gather all that is contained in the Laws of a Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta</note>, of a Draco <note>The first legislator of Athens, known for the severity of his laws</note>, and of other wise lawgivers, together with all that the most prominent philosophers of antiquity have written; it is certain that one will find nothing in them that comes close to the excellence and superiority of the Laws of Faith and of the Gospel. Furthermore, let one read through all the best books of piety <note>original: "Godzaligheid"</note> that exist among Christians—those which promote the peace of society and serve most to God’s glory—and one will find that they are all modeled after these Holy Books, and that everything has been drawn from these Fountains. Is this not proof that nothing more perfect or excellent can be made? And must one not necessarily confess that these Books are the work of God’s Spirit?

<margin>Fourth proof, taken from the fact that we learn from them all that we must know to be blessed.</margin>
IV. The fourth thing that convinces us that these Books are Divine is that we learn from them all that we most desire, and all that we must know to be blessed <note>original: "gelukzalig," referring to eternal happiness or salvation</note>, such as God’s essence and His perfections, His providence, and the honor we owe Him; the beginning of the world and of all creatures; the cause of the miseries and punishments to which human nature is subject; the greatness of our condemnation; what we have deserved, and by what means God’s justice is satisfied; the way that leads to bliss, and what must be done to please God; what our soul shall become after our death, and what our bodies shall become after having lain in the dust for some time, and other things of this nature which it is absolutely necessary for us to know. It will perhaps be said that we desire to know many things that these books do not teach us: but one must make two observations here. The first is that we only ask here for things that concern our Salvation <note>original: "Zaligheid"</note>, and not those that concern human

<column-break/>

sciences; the second is that in the matters that concern Salvation itself, it is only a question of what we *must* know; for the Holy Scripture was not given to us to satisfy an idle curiosity.

Furthermore, it is fitting to note that we find five types of things in these books: 1. Historical narratives. 2. Prophecies. 3. Promises and Threats. 4. Commandments. 5. Doctrines. What is more, among the things these books teach, there are some that are known to us by Nature without any revelation, but which these Books teach us more clearly. There are others of which men have had some knowledge, but a weak, uncertain, and confused knowledge. The Holy Scripture does, with respect to these things, the same as a person would do who helps us read the inscription on a commemorative medal <note>original: "gedenkpenning"</note> that is difficult to read. There are others which men could never have invented with all the ingenuity of their spirit. We shall have opportunity to speak of these things more distinctly.

<margin>Fifth proof taken from the harmony of the Holy Scripture.</margin>
V. The wonderful harmony that exists in all parts of Scripture gives us a fifth proof; for there is nothing in it that conflicts, and it gives us an idea of an infinite wisdom, consistent with the proportion that is seen in the whole. And this precise harmony is all the more wonderful because it is found between the Books of the Old and New Testament, even though those who used their pens to write them had no communication among themselves and were separated from each other by a sequence of centuries. This shows that they were all inspired by the same spirit, and that there was a Supreme Lord above them who held the governance and oversight over all this work. It will perhaps be said that there are contradictions in these books; but it is false that there are any essential ones; they are all apparent contradictions; the greatest contradictions that one sees presented regarding some genealogies or some numbers are things of little importance. Furthermore, if it had pleased God’s Spirit to give us more extensive Revelations, or if we had the books that were common among the Jews, we would find that there is no contradiction: there are things that we do not understand, and which the Jews...

Sixth proof: that the Holy Books tell us everything that can comfort and sanctify us.

VI. I proceed to a sixth proof, consisting in this: that these Books teach us everything that can still the anxieties of our souls and comfort them against the miseries of life, the terrors of death, and the consciousness it has of its sins. That there is now no condemnation for those who are in Jesus Christ and who repent, however great their sins may have been. 3. That they cannot last long and are not to be compared with the Glory prepared for the elect. 6. That death is the door to Heaven for believers, and that it is only terrible for the unrepentant. 7. That it will unite them with Him who is the cause of their being and their happiness; and that nothing

VII. But we find in these books not only all that can comfort us; we also see in them all that can bring us to holiness. They set before our eyes the holiness of God, of Jesus Christ, and of all the believers who lived under both the old and the new covenant; God's hatred for sin; the judgments He has poured out and will pour out upon sinners; the rewards He promises to those who will live holy, righteous, and godly lives; what Christ had to do to atone for sins, and the death He had to undergo to redeem us. Would they have forbidden mere desire, of which Paul said in Romans 7:7 that he would never have known it was sin if the law had not said, "thou shalt not covet" <note>original: "gy en zult niet begeeren"</note>.

If one gathers all that is contained in the laws of a Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta</note>, of a Draco <note>An Athenian lawmaker known for his exceptionally harsh legal code</note>, and of other wise legislators, along with all that the most prominent philosophers of antiquity have written; it is certain that one will find nothing in them that approaches the excellence and superiority of the laws of Faith and of the Gospel. Let one furthermore read through all the best books of piety <note>original: "Godzaligheid"</note> among Christians—those which promote the peace of society and best serve God’s glory—and one will find that they are all modeled after these Holy Books, and that everything has been drawn from these fountains. Is this not proof that nothing more perfect or excellent can be made? And must one not necessarily confess that these Books are the work of God’s Spirit?

<margin>Fourth proof, taken from the fact that we learn from it all that we must know to be blessed.</margin>

IV. The fourth thing that convinces us that these Books are divine is that we learn from them everything we most desire to know, and all that we must know to be blessed: such as God’s essence and His perfections, His providence, and the honor we owe Him; the beginning of the world and of all creatures; the cause of the miseries and punishments to which human nature is subject; the greatness of our corruption <note>original: "verdoovendheid," referring here to the spiritual numbness or depravity of fallen man</note>; what we have deserved, and by what means God’s justice has been satisfied; the path that leads to happiness, and what must be done to please God; what our soul will become after our death, and what our bodies will become after lying for some time in the dust; and other things of this nature which are absolutely necessary for us to know. It may perhaps be said that we desire to know many things which these books do not teach us: but one must make two observations here. The first is that we only ask here for things concerning our salvation, and not those concerning human 

<column-break/>

sciences; the second is that even in matters concerning salvation, it is only about what we *must* know: for the Holy Scripture was not given to us to satisfy a vain curiosity.

<margin>What one finds in the Holy books?</margin>

Furthermore, it is appropriate to note that we find five types of things in these books: 1. Historical accounts. 2. Prophecies. 3. Promises and Threats. 4. Commandments. 5. Doctrines. Moreover, among the things these books teach, there are those known to us by nature without any revelation, but which these books teach us more clearly. There are others of which men have had some knowledge, but a weak, uncertain, and confused knowledge.

Holy Scripture does, in regard to these things, the same thing a person would do who helps us read the inscription on a commemorative medal <note>original: "gedenkpenning"</note> that is difficult to read. There are others that men could never have invented with all the ingenuity of their minds. We shall have the opportunity to speak of these things more distinctly.

<margin>Fifth proof taken from the harmony of the Holy Scripture.</margin>

1. *Obs.* Most things / contained in the Holy Books / and which men would never have invented / are of such a nature / that when they are revealed to us / we find them very much in conformity with our reason / that they fulfill our deficiency / which we feel / and that they have a close connection with the things / that we know.

<meta>This page continues the defense of the Holy Scripture's divine origin. # DIVINE THEOLOGY. BOOK I. CHAPTER XIV. 69

<margin>
To prove the Divinity of the Holy Scripture.
</margin>
the mystery of our Redemption is intertwined with the necessity of satisfying Divine justice; the doctrine of the necessity of satisfaction <note>Theological term "satisfaction" refers to the idea that Christ’s suffering paid the debt for human sin required by God's justice.</note> is intertwined with the doctrine of the universal corruption of Mankind, who had angered Divine Justice; and this universal corruption is known to reason.

3. One must note that the difficulty which reason finds in grasping the mysteries contained in the Books of the Old and New Testament must not cause doubt regarding their truth; either because we find an infinite number of things in Nature which we cannot grasp and yet cannot doubt; or because reason itself acknowledges that it is not possible—being finite as it is—to grasp everything said of an infinite being, and to fathom all the depths of God: so that to wish to reject mysteries solely because they are incomprehensible is to sin against reason.

4. One must note that, to prove the Divinity of Holy Scripture, we do not take our argument from the incomprehensibility of the mysteries themselves; for if the incomprehensibility of a doctrine were a proof of its Divinity, then the most extravagant notions would be the primary Articles of our Faith. Rather, we take our argument from the fact that these mysteries, though elevated above our reason, are intertwined with truths that reason easily understands, and that they constitute the Soul and Essence of the Christian Religion, of whose Divinity a thousand reasons assure us.

5. Finally, one must note that the incomprehensibility of a doctrine is no sign that the doctrine is *against* reason; for to hold this view, one would have to believe that our reason and our understanding are infinite, which one could not maintain.

<margin>
Tenth proof taken from the prophecies.
</margin>
X. The Prophecies found in the Books of the Old and New Testament are an invincible proof of their Divinity; there are many of them in these Books.

1. One finds prophecies there that had their fulfillment a short time later; such as the prophecy of Ahijah concerning the elevation of Jeroboam, the death

<column-break/>

of his Son, and the division of Solomon’s Kingdom; the prophecy of the elevation of Jehu in the place of Joram; the prophecy that Elijah made of the exemplary punishment of Ahab and Jezebel; that of Jeremiah concerning the death of Jehoiakim; those of the misfortunes of Jeconiah, and of the death of the false Prophet Hananiah.

<margin>
1 Kings 16:34.
1 Kings 13:2, 3.
Isaiah 44:28.
</margin>
2. One finds prophecies there that were fulfilled a long time thereafter. This powerful effect of the Scriptures toward the conversion and comfort of mankind is a proof of its Divinity. One should not doubt this if one notes not only that there is nothing but the truth which can produce the effects that the Scripture produces, but also that the stirrings we feel under the contemplation of God’s word have something so lively, so extraordinary, and so different from the stirrings produced in us by human causes, that they must necessarily have a supernatural and Divine origin.

<margin>
Eighth proof: regarding the precise proportionality between the truths of the Gospel and the conscience.

VIII. One will not be surprised by the effectiveness of these books if one considers (and this is an eighth proof of their Divinity) that there is a precise proportionality between the truths they contain and the conscience of man. For they say nothing that the conscience does not approve; they promise nothing but that which the conscience desires; they make no threats except regarding things that the conscience fears; and they offer no rebukes or exhortations except those the conscience finds righteous. This provides clear evidence that He who inspired the Scripture is the same as He who placed the conscience within man.

<margin>
Ninth proof: taken from the sublimity of the mysteries.

IX. The loftiness of the truths and mysteries contained in the Scripture is a proof that can have no contradiction: for how could one believe that men had made a book in which one finds many things

<column-break/>

that exceed the reach of a finite Spirit, and would never have entered the mind of any man, such as the matter of the Trinity, the Incarnation <note>The Christian doctrine that God became flesh in the person of Jesus Christ.</note> of Jesus Christ, the Creation, Resurrection, etc.?

<margin>
Various observations.
</margin>
But to make the force of this proof more deeply felt, one must make these five observations.

1st Observation: Most things contained in the Holy Books, which humans would never have invented, are of such a nature that—once they are revealed to us—we find them very much in harmony with our reason; they fulfill the lack we feel, and they have a close connection with the things we already know.

For example, although we do not understand how something can be made out of nothing; nevertheless, when we are taught that God created all things from nothing, we find that to be very consistent with God's Essence and the nature of created things. With the Essence of God who, being Almighty, was able to produce everything by a single act of His will; and with the nature of created things: for it was necessary that this entire Universe was created from nothing, since there was no matter beforehand. I say the same of the mystery of redemption: reason perceives in this mystery a length, breadth, height, and depth that surpasses all understanding, but approves of what it holds in high regard. It is the same with the doctrine of the General Judgment and the Resurrection of the Dead. As soon as that is revealed to men, they could not deny that it is consistent with reason, which teaches us that God, being Just, must one day reward or punish everyone according to their works; since He does not always do so in this life; and that He must reward or punish the whole man—that is to say, in Soul and in Body; from which it follows that the Bodies must rise.

2nd Observation: One must note that the mysteries which seem most contrary to reason are closely united with the truths of which reason is convinced. For example, the mystery of the plurality of persons in one and the same essence <note>The doctrine of the Trinity: God as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note>—so incomprehensible to reason—is so necessarily linked to the work of our redemption that it could not have been carried out except through the Incarnation of an infinite Person:

### DIVINITY. BOOK I. CHAPTER XIV.

The mystery of our Redemption is intertwined with the necessity of satisfying Divine justice; the doctrine of the necessity of <term>satisfaction</term> <note>The theological concept that Christ's sacrifice paid the debt of human sin to "satisfy" the demands of God’s justice.</note> is linked with the doctrine of the general corruption of mankind, who had provoked Divine Justice; and this general corruption is known to human reason.

3. One must observe that the difficulty reason finds in understanding the mysteries contained in the Books of the Old and New Testament should not cause doubt regarding their truth; partly because we find an infinite number of things in Nature that we cannot understand, yet cannot doubt; and partly because reason itself acknowledges that, being finite as it is, it is impossible for it to comprehend everything said of an infinite Being or to fathom all the depths of God. Thus, to wish to reject mysteries solely because they are incomprehensible is to sin against reason.

<margin>To prove the Divinity of the Holy Scriptures.</margin>
4. One must observe that, in order to prove the Divinity of the Holy Scripture, we do not take our argument from the incomprehensibility of the mysteries. For if the incomprehensibility of a doctrine were a proof of its Divinity, then the most extravagant opinions would be the primary Articles of our Faith. Rather, we draw our argument from the fact that these mysteries—though elevated above our reason—are linked with truths that reason easily understands, and that they constitute the very soul and essence of the Christian religion, of whose Divinity a thousand reasons assure us.

5. Finally, one must observe that the incomprehensibility of a doctrine is no sign that the doctrine is against reason; for to hold such a view, one would have to believe that our reason and understanding are infinite, which is a position that cannot be maintained.

<margin>Tenth proof taken from the prophecies.</margin>

2. One finds there predictions that were fulfilled a long time thereafter.

so much certainty, that one would say, it is much more a narrative of past events, than a prediction of things to come, proceeding from a Spirit to whom all things are present, who sees all things, and reads in the darknesses of the future, because nothing happens except that which He has preordained. This reasoning is within the reach of the common people; for he must be more than blind who does not see that the foretold things have come to pass.

To combat this proof, one will perhaps say that there have been some among the Heathens and the neighboring peoples of Judea who boasted of predicting future things; and that in the writings of the Heathens, certain oracles are found which, according to them, have had their fulfillment.

But I answer thereto:
1. That these same false writers teach us that there have been many false oracles. One also finds a Greek <term>Critic</term> <note>original: Opsgeer</note> named Oenomaus, who wrote against the oracles and struck them down as mere deceptions. Eusebius relates that the Heathen priests, brought to the rack, confessed that they abused the credulity of the people through their pretended oracles; whereas one could not produce a single oracle in the Books of the Old and New Testament that has been found false.

2. I further note that these imagined predictions of the Heathens were only done in secret, and in the presence of a few, and that they were most of the time so ambiguous that they could be interpreted in two completely opposite ways; whereas the Prophets of the Jewish people spoke their oracles in the most solemn assemblies, and they wrote them in books where they could be examined by the entire nation. If some have had some obscurity, there are many that were very clear.

3. Furthermore; these pretended oracles were most of the time given only for the benefit of Princes, who were prepared to give great rewards to the priests, whereas the Prophets spared the Kings no more than their subjects, and set their own interests aside.

I confess that there are some predictions

<column-break/>

that can be made by <term>demons</term> <note>original: Dæmones</note> or evil spirits, because they, through their speed and invisibility, can very quickly know far-off things, and are present at the hidden counsels of men; but there is another sort of prediction that can be attributed to none but God. Such are the predictions of distant outcomes whose preceding causes do not yet exist, and which depend on many circumstances and a sequence of things whose outcomes—if only one were arranged differently—would change the result entirely. Such are those that depend on the uncertainty of the human will, which is very free, and where a choice of things is to be made, where one reason suggests no more cause to choose than the other. Such are the predictions of things that depend on no external circumstances or natural effects, but on God's will alone.

One will perhaps say that the oracles were fabricated after the outcome; thus Porphyry asserted that the Book of Daniel was fabricated; but this <term>Enemy of Christians</term> <note>original: Christenvynd</note> has made himself ridiculous with this saying; for has the authority of the Book of Daniel ever been doubted among the Jews? When they disputed against the Christians, who pressed them with passages from this Prophet, did they ever say that one finds fabrications in it? Josephus relates that the High Priest of the Jews showed Alexander the Great the prophecies of Daniel, which promised him the imperial dominion, and that this Monarch therefore showed the Jews so much kindness. Is the Book of Daniel not translated into Greek with the other Books of the Old Testament, about 300 years before the birth of Christ? Finally, who would dare to say that Jerusalem's final destruction—which was to be carried out by the abominable eagles, that is, by the Roman armies, as Daniel predicts and Christ pointed out from Daniel—was inserted into the writings of this Prophet after the outcome.

These are the strongest proofs of the Divinity of the Holy Scriptures. > “There is but one God the Father, who is the Father of the living Word, His wisdom, consisting of the power and the eternally expressed image; perfect Father of a perfect Son; Father of an only Son. There is but one Lord, one from one, God from God, the expression and Image of the Divinity, the powerful word; wisdom, which encompasses the assembly of all things; and power, which made all creatures; true Son of a true Father; invisible Son of an invisible Father; incorruptible Son of an incorruptible Father; immortal Son of an immortal Father; eternal Son of an eternal Father. And there is but one Holy Spirit, who has his being from God, and who appeared to men through the Son; image of the Son, perfect like him, life, cause of the living, Holy source, Holiness who gives holiness, through whom God the Father is revealed, who is above all and in all things, and God the Son, who is over all; Trinity, perfect without division,

<column-break/>

> nor change in His Glory, in His Eternity, and in His Sovereignty.”

Athanasius has preserved these words from Theognostus of Alexandria.

<margin>On the decrees of the Synod of Nicaea <note>original: "De decret. Syn. Nicen."</note></margin>
> “The existence of the Son is not taken from elsewhere, or brought forth from things that were not; but is generated from the essence of the Father, just as the rays of light are born from the Sun, and the vapor from water: for the vapor is not exactly the same thing as the water, and the rays are not the Sun; yet they are of no other essence. So too the Word is an outflowing of the essence of the Father, yet in such a way that the essence of the Father suffers no reduction by the rays that continually go out from Him. Thus, the existence of the Father suffers no reduction by generating His Son, who is His image.”

The same Athanasius has preserved for us the words of two men named Dionysius; one the Bishop of Alexandria, the other the Bishop of Rome, both enemies of the Sabellians <note>followers of Sabellius, who taught that the Father, Son, and Spirit were merely different "modes" or masks of a single person</note> and of Paul of Samosata.

Dionysius of Rome speaks thus: “I am currently going to oppose those who divide, undermine, and overthrow the pure and godly doctrine of the Church, dividing the complete and absolute Unity into certain powers, separate substances, and into three deities; for I understand that there are among us catechists and teachers who present such a doctrine; wherein they are directly opposed to the sentiment of Sabellius, for the blasphemy of this heretic consists in his asserting that the Son is the Father Himself, and that the Father is the same as the Son; but these others, on the contrary, make in a way three Gods, dividing the Holy Unity into three <term>hypostases <note>A technical theological term for the distinct "persons" of the Trinity; here Dionysius warns against seeing them as three separate gods</note></term>, foreign and entirely separated from one another, etc. It is necessary that the Word of God be united with God, the master of all things; and that the Holy Spirit remain and dwell in God; it is also necessary that the Divine Trinity unite itself into one head, namely, in the Almighty, who is the God of all things, etc. For the rest, those are no less to be rejected who say that the Son is a work of God, wishing to claim that the Lord was made like all other things; for the Scripture attributes to him a Generation, which him...”

<meta>The catchword at the bottom of the page is ", geen" (not/no), indicating the sentence continues on the next page regarding the unique nature of the Son's generation.</meta>

I think that the Confession of Faith—which goes by the name of *Athanasius* <note>Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373) was a champion of Trinitarianism against Arianism.</note>—should be added here.

There are six Formulas of this confession. The 1st is that of *Gilbert Génébrard*, drawn from a manuscript by *Lazare de Baïf*. # DIVINITY. BOOK III. B. CHAPTER XIX.

[addressed] a letter to those of Antioch, signed by many Bishops who were then in Alexandria, because they had been informed that great disputes had arisen among the orthodox in the Eastern Diocese over the use of the word *Hypostasis* <note>A Greek term meaning 'substance' or 'underlying reality,' which caused confusion because it could mean either a distinct 'person' or the 'divine essence' itself.</note>. See here how Athanasius speaks in his own name and in the name of the other Bishops.

<margin>Athanasius' Works, Epistle 1 to the Antiochians.</margin>

> Therefore, if anyone objects to such or similar things, restrain them and bring them to peace; since we have perceived that they are not possessed by anything but stubbornness and a spirit of contention. For having taken knowledge of this disagreement, we found that some people wanted to count it as a crime that [others] said there were *three Hypostases*, because these words are not found in the Scripture and were therefore suspect; and we advised them to hold to the Nicene confession. Meanwhile, as the heat of the dispute among the parties was great, we asked those who were in favor of the *three Hypostases* whether they intended the *Persons* or *Hypostases* to be substances or existences distinct from one another, according to the heresy of the Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who taught that the Son was a created being, lower than the Father.</note>, and whether each *Hypostasis*, according to their thoughts, was separate and existed by itself in the same manner as other creatures or as those born of men; or whether they meant that they were entirely different substances, like gold, silver, and copper; and whether by these words of *three Hypostases* they intended, like the other heretics, to make three principles and three Gods. Thereupon they testified that they had no such thoughts and had never said anything of the kind. We further asked why they then used these words? They answered that they believed in a true and essential Trinity, and not a Trinity of words; a Father who had his existence, a Son truly having his existence, and the Holy Spirit likewise having his existence. But they had never said that there were three Gods and three principles; that they would never tolerate anyone who thought or said that. That they very much desired there to be a Holy Trinity, but nevertheless one single Deity, one single principle; that they recognized a Son, consubstantial <note>original: "medewezig" — meaning sharing the same essence or substance.</note> with the Father, as the Old Fathers had described it; that the Holy Spirit is no

<column-break/>

> creature, and no foreign, but a proper and inseparable being of the essence of the Father and of the Son. We approved of this explanation and examined the others, who had been accused by these [first] ones of recognizing only one *Hypostasis* or Person—namely, whether they said that in the sense of *Sabellius* <note>Sabellius taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were just different 'modes' or masks of one person, rather than three distinct persons.</note>, to separate the Son and the Holy Spirit from the Trinity, and to suggest that the Son had no essence, or the Holy Spirit no *Hypostasis* or existence. These answered that they understood that *Hypostasis* and existence were the same thing, and that they posited one *Hypostasis*, which we hold to be one, both because the Son is of the existence or essence of the Father, and because of the complete identity of nature. For we believe that there is but one Deity, and that this Deity has but one nature, and that the nature of the Father is no other than that of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Thereupon the others, who were accused of having posited *three Hypostases*, agreed with the view of these; as did those who confessed only one *Hypostasis*; they rested in the explanation of the others; and both parties cursed both *Arius* as the enemy of Christ, and *Paul of Samosata* and *Sabellius* as godless, etc.

From this it appears that in the first four centuries, the concern for the Trinity was accepted, and [the Church] was convinced of the Deity of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. I shall only add a word to this. We have two monuments in pagan antiquity from which one can infer what the Christians believed.

<margin>Pliny, Book 10, Epistle 97.</margin>

### IV. CENTURY.

<margin>Epiphanius, *Heresies* 69; Athanasius, Volume 1; Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*; Theodoret, book I, chapter 11, VI; Sozomen, book I, chapter 15; Socrates Scholasticus, book I, chapters 5 & 6.</margin>
IN this Century, Arius <note>Arius (c. 250–336) was a priest in Alexandria whose teachings on the nature of Christ led to the first major schism in the Christian Church.</note>, a teacher in Alexandria, disturbed the Church. One can gather from various writings, and especially from those of Athanasius (who was his opponent), what he and his followers believed:

1. That Christ was God, but lesser than the Father.
2. That he had a beginning and was a creature, created out of nothing before the ages.
3. That he was a "made" God, by the will of his Father.
4. That he is the Son of God through adoption, though like his Father.
5. That the Father created the world through him as an instrument.
6. That the essence of the Father is different from that of the Son; that he is neither co-eternal nor of the same essence <note>original: "medewezen," referring to the Greek term *homoousios*</note> with the Father.
7. That the Holy Spirit is not God, but a creature of the Son.

He had many Bishops of his opinion; the Council of Nicaea, in the year 325, was gathered against him.

<column-break/>

The Arians were divided into many factions.

The first were entirely of the opinion of Arius, whom they call <term>Anomeans</term> <note>From the Greek 'anomoios', meaning 'unlike' or 'dissimilar'.</note>, from a word that in Greek means "dissimilar." <margin>Epiphanius, 76.</margin> This was because they believed that the Son was not similar to his Father; their head was one Aëtius, a Deacon of Antioch; he was called "the Atheist." He had a disciple, Eunomius, and thus they were named Aëtians and Eunomians. He was condemned by the Semi-Arians in the year 358, and in Constantinople in 359 by Constantius, who sent him into exile after having heard the declaration of his faith with horror.

Others said that the Son was similar in essence to the Father, but not <term>consubstantial</term> <note>Meaning 'of one substance'. This group used the term *homoiousios* (similar substance) instead of the Nicene *homoousios* (same substance).</note>; the heads were Basil, Eustathius, etc. They were called <term>Semi-Arians</term>.

<margin>Socrates Scholasticus, book 2, chapter 30.</margin>
Others said that the Son was like the Father; but they did not add "in all things" and "in essence"; the heads <margin>Socrates Scholasticus, book 2, chapter 40.</margin> were one Acacius of Caesarea in Palestine, who subsequently, it is said, accepted the opinion of the orthodox in the year 363. The others rejected all these words and said that the Father was greater than the Son in Honor, in Dignity, and in Divinity. Just as the second Formula of Sirmium states in the year 357, which Hosius <note>Hosius of Corduba, a prominent bishop who presided at Nicaea but was later pressured into signing an Arian creed in his old age.</note> signed.

It would be too long to bring up here all the particular Councils held against and by the Arians.

<margin>Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*; Sulpicius Severus; Vincent of Lérins, book 1, commentary 1; Epiphanius, *Heresies* 74.</margin>
Photinus, Bishop of Sirmium, the capital of Illyria, denied the Trinity; according to him, the Father alone was God, the Holy Spirit was not God, nor a Person of the Trinity; the Christ and Son of God did not exist before Mary, and was not God, but a mere man, though born of a Virgin through the operation of the Holy Spirit. He was condemned by the Councils of Sardis, Milan, and Sirmium.

Macedonius, Patriarch of Constantinople, a Semi-Arian who believed that the Son was like in essence, also maintained that the Holy Spirit was not God, but a creature like the Angels, although of a more exalted rank. His followers were named <term>Pneumatomachi</term>, that is, "Enemies of the Holy Spirit." The Council of Constantinople was held against him under Theodosius the Great in the year 381.

### VI. CENTURY.

<margin>

These sects had their followers in the fifth and sixth Centuries; but it is not necessary to provide their names.

I will only say that a certain *Philoponus* <note>John Philoponus (c. 490–570), an Alexandrian philologist and philosopher.</note>, a philologist <term>Taalgeleerde: a scholar of language and literature, often focusing on classical texts</term> and philosopher of Alexandria, claimed in the sixth Century that there were three Gods. The opinion of *Roscelin*, a cleric of the Church of Compiegne, was condemned in a Council of Soissons in the year 1091, because he taught that the three Persons are three distinct things, like three Angels or three Souls.

In the year 1148, in the 12th Century, *Bernardus* <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux.</note>, at the Council of Reims, had *Gilbert Porreus* <note>Gilbert de la Porrée (c. 1070–1154), Bishop of Poitiers.</note> condemned, who was Bishop of Poitiers and was accused of allowing a quaternity <note>original: "vierheid" — the unorthodox idea that God’s essence is a fourth thing distinct from the three Persons of the Trinity.</note> in God.

In the 16th Century, there were many who contested the Divinity of Christ and the Holy Trinity. Such as *Michael Servetus*, who denied that Christ, before he was born of the Virgin, had any other existence than in the mind of God; *Valentinus Gentilis*, who allowed for three Gods. *Mattheus Gribaldus*, *Pau-*

<column-break/>

*lus Alciatus*, *Georgius Blandrata*, *Petrus Coniza*, *Georgius Paulus*, *François Lismanus*, *Erasmus Joannes*, who was an Arian. *Franciscus Davidis*, *Budneus*, *Christian Francken*, *Bernardus Ochinus*, *Lælius* and *Faustus Socinus* <note>The founders of Socinianism, a rationalist Christian movement that denied the Trinity.</note>, *Andreas Dudithius*, *Valentinus Smalcius*, *Hieronymus Moscorovius*, *Christoffel Ostorodus*, *Georgius Enjedinus*, *Joh. Volkelius*. And in the 17th Century, there have been seen to arise *Theophilus Nicolaus*, *Adam Goslavius*, *Joh. Crellius*, *Joachim Stechmannus*, *Jonas Schlichtingius*, *Wolzogenius*, and others, whose names one finds in the *Antitrinitarian Library* <note>original: "Antitrinitarische Bibliotheek"</note> of *Christopher Sandius*, published in 1684 at Freistadt. They have not all shared the same opinion; but it is not necessary that I describe their views here.

There are those among the *Mahometans* <note>A historical term for Muslims.</note> who say that the world has two Gods: one Eternal, who is God above all things; and a new one, who is Jesus Christ; *Mahomet* said that Jesus was God's Spirit.

To God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God in three Persons, be Honor, Glory, the Kingdom, and Majesty. AMEN.

# THE CHRISTIAN
## THEOLOGY,
### BOOK FOUR.
#### Of God’s Decrees in General.

---

##### CHAPTER I.
###### What is understood by the word Decree,
###### and whether there is such a thing.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'N' depicting a figure walking on a path in a rural landscape with trees and a building in the background.</image-desc>

Now that I have spoken of God’s adorable being, and of the three Persons who possess this being, it is only natural to treat of God’s decrees before I speak of His works. We call a Decree of God that which God has intended, decided, and determined to do or to permit.
The word "Decree" <term>Besluit: in this context, a formal decision or purpose determined by God from eternity</term> is in use in the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to Scholasticism, the method of critical thought and theology dominant in medieval universities and early modern academies.</note> and is taken from the *Vulgate* <note>The Latin translation of the Bible. Original: *vulgata*</note>, as can be seen in Ephesians 2:15 and Colossians 2:14, though often used there in a different sense than we do now.
We cannot doubt God’s decrees; the Scriptures teach us this clearly. Isaiah 46:10: *My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure.* Isaiah 14:24: *The Lord of hosts hath sworn, saying, Surely as I have thought, so shall it come to pass; and as I have purposed, so shall it stand.* Acts 2:23: *Him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain.*
Those who 1. explain this passage as referring to the gift and present that God made of His Son to the Jews to deliver them from their sins, do not understand it; for the root word <note>The original Greek word used in the New Testament.</note> signifies giving someone over to the mercy of their enemies, as the linguists remark. 2. It also cannot be translated

<column-break/>

as a revealed or made-known intention (which we have translated as "determinate counsel"); for it is clear that the text speaks here not of a revealed intention, but of a determined intention, and of a declaration made within God’s own counsel.
Acts 4:28: Peter says that Herod and Pilate were gathered together *to do whatsoever thy hand and thy counsel determined before to be done.* And Paul in Ephesians 1:4-5: *According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world... having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will.* And verse 9: *Having made known unto us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure which he hath purposed in himself.* And verse 11: *We who were predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will.* And Romans 8:28-29: *We know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to (his) purpose. For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate,* etc.
Reason confirms that God is the all-wise being who knows everything, foresees everything, and sustains everything in existence. Now, it befits a wise being to set an end <note>A final goal or purpose.</note> for Himself in all that He does, to arrange all outcomes or possible things that might relate to this end, and not to allow anything to happen against His will; for if this were not so, one could conceive of a being who surpassed Him in wisdom, and without whose will nothing would happen

<meta>catchword: would;</meta>

# DIVINITY. IV. B. II. Chap.

...would; and such a being alone would be worthy of being called God.

Furthermore, if God knows everything—as we proved in the 2nd Book—not only what is possible, but also what is to come, He must necessarily have determined what shall happen: otherwise He could not know for certain what would occur.

Furthermore, because God is independent, it is simultaneously understood that the creatures are absolutely dependent on God; for if this were not so, one could conceive of a more perfect being—namely, one upon whom all creatures depended, while He depended not on them; who could act without them, while they could not act without Him; and whose gaze would be necessary every moment for the existence and activity of the creatures. Now, this dependence on <term>secondary causes: the created means, such as natural laws or human actions, through which God works His will</term> clearly proves that all outcomes must be arranged according to God's will.

The <note>original: "Heidenen" (Heathens or Pagans)</note> ancient philosophers knew this, as many proofs could be provided for it.

### II. CHAPTER.

->*How one must understand God's decrees; and of their Eternity.*<-

Do not think that God makes decrees like men, who, before they go to work, must make a sketch, and subsequently consider what might happen, and who try to carry out their design—but whose spirits are often uncertain and wavering, not knowing which way they shall turn, who then decide one thing and then another, who first think of an end, and then of the means. One must not have such thoughts about God; He sees everything at once and determines it all through a single act of His will. But Scripture attributes decrees to God to teach us that He does everything with great wisdom, that nothing happens against His will, and nothing exists that He did not foresee and determine to either perform or permit.

<margin>What one must distinguish in God’s decrees.</margin>
In God's decrees, one must distinguish three things. 1. God's will, which determines that a thing shall be. 2. The relationship that this will has to the creature or matter,

<meta>catchword: 1. Part.</meta>

<column-break/>

over which God makes any decree. 3. The decreed matter itself. When we consider the act of God's will in these decrees, we do not distinguish it from His essence: for God’s will and essence are the same, and there is nothing in God but God Himself. God could not have been without a decree, because He cannot be without a will.

Just as all beings who work by counsel also work upon some <term>idea: a mental blueprint or concept</term> that they form, it is asked whether there are ideas in God? The question is more curious than it is useful, and it is better to remain silent than to say something that God has not revealed.

The Theologians note the following regarding this: 1. That there are ideas in God, but they are not stirred up from elsewhere, as happens with men. 2. That things <note>original: "den zynd" (existence or being)</note> take their being according to God's ideas, and His ideas are not made according to things; and thus all things are first in God. 3. That these ideas are God’s very essence, who knows His own perfections and wills that there be some traces of them in the creatures. 4. That, strictly speaking, there is but one idea of all things in God, though we perceive many because of the various relationships this single idea of God has to an infinite number of things that are outside of God. 5. That in this sense it is said that the idea of one thing is not the idea of another. 6. That the idea of all the perfections of the creatures is in God; not of their imperfections. 7. Finally, that God indeed knows all the imperfections of His creatures, but He only knows them through the opposite perfections. They cite many other things as well, especially the <term>Scholastic Theologians: university scholars who used formal logic and philosophy to define Christian doctrine</term>. But one reasons about this matter by groping <note>original: "by den tast" (by touch or blindly)</note>, and one quickly falls into extravagances; one becomes entangled in difficulties from which there is no escape. The safest course, then, is to say that one knows nothing of it.

<margin>Of the Eternity of the decrees.</margin>
The Scripture says that God's decrees are eternal. Matt. XXV. 34. *Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.* Eph. I. 4. *According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world.* 1 Cor. II. 7. *We speak the wisdom of God (consisting) in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom, which God...*

<sig>Ee</sig>
<meta>catchword: before</meta>

<keywords>divine decrees, omniscience, dependency of creatures, secondary causes, divine ideas, scholasticism, predestination, eternity of God's will</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the theological argument regarding the eternity of God's decrees, specifically addressing objections that suggest God reacts to human actions in time rather than having determined all things from the beginning.</meta>

<header>THE CHRISTIAN</header>

ordained beforehand, for our Glory, before the world was. 2 Timothy 1:9. *Who has saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to His own purpose and grace, which was given to us in Jesus Christ before the ages began.* 1 Peter 1:20. *Who indeed was foreknown before the foundation of the world.*

The Holy Writers describe God's Eternity to us in no other way. It would be an unfitting thing for a perfect being, before whom all things are naked and revealed, to make His decrees in time and according to the state of affairs; for then one would have to suppose that God learns something daily and takes measures and deliberates according to what He perceives; that cannot be said of God.

<margin>Socinus, Vorstius, Crellius, Remonstrants. <note>These were theological groups and figures—such as the followers of Faustus Socinus and the Arminian Remonstrants—who were often accused of suggesting that God’s knowledge or decrees might be contingent upon human free will.</note></margin>
One must not say that the Scripture gives cause for such thoughts when it portrays God as descending to see the deeds of men and subsequently carrying out His judgments. For we have proven that these words must be understood in a manner worthy of God <note>original: "God-betamelyk-wyze"</note>, to teach us that God does not exercise His judgments upon men unless they have deserved them; just like a Judge who, after a well-conducted investigation, only then condemns those found guilty.

One must also not say that some decrees are Eternal and others are not: for there is no reason why some should be more Eternal than others; and the Scripture does not make this distinction.

It is true that scholars speak of the order of the decrees; they place one before the other, but they indicate thereby that it is for the sake of clearer understanding; for otherwise they say that God, whose wisdom is infinite, has decided everything in one and the same moment.

One will perhaps say that God's existence, in terms of our understanding, precedes His decrees.

I answer that we should not trouble ourselves with that; we shall hear the Scripture, which says that God is Eternal, and that His decrees are Eternal; one must believe both the one and the other.

If there are causes that do not precede their effect <note>original: "gewrogt"</note>, such as the Sun and the Light; then one must not be surprised when it is said that God did not precede His decrees.

But, although God's decrees are Eternal, it does not follow from this that the Creatures

<column-break/>

are Eternal; but only that God has decided from all Eternity what He will do in time with or through His Creatures.

---

### CHAPTER III.

->Concerning the Wisdom, Freedom, and Unchangeability of God's decrees.<-

<margin>Concerning the Wisdom of the decrees.</margin>
One cannot doubt the Wisdom of God's decrees, any more than the Wisdom of God Himself. We have reason to cry out with Paul. Romans 11:33, 34. *O the depth of the riches, both of the Wisdom and of the knowledge of God! How unsearchable are His judgments, and His ways past finding out! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been His counselor?*

This wisdom is evident in all that we can discover of it; and it shall be even more evident when we behold the entire sequence and the wonderful coherence that exists between God's decrees.

<margin>Freedom of the decrees. Matthew 11:26; Jeremiah 18:6; Romans 9:21.</margin>
These decrees are free. *Even so, Father,* said Christ, *for so it seemed good in thy sight.* Matthew 11:26. Jeremiah and Paul testify to the same, where God compares Himself to a Potter. Romans 9:21: *Has not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honor, and another unto dishonor?* This freedom is evident if one considers that God does everything without being determined thereto by any other being, and for righteous and wise reasons, in which true Freedom consists.

Thus, Wisdom does not hinder the Eternity of the decrees.

<margin>Unchangeability of the decrees.</margin>
They are unchangeable. Isaiah 46:10. We shall not distinguish them into general and particular; for God says in this place that He will do all things according to His pleasure, and subsequently He speaks of the deliverance of the Jews, in respect of which God had made particular decrees. God never changes His will, as has been proven: men change their will through ignorance, or weakness, malice, or inconstancy. But this can have no place in God. He knows all, foresees all, does all that He wills, is supremely good, and not subject to frivolous inconstancy.

It is true, God sometimes destroys what He has established; thus He destroyed the established Levitical service <note>The religious laws and rituals of the Old Testament priesthood</note>: But

<meta>catchword: His [zyn]</meta>

<meta>This page continues the theological argument regarding the immutability of God’s decrees. # DIVINITY. Book IV. Part B. Chapter III.

His will does not change. The same God who had decided upon the building up, had also decided upon the tearing down; the matter changes, but God’s will does not. God, who had decreed that men should offer Him such a service for many centuries—as the Books of Moses describe to us—had also decreed to abolish the same with the coming of His Son.

From this immutability, it follows that God has ordained nothing that does not take its effect. Who could prevent it? Could there be anything that could set itself against God's will? Is He not almighty? Or would God find that what He had intended ought not to be carried out? Such talk would accuse God of not having had enough wisdom to foresee the outcomes.

<margin>Socinus, Remonstrants, Crellius, *On God* <note>original Latin: "de Deo"</note>, chapter 32. <note>These were thinkers and groups who argued that human free will could make God's plans "conditional."</note></margin>
From this, it is easy to deduce what one must answer to a proposed question: whether God makes decrees whose execution depends on a condition that often does not happen; this is then called a **conditional decree**. Men distinguish between two kinds of decrees: some are called **absolute**, because they depend on God alone, such as the decree to create the world and to send His Son; others are called **conditional**, whose execution depends on an uncertain condition.

We cannot join in this opinion. We allow that there are decrees which God does not execute except through certain means; but we do not believe that God makes decrees under a condition that often does not occur. For that which hangs on an uncertain condition cannot be certain or immutable. Now, we have proven the certainty and immutability of God’s decrees; consequently, there is no decree whose execution depends on an uncertain stipulation.

One cannot posit such decrees without assuming that He who makes them does not know what shall happen, or that the outcome is not in His power, or at least that He has determined nothing regarding the outcome and leaves things to chance—which cannot be said of God.

To suppose, for example, that God has decreed that Peter or Jacob shall be saved on the condition that he shall believe and be converted, is to suppose either that God does not know whether Peter or Jacob will believe and be converted, and that their faith

<column-break/>

and conversion do not depend on God; or it is to suppose that God is not earnest in taking a decree to save people on the condition of doing what He knows very well they will not do. One cannot say that God does not know that Peter and Jacob will believe; for He has infinite wisdom. One cannot say that the repentance and faith of Peter and Jacob do not depend on God; for the Scripture teaches us that these are God’s gifts. One cannot say, then, that God makes idle and fruitless decrees.

One will say that there are few decrees that do not include some condition. That is true. But these decrees do not *depend* on those conditions. For example: God decrees to save a certain number of persons whom He has chosen out of a corrupt mass <note>original: "bedorve klomp." This refers to the "massa corrupta," the theological idea that all humanity is fallen and God chooses some out of that fallen state.</note>; He demands faith from them, but in demanding it, He produces it. Faith is then a condition without which God does not give salvation to the rational creature; it is a condition that He Himself produces in those He has decreed to save. But one cannot say that God has decreed to save all men on the condition of faith, because there are infinitely many who have not had faith and will not have it; and because one must not attribute idle and fruitless decrees to God.

<margin>Genesis 20:17. 2 Samuel 17:2-3 compared with verse 14, and 24:13. Jeremiah 16:3-4. Jeremiah 17:24-26. Jeremiah 28:18. Jeremiah 42:9, 20.</margin>
One will say that there are conditional promises and threats. I admit it, but there is a great difference between **decrees** and **promises** or **threats**. Promises do not assume that the thing *will* happen, as decrees do: they only make known what is pleasing to God or not, and the connection that exists between the thing God commands and that which He promises. Let it not be said that these conditional promises look toward a decree, and that this decree must therefore be conditional. For the promises only assume that God has decreed to allow such a law to be set before men, and that those who fulfill it shall be saved. For example: if someone fulfilled the law, he would live—that is certain. The promise is: *if you do these things, you shall live.* But it does not follow from this that God has decreed to give life to all men on the condition of fulfilling the law; for God knows that no one can fulfill it. From this, it only follows that God has decreed...

# THE CHRISTIAN [RELIGION]

intended to make known to men what would happen to them if they kept the law perfectly: they would live; and this was to teach them their duty.

Similarly, God threatens death to those who will live according to the flesh. *If you live according to the flesh, you shall die.* Romans 8:13 and John 3:18, 36. *He who does not believe in the Son is already condemned, and the wrath of God remains on him.* But it does not follow from this that God has made a decree to damn all men if they all lived according to the flesh, and if they were all unbelievers; it only follows from this that God has decreed that these two things should be inseparable: a life according to the flesh and death; unbelief and God’s wrath. In the same way, one can reason about Salvation: God has not, through any conditional decree, decided to save all men on the condition of Faith; but He has decreed that faith in Christ would be the infallible means to be saved.

It will be said that God had decreed that the people of Israel should enter into the Promised Land, and yet the opposite occurred. Numbers 14:30.

But that does not prove that there are decrees which do not have their fulfillment.

It only proves these three things:

1. That God had decreed to bring the descendants of Jacob into Canaan, but not all the children of Israel <note>i.e., not every individual who left Egypt, but the nation as a corporate lineage</note>.

2. That God had also decreed not to bring in the unbelieving and rebellious—specifically those who did not enter.

3. Finally, that God nevertheless had decreed to make known to all the people what He required of them, and what He promised to those who would do their duty.

Thus, God’s decree had its effect; for God had not decreed to bring into the Promised Land any but those who were actually brought in.

<margin>That the immutability of the decrees does not take away the freedom of the creature.</margin>
This immutability of God’s decrees does not take away the freedom of the creatures. It is true, one has difficulty understanding how outcomes happen <unclear>infallibly</unclear> <note>original: "affeilbaar", likely a typo for "onfeilbaar" (infallible)</note> and yet men can simultaneously retain their freedom: but these two things are certain.

1. That nothing happens that God has not decreed to do or to permit: for this truth cannot be denied unless one calls into question whether 

<column-break/>

God knows everything from all Eternity and is all-powerful. If something happened that God had not decreed to do or to permit, then something would happen that God had not foreseen or had not been able to prevent.

2. It is also certain that we act freely, and that is enough for us.

One must never deny a matter or a truth under the pretext that one does not see how it agrees with another known truth.

One must only observe that the same decree which decided that things should happen also decided the manner in which they must happen: in such a way that all creatures act in a manner consistent with their nature. Inanimate creatures act through a necessity that is placed upon them. Thus fire necessarily burns what one throws into it, unless something prevents its operation. Free and rational creatures act with reason and freedom.

We must indeed conclude from the immutability of God’s decrees that creatures do not have a "freedom of independence," which belongs to God alone; He, being independent of all other beings, also acts independently of them. Instead, creatures depend on God regarding their being and their actions: for one cannot conceive that a creature, pulled out of nothingness, can exist outside of it in any other way than by the same power that pulled it out; that which is absolutely dependent in its existence cannot be in any state of independence in order to act.

But from this immutability, one cannot draw the conclusion that rational creatures do not have the freedom that is proper to all intelligent beings, through which they act with reason and judgment without being forced to it, except by their own reason.

<margin>Cajetan in Part 1 of Thomas [Aquinas], Question 22, Article 4. <note>Thomas de Vio, known as Gaetanus or Cajetan (1469–1534), was a major Catholic philosopher and commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note></margin>
Various means have been sought to reconcile God's decrees with the freedom of man. Cardinal Cajetan believed that it was a difficulty that one cannot overcome in this life, but others have attempted to solve it.

II. Others deny / that the free acts were decided and determined by God; Suarez, book III, *On Aids*, ch. 17. n. 1. 2. Gabriel Vasquez attributes this opinion to several others.

VI. Among the **Arminians** <note>Followers of Jacobus Arminius, who argued for a more significant role for human free will in salvation compared to strict Calvinism.</note> there are those / who seek to reconcile the freedom of man with the decrees / by proposing:

2. That God / in order to carry out His decrees / does not bend our will except by presenting the matters and motives / that can move it to work; but in such a way / that it is always in its power / not to be affected by these objects.

Others / like Grevinchovius etc. / seek to reconcile it with Middle-knowledge.

1. *On the Will of God, regarding sin*, book II, ch. 8.
*On Free Will*, ch. 4.
</margin>
2. John Strang / Scottish Theologian / after having distinguished a twofold freedom / one which is essential to man / and consists in this / that the will is moved by its own motion / and by the judgment of reason; the other, which consists in indifference; says / that God’s decrees / by which the acts of the will are determined / take away this second freedom / but not the first; because God / who has decreed the acts of man / bends the will in such a manner / that corresponds with its nature. But that regarding **sins** / which God has decreed to permit / God’s decrees take away neither the one / nor the other freedom / since the permission leaves the will in the state / that it can act or not act; and that God / in respect of the things He has decreed should happen according to our free choice / has determined nothing / until after He has foreseen to what our will would determine itself.

3. Amyraldus <note>Moïse Amyraut, a French Reformed theologian who proposed a "hypothetical universalism" that attempted to soften strict predestination.</note>, Professor of Saumur, and many others say / that God’s decrees do not destroy our freedom / because they make it consist only in not being forced / and in acting according to our understanding; they maintain that God does nothing other than preserve the powers of man / and let objects and opportunities come before him; that He / to make us pursue the good / frees our powers from the defects / with which they are infected / grants them new strengths / and raises them above their natural state; And that He / in respect of the evil acts / lets the creature act / and only lets certain objects occur.

<margin>
Perkins, *On the mode & order of predestination*.
Twisse in *Vindication*.
</margin>
4. The other theologians / who explain the manner of cooperation differently / maintain that God’s decrees do not take away freedom / and explain the matter just as the **Thomists** <note>Followers of Thomas Aquinas, who emphasized that God's primary causality works through human secondary causes without violating them.</note> do, such as Perkins, Twisse, and many others.

### CHAPTER IV.
#### Of the Extent and Order of God's Decrees.
---

<margin>Of the variety of the decrees.</margin>
God's decrees cover everything; nothing happens in time that was not decreed from all eternity. Nevertheless, we must not believe that God has decreed everything in the same way. There are things that God has decreed to do alone; there are others that He has decreed to do by means of **secondary causes** <note>In theology, God is the "First Cause," while natural laws or human choices are "secondary causes" through which He works.</note>. Some He has decreed to command; others to do; others only to permit, such as sins, which God cannot do, nor decree to do, because He is the Holy of Holies.

<margin>Of the order of the decrees.</margin>
One might ask if there is any order in these decrees? One should not doubt it, for otherwise there would be only confusion in God’s thoughts. But do not imagine that God knows things as we do, moving from step to step to reach a certain knowledge. The acts of God’s will are not divided, where one would precede and another follow, as if God first saw one thing and subsequently decided another based upon it. We believe that God sees everything in an instant and that He, through a single act of His will, has willed all that is in the world: for we must believe that God does everything in the most perfect way. However, scholars establish an Order of the decrees: 1. To bring their own thoughts into order and to understand things more clearly. 2. Because Scripture, on account of our human weakness, provides a basis for us to consider the works of God’s will distinctly in this way.

Nearly all denominations imagine God’s decrees in a different order.

#### In the Roman Church

<margin>Gabriel Vasquez, Volume 1, Disputation 95, Chapter 1.</margin>
I. **John Duns Scotus** <note>A late medieval Franciscan philosopher and theologian.</note>, along with many others, believed that God first envisioned all humans—both the good and the wicked, such as Peter and Judas—and 

<column-break/>

decided to make Peter blessed <note>original: "zalig," meaning saved or spiritually blissful.</note> before He had foreseen his merits; but that He decided nothing regarding the godless or Judas. Subsequently, He determined to call Peter and give him Glory; but regarding Judas and the godless, He decided nothing. In a third decree, God determined to permit Judas to fall into sin and foresaw that he would die in it. Further, having foreseen what Peter and Judas would do, He decided to give Peter Glory and to punish Judas with eternal punishment. **Corduba** and **Diego Alvarez** believed that in the first instant, before He had foreseen any deed, God had decided to deny Judas happiness and Glory, but not to punish him with the "punishment of sense" <note>The "punishment of sense" (*poena sensus*) refers to physical suffering in hell, distinguished from the "punishment of loss" (*poena damni*), which is the deprivation of God's presence.</note>.

II. **Robert Bellarmine** established this order: 1. God foresaw, he says, that Man, if He created him, would fall into sin with all his descendants. 2. That He subsequently willed to create Man and permit his fall, and thereafter to deliver some from it through His mercy, leaving the others in the **mass of perdition** <note>original: "klomp der verdoemheid"; a reference to the Augustinian *massa damnata*, the idea that all humanity is collectively fallen and deserving of condemnation.</note>. 3. That He further devised suitable means to save the elect, and that among these means, the Incarnation and the suffering of Jesus Christ hold the first place. 4. That He approved these means and chose Christ, and us in Him, before the creation of the world. 5. That God finally charged and commanded that things should happen thus.

III. **Martin Becanus** devised this order: 1. That God decided to create the entire human race for eternal salvation and desired that they should all attain it. 2. That God, according to this will, decided to give grace to Man in the **state of uprightness** <note>The state of humanity before the Fall.</note>, while allowing him the free use of his free will, which includes the permission of sin. 3. That He saw that the first man with all his descendants would fall. 4. That, wishing to prepare a remedy for fallen man, He preordained Jesus Christ and His merits. 5. **Piscator** <note>Johannes Piscator (1546–1625), a German Reformed theologian.</note> sets forth eight decrees of God. The 1st: To make known his Glory through his Mercy in the elect, and through his Justice in the reprobate. The 2nd: To make the Elect blessed and to damn the reprobate. The 3rd: To Justify and Sanctify the Elect, and not the reprobate. The 4th: To call the Elect, and not the reprobate. The 5th: To reconcile the Elect through Jesus Christ, and not the reprobate. The 6th: To elect one and reject the other. The 7th: To allow Sin. The 8th: To Create man.

Mr. Claude <note>Jean Claude (1619–1687) was a renowned French Reformed (Huguenot) theologian known for his clear logic.</note> believed that just as one must naturally establish three orders of things—the right (or law), the case (or act), and the application of the law to the act; and just as there are three attributes in God that correspond to these three orders of things, namely the capacity of Legislator, Steward <note>Or "Economus," the administrator of a household or system.</note>, and Judge; and that he can be considered in respect to men either in the order of Nature or in the order of Grace, so must the decrees be established: 1. That God from Eternity decided to Create the world, and in the World, Man, as a rational creature capable of good. 2. To make known to man his duty, whether through the impression of his perfections in the Universe, or through the impression of the Law of Nature in the conscience of man, or through the first word that God spoke to man in the state of uprightness. This second Right belongs to God as Legislator in the Stewardship of nature. 3. That God, having foreseen the fall of man, had decided not to prevent it, but to let it happen, in order subsequently to draw greater Glory from it. This same decree belongs to God as Steward in the order of Nature. 4. This decree is followed by a decree of God as Supreme Ruler of the Universe, by which he commands the execution of his justice regarding

<column-break/>

That God decided to let this new Law of Grace, grounded on the merits of Jesus Christ, be proclaimed to all men without distinction. This decree is still from God as Legislator. 7. That God decided to divide men into two states: to grant Faith to some through the powerful working of his Spirit, and by means of Faith to incorporate them into the mystical Body of the Savior and give them a share in his merits; and to leave the others in their blindness and natural unbelief. This is a distributive or Stewardship decree, which he calls the general election and reprobation, which determines that there shall be believers and unbelievers. 8. That God, in the execution of this decree, chooses specific Persons among men—Peter, John, etc.—to Faith by means of his Holy Spirit, to be members of the mystical body of Christ through faith; and as for the others, God leaves them in their blindness and unbelief; this is also a Stewardship decree. 9. God sees, as a consequence of his decrees of election and reprobation, the Elect steadfast in Faith to the end, and thus he ordains them to Eternal Life; the reprobate he sees persisting in their unbelief and impenitence; and foreseeing this, he condemns them to Eternal Death. This decree is from God as Judge.
