<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "Divine Decrees"—the logical order of God's plan for salvation and creation. Following the presentation of various theological systems on the previous page, the author now provides five rules for evaluating these systems and outlines the specific order he considers most biblically sound. This view aligns with "Infralapsarianism," a standard Reformed position where God's decree to save some follows his foresight of the Fall of man.</meta>

# THE CHRISTIAN <note>The full header likely reads "The Christian Theology."</note>

...teaches; and not that which our reason suggests; for no one can teach us better what God has done than God himself.

2. One must always pay attention to the concept of a perfect being, and establish no order that is contrary to God’s Wisdom and Holiness.

3. One must carefully note that in this order, no decrees are established that run counter to one another.

4. One must consider the manner in which God has executed his decrees in time.

5. In the decrees, one must carefully and accurately distinguish the causes, the means, what precedes, and the circumstances; these things must not be confused.

According to these Rules, we believe that the most proper order—the one most consistent with Scripture, the most becoming to God, and the one most corresponding to his perfections—is this:

1. That God set out to make known his virtues, his wisdom, power, and other adorable attributes.

2. That he, to that end, decided to Create a World, and in it, intelligent beings who would know and love him, give him honor and homage, and proclaim his virtues and perfections; and among these intelligent beings, men: for we could not believe, nor understand, that God would have decided to do anything regarding man without first having decided to Create him; and this is also what God first accomplished.

3. We then understand that God decided to Create man in a state of righteousness; but nevertheless in a state in which he could change; and to permit that he should fall from the state of his righteousness into sin, and that sin would pass on to his descendants.

4. That God, foreseeing from eternity the fall of 

<column-break/>

man, and seeing the entire human race guilty in Sin and in Death, has out of his Grace chosen some, for whom he has ordained Salvation, while he decided to leave the others in their own ruin and misery.

5. That God decided to send his Son to satisfy <note>original: "voldoen," referring to the theological concept of "satisfaction" or "atonement," where Christ pays the debt of sin to fulfill God's justice.</note> his Justice, and to earn Eternal Life and Glory for those for whom he had ordained Salvation, because his justice did not allow him to ordain Salvation for anyone without being satisfied.

6. That God, knowing that the satisfaction of his Son would be of no use if it were not known and accepted by those for whom Christ has satisfied, decided to let these Saving truths be preached to men; and through the preaching of his word, to gather a congregation, and subsequently to give his Spirit to those for whom his Son died; so that he might produce in them faith and other Christian and moral virtues.

7. Finally, that God decided to eventually give Glory and Immortality to those he has Elected <note>The "Uitverkozen," those chosen by God for salvation.</note>, for whom his Son will have obtained Salvation through the merits of his Death, and whom his Spirit will have sanctified; whereas he decided to punish the impenitent Sinners, who will have lived in Sin, with eternal punishments: which God shall also finally accomplish.

Henceforth we shall follow this order, which we believe to be the most proper and to correspond most with the ideas that Scripture gives us; and following this design, we shall first speak of the Creation of the World, of the Creatures that are in it, of the Angels, and of Man.

# THE CHRISTIAN
<note>The header continues from the title "The Christian Theology."</note>

teaches; and not that which our reason suggests; for no one can teach us better what God has done than God himself.

2. One must always pay attention to the concept of a perfect being and establish no order that is contrary to God’s Wisdom and Holiness.

3. One must carefully note that in this order, one does not establish decrees that conflict with one another.

4. One must consider the manner in which God has executed his decrees in time.

5. One must, in the decrees, carefully and accurately distinguish the causes, the means, the precedents, and the occasions; these things must not be confused.

According to these Rules, we believe that the most proper order—the most conforming with Scripture, the most becoming to God, and the most consistent with his perfections—is this:

1. That God intended to make known his <term>virtues</term><note>The original Dutch "deugden" refers here to God's attributes or divine perfections.</note>, his wisdom, power, and other adorable qualities.

2. That he, to that end, decided to Create a World, and within it rational beings who would know and love him, do him honor and homage, and proclaim his virtues and perfections; and among these rational beings, humans: for we could not believe, nor understand, that God would have decided to do anything regarding man without first having decided to Create him; and this God also fulfilled first.

3. We understand subsequently that God decided to Create man in the <term>state of uprightness</term><note>Refers to "Staat der regtheid," the theological concept of humanity's original moral perfection before the Fall.</note>; but nonetheless in a state in which he could change; and to permit that he should fall out of the state of his uprightness into sin, and that sin would pass unto his descendants.

4. That God, from eternity

<column-break/>

foreseeing the fall of man, and the entire human race being guilty in Sin and in Death, chose some out of his Grace, to whom he ordained Salvation, while he decided to leave the others in their own ruin and misery.

5. That God decided to send his Son to satisfy his Justice, and to earn Eternal Life and Glory for those to whom he had ordained Salvation, because his justice did not allow him to ordain Salvation for anyone without being <term>satisfied</term><note>In this context, "satisfied" refers to the theological doctrine of atonement, where the penalty for sin is paid to fulfill divine justice.</note>.

6. That God, knowing that the satisfaction of his Son would be of no use if it were not known and accepted by those for whom Christ has satisfied, decided to have these Saving truths proclaimed to men, and through the preaching of his word, to gather a congregation, and subsequently to give his Spirit to those for whom his Son died; so that he would bring forth in them faith and other Christian and Moral virtues.

7. Finally, that God decided to one day give Glory and Immortality to those he has Chosen, for whom his Son shall have obtained Salvation through the merits of his Death, and whom his Spirit shall have sanctified; whereas he decided to punish with eternal punishments the impenitent Sinners who shall have lived in Sin: which God shall also fulfill at the last.

We shall henceforth follow this order, which we believe to be the most proper and most in agreement with the ideas that Scripture gives us; and following this design, we shall first speak of the Creation of the World, of the Creatures that are in it, of the Angels, and of Man.

# THE CHRISTIAN THEOLOGY;
## FIFTH BOOK.
### Of Creation.
### CHAPTER I.

->On Creation in general, and that the World is not Eternal.<-

We have established in the previous Book that God first decreed to create the World; and the matter speaks for itself, for it was orderly first to think of the creation of Beings, before deciding what should be done with them.

According to this order, we now treat of Creation.

The Deity is like a Sun, whose brilliance our eyes cannot endure; its great light blinds us, and we cannot look upon it steadily without blinking. But this Sun reveals itself to us in a mirror; thus I call the Universe <note>Original: "Geheel-Al," referring to the totality of the created cosmos.</note>, in which God has impressed an excellent image of his perfections. This is what Paul says in Romans 1:20: *For since the creation of the world His invisible attributes are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even His eternal power and Godhead* etc.

<margin>Why God created Beings (or Creatures).</margin>
It does not befit us to investigate the reasons why God created Beings; we must not penetrate into God’s secrets.

It is enough to note:

1. That God—being perfect and blessed through the contemplation and enjoyment of himself—had no need of Creatures.

2. That, although God needed nothing, it was becoming of a perfect being to bring forth Creatures, over

<column-break/>

whom he could pour out his infinite goodness like a rich stream; for whom his omnipotence was continually active, and through whom his perfections were spread.

Before we speak of the Creatures that God has brought forth, it is necessary to look at Creation in general, and what is understood by the word "to Create."

We understand nothing else by it than the act of God's will, by which he made this Universe; and willed that the things which before were not, should come into being.

The word "Create" signifies in the Scriptures the making of something new by a single act of the will: and the word is used for: 1. Making something out of nothing. Genesis 1:1. *In the beginning God created the Heaven and the Earth.* 2. Making something out of a preceding, but for that purpose unsuitable, substance. Thus it is used in Genesis 1:21, 27. 3. Giving a new power to the Creatures and renewing them, Psalm 104:30. 4. Rebirth <term>wedergeboorte</term><note>The theological concept of spiritual regeneration.</note>. In this sense, a reborn person is called a new creature, Galatians 6:15; and thus David prayed in Psalm 51:10 <note>The Dutch text cites Ps. 51:12 following a different numbering system.</note>, *Create in me a clean heart.* 5. Effecting some great change or making something extraordinary, as in Numbers 16:30 and Jeremiah 31:22.

One generally distinguishes two kinds of Creation; one which has drawn things absolutely out of nothing, without preceding matter from which they could be made. Thus God created the Light, the Angels, the Spiritual Creatures, and the matter out of which all bodily things are composed. The other kind of Creation is that which makes something out of a pre-existing but unsuitable matter, which

had no capacity to receive the new form it obtained. It is indeed a wonder of Nature that a small seed produces a large tree; yet because this seed contains the tree it produces within itself, we call that a birth, and not a creation. But, for example, making a living human from a dead stone is a creation, a matter that exceeds the powers of Nature; God alone can raise children for Abraham from stones <note>A reference to Matthew 3:9, emphasizing God's power to create life where there is none.</note>. In this sense it is said that God created Man from dust, and Eve from a rib of Adam: for neither the dust nor the rib were suitable subjects to receive the form God gave them. They possessed neither the seed of the things brought forth from them, nor the arrangement and preparation that Nature requires in all subjects she wishes to clothe with a new form: so that no less power was needed for this creation than for the first: they both require an infinite strength.

<margin>Whether the World, or matter, is eternal.</margin>
Before Creation there was nothing but God alone; from this it appears that it is a grave error to imagine that the World is Eternal, or at least the matter from which the World is composed. Most Heathens <note>Referring here to non-Christian philosophers of antiquity.</note> believed in the Eternity of the <margin>Aristotle.</margin> World. Some, whose imagination was lost in the vast expanses of the Universe, believed that the World must always have been, because they could not conceive of a power capable of making so great and perfect a work, seeing its stability amidst constant changes. <margin>Pythagoras, Anaxagoras, Socrates, Plato.</margin> Others believed that there was an infinitely wise Being who had set his hand to it; but that before this incomparable Master-Builder <note>Original: "Werkmeester."</note> had touched it, everything was a confused and formless lump; and therefore they acknowledged that God was the Creator of this visible World, but they thought that matter was eternal. Diodorus Siculus says <margin>Library, Book 1.</margin> the Universe was made thus: In the beginning, Heaven and Earth were mixed and had but one form; and these confused bodies being separated over time, they received the form we see; the air remained in constant motion; the fire having climbed upwards, created the Sun and Stars in the orbits in which they are; the troubled and muddy matter remained below due to its weight; finally

<column-break/>

the water separated from the Earth, which in the beginning was soft and marshy, but being made firmer by the heat of the Sun, brought forth animals.

Others, like Epicurus, denied the eternity of the World and contested it with many arguments.

<margin>Lucretius, Book 5.</margin>
Lucretius, a great follower of Epicurus, refuted the Eternity of the World with these reasonings: If Heaven and Earth had no beginning and are Eternal, why have the Poets not sung of anything beyond the war of Thebes and the destruction of Troy? Why would the memory of so many memorable deeds as must have happened been lost? Why would they not have been engraved in the eternal memory of fame? Meanwhile, if I am not mistaken, everything said of history is new; the world is only recently made, and its beginnings are not very old. That is why there are arts that are still being refined and perfected daily.

But although Epicurus and his followers were against the Eternity of the World, they were ridiculous enough to believe that the World had made itself as it is through the accidental meeting of indivisible particles <note>Original: "ondeelbare stofjes," a 17th-century term for atoms.</note>, from which they claimed everything was composed, which would have swirled here and there, without order or law, in the immeasurable and empty space.

Sound reason strongly opposes this.

We have already shown elsewhere, when proving God’s existence, that Eternity is the most excellent of all his perfections, and that it is absurd to attribute it to a being as imperfect as the matter from which the World is composed. Basil says very well <margin>Homily 2 on the Hexameron <note>Basil’s "Hexameron" is a famous series of sermons on the six days of creation.</note></margin> that it is godless to wish to equate matter with the Deity.

We have also proved that, since motion is not essential to matter, some being necessarily impressed upon matter the motion it needed to bring forth the Universe.

Thirdly, we have seen that it is evident there is some being that determined the perfections of matter and thus must have preceded it; from which it clearly follows that matter is not Eternal.

We see in matter constant change...

Certainly, one cannot deny that it is infinitely more provable that an almighty being made this Universe, expanded the Heavens, grounded the Earth, and created all that is in it; that this infinitely good being gave existence and all levels of perfection to so many different kinds of creatures; that this Supreme-wise being placed this excellent masterpiece of the Universe and all its creatures in an amazing order; than to say that the World is Eternal, or that one must attribute this exquisite building to chance. We do not attribute anything to God that includes any contradiction, but the opposite view <note>the view that the world is eternal or accidental</note> cannot be grasped by any thought.

It is a universal tradition that the World had a beginning.

<margin>
Strabo, *Geography*, Book 15. <note>original: "Strab. Geog. l. 15."</note>
</margin>

Dor. l. 1."</note></margin> Thales <note>An early Greek philosopher often called the "first philosopher."</note> said that God had made everything out of water. <margin>Aristotle, *On the Heavens*, Book 1, chapter 10. <note>original: "Arist. de coel. l. 1: c. 10."</note></margin> Aristotle testifies that all philosophers before him believed that the World had come into being.

Lucretius, Book 5. <note>original: "Lucret. l. 5."</note>

It is an unbelievable thing that the World, if it had been eternal, would not have perished already, since it is composed of so many parts that are perishable by their own nature; especially if there were no Supreme Being to prevent all the disorder that could occur. Lucretius also says that if the World had no beginning, these bodies—which are perishable by their own nature—would not have been able to withstand those harsh and violent attacks that would have been dealt to them throughout an eternal duration.

<margin>
Proofs from Scripture against the Eternity of the World.
</margin>
Scripture confirms what Reason teaches: namely, that the World is not Eternal.

1. Scripture speaks of no other Eternal being than that of God.

2. It testifies that God in the beginning created Heaven and Earth. <margin>Genesis 1:1; Revelation 4:11; Nehemiah 9:6; Colossians 1:16.</margin> Genesis 1:1—and that He created all things, Revelation 4:11, Nehemiah 9:6, things visible and invisible, Colossians 1:16.

<column-break/>

Therefore, it is surprising that some Socinians <note>A group of non-trinitarian Christians who emphasized a rationalist approach to Scripture.</note> have dared to say <margin>Volkel, *On Religion*, Book 2, chapter 4. <note>original: "Volk. de Relig. l. II. c. 4." Johannes Volkel was a leading Socinian theologian.</note></margin> that the Creation of the Earth and the water is not spoken of; as if these were not included in the visible and invisible things, and as if Moses did not say that God created Heaven and Earth.

3. VII. 28."</note></margin> in 2 Maccabees 7:28, where it is mentioned that God did not make Heaven and Earth and everything in them from things that already existed. <note>This refers to the concept of *creatio ex nihilo*, or creation out of nothing.</note>

This interpretation is much more proper than the one which claims that Paul intended to teach us nothing other than that God made all the things that are seen out of a formless matter, in which one saw nothing of what is now perceived in it, since everything was mixed together and darkness was upon the Earth. <margin>Crellius, *On Hebrews*. <note>original: "Crellius. in Hebr." Johannes Crellius was a Socinian commentator.</note></margin> 1. The Apostle would have expressed himself differently if this had been his thought. 2. "Not appearing," with respect to material things, means "not existing," and it is in this sense that this expression is used.

Nothing of any weight can be brought against this to prove the Eternity of the World.

1. It is said that one cannot understand how matter and the World could have been created.

Answer: But the eternity of matter is even more incomprehensible. Who can understand another Eternal being besides God? Although we do not grasp Eternity with our intellect, we nevertheless clearly understand that the Being we call God must have been Eternal, but we do not have the same thoughts regarding matter. As soon as one posits something else as Eternal besides God, one posits another God; for whoever says "Eternal" says a being that exists necessarily and is independent.

2. It is said: "Out of nothing, nothing comes." <note>original: "uit niet / komt niet" - referring to the Latin maxim *ex nihilo nihil fit*.</note>

I answer: naturally speaking, nothing comes from nothing here, because every natural cause, being finite, must have a subject upon which it works. But one must not judge God as one judges natural causes; that which cannot happen naturally can happen through God's infinite [power...]

<meta>This page continues the theological defense of the biblical account of Creation. Having previously established that the world had a beginning according to universal tradition and ancient philosophers, the author now addresses specific logical and philosophical objections raised by atheists and rationalists, including Spinoza.</meta>

### THEOLOGY. Book 5. Chapter 1. ###

done by [divine] power. The power of man or of nature is not the measure of the power of God. One cannot say, then, that nature and men cannot produce something from nothing; rather, one must reason: if nature and man can make many things with very little material, then God, who has infinitely more power, can make everything out of nothing.

Furthermore, one must observe that when we say God created the world out of nothing, it does not mean that "nothing" was the starting material from which God made the world—as a potter makes a vessel from clay. Instead, it means that God brought forth a substance that did not exist before. Atheists have never proven that this was an impossible thing.

3. It is said that there is such an opposition and infinite distance between *being* and *not-being* that it is impossible for something to come out of nothing. I answer: 1. This infinite distance only proves that "nothing" and "something" cannot exist at the same time or simultaneously. But that does not prove that something cannot be created where nothing was before. 2. This distance between being and not-being is overcome by God's infinite power.

Parmenides <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher known for the idea that "nothing comes from nothing."</note>, according to the account of Simplicius <note>A 6th-century commentator on Aristotle.</note>, reasoned thus:
> "If any thing made itself out of nothing, there would be no cause that would have made it exist when it began to be; nor any reason why it was not sooner or later."

But this reasoning was groundless, for we clearly understand that an Eternal cause made what we see, and did so when it pleased Him.

Spinoza <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), a Dutch philosopher who argued that God and Nature are the same substance, often accused of atheism by his contemporaries.</note> says that a being that exists through itself cannot have its existence from another being. But he deceived himself greatly: a being that exists through itself, independent of all other beings—as God is—has its existence from no other; but God alone is such a being. Other things exist in themselves independent of accidents <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are properties that can change without changing the essence of a thing.</note>, but they are dependent on God; therefore, they are created by Him.

It is said that one must judge the state and nature of the world at its birth as one judges the world already born; in every birth there is a subject <note>A pre-existing substance or matter.</note> that leaves one form to take on another;

<column-break/>

Thus, it is said, there must have been a subject before the world became what it is, which, leaving the form it then had, acquired that of the world as it is today. 
**Answer:** One must not believe that the first change that gave existence to the world—or how the world came to be—is of the same nature as the productions and births that occur now that the world exists. In nature, as it is now established, the present always follows the past; but it was not the same in the first establishment of nature, when things were first brought forth. When we breathe, there is no breath that was not preceded by another; but when we first begin to draw breath, the first is not preceded by any other.

It is said that we have no concept of Creation.

I answer that we do not have clear concepts of everything; we do not know how our Soul acts upon our Body. It is not possible that a finite being should understand everything that an infinite being does.

It is said that from time to time, overflows, floods, and fires have occurred, which destroyed humans and beasts and completely erased the memory of countless things, so that it is no wonder history seems so recent. But these are merely imaginings. Moses describes the Great Flood, but at the same time says that God created the world. Have these floods and fires then destroyed all the cities, all the temples, all the burial places, pillars, and monuments with which the "old world" they speak of was filled?

It is therefore certain that neither the world nor matter are eternal; the Jewish teachers say: before God created the world, there was only God and His name.

<margin>Rabbi Eliezer ben Israel. See Menasseh [ben Israel], *On Creation*, Problem 3. <note>original: "Rabbi Eliezer ben Israël. Vide Menassé de Creat. Probl. 3." Menasseh ben Israel was a prominent 17th-century Rabbi in Amsterdam.</note></margin>
The question is asked: could the world not have been created from eternity?

I answer: these are two contradictory things—to say that the world is created and that it is eternal. "Created" is as much as to say "having begun to be"; now, everything that has begun is not eternal.

It is said that the world came forth from God like rays from the sun; and that just as the sun was never without its rays, so God was never without...

## CHAPTER II.

### That God Alone Was Able to Create the World, and Has Created It.

Although we could already conclude from what has been said that God created the world, we shall nevertheless set this truth in a clearer light.

There have been philosophers, such as the Epicureans <note>Followers of Epicurus who believed the world was formed by the random collision of atoms rather than divine intent.</note>, who, while recognizing the novelty <note>meaning: the recent beginning</note> of the world, nonetheless did not want the world to be God's work; instead, they claimed it was chance that had made it. We have countered this extravagance elsewhere.

Many heretics in the 1st Century—Simon the Sorcerer and Menander—said that the world was created by the Angels. In the 2nd Century, Saturninus said that the world was created by seven Angels.

There have been heretics, namely the Valentinians and Marcionites <note>Gnostic groups who believed the physical world was inferior or evil.</note>, who, while denying the eternity of the world, 

<column-break/>

claimed that it was created not by the Father of our Lord JESUS Christ, but by some other evil deity whom they regarded as the cause of matter and (which is terrifying) of sin.

But they are all refuted by Scripture and by reason.

Scripture recognizes no other God than the God of Israel, who is the Creator of the world and the Father of Jesus Christ. And reason teaches us, as well as Scripture, that God cannot be the cause of sin.

Reason teaches us that God alone can pull everything out of nothing and do all these wonders that we daily marvel at, without ever being able to marvel at them enough.

<margin>Ps. 89:9, 12, 13.</margin>
Scripture confirms this truth everywhere. Psalm 89:8 <note>Numbered as vs. 9 in the original Dutch text.</note>: "O Lord, God of hosts, who is like unto thee?" and verses 11–12 <note>Numbered as 12–13 in the original.</note>: 
> The heaven is thine, the earth also is thine, the world and the fullness thereof, thou hast founded them; the north and the south, thou hast created them.

<margin>Ps. 121:2.</margin>
Psalm 121:2: 
> My help is from the Lord who made heaven and earth.

<margin>Prov. 3:19.</margin>
Proverbs 3:19: 
> The Lord by wisdom hath founded the earth; by understanding hath he established the heavens.

<margin>Isa. 45:12.</margin>
"I have," says God in Isaiah 45:12, 
> made the earth, and I have created man upon it; it is I, my hands have stretched out the heavens, and I have given the command to all their host.

<margin>Job 9:8. Isa. 45:24.</margin>
The name of Creator of the World is a title of praise that belongs to God alone; Scripture also attributes it to him alone as a sign that distinguishes him from the false deities that the Heathens worship. "To whom then will you liken me?" God asks in Isaiah 

<margin>Isa. 40:25, 26.</margin>
Isaiah 40:25–26, after he had spoken of the idolatry of those who made images for themselves to represent the Deity: 
> Lift up your eyes on high, and see who hath created these things, that bringeth out their host by number, who calleth them all by names, etc.

<margin>Jer. 10:11, 12.</margin>

### DIVINITY. Vol. V. Book II. Chapter.

...who calls things that are not as though they were. Romans 4:17.

The Heathens <note>The author uses "Heathens" to refer to the ancient Greeks and other non-Christian philosophers of antiquity.</note> have known and acknowledged this, as can be proven through *Sophocles*, and through the poems of *Pythagoras*, who are cited by the Early Church Fathers. The first says, "There is one sole God, who made the Heaven and this wide-stretched Earth." The second says further: if anyone wishes to be held as a god, and wants to be called God, he must attempt to make a world <margin>Dissertation 35</margin> like this one, which he can call his world. *Maximus Tyrius* says that it was the will of Jupiter <note>The Roman name for the supreme deity, often used by early modern writers to refer to the concept of God in a classical context.</note> who had made all things.

<margin>The attribute of Creating is incommunicable to the Creature.</margin>
The attribute of Creating is so uniquely God's own that He cannot communicate <note>In theology, an "incommunicable" attribute is a quality of God—like infinity or the power to create from nothing—that cannot be shared with or given to any created being.</note> it to a Creature: we maintain this against the Scholastic Theologians <note>original: "School-God-Geleerden." These were medieval university scholars who used logic and philosophy to explain Christian doctrine.</note>, who believed the opposite. Such as *Durandus* (on Book 2, distinction 1, question 4), *Lombardus* (in Book 4, distinction 5, final chapter), and others brought up by *Vasquez* (disputation 176, chapter 1). Two or three arguments leave us with no doubt.

1. That which requires an infinite power is certainly incommunicable to the Creature, which is finite; now, to Create something out of nothing, solely through the will, is a work of an infinite power, beyond which nothing can be conceived.

2. God assures us that He gives His Glory to no other; but He would be giving His Glory to Creatures if He communicated an infinite power to them.

3. If a Creature Created, the thing that was to be created would exist either because God willed it to exist, or because God had given such power to the Creature that as soon as it commanded something, the thing would immediately exist without God doing anything further; or the thing would be created against God’s will, or without God performing any work therein. If the thing being created is present because God wills it to be present, then it is God who Creates, and not the Creature. One cannot say that God has given the Creature the power to do whatever pleases it through a single act of its will: for a Creature cannot possess such a power. One cannot say that the thing would be created in spite of God, for it is impossible that anything should happen against the will of God, as if He were not powerful enough to prevent it. Finally,

<column-break/>

one cannot say that the thing is created without God concerning Himself with it; for, as we shall see in what follows, it is absurd to suppose that God, who is an all-wise being, would not govern everything through His providence.

It also contradicts our understanding that instruments could have a place in Creation; for Creation happens through the single will of the Creator.

1. *Objection.* Creatures can co-operate to perform miracles. But (1.) in miracles, one presupposes a subject <note>In this context, a "subject" refers to pre-existing matter or a person upon which the miracle is performed, such as water being turned to wine.</note> upon which an instrument can act; whereas in Creation there is no subject. (2.) It is false that the power to perform miracles is communicated to the Creature: although God has often performed miracles in the presence of Creatures.

God alone, then, has created the World and all that is in it.

Those who do not want to admit that God created the World say that some change would have occurred in God if He had created the World, because doing and Creating is something different than not doing and not Creating.

I answer: That one must not judge God as one judges men; we can in no way work or move without some change occurring within us, but it is not so with God; in God, to will is the same as to do; He moves all things without being moved; all change is not within, but outside of God. There has been a World where previously there was none. The names of Creator and Sustainer of the World, which we give Him as a consequence of this deed, signify only the relationship that the World has to the will and power of God. "But," it is said, "did God not then will something that He previously did not will, or did not will sooner?" No; God has willed from Eternity that the World should come to be in time.

It is said: things that have nothing in common cannot be the cause of one another. God being a Spirit, He could not have Created the World <note>This objection suggests that a non-physical spirit could not produce a physical, material world.</note>.

I answer: It is false that an infinite being would not be able to bring forth whatever pleases Him.

Because God created the World, it follows that the World is not God, as the Stoics and Spinoza asserted. I have already refuted this opinion elsewhere.

### CHAPTER III.

->That the three Persons of the Trinity created the Universe.<-

Since we have said in the preceding Books that there are three Persons in the Trinity, the question may be asked whether Creation is the work of the three persons, or of one person?

If we consult the Scripture, which is our rule of conduct, we shall find that the three Persons, who have the same essence, came together in this work. It is true, Creation is particularly attributed to the Father, just as Redemption is to the Son, and Sanctification to the Holy Spirit. But this same Creation is nonetheless ascribed to the Son and the Holy Spirit.

<margin>
John 1:1, 2, 3.
Origen, *Against Celsus*, Book 6.
Athanasius, *Oration 4 against the Arians*.
Hilary of Poitiers, *On the Trinity*, Book 4.
</margin>
With regard to the Son, John teaches us, as we have proven elsewhere, John 1:1 and 3: *In the beginning was the Word; and all things were made through the same.* For he makes a clear allusion to the words of Moses, who presents God to us as creating the World through his word. It is true that no one would have been able to understand this mystery if John had not revealed it to us.

<margin>What is the word through which the World was made?</margin>
One cannot say that it is a spoken word, or Voice, uttered by God Himself; for at the time when there was as yet nothing, of what use would this distinct voice have been, and who could have understood it?

(a) To signify the origin of the World, the Egyptians depicted God as producing an egg from his mouth. The Syrians and Phoenicians also represented their gods,

<column-break/>

who were the Stars among them, as coming forth from an egg. The Indians and Chinese have also had such sentiments, according to the accounts of some travelogues. <note>This note (a) combines the fragment at the bottom of column 1 and the translator's note at the end of the original page regarding ancient creation myths.</note>

One cannot say that this word was a command; for a command, comprised of words, must be given to Creatures capable of receiving the command. One objects that Christ spoke to Lazarus, who was dead. But 1. Lazarus existed <note>original: "was in wezen." Meaning he had an ontological soul or body, unlike the void before creation.</note>, though he was dead. 2. Christ spoke thus for the sake of the bystanders.

One cannot say that one must understand a deed of God's will by it; for if Moses had meant nothing else, it would not have been necessary to repeat it so often: who can believe that God, producing everything by His power, did not desire it and did not think of it?

<margin>Matt. 8:8.</margin>
One cannot say either that the Historian <note>The author refers to Moses as the historian or author of Genesis.</note> intended to teach us that God used no tools to create the Universe; but created everything with as little effort as a work that costs but a word, just as that Man in the Gospel said to Christ, Matt. 8:8: *Only speak a word, and my servant shall be healed.* For if Moses meant nothing else, why use so many detours? Why not say in one word: all things were made by a single act of God's will? Why is he not satisfied with saying that once or twice? Indeed, if there is no mystery in it, then one cannot tolerate this repetition. But John explains the mystery of it to us, John 1:1, etc.

This cannot be understood as the wind, as some Jews—including Menasseh Ben Israel, Maimonides, and Ibn Ezra (Commentary on this passage)—and some Christians have believed. This is because there was as yet no air, nor any exhalation which, driven by its own motion or from elsewhere, moved the air. It is said that Moses showed the Earth so mixed with water that the Earth could not be seen, so that it was necessary for the wind, according to its natural power, to dry the Earth—just as that power is attributed to the wind in the passage through the Red Sea and in Psalm 147:18. But first, it does not matter whether we know if the wind has the power to dry, or if the Red Sea was opened by a drying caused by the wind; the question is whether there was wind in the beginning. Second, in Psalm 147:18, there is nothing that resembles this: it says there that the waters flow away and create streams; this refers to the waters of winter ice and snow, which the spring wind melts into water, creating entire floods—which is the exact opposite of drying. King Solomon (apparently the author of this Psalm) understands the waters that flow when the frost ceases. It is true that waters create a dryness by flowing away, but there must be a place for the flowing waters to go; however, this cannot be applied to the passage in Genesis. For the Earth being covered with water, the waters flowing from one place would have found no other empty place to be received; and a violent wind would have only raised the waves in one place and cast them down in another, without drying anything.

Those who have said that God let the wind blow over the waters so that they would not stink have failed to notice that heat is the cause of rot, and that there was not yet any heat, since the Sun had not yet been created. Some scholars note this, while others add that one reads nowhere in Scripture

<column-break/>

that the wind is called by this name <note>Referring to the specific Hebrew word for Spirit/Wind used in Genesis 1:2.</note>. Genesis 1:6.

God created the World when He judged it to be the right time, and in such a manner as was most appropriate for the manifestation of His Wisdom, Power, and Goodness: so that one, seeing the World, judges it to be a masterpiece worthy of so excellent a Master-builder.

<margin>
What God
did before
He
created the
World.
</margin>
It is ridiculous to ask why God did not choose to create the World earlier or later; for if He had created it earlier or later, one would have always asked the same thing. It is an impudent boldness for the creature to criticize the actions of its Creator.

It is also ungodly to ask what God did before He created the World. The story is told of an old man’s answer to a scoffer who asked him what God did before He created the World. He answered, "God made hell for the curious." Should one not say that God depends on the creature, and can do nothing at all without it? "Before the world was made," says a learned man very well, "God enjoyed Himself, and lived in His unapproachable light; the World has neither established nor disturbed His rest; it added nothing to, nor took anything from, His happiness. That which moved Him to create is for our sake, not for His own state of happiness—to pour out His Goodness outside of Himself, and not to increase His own contentment; to make us partakers of His benefits, and not to draw any advantage from ours."

Time began with the World: for time is nothing other than the successive duration of all produced things, and it is customary to determine it by the apparent motion of the Heavens, because this duration is the most constant, consistent, and generally known of all, and thus the most fit to measure all other motions.

## CHAPTER IV.

### On the Works of Creation.

<margin>
Whether the World was created in an instant, or a point of time?
<note>original: "Phil. lib. de Alleg. leg. Moſ. Maim. apud." — Philo, in his book *On the Allegories of the Laws of Moses*; Maimonides as cited therein.</note>
</margin>

Before I speak of the Works of Creation, I shall answer four questions.

I. Whether the World was created in an instant, or in six days?

I answer: The account of Moses does not allow us to believe that it was in a single instant, as many have believed; for he makes mention of six days and records the work of each day. We see no reason to explain this in an allegorical way, as some <term>Church Fathers</term><note>Early Christian theologians, such as Augustine, who often interpreted the six days of creation symbolically rather than literally.</note> did, which is sufficiently evident from the fact that it is said, "the Earth was void and empty, and darkness was upon the abyss." This could not be said if all things had been completed in a single point

<column-break/>

of time. <margin><note>original: "Ps. X. Procop. Gazæus. Auguſt." — Reference to a Psalm, Procopius of Gaza, and Augustine.</note></margin> Why, <term>My Reader</term><note>The author uses "M. Ben." likely for "Myn Beminden" or "My Beloved/Dear Reader."</note>, would it be said in the Fourth Commandment that God hallowed the Sabbath because He created the World in six days and rested on the seventh, if the World had been created in an instant?

One must not say that it is more fitting for God to make everything in a single point of time. It is no more difficult, nor less glorious for Him, to create the World in six days than in an instant.

One must also not say that God created everything in an instant because He can destroy everything in an instant; for there is no logical consequence from one to the other; besides, it is not a matter of what God *could* have done, but what He *did*.

The passage from <term>Ecclesiasticus</term> XVIII, 1 <note>The author calls this an "irregular book" because it is part of the Apocrypha/Deuterocanon, books not included in the standard Hebrew or Protestant Bibles.</note> causes no difficulty, despite being drawn from an irregular book.

It says there: "The King, who lives eternally, created all things together," or equally. For that is to say: God created the one as well as the other—all of them, none excepted.

One argues against this with Genesis II, 4: "These are the generations of the Heavens and of the Earth when they were created, in the day that the LORD God made the Earth and the Heavens." As if everything was made in one day; but the word "day" here does not mean what we call a day, but time in general; otherwise, Moses would have contradicted himself.

<margin>
Whether every work of God was created [instantaneously]?
</margin>

The second question is whether all the works of God were created without any passage of time?

This question is not so easily solved, and is also of little importance. I would be inclined to side with those who consider that some things were created in an instant—namely, everything that was made out of nothing, for the transition from non-being to being requires no interval of time. But those things made from a substance that already existed were not made without the passage of time, such as the drying of the Earth and the gathering of the waters into one place; for the waters cannot move from one place to another in an instant.

<margin>
Whether God created some creatures a long time before others?
</margin>

The third question is whether there are creatures that God created a long time before the others.

I answer: That God created the Universe in six days; there is no appearance that the Creation of Heaven and Earth...

### THEOLOGY. V. B. IV. Chapter 309

Earth Gen. 1:1, the following proceeded for more than a day.

<margin>Whether God used the Angels to Create the World.</margin>
The fourth question is whether God used the ministry of the Angels in the Creation of the World, or at least for some of the works?

I answer: That the Scripture attributes the Creation solely to God alone. The Angels do not have enough power to do what Moses relates, and God has no need for the ministry of any Angel, because all of nature obeys Him.

After having answered these four questions, I come to the works of Creation; for it is the most unfitting of all absurdities to consider the account of Creation as a parable or a fiction, like those produced by the Heathens, of which the wisest among them were ashamed.

<margin>Gen. 1:1. The Works of the first day.</margin>
1. The Works of the first day are the Heaven—both the Starry Heaven as well as God's Throne and the Seat of His Glory, and the uppermost part of the World, where the Angels and happy Spirits reside before their Creator. There are scholars who believe that the Starry Heaven was created on the second day.

<margin>Gerhard, Calovius, Vossius, etc. <note>Johann Gerhard, Abraham Calovius, and Gerardus Vossius were influential 17th-century Lutheran and Reformed theologians.</note></margin>
2. The Earth, which had no inhabitants nor ornament with which we now see it clothed; everything was surrounded and mixed with water, from which it appears that we do not believe that by "Heaven and Earth" the <term>Chaos</term><note>original: "Bajert" - an old Dutch term for a confused, formless mass.</note> should be understood, as some have believed, including many Heathens. Never does "Heaven and Earth" mean the Chaos in Scripture, except that Chaos or "Bajert" signifies a confused mass: but here the Heaven is distinguished from the Earth, and our opinion is the most common one, and was that of the Early Church Fathers.

<margin>Tertullian, *Against Hermogenes* ch. 19, 25. Lactantius. Ambrose. Athanasius. Chrysostom. Thomas Burnet, *Archaeologiae*.</margin>
It is a daydream to believe that by "Heaven and Earth" indivisible particles <note>referring to atoms</note> must be understood; but it is no less extravagant to claim that the Earth in the beginning was only a crust, directly opposite the rays of the Sun which burned it; that there were neither Mountains nor Rivers until the time of the Flood; that this crust then opening up, many parts fell down and left room for the water; and others were raised up and made Mountains; while others, remaining in their first position, made plains, valleys, and deserts <note>This is a critique of Thomas Burnet’s "Sacred Theory of the Earth," a popular but controversial 17th-century attempt to explain geology via the Bible.</note>: for when one reads Genesis, one clearly sees that the Sea was created on the third day,

<column-break/>

and if one consults Job, the Psalms, Proverbs, etc., one finds that the Mountains have existed from the beginning. <margin>Job 15:7; Proverbs 8:25; Psalm 90:2.</margin>

3. When darkness was upon the face of the Deep (thus the historian <note>Moses, traditionally considered the author of Genesis.</note> calls this terrifying multitude of waters, or rather this mass composed of Earth and Water together), it pleased God to create the Light. One asks: what was Light? The most certain thing is to say that we do not well know.

Some Philosophers have believed that it was a thin substance that moved violently and alternately illuminated one or the other hemisphere; others that it was a brilliant or luminous quality that God had impressed upon all the external parts of the Heavens on the first day, etc. Others have other thoughts.

For the rest, it is without foundation that some believe God created Heaven and Earth a long time before the other creatures; and who therefore translate Gen. 1:1 as: *Before God created Heaven and Earth, the Earth was empty,* etc.

Certainly, God could not begin better than with light, which makes all that we can know of God seen in His works; which makes life sweet through the wonderful variety of objects that it continually presents to the human understanding by means of the senses; and is an excellent symbol of God, the Father of Lights, of the Son, who is the Light of the World, and of the Holy Spirit, who is a Spirit of Light.

Some Jews believe that all Souls were created with the Light.

<margin>The Works of the second day.</margin>
The works of the second day are: 1. The <term>firmament</term><note>original: "uitspanzel" - the expanse of the sky.</note>, which comprises the space from the surface of the globe to the outermost part of the visible Heaven.

<margin>Gen. 1:6. Job 26:8. Ps. 104:3. Jer. 10:13.</margin>
2. The separation of the upper waters—that is, of the clouds and the vapors which are placed in the upper region of the Air—from the lower waters, which are the waters of the Rivers, Fountains, and Seas. The firmament served for that purpose, namely to separate the upper from the lower waters: for, although it is said that the upper waters were above the firmament, one must not understand it as if they were over the entire firmament, but over a part, as appears from the idiom of the original Text.

According to this view / the second day would not lack a blessing. Others approve of these thoughts ; and believe / that the reason / why this day did not have its particular blessing / is / because what God began on this day / was not finished. And these place it in the works of the IIIrd day.

<margin>The Works of the third day. Gen. I. 9.</margin>

There are Jews / who believe / that the Stars are animated : that Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize Torah with Greek philosophy.</note> believed / and Maimonides <note>A preeminent medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher.</note> says / in his *Book of the Foundations of Faith* / chapter 3. that all Stars and Heavenly Spheres have a soul / knowledge / understanding / and lasting life ; that they know him / by whose word the Universe <note>original: "Geheel-Al"</note> became ; that each of these creatures praises their Creator / that they know themselves / that the Angels are above them / but that they are above Mankind. Because it is written Job XXV. 5. *The Stars are not pure in his eyes.* <note>The author is quoting a common theological argument of the time which used this verse to suggest celestial bodies might be moral agents.</note> But those are absurd opinions / which one refutes merely by recounting them.

The Scripture teaches us the various uses / for which the Stars serve.

1. To distinguish day and night by their various light. Gen. I. 18.

2. To distinguish the Seasons.

3. To work through their heat and light.

The Stars are called Signs / because they divide the year into Seasons / Spring, Autumn, Summer, and Winter ; and indicate the Sowing and Mowing time / etc. Possibly also / because they marked the time of the solemn Feasts.

<margin>Against Astrology <note>original: "Sterre-wiggelary" — "wiggelarij" implies divination or sorcery.</note>.</margin>
Meanwhile, it is not to be thought / that they are called Signs / as if they made known / what must happen to Man. That was the opinion of the Priscillianists <note>A 4th-century heretical sect in Spain and Gaul.</note>, who said / that the Fate of all Men was written in the Stars ; and it is also the opinion of those who defend <term>Astrology</term> <note>original: "Planeetkunde," which today means planetary science, but historically referred to judicial astrology.</note> / that one can certainly predict our good or bad fortune through the Stars / if one knows the hour of our birth.

But that opinion is absurd.

1. God reserves for himself alone the knowledge of the future / as appears from Isaiah XLI. 21. 22. 23. Also Daniel says of God / that he reveals the secrets. Daniel II. 28. Therefore, wanting to know the future / is wanting to intrude into that which God has hidden from Mankind.

2. God even mocks the vanity of this science / Isaiah XLVII. 13. *You (namely Babylon) have become weary in the multitude of your counsels, let now those stand up who observe the Heaven, who look into the Stars, who predict by the new Moons,* etc.

3. The Church Fathers have condemned this art. Græc."</note>

<margin>Code concerning Sorcerers and Mathematicians, etc. <note>original: "Cod. de Malet. & Math. &c." Refers to the "Codex de maleficis et mathematicis" in Roman law, where "mathematicians" was a common term for astrologers.</note></margin>
4. The Roman Emperors acted harshly against the astrologers. Augustus banished them from Rome; Tiberius and Claudius from Italy; Vitellius ordered them to be put to death. The Law of Art <note>This likely refers to the "art" of divination or a specific legal article.</note>, which is that of Diocletian and Maximian, says that astrology is an accursed art and is entirely forbidden. Constans and Julian, in the Roman Laws, forbid consulting astrologers, soothsayers, and diviners under penalty of death. Honorius and Theodosius willed that the astrologers be banished from Rome and other cities, and if they do not repent, that they be moved to far-distant places to end their days there. (*On the Jurisdiction of Bishops, Code of Laws.*) <note>original: "L. Mathemat. Cod. de Episcop. Audient."</note>

5. It is a very ridiculous imagination to think that the free will of man depends on any constellations; and to believe that an astronomer, who cannot predict whether it will be heat or cold, or whether the weather will be dry or rainy, could foresee that a Polycrates <note>The tyrant of Samos who was famously crucified.</note> will be crucified; that a Croesus <note>The wealthy king of Lydia who faced execution by Cyrus.</note> will be in the extreme danger of losing his life by a violent death; that a Socrates will die from poisonous hemlock; an Aeschylus from the fall of a tortoise; <note>Legend says the playwright Aeschylus died when an eagle dropped a tortoise on his bald head.</note> an Alexander by poison; another by the sword; that one shall be learned and the other ignorant; that one shall go from being a shepherd to a King, and the other from a King to a schoolmaster; one rich, the other poor.

6. What likelihood is there that a hundred thousand people, possibly born in the same hour and under the same birth sign, share the same fate? And that, although born of parents whose constitution, years, morals, and status are very different, they would have the same inclinations, the same way of life, the same fortunes, and die at the same moment and in the same manner?

7. What likelihood is there that all those who die in a war, in a shipwreck, or from a general plague, would have had the same point of birth? That all the firstborn of the Egyptians, killed by the Angel of Destruction; that all the Egyptians who drowned in the Red Sea; that all the children of Bethlehem whom Herod put to death; that all those Galileans whose blood Pilate mixed with the sacrifices, would have had the same planet or celestial alignment?

But it is enough to have refuted an error whose vanity everyone will experience sooner or later; although astronomers sometimes guess some things by chance, even without following the rules of their art.

<margin>Genesis I: 20, etc. The Works of the fifth Day.</margin>
The work of the fifth day was the production of the water creatures, the fish, and the birds. God willed to make another sort of mechanical bodies, far more excellent than the plants; He willed to create animals which, as well as they, had the power of growing and reproducing; but above that, the power of moving and acting in countless encounters, almost as we do. The composition of these bodies was wonderful, both in terms of the delicacy of the parts of which they had to consist, and because of their number, variety, and perfect union. God began with the creation of the animals with which the air and the water were to be filled.

God then commanded the waters to receive in their womb and to form bodies that had the power of movement within them, in the most imperfect way of all, which consists in gliding and crawling.

At the same time, God commanded the air to be filled with such bodies that also had the power of movement within them; but with a movement as swift and varied as that of the fish was meant to be slow and steady.

<margin>Genesis I: 24. The Works of the sixth day.</margin>
But, since the Earth, which was to be the chief object of the care of her Creator, still had no ornament other than plants, God willed that she, like the air, should also have animals. Therefore, on the sixth day, He commanded her to bring forth an innumerable number of animals, which had as much relation to the Earth as the birds to the air and the fish to the water. <margin>Use of the instruction of Creation.</margin>
This section provides us with excellent lessons.

1. One cannot but highly esteem God's perfections; one sees his **Goodness** manifest in the Creation / his **Wisdom** in the order / his **Fullness** and the **Riches of his Glory**, in the abundance and variety of things / that are in the World / his **constancy** in the duration of what he has brought forth / and his **power**, by which he has drawn all these wonders out of nothing.

2. By observing the Creatures we must elevate ourselves to him / who made them; and not misuse any of them / to the disdain of him who created them for his honor.

3. In our needs and necessities we must observe / that we are Children of him / who created all the goods of the **Universe** / the Riches of Heaven and Earth.

4. Let us think / when we see no human help / nor any second cause remaining for our assistance / that God calls the things / which are not / as if they were.

5. When we are in turmoil and perplexity / let us observe / that God brought forth the **Universe** out of the confusion of the Earthly mass.

6. When we are in the dismal night of adversities / oppressions / and sorrows / we must place our hope and trust in God / who / having drawn the light out of darkness / will make his light shine in our darknesses.

## CHAPTER V.

->Of the Creation of the Angels, and of their Nature.<-

<margin>Were the Angels created by God?</margin>
Since the Scripture often speaks of Angels, it is necessary to know whether they were created by God: for I shall not dwell on proving against the Sadducees that Angels exist. <note>The Sadducees were a Jewish sect during the Second Temple period known for denying the resurrection and the existence of spirits.</note>

In Acts 23:8, it is said that the Sadducees claimed there is neither Angel nor Spirit. It is almost incomprehensible that the Jews, who believed in the Books of Moses and (according to the account of Josephus) <note>Flavius Josephus was a 1st-century Jewish historian.</note> denied all that was written, could deny that there were Angels; this has given scholars cause to investigate what their meaning might have been. Some have said that the Sadducees believed that when the Scripture speaks of Angels, it either means God appearing in a human form, or the good inclinations that God gives to men.

<margin><gloss>Instincts</gloss></margin>
Others have said that the Sadducees did not deny that there were Angels, but only evil Angels. Others say that they only denied that the Angels were immortal beings, but rather were beings that God created and subsequently destroyed.

Whatever opinion the Sadducees may have held regarding the Angels, God's Word—the divinity of which we have proven—is so explicit on this point that it is a wonder there have been Heretics who, while accepting the Scripture, could deny such an established truth: all the more because there is nothing in it that offends reason—to believe in finite beings who are spirits without

<note>(b) We have shown elsewhere that it is ridiculous to understand these words as referring to any creation other than the first.</note>

<column-break/>

bodies; just as there are beings composed of spirit and body, and bodies that are not joined with spirits.

I cannot see how it is possible that people who believe they have a spiritual Soul, and who have thoughts in which they can perceive nothing physical, refuse to recognize spiritual beings who are without a body, nor believe that God often uses the service of these spirits to carry out His commands. No one would dare to say that something which is material does not exist.

Reason and Scripture both teach us that the Angels were created by God. Both teach us that everything which is not God is created, and that Eternity is an incommunicable property of God. Reason says that, however excellent the Angels may be, they are nonetheless finite beings who, consequently not being able to exist of themselves, must necessarily recognize as their origin Him who is the beginning of all things. But the Scripture says expressly in Colossians 1:16: *For by him (namely Christ) were all things created, that are in (b) the Heavens, and that are on the Earth, visible and invisible, whether they be Thrones, or Dominions, or Principalities, or Powers: all things were created by him, and for him.*

<margin>The Angels are not created from any physical matter</margin>
It is easy to understand that the Angels, being Spirits, were not created from any matter like man: for how is it to be understood that Spirits can be drawn from a coarse and extended matter? Therefore, we view as a dream the saying of some Jews that the Angels were made from the primary substances (Elements).

Why Moses does not speak of the Creation of the Angels?
</margin>
It is no wonder that Moses does not mention the Creation of the Angels. His primary objective was to write a historical account of the Church; he speaks of no Angels except when it is necessary to describe what they have done in regard to the believers. Those who write a description of an ornate pleasure-house are not obligated to describe the neighboring peoples; they make mention of them only when it is appropriate and the occasion arises.

This is the true reason for Moses' silence; for it is ridiculous to say that Moses mentions no Angels because of the inclination the Israelites had toward Idolatry, or because they were coarse and not quick-witted enough to understand the nature of Angels. For if these reasons were valid, then Moses should never have spoken of these Heavenly Spirits, yet he does so frequently; and one does not need a more penetrating intellect to grasp that the Angels were created by God than to understand the Creation of other beings.

<margin>
Job XXXVIII. 4--7.
</margin>
It has been believed that the Angels were created on the first day, as it seems can be inferred from Job XXXVIII. 4–7: *Where were you when I laid the foundations of the Earth? Declare, if you have understanding. Who determined its measurements? Surely you know! Or who stretched the line upon it? To what were its foundations fastened? Or who laid its cornerstone, when the morning stars sang together, and all the Children of God shouted for joy?* But this reasoning is not conclusive: it would be valid if it said, "when I founded the Earth, the Children of God praised me," but it does not say that. Thus, we can say that the Angels were created after the foundation of the Earth, shortly before God caused all the waters to gather into their places; which did not happen before the third day, or, as some prefer, on the second day. Meanwhile, I do not oppose the opinion of those who believe that the Angels were possibly created at the same time as the Heavens.

The interpreters are not in agreement regarding what one should understand by the "Host of the Heavens" in Genesis II. 1—whether it means the Angels or the Stars. But even if one understood it to mean the Angels, one could

<column-break/>

not conclude from it with certainty that they were created at the same time as Heaven and Earth.

Consequently, nothing is known for certain regarding the time at which they were created, but one can be assured that they were created in great number, as can be concluded from <margin>Rev. V. 11.</margin> Revelation V. 11: *I heard the voice of many Angels around the Throne, and the Living Creatures, and the Elders; and their number was ten thousand times ten thousand, and thousands of thousands.* And from Daniel VII. 10: <margin>Matt. XXVI. 53.</margin> Matthew XXVI. 53: *A fiery stream issued and came forth from before him; a thousand thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him.*

Regarding the Nature of the Angels, the Scripture teaches us that they are Spirits. <note>Nature</note> Paul places them among the invisible things. <margin>Col. I. 16. Heb. I. 14.</margin> Colossians I. 16. Some of the Church Fathers believed that they had bodies—such as Tatian, Justin, Clement of Alexandria, and Tertullian. The Mahometans <note>An archaic term for Muslims.</note> believe that they are thin bodies created from matter. Voetius <note>Gisbertus Voetius (1589–1676) was a prominent Dutch Reformed theologian.</note> and others also believed this (<note original: "apol. exeg. cap. 7.">Exegetical Apology, chapter 7</note>), <margin>A. Reland, *On the Religion of the Mahometans*.</margin> but they were mistaken.

There are those who excuse those who said the Angels are Corporeal by saying that their objective was only to show that they are true substances, or that they are not spirits as spiritual, simple, and pure as God.

It will perhaps be said that they are compared to the Wind and to a flame of fire. That is true; but if one had to conclude from that that they are corporeal, then one would also have to say that God is corporeal, because he is frequently compared to physical things.

It will be said that the Angels have often made themselves visible to men to carry out God’s commands. I admit it; but one cannot conclude anything else from that than that they assumed bodies, in the same way as the Son of God revealed himself visibly to the Patriarchs.

Furthermore, it would be presumption to determine how and from where they assumed these bodies.

Some say that God created them out of nothing; others that they were made of a substance that had no disposition to become a body, like that with which the Angels appeared; others that they took on the bodies of living men themselves. Others, that these bodies [consisted] of...

It is not very necessary that we trouble ourselves to know what the knowledge and power of angels is; one must confess that we know very little of the matters of spirits.

<margin>
Of the Knowledge of Angels.
</margin>

We are assured that, besides the natural knowledge which these spirits have had since their creation, they acquire more daily, and that God reveals many truths to them which they would not have known by themselves.

It is easy to understand that the knowledge of angels is greater than that of men, since they constantly behold God's face, their hearts are not corrupted, and they have no prejudices.

But we know for certain:

1. That their knowledge is not infinite, and that they do not know many things. Thus Christ says in Matthew 24:36 that they do not know the day of judgment. And Paul teaches us in Ephesians 3:10: "So that now through the church the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places." Peter also teaches us in 1 Peter 1:12 regarding those "things into which angels long to look," even into the depths of the mysteries. God alone, being an infinite being, has infinite wisdom.

He cites Ephesians 3:10 for this purpose. Isidorus <note>Likely Isidore of Pelusium, a prolific letter writer of the early church.</note> generally denied to the angels the knowledge of all objects that were not present. 3. They know God’s perfections much better than men; but one must not imagine that they know them perfectly, because God being infinite, He cannot be perfectly known by any finite being.

4. The manner in which they know corporeal and visible things cannot be explained.

5. One cannot deny that the angels communicate their thoughts to one another; this can be concluded from many passages; but we do not know how. Possibly God has established this order: that when an angel wants to make something known to another angel, that angel knows it; just as He has established this order: that upon certain thoughts of the soul, certain movements of the body immediately follow: for the one is no more incomprehensible than the other.

The meaning is this: if I were as eloquent as the angels would be, if they had a language or tongue; my eloquence would be like the sound of a ringing metal, if it were not animated by love.

# THE CHRISTIAN <note>The header "DE CHRISTELYKE" likely refers to "The Christian Theology" or "The Christian Religion."</note>

Of the Power of the Angels. Psalm 103:20.
</margin>
7. Regarding the Power of the Angels, it is certainly great; thus they are called "mighty in strength"; and they can do innumerable things that exceed human capabilities; but their power is finite; and it is difficult to comprehend, not to say impossible, how they move physical bodies.

8. We are assured that they cannot perform true miracles, because an infinite power is required for that, and consequently, a Divine power; therefore we do not believe that they can raise the dead or create substances. However, we know that God has often performed miracles in the presence of Angels, which are then attributed to them, even though God alone is the cause of them.

<margin>
2 Sam. 24:15, 16. 2 Kings 19:35. Isaiah 37:36.
</margin>

We cannot say if that is the work of an Angel alone, because we do not know the extent of their power.

Of the order of the Angels.
</margin>
<margin>
Colossians 1:16.
</margin>
10. Without doubt, there is some order among the Angels, as is evident from the various names given to them; it is for this reason that Paul, speaking of the Angels, uses the names of various ranks or dignities seen in the States and Kingdoms of the World, where there are **Thrones**, which refers to supreme Rulers and Kings; **Dominions**, which are dignities that, though very high, are nonetheless lower than kings, such as Dukes and Archdukes; **Principalities**, such as Administrators or Governors of Cities and Provinces; and finally **Powers**, which are subordinate Authorities. But we believe it would be reckless to define exactly what the distinction of their order is, and we frankly admit with Augustine that we do not know, without concerning ourselves with all that is brought forward on this matter under the name of the Venerable Dionysius the Areopagite <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite was a 5th-century philosopher whose work *The Celestial Hierarchy* became the standard for angelic rankings in the Middle Ages.</note>.

<margin>
Augustine, *Against the Priscillianists*, chapter 11 <note>original: "contr. Prif. ill. d. 11."</note> & *Enchiridion*, chapter 58.
</margin>
It was the opinion of this Dionysius that there are three Hierarchies of Angels in Heaven, each having three orders, and thus 9 Hierarchies <note>Usually referred to as nine "choirs" or "orders" within three hierarchies.</note>. In the first, one places the **Cherubim**, **Seraphim**, and **Thrones**. In the second, the **Dominions**, the **Principalities**, and **Powers**.

<column-break/>

In the third, the **Virtues** <note>original: "Kragten"</note>, **Archangels**, and **Angels**. It is claimed that these various names are given to them because of the diversity of the properties of their Nature, or because of the various ministries they hold: that some are called **Cherubim** because they surpass the others in Wisdom, which they then teach; others **Seraphim**, because they burn with Divine love and ignite others with the same love; others **Thrones**, because they govern and judge the others. The **Dominions** would assign the Angels their duty; the **Principalities** would manage nations and provinces; the **Powers** would restrain the power of the Devils; the **Virtues** <note>original: "Kragten"</note> would have the authority to perform miracles; the **Archangels** the ministry to announce great matters; and the **Angels** the small ones.

The Jews had previously distinguished ten Hierarchies of Angels; of which some are under the Throne of Majesty, having access to God’s Secret Chambers; others interact and speak with men. They say that four stand before God: **Raphael, Gabriel, Uriel, and Michael**; Michael is at the right hand, Gabriel at the left, Uriel in front, and Raphael behind. Others serve. One sees from the *Introduction to the Jewish Excommunication* <note>original: "Voorbericht der Joodsche Kerk-Ban"</note>, cited by Selden <note>John Selden (1584–1654), an English jurist and scholar of ancient laws.</note> in *On the Law of Nature and of Nations* <note>original: "de Jure Naturæ & Gentium"</note> book 4, chapter 7, that the Jews believe **Uriel** has the governance of the month of *Nisan* (March); **Zephaniel** of the month of *Iyar* (April); **Amniel** of *Sivan* (May); **Peniel** of *Tammuz* (June); **Barkiel** of *Av* <note>OCR reads "Ahh."</note> (July); **Periel** of *Elul* (August); **Zuriel** of *Tishrei* (September); **Zachariel** of *Marcheshvan* (October); **Adoniel** of *Kislev* (November); **Anael** of *Tevet* (December); **Gabriel** of *Shevat* (January); and **Rumiel** of *Adar* (February). They also believe seven Angels rule over the seven days of the week, and four over the four seasons of the year.

But these are mere trifles. Regarding the Hierarchies: 1. Scripture does not speak of them. 2. It says that all Angels are ministering Spirits. 3. According to this opinion, the Seraphim should never have been sent to Earth, yet the contrary appears in Isaiah 6:6. Moreover, Scripture speaks not of many Archangels, but of only one. All these distinctions seem to be taken from the Philosophy of Plato. (See Iamblichus, *On the Egyptian Mysteries*; Proclus, *Commentary on Plato's Alcibiades*). I do not consider it necessary here to give an account of the names of these Heavenly spirits, and to say why they are named Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones.

One must admit that nothing certain can be said about this; therefore, it will be enough to note that the word Angel means *Envoy* <note>original: "Afgezant"</note>, because God indeed sends them to earth to carry out His commands; therefore they are called ministering spirits (Hebrews 1:14) and God’s servants (Psalm 104:4).

God has no need of servants to do what He desires, since He can execute everything through a single act of His will. But He wishes to grant this honor to His creatures, that He chooses to employ them and use them for His glory. Moreover, God acts thus, either for the adornment of the universe—since nothing contributes more to the beauty of the world than seeing that all the creatures of which it is composed, when put together, have a wonderful correspondence with one another: high, middle, and low—or for the comfort of the believers, who thereby perceive how God cares for them, since He uses the ministry of perfect creatures to promote their salvation.

<margin>Whether the Angels are used for the Government of the world.</margin>

# THEOLOGY. Book 5, Chapter 5.

<margin>
Ps. 91:1, 12.
Gen. 19:12, 13, 15, 16, 17.
2 Kings 6:16.
Dan. 6:22 and 3:28.
Acts 5:19.
Luke 16:19–22.
