# DIVINITY. BOOK V. CHAPTER VIII.

### Part 1. Vv
<meta>catchword: the</meta>

...against this view, nothing of weight can be objected.

It is said that, although a man clearly sees that he must act in a certain way for his own benefit and well-being, he is nonetheless always master of his actions, so that he could act otherwise. I answer that he must act in a certain way; if he acted differently, he would bring harm upon himself. When there is no other motive to turn him away from it, he cannot do otherwise than act in this way, as long as he allows himself to be led by reason; thus he will work necessarily, though freely. But not through a **natural necessity**, such as that by which fire burns. <note>Natural necessity refers to physical laws that cannot be changed, whereas the "necessity" of reason is a moral or intellectual certainty.</note>

It is said that if freedom does not consist in **indifference**, and if man is not indifferent, then he shall never deserve a reward. I answer that he would deserve no reward if he were forced to work by an external power, or by a natural necessity, and without reason; but that is not our view. To deserve a reward, it is enough to work with pleasure, with judgment, without compulsion, and with reason. Yet when I speak of a deserved reward, I do not mean to say that the Creature can earn anything from God. <note>The author emphasizes that while human actions can be "rewardable" in a moral sense, a human being (the "Creature") never places God in their debt.</note>

It is said: if we have no freedom of indifference, then warnings and threats will be of no use to us.

I answer: Warnings and threats serve to enlighten our understanding, and our enlightened understanding determines us to do what we do.

It is said in common conversation that freedom is nothing other than pure indifference.

I answer that indeed most people understand freedom this way; but one will feel differently as soon as one thinks of the freedom that is in God; for when we think of that, we do not view freedom as an indifference. <note>God is perfectly free but is not "indifferent" to good and evil; He is necessarily good. This is a common theological argument against the "freedom of indifference."</note>

Having explained the nature of freedom, it is easy to conclude:

<margin>What the freedom of man has been.</margin>
1. That Adam had his Free Will; for freedom is an essential property of the rational creature. It is impossible to conceive of a creature endowed with reason without ascribing to it the

<column-break/>

power to work and to do what seems good to it, with reason; now, to work with reason is always to work freely.

2. It is easy to judge what the freedom of Adam was; it was not a **freedom of independence**, as if he had been master of himself, depending on no one; for the Creature must always depend on his Creator and be subject to His will. But his freedom consisted in this: that he worked according to his own pleasure, not being forced by any being from outside; and that he worked with reason.

One must not understand Adam as being indifferent regarding good or evil, for this indifference would have been a sin; and if Adam had possessed this in the beginning, he would already have been corrupted then; for one cannot be indifferent to good or evil without being corrupted. But to say that Adam was created by God in a state of corruption is to make God the cause of sin; which is godless.

Meanwhile, one must admit that Adam was created in a **changeable state**, in which he could sin and not sin; but this changeable state must not be called "freedom," as it does not deserve to be honored with such high praise.

One must not, therefore, confuse these two expressions: *to be able to sin and not to sin*, and *to be indifferent to good or evil*. A man can be placed in such a state that he shall be able to sin and not to sin, although he always remains Holy and without being corrupted in any way; but one cannot say that a man is indifferent to good and evil without being corrupted. Adam was in the first state, but by no means in the second.

<margin>Augustine, *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 11. <note>Original Latin title: *De Correptione et Gratia*.</note></margin>
The state in which Adam was must also be well distinguished from that in which the blessed will be; just as one must distinguish these two things: *being able to sin and not sin* and *not being able to sin*; *being able to not leave the good* and *not being able to leave the good*; *being able not to die* and *not being able to die*; which Augustine notes very well. The first man was able not to sin; the blessed shall be unable to sin; the first man was able not to die; the blessed shall be unable to die; the first man was able...

<summary>This page argues that human freedom is based on reason and choice rather than total indifference, using the example of Adam's pre-fall state to distinguish between the ability to choose and a sinful lack of moral inclination.</summary>

# CHRISTIAN THEOLOGY

...they will not leave the good; the blessed will not be able to leave it.

### CHAPTER IX.

->Of the Covenant of Nature or of Works, which God made with our first Ancestors.<-

<margin>Socinus Episcop. book 2. ch. 1. <note>Refers to the theologians Faustus Socinus and Simon Episcopius, who questioned the traditional view of the Covenant of Works.</note></margin> After having examined the state in which God created our first ancestors, it is appropriate to investigate whether God made any Covenant with them: some deny it.

Scripture does not speak of this explicitly, at least if we do not wish to cite the passage from Hosea 6:7; but one must admit that the Prophet can be explained otherwise. Meanwhile, the matter speaks for itself; and when we investigate what the Scripture says of Adam, we shall be fully convinced of it. This is what we shall see in the following.

If Moses has not described clearly and with all circumstances the Covenant that God made with Adam, it is because he intended only to explain to us the Covenant of Grace and its administration <term>dispensation; the way God manages human salvation</term>, both before and after the Flood.

<margin>Whether a Covenant can exist between God and Man?</margin> Properly speaking, there could be no Covenant between God and man; because:

1. There is no proportion or comparison between God and man; just as there is none between an Infinite and a Finite being.

If slaves or subjects have no right to make conditions or stipulations with their Lords or Masters, nor the conquered with their conquerors, how much less men with God!

---

<note>(g) The word Covenant, in Hebrew <note>original: *Berit*</note>, comes from another that means "To Cut"; because when one made a covenant, the sacrificial animals were divided, which were then offered, and those making the covenant passed through the middle of these divided offerings: it also comes from a word that means "To Create," "to make," and "to ordain": finally, it descends from another that means "To Choose"; for in covenants, one commonly chose the persons with whom one wished to deal, and the conditions—</note>

<column-break/>

2. There is no proportion between the benefits that God bestows on His creature and the duties He requires of them.

3. Man is always obliged to obey God, even if there were no Covenant.

4. Man cannot contribute anything of himself to this Covenant.

5. Finally, God owes nothing to the Creature and has no need of it. But a Covenant assumes:

1. That the Persons who negotiate are equal, at least in some respects.

2. That they have it in their power to contribute something.

3. That it depends on them to act or not.

4. That they, without this Covenant, are not obligated to the other.

But God, moved only by His Goodness, has thereby willed to invite His creature—who owed Him everything—to His blessed fellowship; and through this display of love, to bind them more strongly to His service.

One can regard God in two respects: either in such a high loftiness that no creature can approach it, and in all the right that His infinity gives Him; or in this moderation which His Goodness and other virtues give to His absolute power. In the first respect, God speaks as an absolute Sovereign; in the second as Creator, or as Father; what He commands in the first capacity must be held as a Law; what He does in the second respect is called a Covenant.

<margin>Jeremiah 33:20-25.</margin> Before we speak of the Covenant that God made with the first man, one must note that the word Covenant (g) is sometimes taken for a steadfast establishment of something: in this sense the word is used in Jeremiah 33:20-25. Thus says the Lord, "If you—"

The Covenant is described as a negotiation through which two or more persons bind themselves to one another to maintain a good harmony, under certain conditions and mutual obligations.

The same word in Greek <note>original: *diathēkē*</note> sometimes signifies a Testament; sometimes a Law; sometimes an agreement.

# THEOLOGY. BOOK 5. CHAPTER IX.

...if you could void my Covenant of the day, and my Covenant of the night, etc. <note>Refers to Jeremiah 33:20, used here to show that "Covenant" can refer to the fixed laws of nature.</note>
The word "Covenant" is also used in another sense; just as Job said, in chapter 31:1, that he had made a Covenant with his eyes, so that he would not allow himself to be led into temptation. It is also used for a simple promise from God. Genesis 9:9, 10, 11.
But in this case, the word Covenant is taken for a mutual agreement between God and Mankind.
<margin>What is to be observed in a Covenant.</margin>
One must note that in every Covenant, six things are observed:
1. Who the persons are that are negotiating.
2. What conditions are required.
3. What promises are presented to those who keep the conditions.
4. What punishments must be feared by those who break the Covenant.
5. The Mediator of the Covenant, if one was necessary.
6. The Signs of the Covenant, and the Seals attached to it.
It is now time to see if one can find all these things in the Covenant that God made with our first ancestors.
<margin>How God and man must be considered in the Covenant of Nature.</margin>
I. In this Covenant, the persons entering into it are God and Man. 1. God, considered as Creator and Supreme Lord (who, being an infinitely wise being, cannot abandon the care of his creature when it has not made itself unworthy of the expressions of his love; who cannot lead it except in a manner consistent with its nature, and through Holy laws; and finally, who could not restrain himself from loving and rewarding his creature when

<column-break/>

it does its duty). 2. Man, considered not only in the capacity of a rational creature, but also as Righteous <note>Original: "Regt" (Upright/Just)</note>, being able to do what God commanded him; and as the First Man, who represented all his descendants and was regarded as the head and Prince of the human race.
God could say to Adam what he said to the Israelites in Deuteronomy 29:14–15: *It is not with you alone that I make a Covenant; it is as much with those who are here, as with those who are not here.* So too, what God said to Adam must be understood as being said to his descendants: *Be fruitful, and multiply.* Genesis 1:28.
II. Regarding the required conditions, God demanded of Adam and his wife:
<margin>Regarding the conditions of the Covenant</margin>
1. That they should learn to know Him as perfectly as they could, whether through revelation, through meditation on God’s works, or through reasoning.
2. That they obeyed the Laws he was to give them, not only this Natural Law that he had engraved in their hearts, but also the particular commands he made known to them, as he indeed did, forbidding them to eat of the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. We shall speak of this Command in what follows. The Jewish Teachers say that Adam received six commands from God: (1) To proclaim His Divine Glory. (2) To do justice. (3) To shed no human blood. (4) To serve no Idols. (5) To commit no robbery. (6) To avoid incest.
3. That their obedience was sincere and not feigned.
4. That they obeyed everything that God would command them.
5. That their obedience was so perfect

<sig>V v 2</sig>

...is proven, not only by Pagan writers but also by the Holy Writers; Jeremiah speaks of this explicitly in Chapter 34:18. This ceremony signified that the one who made the covenant offered himself to be treated like these victims <note>Refers to the ancient ritual of cutting a sacrificial animal in two and walking between the pieces, symbolizing "may I be cut in two if I break this promise."</note> in case they violated or broke the covenant.
One asks how many covenants God made with man: **Amyrault** <note>Moïse Amyraut (1596–1664), an influential French Protestant theologian at the Academy of Saumur.</note>, Professor at Saumur, allows for three: the Natural Covenant with our first ancestors in the Earthly Paradise; the Legal Covenant with the Israelites; and the Covenant of Grace, given in the Go- <meta>catchword: Gospel</meta>

spel: but as the Scripture does not mention two covenants—the Covenant of Works and the Covenant of Grace—it seems more appropriate to me to stick to this distinction: although one could say that there have been three Households <term>dispensations; eras of divine administration</term> and three distributions; for fundamentally one recognizes only two Covenants: the *one* through which God promises life to those who will obey him perfectly; the *other* through which he promises Salvation to those who through faith will embrace the obedience of Jesus Christ and labor toward their sanctification.

It contrasts the views of theologians like Amyraut on the number of divine covenants, ultimately distinguishing between a covenant based on perfect works and one based on grace through Christ.</summary>

<header>THE CHRISTIAN</header>

...made [the creature] as perfect as it could be.

6. Finally, that it was steadfast, and that nothing ever turned them away from it.

It must be noted that God had given man the power <note>The Dutch "kragten" refers to inherent capacities or strengths</note> to obey Him.

<margin>
Of the threat that God made to Man. Gen. 2:17.
</margin>

III. God, having prescribed to man his duty, made a threat to prevent him from deviating from it, contained in these words: *on the day that you eat of it, you shall surely die.* Gen. 2:17.

Here one must note:

1. That God does not threaten man with death except in the case that he sins.

2. That, since God threatens man with death in the event that he should transgress the specific command that He had given him regarding a matter that in itself was neither good nor evil <note>This refers to the fruit of the Tree of Knowledge, which was "indifferent" until God forbade it</note>; so man had to conclude that if he transgressed the other commands against the Holiness of God, he must expect great punishments.

3. That it appears from this threat that God established that the punishment would follow the sin.

It is asked what one must understand by this *death* with which God threatens Adam and Eve?

1. One must not doubt that by this death one must understand the separation of soul and body, which we call temporal death; this is evident from what is said in Gen. 3:19: *In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, till you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken: for dust you are, and to dust you shall return.*

This is clearly a threat; therefore, we cannot approve of those who make a promise out of this threat, as if God were promising man that he would return to the Paradise from which he was taken.

2. It also appears that by this death one must understand all miseries and evils that were to precede death: as one can infer from Gen. 3:16, 17, 18, 19. And because all these miseries are called by the name of "death" in Holy Scripture (Exod. 10:17, 2 Cor. 11:23), it has been very well said that we begin to die the moment we begin to live; and that we do not cease from dying until we are delivered from this body of death by the death of our flesh.

3. This death is what we call the Spiritual

<column-break/>

death, consisting in our separation from God and His communion. Indeed, as soon as man sins, he separates himself from God; and to separate from God, who is the Prince of Life, is to die; thus the Scripture speaks of it in Eph. 2:1, Eph. 4:18, 1 Tim. 5:6.

4. Finally, the death with which God threatens our first ancestors is what we call Eternal death, which shall consist in an eternal separation of sinners from God; as we shall explain more broadly in its proper place.

One cannot take it ill that we give this breadth to the threat God made; either because Moses uses a general word that corresponds with all the types of death of which we have spoken; or because it undeniably appears through many passages of Holy Scripture that all these types of death are consequences of sin.

One must also not find it strange that God made such threats to His creature. God would have to deny Himself to leave the transgression of His laws unpunished; neither His Holiness nor His Justice can tolerate that, as we have proven in the second book of this Theology <note>original: "Godgeleerdheid"</note>.

<margin>
Of the promises of the Covenant of Nature.
</margin>

IV. Regarding the promises of this covenant, Moses says nothing of them: but besides the fact that conscience and reason teach all men that one does not serve God in vain, so one can judge the promise by the threat: for, although God owes nothing to His creature, nevertheless, because Scripture presents Him to us as slow to anger and great in benevolence, and as the rewarder of those who seek Him; so it is not probable that God, who had threatened man with a very severe punishment, would have made him no promise. It is a matter very befitting the Divine goodness to communicate Himself to His holy creature; He cannot refrain from loving the same; now, as soon as one loves, one takes delight in sharing oneself with the beloved.

One cannot deny that the Law had promises of eternal life; that is clearly evident from the conversation that Christ had with a certain man, as spoken of in Matt. 19:16, 17. *Behold,* says the Evangelist, *one came to him and said, "Good Master, what good thing shall I do that I may have eternal life?"*

# THE CHRISTIAN

...however much there have been people who have said that Paradise was the entire earth before it was cursed: if this were so, it would not have been said that God drove Adam out of the Earthly Paradise. It is a ridiculous thought to believe that Paradise is near the Moon, or in the upper reaches of the air. One can consult Basil of Seleucia <note>original: "Basilius Damascenus de fid. Orth. l. 2. c. 11." referring to St. John of Damascus, *On the Orthodox Faith*</note>, Rupert <note>original: "Rupertus. lib. 2. de Trin. c. 37." refers to Rupert of Deutz, *On the Trinity*</note>, Strabo, Bede, Peter Lombard, etc.

<margin>Which location was the Earthly Paradise.</margin>
We leave it to the scholars to dispute in which part of the world Paradise was located; whether it was on the high mountains that border the Caspian Sea, as Kircher <note>Athanasius Kircher, a famous 17th-century Jesuit polymath</note> maintains; or on the Island of Ceylon <note>modern-day Sri Lanka</note>, as the Indians maintain, who claim that they still find the signs of the footsteps Adam made when he fled from God; or in Syria near Damascus, as Melanchthon <note>A key leader of the Protestant Reformation</note> maintained, and others after him, who claimed that the Pishon is the Chrysorrhoas <note>original: "Chryzorrhoas," Greek for "Golden River"</note> and the other river is the Orontus, which others deny because the Orontus, which flowed past the walls of Antioch, did not flow into the land of Cush, and for many other reasons: or on the banks of the River of the Arabs, below Babylonia and Apamea, as Huet maintained. Or between Baghdad and Tikrit, in Mesopotamia, where there is a river that bears the name Odeines, as van Til maintains; or in that part of the world where the Tigris and Euphrates meet, below Mesopotamia and Babylonia, etc. One may consult the famous Bochart on this at the beginning of his *Phaleg* in the latest edition; also the works of Marck and van Til, Professors at Leiden, and of Reland, who believes that Paradise is in that region of Armenia that lies between the sources of the Phasis, Araxes, Tigris, and Euphrates.

We note:

1. That it was a delightful Garden in which God placed our ancestors; so that one should not imagine, as some have done, that Paradise was merely peace of mind and the inner joy of the first man.

2. That it was an outstanding example of Heaven, the Heavenly Paradise; as one will agree if one reads Revelation 22.

3. That it was washed by four rivers; or rather by two, divided into four. These rivers were, according to what almost all scholars believe, the <term>Tigris</term> <note>original: "Tiger"</note> and the <term>Euphrates</term> <note>original: "Eufraat"</note>, not the Ganges and the Nile.

<column-break/>

4. That in this Garden were two very remarkable trees, of which one was called the Tree of Life, and the other the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil.

The Pagans <note>original: "Heidenen"</note> had some knowledge of the Earthly Paradise, because mention is often made in their writings of Jupiter’s Garden, of the Garden of Alcinous, of the Gardens of the Hesperides, etc.

But, without pausing to bring up what the Pagans have said about it, let us only see what must be answered to those questions of whether the *Earthly Paradise still exists?*

We cannot agree with this opinion, which is held by Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine, a highly influential Catholic Cardinal</note>; it has been refuted by Pererius, Oleaster, Jansenius, Suarez, Viegas, and Cornelius à Lapide.

*On the Grace of the First Man* <note>original: "de grat. p. h."</note>, Sixtus.
</margin>
It is said that the waters of the Deluge <note>The Great Flood of Noah</note> were raised fifteen cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of measurement, roughly 18 to 22 inches</note> above the highest mountains. What probability is there that these waters would not have overturned, destroyed, and drowned this place of delight? It was no longer meant to be the dwelling place of guilty mankind.

Theologians add this reason: if Paradise were not destroyed, from where does it come, they ask, that Noah did not go there with his household, instead of setting himself to build an Ark to be his refuge and place of preservation during the time the waters covered the whole earth?

An objection is raised from a passage in <term>Sirach</term> <note>Also known as Ecclesiasticus, a book of the Apocrypha</note>, Chapter 44, verse 17, where it is said that Enoch was translated into Paradise. But these words are not found in the Greek. They are only in the common translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note>, in which it is indeed said that Enoch was translated into Paradise: but it does not say there that it was into the Earthly Paradise.

Objection: It is probable that the olive branch which the dove brought into the Ark was taken from Paradise.

But that is without foundation: when the dove brought an olive branch into the Ark, the waters had already been receding for some time; the Ark stood on the mountains of Ararat: so the dove could easily have pulled a branch from an olive tree that had retained its greenness under the waters.

# CHRISTIAN

## SIXTH BOOK.
### Concerning the fall of the Angels and of Mankind.

# CHAPTER I.
## Why God permitted sin.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial "W" at the start of the chapter, featuring floral patterns and a winged cherubic figure holding a staff within a square frame.</image-desc>

We have stated elsewhere / that God / having decided to create the Angels and mankind / at the same time decided to permit the fall of some of these spirits / and that of man.

Indeed / since nothing happens in the world / without God knowing of it / it would be absurd to believe / that some of the Angels / and afterwards man / would have fallen from their original righteousness / without God having known it beforehand / and subsequently permitted it. We believe then / that God, by the same act through which He decided upon the creation of Angels and men / decided at the same time to permit / that both would use the freedom of action / which He had given them.

It is nonetheless impossible not to be exceedingly amazed / that God permitted sin. Why, people ask, has God / who is so good toward His creatures / permitted them to fall into such great evil? Why has God created Angels / whom He knew would abuse His benefits / and become enemies of His Glory? Either God could have prevented this evil or He could not: if He could have prevented it, how is it / that He did not do so / to keep the creatures in the happy state / in which He had placed them / especially since holiness is the

<column-break/>

most beautiful feature of God's Image / and that which God loves most? If He could not have prevented it, how then can it be said that He is Almighty <term>Almighty: having unlimited power; omnipotent</term>?

One must not say / that God gave to the Angels and to man the freedom of action / the use of which He could not prevent / without doing them a sort of violence / and of which He could not deprive them / without taking away the conditions / which are inseparable from the nature / which He had bestowed upon them. For that would narrowly limit God's power / and expand that of man.

How would it be possible / that God / who through His providence <term>Providence: the protective care and governance of God over the universe</term> governs all other created things / would have so limited Himself / that He would have withdrawn the actions of His creatures from His governance / in such a way that they would be complete masters of their deeds?

On the other hand / if one assumes that there was such freedom in men and in Angels / would it not have been a thousand times better that God had taken it from them / than to let them use it to their ruin? A benefactor / one will say / must not bestow benefits / which he knows in advance will be abused / and serve toward the downfall of those whom he would gift with them.

It is said that a free being is so exalted and so formidable / that its excellence far exceeds the worst consequences / which the abuse of freedom could bring with it.

But one will never be convinced of that / if one examines the infinite calamities / that sin causes. One will always come forward with the ques-

->**THEOLOGY. BOOK VI. CHAPTER II.**<-
Xx 2
<meta>catchword: These</meta>

One might ask whether God should not rather have created us as we shall be in Heaven, so as to be always pleasing to Him. One will not be satisfied with the common answer—namely, that one must distinguish the time of trial from the time of reward—since it will be argued that God could have handled this differently, exposing men to many temptations here while completely freeing them from such in Heaven.

It might perhaps be said that God permitted sin to demonstrate His wisdom, which shines through more clearly in the disorder daily brought forth by the wickedness of men than it would have done in a state of perfect uprightness.

But this answer is insufficient; for it is as if a King were to allow rebellions in his Kingdom simply to have the honor of knowing how to provide the remedies for them. Others say that God’s justice and mercy would have remained unknown without the fall of the Angels and the first man.

But, one will answer, could God not have made His virtues known in some other way? Does not the very concept we have of a perfect Being teach us that God is just and merciful?

Certainly, since Scripture gives us no specific reason for God’s governance in this matter, and gives us enough to understand that there are unfathomable depths within it, let us not presume to plumb these depths.

Let us be satisfied with acknowledging the following truths:

1. That God’s ways may be hidden from us, but they are always righteous.

2. That God has given just laws to all His creatures.

3. That He, being the Holy of Holies, can never be the cause of sin, and He testifies of His abhorrence for it throughout all of Scripture.

4. That He has made all His virtues shine forth in the reconciliation <note>Original: *verzoeninge*, referring to the Atonement of Christ</note> of sin.

5. That He has sent His Son into the world

XIII. en XIV. Pf. XCV."</note>, who did no honor to their dignity since they wavered and fell, and left their own dwelling place—that is, that good Land that God had assigned to them—by renouncing it; whose bodies fell in the Wilderness and were cast into the grave,

6. That the failings of men display the beauty of the opposing virtues.

7. That God governs everything for His own Glory.

## CHAPTER II.

### On the Fall of the Angels and the
### Devils.

In the preceding Book, we showed that all the Angels were created holy and innocent; an observation that must be made again here, so that one does not imagine that some were created with that wickedness which they later possessed. For one cannot hold that view without assuming that God is the cause of sin—which cannot be said without impiety—unless one wished to maintain that the evil Angels are eternal. Thus, one would fall into the views of Marcion and Mani <note>The Marcionites and Manichaeans were early Christian dualist sects</note>, who asserted that there are two eternal principles: one of good and one of evil; impious views to which those who have read the Scriptures unanimously testify.

But, although all the Angels were created holy, it is certain that they did not all remain in the state in which God had placed them. Christ says in John 8:44 that the Devil was a murderer of men from the beginning, and that he did not stand in the truth. Jude speaks in verse 6 of Angels who did not keep their original state <note>original: *beginzel*, referring to their "first estate" or principality</note>, and who left their own dwelling place. (a) It appears that even the Pagans had knowledge of the fall of these evil spirits. (b)

(b) Mention is made of certain poems by Empedocles <note>A Greek pre-Socratic philosopher</note>, in which he said that the demons <note>original: *Demones*, referring to spirits or lesser deities</note> had fallen from the highest part of the air into the Sea to bear their punishment. To this one also attributes the Fable of the Giants, and that of Antea <note>likely referring to Antaeus, the giant son of Gaia</note>.

(c) The word *Demon* is frequently used by writers. Scholars do not agree on the meaning of this word. # DIVINE THEOLOGY. BOOK VI. PART II. Chapter 2.

Demons allowed great honor to be shown to themselves. It is asked what kind of pride they possessed. Some believe that they wanted to make themselves equal to God and deify themselves; others, that they rose up against the Son of God.

The opinion of those who believe that pride was the first sin of the Devils is more likely than that of those who think it was envy; for, as Augustine
<margin>Book II of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis* <note>original: "de Genes. ad liter."</note></margin>
very well notes, Envy follows Pride, but does not precede it: Envy is not the cause of Pride, but Pride is the cause of Envy.

<margin>Justin Martyr, Tertullian, etc.</margin>
Some Church Fathers have believed that the sin of the Angels was unchastity <note>Lust or sexual immorality.</note>. To prove it, they cite Genesis 6:2, where it is said that the Sons of God saw the Daughters of men, that they were beautiful, and they took for themselves wives from all whom they chose. Others have been of the opinion that the union of the Angels with women had produced the race of devils.

But this opinion is ridiculous.
1. It is based on a false principle that the Angels have bodies.
2. It assumes that by the "Sons of God" one must understand the Angels, whereas on the contrary, one is certain that the children of Seth are being spoken of.
3. In short, we perceive nowhere that the Devil tempted Eve to unchastity, but only to disobedience and pride.

Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a prominent Dutch theologian known for Federal Theology.</note> was of the opinion that the sin of the Angels consisted in the seduction of the Woman, since no earlier sin is mentioned, and the Devil is called a murderer from the beginning.

The safest course, in matters of this nature, is to say that nothing is known about it.

It has some appearance of truth that the first sin of the Angels lay in the fact that they did not sufficiently notice what God was, and what duties they had to fulfill. From this it followed that they began to look upon themselves, and to be filled with wonder at themselves. This wonder gave birth to pride, and pride brought them to rebellion; thus they did not remain standing in the truth, nor in the faithfulness they owed to God as subjects to their King, nor in the Rectitude and Holiness in which they were created.

<column-break/>

These evil Angels do all they can to extinguish the Glory of their Creator, but their efforts are useless and vain, although they make all too much of an impression on the minds of the godless. They also neglect nothing in opposing the salvation of men, and in trying to draw them into their rebellion. It is certain that God often gives them free rein, sometimes to punish the wicked, sometimes
<margin>Job 1 and 2.</margin>
to exercise <note>In the sense of "training" or "testing."</note> the good, like Job, sometimes to protect the Believers from pride, like Paul, who testifies
<margin>2 Corinthians 12:7.</margin>
that a messenger of Satan <note>original: "Engel des Satans"</note> would buffet him with fists, so that he would not exalt himself through pride. For it is very likely that it was a Devil who chastised the Apostle in his body.

<margin>Bekker's *The World Bewitched* <note>original: "Betoverde Wereld"</note>.</margin>
It is said <note>Referring to the arguments of Balthasar Bekker, who challenged the belief in witchcraft and demonic possession.</note> that there is no probability that there are spirits who oppose God's will, but that by Satan and Devil—a slanderer, a liar, an enemy—one must understand human passions and the irregular movements of our soul; that one must thus interpret Matthew 13:39, Luke 8:12, Ephesians 4:27, James 4:7, 1 Peter 5:8, Revelation 2:10, etc.; that in 1 Chronicles 21:1 a proud Courtier is spoken of, and that Paul in 2 Corinthians 12:7 has his eye on a cruel enemy he had. But reasoning thus is willfully blinding oneself and distorting the scripture—if not regarding all, then at least regarding some of those places. Besides that, I would like to know whether it is more consistent with the idea one has of God's virtues to set spirits like the Devils against Him than to set men.

Augustine says that God allows the devil to use his power over men either to punish them, or to test them, or to crown them.

One cannot doubt that the Devil tempts men and that he tries to bring them to destruction. The scripture is explicit on this. It says not only that the Devil tempted Christ, but that he also seeks to devour us; that he works with power
<margin>1 Peter 5:8.</margin>
in the children of disobedience;
<margin>2 Corinthians 11:3, Ephesians 2:2, John 13:2.</margin>
that he seduced Eve through his craftiness; filled the heart of Ananias, and inspired Judas to betray Christ.

Against the temptation of our first Ancestors, Bekker objects that it involves great difficulties. I admit it, but it appears at least from this that the Devil tempted Eve, and that he thus

# THE CHRISTIAN <note>Likely part of a title such as "The Christian Religion" or "Christian Theology."</note>

can tempt people. In the following chapter, we shall see the difficulties that reside in this history.

He <margin>Bekker <note>Balthasar Bekker (1634–1698), a Dutch minister who argued against the literal existence of demonic influence and witchcraft.</note></margin> objects to the temptation of Christ, arguing that it should not be interpreted according to the literal word. Instead, he claims that God intended for His Son to imagine the Devil as if he were tempting Him; otherwise, Satan—who is described as very cunning and skilled—would have been reckless to attack Christ directly. One also cannot comprehend how he could have shown all the kingdoms of the world with their glory.

**Answer 1.** But if this matter had occurred as Bekker suggests, Christ would have been tempting Himself, whereas it is explicitly stated that He went into the wilderness to be tempted there by the Devil. **2.** Although there are difficulties in this history, the matter is nevertheless certain. It is established that Christ was tempted by the Devil.

Regarding Job, it is said that he does not complain about the Devil.

**Answer.** He does not do so indeed, because he did not know that the Devil was the cause of the disasters he suffered; but God's Spirit teaches it to us in his history.

It is said that the Devil is a spirit, and that a spirit cannot act upon a body.

**Answer.** That is not true: our soul acts upon our body, but we do not know how.

It is said that the soul acts on the body by virtue of the union that exists between the two.

**Answer.** I admit it; but it follows nonetheless that a spirit can act upon a body. According to Bekker’s own admission, Angels can act upon bodies. One cannot describe his <note>The Devil's.</note> craftiness and artifices, and one must confess that he succeeds only too well with them.

There are those who believe that the Devil, from the time of his fall, has been banished to hell, where he is bound with eternal chains without performing anything more on earth; they say that to hold the common view is the same as placing the Devil on the Throne of God. But they take no notice that we regard the Devil as a slave who does nothing except by the permission of his Master.

It is very well said that those who bind the Devil with strong chains, who banish him from the world, and who cast him into hell where God keeps him prisoner—

<column-break/>

like the alleged Giants <note>The Titans or Giants of Greek mythology who rebelled against the gods.</note> whom Jupiter, according to the fable, sent into the abyss and loaded with great mountains so that they would no longer rise against him—do less to exalt God's power than those who assert that God uses these rebellious spirits. They argue that He makes "galley-rowers" <note>An image of total enslavement; rowers chained to their oars on a ship.</note> of them, who are required to stay by their chains as He desires, and that He binds and unbinds them.

They object using 2 Peter 2:4, where it is said: *For if God spared not the angels that sinned, but cast them down to hell, and delivered them into chains of darkness, to be reserved unto judgment.*

**Answer.** That does not mean that God has already locked them in Hell, but it signifies two things. **1.** That God has condemned the Angels to eternal punishments. **2.** That He keeps them so closely bound to the chains of His providence and justice that they can do nothing without His permission; but it does not follow from this that He does not sometimes give them a bit more room for their wrath.

It is said that our view posits two Gods and introduces pure Manichaeism <note>An ancient dualistic religion that taught a fundamental struggle between a good spiritual world of light and an evil material world of darkness.</note>.

**I Answer** that we speak with the Scriptures. If we call the Devil the *God of this Age* <note>original: "God deezer Eeuwe," referencing 2 Corinthians 4:4.</note>, these are the words of Paul; but it does not follow from this that we believe there are two principles or Gods. We know that the Devil is entirely subject to God, and that no one is Almighty but God.

It is said that our view is insulting to Christ's Glory because we give a greater and more extensive Kingdom on earth to the Devil than to Christ.

**Answer.** It is true that we say the Devil has more people who obey him than Christ; but at the same time we say: **1.** That the Devil would have no subject without Christ’s permission. **2.** That all the subjects whom Satan has overwhelmed, or who have surrendered themselves to him, depend absolutely on Christ, so that He is their Master and lawful King, who can do with them whatever He wills. **3.** Finally, we speak with the Scripture when we say that the number of the reprobate <note>The "rejected" or non-elect.</note> is greater than that of the chosen.

It is said that our view gives occasion for various abuses.

**I Answer** that this happens only by accident, just like all other doctrines of the Scripture; but the abuse of a good doctrine must not take away its use.

# THEOLOGY. VI. B. II. Chapter.

It is not possible to explain how the Devil works upon us; but it is ridiculous to deny that he works, under the pretext that one does not know the manner of it.

If one knew how the Angels are able to communicate their thoughts to one another, and how our spirit works upon our body, one would have no difficulty in understanding the workings of the Devil upon mankind.

<margin>Whether the Devil acts upon bodies.</margin>
It is not possible to deny that the Devil acts upon our bodies when one pays attention to what he did to Job; for it is explicitly said there, *Job II. 7. So Satan went out from the presence of the Lord, and struck Job with painful sores from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head.* <note>The author uses this Old Testament example to prove the Devil’s power over physical health.</note> It appears from the same History that it was Satan, <margin>Job I. 15. 16. 17.</margin> who incited the Chaldeans and the Sabeans to rob him of his goods; who caused the fire to fall from Heaven upon his cattle and ignited the storm; who threw down the house where his children were.

Of these workings of Satan upon bodies, one will be even more convinced if one reads the account of so many possessed persons whom Christ and his Apostles healed.

It is a wonder that there are people who dare to say that the Scripture in this case speaks not according to the truth of the matter, but according to the false ideas of the Jews, who attributed many common occurrences to Devils; so that, even if it is said that the Devils went out of the bodies, and that they terribly agitated those whom they possessed, one must—according to the opinion of these new Teachers <note>A reference to Balthasar Bekker and his followers, who sought to "demythologize" the Bible.</note>—not believe that the Devil worked therein, but that these possessed persons were melancholic <term>nageestige; likely referring to severe depression or mental gloom</term> people, or insane, or those who had the falling sickness <term>epilepsy</term>. However, if it is permitted to interpret the Scripture in this way, there will be nothing that one cannot make it say, and one will henceforth create a Theology that will entirely conflict with those that have come to light until now, and which one will nevertheless want to maintain by twisting the passages in this manner. Why not admit that the Devil plagued bodies in the time of Christ, since he struck Job with sores? Why does one not want to explain the words of the Scripture in their natural meaning, and

one that is not against the truths of the Gospel? If it is true that the common opinion places the Devil upon God’s Son <note>Referring to the Temptation in the Wilderness.</note>, it seems likely that the Savior, through his expressions, would have intended to give cause to believe the same. One must sigh when one sees what freedom people take to explain the words of the Scripture according to their own simplicity. What reasonable sense can one give, according to this new opinion, to the account of Matthew VIII. 28–31? There it is said that two men possessed by the Devil met Jesus in the Country of the Gergesenes, who cried out, *Jesus, thou Son of God, what have we to do with thee? art thou come hither to torment us before the time?* Jesus subsequently gave permission to the Devils, whom he cast out, to enter into a herd of swine. To understand this as a disease that passed from these possessed ones into the pigs is to mock the Scripture and to treat people as fools. One may consult the Messrs. It is also known that many little tales and invented fables are made concerning the Devils: but one must also not believe that, among so many imagined fictions on this subject, there would not be a single true history. # [CHRISTIAN THEOLOGY]

God often uses them <note>Referring to the Angels or heavenly spirits mentioned previously.</note> to execute His decrees; whether because they, being spread throughout the Universe, prevent thousands of things that men intend to do.

One must also not believe that the Devil can do everything that pleases him regarding mankind. We can resist him, and with God’s grace and help, prevent him from carrying out his bold intentions.

To turn away the fiery arrows of the Evil One, one must be clothed with the armor that Paul sets forth. Eph. VI. Such as the *shield of faith*, the *helmet of hope*, the *belt of truth*, the *sword of the spirit*. We must watch and pray, avoiding everything that can give place to this evil spirit, and holding ourselves to Him who has crushed the serpent’s head.

Although he is the cause of many sins that we commit, we must nevertheless not attribute all our sins to him. We ourselves carry the origin of all evil in our own bosom. Therefore we must pay attention to ourselves, as well as to this cruel enemy of our salvation. *O God, lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.* Matt. VI. 13.

## CHAPTER III.

### Concerning the Fall of Man.

The state of happiness of the first man was of no long duration, no more than that of the Angels who did not preserve their original state. He soon lost his glory and crown. One asks, when did Adam sin? Some judge that he was driven out of Paradise on the same day he was led into it. Others believe that he sinned on the tenth day, and that for this reason the Jews established the Day of Atonement on the 10th day of the seventh month. Lev. XXIII, 29. Others maintain it was many years thereafter. The safest course is to admit that one knows nothing of it. Moses described the fall of man. Gen. III.

But above all, we must note that God had given a law to man, not to eat of the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Gen. II, 16, 17.

<column-break/>

<margin>Why God forbade eating from the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil.</margin>
Perhaps one will be surprised that God gave him this prohibition, since it was in itself a very indifferent matter whether to eat from this tree or not. <note>The author uses "indifferent" in the theological sense of *adiaphora*—an action that is neither inherently good nor evil, but becomes so through a command.</note> But one will no longer be surprised when one considers that God, in this case, wished to show man that, although He had given him dominion over the Creatures of this lower World, man nevertheless had to acknowledge God as his Supreme Lord; and that he depended on Him such that he could do nothing against His will.

God acted therein with our first ancestors as Lords do with their <term>vassals</term> <note>original: "Leen-Mannen". In the feudal system, a vassal held land from a lord and had to perform acts of "homage" to show their submission.</note> from whom they demand certain homage. He was not satisfied with giving them a natural Law, which He wrote in their hearts, but He also gave them a particular Law to test their obedience. Thus God wished to make known:
1. That He was Lord of all.
2. That the Dominion He had given him was not independent.
3. That the Creatures were not the supreme good of man.
4. That God’s will is the only rule for our will, and that we must hold ourselves solely to His word.

<margin>Who incited man to sin. 2. Cor. XI. 3. 1. Tim. II. 14. 1. Joh. III. 8.</margin>
It was the Devil who drove man to violate this Law, and who therefore bears not only the name of *Tempter*, but also of *Liar* and *Manslayer* from the beginning. John VIII. 44. It appears that the envy he had conceived against Adam and Eve inspired this cruel intention in him, to drag them into his destruction. And, since it was true, as some have believed, that the first sin of the Angels was the envy they had against this first pair of humans, one could believe that they had imagined that God, being angry with Adam and Eve, would have made them die instantly, and that they would thus occupy the rank that God had given to our first Ancestors among the Creatures.

To succeed in his temptation, the Devil misused a Creature, namely a Serpent, which he used to bring man to destruction, wishing thus to usurp the dominion that the Man and the Woman had over the animals of the field, by making these same animals serve in the downfall of the Woman and the Man. # THEOLOGY, VI. B. Chapter III.

Authority was given over the Woman, and to both Man and Woman over the animals. But Satan arranged this work in such a way that the serpent made himself master of the Woman, and the Woman became mistress over the Man.

<margin>Was it a real Serpent? Rev. 12:9. 2 Cor. 11:3. Aben Ezra. Amyraldus, *On the Tempting Serpent*.</margin>
The question is asked: was it a real serpent? Some believe not, but rather that the name is given to the Devil, as in other places of Scripture. This view is not probable, for if there had been no serpent, why would Moses have provided us with a description of the cunning of this animal? And what would be the meaning of the curse that God pronounced over this serpent, consisting of the fact that it would eat dust? To understand all this in an allegorical manner <note>The author argues against treating the story as purely symbolic, insisting on a literal historical event.</note> is to abuse the Scripture.

<margin>To Maimonides' *Guide for the Perplexed*, Part 2, ch. 30. Amyraldus.</margin>
Some Jews, however, maintain this. Rabbi Shem Tov <note>A 14th-century Spanish Jewish philosopher and commentator.</note> says that the serpent is the faculty of the imagination. Isaac de la Peyrère, the author of the *Pre-Adamites* <note>A controversial 17th-century writer who argued humans existed before Adam.</note>, says that the serpent represents the senses, the woman represents reason, etc.

It is said that if it had been a real serpent, Moses would have described its species. This reasoning is very weak, for in the same way I could prove that Moses’ staff did not change into a real serpent because he does not say what species of serpent it was.

It is said that in Hebrew there is a prefix <note>original: "voorstel-woord". This refers to the definite article "the" (*ha*) in Hebrew (*ha-nachash*), which some argued implied a specific, supernatural entity rather than a common animal.</note> before the word for serpent, which indicates that it was no ordinary serpent. But it is certain that such a prefix is found in many places where ordinary serpents are spoken of, such as Numbers 21:9, Ecclesiastes 10:11, and Amos 5:19.

It is said that Moses could not have said that the serpent was the craftiest of all the beasts of the field.

I answer that those who have made it their work to know the cunning of serpents confirm the testimony of Moses. Besides that, one can very well say that the sense of the words simply means that the serpent was a cunning animal.

It is said that Scripture always attributes the temptation to the Devil. That is true, since it was indeed he, under the form of the serpent.

It is said that it is not probable that God would have wanted to speak to the serpent, which understood nothing. I answer that this should not appear any stranger

<column-break/>

than when God said to all the animals, "Increase and multiply," or when Christ cursed the fig tree. See 1 Kings 17:4, 2 Kings 7:13, Amos 9:3, Jonah 2:10, and Isaiah 45:12.

It is said that it was natural for the serpent to crawl, and thus God would not have condemned a real serpent to do so. I answer that it is probable that the serpent previously crawled without difficulty, whereas after the sin, it crawls in a different manner. The Jews say that it had the form of a camel, and that God cut off its legs.

It is certain, then, that there was a real serpent; but it is no less certain that the Devil spoke through this serpent and that he possessed it. It is the work of a spirit to make an animal speak, and that of an evil spirit to make it say such false and wicked things as the serpent brought forth. Furthermore, the Devil is called the "ancient serpent." Paul, in one of the places cited above, fears that the serpent which seduced Eve might turn the Corinthians away from the simplicity of the Gospel.

<margin>2 Cor. 11:3. Talmud, *Sotah* folio 9.2. *Sanhedrin* folio 29.1. Maimonides from the *Midrash*.</margin>
The Jews, who are fertile in their imaginations, say that Sammael <note>In Jewish lore, the main archangel of death and a figure often identified with Satan.</note>, the Angel of Death—who is the Devil—was riding upon a serpent when he attacked our first Mother. It is very probable that the history of the seductive serpent gave rise to the fables that the Pagans have spread about their *Ophioneus* <note>A serpent-deity in Greek mythology who ruled the world before being cast out.</note>, and about their Dragon who guarded the golden apples in the Hesperian gardens.

<margin>Augustine, *City of God*, book 14, ch. 11.</margin>
<margin>Aelian, book 17, ch. 5. Maximus of Tyre, Dissertation 38.</margin>
It is remarkable that the Pagans have worshipped serpents. Under that form, they honored their Asclepius <note>The Greek god of medicine, often symbolized by a snake-entwined staff.</note>. It is told that, not long ago, the peoples of Samogitia <note>A region in modern-day Lithuania, known for being among the last in Europe to convert from paganism.</note> held a serpent as their God. But it is surprising that in the second century there were heretics foolish enough to believe that the serpent who seduced Adam and Eve was Christ, for which reason they worshipped a serpent; these are called Ophites. See Augustine, *On Heresies*, ch. 17, and Epiphanius, *Heresy 37*.

The first trick of the Devil was then to hide himself under a serpent. It is no wonder that Moses does not speak of the Devil, since he acts solely as a historian.

# THE CHRISTIAN <note>This header is likely a fragment of "The Christian Theology."</note>

<columns>
...others want it to have been a **Basilisk** <note>A legendary reptile reputed to be the king of serpents, said to kill with a single glance.</note>, others a **Lamia** <note>In ancient folklore, a female demon or monster.</note>, others a **Dragon**. I confess that I do not know.

One asks, why did the Devil not take a human form?

I answer, to startle Eve less; for knowing that Adam was the only man in the world, she would have immediately conceived some suspicion of deceit if she had seen another man.

Perhaps the Devil preferred using a serpent over another animal because the form of the serpent in which he appeared resembled a woman, as some have believed. But the matter is quite uncertain. The Devil spoke through the serpent to our first ancestors.

There is no more reason for wonder here than there is regarding the speaking of a **female donkey** <note>A reference to the biblical story of Balaam’s donkey in Numbers 22:28, which was miraculously given the power of speech by God.</note>. Therefore, it is unnecessary to suppose with Josephus <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, a first-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> and others that it was natural for the serpent to speak and walk.

It has some appearance of truth that the Devil made the serpent speak in order to make the Woman believe what he wanted to present to her. She knew that eating the forbidden fruit was deadly. This conviction was based on God’s threat. To take this thought away from her, the Devil countered it with experience; he made the serpent eat the fruit and then speak, so that the Woman—attributing this speech to the power of the fruit—might conclude that if this fruit had the power to make an animal speak and reason, it could well happen that she and her husband would become like **Gods**, knowing good and evil.

<margin>
Why the Woman was not surprised?
</margin>

One asks, why was the Woman not surprised when she heard the serpent speaking, since there is now no one who would not be astonished by it and view it as a miracle?

I answer that our wonder would stem from the knowledge we have that animals do not speak or reason; and this knowledge rests on various experiences and investigations based on them. But the first Woman did not yet have enough experience to judge this. It is then no wonder that the speaking of a serpent did not seem strange to her. Ignorance and doubt do not conflict with the **state of uprightness** <term>state of uprightness: (Latin: *status rectitudinis*) the original condition of human beings before the Fall, characterized by moral innocence and intellectual clarity, though not necessarily exhaustive experience.</term>, but the error of the intellect does.

<column-break/>

<margin>
Why the Serpent first addressed the Woman?
</margin>

One asks, why did the Devil address the Woman first?

I answer, because he believed that the Woman would have less power of resistance, given that God had not made this threat from Genesis 2:16, 17—*In the day that you eat of it, you shall surely die*—directly to her, but to Adam.

<margin>
With what reasoning the Devil tempted Eve?
</margin>

Eve could not have been tempted more cunningly. He spoke to her as if God had forbidden her the use of all the trees of the Garden. Is it also true, he asked, that God said, *You shall not eat from all [the trees] of this Garden?* What appearance of truth is there that God, who has given you dominion over all the creatures of the world, would have forbidden you this beautiful fruit that you see? It would be godless to have such thoughts. This evil spirit did not want to criticize God’s conduct directly, because Eve would then have perceived what this tempting serpent sought. But keeping himself ignorant of what had occurred, he asks if it was really so, that God had forbidden her the use of all trees of the Garden? 2. When the Woman answered this, saying that God had only forbidden her the fruit of the tree that was in the middle of the Garden, and that she would die if she ate of it, Satan contradicted this threat, *You shall not surely die, but God knows, etc.*

<margin>
Gen. III 4. 5.
</margin>

How, he meant to say, would it be possible that such a beautiful fruit would make you die? Thus he tried to make Eve believe <note>original: "diets te maken"</note> either that Adam had not understood God’s meaning well, or that God had not spoken seriously, or that Adam had not told his wife the truth? To remove all doubt, Satan went further. He assured Eve that, far from dying, she and her husband would gain a much greater knowledge if they ate of it, yes, even become as Gods; *God knows, that in the day as you eat of it, your eyes shall be opened, and you shall be as God, knowing good and evil.* From this he let her draw the conclusion that she then should not hesitate to eat of this fruit. He appeals to God—*God knows*—so as not to appear an enemy of God, but he depicts God as being envious that humans would become like Him. Some have believed that the Devil feigned being sent by God to assure her that it was permitted for her to eat of the fruit,

# DIVINITY. VI. B. III. Chapter.

etc. But these thoughts have no basis.

Eve yielded to this temptation, and having observed that the fruit was indeed beautiful, she took from it and involved her husband in the same transgression. Thus the Woman, who was given to the man as a helper like unto himself <note>A reference to the biblical "help meet" from Genesis 2:18.</note>, became the instrument of his ruin.

One cannot say what reasoning she used to convince her husband, whether she recounted the speech of the Tempter to him, or whether she added new reasons of her own. I cannot believe that it was tender love alone, which Adam had for Eve, that moved him—under the hope of forgiveness—to rather scorn his Creator than to displease the Woman, who was a part of himself.

<margin>
Daillé <note>Jean Daillé (1594–1670), a prominent French Huguenot theologian known for his works on the early Church Fathers and biblical commentary.</note> on 1 Tim. II. 14.
</margin>
Whatever the case may be, it is certain that he committed the same sin as Eve. And when Paul says, **1 Tim. II. 14**, *Adam was not deceived, but the woman being deceived, was in the transgression*, he means nothing else than that Adam was not deceived first, and that he was not deceived in the same manner as Eve. "Eve," to use the words of a learned man, "was created last, but sinned first. She had the audacity to swallow the offered poison. They both drank it, but not at the same time. Eve began, and having tasted it at the suggestion of the Serpent, she became the instrument of the Tempter, etc. Thus she opened the door for Sin and Death, and served as a tool for the Devil to corrupt him who was her Head and the stem of the human Race. They were then both deceived, with this distinction: that Adam had no part in the first transgression of Eve. He did not entice her into evil and error; she enticed him into it. Meanwhile, he was no less guilty than she, and it even seems that he bore more guilt, since he ought to have rebuked the Woman for her disobedience to God's command. Some are of the opinion that Adam did not allow himself to be deceived, but that he sinned against his better knowledge, whereas Eve allowed herself to be taken by surprise."

<margin>
Why the Devil attacked the Woman regarding the prohibition
</margin>
The Devil attacked the Woman regarding the prohibition against eating from the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil; for had he tempted her regarding something that ran directly against the law of nature, it would

<column-break/>

<margin>
of eating from the Tree of Knowledge.
</margin>
perhaps have been impossible for him to succeed. The movements of the mind and common knowledge were sufficient to ward off all his deceit: but God's command concerning a matter that was in itself indifferent <note>In theology, "indifferent" (adiaphora) refers to actions that are not inherently moral or immoral, but become so only because they are commanded or forbidden by God.</note>, in which the idea of good and evil was not naturally evident, and which did not demand certain execution by its own nature, made the fallen Angel's undertaking easier.

One asks, what was the first sin of Adam and Eve?

I answer: It is probable,
1. That Eve first doubted whether she had rightly understood God's thought regarding the prohibition.
2. That she, instead of asking the Lord for counsel, found it probable what the Devil had presented to her: namely, that she would not die.
3. That she was subsequently flattered with the vain hope of knowing all things and becoming like God.
4. And finally, that she reached out her hand to the forbidden fruit.

Regarding this, one may then observe:
1. That the beginning of her sin was not paying close attention to God's command; for had she done that, she would not have lent an ear to the Tempter.
2. That she thereafter came to doubt what God had said and gave belief to the words of the Devil.

<margin>
What the cause of man's fall was.
</margin>
One asks, what was the cause of man's fall?

I answer: God cannot be accused of it without blasphemy; for He expressly forbade the eating of the fruit; and to turn man away from it, He threatened him with death if he should partake of it. He gave him the enjoyment of all other trees; He had provided him with all necessary powers to do all that He had commanded; and He did not withdraw any benefit that He had previously bestowed upon him.

3. The Devil must also not be viewed as the true cause of man's fall. He did him no violence; he only made use of the way of persuasion, and his reasons were not so powerful that it would not have been easy to refute them: for Satan spoke against an express command of God. Never would he have conquered man if man had not begun to look upon himself.

One must also not place [the blame] on the tree—

<meta>This page continues the theological examination of the Fall of Man. Having previously discussed the Serpent's role and Eve's initial transgression, the text now focuses on the mechanics of Adam's free will, the nature of his original holiness, and the specific reasons why a perfect being was capable of falling into sin.</meta>

# THE CHRISTIAN <note>Likely part of a larger title such as "The Christian Religion" or "The Christian Theology."</note>

lay. The beauty of the fruit and the desire to gain knowledge by eating from it should not have caused man to waver, nor outweighed God’s command.

Man's will alone was the true cause of his fall, determining itself through its own motion toward an object that his misled understanding presented to him, but which God had forbidden. What caused him to listen to the Devil’s temptation was the natural desire we have to obtain and possess what we do not have. A pagan philosopher <note>Likely a reference to the Platonic or Neoplatonic idea that the soul's self-determination is the origin of moral failing.</note> has acknowledged that the human soul is the sole cause of evil, by reason of man's freedom.

One asks, how is it possible that man, who was upright, allowed himself to be taken in by the false reasoning of the tempter? Is it conceivable, it is said, that a will perfectly holy and pure could, in a single stroke, produce such acts of disobedience and contempt for God’s commands?

I answer that one should not wonder at this so greatly, since man was not so strengthened and confirmed in holiness that he could not lose it. He was holy and righteous, but he could cease to be so. He was oriented toward the good, but this orientation could be changed and overturned through a temptation, combined with some neglect on the man's part, followed by a false judgment and a hasty consent. Thus, man’s fall should seem no more miraculous to us than when we see someone who was standing upright fall, or someone who was at rest move.

Furthermore, one must note that Adam did not yet have experience, and that he did not possess the sciences <note>original: "Wetenschappen." In this context, it refers to systematic knowledge or the wisdom gained through long observation.</note> that we acquire when we view objects from all sides and see them from various perspectives and in different lights. Therefore, it is not strange that he allowed himself to be misled by the Devil, who presented evil to him under the guise of good, and that he passed a judgment contrary to the nature of things by rushing his decision.

One asks whether man was in a state in which he could have protected himself from his fall?

I answer that he could have protected himself from it.

<column-break/>

God had given him a help <note>A reference to the theological concept of "sufficient grace," meaning the innate ability provided by God to resist sin.</note> with which he could have remained steadfast if he had willed it. Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a central figure in the development of Western Christian thought regarding original sin and grace.</note> compares this to the help that food gives to the life of those who wish to consume it; whereas one cannot live on food if one refuses to use it. Adam had only to pray to Him and ask God for counsel. He should have taken time to reflect on the objects that were opposed to those proposed by Satan. Thus, he would easily have discovered the deceits and snares of the tempter.

It is said that the impression which objects make on the understanding is not voluntary, and consequently it is not in our power to suspend it.

I answer that one can always suspend judgment on a proposal made to us.

One asks whether being able to be deceived and being able to fall is a defect?

I answer: Yes, it is a defect, an imperfection of the creature as a creature, and a weakness; but if man is on his guard and does not rush his judgment, this weakness and this imperfection will not lead to sin.

One asks why God did not place man in a state where he would always be holy, without ever ceasing to be so.

I answer in a word: that it was God’s good pleasure <note>original: "welbehagen." This refers to God’s sovereign will, which is considered the ultimate reason for the order of creation, beyond human questioning.</note> to have it so. All other reasons brought forward are not sufficient.

<margin>How God intervened in the fall of Adam</margin>
If one is eager to know how God intervened in the fall of Adam, I answer that it is better to remain silent on this matter than to speak too much of it.

One will not be mistaken in saying:

1. That God incited neither Satan to tempt Adam, nor man to fall away. God preserve us from such thoughts regarding a holy being!

2. That God withdrew nothing from man that He had previously given him, for then He would have punished man before he had sinned. Now, there is no punishment where sin does not precede it. Besides that, if God had taken away any help that was previously given to man, it would seem that He would have been the cause of the sin—much as when the pillars upon which a building rests are removed, it must necessarily fall.

<summary>This page explores the theological reasons for Adam's fall, arguing that while Adam was holy, he was not immutable, and his fall resulted from a hasty judgment and the exercise of free will rather than a lack of divine help. The author emphasizes that God did not cause the sin nor withdraw His grace beforehand, as that would constitute unjust punishment before a crime was committed.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of the Fall of Man. This page addresses the difficult question of God’s sovereignty and foreknowledge in relation to human transgression.</meta>

### THEOLOGY. BOOK VI. CHAPTER III.

3. It is certain that God foresaw man’s fall; otherwise, His knowledge would not be infinite.
4. Nor should one doubt that God decreed from all eternity to permit the fall of man; for otherwise, it could not have been certain that he would sin or not sin. If, according to the testimony of Christ, not a single sparrow <note>A reference to Matthew 10:29: "Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Yet not one of them will fall to the ground outside your Father’s care."</note> can fall to the earth without the will of our Heavenly Father, who would not be convinced that a fall—which turned the entire universe upside down and displaced the whole order of nature—did not happen without the will and foreknowledge of God?
5. It cannot be denied that God gave Satan free rein; for if He had restrained him, he would not have tempted our first ancestors.
6. By forbidding the Tree of Knowledge, God provided a harmless occasion for the devil to tempt Adam and Eve.
7. It appears clearly that God did not prevent the fall of Adam, though He was able to prevent it, since nothing is impossible for Him.
8. That God, in the moment of temptation, did not provide him with an additional grace that would have so confirmed him in holiness that he would never have fallen from it, was because He wished to test his obedience and faithfulness.
9. It is also certain that God did not refuse Adam any grace that he had requested of Him.
10. Finally, it is established that God maintained the natural faculties <note>The inherent powers of the mind and soul, such as reason and will.</note> of man.

We must abide by these general observations and henceforth worship God’s ways in silence, recognizing that He always acts with justice and supreme wisdom; so much so, that one could not suspect Him of sin without a heaven-defying godlessness.
One cannot say that God is the cause of sin, either because He foresaw it (for God’s foreknowledge and infinite wisdom are not the cause of the outcomes); or because He had decreed to let the fall happen (for this decree placed no coercive force upon the freedom of man); or because He permitted the temptation of the devil (for He did not give the devil the will to tempt man, nor did He approve of this temptation); or because He

<column-break/>

created man in a state in which he was capable of falling; for He did not create man with any evil inclination; He made him holy and righteous. Nor can it be said He is the cause because He did not give him grace sufficient to prevent his fall; for He had given him enough strength to remain in the state in which he was placed. God was not obligated to give him more. Nor because He had forbidden him the use of the Tree of Knowledge; for Adam could easily have refrained from eating of it. Nor because He had created a Tree which became the occasion of man's fall; for this Tree was a very harmless occasion.

<margin>
Why God permitted the fall of man.
</margin>
If it is asked further why God permitted Satan to tempt man, and why man succumbed to the temptation:
I answer with *Augustine* <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian who wrote extensively on original sin and divine grace.</note> that I adore the depths of God’s counsel, but I do not dare to fathom them.
I only note:
1. That God showed His hatred of sin by punishing it, even in His own Son.
2. That God, on the occasion of sin, poured out the unspeakable riches of His mercy and raised His goodness to an infinite degree.
3. Finally, that sin gave God the occasion to make all His virtues known.

<margin>
The greatness of Adam's fall.
</margin>
Adam’s sin was a heap and entanglement of many sins.
One sees in it a disordered desire for a fruit that was forbidden by his Creator.
A distrust of God’s truth and sincerity.
A doubt regarding God’s love and goodness toward him.
A desire to make himself equal to God, and a most punishable pride.
A desire for independence and excessive self-love; a shameful ingratitude and contempt for God.
One can further judge the greatness of this sin if one takes into consideration:
1. That he who sinned was created without any inclination toward evil.
2. That he was overwhelmed with God’s blessings.
3. That he had just come from the hands of his Maker, and had done almost nothing yet for his Creator.

4. That he sinned in Paradise, where everything preached to him the Power, the Greatness, the Wisdom, and the Goodness of God.
<margin>Augustine, *The City of God*, Book 14, Chapter 15.</margin>
5. That it was very easy to refrain from the Tree of Knowledge in a place where there were so many other fruits, as <note>original: "Augustinus"</note> Augustine remarks. If one cannot sufficiently marvel at the obedience of Abraham—because what God commanded him was very difficult—then one cannot sufficiently condemn the disobedience of Adam, because nothing was easier than to keep what God had commanded him.
6. Finally, that one cannot offend their Creator more than by preferring to believe the word of a Serpent over the word of their God.

If, according to <term>Navarra</term><note>Martin de Azpilcueta (1491–1586), a famous Spanish canonist and moral theologian.</note>, <term>Lessius</term><note>Leonardus Lessius (1554–1623), a Flemish Jesuit known for his influential works on justice and law.</note>, and <term>Gregory of Valencia</term><note>A Spanish Jesuit theologian (1550–1603) who was a prominent figure in the Counter-Reformation.</note>, it were a provable opinion that <term>penal laws</term><note>Laws that supposedly only obligate the person to accept the punishment if caught, rather than binding the conscience to avoid the act itself.</note> lay no obligation upon the conscience, then Adam and Eve would have had reason to flatter themselves that by eating from the forbidden tree, they would not sin. But this is a godless opinion.
