### CHAPTER IV.

->Concerning the harmful consequences of the first sins, with respect to our first Ancestors.<-

Just as the sin of our first ancestors greatly kindled God’s wrath, so it also had very harmful consequences.
<margin>
Valentin Smalcius's work against Wolfgang Franz, Disputation 7.
Socinus, *Theological Lectures*, Chapter 3.
</margin>
1. One cannot doubt that they lost the most beautiful features of <term>God’s Image</term><note>The *Imago Dei*, the theological concept that humans are created to reflect God's character.</note>, consisting in an unblemished holiness. Indeed, they did not lose the entire Image of God after which they were created. God willed that some remnants of this unhappy loss should remain, so that from them one might know how glorious the Image was before it was defaced, and to erect another beautiful building upon the ruins of this fallen house. It is even certain that God, through His Spirit, prevented the disorder within our first ancestors from bursting out as far as it otherwise would have done. But meanwhile, Adam felt from then on what he had not perceived before: a flesh that rose up against his spirit; a law of the members that strove

<column-break/>

against the law of his mind; passions that set themselves against reason and very often carried it away toward irregular desires; guilty inclinations; thoughts that do not become a creature; and an all too great love for the created and the visible.
2. Just as they were separated by sin from the Prince of Life, who is God, so in this regard the sentence that God had pronounced over them began to be carried out. On the day they ate from the forbidden Tree, they died the death of the soul, which consists in the separation from God through sin.
3. They became the objects of God's wrath, and God would have condemned them to the eternal pains He has prepared for the godless, had He not had compassion on them. Also, God called Adam immediately after he had sinned and said, *Adam, where are you?* <margin>Genesis 3:9.</margin> To summon him, as it were, before His judgment seat so that he might give an account of his conduct; to reproach him for his unbelief, rebelliousness, ingratitude, and pride; and to show him from what a high step of glory and happiness he had fallen into the utmost calamity.
4. Their eyes were opened, and they realized that they were naked, and they were ashamed of it. As soon as their soul was stripped of this garment of holiness, the nakedness of their bodies made them afraid, and they stood ashamed over it.
5. Their conscience was troubled, and in place of that quiet peacefulness which it previously enjoyed, it became disturbed. The voice of God, which was their joy, struck terror into them, and they sought to hide themselves from the One who sees all and whom they had so shamefully offended.
6. They were driven out of Paradise, that place of <term>delight</term><note>The original Dutch *wellust* here refers to "pleasure" or "delight" in the context of Eden's beauty, rather than the modern sense of "lust."</note> which the Almighty had planted and adorned with His hand; they were deprived of its fruits, which they previously had use of.
7. From that moment, they were exposed to all the evils and diseases that thwart and shorten our lives, and they noticed that they would imperceptibly lose the life God had given them and return to dust, from which God had made them, just as they indeed experienced after having lived for some time on earth.

One cannot be sufficiently amazed at God's goodness / that he did not crush these first two sinners with one blow / and that he gave their lives a long course. We do not know / how long Eve lived; but Scripture teaches us that Adam reached 930 years.

One answers, that no mention is made of it / so that he might be regarded solely as the beginning of nature / and the boundary of grace; as the origin of sins / and through sin, death / so as to leave to Christ the honor and thanksgiving for our salvation.

# THE CHRISTIAN [DIVINITY]

...as a fall, as an injustice and godlessness, as a debt of guilt.

<margin>
On the
nature
of
sin.
</margin>
John describes the nature of sin when he says in 1 John 3:4: "Sin is that which is against the Law." <note>original: "De zonde is, dat tegen de Wet is." Modern translations usually render this as "sin is lawlessness."</note>

<margin>
* This
passage is
translated
according to
the French
version.
James 4:12.
</margin>
By "the Law," one understands the Law of God, who is the only Lawgiver who can save and destroy; for human laws do not bind the conscience by their own power, but only because of the Law of God, which commands us to obey our authorities. Therefore, we are not bound to obey men except when they command us in things that do not conflict with God’s Law; otherwise, we must always remember that word of Peter: "It is better to obey God than men."

<margin>
Acts
4:19.
</margin>
To understand this matter well, we must observe that the most perfect rule of goodness is God’s own being—His holiness and His purity—according to which God always acts. He cannot deny Himself, so there are things that would be evil solely because of their contradiction of God’s purity, even if God had not explicitly forbidden them—such as being a slanderer, an unbeliever, etc. Other things are not evil except because God has forbidden them, such as eating from the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil. Such were all the <term>Ceremonial Laws</term><note>Religious laws regarding rituals, sacrifices, and purity which were specific to the Israelites, as opposed to universal Moral Laws.</note> that God had given to His people. Those who have received these Laws are obliged to keep them solely because of God’s authority.

<margin>
2 Tim.
2:13.
</margin>
But regarding the other Laws, which are grounded in God’s essence and holiness, we are bound to obey them even if God had commanded us nothing concerning them. 

It is probable that the Apostle, in 1 John 3:4, uses the word "Law" for the expression of God's holiness (if I may be permitted to speak thus) which we find in the <term>Moral Law</term><note>The universal ethical principles, summarized in the Ten Commandments, which Christians believe apply to all people at all times.</note>, and which Christ explained in His Gospel according to the perfect knowledge He had of His Father’s will and being. Just as God's Law commands some things and forbids others, we oppose this Law either by not doing what it commands or by doing what it forbids. This is called a **sin of commission** and a **sin of omission**. In the latter, one sometimes falls voluntarily, when one does not want to do what one is bound to do; sometimes because one pays no attention to it or does not think of one's duty. Sometimes this omission is joined with deeds that are in them-

<column-break/>

selves good, but which are not so at certain times—for instance, when someone, being too attached to his profession, forgets to pray to God. Sometimes this omission arises from a faulty action, such as when someone, being drunk, has forgotten to do what he was bound to do. Sins of commission happen in many ways: 1. When one does something that one must not do, such as killing someone, etc. 2. When one performs a work that is good in itself but from an evil principle, such as giving alms without love and faith, but out of pride. 3. When one does not bring what one does to God’s glory. 4. When one does certain things at certain times or in certain places where they should not be done. 5. One sins in thoughts, words, and deeds. 

Furthermore, since the Law demands a perfect holiness and sincerity, we go against it when we do not possess the holiness it requires and are inclined toward evil.

<margin>
The es-
sence of
sin.
</margin>
The essence of sin, then, consists in a deprivation of the righteousness and holiness that ought to be in a rational creature, into whose heart God has poured a natural law, and for whom He has prescribed a perfect rule in the Law proclaimed on Sinai. Therefore, to know if something is a sin, one must observe whether it is against the holiness that the Law requires. 

It is not always necessary, therefore, that an act be done voluntarily with premeditation and with an actual knowledge of the malice inherent in it. For, as has been very well noted, if one had to essentially know the wickedness of the act one intended to do in order to make oneself guilty of sin, it would follow that there would be no "sin of surprise" <note>Sins committed suddenly or without thinking.</note>, nor of inattentiveness, nor of ignorance. The sin someone commits while drunk would not be a true sin, nor would the sin of habit or innate inclination—which one commits without notice and in a violent fit of temper. And everyone who, in good faith, assumed a matter was permitted would commit no sin by doing it, and there would be no sin of ignorance.

CHRISTIAN <note>The header "DE CHRISTELYKE" likely continues from the previous page as "The Christian Divinity" or "The Christian Theology."</note>

One asks whether sin deserves an infinite punishment? I answer, in general, yes; yet I add to this that this punishment cannot be infinite except in duration with respect to the creatures. But that it is enough to atone for it that the Person who suffers for the sin be infinite, as we shall show elsewhere. Meanwhile, one cannot doubt whether sin deserves an infinite punishment if one considers that—although it seems there is no proportion not only between a single sin but all the sins of a life as short as ours and eternal punishments—it is nonetheless just that those who have offended an infinite Majesty should be punished with an infinite punishment and never come into grace with God, unless someone satisfies His justice for them and in their place.

God imposes an infinite punishment in duration, but not in <term>degrees</term><note>The author distinguishes between how long a punishment lasts (duration) and how intense it is (degrees). This allows for the theological idea that some people are punished more severely than others in hell, while all remain there eternally.</note>; since the creature, being finite, could not bear a punishment infinite in degrees; and because there would then be no inequality in the punishments if God, to satisfy His justice, imposed on the creature all the punishments it could bear—which is against the Scripture, which teaches us that one shall be punished less and the other more.

Furthermore, although sinners always deserve punishment, they can nonetheless be delivered from it if someone stands in their place who stills God’s wrath for them.

<margin>Romans 8:1.</margin> This causes Paul to say in Romans 8:1 that there is no condemnation for those who are in Jesus Christ, since Christ has delivered them from it. But, having seen what sin works in us in general, and what punishment it deserves, let us now consider what harmful consequences it has had with respect to Adam’s descendants, to which we shall devote the following chapters.

## CHAPTER VI.

->Of the harmful consequences of the first sin of Adam with respect to his descendants, along with the explanation of Romans 5:12, etc.<-

Adam has made his descendants guilty and punishable through sin. Paul teaches us this in Romans 5, where he places this matter in the light of day.

His purpose was to prove that we are justified through the obedience of Christ; but because there were many who could not understand how the righteousness or obedience of Christ could be <term>imputed</term><note>Imputation is a legal term meaning to "credit" someone with something. Here, it refers to God crediting Christ's perfect life to the believer's "account."</note> to us, he makes a comparison between Adam and Christ. He shows that one should no more be surprised by the imputation of Christ’s righteousness than by the imputation of Adam’s sins to his descendants. He therefore presents Adam and Christ as two "heads"—the first of the human race, the other of the believers; the one who brings death to his descendants, the other who grants salvation and life to his members.

The Apostle begins the comparison in this verse and shows that Adam introduced sin into the world and brought death upon all men because they are all considered to have sinned in him. Now, how are all men considered to have sinned in Adam, except through the imputation of Adam's sin?

One can give no other sense to these words without doing them violence.

**I.** It is incomprehensible, it is said, that God <term>imputes</term> the sin of Adam to his descendants, who were not yet born.

**2.** God, having made a <term>covenant</term><note>A 'covenant' is a formal, binding agreement or treaty between God and mankind, often involving promises of life for obedience and death for disobedience.</note> with Adam, was able to enter into it with him under these conditions: that should he violate it, not only would he himself suffer for it, but also his offspring.

<margin>Benoist.</margin>
It is very well noted that in the free gifts of grace, which are offered to someone voluntarily and without obligation, the one who is the giver can set such conditions as he pleases. Now all the covenants that God makes with man are free graces, which He grants him without obligation and through pure loving-kindness. God can then be accused of no injustice if He closed a covenant with Adam under these conditions: that He would follow him and his offspring with His graces, provided they kept His commandments; but that he would lose the same for his descendants, as well as for himself, if he transgressed them.

**3.** One cannot deny that Adam was the Head of the human race, and as the King of all men; it

<column-break/>

is then no wonder that the transgression he committed is imputed to his subjects. A Prince forms but one body with his People.

**4.** But there is more. Adam was the Father of men. They are all his children. Now it is something that nature itself teaches: that children follow the status of their Parents. Whether the Parents are Noble or Slave, Rich or Poor, the children are in the same state. One has always viewed children as a part of the Parents.

<margin>Law: *Regarding those who are guilty of High Treason* <note>original: "L. Quib C. ad Leg. Jul. Majest." referring to the Lex Julia Majestatis in Roman Law.</note></margin>

**III.** It is said that God having forgiven Adam the sin, it is not probable that He has imputed to his descendants a sin which He had forgiven the one who committed it.

**2.** That it is easy to conceive that God was free to act thus. Adam's sin is of this latter kind, because he represented the entire human race. Therefore one also sees that the punishments of Adam and of Eve are spread out over all their children.

**V.** One objects not only to Genesis 18:25, where it is said that God does not make the righteous die with the wicked. But above all, Ezekiel 18:20, where God speaks thus:

> the Soul that sins, it shall die; the Son shall not bear the iniquity of the Father, and the Father shall not bear the iniquity of the Son. The righteousness of the Righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.

One adds to this Deuteronomy 24:16, where it is forbidden to kill the children for the Fathers, and further all the places where, as in Matthew 16:27, Romans 2:6, and 2 Corinthians 5:10, it stands written that God will repay everyone according to his works.

**Answer.** These are weak reasonings. If one must take these passages so strictly, how does it happen that God <term>imputes</term><note>To 'impute' is a legal term meaning to attribute the actions or debts of one person to another. The author argues that God treats humanity as a single legal entity under Adam.</note> the sin of the Fathers to the children, and of kings to the subjects, even that of one Man to a whole people? For Achan's transgression, all the Israelites were punished. Joshua 7:10, 11. Then the Lord said to Joshua,

> Israel has sinned, they have transgressed my covenant, they have also taken of the accursed thing.

It was meanwhile Achan alone who had taken from it.

Because Saul did not keep the word that Joshua had given to the Gibeonites, God struck the people of Israel with a three-year famine. 1 Samuel 21:1. <note>The text cites 1 Samuel 21, but this event is recorded in 2 Samuel 21.</note> In the general Deluge, and in the destruction of Sodom, the children perished with and because of the Parents.

The whole house and lineage of Ham was subjected to the curse that Ham alone had deserved. Genesis 9:25.

Because of Pharaoh's hardening, all the firstborn of Egypt were killed by the destroying Angel. Exodus 11.

Because of the crimes of their Husbands and Fathers, the Women and children of the Canaanites were condemned by God to be rooted out to the ground as cursed ones. Deuteronomy 20:13, 14, 16. God commanded Saul to destroy the Amalekites—

—because their Fathers four hundred years before had set themselves against the passage of the Israelites. 1 Samuel 15:2, 3.

See here God's threat. Leviticus 26:38, 39.

> You shall perish among the Heathen, and the land of your enemies shall consume you, and those who are left among you shall pine away for their iniquity in the lands of your enemies; yes, also for the iniquity of their Fathers shall they pine away with them.

Christ testifies against the Jews in Matthew 23:35: That he will cause to come upon them all the righteous blood that has been shed on the earth, from the blood of Abel the righteous onward.

<margin>Exodus 20:5.</margin>
God declares in his Law, Exodus 20:5, that he will visit the crime of the Fathers upon the children, unto the third and the fourth generation. Because of the sin of David, consisting in the counting of his subjects, God made seventy thousand people die. These examples show enough that one must not consider it such an unusual thing that God imputes Adam's sin to his offspring.

Against all these Scripture passages one brings in: **1.** That God punishes the children when they follow the sins of their Fathers. **Answer.** This is an absurd answer, because besides the fact that God would then visit the children for their own sins and not for those of their Parents, we have brought forward examples of children killed for their Parents' sake, where one cannot say that they had followed their Parents. Secondly, if it only spoke of children who follow their Parents, then the Lawgiver would not only say that he would visit them until the fourth generation, for he will always visit them. One says, **2.** That God only punishes with temporal punishments. **Answer.** But to deprive someone of his covenant and of all its benefits, as he punished the whole lineage of Ham, is that only a temporal punishment? One says, **3.** It is only until the third or fourth generation. **Answer.** But can one say that Ham's descendants were only cast out of God's covenant until the fourth generation? If there were furthermore any distinction between these examples and that of Adam, one could conclude nothing from that against our opinion.

**II.** Regarding Ezekiel 18:20, one must note that the Jews, although they were innocent, complained that they were being punished for their parents; that their fathers had eaten unripe grapes, and that the children's teeth had become blunt. <note>original: "stomp," commonly translated in English Bibles as "set on edge." This refers to the proverb that children suffer for their parents' tastes/sins.</note> The Prophet declares to them on God's behalf that He shall not punish them for the sins of their fathers, as He had the right to do, but for their own sins, and that, consequently, the soul that had sinned should die. This is, therefore, a specific case.

**III.** Deuteronomy 24:16 teaches the Judges how they must deal with criminals, but no conclusion can be drawn from that [regarding God]. God has the right to do many things that He may forbid others from doing, and we have seen how He desired that His people should root out the children of the Canaanites as well as their parents.

<margin>Matthew 16:27; Romans 1:5.</margin>
**IV.** Finally, when it is said that God will repay everyone according to his works, God’s Spirit does not intend to deny in this case that God <term>imputes</term><note>To 'impute' is to legally charge or attribute something to someone's account.</note> the sin of Adam to us (2 Corinthians 5:10), but He only wants to make us understand how closely we must pay attention to our works, since God will demand an account of them from us.

**V.** It is said that if the first sin of Adam were imputed to us, his righteousness would also have been imputed.

**I Answer** that his righteousness would indeed have been imputed to us there, so that we would not be born guilty, but would come into the world in that state in which Adam was created; from which we draw yet another proof for <term>imputation</term>.

It is a fundamental rule, grounded on the purest light of reason, that those who share in the benefits of a <term>covenant</term><note>A legal and spiritual agreement between God and humanity. The author views Adam as the "federal head" or legal representative of all people.</note> must also share in the inconveniences. It follows then that, since Adam's posterity would have shared in the righteousness of the first man if he had remained steadfast in righteousness, they must likewise have shared in his sins.

One raises several other difficulties, but these can easily be resolved by the principles we

<column-break/>

have set down.

It is said that if the first sin of Adam is imputed to us, his other sins must also be imputed to us. I answer that only the first sin must be imputed to us, because by that sin Adam broke the covenant that God had made with him as the head of the human race.

It is said that all his other actions, even the most natural ones, should also be imputed to us. I answer that since we are dealing here with an imputation followed by a punishment, there are no other acts besides moral ones that are imputed, as none but these are punished.

It is said that if sin is imputed to all the descendants of Adam, the same must also be imputed to Christ.

I Answer that this is not a valid conclusion, since it depended upon God to make an exception and to free the Lord Christ from that imputation, whom He sent to make satisfaction for our transgressions. I will not bring other reasons here. <margin>in the Theological Ecclesiastical Epistles 66.</margin> Arminius <note>Jacobus Arminius (1560–1609) was a Dutch theologian whose views led to the formation of the Remonstrant movement. He had a nuanced view of how sin was passed down.</note> asserts in one of his letters that Christ was not in the loins of Adam before he sinned, and thus did not sin in Adam. He proves this: 1. Because he would have to have been there by virtue of this blessing, "increase and multiply," which is not so. 2. Because Christ would then have come from Adam’s loins even if Adam had not sinned, which is not true. But he says that He was in Adam’s loins after his sin, by virtue of the promise, "the seed of the woman," etc.; and that He was in those of Abraham by virtue of this blessing, "in your seed," etc.

It is said that no one ever prayed for the forgiveness of Adam's sin; that is granted, but one must pray to God that He not punish us for this sin.

It is asked whether God would damn a perfectly holy man for the sin of Adam alone?

I answer that where Scripture constrains us, we must decide nothing. Meanwhile, I confess that I do not believe it; but one can conclude nothing from that against the doctrine of imputation.

## VII. CHAPTER.
### Of Original Sin.

**The** sin of our first Father ensures / that we come into the world not only guilty / but corrupted.

From him we have the corruption / which since his fall has clung to human nature / defiled it / and made it worthy of God’s aversion. Cyprian <note>A 3rd-century Bishop of Carthage.</note> calls this the "domestic evil," and Augustine calls it "Original Sin," because we have it from our origin / that is to say / as soon as we begin to exist / and because it is the source-vein of all other sins.

David teaches us this truth in the 51st Psalm, which he left to us as a monument of his repentance; for having pleaded with God in this Song for the forgiveness of his sins / the cause of his tears / he climbs up to the source of his corruption / and confesses that he was corrupt from his conception. *I was born in iniquity, and in sin did my Mother conceive me.* verse 7. Now he who confesses / that he was conceived, made, and born in sin / acknowledges / that he brought corruption and sin into the world from his Mother’s womb / and this is what is called original sin.

It is said, 1. That David here speaks not of Adam, but of his Mother. I answer, that the proof is therefore no less powerful; for we agree / that the sin of Adam is communicated to us by means of our Parents. But he is the first origin of [it].

2. It is said, that he speaks only of his Mother / and of his Mother’s sin / just as one says / that someone is born in adultery. I answer: 1. That it is clear / that David here makes confession of his own sin / and not of that of his Mother / which is not the point here. 2. One cannot object to this / without falsely suggesting / that the Parents of David sinned in the begetting of this Prophet /

<column-break/>

as if he were conceived in an illicit encounter. 3. God's Word clearly shows / that it is spoken here of David, being conceived and formed.

3. It is said, that it is a hyperbolic <term>manner of speaking</term><note>An exaggerated or figurative rhetorical device.</note> / by which David acknowledged / that from his youth / and as soon as reason had begun to teach him to distinguish good from evil / he had been inclined toward sin and impurity / and that consequently this expression signifies nothing else / than a long and old habit of doing evil / in the same sense / as he rebukes his enemies. *The wicked are estranged from the womb; the liars go astray from the (mother's) belly.* Ps. 58:4. And God says against the Israelites in Isa. 48:8. *That they were transgressors from the belly.* Answer. But who does not see / that these and other phrases / which are brought forward / are not like this one / *I was born in iniquity, etc!* for it is clear / that here no actual sin is spoken of / as in the places that are cited: but of a sin / in which one is conceived / and of a corruption / that one has from one's Mother. Why explain David's words / as if he spoke of the time / in which reason taught him to distinguish good from evil / since it clearly appears / that the Prophet speaks of a time / which long precedes the use of reason; besides which, one can very well make use of all the quoted texts / to prove original sin / as many learned men have done.

4. It is said, that / if one must conclude from David's expression / that he was truly conceived in sin / one could also conclude / that many holy Men were born in an original holiness / and that they were free from all corruption / like Job, who says / *From my youth he was brought up with me, as (by) a Father, and from my Mother's womb, I have guided her.* Job 31:18.

David uses the same manner of speaking in Ps. 22:11. *Upon you I was cast from the womb, from my Mother's belly you have been my God.* And Ps. 71:6. *Upon you I have leaned from the belly, from my Mother's womb you are my helper.*

I answer, that / if Job and David had said / that they were conceived in righteousness / just as David says / that he was conceived in sin / one would

is said in **Romans 8:7, 8**. *The carnal mind <note>The Dutch "bedenken des vleesch" refers to the mindset or orientation of the "flesh"—the fallen human nature.</note> is enmity against God: for it does not subject itself to the law of God, nor indeed can it; and those who are in the flesh cannot please God.* In this sense it must be taken here; it is then as if *Christ* said / that all that is born of flesh / as all humans are born / is corrupted / just as that which is born of the spirit / that is, reborn by God’s spirit / cleansed by this spiritual water / purified by this Heavenly fire / partakes in the nature of its origin / in its desires / thoughts / and feelings.

From this reasoning of *Christ* one can easily draw these two consequences.

First, that all who are born as we are / come into the world corrupted: For all that is born of flesh, is flesh. Consequently, we do not corrupt ourselves merely by following evil examples / but that corruption is a poison / with which we are born / that has infected us from the first moment of our lives / and that we bring with us into the world.

Secondly, that (with the exception of *Christ* alone / who is God and Man / conceived by the Holy Spirit) there is no human / but he is born in corruption / because they are all born of flesh.

It is said, that the word flesh should not be taken for corruption: but that it signifies a body / in contrast to a spiritual substance; that it is an answer of *Christ* to the coarse objection of *Nicodemus*, who had said / *how can a man be born, being (now) old, can he also enter a second time into his Mother’s womb and be born? John 3:4.* It is then posited / that *Christ* answers this Teacher / that he was not speaking of a physical and earthly birth / which would have no power at all / to make us enter into God's Kingdom / even if it were repeated a hundred times / since all that comes from flesh / is earthly / mortal / weak and frail / like the flesh / from which it proceeds.

I answer, that one must wish to be blind / not to see / that "flesh" here is taken for corruption. For 1. It is set against the spirit. Now "spirit" is not used here for the soul, as one would have to posit / if "flesh" signified the body. 2. A "flesh" is spoken of here / that needs to be reborn; now

<column-break/>

rebirth presupposes corruption. 3. *Christ* speaks of a flesh, with which one cannot enter into God’s Kingdom / that is / being a member of *Christ's* Church / and having a share in salvation. Now if "flesh" meant nothing other / than an earthly and mortal nature / that does not prevent us from being a member of *Christ*. Corruption alone prevents us from that. 4. Finally, I ask / why that which is born of flesh / is mortal and weak? Is it not because of the sin / that clings to it / and has death as its wages?

Furthermore, what *Christ* says / agrees with that of *Job*. **Job 14:4**. *Who shall bring a clean thing out of an unclean? Not one.*

It is said: 1. That an impurity is spoken of here / that can even be in the Angels / who are not pure before God.

I answer, that *Job* speaks of an impurity / that subjects humans to death / now that is not in the Angels.

It is said: 2. That here not a moral / but a natural impurity must be understood.

I answer, that a moral impurity is spoken of here / because it exposes humans to many evils / and to God’s judgment. One can call it natural / because it is natural to us / and that we come into the world with it; but it is called moral / because it corrupts the heart of man.

We are then born infected / since we draw our origin from an unclean source / and that makes us / by nature children of wrath. **Ephesians 2:3.**

1. It is objected: That *Paul* says / we *were* children of wrath / and not / we *are*; therefore this signifies something / that was no longer in the Ephesians. Now / it is said, those who recognize original sin / are of the opinion / that it is never annihilated / until the hour of death.

I answer, That the phrasing of *Paul* does not weaken the strength of the proof / that theologians draw from this passage. It is true / that we are by nature always corrupted / but the believers / who are converted / though by nature corrupted / are no longer children of wrath / because *Christ* has freed them from his Father’s wrath and from damnation. The grace / that has governed them / does not prevent them from being born with an infected nature / but ensures / that they are protected from the arrows of God’s anger.

2. It is said, That *Paul* here has in view

I answer, That it is clear / that Paul speaks here of everyone in common / *we were by nature children of wrath, even as the others.* <note>Referencing Ephesians 2:3. The author is arguing that "we" includes Paul himself and all believers, not just the former pagans.</note>

3. It is said, That Paul speaks of sins / that the Ephesians themselves had committed / since he adds / that they had *walked* therein / which indicates an old and pleasant habit / and not a condition of nature.

I answer, That Paul in this place ascends from the streams to their source / from actual sins to original sin. *We have all walked*, see there the actual sins; *we were children of wrath by nature*, see there the original sin.

4. It is said, That to be a child of wrath by nature / does not concern birth / because natural things do not change; now those who were by nature children of God's wrath / become children of His love / through the proclamation of the Gospel and through faith in Christ.

I answer, That it is easy to understand / how those / who from their mother's womb had a corrupt nature / and were thereby exposed to God's wrath / were delivered from the same by the blood of Christ and sanctified by His spirit.

5. It is said, That to be a child of wrath by nature / only means / that one is truly worthy of God's wrath / just as Galatians 2:15: *We are Jews by nature*, that is truly; and Galatians 4:8: *You served those, who by nature were no Gods*, that is / who truly were no Gods.

I answer, That it does not only mean to be worthy of God's wrath / but to be worthy of it through the state of nature; and as for the cited passages / to be a Jew by nature, is to be such by a natural right / and not for any other cause / that grafts someone into the body of the Jews / and lets them share in their privileges. To be no God by nature, is to have no Divine existence / to be not worthy by nature / to be worshipped as God. If being a child of wrath by nature only meant being truly worthy of God's wrath / one could say / that we are by nature children of God / because we truly are; but the scripture does not say that.

<column-break/>

6. It is said, That nature signifies a long habit / that habit is a second nature / and that one thus says / that someone is a thief by nature / to indicate / that he has practiced that trade for a long time.

I answer, 1. That this explanation cannot stand here / for Paul does not only say that we were sinners by our nature / but *children of wrath* / which is the punishment of sin. 2. When one says / that someone is a thief by nature / one does not only mean that he is accustomed to stealing / but that he has a natural inclination toward theft / which signifies a ground of natural corruption.

A third proof for original sin / we take from death / which all of Adam's children must undergo / even those who have not yet come to the use of reason: for / as we have often said / *Death is the wages of sin.* <note>original: "De dood is de bezolding der zonde" (Romans 6:23).</note> Since then the children die / they must necessarily be corrupt. With what fairness / asked Fulgentius, <note>Fulgentius of Ruspe (c. 467–533 AD), a North African bishop and staunch defender of Augustinian theology against Pelagianism.</note> would a child be subject to the wages of sin / if it did not have the stain of sin?

It is said, That from the death of children it does not follow / that they are sinners / since the beasts die. I answer, that it is absurd / not to say something worse / to compare the death of children to that of beasts.

The consequence / that we draw from the dying of children / we cannot pass by / because the scripture teaches it to us.

It is said, That children die / because they have their origin from Adam / who after sin was subjected to death. But why does one insist / that they have more of the death of Adam than the sin / since death is a consequence of sin / if it is true / as those who oppose us in this assert / that the sin of Adam was not imputed to his posterity? why does one want / for them to be subject to death / which Adam was subjected to through sin?

If children are born without the stain of sin / what reason is there that they need a Savior? <term>Zaligmaker</term> <note>Literally "Blessed-maker" or "One who makes whole/blessed," the standard Dutch term for Savior.</note> for where there is no sin / no redemption is necessary.

...saves the sinner. 2. Christ does not give eternal life except to those for whom He has died and has satisfied Divine justice. Now, He has not made satisfaction except for those who were tainted with sin.

If children were born unstained, how is it to be understood that corruption is so universal? How is it possible that among so many people not one is found holy, who does not allow himself to be carried away by the stream of sins? Moreover, if it is true—as we shall prove in its proper place—that Circumcision and Baptism were seals of the righteousness of faith and of the forgiveness of sins, one must necessarily conclude that the children to whom the covenant-signs were administered and are still administered, are tainted with sin. Meanwhile, it is admitted that they have actual sins; consequently, they have another sin within them, namely, original sin.

<margin>Limborch.</margin>
<note>Philippus van Limborch (1633–1712) was a prominent Remonstrant (Arminian) theologian who questioned the traditional Reformed view of original sin.</note> It is said, 1. That Christ did not command infant baptism, and that there is no example of it in Scripture. 2. That Baptism signifies not a cleansing of sins but an obligation to holiness of life and a promise of eternal life. 3. That Christ, who was without sin, was baptized.

Answer. 1. It is surprising that the Remonstrants <note>A group of Dutch Protestants who followed the teachings of Jacobus Arminius; they often held more moderate views on human depravity than the strict Calvinists.</note> would rather side with the Anabaptists <note>The "Wederdoopers," a radical Reformation movement that rejected infant baptism, believing only adult believers should be baptized.</note> than acknowledge original sin. 2. In our treatise on Baptism, we shall answer the Anabaptists. 3. It is well known that the forgiveness of sins is joined to Baptism in Scripture; if children are then baptized, one must firmly establish that they are tainted. 4. It is a strained comparison to equate the Baptism that Christ received with our own.

Origen proved the corruption of our nature through Baptism. See Homily 8 on Leviticus, which is attributed to him. He nevertheless had many extravagant thoughts on this subject.

<margin>Origen, *On First Principles* <note>original: "περί ἀρχῶν"</note>, book I, chap. 8; book II, chap. 8; book III, chap. I.</margin>
He believed that souls were created long before God united them with bodies; that using their free will in Heaven, they sinned—some more, and some less; and that God, wishing to punish them according to the number and the appropriateness of their crimes, joined them together with bodies. Thus, he regarded the body as a prison in which souls are locked up. As an

<column-break/>

<margin>In John, Volume 2. In Leviticus, Homily 8. In Matthew 11, § 7.</margin>
example, he brought forward children, where some are more wicked than others. He said that Jacob had tripped the heel of Esau, and that John the Baptist had leaped for joy in his mother’s womb. His opinion on the pre-existence of souls was that which Orpheus, Philolaus, and Plato had held. Meanwhile, Origen confessed that no man was innocent, even if he had lived but one day, relying on Psalm 51: *I was conceived in sin.* He proved that the baptism of children would be useless to them if they had no stain that needed to be washed away. And he claimed that this was the reason why the Saints never celebrated the day of their birth.

Finally, the evil inclinations that are discovered in us from earliest youth—in some more than in others—those secret resistances against reason and good upbringing which the wise of the world have seen in man, confirm our sentiment.

<margin>Tractate Sanhedrin, Babylonian Gemara, chap. 11, § 7.</margin>
The Jews recognized natural corruption; one finds evidence of this in the Talmud <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah and the Gemara.</note> which leaves no doubt about it.

<margin>Vossius, *History of Pelagianism*, book II, part I, Thesis I. Theodoret in Photius, chap. 177. Chrysostom, *Homily to the Neophytes*.</margin>
The most orthodox Antiquity has taught this truth, just as Augustine proved against Julian <note>Julian of Eclanum, a defender of Pelagianism who argued against Augustine’s views on original sin.</note> from Irenaeus, Cyprian, Hilary, Gregory Nazianzen, Basil, and Ambrose. It was defended in many Councils: of Milevis, of Toledo, of Orange, etc. Although some Church Fathers seem to have denied original sin, such as Theodore of Mopsuestia, and a certain Chrysostom, and before them Rufinus.

<margin>Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book 1, chap. 3. Johannes de Laet, *History of Pelagianism*, p. IV, chap. I. Augustine in Jansen, *On the State of Nature*.</margin>
Irenaeus says that Christ came into the world so that we might regain God’s Image, which we had lost in Adam; since on the one hand it was impossible that man, who was wounded and overcome by sin, could triumph over corruption, and on the other hand it was even more impossible that man, persisting in his sin, could be brought into Heaven.

<margin>Cyprian, *On the Lapsed*, book 1. Bellarmine, *On the loss of grace and the state of sin*, book IV, chap. 6, 7.</margin>
Cyprian, writing for Bishop Fidus the decrees of a Council of Carthage over which he had presided, addresses him thus: "If the greatest sinners, coming to the faith, receive the forgiveness of sins and Baptism, how much less must one refuse it to a child who is just born, and has not sinned, except insofar as he is born of Adam according to the flesh, and through his first birth..."

# DIVINITY. VI. Book VII. Chapter.

<margin>Letter 64 and *On the Benefit of Patience* <note>Original: "Ep. 64. & de bono pat." refers to the works of Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258 AD).</note></margin>
> "...has become a partaker in the contagion of the ancient death. He must be all the more easily admitted to the forgiveness of sins, as these are not his own sins, but those of another, which are forgiven him."

In another letter he says that if God forgives adults their sins, He will show all the more grace to newborn children, since they are not guilty of anything other than the sin they bring into the world from their mother’s womb, and which Adam shared with them.

<margin>Quoted by Augustine, *Against Julian*, Book 1, Chapter 2. <note>Julian of Eclanum was a defender of Pelagius and a primary opponent of St. Augustine.</note></margin>
Rhéticius, Bishop of Autun at the end of the 3rd century, said "that children are relieved of their ancient crimes through baptism, and that this sacrament erased the acts of their first ignorance, and purified man from the sins that were born with him."

<margin>Optatus of Milevis, Book IV, p. 79. Augustine *Against Julian*, Book 3, Chapter 3; Book 1, Chapter 2.</margin>
Some scholars are of the opinion that the faith of the Church in the 4th century can be proven by three ceremonies. 1. Through infant baptism for the forgiveness of sins. 2. Through the breathing upon <note>The practice of "insufflation," where the priest breathed on the candidate to symbolize the driving out of the devil and the gift of the Holy Spirit.</note> and the exorcism. 3. Through the Lord's Supper <note>Communion or the Eucharist.</note> given to children. Olympus, Bishop of Spain in the 5th century, assured that sin is born with man, and that the corruption of Adam is communicated with conception. See Hilary on *Matthew 10*, who said that since the fall of our first ancestors, sin is the father of our bodies and wickedness the mother of our souls.

See also *Athanasius, Oration XI Against the Arians*; *Cyril of Jerusalem, Canon 2, p. 7*. These believe that Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, known for his "Golden Mouth" preaching; some debated his views on original sin because he emphasized human will in his sermons.</note> denied original sin because of what he said in a discourse on *Romans 8* to the newly baptized <term>Neophytes</term> <note>From the Greek 'neophytos', meaning 'newly planted'—a term for people recently converted or baptized into the Church.</note>. Others have attempted to justify him. <margin>Augustine *Against Julian*, Book 1, Ch. 2; Thomas Aquinas 1. 2. q. 82; Thomas *On the Human Will*, Discourse 5, Section 1.</margin>

In the year 415, there was a Council at Diospolis <note>Modern-day Lod, Israel.</note>, formerly called Lydda, a city in Palestine, which was gathered against the views of Pelagius <note>Pelagius (c. 354–418 AD) was a monk who taught that human nature was basically good and that humans could achieve salvation through their own efforts without divine grace, a view the Church later condemned as heresy.</note>, who maintained that Adam alone had been harmed and that there was no original sin passing from parents to children, and that all men are born in the same state of perfection as Adam, except that he was not a child. Augustine cites the proceedings of this Council in the *Book of the Acts of Pelagius*; a summary can be found in his 106th Letter.

<column-break/>

Prosper <note>Prosper of Aquitaine, a disciple of Augustine.</note> praises the Fathers of this church assembly. But Jerome says they allowed themselves to be misled by the hypocrisies of Pelagius, who denied the errors he was accused of and gave an apparently orthodox explanation to what he or Celestius had proposed.

The Council of Carthage in the year 418 made many decrees against the errors of Pelagius.

> The 1st was contained in these words:
> "Whoever says that Adam, the first man,
> was made mortal in such a way
> that, whether he had sinned or not,
> he would have died or departed from this body,
> not through the deserts of sin,
> but by the necessity of nature:
> Let him be cursed." <note>Traditional ecclesiastical phrase: "Anathema sit."</note>

The 2nd reads as follows:

> "Whoever denies that newborn
> children must be baptized, or who says that
> they are indeed baptized for the forgiveness of
> sins, but that they do not have the original sin
> of Adam which is erased by the
> bath of rebirth—from which it follows
> that the form of baptism for the
> forgiveness of sins is not true, but
> false: Let him be cursed. Since
> the words of Paul—'through one
> man sin entered the world,
> etc.' and 'they have all sinned in him'—
> must not be understood otherwise
> than as the universal Church, which
> is spread everywhere, has always understood them.
> They add that little children,
> who have as yet committed no sins in themselves,
> are baptized for the forgiveness of sin,
> so that what they have contracted
> by nature may be cleansed by
> rebirth."

Nothing can be said more explicitly than what one reads in a letter from the African Bishops at the beginning of the third book of Fulgentius *On Predestination*.

The Second Council of Orange <note>Held in 529 AD, this council was crucial in settling the Pelagian controversy in the West, affirming the necessity of God's grace.</note> is no less explicit in the first two decrees. The 2nd contains these words:

> "If anyone asserts that the sin
> of Adam was harmful to him alone, and
> not to his descendants, or that the death
> of the body, which is the punishment for sin,
> passed through one man to the whole
> human race, he does God
> wrong and contradicts the Apostle,
> who says: 'through one man sin entered
> the world, and through sin death
> came to all men, in whom
> they all have sinned.'"

<meta>This page continues the historical survey of the doctrine of original sin, transitioning from the early Church Fathers to the decrees of the Councils and the views of various theological groups during and after the Reformation. # CHRISTIAN [DIVINITY]

The *VIth Council* of *Toledo* in the year 638 confirms the same doctrine.

It has been contested: I. by the *Pelagians* <note>Followers of Pelagius, who argued that humans have the free will to achieve salvation without divine grace and denied the inheritance of Adam's sin.</note>, according to the account of *Augustine* (*On the Gift of Perseverance* <note>Original: "l. II. de bon. persev. c. 2."</note> & *On Heresies* <note>Original: "de Haer. c. 88."</note>). II. by the *Socinians* <note>A group that emerged during the Reformation, led by Fausto Sozzini, who rejected several traditional doctrines including the Trinity and original sin.</note> (*Socinus's Theological Lectures* <note>Original: "Soc. Prael. c. 4."</note> & *On Christ the Savior* <note>Original: "ad 1. art. Cuten. de Christo Servat. p. IV. c. 6."</note> *Racovian Catechism* <note>The primary statement of Socinian belief.</note> title: *On Free Will* <note>Original: "de Lib. arb. c. 18. & c. 10."</note> *On the Prophetic Office of Christ* <note>Original: "de Proph. Christi mun."</note> Smalcius *Discourse IV on Justification* and in the discourse *On Original Sin* <note>Original: "de pecc. Orig."</note> *Discourse 2 on Repentance* <note>Original: "de poenit."</note> *On Free Will* <note>Original: "de Lib. arbitr."</note> *Discourse 8. Homily III on John 1. Volkelius Book 5. ch. 13. Ostorodus Institutes ch. 33.*)

One must, however, note that the *Socinians* believe that most men are born corrupt. But they will not allow that this corruption comes from *Adam*, but rather from other men, who have passed their evil nature down to their children. *Socinus's Lectures ch. IV. V. Smalcius Homily III on John. Ostorodus Institutes ch. 34.* III. by the *Remonstrants* <note>Followers of Jacobus Arminius who disagreed with the strict Calvinist view of predestination and total depravity.</note>. In the preface of their defense, they say that there are five opinions regarding original sin that are difficult to understand. *Ochinus* <note>Bernardino Ochino, an Italian reformer.</note> had noted the same. *Dialogue II. 1. Episcopius*, writing against *Heidanus*, calls original sin a "fabrication of *Augustine*." It appears from their defense *ch. 7* that they do not consider original sin to be a sin that can bring God's hatred upon us, nor a punishment that has passed from *Adam* to his descendants. Rather, they see it as a weakness and defect; see *Curcellaeus's Dissertation 2. Arminius* nevertheless believed in original sin; see his oration on the High-Priesthood of *Christ*, and his answer to *XXXI Articles XIII, XIV. Corvinus*, writing against *Tilenus*, says that *Adam’s* sin is imputed to us. IV. by some Roman Catholics. *Durand of Saint-Pourçain* holds the same opinion as the *Remonstrants*, in *Commentary on the Sentences* <note>Original: "II. dist. XXX. q. 1."</note>. He is refuted by *Vasquez* in *Commentary on Thomas Aquinas* <note>Original: "I. II. Thom. Disp. 131."</note>. *Ambrose Catharinus* and *Albert Pighius* only allow for the imputation <note>The legal accounting of Adam's sin to his descendants, rather than an inherited internal corruption.</note> of the sin. V. by some *Anabaptists* (*Colloquy of Frankenthal, Article 2, art. 4.*) It is a false accusation that *Zwingli* is said to have denied original sin. See *Bullinger's Decades, Sermon X* & *Against the Anabaptists Book I. ch. 12. Gualtherus* in the defense of *Zwingli*, at the beginning of the works of this Teacher. The *Colloquy of Marburg* in the year 1529, and the *Confession of Faith* <note>Likely the Augsburg Confession or Zwingli’s Fidei Ratio.</note> presented to *Charles V* in the year 1530.

Several difficulties are raised regarding this subject, which I shall answer.

<column-break/>

1. It is objected: That **God** never forbade original sin in His law, and that consequently it is not a sin.

I answer: That one should not wonder that the Law does not forbid original sin, because the Law presupposes man to be innocent, and only forbids deadly sin, such as *Adam* could commit. Furthermore, one cannot deny that the Law commands a perfect holiness, which this corruption contradicts.

2. It is objected: That one feels no remorse of conscience for the sin of *Adam*, nor for the original sin that it is claimed we have inherited from him.

I answer: 1. That, since we commonly have no remorse except for what we ourselves have done—when one sees that one could have avoided it—it is no wonder that one feels no remorse for original corruption.

2. That without the Law, *Paul* would have felt no remorse for concupiscence <note>The inclination of our nature toward sin; lustful desire.</note>, since he admits that he would not have known it to be sin. Yet one would not dare to say that concupiscence is not a sin.

3. That the Saints daily sigh because they must carry about what they have inherited from *Adam*, and they feel the law that is in their members fighting against the law of the mind.

3. It is objected: That marriage should have been forbidden to stop this propagation of sin.

That was the great argument of the *Pelagians*, but it carried little weight, since marriage is not the cause of original sin, and the same would have taken place in the state of righteousness for the multiplication of the human race.

4. It is objected: that Scripture almost always speaks of the innocence of children, as those who know no difference between good and evil. *Deut. I. 39. Ps. CVI. 38. Rom. IX. 11. Matt. XVIII. 3, 4. XIX. 14. 1 Cor. XV. 20. Jonah IV. 11.*

Answer: All these passages prove nothing. It is said there that children do not know the difference between the right and left hand. Who doubts that? But can one conclude from this that they have no natural corruption?

If they are called holy in *1 Cor. VII*...

<meta>This page continues a series of theological rebuttals concerning the doctrine of original sin. # THEOLOGY. BOOK VI. CHAPTER VII.

VII. 14. It is because they were born into the covenant, to distinguish them from the children of unbelievers.

In Psalm 106:38, it is said that the Israelites had shed the innocent blood of their sons and daughters, since these harmless children had indeed not deserved to be put to death in such a manner. One could have said the same of many adults. In Romans 9:11 <note>The text says Romans 9:14, but the reference to Jacob and Esau doing neither good nor evil is verse 11.</note> it stands written that Esau and Jacob had done neither good nor evil; that is true; but they were both conceived in sin. In Matthew 18 and 1 Corinthians 14, we are exhorted to imitate children, and indeed it were to be wished that we did no more evil than they.

5. It is objected: *That it is a fundamental principle in ethics and in civil society that all sin must be committed knowingly and without compulsion to deserve chastisement, and that one is not held punishable except for voluntary acts that could have been avoided.*

I answer: 1. That this is a false fundamental principle, as we have already shown elsewhere. The same principle serves to excuse all sins of weakness, of neglect, of surprise, as well as the movements of lust.

One may consult what I have said regarding the nature of sin, and what the learned have judged regarding <note>original: "Pêche Philosophique"</note> philosophical sin <note>A term used in theological debates to describe a moral error made without conscious reference to God's law.</note>. 2. Even if one granted this principle, it should not be extended further than to actual sins; but that does not prevent one from calling the original corruption "sin," this word being used for that which is contrary to the holiness that the Law demands.

6. It is objected: *That one perceives no reason why the corruption of Adam should pass to his descendants; that Adam could not have communicated the same, neither as a natural nor as a moral cause.*

I answer, without pausing to explain these <term>Scholastic terms</term> <note>Academic vocabulary used in formal theological and philosophical debate.</note>, that it is easy to understand how God, having imputed the sin of Adam to his descendants (as we have proven), permitted that the corruption, with which Adam had become infected through his first and many other sins, passed to his offspring. It is true, Adam is no more, but his cor-

<column-break/>

ruption has come upon his children, and from his children upon his children's children, thus down to the very last descendants.

7. It is objected: *That one cannot say we have naturally that which we have only acquired through various and repeated acts, and that the inclination to evil is not acquired except through such acts.*

I answer: That it is not true that we have that inclination only through repeated acts; we have it naturally, and increase the same by constantly doing evil. Besides that, one must make a distinction between a general inclination to evil and an inclination to certain particular sins. We have the former naturally; we acquire the latter.

8. It is objected: *That what is natural is not sin.*

I answer: That one must distinguish here; that which is natural—that is, that which constitutes the nature of man as man—is not sin; God is the Creator of nature. But that which is called "nature" only because we come into the world with it, and which infects our nature, can rightly bear the name of sin.

9. It is objected: *That original sin is either an act of every man, or a <term>habit</term> <note>original: "hebbelijkheid," referring to a "habitus" or an ingrained disposition of the soul.</note>. It cannot be an act of every man, for Adam alone sinned: it can also not be a habit, for it is not an acquired habit, seeing as children are not capable of that; nor is it a natural or an infused habit, since God is the cause of both the one and the other.*

I answer: That original sin, properly speaking, is neither act nor habit, but an evil disposition <note>original: "quaade gesteltheid"</note> that is natural to us, and of which God is not the cause.

If one wishes to call it a natural habit, one may give it that name—one is master of the use of words—but then I deny that God is the cause of natural evil habits.

10. It is objected: *That among the punishments with which God threatened our first ancestors, this original corruption is not found.*

I answer: Among those, various other punishments of sin are also not mentioned, such as diseases, etc. Furthermore, what Moses does not teach us, the other Holy Writers do teach.

The author maintains that while humans are born into God's covenant, they nonetheless carry a natural inclination toward evil inherited from Adam.</summary>

# THE CHRISTIAN <note>Presumably "The Christian Theology"</note>

11. **It is objected:** That if Adam's first sin were imputed to us, then **original corruption** would have to be viewed as a punishment for that first sin; and that it is ridiculous to say that a sin is the punishment for another sin.

**I answer:** That even if it were ridiculous to say that one sin is the punishment for another, our position would still hold, because we would show that, even if the punishment does not consist in the corruption itself, it nonetheless consists in the act of God—namely, that we are born corrupt from a corrupt human being. I add further that, if one reads the Scriptures carefully and pays close attention to this matter, one will find that it can indeed be said that a sin is the punishment for another sin. The reasons brought against this seem to me of no importance, because people form a concept of the punishment of sin as if there were only one kind of sin. See 2 Samuel 13:11–12; Romans 1:24–27; 1 Kings 22:20.

12. **It is objected:** That if children were infected with original sin, it would not be said that the **Kingdom of Heaven** belongs to them.

**I answer:** That for the same reason, I could prove that believers are no longer stained with sin, since the Kingdom of Heaven is also promised to them. The Kingdom of Heaven belongs to children not because they are not corrupted, but because Christ has earned salvation for them, and the grace of the Holy Spirit sanctifies them.

13. **It is objected:** That one cannot comprehend how sin can be transferred <note>or "transmitted" from one generation to the next</note>.

**I answer:** That is a foolish thing to say. One must never deny that a thing *is* simply because one does not understand *how* it could have come to be. That is just as ridiculous as if someone were to claim that a person who has fallen into a deep well is not actually in it, simply because he does not understand how he could have fallen in.

<margin>
Ostorodt,
*Institutes*, ch. 33.
Socinus,
*Theological Prelections*,
ch. 4. Völkel,
Bk. V, ch. 28.
<note>These refer to Socinian authors who denied the orthodox doctrine of original sin.</note>
</margin>

14. The **Pelagians** <note>Followers of Pelagius (c. 354–418 AD), who taught that human nature is essentially good and that humans can choose God without special divine grace.</note> objected that the soul, being created pure by God at the moment of its union with the body, could be neither guilty nor sinful.

But it was easy to answer them: that the soul acquires the stain of original sin through its union [with the body]. Sometimes Augustine answers them in a different way; but it

<column-break/>

seems that he was in favor of the opinion that the soul is procreated by the parents <note>A theological view known as Traducianism, which suggests souls are generated by parents rather than created individually by God.</note>; which is an error.

15. **It is objected:** That a single act cannot create a **habit** <note>In the sense of a settled disposition or state of being; from the Latin *habitus*.</note>, and that consequently a single sin of Adam could not have defiled and corrupted the whole Adam and all his descendants.

1. **I answer:** That because Adam's sin angered God and stripped man of his perfect righteousness—whereupon countless other sins followed—it is easy to understand that he became corrupted.

2. That he subsequently passed this corruption on to his descendants.

16. **It is objected:** That one sees pious children being born to parents who are not pious.

**I answer:** That this is true, but they are such because they are born again through God’s Spirit; for from their mother’s womb they bring corruption and sin with them into the world.

I end this Chapter with this remark: that when one admits original sin, one understands the true cause of the deep darkness in which our intellect is buried; the particularly deep and corrupt inclinations that we constantly feel rising within us; that leaning toward pleasures which separates us from the contemplation of the **essential good**; the cause of the disorders of our imagination and the rebellion of our senses; and the reason for all those terrible evils under which men are oppressed, from their birth until the hour of their death.

everyone comes into the world with some inclination toward sin / for / they say / everyone is by nature inclined to that which gratifies the flesh; now / they add to this / everything that pleases the flesh is against God's will. It follows then / they conclude / that everyone is inclined to sinning, but they do not want to admit that this inclination is actually sin. <note>The author is likely arguing against the Remonstrants (Arminians), such as Philippus van Limborch, who viewed the "inclination" as a natural weakness rather than inherent guilt.</note>

It is a wonder / that they find it difficult to call something sin which they themselves confess is against God's will / and against the holiness / that the Law demands: for that inclination toward things against God's will and Law / cannot be viewed as an indifferent condition. It is therefore evil / and consequently one must call it a sin / in the sense that we have described. Meanwhile, they are right to say / that in everyone / who is born / there is a natural inclination toward things / that please the flesh / and a love for the visible. But one must observe / that this inclination causes great disorder in all the faculties of man / in his understanding / in his will / and in all his passions.

To unfold this matter properly / let us observe:

I. That original sin has not corrupted the very <term>substance</term><note>The "substance" or "essence" (Dutch: *zelfstandigheid*) refers to what a thing fundamentally is, rather than just how it behaves.</note> of the soul / as Matthias Flacius Illyricus believed / and defended in a public debate against Strigelius, in the presence of Johann Friedrich, Duke of Saxe-Weimar, even asserting that sin is the substance of the soul. An error / which was also maintained by one Cyriacus Spangenberg. <note>Matthias Flacius Illyricus (1520–1575) was a Lutheran reformer who famously argued that original sin was not just an accident of the soul, but had become the very essence of human nature after the Fall.</note>

The falsehood of the opinion of Flacius Illyricus cannot be doubted / if one pays attention: 1. That all substance is created by God. One cannot say without godlessness / that God is the author of sin. 2. That / if sin were the nature itself of man / it would follow from this / that Christ / by taking on our nature / would also have taken on sin / which cannot be said. 3. It would also follow / that man / when he is sanctified / takes on another nature. One could bring many other reasons / to show the absurdity of this opinion. I will only say / that the Scripture distinguishes our nature from sin / and the corruption that clings to it (Hebrews 12:1) or that dwells in it; therefore, one must not mix them together.

<column-break/>

It is said: That Original Sin is presented to us in Scripture as a Body (Romans 6:6). And as the flesh of the <term>old man</term> <note>A biblical term referring to the unregenerate human nature dominated by sin.</note>. That is true; but one cannot conclude from that that the substance of our soul has been corrupted. Everyone understands well enough the reason for these expressions. Sin is a body / but one that has for its members fornication, adultery, etc. (Colossians 3:5).

Flacius made himself ridiculous / by believing / that the work of the flesh was a substance.

II. But / although we must not fall into the error of this Teacher / we must see to it / that we do not view Original Sin as a mere deprivation of the righteousness / with which Adam was created. Original Sin encompasses two things / both this deprivation of Adam's righteousness / and a general disorder. Not only a lack of light in the understanding / and of uprightness in the will / but also a source of prejudices and errors in the understanding / and a ground of malice and rebellion in the will / an entire irregularity in the passions / an inability toward good and an inclination toward evil / a pull toward fleshly lusts / and a love for sensory things.

The Scripture gives us cause for this thought; it calls our sin **Flesh, Lust, Law of the members, Body of death, Old man**; terms / which signify something positive. <note>By "positive," the author means that sin is an active, existing force or condition, not just the "absence" of goodness.</note>

The effects of sin strengthen us in this truth: for those are positive effects / such as murders, adulteries, evil desires, and many others.

Certainly / one can reason about original sin / as one does about the virtue that is in us; for the effects of sin are no less substantial / than those which virtue produces.

It is said: That everything which is positive / comes from God. That is not so. All substance is from God / but not all qualities / all habits / all dispositions. They are from God if they are good / for God is the cause of all good / but they are not from God / if they are evil.

It is then clear / that Original Sin has its seat in all the faculties of the soul. It darkens the understanding / corrupts the will / and inflames the passions.

It is sometimes called lust <note>The Dutch word is *begeerlykheid*, often translated in theological contexts as concupiscence—the disordered desire for worldly things.</note>...

<meta>The catchword at the bottom is "naamly" (namely), indicating the next page will define or elaborate on the nature of this lust.</meta>

...called / of which we / in treating the Law / shall speak.

One cannot fully comprehend / how this sin exists in children / who are still within their mother’s body; but what we have said / and will yet say / can provide us some understanding of it.

There are many Philosophers and Divines / who believe / that children themselves think while in their mother's womb / and that John the Baptist possessed thought / when he leaped. If this opinion were true / one would have less difficulty understanding / wherein Original Sin consists. But it is not easy to make a certain conclusion about such an obscure matter.

All the children of Adam have inherited this corruption from him / which is natural to us all / except for Christ alone / who was not born as other men are / but was conceived by the Holy Spirit.

It appears then / how we must answer a question / that is often asked concerning the Blessed Virgin / whether she was free from original sin.

These six things are certain:

1. That the privilege / of being born without any corruption / is so great and noteworthy / that / if the Virgin Mary had possessed it / it is probable / that the Scripture would have said something about it. However, it does not speak of this. It says / that Christ was without sin / but it mentions nothing of the kind concerning the Blessed Virgin.

<meta>This page continues the historical survey of theological opposition to the doctrine of the Immaculate Conception, moving from the 12th century through the late 15th century, detailing the conflict between the Dominican and Franciscan orders.</meta>

<header>THE CHRISTIAN</header>

The Papal law <note>The *Decretum Gratiani*, the collection of canon law compiled around 1140.</note> which he wrote 14 or 15 years after Bernard's letter, makes no mention of this Feast, though he lists all the Feasts of that time. One reads these words in the notes (<gloss>Glossa</gloss>) that were made on his writings more than a hundred years after his death:
> “No mention is made here of the Feast
> “of the conception, since it ought not
> “to be celebrated, as is done in many other
> “places and especially in England.
> “The reason is that the Virgin was
> “conceived in sin, just like
> “other saints, with the sole exception of the 
> “Person of our Lord Jesus
> “Christ.”

<margin>Ration. Div. off. l. 7. c. 7. <note>Rationale Divinorum Officiorum by Durandus of Mende.</note></margin>
Durand, Bishop of Mende, who lived in the year 1280, says only that it was celebrated by some.

Thomas Aquinas, who died in the year 1274, says that neither the Roman nor many other churches celebrated this Feast, but that they tolerated the custom of some churches that did celebrate it.

<margin>Bandel. de Concep. B.V. <note>Vincent Bandello, a Dominican who wrote against the Immaculate Conception.</note></margin>
In the 13th Century, many teachers refuted this error of the immaculate conception, and among others Anthony of Padua, Bonaventure, Alexander of Hales, Occam, Alvares, Lyranus, etc.

Five Popes of Rome—Innocent II, Innocent III, Honorius III, Clement V, and Innocent V—have maintained that the Virgin was conceived in sin.

<margin>In 3. Sent. d. 3. q. 1. <note>Refers to Scotus’s commentary on the *Sentences* of Peter Lombard.</note></margin>
At the beginning of the 14th Century, one Johannes Scotus, surnamed the Sharp-Witted <note>original: "Spitsvinnige," translating his Latin title *Doctor Subtilis* or the Subtle Doctor.</note>, said that God could have brought it about that the Virgin Mary was not born in sin, or that she was only in it for a moment, etc., but that it is known only to God what happened to the Blessed Virgin. Meanwhile, if it is not against Scripture, it is fitting to attribute to Mary that which is most excellent.

The Franciscans follow the teaching of Scotus and promote the opinion of the immaculate conception very strongly.

<margin>In 3. Sent. Dist. 3. Art. 1.</margin>
The Dominicans strongly opposed this, following the opinion of Thomas, who says that the Virgin was conceived in sin. Regarding the opinion of Thomas, see Cardinal Sfondrati in a book titled <margin>\* *The Defended Innocence*</margin> \* *l'Innocence defenduë*, in the year 1695, in folio.

Meanwhile, the opinion of the Franciscans had more followers. Jean de Montson, Chaplain of the Order of Preach-

<column-break/>

ers <note>The Dominicans</note>, Teacher of the Faculty of Paris, having proposed among other propositions this one in the year 1387—that the Virgin was born with original sin—was condemned by the Faculty and University of Paris. See du Pin, Vol. XII, p. 141, and in the Works of Gerson, Vol. I, col. 693.

In the year 1439, the Council of Basel made a decree (Session 36) by which it declared that the opinion of the immaculate conception of the Virgin, free from all original and actual sins, must be embraced and accepted by all Catholics. And this decree was accepted by those who approved of this Council, but it was rejected by others. The Dominicans condemned this Church assembly. There was someone who used to say, “The Council of Basel has given birth to a Basilisk.” <note>A wordplay on Basel and the mythical deadly serpent.</note>

In the year 1476, Pope Sixtus IV, a Franciscan, confirmed the new ecclesiastical service of the immaculate conception of the Virgin, composed by Leonardo Nogarola, Prothonotary of the Roman Court at Verona, and promised many indulgences to those who would celebrate it.

While this Bull and this ecclesiastical service caused a great uproar, and the teachers tore each other apart, Sixtus issued another Bull in the year 1483, in which he declared that everyone was free to believe what they wished, since the Roman Church and the Apostolic See had not yet decided anything. That meanwhile, one party should not accuse the other of heresy. He nevertheless shows in this Bull that he favored the Franciscans more than the Dominicans.

In the year 1494, Abbot Trithemius asserted, through a book he wrote in honor of Saint Anne, Mary’s mother, that the Blessed Virgin had been preserved from original sin. Wigand Kuchenmeister <note>original: "Wigandus Cauponis"</note> opposed this. Peace was finally made after Wigand fell silent. That did not prevent the Dominicans from appealing to Pope Alexander.

In the year 1497, 82 teachers of Theology in Paris bound themselves to admit no one to the universities who had not pledged by oath to defend the immaculate conception.

It concludes with the 1497 Parisian decree requiring an oath to defend the doctrine for university admission.</summary>

<header>THEOLOGY. VI. BOOK. IX. CHAPTER.</header>

But a Jacobin <note>A common name for the Dominican Order in France, derived from their Saint-Jacques monastery in Paris.</note> from Rouen, named Saint Jan du Verger, preached the opposite in Dieppe on the 19th of September of that same year.

In the year 1499, the Theological Faculty of the Universities of Cologne supported the same opinion.

In the year 1501, this Faculty did the same as that of Paris.

In the year 1502, two Cardinals made a decree by order of Alexander VI, through which they confirmed that of Sixtus IV, which forbade the two parties from accusing each other of heresy regarding this matter.

In the year 1509, the Dominicans in Bern—wishing to employ devilish means to uphold their opinion, which nevertheless agreed with God's word—were punished according to their deserts. <note>This refers to the "Jetzer Affair," where four Dominicans were burned at the stake for faking apparitions and miracles to "prove" that Mary was conceived with Original Sin.</note>

In the Council of Trent, the war began again between the Dominicans and Franciscans; but they wished to decide nothing. Meanwhile, to give the Franciscans some satisfaction and yet not condemn the Jacobins <note>Dominicans</note>, a provision was added to the end of the decree: That in all that had been said on both sides, there was no intention to bring any prejudice against the opinion of the immaculate conception, and that the meaning of the Council was that the decree of Sixtus IV should remain in effect.

In the year 1570, Pope Pius V forbade disputing this matter in sermons, or writing about it in the common mother tongue <note>The vernacular, or the language of the people, rather than Latin.</note>; though he allowed it to be handled in the Universities.

In the year 1616, Pope Paul V renewed the decrees of Sixtus IV and Pius V, and added new punishments for those who violated them.

In the year 1617, the same Pope forbade saying in public gatherings that the Blessed Virgin was conceived in sin.

All these Bulls <note>Official papal edicts or charters.</note> caused great movements in Spain.

Pope Gregory XV, having renewed the Decrees of Sixtus IV and Paul V in the year 1622, added that no one should be authorized to say that the Virgin was conceived in sin, except for those to whom the Papal See would permit it; and that his intention was not at all to do any prejudice by this decree to the opinion of those who denied the

<column-break/>

immaculate conception.

Finally, in the year 1611, Alexander VII renewed all the decrees that had been issued in favor of the opinion of those who maintained that the soul of the Blessed Virgin had been preserved from original sin.

There you have the account of this great dispute. Simon Santagata, Canon of Bologna, cites 5,000 writers who have defended the immaculate conception of the Virgin Mary in the Roman Church. There are possibly just as many who have contested this opinion in our Church. Heidegger, Professor at Zurich, and Friedrich Ulrich Calixtus, Professor at Helmstedt, have written the history of this conception.
