<margin>Augustine to Jerome, Letter 29.</margin>
**T**here is nothing more investigated regarding original sin than the manner in which it passes from the Parents to the Children. This is a very difficult inquiry, in which one cannot be fully satisfied. Therefore Augustine said that one should strive more to be delivered from these sins through Christ than to know how one received them from Adam; just as one who has fallen into a well should not investigate so much the manner in which he fell into it, as the means by which he shall get out of it.

However, to say something on this matter, we must establish some fundamental principles.

The 1st is, that we do not have our souls from our Parents, but from God, as the Scripture and sound reason teach. <note>This theological position is known as "Creationism"—the belief that God creates a new soul for every human body—as opposed to "Traducianism," which suggests souls are generated by parents.</note>

Indeed, if we had our souls from our Parents, there would be no difficulty regarding the manner in which Original Sin passes to the children: but, when one examines the Scripture and consults reason, one cannot enter into the aforementioned opinion.

The 2nd is, that the soul is not created impure. Such a thing cannot be said,

...without accusing God of being the cause of sin. For nothing that is impure can proceed from God.
   These two principles clearly show that **Original Sin** is not transmitted by means of the soul. It must, therefore, be through the way of the body.
   The 3rd principle is that, while the child is in the mother's womb and still forms a whole with her, it is probable that objects make the same impression on the brain and the heart of the child as they do on those of the mother. The blood and the <term>animal spirits<note>In early modern medicine, "animal spirits" were thought to be volatile fluids that acted as messengers between the brain, nerves, and muscles.</note></term> of the mother have communion with those of the child; the mother’s brain relates not only to all parts of her own body but also to the brain of the child, and through that, to all the parts of the child's body, which is very weak and tender.
   This provides the reason why women who, during their pregnancy, see someone with a mark on a certain part of the face, will imprint that same mark upon their child. It also explains how a mother communicates her own weaknesses of spirit to her children—as all the world knows, there are entire families afflicted with great weaknesses of *imagination* which they have inherited from their fathers or mothers. It explains how children have been seen whose bodies were broken in the same places where criminals were being <term>broken on the wheel<note>A common historical form of execution where a criminal's limbs were shattered by blows from an iron-rimmed wheel.</note></term>, because every blow that the mothers had seen given to the criminal had struck their imagination and, by a physical reaction, the tender brain of their unborn fruit.
   The 4th principle is that the soul is so closely united with the body that certain movements of the body cause certain thoughts to arise in the soul, just as certain thoughts of the soul stir certain movements in the body. And it is probable that God, in fashioning the nature of man through the union of a spiritual soul with a material body, established this order: that not only would the bodies of children receive almost the same impressions as the bodies of the parents (unless some foreign cause disturbed them), but also that the soul, united with the body, would have certain inclinations whenever the body received certain pressures. These are two laws that would have brought no harm to mankind,

<column-break/>

had Adam, remaining in the **state of righteousness** <note>Also known as "original justice," the condition of perfect moral integrity before the Fall.</note>, preserved his body in that condition in which it was created by God.
   The 5th principle is that through the corruption of the heart and the spirit of the mother, all objects tend to fix the soul to fleshly and sensory things.
   The 6th basic principle is that the movements which occur in the brains of children also make deep impressions there (according to our established rule), which attach their newly-created soul to the sensory and the material. From this, it follows that the souls of children transfer everything to their bodies. This is clarified by the following comparison.
<margin>Jurieu, *On Nature and Grace*, p. 210. <note>Pierre Jurieu (1637–1713) was a prominent French Protestant theologian known for his defense of the Reformed faith.</note></margin>
> "If God,"
> it is said, "placed the body into which He wished to pour a soul into the midst of a burning liquid before the soul was infused, the soul, upon entering it, would suddenly be seized with a feeling of pain; on the contrary, if the body, not yet animated, were in a sweet bath, the soul, upon entering it, would have a sensation of joy. In the same way, the body that is in the mother's womb, having already turned toward corruption before it is animated, and retaining that turn which bends the soul toward the love of fleshly things, as soon as the soul has entered therein, it receives these impressions; and there arise in the soul of the child the same passions that are stirred in the mother."

   These principles can already—though not perfectly—give us to understand how sin passes from the parents to the children.
   But, to shed more light on this matter, one must note two things.
   1. That the soul is not created with the same powers that the soul of Adam had in the state of righteousness: for if it had those same powers, it would be able to resist the impressions of the body.
   2. That God's righteous judgment intervenes, which, imputing Adam's sin to all his posterity, allows his corruption to pass to his descendants. Without these observations, one will never be able to have a true concept of this transition.

# DIVINITY. VI. BOOK. IX. CHAPTER.

->Answer.<- One is mistaken. The soul is united with the body by virtue of the decree that God made to multiply the human race through procreation; but as soon as the soul is united with the body—which we have from Adam—Adam's sin is <term>imputed<note>Theologically, "imputation" refers to the legal crediting of one person's actions (either Adam's sin or Christ's righteousness) to another's account.</note></term> to it.

Furthermore, it is not necessary for one to torment oneself to know exactly how **Original Sin** is communicated, but we must pray to God that He, through His Spirit, might overcome our corruption and look upon us in His Son Jesus Christ, and not in ourselves, for we deserve nothing but death. This leads me, in order, to the discussion of the punishment of **Original Sin**.

Certainly, the opinion of the <term>orthodox church<note>Referring here to the established Reformed or Calvinist tradition which the author is defending.</note></term> has always been that children—whether because of the imputed sin of Adam, or because of that which they bring into the world from their mother’s womb—are born as children of wrath and subject to eternal damnation.

The renowned <term>Vossius<note>Gerardus Joannes Vossius (1577–1649), a famous Dutch scholar and theologian.</note></term> (Disp. XXVII. I. p. 15) cites <note>original: "Augustinus in Lib. V. cont. Jul. c. VIII. I. I. de pecc. merit. & remiss. c. XV. XXIII. I. III. de Orig. ani. c. X. I. X. de verb. Ap. Ser. XIV."</note> Augustine in his fifth book against Julian, and his works on the merit and remission of sins, the origin of the soul, and several others, including Paulinus’s book to Zosimus, Orosius’s *Apology for Free Will* <note>original: "Apol. de Arb. Libert."</note>, Prosper against Cassian <note>original: "contra collat."</note> in chapter XIX, and various others.

Indeed, Adam's descendants are subject to the same punishment deserved by him whose sin is imputed and whose corruption is shared. Now, we have proven that the punishment pronounced against Adam consists of temporal and eternal death; it follows then that Adam's children come into the world subject to this same punishment. But notwithstanding this, I am convinced that most will be lost for their own sins, and that all children born of believing parents who die in their infancy obtain Salvation through God’s mercy.

Some objections are made, which I shall resolve with no small benefit.

<margin>Limborch <note>Philippus van Limborch (1633–1712), a prominent Remonstrant theologian who challenged strict Calvinist doctrines.</note></margin>
1. It is said that Adam was not punished with eternal punishment. That is true, but God is not bound to show the same grace to the descendants of Adam; however, He has shown it to several.

2. It is said that, if God condemned the largest part of the human race to eternal fire because of A-

<meta>catchword: Part I,</meta>

<column-break/>

dam’s sin—whether imputed or communicated and clinging—then an act of Adam would have more power to damn us than the blood of Christ has to save us, which is contrary to Romans 5:15. *But not as the offense,* says Paul there, *so also is the free gift.*

I answer, 1. That no one has ever said that God condemns the majority of people to eternal fire for the sin of Adam alone. Many more are condemned for their own deeds than for Adam's sin. 2. That one could reason in the same way about the certainty that exists, according to the testimony of the whole world, that more are lost than saved. One would then say that it follows likewise that the Devil and the world have more power to damn us than the blood of Christ has to preserve us, which would be a ridiculous reasoning. 3. That even if Christ saved fewer people than He does, it would not follow that Christ's blood has less power to save us than the sin of Adam has to bring us to destruction; for He saves all those whom He wills to save. 4. That Romans 5:15 is poorly explained. Paul there compares grace with the offense, not regarding the number of those who share in the grace or those to whom the offense is imputed; for in this regard, sin would exceed grace, since many more die in Adam than are made alive in Christ. But the Apostle exalts grace above the offense in this: that one offense caused the damnation of many, but the righteousness of Christ brings forth the forgiveness of many offenses for us—besides the fact that it is much harder and more glorious to save a single person than to cast a hundred into destruction.

3. It is said that, if **Original Sin** subjected us to eternal punishment, God would be cruel by causing us to come into the world only to be lost.

But who does not see that by the same argument, I could show that God should not let any person come into the world except those He simultaneously wanted to save, since it would be a thousand times better never to be born than...

# THE CHRISTIAN

...than to be born and to be damned. 

Furthermore, how many are there whom God saves, and to whom He <term>imputes<note>In this context, to "impute" means to legally assign the guilt of a sin to someone's account.</note></term> neither their own nor Adam's sin, and how many are lost who perish for nothing but their own sin! It does not belong to us to rebuke God's justice under the pretext that we can give no reason for His handling and for all the ways of His providence; it is enough for us to know that God always acts justly, and to believe what He tells us in His word.

4. **It is said.** That from our doctrine it follows that humans have been less loved by God than the fallen angels, because the angels were punished only for their own sins which they committed voluntarily, whereas humans are condemned to Hell for a sin committed before they were born, and to which they contributed nothing.

**I answer**, 1. That it appears God loved humans more than the angels, since He has saved many humans and none of the fallen angels, and that Christ assumed <term>Human Nature<note>The "Incarnation," where God became man in the person of Jesus.</note></term> and not that of the angels. 2. This reasoning assumes that all people are punished solely for Adam's sin, which is false. 3. In short, we have shown elsewhere by what right God was able to impute Adam's sin to his posterity.

5. **It is said.** That if **Original Sin** deserves any punishments, they must be made proportional to the crime, and that if the crime consists only in the deprivation of original righteousness, the punishment likewise must consist in some deprivation of happiness alone.

**I answer.** 1. That it does not belong to us to determine the punishments that God must bring upon men. 2. That God has the right to punish with eternal punishment every creature found in a state of sin. 3. That just as **Original Sin** consists not only in the deprivation of an original righteousness, but in something positive, the punishment must also be substantial.

6. **The question is asked.** What one must believe regarding the salvation of children who die in their infancy and who are infected with nothing but **Original Sin**. **I answer.** That if they are children born into God’s <term>covenant<note>In Reformed theology, children of believers were considered part of God's "Covenant of Grace" from birth.</note></term>, it is more than probable that God does not impute to them the **Original Sin** in which they were con-

<column-break/>

-ceived, as I have said.

7. **The question is asked.** What we think of the children of the **Heathens** who happen to die in their infancy. **I answer.** That the Scripture says they are unclean, and that nothing that is unclean shall enter into the Kingdom of Heaven. We can say no more about it and leave them to God's judgment.

8. **It is said.** That since they have not transgressed the conditions of the covenant, they should not be subject to damnation. **I answer.** That one can draw no other conclusion from this than that they will be dealt with in a different manner than those who have actually failed to meet the demands of the covenant.

9. **It is said.** That since God has forgiven Adam his sin, the children, who are guilty of this sin alone, should not be punished. **I answer.** That it does not belong to us to determine what God must do. He willed to forgive Adam his sin, but He does not grant the same grace to all his descendants.

### CHAPTER X.

->Of actual sin, and of the various kinds of sins.<-

---

An evil tree brings forth evil fruit, and from an impure spring flow impure waters. **Original sin** is the evil tree and the impure spring. <term>Actual sins<note>Known in Latin as *peccatum actuale*, these are specific individual acts of sin, as opposed to the inherited state of Original Sin.</note></term> are the names given to all those into which we daily fall, whether by not doing what the Law commands, or by doing what it forbids. 
There are various kinds of these, which we shall examine somewhat more closely.

1. Sin, as has been said, is distinguished into **sin of commission** and **sin of omission**. It is called **omission** when one does not do what the Law commands, and **commission** when one does what the Law forbids. Everyone knows that the Law commands some things and forbids others. It commands the good and forbids the evil: one transgresses the Law in these two ways.

<meta>This page transitions from a discussion on the justice of God regarding Original Sin to a detailed classification of actual sins, specifically focusing on sins of omission and the various ways humans sin through thought, word, and deed.</meta>

# DIVINITY. VI. BOOK. CHAPTER X.

It seems that the sin of **omission** <note>Dutch: *nalaatigheid*, literally "negligence" or "leaving undone."</note> should not be called a sin, since the omission of an act, it is said, is not an act itself.

->Yet one shall agree that it is a sin.<-

<margin>James IV. 17. Matt. III. 10. John XV. 2. Luke XII. 47.</margin>
1. When one pays attention to what the Scripture says. James 4:17: *Therefore to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin.* Matthew 3:10: *Every tree which bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire.* John 15:2: *Every branch in me that beareth not fruit my Father taketh away.* Luke 12:47: *And that servant, which knew his lord's will, and did it not, shall be beaten with many stripes.*

2. When one considers that a sin of omission is almost always accompanied by an act of our **will**, through which we do not want to do what we are obligated to do. Or, it is preceded by an act that is the cause or occasion for it, or which prevents us from fulfilling our duty. When we do not do what the Law commands, it is either because we do not want to do it—as when someone says, *I will not perform acts of charity, I will not give alms; I will not hear God's word, I will not go to Church*—or because we want to do something else that prevents us from doing what God commands—such as when someone wants to sleep when it is time to go to Church—or because we have done something that has made us unable to fulfill our duty—as when someone has poorly spent the money that he should have set aside for the poor, for that leaves him unable to practice charity.

It also frequently happens that one falls into this sin of omission through **ignorance** or through **inattention**.

One must observe that in all sins, both an omission and a <term>commission<note>Dutch: *bedryf*. In theology, a "sin of commission" is doing what is forbidden, while a "sin of omission" is failing to do what is commanded.</note></term> can be found, to use these **Scholastic** modes of speech; that is to say, that one does what one ought not to do, and does not do what one must do.

II. We sin with **thoughts**, **words**, and **works**.

<margin>Matt. V. 28. Matt. XV 19. Prov. VI. 18.</margin>
1. With **thoughts**. Matthew 5:28: *Whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.* From the heart proceed evil thoughts. Solomon speaks in Proverbs 6:18 of *A heart that deviseth wicked imaginations.* With **words**. Such

<column-break/>

sins are slanders, uncleanness, lies, insults, dishonest and unchaste words, and even **idle words**, Matthew 12:36. We have explained in our <term>ethics<note>Dutch: *zedekunde*, the study of moral conduct.</note></term> what these idle or useless words are. Some translate this as "false" or "harmful" words. 1. But it is certain that the Greek word <note>original Greek: *argos*</note> for "idle" means that which does nothing, or serves no purpose. Matthew uses it thus in 20:3 and 6 to describe the people who were in the market without doing anything. 2. It is certain that those who translate the root word differently limit the thoughts of Christ too narrowly.

3. Finally, we sin with **works** (deeds), which needs no proof. One only has to note that we almost always sin in all these ways at the same time.

III. One also distinguishes between sins of the **flesh** and sins of the **spirit**. Sins, or defilements of the flesh (2 Cor. 7:1), are those named that occur through the members of our bodies, and which would not be committed if we had no body. Such are murder, adultery, theft, gluttony, and drunkenness. Sins of the spirit are those for which our body is not necessary, although it is commonly the cause of many fleshly acts. Such are ambition, pride, hatred, and envy, which are placed among the "works of the flesh" in Galatians 5:19.

IV. One distinguishes between that which is sin by its **own nature**, as an evil deed, and that which is sin only in respect to certain **circumstances**. For example, giving alms out of pride is a sin—not the gift in itself, but because of the vanity of the giver. In this sense, it has been said that the **virtues of the Heathens** were "shining sins" <note>This refers to the Augustinian idea (*splendida peccata*) that even seemingly good deeds by non-believers are sinful because they lack the proper motivation of love for God.</note> because all their deeds did not proceed from a true love for God, nor did they serve His glory. They sprang from self-love and had no other end than empty honor.

<margin>Levit. IV. 2. Luke XXIII 34. Acts III 17. I Tim. I. 13. John XVI 2. Num. XXXV. 11. etc.</margin>
V. One distinguishes between the sin committed through **ignorance**, and that committed **against better knowledge**. Both are spoken of in the Scripture. Of those who crucified the Lord of glory, it is said that they knew not what they did. Christ gives them this testimony. Peter says in Acts 3:17: *I wot that through ignorance ye did it.*

One asks whether there is such a thing as an innocent error, just as there is such an ignorance.

I answer: *Undoubtedly no*; ignorance being a simple deprivation of knowledge, God can be the cause of it in various cases without prejudice to his holiness and truth.

But error, being a moral disorder and an evil use of the intellect, cannot be attributed to God as its source without blasphemy. Furthermore, a person may be unable to know certain historical truths with certainty; but he is never driven by a hard compulsion to make a false judgment, because one must not affirm a proposition unless one is convinced that it is true. Now, one can never be completely convinced of the truth of a proposition that is false. One must then suspend one’s judgment until one has clear and distinct ideas of the truth or falsehood of the proposition that presents itself to our understanding. And this suspension is within our power. All our errors, even the "innocent" ones, are effects of our natural corruption and desire <term>begeerlykheid: often translated as concupiscence; the innate inclination toward sin and worldly desires</term>.

<margin>Saurin</margin>
A learned man <note>referring to Jacques Saurin (1677–1730), a famous French Protestant preacher known for his eloquent sermons</note> has very rightly said that to distinguish someone in error through no fault of their own is to destroy God’s holiness and man’s freedom: for it is to suppose either that God clearly and distinctly sees that what is true is false, and the false true, or that He determines man in an irresistible way to believe a thing without reason, and to imagine that the reasons for which he believes it are convincing, even though they are not; or to want to believe it oneself, whatever the cost, even though they believe they have no reason to believe. Now, all of this is unworthy of God. Meanwhile, one must note that all errors are not of the same consequence. There are some that concern neither God nor our fellow man. Those who fall into these do not offend God, except insofar as they

<column-break/>

misuse their reason; but there are errors that offend the Divinity and the holiness of man, and those errors are inexcusable <note>original: "onvergelpelyk," likely a variation of "onvergeeflyk" meaning unpardonable or inexcusable</note>, some much more so than others.

One asks whether one can rightly accuse someone who is in error of obstinacy. <margin>* The author of the Philosophical Commentary.</margin> * The creator of the *Philosophical Commentary* <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), whose "Commentaire Philosophique" argued for religious tolerance and the rights of the "erring conscience"</note> argues that one must not accuse such a person, if it appears that he errs in good faith, just as one cannot accuse someone of obstinacy who finds sweet what others find bitter.

<margin>Saurin</margin>
Answer: It has been very well noted that this writer confuses taste—the objects of the senses—with the judgment of the truth or falsehood of a proposition. When someone finds a fruit sweet that is bitter to another, neither one is deceived. The same fruit happens to produce in one the feeling that is called sweetness, and in the other what is called bitterness; but it would be ridiculous to say that 2 and 2 make four in respect to some, and 5 in respect to others. Truth is independent of the feelings of men. 2. Since the heart of man is deceitful above all things, it is more than likely that there is always some passion that closes our understanding to the truth.

One asks whether the errors that do not restrain our desires should be viewed as effects of our corruption and as sins.

<margin>Saurin's Reflections</margin>
I answer: 1. That since God can no more be the cause of error than of sin, we must seek the cause of it in ourselves. 2. That there is not one of our sentiments that does not have something of our passions in it. Thus, many thousands of people believe a liberal fiction that honors their nation, and at which other nations scoff. It is pride that produces and nurtures this error. Theological errors have the same origin; therefore they are punishable, as one cannot be too modest nor too careful to close one’s eyes to the voice of the passions and of desire when one is about to give a judgment upon which God’s honor and our eternal salvation depend. 3. That most errors flatter either reason or the senses, and therefore they are effects either of the inflexibility of our proud and inflated reason,

VI. One distinguishes between **sins of weakness** and **sins of malice**. Some call "weakness" all sins that are not committed with premeditated counsel and evident contempt for God and His Majesty.

Others call "weakness" all those small sins into which we fall daily, whether through inattention or by being caught off guard, being carried away by a passion that has not left us time to reflect within ourselves.

One calls **sins of malice** those which we commit after mature consideration, "with a raised hand" <note>original: "met opgeheve hand"; a biblical idiom for acting with defiant, intentional rebellion</note>, to speak with the Scripture. Such are the crimes committed through pride, which David prayed to be kept from.

<margin>*Ps. XIX. 14.* <note>Psalm 19:13 in modern English Bibles: "Keep back your servant also from presumptuous sins."</note></margin> One also calls them sins against the conscience. One must note that there are two ways in which one sins against the conscience. There are people who—without regarding what their conscience (which speaks to them on God's behalf) presents to them—give themselves over to their desires and *want* to give themselves over. This is the sin of those of whom Paul speaks in *Hebrews X, 26*: *Those who sin willfully after they have received the knowledge of the truth.* And, in a word, of all whom God gives over to their own minds. But there are others who, enticed by the attractions of the world and the sweetness of sin, allow themselves to be seduced by sin against the prompting of their conscience. This does not happen without struggle and resistance.

Thus it sometimes happens that even the reborn <term>wedergeborene: those who have undergone spiritual renewal or "regeneration"</term> themselves sin against their consciences, and those are the sins that cost them so many sighs and tears.

VII. One distinguishes sin into **reigning** <term>heerschende: dominating or ruling over the person</term> and **non-reigning**; but these words are explained in various ways. Some understand by *reigning sin* the sins of the unregenerate in general, whether they must

<column-break/>

die in their sins, or whether they will have repentance for them; whether they sin with a gnawing conscience or with full consent; whether they sin by surprise and without forethought, or whether they sin premeditatedly. The reigning sin is then, according to their view, the dominion of natural corruption before it is changed by grace.

Others understand by *reigning sin* every crime that involves a person in death-deserving guilt, whether it is a reborn or an unregenerate person who commits it. Thus, according to their thoughts, every sin that overcomes the person is a reigning sin.

Finally, others understand it as a sin that has strengthened itself in us through a long-standing habit, which keeps us captive, makes us slaves of sin, and subjects us to its dominion.

As for the **non-reigning sin**, some understand it as the corruption of the heart that has been brought under subjection by grace, but which nevertheless, in particular cases and regarding certain objects, triumphs over the believers themselves. Others understand it as all sorts of sins that believers resist through the grace of the Holy Spirit, and which consequently do not subject them to eternal death because they repent of them and obtain forgiveness.

Among the sins, there are some called **crying sins** <note>original: "schreeuwende zonden"; sins considered so grave that they are said to "cry out" to heaven for divine justice</note>, such as the shedding of innocent blood (*Genesis IV. 10*). The sin of robbery (*Habakkuk II. 11*). The sin of those who withhold the laborer’s wages (*James V. 4*). The sin of those who oppress the Poor, Orphans, Widows, and God’s people (*Exodus III. 7; XXII, 23, 24*). The sin of Sodom (*Genesis XVIII. 20*).

VIII. One distinguishes sin as consisting either in a **single act** or in **habit**. The first can be committed by an honest man without him having a particular inclination toward it. One calls **sins of habit** or "habituality" those we commit through an old habit and the inclination we have toward that sin. Among the sins consisting of a single act, there are some where reason is caught off guard and carried away by a strong impulse. There are others that one commits premeditatedly, like the sins of guile and deceit.

Finally, one distinguishes the sins that God forgives from those He does not forgive, where...

## CHAPTER XI.

### Concerning the disparity of sin, and whether every sin deserves death.

It appears / that all sins are not equal / as it is said / that the *Stoic Philosophers* believed / and with which **Jovinianus** <note>A 4th-century Christian monk who opposed the idea that some sins were inherently worse than others</note> himself was even accused / although **Alfonso de Castro** <note>A 16th-century Spanish Franciscan theologian known for his writings against heresies</note> denies this of him. There is as much variety in sin / as there are different species that can be contained under one genus.

There are sins that cannot coexist with communion with God / and with true sanctification; there are those into which a true believer can fall / without falling away from his faith; there are those that deeply wound the conscience; there are those that do not wound the conscience / and do not inflict a mortal injury. There are those that actually subject a person to God's wrath / and consequently to eternal death / if he does not repent of them / such as those which **Paul** mentions in 1 Cor. 6:10, Gal. 5:21, and Col. 3:6. There are those that do not subject a man to God's disfavor / and do not expose him to His vengeance / provided they are not committed maliciously. There are those that one cannot think of without horror. There are others that are not so gruesome. Everyone knows / that there is a difference between a **parricide** <note>One who kills their own father</note> / and one who commits **incest**; between a rude mockery / an involuntary wandering of thoughts during worship / and an unchaste look. There are those that one can easily avoid. Others, into which one almost falls / before one knows it. There are those of such a nature / that we / if we died in the act of committing them / and without true repentance / would be damned. There are others, which do not separate us from God's love / which do not deprive us of the workings of His mercy / and do not shut us out of the Kingdom of Heaven. There are those that one must actually forsake / and leave behind / otherwise there is no hope of Salvation. There are others, from which we

<column-break/>

must strive to abstain / but if our weakness / despite our resistance / causes us to fall into them / we may hope / that God will not reckon them against us.

->**There is then disparity in sin.**<-

The Teachers of the **Roman Church** etc. distinguish sin into **mortal** and **venial** <term>venial: from the Latin 'venia' meaning pardon; sins that are considered "forgivable" or less grave in Catholic theology</term> sins. They say / that a sin can be called venial / either when it is committed through ignorance and weakness. Opposite this sin stands one / which is called mortal / and is committed out of malice. Opposite this sin stands a sin / which is by its nature unpardonable; or it is called venial by nature.

We have no disagreement with the Roman Church / regarding the first two meanings / but we simply deny / that there is any Sin / which by its own nature and essence does not deserve death. They distinguish three more types of venial Sins.

The first, which indeed have an evil matter as their object / but which are not against the love / that we owe to God and our neighbor / such as an **idle word**, or **immoderate laughter**. The second, which are not voluntary / such as the **first stirrings of anger and envy** / which suddenly surprise us. The third, which are so minor / that one hardly takes notice of them / such as **stealing a penny**.

We must however observe / that there are Teachers among them who believe / that all sins cannot be justly punished with an eternal punishment / but that God's goodness ensures / that they are only punished temporarily. Some objections are raised that do not hold much weight.

1. It is said that **James** only says of sin that is "full-grown" that it brings forth death <note>Referencing James 1:15</note>. That is true; but he does not mean to say that sin only first deserves death after it is full-grown. He does not distinguish between several types of sins, where some deserve death and others do not. Rather, he describes the various stages through which sin passes and the progress of temptation. We shall have the opportunity to deal with this in another place.

2. One objects from 1 Cor. 3:15, where **Paul** says that he who has built "hay, wood, stubble" on a good foundation shall be saved.

I Answer: 1. That "hay, wood, stubble" does not signify light sins, but new, vain, and strange doctrines; **Bellarmine** admits this in *On Purgatory*. 2. The point of dispute is not to know whether those who commit light sins will be saved, but whether they do not deserve death. This passage does not prove that they do not.

3. It is said that **John** calls the sin against the Holy Spirit a "sin unto death," 1 John 5:16; consequently, it is argued, there are sins that do not deserve death.

Answer: This reasoning would prove that murder, adultery, etc., are not sins that deserve death, which one would not dare to say. All sins, except the sin against the Holy Spirit, are distinguished from the "sin unto death"; not because they do not deserve death, but because God forgives them to those who repent of them, whereas the sin against the Holy Spirit is absolutely unpardonable and one never repents of it.

### CHAPTER XII.

#### On the Sin against the Holy Spirit.

Since the Sin against the Holy Spirit is the greatest of all sins, and one that is never forgiven, it is necessary to know its nature and essence accurately in order to avoid it. To this end, we arrange this Chapter.

This sin is spoken of in Matthew 12:31, 32. *Therefore I say to you, every sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven men, but the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven men. And whoever shall have spoken a (certain) word against the Son of Man, it shall be forgiven him; but whoever shall have spoken against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this age, nor in the one to come.* Mark records Christ speaking thus in Mark 3:28, 29. *Truly I say to you, that all sins shall be forgiven the children of men, and all kinds of blasphemies with which they shall have blasphemed, But whoever shall have blasphemed against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness forever, but he is guilty of eternal judgment.* From which it appears that Matthew is explained by Mark. In verse 30, he adds that Christ said this against the Pharisees because they said of him, *He has an unclean spirit.*

There is therefore no doubt that there is a sin against the Holy Spirit, but we must investigate what it consists of.

sin is very great, we nevertheless see that 
God calls many of these people to the true 
faith.

commit these sins; for under the new dis-

IV. One must not confuse the sin of Heresy 
with the sin against the Holy Spirit. 
One can return from Heresy, but from

V. All those who have the habit of com-

These habitual sins cannot, I admit,

often happens that such people repent.

many who have been so unfortunate as to 
fall away have risen again, weeping for

Apostle been accused of sinning against the 
Holy Spirit.

I also do not believe that the sin against

<margin>Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 9. Basil, *Shorter Rules*, 23.</margin>

> "He who shall have spoken any word against the Son

Indeed, one must not be surprised that such a sin is unpardonable, especially when one considers:

1. That the Pharisees attacked the miracles which Christ wrought to confirm the truth of his mission.
2. That they could know that these miracles could not happen except through a Divine power.
3. That they did this through a surrendered <note>original: *overgegevene* — meaning a state of being completely handed over to or consumed by evil.</note> wickedness, and not out of fear of any punishment, because the Lord rebuked their hypocrisy, and because they were fearful of losing their authority.
5. <note>The original text skips number 4 in the list.</note> Finally, that they were confirmed in this malice.

But, although I believe that one has reason to say that the Pharisees, who spoke of Christ in such a way, sinned against the Holy Spirit, this matter is nevertheless full of difficulty.

1. It is a very uncertain matter whether the Pharisees believed that the miracles of Christ could not be done except by a Divine power, or whether they were of the opinion that the Devil could do such things. I grant that they would have been in a great error; since it is certain that the Devil could not do what Christ did; but the error makes them much less guilty than they would have been if, believing that these miracles proceeded from a Divine power, they had attributed them to

<column-break/>

the Devil.

2. One could interpret the words of Christ otherwise, and say that Christ wishes to give the reason why he does not excommunicate <note>original: *in den ban slaat* — literally "strikes into the ban," referring to the formal ecclesiastical punishment of excommunication or anathema.</note> those who attributed his miracles to Beelzebub, but that he occupies himself with showing them the falsehood of their reasoning; namely, because it was a blasphemy against the Son of man, which could be forgiven, nothing being unpardonable but the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit.

To know this sin even better, one must see whether the scripture speaks of it only in the places that we have cited from Matthew and Mark.

When we read the 6th and 10th Chapters of Paul to the Hebrews, it is impossible that we should not recognize that the sin against the Holy Spirit is spoken of in both those places. Hebrews 6:4, 5, 6:
> It is impossible, says the Apostle, for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted of the Heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the age to come, and fall away, (I say) to renew them again unto repentance; seeing they crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh, and put him to an open shame.

For, he says, Hebrews 10:26–31:
> if we sin willfully after we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remains no more sacrifice for sins, but a certain fearful looking for of judgment and fiery indignation, which shall devour the adversaries. He that despised Moses' Law died without mercy under two or three witnesses. Of how much sorer punishment, suppose ye, shall he be thought worthy, who hath trodden under foot the Son of God, and hath counted the blood of the Covenant, wherewith he was sanctified, an unholy thing, and hath done despite unto the Spirit of grace. For we know him that hath said; Vengeance belongeth unto me, I will recompense, saith the Lord, and again the Lord shall judge his people; it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.

# THE CHRISTIAN [THEOLOGY]

<columns>
...fell back into sins; others understand this to refer to the Jews who, after they had been baptized and had received the gift of miracles—which the first Christians received through the laying on of hands—returned to the Synagogue, where they poured out their blasphemies against the Lord Christ.
The majority of those who hold this view explain these words, *it is impossible for those who were once enlightened to be renewed*, as if one must understand "enlightenment" to mean "baptism," according to the style of the Church Fathers <note>The early Greek Fathers often used the term *photismos* (enlightenment) as a synonym for baptism.</note>, and as if Paul meant to say that it was impossible for them to be renewed unto repentance because they could be baptized only once.
But I confess that this reasoning does not please me.
1. Paul never called Baptism an "enlightenment"; it was only long afterward that Baptism was named thus.
2. I also cannot approve of interpreting "to be renewed unto repentance" as "to be rebaptized."
3. Most who favor this explanation imagine that those who could not be rebaptized could no longer have faith or remorse.
These thoughts, it seems to me, have no basis. In my judgment, Paul speaks in those two places <note>Referring to Hebrews 6:4-6 and Hebrews 10:26.</note> of the sin against the Holy Spirit; and here is my proof.
Christ presents to us, in Matthew, the sin against the Holy Spirit as the only sin that is unpardonable. Now the Apostle speaks of a sin from which one cannot return, and for which no further sacrifice remains. From this, it appears to me to follow that Paul speaks of the same sin of which Christ had spoken, and of which the Pharisees had made themselves guilty. This being presupposed, we shall draw from these passages the characteristics of the sin against the Holy Spirit.
The 1st Characteristic is that it is a sin that is not committed except by those who know the truth. Paul notes this when he says: 1. That they were *enlightened*, which means that they have known the true Evangelical Doctrine and that they have been instructed in Religion. 2. That they *have tasted the heavenly gift and the good word of God*, that is, that they have acknowledged that the Gospel was the good word, that they had tasted it, and that they had a reasonably lively feeling of the advantages it contains.

<column-break/>

3. That they have had the *knowledge of the truth*. Heb. X. 26.
The 2nd Characteristic of this sin is that it is committed by those who have received some grace of the Holy Spirit; the Apostle notes this when he says that they have been made *partakers of the Holy Spirit*. For, although one can apply these words to the miraculous gifts of the Holy Spirit—which were then distributed in the first century of the Christian Church and consisted of either the gift of tongues or healing, etc.—nothing prevents us from understanding the same as the internal gifts and grace of the Holy Spirit; for one must observe that it is not the believers alone who have a share in the grace of the Holy Spirit; it is true they alone are those whom the Holy Spirit converts and incorporates into the communion of the Savior; they alone are those whom He sanctifies and fills with perfect consolation; but there are graces of the Holy Spirit that are common to the good and the wicked alike.
For example, it is the Holy Spirit who restrains the obstinate passions of the greatest villains and who keeps them from doing as much evil as they otherwise would. It is the Holy Spirit who curbs them and moves them through the gnawings of their conscience, which He awakens. It is the Holy Spirit who convinces so many people of the truth and sweetness of the Gospel, and who sometimes gives them the strength to embrace the true faith.
Thus, it is easy to understand how those who sin against the Holy Spirit have received some grace of the Holy Spirit; indeed, it is necessary that one presupposes it.
The 3rd Characteristic of this sin is that it must be committed *willfully*. *If we sin willfully*, says the Apostle; that is to say, without being forced to do so, and against the light of the conscience.
There are two ways to do something willfully. The one is when one does it with one's full will; the other, when one does it with a conflicting will that is tossed back and forth by the reasons that present themselves for and against—as in the case of a Merchant who throws his goods into the sea, partly with and partly against his will <note>A classic philosophical example of "mixed" voluntary action: the merchant wants to save his life, but does not want to lose his cargo.</note>. He wills and he wills not. When it is said that those who sin against the Holy Spirit sin "willfully," we do not speak of those who, either terrified by the fear of death or blinded by the glitter of honors and riches, abandon the truth; but of those who the truth...

</columns>

# THEOLOGY. VI. B. XII. Chapter.
->397<-

...abandoned [the truth] voluntarily in a time in which nothing forced them to do so, but rather several things bound them to hold it fast.

<margin>Heb. X. 29.</margin>
The **IV. Characteristic** is that this sin is a total abandonment of the truth of our Savior, through which one shows that they value the world and its pleasures more than Him. Paul notes this when he says that they *trample the Son of God underfoot*, that they *treat the blood of the Covenant as unholy*, and *insult the Spirit of grace* by opposing the good stirrings that He awakens in their hearts.

<margin>Heb. XII. 16.</margin>
The **V. Characteristic** is that this abandonment of the truth is paired with the contempt of the truth. These words further signify this: *Trampling the Son of God underfoot, treating the blood of the covenant as unholy*; for through these expressions, Paul shows us that such people reject the Savior, esteeming Him less than the goods of the earth, and viewing His blood as a trivial and contemptible thing. The Apostle points this out more closely when he compares those people to those who despised the Law of Moses, and to the *unholy Esau*, who sold his birthright for a dish of lentils. <note>original: "geregt van linzen"</note> Hebr. XII. 16.

The **VI. Characteristic** is that this contempt is often accompanied by **hatred**, when these unfortunate souls see that the Gospel comes to disturb their false joy; the presence of the confessors of the truth disturbs them, because it seems as if they reproach them for their apostasy and cowardice. It also often happens that these God-forgetting people persecute the truth and those who proclaim it, just as the Jews persecuted our Savior and His Disciples. They blaspheme not only the Spirit of grace but also those in whom this Spirit dwells.

Finally, the **VII. Characteristic** is that those who fall into this abominable sin become so hardened in it that they remain in it until the end. This leads Paul to say that *it is impossible for them to be renewed unto repentance*. It appears then that the sin against the Holy Spirit is a malicious rejection and, if I may speak so, a total denial of the truths of the Gospel, which were previously known, accompanied by contempt and hatred, and almost always paired with persecution, but always with final impenitence.

<column-break/>

Several questions are asked regarding this.

I. One asks, how is it possible that there could be a person in the world who, knowing the truth and utility of the Gospel, rejects, despises, hates, and persecutes it? How can anyone be so maddened?

<margin>Claude on this subject.</margin>
<note>This likely refers to Jean Claude (1619–1687), a prominent French Protestant theologian famous for his defenses of the Reformation.</note>
I answer that one should not be surprised by this, because those who fall into this sin embrace the Gospel not so much because they have been moved by the preciousness and excellence of its truths, but because they have been touched by the idea of the good that God promises in His fellowship, and of the blessedness that the Gospel makes us hope for; or because they found some temporal advantage in the profession of Christianity, and believed that they could easily pair Christ with the world, the Gospel with the advantages of this Age and their own passions. 

But when they notice that they cannot profess the truth except by curbing their urges, by giving up their pleasure, by exposing themselves from time to time to various persecutions, by enduring many kinds of temptations, the laying down of their offices, the leaving behind of their goods and the comforts of this life, and the losing of that which is most pleasant and desirable to the flesh—then they find that they have miserably deceived themselves in believing that they could easily reconcile Christ with the world and pair the Gospel with their passions. 

And seeing themselves forced to abandon either one or the other, as they take nothing more to heart than the comforts of this present life, caring little for the future, they reject Christ and His truth, even with fury, reflecting on how narrow an escape they had from losing—for the love of Christ—that which they hold as their highest good: namely, their offices of honor, their prestige, and all those temporal goods which are the **Godhead** they worship. The salvation of Jesus, which seemed so advantageous to them when they thought only of the Glory He has obtained for those who love Him, makes them afraid when they remember with what misery, pain, disdain, and loss the confession of the Gospel is accompanied; and, as has been very well said, the idea of the future good that shines in salvation and gladdens their hope is swallowed up in their soul by the present miseries that befall them.

# THE CHRISTIAN
->398<-

I further answer that one does not fall suddenly into this sin, and that one falls into it when it seems that one ought not to fall into it. It happens sometimes that there are those who abandon the true religion through the transport of their passions. Once the "thirst" <note>Likely referring to the heat of the moment or a temporary craving for worldly things.</note> has passed, they feel remorse for it, but they lack the strength to give the glory to God. They even attempt to adapt themselves to the false religion which they have embraced, and they grow accustomed to its practice against their own conscience. Subsequently, seeing that they can satisfy their passions in this way, they come to despise the true religion which they had left, and they mock it. This contempt is sometimes followed by hatred against those who profess the truth, because they cannot endure their presence without feeling shame; from hatred, they pass over to persecution, and they often die in that state.

II. The question is asked: why is this sin called the sin against the Holy Spirit?

It is not because it only strikes against the third Person of the Holy Trinity, for all sins offend the three adorable Persons; rather, it is because it is committed against the enlightenment of the Holy Spirit, to whom the Scripture, in the **Economy of Salvation** <term>Economy of Salvation: The divine plan or arrangement for the salvation of humanity.</term>, attributes the care of enlightening mankind. A great man has said very well:
<margin>Claude</margin> <note>Jean Claude (1619–1687), a famous French Reformed theologian.</note> "That he who sins against the Law is said to sin against the Father; that he who rejects the Gospel when it is proclaimed to him is said to sin against the Son; but that he who resists the light which he has already received, and who makes for himself a bulwark and shield out of the wickedness of his heart and the deceits of his mind against the inspirations of grace, sins against the Holy Spirit."

III. The question is asked: whether all people can fall into this sin.

I answer, 1. That those who do not know the Gospel can never fall into this sin, but indeed those who are called "temporary believers," who received the Gospel with joy, but who thereafter abandoned it.

I answer, 2. That the elect and the faithful <note>The "elect" refers to those predestined for salvation according to Reformed theology.</note> cannot fall into this sin, as shall clearly appear when we treat the **perseverance of the Saints** <term>Perseverance of the Saints: The doctrine that those truly saved by God will never finally fall away from the faith.</term>. We do not deny that the faithful could commit great sins that would make them worthy of eternal death. We do not deny that it could happen that the faithful,

<column-break/>

terrified by the fear of death, or by the violence of persecution, or by the power of some passions, would leave the true faith. But we maintain that they shall not remain long in that state, because God comes to pull them out of it by His almighty hand. The weakness of their nature yields to the conquering power of grace. Their faith, which was like a fire covered under ashes, begins to ignite and shine forth again; and if they have been unfruitful for some time, like trees in the winter, one sees them bring forth beautiful fruits as soon as the **Sun of Righteousness** <note>A biblical title for Christ (Malachi 4:2).</note> comes to cast its rays upon them again.

IV. The question is asked: whether one finds anyone nowadays who falls into this sin.

Answer: Those who believe that none sin against the Holy Spirit except those who attributed the miracles of Christ to Beelzebub are of the opinion that the Pharisees alone committed this sin. But we are not of that thought. We believe that there are many today who still commit it, since many sin willfully after they have known the truth, and hold the **blood of the covenant** to be unholy.

The sin against the Holy Spirit is regarded as the greatest of all sins, since it is unpardonable. Now, it is certain that the sin of Christians—who abandon, hate, despise, and persecute the truth they know—is a weightier sin than that of the Pharisees, who, blinded by their prejudices and by their envy, judged poorly of Christ's miracles. Those who crucify the Lord Jesus anew, whom they have recognized as the true Messiah, sin much more heavily than those who crucified Him while believing Him to be a deceiver.

A learned English writer named **Daniel Whitby** <note>Daniel Whitby (1638–1726) was an English theologian and biblical commentator.</note> in his commentary on the New Testament, believes that this sin was not committed in the time of our Savior, because the Holy Spirit had not yet been given. This opinion seems more probable to me than the view of those who believe that this sin was only committed by the Pharisees. Meanwhile, we are of the opinion that one can say that the sin against the Holy Spirit was committed by the Pharisees, and is still committed today by many Christians.

# DIVINITY. Book VI. Part B. Chapter XII.

...ed. But we are at the same time of the opinion that there are several kinds of this sin.

Those who completely renounce Christianity and have persecuted the Christian faith are the most guilty of all who sin against the Holy Spirit, because they absolutely reject Christ and His fellowship.

Those who, after obtaining knowledge of the Gospel, reach the point where they have no fear of God nor show any regret toward Him, and who view the threats of God's word as trifles, must also be placed in the number of those who sin against the Holy Spirit.

We shall observe ourselves that, although it is certain that this sin is particularly committed under the *New Dispensation* <term>New Dispensation: The era of human history following the coming of Christ, characterized by the "New Covenant" and greater spiritual light.</term> where they have a much greater light (it is also distinguished in Hebrews 2 and 10 from the transgression of the Law), it nonetheless took place in some manner under the *Old Testament* among those who despised the Law of Moses and hardened their hearts against God's voice. I do not believe, however, that Cain and Saul sinned against the Holy Spirit, as some have been of the opinion.

1. Christ says of this sin that it shall be forgiven neither in this nor in the coming Age, which is to say, never. We shall give the reason for this expression elsewhere. Indeed, where there is no conversion, there is no forgiveness. Now Paul says that they cannot be renewed unto repentance. It is not that their wickedness is of such a nature that it cannot be overcome by grace—for nothing is impossible for God—but it is that God, who is the giver of repentance, would give them over to their destruction through a righteous judgment. When the Holy Spirit is not only hindered but grieved in His workings; <margin>Claude <note>Jean Claude (1619–1687), a renowned French Reformed theologian often cited in Dutch works of this period.</note></margin> when, says a learned writer, the Holy Spirit is blasphemed and rejected through an excess of human callousness, He holds, so to speak, an aversion to an object that has made itself unworthy of His impressions.

Secondly, Divine justice does not will that God forgive those who have sinned against the Holy Spirit. He who has violated the Law of the Father finds a means of forgiveness in the satisfaction of the Son. He who happens to offend the Son through unbelief and through ignorance 

<column-break/>

can be converted through the grace of the Holy Spirit, who causes his ignorance to vanish and overcomes his unbelief. But he who offers an insult to the Holy Spirit has nothing more to hope for. <margin>Claude</margin> The aforementioned writer has very well said, "that when the justice and the sovereignty of God are violated, one still finds a refuge in His mercy, which is revealed to us in the Gospel. If this Evangelical Mercy is offended without knowing it, through a preconceived error, there is still in God a hidden mercy that can enlighten man; and that mercy is a principle that is still intact, that has not yet suffered offense, and consequently can make everything right by pouring the light of grace into the soul. But if that hidden mercy is injured and despised, then all access to God is closed, and mercy, thus insulted, changes into a burning wrath."

2. Paul says that there is no sacrifice for this sin, alluding to the sins for which God had instituted no sacrifice <note>Under Mosaic Law, certain intentional or high-handed sins had no prescribed animal sacrifice for atonement.</note>. They have rejected Christ in His salvation; they have insulted His Spirit. There is then nothing to expect for them. Every sacrifice is offered to offended justice, so that it may give place to mercy. But there is no sacrifice that can be offered to a despised mercy, and mercy is angered when one rejects it under the name of mercy itself and as being such.

3. Finally, John says that one must not pray for the sin which he calls a sin unto death. <margin>1 John 5:16</margin> *If anyone sees his brother sinning a sin not unto death, he shall pray (to God), and He shall give him life, to those (I say) who sin not unto death. There is a sin unto death; for that (sin) I do not say that he should pray.* Here are several things to be noted.

1. # DIVINITY. VI. B. CHAPTER XIII.

### CHAPTER XIII.

->Of the free will of Man in the state of sin, and of his impotence to do good from and by himself.<-

We have considered the free will of man in the state of righteousness <note>The "state of righteousness" refers to the theological concept of humanity's condition before the Fall, when Adam and Eve were believed to be in perfect harmony with God's will.</note>; we must now see what man's free will is in the state of sin. Elsewhere we have shown that freedom consists in acting with reason, without being forced to do so by another; and we have proven that this freedom is so essential to a rational creature that, in whatever state it may be, it cannot exist without this freedom.

It is certain, then, that sin has not taken this freedom away from man, since man cannot lose it without ceasing to be human.

Spinoza <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), a Dutch philosopher who argued for determinism—the idea that humans only believe they are free because they are conscious of their actions but ignorant of the causes that determine them.</note> maintained that we only consider man to be free because we do not know the sequence of causes that make him act. But, although we do not know the sequence of causes that make men act, we nevertheless do not fail to say that man is free, because he does what pleases him. The reasons that incite him to do what he does do not diminish his freedom; for, if he did not find them good, he would not do it.

But one must note that, besides this freedom which is essential to human nature, Adam possessed another in the state of righteousness, consisting in being absolutely free from sin. He lost this second freedom by sinning, but he never lost the first. Therefore, all his children are born free, possessing that first freedom by which we act according to our own discretion; but because they come into the world as sinners, they are by nature slaves to sin, and they misuse the first freedom by applying it to nothing but evil, and without the assistance of God's grace, they can do no good.

<column-break/>

It is true that man, regarding natural things, has the same powers that Adam had; he can do them or not do them according to his will: eat, drink, sleep, etc.

<margin>
Socinus, *Theological Lectures*, ch. 5. Volkel, *On the True Religion*, book V, ch. 18. Bellarmine, *On Grace and Free Will*, book V, ch. 9. All the *Articles of the Hague Conference*, art. 3 <note>The Hague Conference (1611) was a pivotal meeting between Remonstrants (Arminians) and Counter-Remonstrants (Calvinists) in the Dutch Republic.</note>.
</margin>
It is also true that man, regarding matters concerning civil life, still has powers, though one must admit he does not have as many as Adam, because sin has filled his understanding with a false light, and his will often deceives itself regarding what it chooses or rejects. But regarding spiritual goods, we believe that man, being corrupted by nature, can do nothing of himself that is pleasing to God, because he has made himself a slave to sin.

The whole of Scripture teaches us this truth. This appears first from all the places where it is said that man of himself can do nothing. <margin>Grevinchovius <note>Nicolaas Grevinchovius (d. 1632), a prominent Dutch Remonstrant theologian.</note>.</margin> Romans 8:7: *The carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be.* 1 Corinthians 2:14: *The natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God.* John 6:44: *No man can come to me,* says Christ, *except the Father which hath sent me draw him.* Jeremiah 13:23: *Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil.* John 15:5: *Without me,* says Christ, *ye can do nothing.* 2 Corinthians 3:5: *Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God.* Matthew 7:18: *A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit.*

<margin>Limborch, *Christian Theology*, book IV, ch. 14 <note>Philippus van Limborch (1633–1712) was a leading Remonstrant theologian and professor in Amsterdam.</note>.</margin>
1. Regarding these passages, it is commonly said that all these ways of speaking—which establish the total impotence of man to do any good of himself—must not be taken literally, and that they are hyperbolic expressions used by the common people. But if that is so, why is it that they are found everywhere in Scripture? Why is it that all the holy writers use the same language? Why is it that God's Spirit tells us nothing that can reveal the true sense of these words?

2. It is said that these words, *he cannot*, only mean that this does not commonly...

# THE CHRISTIAN

commonly happens, or when it is testified that man can do no good, people want to interpret it as merely saying that he does not do it. But, to be convinced of the contrary, one has only to read these Scripture passages. If one were to give it that meaning, would Paul say that the flesh does not submit, and *cannot* submit? Would Christ say that a bad tree does not bring forth good fruit, and *cannot* bring forth? Does that mean it is not *accustomed* to bringing forth good fruit? Can one explain Jeremiah with any appearance of reason thus: *Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil.* <note>Jeremiah 13:23. The original Dutch uses "Moorman" (Moor), referring to an Ethiopian or person of dark skin, a standard biblical metaphor of the era for unchangeable nature.</note> Does this question and this parable not signify a total impotence to do good?

3. It is also said that these words, *he cannot*, mean *he will not*. I answer that it is true that the impotence of man is voluntary, as we shall see in the following; but the will of man is so corrupt that, unless the grace of God changes it, it always incites man to evil.

<margin>Bellarmine, *On Free Will*, chapter X.</margin>
4. It is said that Paul in Romans 8:7 speaks not of the state of an absolutely unregenerate man, nor of the "higher faculty" of the soul, but of the "lower faculty," which is called the carnal mind. Answer: But, besides that this distinction between higher and lower faculties is imaginary <note>The author argues against the Scholastic view that the human mind is split into a "higher" part (reason) that remains pure and a "lower" part (passions) that is corrupted by sin.</note>, one must note: 1. That the word we have translated as the "carnal mind" in Paul’s language <term>vleesch-gezindheid</term> signifies understanding or prudence, just as the Vulgate <note>The late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible.</note> has rendered it. Now, understanding and prudence belong to the faculty called the higher faculty. 2. Scripture includes under the word "flesh" the corruption of all our soul's faculties. Among the works of the flesh Paul places idolatry and heresy (Galatians 5:20), and in John 3:6 he calls everything that must be born again "flesh."

<margin>Limborch, *Christian Theology*, book IV, chapter 14.</margin>
5. It is said that when Christ (Matthew 7:18, 12:33, Luke 6:43) teaches us that a bad tree cannot bring forth good fruit, one must not take these words more literally than when he says a good tree cannot bring forth bad fruit. Now,

<column-break/>

it is said, a good tree sometimes bears bad fruit, or those not entirely ripe, or those infected by worms. Answer: Who does not see that one can never say a good tree bears bad fruit if the fruit it produces does not ripen or is spoiled by some vermin? This does not prevent a good tree from bearing fruit that is good by nature but corrupted by an external cause. On the other hand, there is a great difference between a believer and an unbeliever. A believer is such a good tree that has within itself an evil seed that has not been entirely rooted out. One must not be surprised then that a believer all too often brings forth bad fruit. It is not so with the corrupt man; there is nothing in him that can bear good fruit. It is added here that if one were to explain this passage literally, it would follow that man is good or evil by virtue of a natural necessity, just as a tree is good or evil by virtue of a natural necessity. I answer that we take these words literally only insofar as, just as a bad tree by nature cannot bear good fruit unless it is changed by God’s omnipotence, so man, who is conceived in sin, can do no work by his own strength that is pleasing to God unless he be recreated and wholly renewed by grace.

6. It is said that when Paul testifies that the natural man cannot understand the things of God (1 Corinthians 2:14), these words do not mean he can have no knowledge of God’s word, but they mean he cannot grasp the excellence of spiritual things above fleshly things; that he cannot grasp them so as to give his consent to what the word teaches him and direct his conduct accordingly. I answer: That we demand nothing more, and that this is enough to show the impotence that we attribute to the corrupt man.

7. One objects: That when Paul says we are not sufficient of ourselves to think anything, these words only concern the duties of the Apostleship. I confess that Paul speaks thus in respect to his Apostleship. But look here at his reasoning. If we are not sufficient of ourselves to have one good thought, how much less can we fulfill the duties of the Holy Ministry if God does not give us the capacity for it? The manner in which Paul speaks does not allow us to doubt that he reasons thus: for after he has said in general that all our sufficiency comes from God, he adds, *who also hath made us able ministers of the New Testament.* <margin>2 Corinthians 3:5-6.</margin> If a great Apostle was not ashamed to acknowledge that he had no sufficiency of himself, why should anyone in their own calling be ashamed to make the same confession? People further say that one should not translate "we are not sufficient of ourselves to *think* anything," but rather to *devise* or *invent*. I answer: 1. That the root word is very rarely used in that sense. 2. That by taking it in that meaning, one would make Paul say a ridiculous thing, as if he meant to suggest that we are not sufficient of ourselves to *invent* the Gospel. Furthermore, one does not see why Paul says *of ourselves as from ourselves*, for men did not invent the heavenly mysteries through God’s assistance; rather, they were revealed to them, where this addition *of ourselves as from ourselves* fits very well with Paul's reasoning. Augustine <margin>On the Gift of Perseverance, Book II, chapter 13.</margin> <note>original: "de bono persev. l. II. c. 13."</note> remarks:

> think anything." And in another place 
<note>Augustine to Boniface, Book II, chapter 8.</note> he makes this observation: that thinking is less than desiring, and consequently, since we can think nothing good of ourselves, we are even less capable of doing anything good without God's help.

We draw a second proof from all the passages where man in his natural state is depicted as a *slave to sin* and to the Devil.

Formerly, there were three kinds of slaves. Some were born slaves, others were sold into slavery, and others were made slaves in war.

<margin>Romans 6:16-17.</margin>
Scripture depicts men as <margin>John 8:34.</margin> being born children of wrath, and consequently <margin>1 Peter 2:19.</margin> *slaves*, as *sold under sin*, as made into slaves by the one who has overcome us; being in the snares of Satan. <margin>In the Low-Dutch translation it says, "in your bondage"</margin> <note>original: "Neder-duytsche overzet-ting." The author is noting a specific phrasing in the Dutch Bible of his time.</note> In short, as slaves who cannot obtain their freedom except through the Son, namely Jesus Christ. *John 8:36.*

This slavery contains two things. 1. A constant obligation to the one whose slave you are, until you are restored to freedom. 2. That he who is thus a slave works only for the benefit of his Master.

Since man is then described to us by nature as a slave of Sin and the Devil, it follows that he is enslaved and subjected to the Devil and to Sin, and that he can do nothing but what these second masters want.

<margin>Romans 6:17-18.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of human corruption and the necessity of divine grace, specifically addressing the concept of "slavery to sin" as described by the Apostle Paul.</meta>

->THE CHRISTIAN<-

that there is a great difference between the manner in which believers are made slaves of righteousness and the manner in which humans are born as slaves of sin. Everyone knows that the grace which has freed the believer from the slavery of sin and subjected them to the gentle rule of righteousness has not sanctified them so completely that no remnants of sin remain in them, which still often cause them to sin. But humans are born entirely under the dominion of sin.

I say secondly: That Paul's aim is not so much to describe the *state* in which believers find themselves, as it is to describe their *obligation*. He wants them to understand that, since they were formerly so subject to sin that they offered all their members as instruments of unrighteousness, they ought now—having been redeemed—to give themselves over entirely to the righteousness to which grace has subjected them.

II. It is said that there is a great difference between physical slavery and the slavery of sin. The first is usually an unwilling state, while the second is a completely willing slavery. I admit this, but it actually strengthens our reasoning: for the sinner is a slave to sin to such an extent that he *wants* to be one; he does not want to leave his prison, he kisses his chains, and he worships his tyrant—whereas other slaves long for their freedom and do everything in their power to obtain it.

III. It is said that the sinner, being a slave of sin, is therefore no less free.

I make a distinction here. He is no less free regarding that freedom which is essential to all rational creatures <note>This refers to "natural liberty," the basic human capacity to think and act, which remains even if the moral direction of those acts is corrupted.</note>; but he is meanwhile so subjected to the dominion of sin that he does nothing except what his tyrant desires. One can compare sin to a person in love. This person is free, for no one forces him to do what he does. However, his passion makes him such a slave to the person he loves that he has no other will than that of his mistress.

IV. It is said that man, through the slavery of sin, has not lost the freedom and power to receive the grace offered to him and to cooperate with it—just as some-

<column-break/>

one, it is said, who has fallen into a well has indeed lost the freedom to walk, but not the freedom to move and to hold onto a rope.

I answer: That the sinner by nature resists and rejects the grace offered to him, far from accepting it. Thus, there is a difference between him and someone who has fallen into a well. The latter wants to get out, but the sinner wants to remain in sin; he takes delight in it; he places his pleasure in it.

To prove the inability of man in the state of sin, we draw a third proof from the fact that humans are shown to us as *blind, and being entirely darkness* (Ephesians 5:8); as having a *deceitful and desperately wicked heart* (Jeremiah 17:9); *a heart where the thoughts are evil every day* (Genesis 6:5); *an uncircumcised heart; a heart harder than diamond* (Zechariah 7:12); and *a heart of stone* (Ezekiel 36:26), in which the heavenly seed can take no root. A heart that is dead and without life, like stone; a heart that resists the hammer of God’s word and will not receive the impression and seal of God. An earthly, unfeeling, stubborn heart. A heart that bears no fruit. From all these expressions, we draw a powerful proof to show that man has no strength—neither in his understanding nor in his will—to pursue spiritual things, and that without grace, he can neither know divine truths nor do good works.

1. It is said: That when sinners are called *blind*, that expression only signifies their ignorance in spiritual matters, but not their inability to be converted and enlightened. **Answer.** We do not deny that they can be enlightened by grace; but we maintain that by nature they cannot comprehend heavenly things, and we prove it not only from the name *blind* which the Scripture gives them, but from various similar expressions.

2. It is said: That Christ testifies in John 9:41 that if the Pharisees were *blind*, they would have committed no sin; but that, according to our view, the state of blindness in a sinner is a state of deficiency.

<meta>The catchword at the bottom of the page is "Antw." (Answer), indicating the rebuttal to the second objection will follow on the next page.</meta>
