As for evil deeds, we shall deal with them in the following chapter, in which we shall see how God works without anyone being able to accuse Him of being the cause of sin.

I have only two points to investigate here.
1. The first is: how does Providence in the governance of God agree with the freedom of man?
2. One must confess that, just as nothing is more becoming to God, and nothing more satisfies the idea we have of the infinitely wise and perfect Supreme Being, than the manner in which God makes everything that happens in the world—even through free beings—serve the execution of His purposes; so also is there nothing more difficult to understand. This difficulty is the reason why freethinkers <note>original: *vrygeesten*; those who reject traditional religious authority and dogma</note> and the ungodly reject Providence.

In the meantime, nothing is more unjust than their behavior: for, although we cannot reconcile Providence with the freedom of man, our reason and the Scripture nevertheless teach us that God governs all things and that we depend on Him; and at the same time, we feel that we are free.

# THEOLOGY. VII. B. IV. Chapter.

,, ...stuck in insurmountable difficulties, if we undertook to bring the freedom of our will into agreement with His decrees; because, in order to do so, we would have to comprehend—that is, to embrace and define with our understanding—the extent of our freedom and that of the ways of eternal providence, which, being infinite, cannot be understood by any finite mind.

But one will find that providence agrees very well with our freedom, when one takes into consideration:

1. That God always makes causes act in accordance with their nature, except in the case of miracles.

<margin>Augustine, *The City of God*, Book VII, chapter 39.</margin>
2. That freedom consists in this: that a person does what they do with knowledge, after ripe deliberation, and after their understanding has shown them that they must act in that way.

3. That only two things are required for an act to be free. 1. That the creature who acts is not determined to that work by its nature <note>Meaning the creature is not a purely mechanical or instinctive being like a stone or a simple animal.</note>, and that it is not forced to it by any other creature. 2. That it acts following prior knowledge and judgment.

4. That God does not force us, but that He bends our will to want what He wants. And that in this way, He does no violence to our freedom. Everything that the will wants, in the very act of wanting it, it wants freely; whether that which bends the will is an internal cause that pre-determines it, or an external object that powerfully draws it.

What leads people to believe that the <term>concurrence</term> <note>The theological concept of God's power cooperating with human actions.</note> of God destroys human freedom is the natural tendency to think that freedom requires the exclusion of all necessity, and in this, they are mistaken: freedom can only be harmed by what we call compulsion. One can force someone to do what they do not want to do, but one cannot force someone to *want* what they do not want. All beings who act with knowledge, who are not determined by their nature to do something, and who are not forced by other beings, act freely.

Those who believe that the foreknowledge and the providence of God are the same thing seem to easily reconcile providence with human freedom, because God's foreknowledge imposes no necessity. It sees what must and will happen, but it is not the cause of a thing happening, just like a doctor

<meta>Part I.</meta>

<column-break/>

who foresees what will happen to the sick. But we have shown elsewhere that providence is not mere foreknowledge.

Those who believe that God lets creatures do whatever they want, whether good or evil, also find it easy to reconcile providence with human freedom. But this opinion goes against the passages we have cited above and will yet cite, and we have also proved elsewhere that God's permission is not a "hollow" permission. Those who only attribute to God a general and indifferent concurrence <note>The idea that God provides the energy for an action but remains neutral toward the choice itself.</note> also have no trouble reconciling providence with human freedom. But we have refuted this opinion in the previous chapter. Furthermore, one can ask all those who acknowledge God's foreknowledge whether they do not believe that everything God has foreseen happens infallibly. They would not dare deny it. If the outcome is now infallible, how will they reconcile this with the "freedom of indifference" <note>The philosophical idea that the human will is a neutral "balance" that can tip either way regardless of prior influences.</note> which they attribute to man? They must, against their own will, confess that man cannot act otherwise; for if he could have acted otherwise, the foreseen outcome would not have been a certain and infallible outcome. Thus, it appears that it is a very difficult matter to reconcile providence with human freedom.

2. The second point we must investigate is how one can posit a providence while at the same time acknowledging that there are certain things called <term>contingent</term> <note>From the Latin *contingens*; events that appear to happen by chance or could have happened otherwise.</note>, which is to say, things that can be and not be.

One can easily clarify this point by saying that everything from our perspective can be called "contingent," although it is established and decided by God: for we do not know what God has decided, whether He has decided that a thing shall or shall not happen. We do not know the chain of things that are called contingent as we do other things.

I only add one observation here: that in the governance of the world, God sometimes works through the means of <term>secondary causes</term> <note>Created instruments like people, animals, or nature that God uses to achieve His ends.</note>, sometimes immediately by Himself, sometimes through the service of angels and men, sometimes through irrational creatures, although He can do everything immediately without needing any creatures. Sometimes He follows the laws He has prescribed for Himself in the governance of the world, according to the order He has established. Sometimes He goes beyond these laws—

## CHAPTER V.

->On the manner in which Providence<-
->intervenes in the sins<-
->of men<-

We cannot doubt that providence intervenes in the sins of men, because it is certain that nothing happens in the world without God knowing it (since He is omniscient), nor against His will (since He is almighty), and without Him having some purpose in permitting it to happen, and without Him sustaining the powers of the creatures He uses. 

But one must admit that there is nothing more difficult to explain than the manner in which providence intervenes in sin, because one so easily strikes against the "rocks" <note>A metaphor for falling into heresy or logical error.</note> that lie here. 

There have been heretics, such as the <term>Manichaeans</term> <note>Followers of a dualistic religion that believed the universe was a struggle between equal forces of Good and Evil.</note>, who believed that there are two principles: one of good and another of evil. They took this theology from the Persians, who had their Oromasdes and Arimanius <note>Refers to Ahura Mazda and Angra Mainyu in Zoroastrianism; the good and evil spirits.</note>. 

Others have been of the opinion that God was the cause of sin, such as the followers of Simon the Sorcerer, the Florinians, and the Priscillians. 

May God preserve us from falling into such terrible errors. 

Reason and Scripture both refute them. 
1. They both teach us that there is but one eternal principle of all things. 
2. That this principle is God. 
3. That God is a most perfect 

<column-break/>

being. 
4. That He, above all, hates sin and is perfectly holy. 
5. Finally, that He punishes sin and will punish it severely. If there were two principles, how is it that the world is governed in such an orderly fashion? 

One might say that there is a treaty between them both. But can a principle that is essentially good consent to evil? One says that He is forced to it, but if that is true, the principle that allowed itself to be forced is no God: for a good principle would be no God if there were an evil principle equal to it, because it would not be almighty. 

One must then investigate how God intervenes in sin, since it is established that He is not the cause of it. 

There are several opinions on this. 
Durandus believed that God only sustains the power to work in <term>secondary causes</term> <note>Theological term for the actions of creatures or nature, as opposed to God being the "Primary Cause."</note>. This opinion is refuted by most <term>School-theologians</term> <note>Also known as Scholastics; medieval and early modern university scholars.</note>, as Vasquez notes (in 1., 2, Disputation 129, chapter 3). 

Scotus (in 2. distinction 37, question 2) was of the mind that the wickedness comes only from the side of the creature, because the created will is bound to do good works, but God is not obliged to make the works of men right. He would, however, do this if men's will did not resist His. Thus, he makes God's will dependent on that of man. Thomas and the <term>Thomists</term> <note>Followers of the teachings of Thomas Aquinas.</note> oppose this view. Some of them, according to the testimony of Vasquez (in 1. disputation 125, chapter 5), believed that one should not attribute sin to God because, they said, when He <term>concurs</term> <note>Co-operates or acts alongside.</note> in the act of sin, He does not go against the rules of sound reason. To this view one can bring the opinion of those who claimed that God cannot sin because He is subject to no law. 

But although these writers proved through their reasoning that God does not sin, they would not thereby prove that He is not the cause of sin if He produced the act of sin in man. On the other hand, it is certain that although God is not subject to the law as men are, He nevertheless never acts against His own perfections. 

Vasquez (in 1. 2. question 129, chapters 2, 3, 4, 5, 6), after he had refuted many other opinions from those of his own community, believes...

# DIVINE THEOLOGY. VII. Book V. Chapter V.

...maintains that God is the natural cause of the entire act from which sin arises, but that He is not the moral cause of it, because He neither advises nor commands it.

The <term>Dominicans</term> <note>A Roman Catholic religious order following the teachings of St. Dominic.</note> and the <term>Thomists</term> <note>Theologians who follow the system of Thomas Aquinas; they emphasize God's absolute sovereignty in every action.</note> were of the opinion that God determines <term>secondary causes</term> <note>The actions of created things, like humans or nature, which are moved by God, the "Primary Cause."</note> beforehand, and that He brings them into action, and is therefore called the "First Mover." (See: Dominican Bannes; Diego Alvarez, *On Help*; Estius, *On the Second Book of Sentences*, distinction 24, paragraph 14). This also seems to have been the opinion of the <term>Catechism of the Council of Trent</term> <note>The official manual of Catholic doctrine produced in the 16th century.</note>. For there it is said on page 32 that God moves and works upon those things that move and work in such a manner, through a secret power that is their own; that, although He does not hinder the action of secondary causes, He nonetheless precedes them through His hidden power, which extends to all things: for, as the <term>Wise Man</term> <note>Likely referring to the author of the biblical Book of Wisdom or Solomon.</note> says, He works mightily in all things.

The <term>Molinists</term> <note>Followers of the Jesuit Luis de Molina, who sought to preserve human free will against strict predestination.</note> and the <term>Jesuits</term> oppose this "predetermination" and only allow for an "indifferent concurrence" <note>A theory where God provides the necessary power for an act, but the human will alone decides whether to use that power for good or evil.</note>, of which I have spoken above. (See: Molina, *The Concord of Free Will*, etc., and question 14, dispute 26; Leonardus Lessius, *On Efficacious Grace*, chapter 2; Annat, *Treatise on Middle Knowledge*, dispute 4, § 3; Diego Ruiz, *Treatise on the Will of God*).

The <term>Arminians</term> <note>Followers of Jacobus Arminius; a group of Dutch Protestants who argued for human cooperation with divine grace.</note> are also in favor of an indifferent concurrence. (See: Arminius, *Against Perkins*; Grevinchoven, *Against Ames*, section 32; Corvinus, *Against Tilenus*, chapter 9; Episcopius; Limborch).

Most teachers among the <term>Reformed</term> <note>Calvinist theologians who emphasize God's sovereignty and the total depravity of man.</note> favor the opinion of the Thomists regarding predetermination. Elsewhere we shall speak of the opinion of <term>John Strang</term> <note>A 17th-century Scottish theologian who wrote extensively on the nature of God's will and the origin of sin.</note>, a Scottish Divine.

Many here remain silent and confess their ignorance, and that is by far the best course.

However, to clarify this matter as much as possible, one must distinguish three things: the beginning, the progress, and the end of sin.

Regarding the beginning, here is what Scripture teaches us of it.

<margin>Psalm 81:13.</margin>
1. That God permits sin. *I gave them over to their own hearts' lusts, and they walked in their own counsels,* says the Lord in the 81st Psalm, verse 13, speaking of the Israelites. Paul testifies that God in times past *suffered the nations to walk in their own ways,* Acts 14:16. Even if Scripture did not teach this, reason would make it known to us, for nothing can happen against God's will.

<column-break/>

We have already shown that it is very difficult to say why God has permitted sin, but it is certain that sin gave God the occasion to manifest all His virtues. Those who object to this do not pay enough attention to God's purpose; for He did not only intend to make His goodness known (otherwise He would have made all men blessed and holy), but He also wished to display His wisdom and His other perfections.

To understand as much as possible wherein this "permission" consists, one must make the following observations.

One must guard against believing that this permission includes approval.

It is as impossible for God to approve of sin as it is impossible for Him to commit it. All of Scripture teaches us that God condemns and punishes sin.

One must also not believe that this permission is an "idle tolerance," which endures either what it does not know or what it cannot prevent; for there is nothing more unworthy of God than to suppose either that He does not know what happens in the world, or that He does not have the power to prevent it.

Permission, then, does not consist merely in God providing no hindrance. One proof will be enough to demonstrate this.

When God permits sin by not preventing it, He does so either because He does *not want* to prevent it, or because He *does not think* of it. If one says it is because God does not think of it, one attributes something to God that is unworthy of the Perfect Being. If one says it is because God does not *want* to prevent the sin, then God’s permission will include not only that He does not prevent the sin, but also that He truly does not *wish* to prevent it—not for lack of power, but for wise reasons that are unknown to us.

To form a good understanding of this permission, one must observe that God can prevent and hinder sin in several ways.

1. God hinders sin when He forbids men to commit it, and when He adds heavy threats to His prohibition. In this manner, God always prevents sinning. But there are other means by which He could prevent the commission of sin, which He does not always use.

# THEOLOGY. Book VII. Chapter V.

God's permission allows them to have these same evil thoughts; there is no more difficulty in this than there is in understanding how one Angel can communicate his thoughts to another Angel if he wishes. However, it is certain that both one and the other exceed the reach of our weak understanding. It is enough, then, to know that God gives over the sinners—who have so greatly abused the riches of His mercy—to the Devil, who forgets nothing in his efforts to incite them to all kinds of sins; but one must not torment one's spirit to know the exact manner in which the Devil works.

The fifth thing that God does is that He causes certain thoughts to bubble up in man which are good in themselves, or at least <term>indifferent</term> <note>Meaning neither inherently good nor evil, but neutral.</note>, but which lead him to sin by chance. Thus, He allowed the brothers of Joseph to think of the love that Jacob bore for Joseph; this thought incited these degenerate brothers, who were full of envy, toward the evil that they committed against this innocent youth.

<margin>John 18:14.</margin>
Thus, He caused it to arise in the thoughts of Caiaphas that it was useful for one man to die for all the people. A true fundamental principle; but from it, this High Priest concluded that it was good to kill Christ as a rebel, out of fear that the Romans would uproot the temple and the people for His sake.

<margin>Exodus 14:4. 2 Samuel 16:10.</margin>
See there what we can clearly derive from God’s word. But it is asked whether God does more. It seems that the Scripture wishes to give us to understand that He does something further when it says that God hardened the heart of Pharaoh, that He commanded Shimei to curse David, etc., etc.

But the safest course in this matter is to confess one's ignorance and to remain in a deep silence, so as not to attribute anything to God that is unbecoming of the most perfect, holy, and wise Being.

However, to satisfy those who are eager to know the theological opinions, I will say that most are of the mind that God, through His <term>concurrence</term> <note>original: "zamenloop"; a theological concept where God provides the underlying power for an action, while the human provides the moral direction.</note>, is the cause of the act, but not of the wickedness of the act.

To set this in its proper light, they note: 1. That one and the same act can have two causes. The soul of man, they say, causes him to walk through the influence of the spirits descending from the brain, where they have their seat, into the nerves and tendons of the legs and feet. Now, if this man limps, neither the soul nor the spirits

<column-break/>

are the cause of it, but rather the leg, which has a poor condition. Thus, they add, when God moves and works within someone who commits a sin, He indeed determines him beforehand to the act, but not to the evil of the act. The movement is in and comes from God, but the "unsuitability" <note>Or lack of harmony with God's law.</note> perceived in the movement comes from the man. A Magistrate, they continue, can be called the cause of the death of a criminal; but he cannot be the cause of the felony for which the executioner takes the man's life.

2. They note that acts in themselves are neither good nor evil, but it is the specific circumstances that make them good or evil. For example, killing can be a good act and an evil act. A good one, if it is commanded by the Authorities; an evil one if it is committed by a murderer.

3. They give us to consider that most passions in themselves are neither good nor evil; love, desire, hatred, etc., have nothing evil within them. Thus, they say, God can indeed cause passions to rise, and yet not determine them toward evil.

4. They say that there are many acts which are good regarding the substance of the deed, and do not become evil except by the manner in which they are done. For example, praying, fasting, and giving alms are in themselves good works, but they become evil when one does them out of a spirit of pride. In such acts, it is easy to conceive how the act can come from God, and the defect from the man.

5. They say that one can distinguish these two things even in sins of omission. For before every sin of omission, some act of the will precedes or accompanies it; now, it is the acts that precede or accompany it that are the cause of the sin of omission.

6. When one is presented with certain acts that seem evil by their nature, such as hating God, and in which it is very difficult to understand how God can concur with the substance of the act without being the cause of the evil within the act—because the evil of the act seems inseparable from the act itself—they say that even there one can distinguish the act from the evil of the act: the movement of hatred from the direction of hatred against God.

That God, without sin, can concur with this movement of hatred, which in itself is not evil, but that the—

# THE CHRISTIAN [THEOLOGY]

...determination of the movement of hatred—viewed from God's side—is essentially the moral element that is evil. Those who wish to explain this matter differently distinguish three types of "being" in a creature: a **natural being** which they have in common with all creatures, a **moral being**, and a **blessed being**. For example, they say that in the Angels one finds a **natural being**, inasmuch as they are substances; a **moral being**, inasmuch as they are Holy; and a **blessed being**, inasmuch as they possess glory. But, they say, there are rational creatures who possess only the **natural being**, such as the Devils, who do not possess the **moral being**, which according to their view consists of the "good" and "blessed" being. They believe that against each of these beings stands a "nothingness": against the natural being stands absolute nothingness; against the moral being stands sinful nothingness; and against the blessed being stands miserable nothingness. They add that God can provide the necessary **concurrence** <note>original: "zamenloop" — the theological concept of God's cooperation or simultaneous action with a created being.</note> simply to exist for the creature, yet refuse the concurrence necessary to be good, and that the creature must therefore fall into "sinful nothingness."

and Grace. ch. 10
</margin>
The famous **Jurieu** <note>Pierre Jurieu (1637–1713) was a prominent French Protestant theologian known for his defense of the Reformed faith.</note>, who brought this view into play and believes—along with our theologians and the **Thomists** <note>Followers of the theological system of Thomas Aquinas.</note>—that God predetermines the **will**, explains this with an example. "Let us," he says, "imagine a stone lying still. A hand picks it up and, in lifting it, gives it a motion that we call diagonal—not in a straight line, but in a curved line extending from the earth toward heaven. But the stone, instead of continuing that way, as soon as it leaves the hand, abandons the line leading it upward to heaven and begins to sink toward the earth; and after describing a long curved line in the air, it falls on a certain spot on the ground. It is not the hand that determined the stone to fall. On the contrary, if the stone had followed the movement of the hand, it would have climbed toward heaven. It is essentially the weight of the stone that determines its fall. Meanwhile, it is the hand that gave it the initial movement." Similarly, he says, it is God who predetermines the will to an act of **Love** or of **Hatred**, but God is not the cause of this love falling upon a fleshly lust, or this hatred being directed against God. It is the fault

<meta>catchword: of</meta>

<column-break/>

of the wickedness and corruption of the **Will**.

A Scottish theologian named **Strangius** <note>John Strang (1584–1654), a Scottish minister and Principal of the University of Glasgow.</note> believed that God determines the Will in good and righteous deeds. But he believed that the Will determines itself in sinful deeds—not by making any movement toward evil without God, but through a certain inclination toward evil which God sees, and according to which God gives the creature the **concurrence** it needs to move.

One might perhaps transition to another view, and I shall propose it for those who cannot reconcile themselves to what has been put forward. It consists of this: concerning the act of hatred against God, and concerning all acts which are considered sinful in themselves (for as for others, there is no difficulty), one can say that God is in no way the cause of the act of hatred, but that He is the cause of the movements that precede this act of hatred. To explain this more clearly, I note: 

1. In order for a movement of hatred to arise in my soul, certain movements must first necessarily arise in my body, which dispose me to hate what is presented to me. Thus, there are moments in which everything displeases us and we can tolerate no one. These movements and these thoughts are not evil in themselves; but the determination of these movements and of these thoughts against God (who is supremely lovable)—which determination follows these movements and these thoughts and depends on our **will**—is a great sin. 

2. I understand that nothing prevents God—acting either upon our blood, or upon our spirit, or upon our **humors** <note>original: "zappen" — literally "juices," referring to the Four Humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control human temperament.</note>—from producing these movements and thoughts that dispose us to hate. But because the passions always choose a particular object, and because one commonly—when thus disposed to hate everything—hates that which then presents itself (especially when what presents itself has power over us), it is easy to understand that when someone who is corrupt and finds himself in this state of soul thinks of God, and considers that God will not allow him the enjoyment of his lusts, he commits a calculated crime by directing his hatred against God. 

3. I note that one does not come to this with a single blow...

# THEOLOGY. VII. B. V. Chapter.

this hatred comes only by degrees. Various thoughts precede it, some of which are themselves quite innocent and can be prompted by God. 4. If one asks how God provokes these movements and thoughts, since He knows that such terrible sin will follow? I answer that one cannot truly give a reason for this action, but one also cannot say why God has permitted a sin that He was able to prevent? Why He allows objects to appear before sinners which He knows will cause them to sin? Why He sustains the powers which He knows they will misuse? Besides that, God’s action is not to be reproached <note>original: "waaken" — likely a typo for "laken" (to blame/reproach) or "wraken" (to reject)</note>, because the movements and thoughts of which I have spoken do not, in themselves, incite man to sin, but do so only by accident <note>term: "toeval" (contingency/accident) — in a philosophical sense, something that happens but is not part of the essential nature of the cause.</note>, springing from his corrupt nature, of which God is not the cause. Add to this that God powerfully exhorts us to flee from sin, and that He threatens sinners with the most hideous punishments. One can investigate this sentiment further. The surest and best path is to hold to the Scripture.

But, it is said, how is it possible that God is not the cause of sin, since He permits the sin which He can prevent; sustains the faculties and powers of man which He knows man will misuse; places sinners in such circumstances in which He foresees they will sin; and presents objects to them which He knows will bring them to a fall, etc.?

I acknowledge that these are great difficulties. However, one can deny none of these propositions; it is certain that God permits sin, that He sustains the powers of sinners, etc., etc. Scripture and reason convince us of it. But one also knows with certainty that God is not, nor can be, the cause of sin.

One must then believe both the one and the other, without racking one's brain <note>original: "’t hooft verder te breeken" — literally 'breaking the head further'</note> any further. It is true that God permits the sin which He could prevent, but He has had greater reasons to permit it than to ward it off. If He does not prevent the sin which He foresees, He does not produce it, and He does not force man to commit it. The end <note>gloss: "The purpose or goal"</note> that He proposes for Himself in the permission of sin is a greater and much weightier good than all the evil He foresees. It is also true

<column-break/>

that He places man in circumstances in which He foresees that he will sin; but does man not have, at the same time, a hundred reasons not to sin? Furthermore, He governs everything with a wondrous wisdom and makes the sins of men serve His glory, as we have already noted.

It is said that anyone who permits a sin which he can prevent is guilty. I answer, 1. That everyone is commanded to ward off the evil that he can prevent, and that one consequently makes oneself guilty if one permits it. But God has not prescribed such laws for Himself.

2. Men must ward off evil because, once it has happened, they can offer no help therein; but God can come to the aid of all evils in a moment.

It is said that he who produces a creature is the cause of the sin which the creature commits.

Answer. That is not so. If God, in the production of creatures, breathed into them a corrupt soul, He would be the cause of the sins which that corrupt soul would commit. But the soul comes unblemished and sinless from God’s hands. If one does not accuse a father of being the cause of the crimes his son commits, even though he has shared his corruption with him, how much less must one attribute our sinful deeds to God, since He has given us a pure soul. God has endowed the soul with understanding and will, but He has not occupied the understanding with prejudices; He has produced no evil disposition in the will. It is not always true that the cause of a cause <note>term: "oorzaak van een oorzaak" — the Scholastic principle *causa causae est causa causati* (the cause of the cause is the cause of the effect).</note>—to speak with the Scholastic theologians <note>original: "School-Godgeleerden" — medieval and early modern academics who used logic and philosophy to explain Christian doctrine.</note>—is always the cause of the result that the second cause produces. The suffering of Christ is the meritorious cause <note>term: "verdienende oorzaak" — the legal/theological basis by which a reward is earned.</note> of our salvation; but all who were the cause of Christ’s death, such as the Jews, Pilate, etc., must not be viewed as the cause of our redemption. If human nature, as human nature, committed sin by the same necessity as fire necessarily burns, one would not be able to understand how God gave us such a nature without being the cause of sin. But there is nothing here that resembles that. Meanwhile, one must acknowledge that there are depths in this matter in which one loses oneself if one [tries to]...

# THE CHRISTIAN [THEOLOGY]

reasons. One must be satisfied with these two things: 1. That nothing happens without God’s permission. 2. But that God is not the cause of sin.

It is said that, if one cannot blame <note>original: "wraaken" — to reject or find fault with</note> God, [considering] that He often allows circumstances to arise which He knows men will misuse; then one must also blame a man who gives a sword to a madman, knowing beforehand that he will do evil with it.

I answer, 1. that it is by no means God’s intention, when He causes the opportunities which men misuse to arise, to lead them into sin. He has other reasons, which are unknown to us and are fitting for God. It is true that, in providing these opportunities, He knows that men will make a bad use of them: but He also knows that the good which will come from what He does will be much greater than the evil that men will commit. Far from causing them to sin by providing these opportunities, He warns them against sin at the very same moment in which He provides them. 2. When a Magistrate, wishing to put a punishable criminal to death, gives a sword to a madman, even though he foresees that the madman will stab this man to death as soon as he meets him, the Magistrate is not guilty before God. He did not make this man mad, but he utilized his madness to punish a guilty person. God never incites man to do evil, but He often uses sinners to carry out His judgments; they are not for that reason less guilty, and He is not for that reason less holy.

Let this be enough regarding the way in which God intervenes in sin before it is committed. Let us now see what He does during the time in which men sin. One can say that God does three things.

I. He directs the sinners in such a way that, although He does not instill in them the loathsome will to sin (which would be against His holiness), He nevertheless ensures that they practice their malice toward certain objects <note>In this context, "objects" refers to the targets or victims of the sinful act.</note> rather than others; and those against whom they practice it are usually those whom God intends to chastise and punish. Thus the Prophet Ezekiel notes that

<column-break/>

<margin>Ezekiel 21:26, 27, 28. etc.</margin>
when the King of Babylon wanted to know by casting lots whether he should attack the children of Ammon or the Jews, it pleased God to allow the lot to fall on the Jews, whom God had decided to punish.

II. God causes sin to result in an entirely different end than what man intends. Thus God ensured that the wickedness of Joseph’s [brothers], by wishing to overshadow his luster and thwart his happiness, gave him the occasion to climb to the highest steps of honor and prestige. In the same way, the murder of the children of Bethlehem, which Herod the Great ordered, served to make known the birth of the Lord Jesus Christ.

III. God sets boundaries upon sins so that they do not multiply beyond measure, extend too far, or last too long. This He does in various ways: either by enlightening the minds of the sinners and restraining their lusts, or by curbing their passions, or by turning away the opportunities they seek to do evil, or by resisting their mad drive, or in other ways which I shall pass over. Thus He prevented Satan from taking the life of Job,

He also determines the time, and does not allow the wicked to always carry out their intentions when they desire. The Jews wanted to seize Jesus, but it is written that no one laid hands on Him because His hour had not yet come.

God does even more things when sin is committed.

I. He directs them to a good end, contrary to the intention of those who commit them. Thus God made the selling of Joseph serve for the preservation of the house of Jacob and of the entire Kingdom of Egypt. Thus the sin of the Jews who crucified Christ brought forth eternal redemption for the human race.

## VI. CHAPTER.

### Explanation of various passages of scripture, which produce some difficulty regarding this matter.

It only remains now for me to explain some passages which seem to lay the cause of sin upon God.

We shall begin with those where it is said that God hardens the sinners. Exod. IV: 21. VII. 3. IX. 12. X. 27. XI. 10. Deut. II: 30. Jos. XI. 20. Joh. XII: 40. Rom. IX 18. etc. One has no difficulty in understanding how sinners harden their own hearts, as is often said in scripture. Exod. VII, 13, 14. VIII: 15, 19, 32. Zach. VII: 11, 12.

It is easy to perceive that someone who, being corrupted by nature through the daily sins he commits, becomes so accustomed to angering God that he does nothing else; and that he, loving nothing but the enjoyment of sins, resists God's voice, which invites him to a holy life. One understands that the prejudices with which he is preoccupied by the world make of his understanding a stony path, through which the seed of God's word cannot penetrate.

But one is surprised to read that God hardens the heart of Pharaoh. This seems to be against his goodness, holiness, and righteousness. However, it is certain that it is frequently testified of God.

One must then see how God hardens the sinners, and subsequently examine

->Part I.<-

<column-break/>

whether there is anything in his actions that runs counter to these virtues.

I will not dwell on refuting the delusions <note>original: "herssenbeelden" — literally 'brain-images', referring to fantasies or unfounded ideas</note> of the Manichaeans <note>Followers of Mani who believed in a dualistic struggle between Good and Evil</note> and of the (b) Marcionites; in their spirit <note>original: "geis," likely a typo for "geest"</note> nowadays no one is of their opinion anymore.

I will also not involve myself in all the opinions of the theologians. This would lead me too far astray.

There are those who have believed that God hardens men by permitting and not preventing them from hardening themselves in evil, like a Physician who leaves his patient and lets his ailment canker <note>original: "inkankeren" — to fester or become malignant like a cancer</note>; like a Father of a household who does not prevent his servants from giving themselves over to drink; like a Commander-in-Chief who retreats when his soldiers are in hand-to-hand combat with their enemy. But this opinion does not satisfy.

The expressions of Scripture are too strong to understand them as mere permission—*I will harden the heart*, etc.—they indicate that God is active.

Now to suppose that God does nothing else than not preventing the hardening of man's heart is to suppose God in inactivity, or as not working. There are those of the opinion that God only hardens men by enduring them and exercising his long-suffering toward them. But I find this still too weak to satisfy the expressions of Scripture.

It appears that when it is said that God hardens, it is a punishment which he imposes.

Now God's forbearance is a grace. Others say that God hardens man when he makes his hardening known, and that he foresees it. But this is a forced interpretation. One must go further here, provided one takes care, as we have said elsewhere, to avoid attributing any cause of sin to God.

Therefore, to have some understanding of the manner in which God hardens the sinners, it is necessary to establish some general grounds, such as:

1. That man is by nature corrupt, and that he can do nothing but evil if he is left to himself.

2. That by committing many sins,

# THEOLOGY. VII. Book. VI. Chapter.

7. It is true that God added other signs to the first ones, but they were harmful and deadly signs for the entire Kingdom of Egypt; consequently, they embittered Pharaoh more than they calmed him.

8. When God sent him the plague of the <term>frogs<note>The original Dutch uses "listvoschen," likely an archaic variant or OCR error for "vorschen" (frogs), which is the second plague described in Exodus.</note></term>, He did not give him to understand in darkness that no one could deliver him from it but He; instead, the ease with which he was freed from this plague hardened his heart, especially since his Magicians had also managed to make frogs appear.

9. Although they could not imitate Moses when he had brought the lice over the land, Pharaoh's heart did not become any softer, because this plague seemed to him of less importance than that of the frogs; and furthermore, he believed that the God of Israel had exhausted His power to visit him with anything heavier.

10. The loving-kindness with which God delivered him each time from every plague, through the <term>intercession<note>A formal plea or prayer on behalf of another; here, Moses praying to God to stop the plagues.</note></term> of Moses, also contributed not a little to his hardening. Thus, this Prince was not touched by God’s punishments as he should have been; it was with him as with a stream that swells more because of the dikes one throws up against it, and overflows with more violence when the dikes are broken through, or like an anvil that becomes harder with every hammer blow.

11. The saying of Moses in Exodus 10:26, that the flocks would depart with the people without leaving a single hoof behind, also hardened Pharaoh, because he clearly saw that this people would not return.

12. The last plague, which in all appearance should have softened his heart the most, hardened it more than all the preceding ones. He realized how much his Kingdom would lose by the departure of this people. His greed, ambition, and other passions, which had left him in a little peace after he understood that his firstborn Son had died and there was a corpse in every house, came to a boil again when the people marched out, because he realized in one blow how much his income and his power were about to diminish.

13. The carrying away of silver vessels, etc., etc., which belonged to the Egyptians, embittered this Prince not a little.

<margin>
Exodus
13.
14:2, 3.
</margin>

<column-break/>

ites had taken, because he hoped that he would have defeated them in their departure, or returned them to their first slavery. Add to this that God gave him over to his own lusts, and you will discover the way in which God hardened the heart of Pharaoh.

God could indeed have dealt with him in other ways; but they are either unknown to us, or they amount to those we have presented and are easy to discover.

However it may be, it is certain that in what we have said, there is nothing that runs contrary to the holiness and justice of God, as one will notice if one considers each proposition individually and more closely.

One sees, therefore, that God incites no one to evil; that nothing He does regarding sinners can incite them to it of itself; that He, if He does not give His grace to all, is not obliged to do so; and, if He takes away the same from those to whom He had given it, it is an effect of a righteous judgment.

Rather, sinners harden their own hearts through the *very same means* that ought to have brought them to conversion. When an eye that is inflamed looks toward the Sun, it becomes even more fiery. Is the blame for this placed upon the Sun? Not at all; it is attributed to the poor condition of the eye. To explain this further, one must observe:

1. That man is by nature blind, and that he is born blind.

2. That God enlightens the human understanding in various ways. He impresses upon it natural concepts <note>original: "natuurlijke begrippen"</note> which serve to guide him regarding the things of this life. He often gives him great talents to understand the sciences, arts, etc. He causes His law to be proclaimed to him, and He accompanies the proclamation of His Gospel with some grace of His Spirit, which reveals to him the knowledge of salvation. Therefore Paul says, speaking even of the temporary believers <note>original: "tytgeloovigen," referring to those who believe only for a season</note>, that they are enlightened.

4. From this it follows that God can blind man in various ways; whether by taking away the light He had given him because he misused it; or by no longer letting him hear the Gospel; or by handing him over to the passions that blind him.

5. Thus it happens that what should have enlightened man blinds him by accident, and what should have driven away his darkness increases it.

6. From all this, one can deduce that there is a threefold blindness in sinners: a natural one; one they inflict upon themselves; and one that is the punishment God imposes on them when He gives them over to themselves.

...that is, to mislead, and if he brings a command, would I the Lord have misled that Prophet? On the contrary, I will stretch out my hand against him. But one cannot accept this explanation when one examines the original text <note>original: "Grond-text"</note>.

There are those who believe that the Lord declares here that He will punish the false prophet for his deceit and deprive him of his senses; but this interpretation does not agree with the original words. The word that has been translated as *persuaded* <note>The Dutch word used here is "overreden," likely referring to Ezekiel 14:9</note> actually means to draw or lure toward oneself, whether to good or evil, or to indifferent deeds, through gentle ways, through persuasive expressions, or other flattering manners; whether by giving gifts or by stroking the affections with alluring objects. When someone is lured toward evil through such paths, this enticement is not called mere persuasion, but a deception.

To understand the Prophet's meaning, one must know that God, being justly angered against His people, testifies to them that if they do not abandon their false gods, He will no longer give them an answer when they ask Him for counsel. And if it happens that a false prophet allows himself to be misled by those who come to him for advice—by their persuasions, caresses, promises, and gifts—and thus, being misled, makes a false prophecy, "it is I," says the Lord, "who have misled this prophet," not by breathing in the lies he spreads, but by not revealing my will to him and by giving him over to his passions, which cause him to have a blind devotion to those who ask him for counsel. I will act thus to punish the hypocrisy <note>original: "veinzerye"</note>, idolatry, and sins of my people; but afterward, I will punish both the one who asks for counsel and the one who gives it.

### THE CHRISTIAN GOD

God sent him to punish him.
<margin>

12:11,

</margin>
> Nathan spoke thus to David. 2 Samuel 12:11, 12. Thus says the Lord: behold, I will raise up evil against you out of your own house, and I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor <note>In this context, the "neighbor" refers to David’s own son, Absalom.</note>; he shall lie with your wives in the sight of this sun; for you did it in secret, but I will do this thing before all Israel and before the Sun.

Who can judge otherwise than that God is the cause of Sin? But that is far from the truth. One must distinguish between what God intended to do and what Absalom was to carry out.

God says that He will give David’s wives into the hands of his neighbor, but He testifies at the same time that Absalom would commit an act of incest <note>original: "bloedschande"</note>, to which he was driven by the counsel of Ahithophel. One must not be surprised that everything is attributed to God. God wished to punish David for his adultery.

To that end, He willed that the dignity of the crown should fall into Absalom’s hands and deprive David of it for a time; it is for this reason that everything this dehumanized son—clothed in royal authority—attempted, and everything God permitted him to undertake to punish David, is attributed to God.

In the same sense, someone who has provided the occasion for something to be done is said to have done it themselves. This is how God attributes the persecutions of the Church to Himself—not because He incites men to persecute the Church, but because, intending to chastise His children or to test their faith and patience, He allows bloodthirsty and godless men to rule, who unfortunately abuse their authority and power to persecute God’s children. It was, then, God who gave David’s wives over to Absalom by a righteous judgment, in order to punish a king who had stolen another man’s wife. God’s act was holy and righteous; but Absalom’s heart being corrupt, he abused his father’s wives through a shameful incest; his conduct was detestable. God did not breathe this crime into him, but He permitted it to be committed. One might say: but surely God knew that by handing these wives over to Absalom, this immoral son would abuse them? I admit this; but God did not drive Absalom to commit this sin; rather, Absalom’s own lust seduced him, and it was Ahitho-

<column-break/>

phel who stirred it up. God had reason to punish David, but He was not bound to prevent Absalom’s sin.

<margin>
2 Sam.
16:10,
12
</margin>
Another passage is raised as an objection, which seems to present more difficulty. 2 Samuel 16:10, 12, David says of Shimei: *let him curse; for the Lord has said to him, curse David.*

It is clear that one must not take these words literally. What likelihood is there that David believed that God—who so strictly forbids in His law the cursing of the princes of His people—would have given a command to Shimei to curse the king? If David had believed it, would he have viewed what Shimei did as a sin? One would much rather have to praise him for obeying God’s command, just as one praises Abraham, who fulfilled the command God gave him to offer up his son. But far from David approving the act of this rebellious subject, he instead charged his son Solomon on his deathbed to punish him for it.

What then does David mean by this expression? To understand it well, one must take into account:

1. That Shimei was a malicious man.
2. That he was a secret enemy of David, for he was of the house of Saul and could not endure that David had succeeded Saul; but he hid his hatred, fearing David’s power.
3. That God caused him to encounter David—whom he hated and feared—in a state where he could heap insults upon him without punishment, because David was stripped of the authority and power of which Shimei had been afraid.
4. That God, who could certainly have prevented this bold courtier from insulting his King, did not wish to prevent it because He had resolved to humble David; therefore He gave free rein to this mad dog. This is what David recognizes; he views this action of Providence—which exposed him to Shimei’s encounter and rage—as if it were a command from God Himself. "It is God who wishes to humble me thus: I must worship His providence, which punishes me through one of my subjects, and has therefore given him over to the disorder of his own heart." This led Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393 – c. 458 AD), an influential theologian and bishop of the early Christian church.</note> to say that David regarded God as the one who chastened him, and Shimei as the rod by which he felt the blow. The holy Prophet, he adds, must not

# THEOLOGY. VII. B. VI. Chapter.

not against the rod with which he is struck, out of awe for the hand of which the rod was only an instrument. <note>The author is likely concluding an argument from the previous page that a believer should submit to God's discipline even when it comes through a human "instrument" or "rod."</note>

<margin>2 Sam. 24:1</margin> I move now to another passage, found in 2 Samuel 24:1, where it is said that the anger of the Lord was again kindled against Israel, and that he incited David against them, saying, "Go, number Israel and Judah." Thus reads the original text. But when one reads 1 Chronicles 21, where it clearly states that Satan stood up against Israel and incited David to number Israel, one sees clearly that when it is said there that God incited David, etc., it signifies that through His righteous judgment and through the hidden ways of His providence, He had permitted Satan to lead David into this sin, in order to punish Israel and to humble David, who was puffed up by pride at seeing so many people subject to his scepter. There are some interpreters who explain this passage thus: "The anger of the Lord kindled against Israel, so that David was set against them to say, go, number Israel." In that way, there would be no difficulty, for it would only mean that David was driven to the numbering of the people by his own ambition <note>original: "staatzugt"</note>, or by Satan.

Similar manners of speaking are found elsewhere in Matthew 1:23, 5:15, 7:16, 9:17; Luke 6:38, 11:22, 12:11, 20, 48; 14:35, 16:4, 9, 21:16; John 12:40, 15:6; Revelation 16:15.

One encounters an even more difficult passage in 1 Kings 22:19–23, where the Prophet Micaiah speaks thus to Jehoshaphat and Ahab: "I saw the Lord sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing beside him on his right hand and on his left. And the Lord said, 'Who will entice Ahab, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?' And one said one thing, and another said another. Then a spirit came forward and stood before the Lord, saying, 'I will entice him.' And the Lord said to him, 'By what means?' And he said, 'I will go out, and will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.' And he said, 'You are to entice him, and you shall succeed; go out and do so.' Now therefore behold, the Lord has put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these your prophets; the Lord has spoken evil concerning you."

One has only to read this passage to see that it must not be taken

<column-break/>

literally; for, if it were to be interpreted that way, one would have to say that God needs to take counsel, and that He is uncertain about what He ought to do.

It is clear that Micaiah means nothing other than that God, righteously angered against Ahab, permitted a spirit of error to mislead him and to incite him to a war that would be fatal for him. Indeed, the justice and the wisdom of God—who can neither deceive nor be deceived—nevertheless allows a spirit of error to exercise its power upon men who close their eyes and ears, like this godless king, so as not to see or hear the truth.

But, it is said, the Scripture says that God commanded the Devil to act so. It is true: but Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–458 AD) was an influential theologian and bishop in the early Christian church.</note> rightly observes that this is done to teach us that Satan, with all the will he has to deceive men, can mislead no one unless God permits it. This always implies a righteous judgment that punishes those who are willfully blind.

For since they do not wish to hear God when He exhorts them to their duty, they deserve to be given over to their own darkness and to that of the lying spirit.

<margin>Job 12:16</margin> Some object with Job 12:16: "With him are strength and wisdom; the deceived and the deceiver are his."

These words prove nothing else than that all things are under God’s governance; that if someone errs, or makes another err, such happens with God’s permission; that nothing occurs against His will; and that both the one who misleads and the one who is misled depend absolutely on God.

<margin>Prov. 16:4</margin> Some object with Proverbs 16:4: "The Lord has made all things for himself, or so that they correspond to one another; even the wicked for the day of evil." But Solomon does not mean to say that God is the cause of evil, or that He created man wicked. He made man, who corrupted himself, and He ordains everything toward the righteous punishment which he has deserved.

Some object with Psalm 119:36 and 141:4: "Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to greed; Incline not my heart to any evil thing."

Who does not see that it is as if the Prophet said: "Lord, do not abandon me to my [own heart]..."

<meta>This page continues the theological defense of God’s character, specifically addressing how certain biblical passages that seem to suggest God causes sin should be interpreted as divine permission or the withdrawal of restraint rather than active incitement.</meta>

# THE CHRISTIAN

passions that would incite me to filthy lucre <term>filthy lucre: shameful or ill-gotten financial gain</term> or other sin.

<margin>Revelation XVII. 13.</margin>
One objects with *Revelation XVII: 13*, where it is said that God put it into the hearts of the Kings to give their kingdom to the beast.

This does not mean that God breathed this intention into them. But rather: 1. That He permitted the Kings, captivated by the splendor of the Beast, to subject themselves to it. 2. That He gave them over to their own passions. 3. That He was able to raise in them such thoughts which, though indifferent <note>meaning neutral or non-moral in themselves</note> in their own nature, provided the occasion by chance for other evil thoughts, which led them to the subjection of their Kingdoms to the Beast.

<margin>Isaiah LXIII. 17.</margin>
One objects with *Isaiah LXIII. 17*, where the Jewish people speak thus to God: *Lord, why do you make us wander from your ways, why do you harden our hearts so that we do not fear you?*

One could say that it is the distress in which the people found themselves that makes them speak this way, and that consequently one should not pay it much heed. But beyond that, it is easy to understand that the people do not wish to accuse God of making them go astray, but that it is a kind of humble question or confession in the form of a question: why have you, Lord, permitted us to wander from your ways? Why have you given us over to our passions? Why have you not made our hardened hearts soft? Why have you not restrained our flesh, which rose up against you? It is true that we have made ourselves unworthy of your grace; but, Lord, return, etc. etc.

<margin>Romans I. 24.</margin>
One objects with *Romans I: 24*: *Therefore God also gave them over in the lusts of their hearts to impurity, to dishonor their bodies among themselves.*

One cannot conclude from this that God is the cause of the sins committed among the Heathen. Paul only wishes to teach us that God, justly angered against the Heathen for their sins, gave them over to themselves. It is true that terrible outrages followed upon this "giving over," but the sole cause of the same is the corruption of the Heathen. The abandonment by God is only the cause by chance, and only insofar as the corrupt-

<column-break/>

ion of man, being no longer held back by any bridle, brings forth all kinds of evil deeds; just like water, when held by nothing, has its free course over the land. God had still preserved some seeds of righteousness among them, but regarding the impurities of the flesh, He had loosened the reins on all their lusts.

Lastly, one objects with *2 Thessalonians II: 11. For this reason God will send them a strong delusion, that they should believe the lie.*

<margin>2 Thessalonians II. 11.</margin>
Everyone sees that Paul wants to teach us here how God acts toward those who reject and abandon the truth, which had been confirmed to them by miracles.

1. God permits a false doctrine to be preached to them, which flatters their desires, and permits it to be confirmed by false miracles. 2. He permits the reasons used to make the lie acceptable to lead them entirely away from the truth. 3. He does not give them His grace, by which they would recover from their errors. 4. He leaves them to themselves and gives them over to their perverse mind; so that, being thus given over to their passions, they believe the lies and the errors that they are taught.

I cannot refrain from noting here that all our churches and Church-Teachers have unanimously acknowledged that God is not the cause of sin. It is true that some have used certain harsh expressions, but it is necessary to note regarding them:

<margin>Zwingli, *On the Providence of God*, ch. 6, p. 366. Calvin, *Institutes*, book 1, ch. 18, § 1; ch. 18, § 4; ch. 6, § 5. In the Notes.</margin>
1. That almost all their expressions are taken from Scripture, or modeled after those of Scripture. One may compare what *Zwingli* and *Calvin* say with *2 Samuel XXIV: 1*. Calvin, *Institutes*, book 1, ch. 17, § 11 with *2 Samuel XVI: 11, Isaiah X: 7*. Calvin, *Institutes*, § 4, *Against the Libertines*, ch. 14. Beza in *Aphorism 22* and *Treatise on Predestination against Castalio*, vol. 1, p. 373, with *Isaiah X: 5, 6, 15*. Calvin, book 2, *Institutes*, ch. 6, § 2 with *Acts II: 23, IV: 27, 28, Genesis XLV: 7, 8*. *Institutes*, ch. 11, § 2 with *Job XII: 14, 2 Thessalonians II: 11*. Zwingli, *On Providence*, ch. 6, with *1 Samuel XII: 11, 12*.

<margin>See Piscator, Bucer, Vorstius, *To Amica*</margin>
2. That most of their expressions, which are criticized, can be taken in a good sense, like this one from *Zwingli* regarding providence: *how shall one know justice,* he asks, *if there is no injustice?* § 5. See *Piscator* and others, like *Zanchius*, book 5, *On the Nature of God*, ch. 2, part 4, p. 565. Bucer on *Romans I*.

### CHAPTER VII.

->On the misuse that various people make of the Doctrine of Providence, and on the good use that one must make of it.<-

<margin>
Ezek.
XVIII.
29.
XXXIII.
20.
</margin>
There are many people who misuse the doctrine of Providence, such as:
1. Those who murmur against God and accuse Him of injustice, or complain about Him as if He were unjust, when He gives the wicked an abundance of goods and leaves the good in poverty. Ezekiel speaks of certain godless people of his time who dared to say, *The way of the Lord is not right* (Ezekiel 18:29). Scripture even makes mention of believers who, in their adversities, let some complaints escape them, such as Job, Asaph, etc.

<margin>
Job. XXI.
7. 8. Ps.
LXXIII.
2. 3.
Jer. XII.
1,
</margin>
2. Those who wish to excuse their sins by saying that they could not have done otherwise, and that God willed it so.
3. Those who remain in a punishable idleness and deep anxiety, despising the means that Providence gives them to work out their salvation.
4. Those who recklessly expose themselves to dangers without being called to do so and without necessity, imagining that God will always perform miracles for them.
5. Those who fall into despair in their adversities, as if there were no longer any way

<column-break/>

out, and who take their own lives in that state.
6. Those who are in constant worry regarding what will happen to them, saying: *What shall we eat, what shall we drink, wherewithal shall we be clothed?* (Matthew 6:25).
7. Finally, those who bind themselves too much to <term>secondary causes: the physical or human means through which God works, rather than God Himself</term>, and who trust more in the arm of the flesh than in God.

True believers make a good use of the doctrine of Providence.
1. They worship God as the dispenser of all things, who governs the whole Universe through His wisdom and power; who holds infinite treasures of goods in His hand; who exalts some and humbles others; who creates light and darkness, peace and war, prosperity and adversity; from whose mouth good and evil proceed.
2. They fear Him as one who can arm all creatures against them and do with them according to His pleasure.
3. They take refuge in Him in all their needs, as He who ordains everything, and they thank Him for all good outcomes, without <note>original: "hunne netten te wierooken"</note> "burning incense to their own nets" <note>a biblical metaphor meaning to take credit for one's own success instead of thanking God</note> or attributing anything to their own prudence, conduct, and power.
4. They possess their souls with patience in their misfortunes and say with the Prophet (Psalm 39:9): *I will not open my mouth: for you have done it,* etc.
5. They cast all their worries upon God because He cares for them; knowing that He who feeds the birds of the air, clothes the lilies of the field, makes manna rain from Heaven to feed His people in the Wilderness, and who makes water flow from a dry rock for them to drink, can fulfill all their needs.
6. They are full of confidence in the midst of their cruelest enemies, being assured that not a hair of their heads will fall without His will; that God inclines and bends the hearts of men as it pleases Him. That He reconciles their enemies when their ways are right; that there is nothing that can separate God's children from His love; that He sets limits to the passion of the wicked, just as to the Sea, saying: *Thus far, and no further, shall the turbulence of your waves go.*

<margin>
Job XIII.
15.
</margin>
7. They place their entire trust in God and say with Job, *Even if He were to kill me.*

### FIRST CHAPTER.
->Concerning the decree of counsel that God has made to save men in general, and whether it is necessary to explain the Doctrine of Predestination.<-

<image-desc>Ornate decorative drop cap 'W' at the start of the first column, featuring foliage and scrollwork motifs.</image-desc> We have spoken in the preceding Books of the fall of man, of sin, of the various kinds of sins, of the manner in which God permits them, and finally, what they deserve: namely, an eternal death.

It seems that one should conclude from this that all men who have sinned shall perish eternally; but the Scripture does not allow us to make such a determination. It teaches us that God did not will that all the children of Adam should be lost, as they deserve, and that He has from all eternity decided to save some, leaving the others in their damnation. This we shall prove in the following sections through various explicit passages.

It should seem strange to no one that God has made decrees concerning the salvation of men, since we have proven in other places that nothing happens in the world that God has not previously decided to do or to permit, and that nothing happens against His will, or without it being known to Him.

One asks whether it is necessary to treat these matters and explain them to the people?

<column-break/>

In the time of **Augustine** <note>A 4th-century Church Father whose writings on grace and predestination became foundational for Western theology.</note>, there were some who did not approve of this Church Father treating this subject, and in the present day one still finds those who are of the same opinion. But this is without foundation. There is no reason that obliges us not to speak of this subject that would not also oblige us to remain silent about other mysteries: such as the mystery of the **Trinity**, of the **Incarnation**, and of various others which the Godless <note>original: "Ongoddisten," referring here to atheists or those who reject religious authority.</note> abuse.

The Apostles spoke and wrote of this several times, although they well foresaw the evil use that the wicked would make of it through their objections. Why then should we not speak of it, just as they have done?

<margin>Luke 10:20.</margin>
Is it right that we pay more attention to the unholy and to the free-thinkers <note>original: "vry-geesten," a term used in the 17th and 18th centuries for those who questioned orthodox religious doctrines.</note>, who trample all holy things underfoot, than to the believers, who draw comfort from this doctrine? <margin>2 Thess. 2:13.</margin> Also, the Lord Christ wants His disciples to rejoice—not because the spirits were subject to them, but because their names are written in Heaven; and Paul wants the **Thessalonians** to thank the Lord that He has called them from the beginning to salvation in sanctification of the Spirit.

It is true that in that mystery there are depths which flesh and blood <note>A biblical idiom for human nature or limited human understanding.</note> must not venture to sound; but one must distinguish what God has wished to reveal to us and what He has hidden from us.

We must leave the hidden things to God, and only contemplate those which He has made known to us for our comfort.

<header>THE CHRISTIAN [THEOLOGY]</header>

It is also true that one must use caution in presenting this mystery. This topic should not be taught to those who do not yet know the clearest truths of Christianity, and who have need of milk, and are not yet fit to bear solid food <note>This is a reference to 1 Corinthians 3:2 and Hebrews 5:12, where "milk" represents basic teachings and "solid food" represents complex spiritual mysteries.</note>. One must follow Paul, who, wishing to convert the Jews, first spoke to them of the forgiveness of sins promised to believers and of the resurrection of our Savior; one must follow Christ, who, to convert Nicodemus, contented himself with proposing that he who believes in Him shall not perish, but he who does not believe is already condemned. It is not necessary to entertain the common people with the various opinions of the learned on this subject. It is enough to teach them only what God says, and to that end, one must use the expressions of the Scriptures as much as possible.

It is not a doctrine that one should preach about frequently, but only on certain occasions: 1. for example, when the sequence of the books of Scripture that we are explaining obliges us to do so; 2. when one sees great strife arising in the Church between those who are considered the most zealous and holy; it is on such an occasion that most theologians believe Paul makes mention of this in the second letter to Timothy 2:19, where, having spoken of those who had turned away from the truth, he adds these words: *the foundation of God stands sure, God knows those who are His own.* 3. When we find believers who, in times of persecution, are fearful that they will not be able to withstand the strength of the temptations and that they will be eternally lost. One can comfort them through the explanation of this Article of faith. This, Paul does extensively in Romans 8.

When this doctrine is taught, it is necessary to show:

1. That God had the right to condemn us all to eternal pains.

2. That it is a work of infinite goodness that He did not will that all men should perish.

3. That we must not torment ourselves to know whether we are ordained to salvation from eternity or not; but that we must be convinced that if we have faith and love, we shall be saved; whereas, if we have neither faith

<column-break/>

nor love, we shall be condemned.

4. Finally, that those who are preordained to eternal salvation have no reason at all to exalt themselves above others, as if they had made themselves worthy of such a distinction; and those who are not have no reason to complain, since they have deserved nothing but death.

At the end of this book, we shall consider the use that can be drawn from this doctrine. Meanwhile, to say something more specific about the general decree that God has made regarding the salvation of men, it is necessary to make some observations and take heed:

1. That God has established, regarding all men individually, everything that must happen to them, whether they shall be saved or not; this foresight requires no proof.

2. That these decrees are eternal, as we shall prove in the following.

3. That when God made these decrees, He had already decided to create man and to permit his fall; He viewed all the children of Adam as fallen: for it would be absurd to decree the salvation of men whom one had not yet decided to create, and who would have no need of salvation.

Besides that, it seems to be against God's goodness to create men simply to damn them, and against His justice to condemn to eternal death those who have not yet sinned.

It is a matter much disputed among theologians—namely, how God viewed men when He ordained them to glory.

Those in the Roman Church who believe that predestination is that decree of God by which He established everything concerning men are of the opinion that God viewed them only as "possible" and "capable of being created," as held by *Alfonso Mendoza in "Questions on Predestination" <note>original Latin: "quæst. de Prædest."</note>, Estius in "Book of Sentences," Distinction 40, paragraph 6 <note>original Latin: "in l. Sentent. Dist. 40 parag. 6." Estius was a major Catholic commentator on Peter Lombard's "Sentences."</note>, Giacomo Nacchianti, Albert Pighius, Pietro Galatino, Lancelot Politi, and John Duns Scotus.* But the most common opinion is that when God ordained men to salvation, He viewed them as having fallen in Adam.

# THEOLOGY. VIII. B. I. Chapter.

Church, some have been of the opinion that God viewed humans as *creatable*, or at least as being *capable of falling into sin*. <note>This is the "Supralapsarian" view—the idea that God's decree of election occurred "above" or "before" the decree to allow the Fall of man.</note> This was the opinion of Zanchius, Beza, Piscator, Perkins, Ursinus, Gomarus, Polanus, Voetius, Twisse, etc. etc.
Others believe that God viewed humans as *having fallen in Adam*; this is the opinion of most of our theologians and that which most closely corresponds with the decrees of the Synod of Dordrecht. <note>This is the "Infralapsarian" view—the idea that God viewed humanity as a "corrupt mass" after the Fall when He chose whom to save. The Synod of Dordrecht (1618–1619) was the international gathering that standardized Dutch Reformed doctrine.</note> Others maintain that God viewed humans as *being called to the fellowship of Christ* through the preaching of the Gospel; this is the opinion of Georgius Sohnius, theologian of Heidelberg, of Testard, and of Amyraut. These believe that the first effect of election is the gift of faith. The Arminians <note>Followers of Jacobus Arminius; they argued that election was based on God's foreknowledge of an individual's future faith, rather than an absolute decree.</note> also hold that God viewed humans as *redeemed by Christ*, whether they be believers or unbelievers. Regarding the first view, I confess it seems much more natural to me to say that, when God preordained humans, He had already decided to create them and allow their fall (Salvation and damnation presuppose a being that exists, or is supposed to exist); now, before God decided to create humans, one cannot suppose they exist. Furthermore, if God had only considered humans as *coming to be created* when He decided to save or damn them, He could have established the salvation or destruction of an infinite number of people who were never created and will never be created, but who could have been created if God had willed it. Now there is no one who does not understand that it is unbefitting for a supreme wise being to make unnecessary decrees. Add to this that Salvation presupposes that one is lost; it is therefore necessary to posit that God regarded humans as *lost in Adam* when He decided to make them blessed. Scripture teaches us this when it says that believers are chosen in Christ, Ephesians 1:4: *Just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him in love.* If it is now necessary that we

<column-break/>

be redeemed, it follows that we are viewed as miserable and as lost. But, it is said, when Paul presents God under <margin>Romans 9:21</margin> the image of a Potter who makes from one *lump* a vessel for honor and a vessel for dishonor, does he not make us understand well that God did not view humans as having fallen in Adam when He preordained them? For, it is said, it comes down here to a lump that is not corrupt; but there one deceives oneself, for Paul speaks of a lump from which God makes vessels of wrath and of mercy; now, wrath and mercy presuppose misery and sins. He speaks of a lump from which those who are made from it can be hated, like Esau, and from which Pharaoh was brought forth. One will perhaps say that it appears that a *pure* lump is spoken of here, because a lump is discussed from which children came who had done neither good nor evil (verse 11). But it is clear that when it is said that these children had done no good or evil, it is only to teach us that Jacob had not yet done any good that could have obligated God to choose him over Esau, and that Esau had not yet done any evil that could have moved God to hate him rather than Jacob, and thus the election of Jacob depended solely on God's good pleasure. One will perhaps still say that Paul speaks here of a lump from which one makes vessels for dishonor. That is true, yet by *dishonor* one must not understand sin, but the *punishment* for sin. Vessels for dishonor are the creatures who are preordained to destruction; now, that punishment, as stated, presupposes sin and preceding corruption. One will furthermore say that here a lump is being discussed from which Adam was made: one is mistaken; a lump is spoken of from which God makes *vessels of wrath*. But, it is said, if a corrupt lump were seen here, there would be no more difficulty in this matter. One is mistaken; for one always has reason to ask: why does God choose one rather than the other? But, one will say at last, if this is so, then Adam and Eve will not have been preordained, since they were brought forth from a corrupt lump. <note>The author is posing a potential counter-argument here: if the "lump" is always the fallen human race, how could Adam and Eve, who were created perfect, fit into this decree?</note>
