## CHAPTER II.

->Regarding various expressions that the Scripture uses to show us the decree that God has made to save humanity, and regarding their election in particular.<-

The Scripture uses four specific manners of speaking to express the decree that God has taken to save humanity. It says that God **foreknew** us (Romans 8:29, Romans 11:2, 1 Peter 1:2); that he **predestined** <note>Dutch: *te voren verordineerd*</note> us (Ephesians 1:5); that he **chose** us (Ephesians 1:4). Finally, it speaks of the **purpose** of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will (Ephesians 1:11).

The word **Foreknowledge** does not only mean the infinite knowledge of God, by which all things are naked and exposed before him; for in the places where one finds this manner of speaking, it refers to a foreknowledge that concerns believers in particular, whereas the general knowledge of God extends over all creatures, both good and evil. Rather, this expression includes a *knowledge of love*, if I may speak so; and a knowledge that is accompanied by a decree in which God has established to give signs of his love to those whom he has thus known. It is called a foreknowledge to indicate the eternity of God's love, which preceded all ages. Let us here make two observations, which will not be in vain for a proper understanding of some passages of Scripture.

The first concerns the word **Foreknowledge**. Sometimes it is taken to mean both the love of God and his **Election** at the same time. Thus one must understand what Paul says in Romans 8:29: *those whom God foreknew*, that is to say, those whom God has loved from all eternity, before they had anything lovable in them, and

<column-break/>

whom he, by an act of his love, has separated from others in order to share his glory with them. Sometimes the word **Foreknowledge** includes nothing other than love; thus it is taken in 1 Peter 1:2, where the Apostle mentions those who are *elect according to the foreknowledge of God*.

<margin>2 Timothy 2:19.</margin>
The second observation is that the Scripture, which says that God has foreknown people from all eternity, also speaks of another knowledge that God has *in time*. *God knows those who are his*, says Paul in 2 Timothy 2:19; and this knowledge includes the love and the protection with which God favors his children as long as they are in the world. The Scripture even speaks further of a knowledge by which he will recognize us as his own on the Last Day, in contrast to the godless, to whom he shall say: *I do not know you.*

**Predestination** <note>Dutch: *Voorverordineering*</note> specifically includes the arrangement of the means that God has established to bring us to salvation. That is why Paul says that *God predestined us to be conformed to the image of his Son* (Romans 8:29) and that *he predestined us for adoption as children through Jesus Christ in himself, according to the good pleasure of his will* (Ephesians 1:5).

One must only note here that the phrase "to predestine" <note>Dutch: *te voren ordineeren*</note> is a general manner of speaking, which the Scripture also uses on other occasions, such as when it is said in Acts 4:28 that Herod and Pontius Pilate did *whatever your hand and your counsel predestined to occur*. From this it follows that the Church Fathers have used it to express predestination to eternal destruction <note>Often referred to as "reprobation" in theological texts.</note> as well as predestination to eternal salvation.

Thus **Augustine** <note>A 4th-century theologian central to Western Christian thought.</note> takes it in the 42nd and 48th treatises on *John*, in the second book of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, Chapter 18, and in the *Enchiridion* (Handbook) to Laurence, Chapter 100. Also in the book *On the Perfection of Righteousness*, and in the 15th book of *The City of God*, Chapter 1. **Prosper** <note>Prosper of Aquitaine, a disciple of Augustine.</note> uses it in the answer to the objections of the Gauls <note>original: "Gauloisen"</note>, 14th objection. **Fulgentius** <note>Fulgentius of Ruspe, a 6th-century North African bishop.</note> in the book to Monimus, to which one can also add the Church decrees...

<header>THEOLOGY. BOOK VIII. CHAPTER II.</header>

<margin><unclear>Mendoza</unclear></margin>
...of Valence, Langres, and Toul, and the Church of Lyon, to say nothing of Gottschalk <note>Gottschalk of Orbais (c. 800–868) was a Carolingian theologian known for his early and controversial defense of double predestination.</note>.

<margin><unclear>VII. B.</unclear></margin>
<margin><unclear>XI. m.</unclear></margin>
<margin><unclear>T. 1. Cap.</unclear></margin>
<margin><unclear>XII. n.</unclear></margin>
Some scholars of the Roman Church take the word **Predestination** <note>Dutch: *Voorverordineering*</note> to refer only to the decree by which God established the giving of heavenly glory to certain people. Gabriel Biel, Occam (one may consult Gregory of Valence, Volume 1, Disputation 1, Question 23, Point 3), others for the decree that ordains the means to salvation (Becanus, *Summary of Theology*, Volume 1, Chapter 14, Question 2, Conclusion 1). Others take it for the eternal decree through which God has destined certain people for the supernatural enjoyment of salvation through supernatural means, such as Eustachius of Saint Paul, Petrus of Saint Joseph, Gregory of Valence, and Estius. Others, like Jansenius in *On the Grace of God the Savior* <note>Original: *de Grat. Dei Serv.*</note> Book IX, Chapter 3, understand by it the decree through which God has destined some to glory and others to destruction.

Others believe that **Predestination** is the first decree of God, and that all others followed upon it, even that of the creation of the world (Alphonse Mendoza in *Scholastic Questions on Predestination*, Section 6 <note>Original: *quæst. Sch. de prædest.*</note>). Those who hold this view place creation, the permission of sin, etc., among the effects of Predestination.

Regarding the Protestants: some take the word **Predestination** for the decree that destines one to salvation and the other to destruction, such as Zanchius, Beza, Ursinus, Perkins, Polanus, Bucanus, and the Synod of Dordrecht. Others take it for the decree that destines certain people to salvation and to the means that lead to salvation.

The word **will** or **firm purpose** indicates the certainty of the outcome—namely, that the things God has established will certainly happen. Paul uses it in this sense in Ephesians 1:11: *In him,* he says, *in whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will.*

Finally, the word **Election** indicates the choice that God has made of certain persons, to the exclusion of others; but one must take note that the word Election sometimes signifies the choice one makes of someone to be

<column-break/>

raised to a worldly or spiritual office, as in 1 Samuel 10:24, Luke 6:13, Acts 1:2, John 6:70, etc. Sometimes it signifies the choice God made of a certain people to enter into a covenant with them; it is in this sense that the people of Israel are called the "chosen people" (Deuteronomy 4:37, 7:7). Sometimes it refers to the separation that God makes in time, through his efficacious grace, of certain people whom he wishes to lead to glory and to whom he gives faith. In this place, we take it for the eternal decree of God, in the same way that Paul uses it in Ephesians 1:4, when he says that *God has chosen us in Christ before the foundation of the world.*

<margin>Alph. Mendoza, *Scholastic Questions on Predestination*, Section 2. Severus on 1 Peter 1:1.</margin>
In the Roman Church, some take the word **Election** for the decree through which God assigns glory to certain persons. Others understand it as the decree to give grace and glory. Among Protestants, the word Election is taken in the sense we have noted; however, there are some who understand it as the decree to efficaciously call certain people to Christ and to give them a living faith, such as Testard, Louis Cappel, and Moïse Amyraut <note>These theologians were associated with the Academy of Saumur and the "Amyraldian" view, which attempted to soften strict Calvinist predestination with a form of hypothetical universalism.</note>.

But by **Election**, we understand 그 eternal and unchangeable decree of God, through which he established out of pure grace, before the foundation of the ages, to draw some out of the miserable state into which he foresaw that the rebellion and the fall of Adam would cause the human race to collapse, and to provide them with salvation through his Son Jesus Christ, although they were no better nor more excellent than others whom he has left behind.

I. We say, then, that **Election** is an eternal decree; Paul teaches us this when he says that *God has chosen us before the foundation of the world* (Ephesians 1:4), and Christ says that *the Kingdom of Heaven was prepared for the blessed of his Father from before the foundation of the world* (Matthew 25:34).

It is said that Paul, in teaching that God chose us, means to say that he *decided* to choose us.

**Answer.** Besides there being no necessity to accept this interpretation, it would nonetheless always follow that the decree of Election is eternal.

### IV.
We observe that **Election** concerns only a certain number of people whom God appoints to salvation, so that one does not believe that all people are chosen, as Samuel Huberus <note>Samuel Huberus (1547–1624) was a Swiss Lutheran theologian who controversially argued for "universal election," the idea that God had chosen all of humanity for salvation, though many reject it.</note> believed. The word **Election** [Choosing] itself shows that all people cannot have a part in it: for whoever says "an election" implies that others are passed by. Scripture confirms this truth.

Various passages, which I have already cited, do not allow for doubt on this matter; but one can add several others to them. Just as nothing happens in time that God has not established from eternity, so one can conclude that God has not chosen all people and had no intention to save them all from the fact that Scripture says that God shows mercy to one and that he hardens the other <note>A reference to Romans 9:18: "Therefore God has mercy on whom he wants to have mercy, and he hardens whom he wants to harden."</note>; that he reveals his mysteries to children and hides the same from the wise, etc <note>A reference to Matthew 11:25.</note>. Reason itself teaches us that since God will not grant salvation to everyone, this is proof that he had not pre-destined the same for them all; because if he had destined it for them, he would undoubtedly give it to them. He would also not fail to provide them all with the means to reach it; indeed, one cannot conceive that God, who has all means in his hand, would have decided from all eternity to give salvation to all, on the condition of faith, and yet in the meantime he does not let his word be preached to all, and that he does not give faith to all: for he who sincerely desires the ends must also desire the means leading to them.

It is said that he who desires the ends absolutely, and without any condition, must also desire the means that can bring him to it; but that it is not the same with him who desires the ends only under certain conditions, as it is assumed that God desires the salvation of men.

Answer. This assumes what is in dispute, namely, that there are conditional decrees in God. Besides that, when one desires an end with a serious will, one must also seriously desire the means that lead to it.

It is said that he who desires the end also wants the means, but that in order to

<column-break/>

desire the means, one does not always have to want those to whom they are offered to actually use them; that it can coexist with wanting to offer them in such a way that those to whom they are offered can use them if they desire it; just as it cannot be denied that a Father desires nothing else but that his children live well, since he offers them the means to that through his admonitions and promises, although he cannot make them actually use the means that he proposes to them.

Answer. This does not weaken our proof, for he who sincerely desires the end must also, as much as is in him, desire all the means necessary to arrive there; he must not only offer them, but he must produce them, if it is in his power, as one cannot doubt that such depends on God's power; whereas, on the contrary, it does not depend on a Father to produce good inclinations in the heart of his children.

This truth seems to conflict with some passages of Scripture, but it is very easy to explain them.

1. When Christ, in John III. 16, speaking to Nicodemus, says:

it is to teach us these three truths. 1. That God, who could justly have let the entire human race perish and condemned them to eternal pains, like the fallen Angels, nevertheless loved them so much that he did not want to deal with them so severely. 2. One will object, that / just as one cannot say that a Prince loves a City / consisting of 10,000 Inhabitants / if he did not preserve more than a few hundred of them / so one also cannot say / that God has loved the human race / if it is a truth that he has decided to preserve so few.

I answer: 1. That one can very well say / that a Prince loves a City / where he only wishes to preserve some inhabitants / if the same has made itself worthy of being rooted out with all its inhabitants.

2. The proof / that we draw from this Chapter <note>Referring to Romans 9.</note> / is therefore of great emphasis.

One will say, that it does not speak of eternal Election, but of an election / which happens in time / through which God converts some and passes others by.

But **I.** One cannot deny / that there are verses in this Chapter / that mention Election and Reprobation / as in particular / vs. 22. and 23.

**2.** Even if one granted / that here it is not seen as the election / which happens in time / the proof would be no less powerful / for / if it is a truth / that God distributes his gifts in time / and converts people / although they have nothing in themselves / that can oblige him to do so / it is an even greater truth / that God has decreed from eternity to give his grace / without foreseen works. If temporal election does not presuppose the foresight of faith and of works / then eternal election presupposes the same much less.

God calls and justifies them; he makes them persevere in the faith; he brings them at last to salvation. It depends here on a calling / that goes before justification / and is inseparable from justification. It is therefore a calling to faith / through which we are justified. Finally, the Apostle looks to a calling / which is an immediate effect of Election, which cannot be said of the calling to the cross alone.

Certainly one cannot deny / that here it is seen as an eternal decree / before which God has established / to communicate all kinds of spiritual blessings to certain people /

It is said, that Paul does not look at election to glory, but to grace.

Answer, 1. From that it would then follow / that election to grace does not presuppose the <term>foresight of faith: the idea that God chooses people because he sees in advance that they will believe (original: voorbeschouwing van het geloof)</term>.
2. Faith follows / but does not go before.

<margin>Volkel <note>Johannes Volkel (c. 1565–1618), a leading Socinian theologian who argued against traditional views of predestination.</note> L. V. c. 17. p. 523. Remon. <note>The Remonstrants, or Arminians, who opposed the strict Calvinist doctrine of unconditional election.</note></margin>
It is said, that it does not say / those who were *previously* ordained, but simply those who *were* ordained.
I answer, that this is mere hair-splitting / and that it comes to the same thing / as can be concluded from the phrasing / that Luke uses / which is similar to that used in the same sense / *Rom. IX, 23.*

It is said, That it is not said / that those who were ordained *by God* / believed / but simply those who were ordained.
I answer, that one cannot understand it otherwise : for either they had ordained themselves / which is a pure <term>Pelagian thesis: the belief that humans can take the first step toward salvation without divine grace (original: Pelagiaansche stelling)</term> ; or they were ordained by God.

<margin>Volk: Rem.</margin>

IV. If Election presupposes the foresight of faith / then God foresees faith in those whom he chooses / either as a disposition / that proceeds from them / or as a work of his grace.
<margin>Eph. II. 8.</margin>
One cannot say / that God foresees faith in those whom he chooses / as a matter that depends on them ; for the Scripture says very explicitly / that faith is a gift of God. If he foresaw it as one of his gifts / and as a work of his grace / one must suppose / that he has made a decree / through which he intended to give faith.
This is the decree / that we call Election. Election then does not presuppose the foresight of faith. One can make no substantial objection against this truth.

I speak of Adults, yet it does not follow from this / that God did not previously designate certain persons for salvation / until after he had foreseen / that they would believe. The only conclusion / that one must draw from this / is / that God having previously designated salvation for some / he also at the same time established to give them faith. All the places / that are brought forward / prove the necessity of faith to be saved / but they do not prove / that the foresight of faith precedes election.

I answer, that it is true / that God in time makes men saved / in the same way as he has decreed from all eternity to make them saved / and that consequently / just as he in time only makes saved those who believe / so he has also decreed to save no one / except those who shall believe : but from this it follows in no way / that faith is the cause of the pre-destination to salvation. 3. It is said, *Heb. XI. 6.* For without faith it is impossible to please God, and that God consequently could only have chosen those / in whom he foresaw faith.

What is it that God could have foreseen in his Creatures / except what he himself has given them / and that therefore his election follows / which is the source of all saving grace.

God then ordained beforehand those / whom he foreknew / not because they were conformed to Jesus Christ / but so that they should become so.

6. A passage is cited from James, in which it is said / that God has chosen the poor of this world, (to be) rich (in) faith, and heirs of the Kingdom, *James II. 5.*

Because they / although they were excluded from earthly inheritances / would nonetheless be heirs of the Kingdom of God. One cannot then say / that God has chosen the poor / because he foresaw / that they would be rich in faith; for then one would also have to say / that he chose them / and prepared salvation for them / because he foresaw that they would be heirs of his Kingdom: but one must say / that God / who has chosen many poor / makes the same rich in faith / and that he will make them heirs of his Kingdom.

I answer, that / since God wants to use their service to bring men to salvation / they must labor therein with zeal / leaving the outcome to <term>Providence: God’s divine guidance and care over the world (original: Voorzienigheid)</term>.

        "just as [one] does. Since no injustice is found therein, one must also acknowledge that there is no <term>respect of persons: showing partiality or favoritism based on status rather than merit (original: aanneeming des perzoons)</term> in it. Otherwise, those with little knowledge might say that there was indeed respect of persons with that Master of the house in the Gospel, who gave as much reward to those who had worked only one hour in his Vineyard as to those who had endured the heat of the whole day; thus equaling in reward those who had been so unequal in labor. But what did the Master of the house answer to those who grumbled against him, and seemed to accuse him of respect of persons? 'Friend,' he said to one of them, 'I have done you no wrong: did you not agree with me for a <term>penny: a standard day's wage, referring to the biblical denarius (original: penning)</term> a day? Take what belongs to you, and go your way; I wish to give to this last one as much as to you. Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with what is mine? And is your eye evil because I am good?' There is no other right to be demanded; it consists only in this one word: *I desire it so*. I have paid you, I have forgiven the other, and because I have forgiven him, I have not taken from you, nor deducted what I owed you. Is it not lawful for me to do with what belongs to me as I wish? Just as there is, therefore, no respect of persons here—because, although one receives a great advantage for nothing, the other does not suffer by it, since nothing is taken from him of what was owed to him—likewise there is no respect of persons when, according to God's decree, one is called and the other is not. This is because God gives freely to the one who is called a good that He did not owe him, of which the Calling is the fundamental principle; and He allows the one who is not called to suffer the evil he deserved, because all men are guilty in the one through whom sin entered the world. For one can in no way pretend that there is any respect of persons when someone, having two debtors who owe him the same amount, forgives the one and demands from the other what is owed."

    *   *Drafting Transition and Column 2:*
        "Thus, respect of persons only takes place when one must give to each what is rightfully <column-break/> due to him / and in that way it remains certain that with God there is no respect of persons / because He can do no wrong. But when one gives freely what one owes to no one / there is no respect of persons / by giving to one what one refuses to another. One may consult / what Fulgentius says <note>Saint Fulgentius of Ruspe (467–533 AD), an African bishop and theologian</note> (*Book on the Incarnation and Grace to Peter*, chapter 2) & Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential medieval philosopher and theologian</note> (*Summa Theologica* II-II, question 63, article 1, reply 3; also I, question 23, article 5, reply 3)."

        "The second observation is / that the eternal decree of God / through which He has chosen men / includes two things / the appointment of the elect to Salvation / and the appointment of the means / that lead to salvation. Augustine says / that <term>predestination: the divine foreordaining of what will happen, especially regarding the salvation of some and not others (original: voorbeordinering)</term> is the eternal knowledge and preparation of the grace / by which those who are saved / are surely saved. Thus God / in choosing and in appointing men to <term>Glory: the splendor and bliss of heaven (original: Heerlykheid)</term> / simultaneously decided to send His Son / to obtain salvation for them / to call them to the knowledge of the truth / to justify them / to sanctify them through His spirit / and to produce in them faith and Christian virtues / to make them persevere to the end / and finally to give the glory / which He has prepared for them. Christ is therefore the first means / through which God carries out the decree of election / and that is what Paul teaches us in 1 Thessalonians 5:9. Where he says / <margin>1 Thess. 5:9.</margin> *God has not appointed us to wrath, but to the obtaining of salvation, through our Lord Jesus Christ.* If one asks / how God could appoint salvation to men / who had offended Him / without violating His justice / one must answer / that God / in determining to make them saved / simultaneously determined in His decree to send His Son to satisfy His justice. <summary>This page refutes the charge that predestination implies divine partiality, using the Parable of the Workers in the Vineyard to argue that God may bestow unmerited grace on some without being unjust to others. It further explains that God's decree of election includes both the end (salvation) and the means (Christ's sacrifice and the work of the Holy Spirit).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the defense of the doctrine of Election (Predestination) against common objections. The previous page established that God is not "partial" or a "respecter of persons" when He chooses some for salvation, using the analogy of a homeowner and his workers.</meta>

# THE CHRISTIAN

nothing can be concluded against the truth that we have established. **Paul** intends to say nothing else than that a person who applies himself to cleansing himself from the defilements of sin will indeed be a sanctified vessel, and show that he is a chosen vessel, previously destined for glory. This is in the same sense as **Christ** said, *love your enemies, so that*

<margin>Matthew 6:44, 45 <note>The text cites Matthew 6, though these verses are traditionally found in Matthew 5:44-45.</note></margin>
*you may be children of your Father, who is in Heaven;* that is to say, to make it evident that you are children of the Father of mercy.

9. It is said that this doctrine makes man careless and causes the practice of godliness to grow cold.

But one is greatly mistaken; for, when we say that God has chosen us according to His good pleasure, without having foreseen any quality in us, we add to this that God will not give salvation except to believers, and only to those who seek to work out their salvation. <note>The author is balancing the idea of "unconditional election" with the necessity of living a holy life.</note>

10. It is said that by this view, prayers are made useless; for why, it is asked, should one seek to prevail upon God through prayers if it is a truth that He has determined from all eternity everything that must happen?

I answer that God, who has taught us that He chose us before the foundation of the ages, demands from us the duty of our prayers, and that we cannot release ourselves from this without offending Him. We shall examine this more closely when we deal with the subject of Prayer.

11. It is said that this doctrine strives against the Gospel; for the Gospel, it is said, commands us to have repentance, whereas this doctrine supposes that God wants to save men without having foreseen their repentance, and that He produces this repentance in them.

I answer: 1. That although the decree of Election does not follow the foresight of repentance, God has nonetheless resolved to give salvation only to the penitent. 2. That penitence is simultaneously a duty of man and a gift of God.

12. It is said that this doctrine contradicts what the Scripture teaches us of eternal life, which it depicts to us as the inheritance of God’s children, the reward of their obedience, and the crown of those who shall have fought the good fight, etc.

Answer: One fails to notice that we say

<column-break/>

that eternal life will not be given except to the believers who remain faithful until death.

13. It is said that this doctrine causes Pastors and Teachers to neglect the duties of their ministry, because the same can be of no benefit except for those who shall be saved, and who cannot be lost.

I answer that, since God wishes to use their service to bring men to salvation, they must labor therein with zeal, leaving the outcome to Providence.

What we have said is enough to explain this matter. But notwithstanding this, we shall make a few more remarks about it.

1. The first is that God, in choosing men, acts as a Merciful Father and a Sovereign Lord <term>Sovereign Lord: A ruler with absolute, independent authority (original: Vrye Heer)</term>, who does what pleases Him. Therefore, if one asks: Why has God chosen certain persons? one must answer that it is a work of His infinite mercy toward the human race, which moved Him not to let all perish who deserved it. But if one asks: Why did God choose **Peter** rather than **Paul**, since they both deserved death? one must answer: Because it so pleased Him. He is like a Potter who, from one lump of clay, makes one vessel for honor and another for dishonor. <note>This refers to the "Potter and the Clay" analogy found in Romans 9:21.</note> We have reason, then, to adore God's mercy toward men, in that He wished to spare some of the human race, although He could have punished them all; but we must not value the Supreme Power He has over them any less highly.

One must not accuse God of being a respecter of persons <note>original: "Aannemer des perzoons," meaning one who shows favoritism or partiality based on status.</note>, as **Augustine** very well remarks. "One calls it respect of persons," he says, "when someone who must pass judgment on a matter leaves aside the justice of the case and favors one to the detriment of the other, because he finds something in his person that draws his esteem or his compassion. But if someone had two debtors, and he wished to forgive the debt of one and make the other pay his, what could one have to say about that, except that he gives to whom he wills, and harms no one?"

<margin>Book 4 to Boniface, chapter 7 <note>Referring to Augustine's "Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians," written to Pope Boniface.</note></margin>

Thus, partiality only takes place when one must give to each what is due to them by

<column-break/>

right; and in that way it remains certain that with God there is no partiality, because He can do no wrong. But when one gives freely what is owed to no one, there is no partiality in giving to one what is refused to another. One may consult what Fulgentius says <note>original: "Lib. de inc. &. grat. ad Petrum. c. 2." — referring to Saint Fulgentius of Ruspe's 6th-century work *On the Incarnation and Grace, addressed to Peter*, chapter 2.</note> and Thomas [Aquinas] <note>original: "2. 2. q. 63. art. 1. ad. 3. item 1. p. q 23. a. 5. ad. 3." — referring to the *Summa Theologica*, various parts regarding partiality and predestination.</note>.

The second observation is that the eternal decree of God, through which He has chosen men, includes two things: the destiny of the elect to salvation, and the arrangement of the means that lead to salvation. **Augustine** says that predestination is the eternal knowledge and preparation of grace, through which those who are saved are certainly saved. Thus God, in choosing and destining men for glory, simultaneously decided to send His Son to obtain salvation for them, to call them to the knowledge of the truth, to justify them, to sanctify them through His spirit, and to produce in them faith and Christian virtues, to make them persevere to the end, and finally to give the glory He has prepared for them. **Christ** is therefore the first means through which God carries out the decree of election, and this is what **Paul** teaches us in **1 Thessalonians 5:9**, where he says: *God has not appointed us to wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ.*

<margin>
1 Thessalonians 5:9.
</margin>

If one asks how God could assign salvation to men who had angered Him without wounding His justice, one must answer that God, in determining to save them, simultaneously established in His decree to send His Son to satisfy His justice. **Christ** is then the cause and the foundation of our salvation: but the mercy and the good pleasure of God is alone the cause of our election.

<margin>
Arminians: *Conference of The Hague*; *Acts of the Synod*. <note>Refers to the debates between the Remonstrants (Arminians) and the orthodox Calvinists in the early 17th century.</note>
</margin>

It is therefore wrong to charge our doctrine with the accusation that it overthrows the merits of **Christ**.

<margin>

</margin>

When the Apostle says then, in **Ephesians 1:4**, *that we are chosen in Christ*, it is to teach us that God, in choosing men, decided to give them to **Christ**. In the same decree in which He destined men for glory, He also established to give them to **Christ**, and to send **Christ** into the world to [be] for them...

## CHAPTER IV.

### Of the View of the Ancient Church regarding the matter of Predestination.

<margin>
<note>original: "Tom. I. Theol. Dogm. l, IX, c, 5, 6, Aug, de bon, Pers, c, 20, p, 1288. T, VII."</note>
Volume I, Dogmatic Theology, Book IX, chapters 5, 6. Augustine, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 20, page 1288, Volume VII.
</margin>
It has been well noted that in the disputes which have been held for a long time over Grace, Election, and Predestination, one must give less weight to the teachings of the Church Fathers who lived before the heresy of Pelagius <note>Pelagius (c. 354–418) was a monk who argued that humans could take the first steps toward salvation by their own free will without divine grace, a view later declared heretical.</note> than to those of the Church Fathers who arose afterward, because the latter investigated these matters with greater precision. This is acknowledged by the Jesuit Petavius. „ Every „ new faction of heretics, says Au- „ gustine, that arises in the Church, gives „ occasion, through the disputes they „ stir up, to explain and protect the „ truths of the Scripture which they „ oppose much more broadly and „ accurately than would have been „ done otherwise.

The Fathers, while disputing with the Manichaeans <note>Followers of Manichaeism, a dualistic religion that taught a radical struggle between good and evil; Augustine famously converted from this faith to Christianity.</note>, set the powers of free will a little too high. Meanwhile, many of them favor the truth that we defend, and they have been of great service in combating the errors that we perhaps oppose.

But, so as not to occupy ourselves with the views of the Church Fathers who lived before Pelagius, let us examine what the Church taught when this heretic arose, and what those who came after him believed.

<margin>
<note>original: "Lib. de Praed. T. VII. f. 19."</note>
Book *On Predestination*, Volume VII, folio 19.
</margin>
From the works of Augustine, it appears that in his time there were three doctrines concerning predestination.

The First was that of Augustine and the Church, which ascribed everything to God. The second was that of Pelagius, who attributed everything to man. The third, that of the Semi-Pelagians <note>A group that sought a middle ground, teaching that God’s grace is necessary but that humans must take the first step toward faith.</note>, who indeed divided the work of grace between God and man, but nonetheless ascribed more to man than to God. The Pelagians based pre-

<column-break/>

<margin>
<note>original: "Aug. lib. de Praed. c. 18."</note>
Augustine, Book *On Predestination*, chapter 18.
</margin>
destination, or rather God's election, upon the foresight of human merits. The Semi-Pelagians, acknowledging that grace is necessary for all good works, ascribed only the beginning of faith to the will, and asserted that Predestination was grounded on the foreknowledge of the merits of this first beginning, which according to them was to be ascribed to man alone. They even said that children who happened to die in their childhood years were predestined according to the life that God foresaw they would have led if they had lived longer.

<margin>
<note>original: "Prosp. Ep. ad Aug. et Resp. ad Capit. Gall."</note>
Prosper of Aquitaine, *Epistle to Augustine* and *Response to the Gallic Chapters*.
</margin>
They also distinguished two decrees: one general and conditional to make all men blessed, and one particular and absolute to preserve only those whose faith God had foreseen.

But Augustine, maintaining with the whole Church that every good quality in man is a gift from God, from the first principle of faith to perseverance itself—and a gift that springs solely <note>original: "enkellyt," likely a typo for "enkellyk" (purely/solely)</note> from a grace which not only includes all merits but is granted to sinners who are entirely unworthy of it—held fast that predestination is wholly and entirely of grace.

If one examines the works of this ancient Teacher, one will find therein most of the arguments that we have brought forward in the preceding Chapter. He makes use in several places of the Epistle to the Ephesians, Chapter 1, which we have also cited, and uses the same against the Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians in his book *On the Predestination of the Saints*. <margin>Volume VII, page 1256.</margin> Chapter 19: „ Perhaps, he says, those „ for whom we write will say that „ it is true that the doctrine of the „ Pelagians is struck to the ground „ by this passage of the Apostle, „ where he says that we are „ predestined in Christ, before the „ foundation of the world, out of „ regard for the love he has borne „ us, so that we should be holy „ and blameless before his eyes; „ since to say, as the heretics do, „ that once we have accepted the „ commandments of the Gospel, „ our free will is what makes us „ holy and blameless through love, „ and that it is through the „ knowledge he had from eternity „ that this must happen so, that he „ has predestined us in Christ „ before the creation of the world, „ is to [contradict] the Apostle in...

<meta>catchword: „ aan- (accepted)</meta>

The Church highly approved the teachings of *Augustine* and contested those of *Pelagius* and the *Semi-Pelagians* <note>Those who attempted a middle ground, suggesting that humans can take the first step toward God, but require grace for the rest.</note> in various *Church Assemblies* and in particular, in
those held at *Carthage* and *Milevis* against *Pelagius* and *Celestius*, in the years 416, 417, and 418.
The Popes *Celestine* and *Innocent* declared themselves against these heretics and

<column-break/>

upheld the doctrine of *Augustine*.
*Prosper* <note>Prosper of Aquitaine, a lay theologian and disciple of Augustine.</note> defended the same among the *Gauls*.
Pope *Leo* stood for them no less fervently, as can be seen in his letters, and he confirmed all that had been done against the *Pelagians* by the *Councils* of *Africa* and others. He even took *Prosper*
<margin>Letter 86</margin> as his secretary.
Pope *Gelasius* also took up the cause for *Augustine* and made known how much he esteemed the book *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, while he placed all the works of *Cassian* and *Faustus* <note>John Cassian and Faustus of Riez, whose writings were seen as leaning toward Semi-Pelagianism.</note> among the number of the irregular (*Apocrypha*), that is to say, those which were rejected.
In the 6th century, Pope *Hormisdas* was of the same opinion; and the doctrine of *Augustine* was defended by *Johannes Maxentius*, monk and priest in *Antioch*, by *Fulgentius*, by *Caesarius*, Bishop of *Arles*, by Bishop *Primasius*, by *Ferrandus*, deacon of *Carthage*, by the renowned bishops and confessors of the faith who were exiled to *Sardinia* for the Gospel, by the Second Council of *Orange* in the year 529, etc., by *Cassiodorus*, etc. In the 7th century by *Gregory the Great*, *Isidore of Seville*, etc.
In the 8th century by Pope *Adrian I*.
In the 9th century there were also several who stood for the doctrine of *Augustine*, and among others the world-famous *Gottschalk*, who suffered much through the persecutions of *Hincmar* <note>Hincmar of Reims, who had Gottschalk imprisoned and whipped for his strict views on "double predestination."</note>, yet was defended by many, and among others by *Remigius*, Archbishop of *Lyon*, who showed that the *Church Assembly* of *Quierzy* (where *Gottschalk* had been condemned to be scourged) had acted unjustly.
Ratramnus, monk of Corbie, taught the doctrine of <term>Predestination</term> <note>original: "Voorverordineering"</note> through grace in the two books he wrote on this subject and dedicated to Emperor *Charles the Bald*.
*Prudentius*, Bishop of *Troyes*, took up the defense of the same doctrine and declared in his letter to *Hincmar* and *Pardulus* that no one with more care than *Augustine* had applied himself to the most hidden secrets of the scriptures, discovered them with more attentiveness, built them up with more sincerity, held them fast with more faithfulness, defended them with more power, proclaimed them with more heartiness, and spread them abundantly like a holy seed, and resolved the difficulties that occur therein with more discretion and order. This *Prudentius* wrote against *Johannes Scotus Erigena*.

*Lupus Servatus*, Priest at *Mainz*, published a Book / in which he maintains the same Doctrine of gracious predestination.

*Florus*, Deacon of the Church of *Lyons*, defended the same truth in his Book against the XIX Articles of *John the Scot* <note>original: "Johannes den Schotman;" referring to Johannes Scotus Eriugena (c. 815–877), whose views on predestination were controversial and often condemned by his contemporaries.</note>, and *Remy*, Archbishop of the same City / also stood for this matter with much

Pope *Nicholas I* confirmed these decrees / as *Prudentius*, Bishop of *Troyes*, has noted in his *Annals*.

But above all, *Bernard* in the 12th Century gave striking evidence / that he was in favor of the opinion of this Bishop of *Hippo* <note>Saint Augustine.</note>. The Abbot *Gilbert*, a Student of *Bernard*, also maintained the same.

*Ailred*, Abbot of *Rievaulx* in *Great Britain*, defended Predestination out of pure grace / in his work that bears the title *Mirror of Charity* <note>original: "Spiegel der Liefde;" Latin: *Speculum Caritatis*.</note>, and he proves / that it is the particular Love / which God has had from all eternity for some people / and not for others / that makes the distinction / that exists between them. They are all equally condemned. But he gives the greatest number to his justice...

After the holding of the Council of Trent <note>The 16th-century ecumenical council that defined Catholic doctrine in response to the Protestant Reformation.</note>, which did not wish to decide this dispute / great contentions arose between the Franciscans and the Jacobins <note>In this context, 'Jacobins' refers to the Dominicans, who were often called so in France because of their primary house on the Rue Saint-Jacques.</note>. These latter held with Augustine, and had as their head Domingo de Soto; the others pleaded for the opposite opinion / and had as their head Andreas Vega. The Jesuits embraced the latter strictly / but not all of them. Bellarmine, Pererius, Lorinus, Ribera, Suarez, etc. defended the opinion of Augustine and of Thomas. Jansenius <note>Cornelius Jansen (1585–1638), whose writings on Augustine sparked the Jansenist controversy regarding predestination.</note> supported the same with all his might. Ambrosius Catharinus wanted to strike out on another path; He proposed two elections / one absolute, which depends entirely on God's good pleasure / like the election of Mary, of Peter, and Paul. Vázquez <note>Gabriel Vázquez (1549–1604), a prominent Spanish Jesuit theologian.</note>, who opposes this opinion / recognizes a predestination / by which God has assigned to certain men the gifts of grace / which surely lead them to salvation.

One can further read on this matter the work of Mr. Maugain / as well as the Book of Mr. Germain, Doctor of Theology / which was published under the Title of *Tradition of the Roman Church, on the Predestination of the Saints*.

THE CHRISTIAN

## V. CHAPTER.

### Of the firmness and certainty / of Election.
<note>In this context, "Election" refers to the theological belief that God has chosen specific individuals for eternal salvation before the beginning of time.</note>

Until now we have seen / how God / who did not want all people to perish / has chosen some / for whom he has intended eternal glory. One must not doubt / that he will put them in possession of it; for God's election is firm / certain / and unchangeable: and we know no election / that would not be firm. This must be proven.

<margin>Remonstrant Apology chapter XVI. 4. etc. Volkel. Socinus, Prelections chapter 11.</margin> <note>These references point to the theological opponents of the author: the Remonstrants (followers of Arminius) and Socinians, who argued that God's choice was based on human actions and could therefore change.</note>
I. There is no reason / that obliges us to judge the decree of Election differently / than the other decrees of God. Who does not know now / that scripture speaks of them / as so many irrevocable and unchangeable sentences / *My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure, says the Lord through Isaiah Chapter XLVI. 10.* Paul speaks in Hebrews VI. 17. Of the unchangeable firmness of God’s counsel. Since it is written, *that the gifts and the Calling of God are without repentance,* Romans XI. 29. do we then not have reason / to speak and teach the same language / regarding the election of God; if God changed the decree of his election / it would have to be / either because he did not foresee what was to happen / or because he cannot carry out what he had intended / or through inconstancy and lightheadedness. One can say none of these about God. One cannot say / that he did not foresee the outcomes: for he sees everything / and all things are naked and exposed before his eyes. One cannot say / that he does not have the power / to do what he has decided. What is impossible for him who created the world out of nothing? Finally / one cannot, without godlessness / accuse God of inconstancy or lightheadedness,

<margin>Numbers XXIII. 19. Isaiah XLVI. 10. Hebrews VI. 17. Romans XI. 29.</margin>
<margin>James I. 17. Numbers XXIII. 19.</margin>
There is with him no change or shadow of turning James I, 17. God is not a man, that he should lie, nor a son of man, that he should repent; would he say it, and not do it? or speak, and not make it certain? Numbers XXIII. 19.

II. To these general observations one must add several specific thoughts.

<column-break/>

Paul, describing the Divine Chain of Salvation / shows that all the links are so closely attached to each other / that one cannot separate them. *Whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many Brothers. And whom he predestined, these he also called, and whom he called, these he also justified, and whom he justified, these he also glorified.* Romans VIII. 29. 30. Here it appears / that God joins foreknowledge and preordination / which are the two acts of God's eternal election (the one concerns the end / and the other the means) not only with calling and justification / which occur in time / but with the glory / that must follow / to assure us that of all / who were preordained before the foundation of the world / there is no one / who will not certainly / after the completion of the ages / be glorified. If now election were not unchangeable / it could happen / that those whom God foreknew and preordained / would not be glorified. These two things stand firm / that all those / whom God will glorify / will have been justified / called / and preordained / and that all / whom God preordains / justifies / and calls / shall be glorified; whichever way one views preordination, calling, and glorification / they are linked with each other in the closest manner.

> One will say, that God will glorify those whom he foresaw / would believe to the end.

Answer. 1. Those who make this objection / do not notice that Paul places calling / through which God works faith in us / after preordination. One can therefore not say / that God has glorified those whom he foresaw / would believe. 2. God will glorify those / whom he has foreknown / and whom he shall have called / and in whom he shall have produced true faith: but one must not say / that he will glorify those whom he shall have foreseen / would believe until the end.

One says, that God will glorify those / whom he has preordained / If they are steadfast in loving him / and doing their duty.

<vocab>Election: God's sovereign choice of individuals for salvation. Predestination: The doctrine that God has ordained all that will happen, especially concerning salvation. Divine Chain: A theological term for the sequence of salvation steps in Romans 8. Justification: Being declared righteous by God. Remonstrants: Dutch Protestants who opposed the strict Calvinist view of predestination. Socinus: A 16th-century theologian who denied the Trinity and strict predestination.</vocab>

->DIVINITY. VIII. B. V. Chapter.<-

**Answer.** It is without basis to claim that Paul’s reasoning is conditional; for it clearly shows that God himself produces the condition—consisting of faith and perseverance—within the elect.

<margin>Phil. IV. 3.</margin>
**III.** A third proof for the certainty of God’s election lies in the recording of the names of the elect in heaven in the book of life. Paul, speaking of his fellow workers, says in Philippians 4:3, *that their names are written in the book of life.*

<margin>
Heb. XII. 23.
Rev. XIII. 8.
</margin>
In the Letter to the Hebrews, Chapter 12:23, he mentions the firstborn who are written in heaven. John, in the Revelation, Chapter 13:8, mentions those whose names are *not* written in the Lamb’s book of life. There are those who make a distinction between the "Book of the Lamb" and the "Book of Life." They say that in the first, the names of those who will remain steadfast in faith and be saved are recorded; and in the second, all believers are recorded, under the condition of perseverance. But it appears clearly enough from the passage itself that it is one and the same book.

It is said that one must distinguish between a double recording. One, made from eternity based on the foresight of perseverance, which is unerring; and another, which happens in time according to the present state of the believers; and they add that this latter one can be erased. But this <unclear>notion</unclear> <note>original: "gebooten"; likely a typo for "gevoelen" meaning "opinion" or "view"</note> offends God’s Majesty, as if His decree depended on the movements of our inconstant will.

<margin>Luke X. 20.</margin>
Christ wants His disciples to rejoice that their names are written in heaven. Luke 10:20. This is a manner of speaking that indicates the firmness and the certainty of the salvation of the elect children of God, in contrast to those who perish,

<margin>Jer. XVII. 13.</margin>
whose names are marked on the earth and in the sand, where they can easily be wiped out. If Pilate

<margin>John XIX. 22.</margin>
could say, John 19:22, *What I have written, I have written,* <note>original: "Dat ik geschreven hebbe, dat heb ik geschreeven," referring to the Latin "Quod scripsi, scripsi."</note> how could we believe that God—who has no part in our flaws or our mistakes—would want to scratch out the name of His elect, which He has written therein? Why would Christ have exhorted His disciples to rejoice that their names are written in heaven if this writing could be erased?

Part I.

<column-break/>

One must take good note that Christ says, *rejoice that your names **are** written,* and not that they *shall be* written, as some would wish to distort this passage. It is said that Judas was one of those to whom Christ said that their names are written in heaven. But that does not appear to be the case. Christ, expressing himself thus, was not speaking to the Apostles, but to the seventy disciples. Even if He had spoken to the Apostles, Judas was not included, but excluded: for how could one say of such a traitor that he stands recorded in the Book of Life?

To understand these manners of speaking, which occur often, one must note that the Scripture mentions many "Books of God."

<margin>Isa. XXXIV. 16.</margin>
1. It appears that it speaks of the world, or at least of Heaven, as a book.

<margin>
Rev. VI. 14.
Ps. XIX. 4.
Rom. II. 15.
</margin>
2. It speaks frequently of the Book of the Law, of the Book of the Covenant, of the Book of the Lord, etc.

3. The conscience can also be regarded as a book in which God has written His Law. Besides these books, three others are mentioned. 1. The **Book of Providence**, of which David speaks in Psalm 139:16: *Your eyes saw my unformed substance, and all these things were written in your book, in the days when they were being formed, when as yet there was none of them.* And to assure us that God has a special knowledge of our tears, he says in Psalm 56:9 that they are not only in His bottle, but in His Register. 2. Mention is made of the **Book of Judgment**, in which everything concerning the conduct of rational creatures—their good and evil works, their prosperity and adversity—is written. Isaiah 65:6: *Behold, it is written before my face; I will not keep silent, but I will repay, even repay into their bosom.* Malachi 3:16: *Then those who feared the Lord spoke to one another: the Lord paid attention and heard them, and a Book of Remembrance was written before His face for those who feared the Lord and esteemed His name,* to give us to understand that God will remember the godliness of His children and that He will reward them. Here one can also bring in what is written by the Prophet Daniel, Dan. 7:10: *the court sat in judgment, and the books were opened.*

# THE CHRISTIAN <note>The header "DE CHRISTELYKE" is incomplete, likely referring to "The Christian Religion" or "The Christian Divinity."</note>

as well as Revelation 20:12: *And the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works.* 3. Finally, mention is made of a **Book of Life**, by which Holy Scripture understands the decree of God's **election** <term>Election: The theological doctrine that God chooses certain individuals for salvation before the beginning of time.</term> / and which it compares to a book / in which the names of all the **Elect** are written.

It appears, then / that one must not take these expressions literally / as if God had a physical book / in which the names of those / whom he wishes to save / are written. Through this, the Scripture gives us to understand / that God has a perfect and infallible knowledge / and that his election stands firm.

One cannot deny / that we know written things / which stand expressed before our eyes / more distinctly / than those which are told to us by a living voice. Words disappear and fly into the air; what is written remains. God accommodates himself here to the weak understanding of men / among whom books are of great use.

Some are of the opinion / that / when the Books of God are spoken of / in which the names of the elect are written / it is an allusion to what happens in war / where those who take up service / are written down / as if God wanted to take his elect into his service / to fight for his honor.

Others are of the opinion / that it is an allusion to what happens in communities / where the names of those / who enter into them / are written down. The most probable of all is / that it is an allusion to the writing down of the names of **Citizens** / who already had or had obtained the **Right of Citizenship** <term>Burgerregt: The legal status and privileges belonging to a citizen of a city or state.</term> / in certain public books / which were set aside for that purpose in ancient times in all lands. Not to mention the Romans and other nations / where this registration was in use / let us cast our eye on the custom of the Jewish people / see Nehemiah 7:5, 12:23, and compare Ezekiel 13:9.

<margin>Ezekiel 13:9.</margin>
*My hand shall be against the prophets who see vanity and divine lies; they shall not be in the assembly of my people, nor shall they be written in the record of the house of Israel, nor shall they enter into the land of Israel.* God notes here three punishments / which he will impose upon the false prophets. 1. That they shall no longer attend the Council of the people / where the prophets could appear.

<column-break/>

2. That they shall not be written in the Book / where the names of the true members of Israel's **commonwealth** were written / to have a share in its privileges. 3. That they should be driven out of the land of Israel / where even strangers might enter.

The Holy Spirit / alluding to this custom / presents the elect as being written in a book / to signify that they are the true citizens of the **Heavenly Jerusalem** / and the true children of Abraham, to whom Heaven and Bliss belong. But it is not the same with these Heavenly Citizens / as with those of a city; they can never lose their citizenship in Heaven / because it is founded upon God's promises / and the infinite merits of Christ.

From what has been said, it then appears / that Election is firm and certain / and that those whom God has chosen / will undoubtedly be eternally blessed. Their names are written / not on the earth or on paper / where they could be erased / not in public registers or name-books / which can be consumed by fire / not on marble stone and on steel / which time can destroy / but in the Heavens / above all the power of all-destroying time. That is also why Christ / after he had said in Matthew 24:24 that false prophets and false Christs shall arise, who shall show signs and wonders, to seduce the elect, adds / *if it were possible.* These four words / (*if it were possible*) / indicate that the thing is impossible.

1. Christ shows us here, then, the efforts / that the false teachers would put into action / to seduce all kinds of people / who can be seduced. 2. The boundaries / that God had set against this. Paul confirms the same truth in those glorious words / which one finds in

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of God's sovereignty, transitioning from the "Perseverance of the Saints" on the previous page to the more difficult doctrine of "Reprobation"—the decision of God to pass over some while choosing others for salvation. It defines the nature and timing of this decree.</meta>

# THEOLOGY. VIII. B. CHAPTER VI. 479

It appears that this word first began to be used in the time of <note>Godeschalcus, or Gottschalk of Orbais (c. 800–868), was a Carolingian monk whose teachings on "double predestination"—that God predestines some to hell just as he does others to heaven—caused great controversy in the medieval church.</note> Godeschalcus. It is taken from *Psalm 15:4*, "who looks with contempt upon the <term>reprobate</term><note>The original Dutch uses 'verworpenen,' meaning those who are rejected or cast away. In a theological context, this refers to those not chosen by God for salvation.</note>," etc. thus it stands in the Hebrew; and from *Isaiah 41:9*, "You are my servant, I have chosen you, and have not rejected you." Paul uses a word that has also been translated as "reprobate." *1 Cor. 9:27, 2 Cor. 13:5, 6, 7, 2 Tim. 3:8, Titus 1:16, Heb. 6:8.*

One cannot deny that God has rejected some of His creatures, since He has not chosen them all. Paul speaks in *Romans 9:22* of "vessels of wrath, prepared for destruction." Jude verse 4 speaks of certain men who have crept in, who were "marked out long ago for this condemnation."

One can also not deny that this rejection occurred from all eternity. For there is no reason to judge Rejection any differently than Election. Now we have proven through the Scriptures that Election is eternal. Moreover, the concept that we have of God as the most perfect Being does not allow us to believe that anything happens in time that was not decided from all eternity; nor should we ascribe to Him purposes that were only designed in time and depend upon secondary causes.

Reprobation is then that eternal decree of God, by which, at the same time He decided to give salvation to some (though they deserved nothing but death), He determined to leave others in their corruption; and foreseeing that they would commit countless sins, He decided to punish them eternally for them.

Thus we distinguish two acts in this decree.

1. The first is that by which God—all men being in the same state of corruption—decided to leave many in it without taking pity on them, just as He did for the elect. This must not be understood as if God determined to show them no grace at all; for He preserves them, He fills them with temporal goods; there are infinite numbers to whom He causes His Gospel to be proclaimed, and He enlightens some by the light of His Spirit; for which reason Paul says of the <term>temporary believers</term><note>Those who appear to have faith for a time but do not persevere; a common concept in Reformed theology to explain why some "fall away."</note> in *Hebrews 6:4* that they "have been enlightened." But He has decided not to give them all the same grace that He imparts to the elect, and through which

<column-break/>

He grafts them into the communion of His Son, makes them members of His mystical body, and establishes them as His heirs and co-heirs with Christ.

The second act is that by which God decided to pour out His judgments upon those whom He has left in their corruption, and to punish them eternally; and this because He foresees that they will misuse the light of nature or of the Gospel, and that they will fall into the most abominable sins, which are worthy of all His wrath.

Consequently, God can be viewed in the decree of reprobation as a **Sovereign Lord**, who does all that He wills, like a **Potter** who makes from one lump of clay vessels for honor and for dishonor; and as a **Supreme Judge**, who causes the guilty to suffer the punishment they deserve. When He leaves Peter in his natural corruption and chooses Jacob, He acts as Sovereign Lord; but when He condemns Peter to eternal punishment for his sins, He acts as Supreme Judge. To place this matter in a greater light, one must answer several questions.

1. It is commonly asked, what is the cause of reprobation?

I answer: sin. For if there had been no sin, God would have rejected no one. Augustine says that God would not have been a "venging God" <note>Original: "wreekende God."</note> if man had not sinned.

2. It is asked, why God preferred to leave Anthony rather than John; and why He preferred to choose John rather than Anthony?

To this question one must not answer that sin is the cause; for Anthony and John were both included in the same lump of corruption, and consequently deserved to be treated in the same way; and if God had done so, no one would have had reason to complain. One must then say that it is God’s **good pleasure** alone which moved Him to leave the one and accept the other. Paul puts these words into our mouths: "He has mercy on whom He will have mercy, and He hardens whom He will harden." This He explains through the parable of the potter, which we have cited so often. However one explains these words in *Romans 9:13*, "Jacob I have loved and Esau I have hated," it is certain that one

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Reprobation—the theological concept of God's decision to withhold salvation from certain individuals—addressing common objections to this difficult doctrine. It focuses specifically on the biblical example of Jacob and Esau from Romans 9 to argue that God’s choice is based on His sovereign will rather than human merit or temporal success.</meta>

<center>### THE CHRISTIAN ###</center>

...one can say of all people what Paul says of these two brothers, namely, that before they had done good or evil, God loved the one and hated the other.

People say that here it only speaks of the descendants of Jacob and Esau, and of temporal blessings.

Answer: 1. It is clear that Paul reasons about the persons of Jacob and Esau themselves; for he says explicitly, *before the children had done good or evil*. It is said, etc. 2. To be loved and hated by God means more than being filled with temporal blessings or being deprived of them. 3. It appears that the ungodly Esau possessed more goods than Jacob.

3. One asks, Why does God condemn to eternal punishment those who have lived wickedly?

I answer that their sins are the cause of their damnation. When one pays close attention to these three questions, many difficulties can be solved and many objections answered.

It appears then that it is not the same with <term>reprobering</term><note>Also known as Reprobation; the theological doctrine that God, in His sovereignty, decides to pass over some people, leaving them to the consequences of their sin rather than choosing them for salvation.</note> as it is with <term>election</term><note>God's sovereign choice of individuals for salvation through His grace, independent of their own merit.</note>: election places nothing in the person that deserves being chosen, because it is an act of mercy. But reprobation, which is an act of <term>justice</term><note>In this context, 'justice' refers to God's righteous judgment against sin, which the author argues is the basis for rejection.</note>, necessarily presupposes sin.

Some objections are made here:

1. It is said that this doctrine conflicts with God's justice, since it presupposes that God acts in such an unequal way with people who are all sinners.

I answer that one would be right if we taught that God punishes people and condemns them to death without considering their crimes. But we maintain that God rejects only sinners, who consequently deserve to be punished. Although God treats people—who were equally sinners—in an unequal way, He nevertheless does nothing against His justice. 1. Because He is free to show mercy to whom He will, without anyone being able to take offense; 2. Because if He has destined some to salvation, He has found a way to satisfy His justice in their place through the sending of His Son into the world.

Sinners have no reason to complain, for God was not bound

<column-break/>

to have mercy on them, and the good have no cause to boast, because they have deserved nothing from God. The former must worship His justice. The others must praise His mercy; and we all have reason to cry out, <note>original: "O Diepte der wysheid enz."</note> *O the depth of the wisdom* etc. <note>This is a reference to Romans 11:33, a common refrain in Reformed theology when addressing the mysteries of God's decrees.</note>

2. It is said that if God had rejected some people, He would not have the <term>Gospel</term><note>The 'good news' of salvation through Jesus Christ.</note> proclaimed to them as He does, because to present the promises of salvation to them would be as much as mocking them.

I answer that although God has rejected many, He nevertheless has wise reasons for having the Gospel preached to them, as we shall see in our treatise on <term>The Calling</term><note>Refers to the theological concept of the 'external call' (the preaching of the word to everyone) versus the 'internal call' (the work of the Holy Spirit in the hearts of the elect).</note>.

Even if we did not know any of these reasons, that should cause us no more trouble than so many other decrees and actions of God for which we cannot give a reason, and which exceed the reach of our understanding. It is enough that we believe what the Scripture teaches us:

1. That God does not have mercy on everyone.

2. That consequently God has decided from all eternity not to have mercy on everyone, since nothing happens in time that was not established before the foundation of the world. 3. That meanwhile God has His Gospel proclaimed to many to whom He does not show His mercy.

3. It is said that the doctrine of reprobation opposes God's kindness.

Answer: One would then also have to say that the entire world will be saved because, if it is not saved, God would not have infinite kindness. God is kind, and His kindness is unspeakable, that is true; but He is absolutely free in His actions.

4. It is said that the doctrine of reprobation makes God the cause of sin.

I answer that this is untrue; 1. Because God rejects only those who are already sinners. 2. God drives no one to sin through the decree of reprobation. It is true that God decided not to give converting grace to all people, but He is not obligated to do so.

5. But, it is said, how can God punish people for committing sins which they could not avoid, being abandoned by God?

I answer that God always has just reasons to punish sinners who have willfully committed infinite sins...

**The question is asked**, whether it would not have better suited the wisdom and goodness of God not to give life to those He foresaw would misuse His grace.

**Answer.** It does not befit us to rebuke God's actions; we must adore them and not criticize. If they do not align with our ideas, we must reform our ideas, but not reject God's decree. God, through a wisdom that surpasses our understanding, has judged that it was more fitting to draw good out of evil than to permit no evil at all.

**Secondly, God frequently makes use of the wicked** to nurture the arts and sciences, and to provide His elect with many of the goods they possess. Through their means, God teaches His children what they themselves are and would do, if God had abandoned them as He abandons others. He gives them cause to have more gratitude for the benefits they have received from Him, while He lets the others walk in their own ways; in short, He uses the wicked to test the faith and patience of the pious, and to make their zeal shine forth, and at the same time to make His virtues known. Furthermore, it will not be unhelpful to cite the diversity of opinions among various denominations on this subject.

**In the Reformed Church.**

1. There are those who trace the permission of sin back to the decree of reprobation <note>This refers to the "Supralapsarian" view, which argues God decided who would be saved or lost before even considering the Fall of mankind.</note>, and these describe predestination thus: **It is the eternal and unchangeable decree of God to create men, to permit their fall into sin and eternal death, to send His Son into the world, to save some through His word and spirit for His Son's sake, to justify, raise, and glorify them, and to leave the others in sin and death, and to condemn them to eternal pains.** This is the description made by **Ursinus** in his *Explanation of the Catechism, part 2, chapter on Predestination, 92* <note>original: "Expl. Catech. part. 2. cap. de Præd. 92."</note>; **Zanchius** in *Volume 7, Treatise on Predestination, number 9* <note>original: "T. 7. Tract. de Præd. n. 9."</note>; **Bucanus**

2. **The most common opinion is** that which we have explained, being the view of the Synod of Dordrecht <note>Commonly known as the Synod of Dort (1618–1619), which solidified the Five Points of Calvinism.</note>. Others are of the opinion that it consists in the first act, such as the Synod of Dordrecht, **Rivetus**, and English theologians. Those of the Academy of Saumur <note>A French Protestant university known for "Amyraldism," a more moderate form of Calvinism.</note> limit Reprobation only to the denial of saving grace: **Theses of Saumur on Election and Reprobation, Thesis 36** <note>original: "Th. 3. **The first theologians** who are for "election before the fall" place among the effects of Reprobation the creation of the reprobates and the deprivation of grace, by which they also understand the permission of sin: **Polanus, *Syntagma Theologiae*, book 4, chapter 10, Thesis 3** <note>original: "Polan. The permission of those sins that follow original sin in the reprobates. 2. The denial of the grace that God grants to the elect, and finally eternal death. The renowned

Regarding the theologians of Saumur, who distinguish reprobation from damnation, they place only the denial of efficacious grace—which produces faith and conversion in believers—among the effects of Reprobation.

4. **With respect to the theologians who are for "election before the fall,"** some believe that the object of Reprobation is "creatable man" <note>Man considered before the act of creation.</note>, such as **Polanus, Beza, Zanchius, Gomarus, Ursinus, Bucanus, Twissus**, etc. Others argue that it is the "created, but not yet fallen man," such as **Junius.**

Polanus, *Syntagma of Theology*, book IV, chapter 10, theses 2, 3. Zanchius, book V, *On the Nature of God*, chapter 2. Beza, etc.

8. A number of others, who also follow the Synod of Dordrecht, believe that the "negative act" of Reprobation <note>The "negative act" refers to God's decision to "pass over" or not elect someone, as opposed to the "positive act" of sentencing them to punishment.</note> has no cause other than God’s good pleasure. However, they believe the "positive act" has sin as its cause. Others make the distinctions that we have presented in this chapter.

### In the Roman Church.

1. Some limit Reprobation to that eternal decree by which some are excluded from the Kingdom of Heaven and subjected to eternal punishments. Lombard, book 1, *Sentences*, distinction 40; Durandus, distinction 40, question 2; Molina.

2. Others believe that Reprobation encompasses not only the deprivation of Heavenly Glory but also the permission of sin and the lack of grace. Thomas [Aquinas], Part 1 of the *Summa [Theologica]*, question 23, Article 3. Gregory of Valencia.

3. Some attribute Reprobation only to the surrendering of man to sin and the hardening of the heart—through which God, to punish preceding sins, allows some to fall into much heavier sins. Others include the permission of all kinds of sins. Some believe that Reprobation consists of two positive acts: one concerning the permission of sin and the withholding of grace (which is necessary to avoid sinning), and the other concerning eternal punishments. Gregory of Valencia, *On Reprobation*, part 1. Bañez on the first part of Thomas [Aquinas], question 23, article 2, doubt 2, conclusion 3. Estius on the first book of the *Sentences*, distinction 40, paragraph 16. There are even those who believe that at the same time God ordained some to eternal life, He made a definite decree to exclude others from His Kingdom before He had foreseen any of their sins. Alvarez, book 12, *On the Aids of Divine Grace*, disputation 109, section 51, conclusions 1 & 3. Others distinguish two decrees: one positive and one exclusive, similar to the Reformed teachers. Puteanus, *General Questions on Reprobation*, doubt

<column-break/>

2, conclusion 1. St. Joseph in *The Idea of Speculative Theology*, book 1, chapter 20. Eustachius of St. Paul, *Summary*, treatise 1, disputation 17, question 2.

4. Some believe that man, *before* his fall, is the object of Reprobation. Estius in distinction 40, book 1 of the *Sentences*. Others are of the opinion that it is *fallen* man. As seen in Peter of St. Joseph, *Speculative Theology*, chapter 20, resolution 5. Eustachius of St. Paul, treatise 1, *Summary of Theology*, disputation 17. Others believe it is man considered as dying in sin.

5. Some, who limit Reprobation only to the will to damn certain individuals, believe that the cause of the Reprobation of some is the foreknowledge <note>original: "voorbeschouwing"</note> of their persistence in sin. Others, who include the permission of sin in Reprobation, are of the opinion that there is no cause for it other than the will of God; and those who, with Alvarez, Estius, and Rispolis, believe that the object of Reprobation is man as a "creatable" being <note>original: "schepbaare mensch" — referring to man as a potential creature before the decree of creation</note>, are of the same mind. One can also consult Cajetan on this; Sixtus of Siena, *Holy Library*, book 6, annotation 252, book 2, letter R. Domingo Bañez on the first part of Thomas [Aquinas], question 23. Puteanus, Petrus Soto, Thelmannus, Guillandus; it was also the opinion of the old Scholastics, Gregory of Rimini, Lyranus on Romans 9; Marsilius of Inghen, in book 1 of the *Sentences*, distinction 42, question 4. Others believe that Reprobation—viewed strictly in terms of the "negative act," which consists of the refusal of grace—has the sin of the first man [Adam] as its cause. As seen in Vasquez, volume 1, disputation 95, chapter 3, and Becanus.

Others are of the opinion that original sin <note>original: "erfzonde"</note> must be considered the cause, such as Peter of St. Joseph, *The Idea of Speculative Theology*, book 1, chapter 20, resolution 5.

Others limit Original Sin here to children who die without Baptism, as the sole cause of their Reprobation.

Others believe that it is actual sin <note>Sin committed through one's own actions, rather than inherited sin.</note> in those to whom original sin was forgiven through Baptism.

Others view both inherited and actual sin as the cause, as in the reprobate to whom original sin was never forgiven. Domingo de Soto on Romans 9 and Petrus de Soto.

Others, like Bellarmine, *On Grace and Free Will*, book 2, final chapter, believe that the negative act indeed follows the foreknowledge of Original Sin, but that this sin is not the "meriting cause" of it.
