DIVINITY. VIII. B. VII. Chapter.

## CHAPTER VII.

->On the proper use that one should make of<-
->the Doctrine of Election and<-
->Reprobation; and on the<-
->misuse that some<-
->commit regarding this.<-

There are those who, to their own misfortune, misuse the doctrine that we have established, and who take occasion from it to fall into despair <note>The Dutch "wanhoopen" refers here to the spiritual crisis of believing one is eternally rejected by God.</note>, through a false imagination that they are among the number of the reprobate <note>The "reprobate" are those not chosen by God for salvation.</note>, and that they, whatever they might do, cannot be saved.

It is easy to show that they are making a poor use of a holy Doctrine.

1. They are wrong to think that they are reprobate, because it is a matter upon which no one can pass a decisive judgment. God’s decrees are hidden from us, and it is not for us to fathom them. It is indeed certain that there are reprobates and elect, but we do not know with any certainty who the elect are and who the reprobate are. Those who are elect can know that they are so <note>Through the "internal testimony" of faith and the Holy Spirit.</note>, but the reprobate cannot know it, because they do not know whether God will yet convert them. A Sinner can certainly see that he bears the marks of a reprobate, or to put it better, that he lives like a reprobate; but he cannot pronounce with any certainty that he is reprobate, because he does not know what God intends for him. He must not, therefore, draw a certain conclusion from an uncertain principle, saying: "whatever I may do, I shall be damned, so I may as well do whatever I desire."

2. One can demonstrate the extravagance of those who reason thus through two common examples. Suppose that there are many sick people in a hospital <note>original: "gasthuis," an infirmary or guest house for the poor and ill.</note>, to whom an Angel from God has come to say that some of them will recover, but that the others shall die. Would one not regard as insane the man who, after this revelation, would begin to imagine—without reason and without grounds—that he must die, and who in this conviction would refuse to take either food or medicine, or who would kill himself out of despair?

<column-break/>

Consider here another example. Suppose that an Angel at the head of an Army announced that the greater part of the Soldiers of which it consists shall fall in battle, and that only a few will escape; would one not consider him mad who, assuming from this that he will be killed no matter what he does, would—like a Raving man—expose himself to thousands of dangers? One must judge the same of someone who, knowing that there are Elect and Reprobate, would imagine that he is a reprobate, and in that thought live like a reprobate. Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), whose writings on grace and predestination heavily influenced both Catholic and Protestant theology.</note> says very well that one must never despair of the salvation of anyone whom God’s forbearance allows to live, and much less of one’s own. For, although one must not hold oneself certain of election before having found faith and other Christian virtues in one's heart, there are nevertheless many things that should convince someone—to whom God allows His Gospel to be proclaimed and at whose heart He knocks daily—that God has not entirely abandoned him. I confess that this is not enough to prove that one is an elect person, but it is enough to be convinced for oneself that one is also not a reprobate. The converted Thief on the cross <note>referring to the "Penitent Thief" (Dismas) crucified alongside Jesus.</note>, who previously lost himself in all kinds of sins, would have had great misfortune to believe that he was reprobate, since he ended his life so well.

3. Those who say, "If I am reprobate, I shall—whether I believe and dispose myself to virtue or not—be damned," are reasoning entirely illogically <note>original: "gansch buiten den haak," literally "entirely off the hook."</note>. For where has God revealed to us that those who believe and pursue their sanctification shall be lost? <margin>John 3:16.</margin> Does the Scripture not say the opposite? *Whoever believes shall be saved,* John 3:16. <note>original: "die gelooft zal hebben / zal zalig worden."</note>

That the Doctrine of predestination <term>voor-verordineeringe</term> <note>The eternal decree of God by which He has settled the fate of all people.</note> brings man to despair is far from the truth; it is a full fountain of consolations. Everyone knows that the believer is exposed to all kinds of seductions and temptations: but what comforts them therein is that God’s Elect shall not perish. We have already brought up a passage that is very fitting here. Matt. 24:24. *For there shall arise false Christs, and false Prophets, and shall shew great signs and wonders; insomuch that, if it [were possible...]*

THE CHRISTIAN

(if it were possible) would also deceive the Elect <note>The "Elect" refers to those chosen by God for salvation from before the beginning of time.</note>. From this, the Elect conclude that they will not be dragged into destruction by any deception.

<margin>Matt. 24:21, 22.</margin>
The believers are also exposed to various persecutions; but what comforts them is the doctrine of election. For then, says Christ, there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor ever shall be, etc. but for the sake of the elect, those days will be shortened. Matt. 24:21, 22. <margin>Dan. 12:1.</margin> There will be a time of distress, says Daniel, etc. but at that time your people will be delivered, everyone who is found written in the Book <note>The "Book of Life," a biblical metaphor for the record of those destined for heaven.</note>. Dan. 12:1.

Nothing disturbs believers so much as the apostasy <note>Falling away from the faith.</note> of those who should have stood for the truth. Against this offense, scripture arms us when it teaches us that the foundation of God stands firm, 2 Tim. 2:19.

<margin>Luke 12:32.</margin>
Is there a doctrine more suitable to comfort us than this, which assures us that God loved us before the foundation of the world, and that He will consequently love us to the end; that He who loved us when we deserved His hatred, will love us even more now that we have become His children and are recreated in His image; that He who loved us when we were His enemies, will now, having been reconciled with Him, love us even more. In whatever distress the believer may be, the doctrine of election serves as a wonderful comfort. Fear not, little flock, said Christ, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the Kingdom. Luke 12:32.

There are some who misuse the doctrine of Election in another way; whatever I may do, these say, it does not matter; if I am chosen, I must be saved; I can freely follow the impulses of my passions and the current of the world, and, like others, live in all kinds of pleasures. The virtues that I could practice, or the sins with which I could defile myself, cannot change God’s eternal decree.

Regarding these, I note:

1. That no one but unholy and abandoned villains can reason thus: I am preordained, therefore I am free to live like a castaway <note>Dutch: "verworpeling," referring to one rejected by God.</note>: to say that one is preordained means that God, through

<column-break/>

<margin>Col. 3:12.</margin>
an effect of His grace, which cannot be praised enough, has assigned salvation and glory to us, even though we were worthy of death. How is it now possible that someone who believes God has shown him this grace can say: God loved me so much, and I want to hate Him; He opens heaven to me, and I want to live as if hell were prepared for me; He makes His grace abound where my sins were abounding; I want to make my sins abound where His grace is abundant. One must be a monster of ingratitude to use such language. Paul warns us against it and desires that we, on the contrary, as God’s chosen ones, clothe ourselves in Christian virtues.

<margin>Eph. 2:10.</margin>
2. I note that it is not true that an elect person will be saved regardless of what he may do. For who does not know that the same God who preordained people for salvation also appointed them to the means that lead to salvation, and that these means are faith and holiness, etc. That kind of people reason as ridiculously as someone would to whom God, as to Hezekiah, would say: you shall live another fifteen years, and on that ground would boast and say: I do what I do, whether I eat or not, whether I take care of my life or put it at risk, I shall not die. Certainly, Paul was a chosen vessel, preordained from all eternity; I ask whether he would have been saved if he had continued to persecute Christ and His church, and to constantly blaspheme against God? Although it is true that all the elect will be saved, it is not true that they will be saved while doing and acting as they please and what they please. God, who has chosen them and written their names in the book of life, has also created them in Christ to do good works, which God prepared beforehand so that we should walk in them. Eph. 2:10. And He declares that no one shall see God without sanctification <note>The process of becoming holy through the Holy Spirit.</note>.

3. Finally, I note that although all the elect will be saved, they will only be saved for Christ’s sake, whom they will have embraced through faith and followed through good works.

...leads to an unrestrained life; instead, it provides us with many motives for the practice of godliness.

1. It ignites our hearts with a holy love toward God: for how could one not love Him who loved us so much and first?

2. It awakens us to the pursuit of sanctification; for God has chosen us, so that we should be holy and blameless before His face.

3. It produces humility in us, by making us understand that we have nothing that we have not received, and that God has distinguished us from others.

4. It fills us with full assurance of salvation, and makes us cry out, Romans 8:31: *If God be for us, who can be against us?* and verse 33: *Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifieth*, etc.

5. Finally, it instills in us the fear of appearing before Him to whom we owe everything, and spurs us on to work out our salvation with fear and trembling.

<margin>Volume 1, Dogmatic Theology, Book 3, On God, Chapter 15, Article 6.</margin>
Furthermore, the Jesuit <note>Dionysius Petavius (1583–1652), a prominent French Jesuit theologian known for his work on the history of dogma.</note> Petavius rightly notes that all the objections that can be made against the doctrine of gracious predestination apply to all the ways in which this mystery is explained. The doctrine of God’s foreknowledge gives as much cause for all these objections as the doctrine of gracious predestination. For, as Mr. Nicole says in his *Theological Instructions on the Faith*: it is certain 
<margin>page 175.</margin>
that God has not only foreseen the end of every human being, but also all their deeds and all their actions which they will do to reach that end; so that, whether God be the primary cause of good works, or the will of man, the same man will go the same way for a long time and come to his end through the same chain of deeds known to God. Thus also, he adds, whether grace be efficacious of itself and draws the consent of the will infallibly after it; or whether it be not so, except only for those whom God has chosen out of a special love and favored with the gifts of grace to which He foresees they will consent—as most theologians who are called <term>Congruists</term> <note>A group of Jesuit theologians who argued that God offers grace in "congruity" (harmony) with a person's circumstances, knowing they will freely choose to accept it.</note> teach—or whether these gifts of grace to which the will

<column-break/>

consents are not given out of a special love from God, but through certain general laws of Providence, as others teach; it is clear that, according to all these opinions, the effect of grace always proceeds with equal certainty, and that man acts in the same way. "What concerns man," he says, "regarding this doctrine is only the certainty of the outcome; they are only fearful of damnation."

## VIII. CHAPTER.

->On the Election and the Reprobation of Angels.<-

There is nothing left for me to finish this subject but the treatise on the Election and Reprobation <note>"Reprobation" refers to God's decision to leave some to their own sin and its consequences, the opposite of election.</note> of the Angels. Even if Scripture did not speak of it, reason would teach us that there are elect and reprobate angels: for, since (as we have often said) nothing happens, and nothing must happen in time, that is not firmly decided in God’s counsel, it is clear that the glory which the good angels enjoy, and the punishment which the evil ones must suffer and which they already begin to bear, was assigned to them from all eternity.

Scripture does not speak with express words of the Election of Angels, unless one wished to apply this passage from Paul, 1 Timothy 5:21: *I charge thee before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, and the elect angels.* For nothing prevents us from saying that they are called "elect," not only to distinguish them from the evil angels who are rejected and have left their habitation, and to indicate the excellence of their nature, but also to signify that God has chosen them from all eternity to be vessels of honor forever.

<margin>Matthew 25:41. 2 Peter 2:4. Jude verse 6.</margin>
One can clearly derive the Reprobation of the evil angels from what Christ says in Matthew 25:41, of the *everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels.* 2 Peter 2:4 speaks of the *judgment* for which they are preserved, and Jude verse 6 speaks of the *eternal chains* under which they are kept in darkness until the judgment...

When we spoke of the election of men, we said that God, in appointing them to salvation, had decided to provide them salvation through Christ, and that we are chosen in Him; but we cannot say the same of the Angels.

I well know that some have been of the opinion that Christ is the Mediator of the Angels, and that through His death He earned for them their confirmation in the happy state in which they exist. But there is no reason that obliges us to enter into that opinion.

### CHAPTER I.

->The order that will be followed in this Book.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'I' containing floral scrollwork.</image-desc>
In the preceding Book we have seen / that God did not wish / that the entire human race should perish / but that He chose some for Himself before the foundation of the world, that they should be holy and blameless before His face in love, having predestined them, to adopt them as children in Christ, according to the good pleasure of His will, to the praise of the Glory of His grace. Ephesians 1:4, 5, 6.

We have observed / how God / from all eternity / has assigned them Salvation and eternal Glory. Now we must investigate what God has done in time / to regain this salvation for them / consisting in the sending of His Son. We then intend to treat this Son / to consider Him as the Mediator <note>A 'Mediator' is a go-between who reconciles two parties—in this case, God and humanity.</note> of mankind / and to unfold all that He / to obtain for us Salvation and immortality / has suffered.

To lay out this subject with all clarity / we intend to follow this order. **1.** That it was necessary / that God's justice be satisfied <note>original: "voldaan" - in theology, 'satisfaction' refers to the idea that a debt or penalty must be paid to meet the requirements of divine justice.</note> to save mankind. **2.** That it was not absolutely necessary / that the sinners satisfied His justice for themselves.

<column-break/>

**3.** That a Divine Person alone could satisfy for us. **4.** We shall see / how this could happen / since all the Persons of the holy Trinity were equally offended <note>original: "beledigt" - in this context, it refers to the violation of God's holy law and honor by sin.</note>. **5.** Why God did not send His Son immediately after the Fall of Man. **6.** By what prophecies <note>original: "Godspraaken" - literally 'God-speeches' or oracles.</note> this Son was promised, etc. **7.** We shall show / that the Messiah has come / and that Jesus / the Son of Mary / is the true Messiah. **8.** We shall treat the Law / which God gave to His people / and why God willed / that His Law be proclaimed before the coming of His Son. **9.** We shall show what state the ancient Church was in / before Christ came into the world. **10.** Why He assumed human nature; whether there are two Persons in Christ / and how His two natures are united. **11.** What the two states of Christ were <note>This refers to the 'State of Humiliation' (His life and death) and the 'State of Exaltation' (His resurrection and glory).</note>. **12.** We shall treat His conception and birth. **13.** Of the principal things / that one must note in His life. **14.** Of His suffering and death / and of the fruits of His death. **15.** Of His burial and descent into Hell. **16.** Of His Resurrection. **17.** Of His Ascension. **18.** Of His Sitting at the right hand of God. **19.** Of His Mediatorial office. **20.** Of His three Offices <note>These are traditionally the offices of Prophet, Priest, and King.</note>. **21.** Of His Prophetic. **22.** And High-Priestly Office. **23.** Of the Truth of His satisfaction. **24.** And of its perfection. **25.** Of His Intercession. **26.** Of the excellence of His Priesthood above the Levitical one / and of its fruits. **27.** Of His Kingly Office. **28.** How Christ [makes us] part- <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "ge-", likely leading to "gedeeltig" or "deelachtig," meaning "to make us partakers" of His benefits.</note>

## CHAPTER II.

->Whether it was necessary to satisfy God for the sins of mankind.<-

<margin>What the Word 'Satisfy' signifies.</margin>
**I**n order to rightly understand the reason / for which it was necessary / that Christ came into the world to acquire for us the salvation / which God has destined for us / one must prove three things. **1.** That it was absolutely necessary to satisfy Divine justice / and that / without satisfaction / God could not make men blessed. **2.** That it was not necessary / that men satisfied for themselves / and that they were unable to do so. **3.** That a Divine Person must bring about this satisfaction.

The question / which we must then investigate / is / whether it was absolutely necessary / to satisfy Divine justice. But first one must take note / that the word satisfy (a) is taken in this place for paying that which Divine justice demanded from Sinners for their sins. The Scripture does not use this specific expression / but it makes use of many others / which signify the same truth / like the words *Redemption, Reconciliation, price or ransom of Redemption*, and such like.

This being laid down as a foundation / it is easy to establish the necessity of a satisfaction. Many reasons prove the same.

<column-break/>

<margin>Proofs of the necessity of the Satisfaction against the Socinians.</margin>
**I.** Even if there were no other proof / than that taken from the death of Christ / after His Divinity has been proven / it is more than convincing. For is there any shadow of appearance / that God would have exposed His Son to so many indignities and pains / that He would have sent Him into the world / to take on human nature with all its sinless weaknesses / to appear in the likeness of sinful flesh / to nail Him to the cursed wooden cross / and to die as an evildoer / if it were indeed of no absolute necessity to satisfy His justice? Is there the least probability / that He would have thus dealt with His Son / His beloved Son / His perfect Image / in whom He had His good pleasure / if He could have forgiven men their sins without satisfaction / and that it was only necessary / to proclaim salvation to men / to give examples of Holiness and patience / and to seal the truth of God with His blood? Can that enter into a human heart?

<note>The 'Socinians' were a group of thinkers who argued that Christ's death was merely an example of obedience and a seal of his teaching, rather than a necessary legal payment for sin.</note>

---

<note>Footnote (a) spans the bottom of both columns</note>

(a) The Latins <note>original: "De Latynen" - referring to Latin-speaking authors and legalists.</note> have used this in several senses. **1.** When someone granted another's desire, they said that he satisfied him; and one still says today in the French Language, that someone gives another much satisfaction, to say, that he pleases him. **2.** When someone by his works or words testified, that he repented having offended another, and that he asked for mercy, they said, that he had satisfied. The formula, which they used in this case, reads thus, *I wished not to have done it, I am prepared to swear, that you did not deserve this wrong.* <note>original Latin: "non velle factum, iuraturum se non merito fecisse."</note> The French also take this word in the same sense. **3.** When someone paid his debts, or fulfilled his word, the Latins said that he satisfied. Thus one also speaks in French. **4.** The ancient Fathers <note>Early Christian theologians of the first few centuries.</note> called the acknowledging of sins before God, and the calling upon His grace, to satisfy God. They gave the name of satisfaction to all the works of penitence, such as the confession of sins, and change of life and conduct. In that sense Cyprian <note>A 3rd-century Bishop of Carthage.</note> exhorted the Heathens, *We exhort you, while you have the time, to satisfy God, and to go out from the deep abyss of dark superstition, to follow in the beautiful light of the true Religion.* <note>original Latin from Cyprian's 'Ad Demetrianum': "Hortamur vos... dum locus datur, Deo satisfacere..."</note> **5.** One called 'satisfactions' the public testimonies, which the Sinners gave of their repentance in the Church, for the edification of the believers, and that was called Regular satisfactions. Here the word *satisfaction* is taken for the price, which has been paid to Divine justice for sins.

# THEOLOGY. BOOK IX. CHAPTER II.

II. But besides this reason, there are many others. Certainly, if it is true that God is by nature infinitely Holy and Righteous; that He completely hates and curses sin as something that strives against His justice, it is clear that He cannot fail to punish it, and that He cannot forgive it without having received some satisfaction. Now, we have proven in our *Treatise on God’s Perfections* that He is righteous by nature, that He hates all who commit iniquity, and that His eyes are too pure to behold evil. It follows then that He must necessarily punish sin, and that He cannot forgive it without satisfaction. I do not wish to repeat here what I have said elsewhere. I request my readers to please read the chapter on God’s Justice; they will find there the answers to the strongest objections that can be brought against this point.

I shall add only one here. It is said that, since God can punish those whom He does not hate and whom He loves—as in the case of innocent men—He could also grant forgiveness to those whom He hates. I answer that it is not true that God can punish those whom He does not hate: for that would conflict with His virtues. If He punished *Christ*, it was for the reason that He took the place of the sinners whom He hated <note>In Reformed theology, this refers to 'Penal Substitution,' where Christ legally takes on the guilt and the resulting wrath of God on behalf of the elect.</note>.

One objects with *Job 4:18* and *15:15*, from which one wishes to conclude that God can reject the holy Angels.

Answer: Nothing of the sort can be derived from these passages.

It is not the same with our God as it is with the false deities of the Heathens: the Heathens imagined that their Gods were satisfied with some appearance of satisfaction; they also sometimes offered them painted sacrifices, and they believed that their *Jupiter* allowed himself to be reconciled with the fires that were built in his honor. *Porphyrius* <note>original: "Porphyrius"; a Neoplatonist philosopher who was a prominent critic of early Christianity.</note> writes that *Pythagoras* offered an Ox made of dough; and *Athenæus* <note>original: "Athenæus"; a Greek rhetorician and grammarian.</note> relates that *Empedocles*, a disciple of *Pythagoras*, had an Ox—made of Myrrh, Frankincense, and all kinds of spices—distributed to those present at the Olympic games where he had been crowned. The poor among the Egyptians offered a Pig made of dough to *Bacchus* <note>The Roman name for Dionysus, the god of wine and ritual.</note>. Mr. *Thevenot* <note>Jean de Thévenot (1633–1667), a famous French traveler whose accounts of the East were widely read in the 17th century.</note>, in his *Indian Travelogues*

<column-break/>

Part III, chapter 47, speaking of the *Brahmins* of *Telangana*, a province of *Hindustan*, says that on a certain day of joy they make a cow of dough, which they fill with honey, and thereafter slit its throat and cut it into pieces. He adds that the honey, which drips from all sides, represents the blood of the Cow, and that they eat the dough instead of its flesh.

Our God is a consuming fire, and His justice is so strict that it does not forgive sin where it has not been satisfied. If God did not punish sin, He could just as well not hate it: for when the Scripture ascribes hatred to God, it means by this expression the constant will He has to punish or destroy all that is against His virtues. If it were now possible for God not to hate sin, it would be possible for Him to love it; which is a godless thing to say.

Certainly, if it is not possible for God to leave holiness without reward when He finds it in His creatures, it is even less possible that He leaves their sin without punishment, since the exercise of justice is much more necessary than that of His mercy.

It is a natural knowledge imprinted in the hearts of men that the Deity must punish the insult offered to Him; from this come the terrors of conscience, of which we have dealt elsewhere, and the sacrifices of men that the Heathens offered to their Gods. <margin>Acts 28:4.</margin> The Barbarians of the Island of *Malta* were convinced of this: seeing that a Viper had seized the hand of *Paul*, they said that he was a murderer whom Divine justice would not allow to live.

Those who most oppose the necessity of satisfaction are forced to acknowledge that God cannot leave the impenitent and rebellious unpunished. Now, impenitence is not punishable except insofar as it is an intent to do evil. Impenitence, considered in its essence, is a Perseverance, and perseverance is good or evil according to the various applications one makes of it. It is good in respect to virtue, and evil in respect to vice; from which it follows that perseverance is not actually what God's justice takes as its...

The Lord Sherlock, in his treatise on the happiness of the Pious / <note>William Sherlock (c. 1641–1707) was an influential Anglican clergyman; the author is likely referencing his *A Practical Discourse Concerning Death* or *A Discourse Concerning the Happiness of Good Men*.</note> insists only on this last proof. One will perhaps say, that God’s threats are conditional / as many of them appear in Scripture.

The first can be left unexecuted; but the second must necessarily be put into effect / unless satisfaction was made for those who have transgressed His commandments.

God did not want / men to be ignorant / that it is necessary / that justice be satisfied. Therefore He had / as we shall show elsewhere / instituted all the sacrifices / which had to be brought to Him / and which by themselves could not atone for sin.

II. It is said, that everyone can waive their rights / and consequently / that God can forgive without satisfaction / since he is the Lord and Master of all men.

I answer, that it is true / that there are certain rights / which one can surrender / for example / a creditor can cancel a debt; someone who is insulted / can choose not to demand satisfaction; a Master can do with his servants as he wills. But I add to this, that the high Authority cannot allow / the laws of the State to be violated with impunity. Now, in this matter, God cannot be viewed as a privately insulted Person / or as a private creditor / but as the supreme Judge and Master of the world / and consequently he cannot leave the transgression of his commandments unpunished.

<margin>Socinus, *Theological Lectures*, chapter 16.</margin>
III. It is said, that sins are depicted to us as debts, and that God therefore must be viewed as a creditor. But one pays no heed to the reason / for which sins are portrayed as debts. This is done to teach us two truths. 1. That our sins give God the same right to punish us / as the debts / that one has made / give a right to a creditor to act against his debtor. 2. That / just as a creditor no longer has a right to act against his debtor / once he has canceled his debt / one also has no need to fear Divine justice / when God has forgiven us our sins; but one must not conclude from this / that it is as easy for God to forgive sins without satisfaction / as it is for a creditor / to cancel a debt; for by canceling what is owed to us / one does not wrong the Law; but one cannot leave the transgression of laws unpunished / without overturning the laws themselves.

Certainly / if one had to conclude from the fact that sins are called debts / that—

God can forgive them without satisfaction / it would also follow / that God could release us from showing him obedience / which is also called a debt. One could likewise conclude / that God could forgive us / even if we lived in impenitence / something which the deniers of the necessity of satisfaction would not wish to grant.

IV. It is said, that Princes and Authorities often show mercy to those who have violated the laws of the State.
I answer, 1. That Princes sometimes forgive the violation of the Laws of the State / because they can act in no other way. But it is not so with God / who is neither bound nor forced to show mercy. 2. That Princes many times do what they ought not to do / and that their actions are not always as they should be. They sometimes imagine / that they are above the laws / and that they can release others from them / instead of keeping in mind what one reads in the fourth Book of the Laws of **Theodosius** <note>Theodosius II (401–450 AD) was a Roman Emperor; his legal code, the *Codex Theodosianus*, was a primary source of Roman law in the West.</note> / that the Prince is bound to the laws.

I answer, that God demands no more from sinners than their faith and conversion / because he has received the satisfaction of his Son on their behalf. But it must not be concluded from this / that God can forgive them without satisfaction.

<margin>Twisse in *A Vindication of Grace*.</margin>

Who does not see / that one does not use this parable there to teach us that he is a thief / but to show us that his coming will be sudden and unexpected. <note>The author refers to the common biblical metaphor where the "Day of the Lord" comes like a thief—meaning unexpectedly—rather than suggesting any moral likeness.</note> One must then here also pay attention to the aim of the Lord Christ. That is what Christ proposes to himself in this parable / one must seek no other mystery in it. To another, this King simply remits a debt of talent-pounds. Now we gladly admit / that a private creditor can waive some of his rights.

**VIII.** It is said, that he exhorts us to forgive our brothers their sins / just as God forgives us ours. Now, it is said, we must demand no <term>satisfaction</term> <note>Satisfaction: in this context, a legal payment or penalty that "satisfies" the requirements of justice.</note> for that.

I answer, that the insight of the spirit / when he exhorts us to forgive the insults / that we have received / just as God forgives those which we do to him / is / to teach us that we must as earnestly forgive the wrong suffered / as God forgives us our crimes ; for / if one wanted to press the parable too far / one would have to say that one must not forgive / except to those who have repentance for having wronged us / just as God only forgives the truly <term>penitent</term> <note>Penitent: those who are sincerely sorry for their sins and intend to change.</note>. Who does not know that there is an infinite difference between God and men? He is the Judge of the earth / who is bound to maintain order : but men are private persons / who have no power to punish.

**IX.** It is said, that / if God has loved us to such an extent / that he has given us his Son / before he has received any satisfaction / he could also well make us blessed without satisfaction.

Answer ; this conclusion does not follow. For God could love men enough as his creatures / to give them—

<column-break/>

—any satisfaction received / and to give them the means / leading to salvation : but among these means / it was necessary / that there was one for the satisfaction of his justice. Otherwise he would not have preserved the human race. To make this matter more understandable / one must observe / that God made these two decrees at the same time / one to destine salvation to some men / and another to send his Son into the world / for the satisfaction of his justice and reconciliation of sins.

<margin>Twisse, *Vindication of Grace*. <note>original: "Twiss. Vind. Grat." refers to William Twisse (1578–1646), a prominent English theologian and Prolocutor of the Westminster Assembly.</note></margin>
**X.** It is said, that / if God could not forgive sin without satisfaction / it would be / either because it includes a contradiction that sin be not punished / or because God's justice opposes it / or by lack of God's Omnipotence.

I answer, that it is / because God can never act against his perfections / and by consequence against his justice ; and that it follows / that God / who is a righteous being / does not go against his justice.

**XI.** It is said, that / if God must necessarily punish sin / it would be / either with a temporal punishment / and then it would follow from that / that sin deserves no eternal punishment / or with an eternal punishment / and then the sinner would have to exist eternally / without God being able to <term>annihilate</term> <note>Annihilate: to completely destroy or reduce to nothing. Some theologians argued God could just "delete" a sinner rather than punishing them forever.</note> him.

I answer, that we certainly know / that God cannot release himself from punishing sin / and that sin deserves a punishment / that is proportionate to God's offended Majesty. But beyond that we know no more. We know that God can bring creatures to nothing ; but we know not / whether this annihilation would be a punishment / that satisfied Divine justice. We have much more reason to believe / that it is only eternal punishments / which are proportional to the sins / that we have committed.

**XII.** It is said, that God would do no one wrong / if he forgave without satisfaction.

I answer, 1. That God would deny himself and his perfections.
2. That one could say by the same way of reasoning / that God could forgive the sins of the impenitent / because he would [do no one] wrong therewith...

## CHAPTER III.

### Whether it is necessary that the sinners themselves satisfy Divine justice.

From what has been said / it appears that it was necessary to satisfy Divine justice for the sins of men. A second problem is proposed / and it is asked whether it was necessary / that the sinners themselves should satisfy it.

To answer this / we say three things.

1. That all sinners deserve to be punished / and that their punishment itself is very consistent with the nature of the matter and with order.

2. That, therefore, Divine justice could have demanded / that the sinners themselves suffered for their sin / without having reason to complain about its severity.

3. That, meanwhile, Justice has been able to step away from some of its severity / and allow another to suffer for mankind in their place.

To understand this truth / one must observe that these are two very distinct matters: not punishing the sin / or not punishing the sinner. The justice and holiness of God do not allow him / to leave the sin unpunished / but they do not oppose the forgiveness of sinners. God / as holy and righteous / cannot refrain from hating sin / and he cannot hate it without punishing it / because / as we have proven elsewhere / to hate in God / means to will to punish. It would then run against his Justice and Holiness if the sin remained unpunished / but these are by no means offended if God / having punished the sin / forgives the sinner / because he / by the punishing of the sins / has satisfied his justice. This way of punishing the sin / and leaving the sinner free / suits God's wisdom: for thus he has found the means / to reconcile his mercy with his justice. If all men had been required to satisfy Divine justice /

<column-break/>

they would all have been subject to eternal death / and there would have been no place for the exercise of mercy: but / another having been placed in the stead of the sinners / justice has enjoyed that which it desired / and mercy has been able to have its course.

Justice has punished the sin / and received the <term>satisfaction</term> <note>Satisfaction: the legal fulfillment of a debt or penalty.</note> for the sinners: but mercy has acquitted the sinner of what he owed / because of the satisfaction of the one who placed himself in his stead and satisfied the debt; consequently, these two things are not contradictory in this matter / satisfaction and forgiveness: the <term>surety</term> <note>Surety: a person who takes legal responsibility for another's debt or behavior.</note> and the mediator of men has satisfied for them / and God forgives them the crimes / for which he had the right to punish them in their own persons.

But / it is said, is it not against God's justice to punish an innocent person for the guilty?

I answer, that this does not conflict with justice / when these conditions are observed.

<margin>
Under what conditions an innocent person can be <unclear>substituted</unclear> for a guilty person.
</margin>
1. That the sin be punished / and that with a punishment proportionate to the greatness of the love / that God has for holiness / and of the hatred / that he has against sin.

2. That the innocent person / who offers himself to suffer / suffers willingly / and that no violence is done to him.

3. That this innocent person be master of his own life / to do with it what he desires.

4. That he can perfectly satisfy for those / for whom he offers himself.

5. That he can deliver himself from death by his own power / and thus the commonwealth <note>The author uses 'gemeenebest' (commonwealth) to imply the moral order of the universe or society, which should not suffer the permanent loss of a righteous person.</note> comes to suffer nothing through the loss of an honorable man.

6. That God be more glorified thereby / than he would be through the punishment of the guilty themselves.

7. That God approves / that an innocent person places himself in the stead of the sinners.

8. That the innocent person has the same nature as the guilty / so that the sin may be punished in the same nature / in which it was committed.

When these conditions are met / one sees / that justice is in no way compromised.

The reason / why some do not wish / for an innocent person to suffer for a guilty one, is: 1. That few are found who would be willing to die for another / as Paul noted in Romans 5:7. 2. It would not be fair to deprive the Commonwealth <note>original: "Gemeenebest," referring to the organized society or state</note> of a citizen / who is honest and innocent / in order to spare villains / who disturb human society. <margin>John 10:18.</margin>
John 10:18. *No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of myself; I have the power to lay it down, and I have the power to take it again.* He also willingly offered himself to God. Saying / *Behold, here I am, O God, to do your will.*

<margin>Ps. 40:8, 9.</margin>
<margin>Heb. 10:8, 9, 10.</margin>
He was able to give a sufficient ransom / to pay for sins. He was able to raise himself up / as he indeed did. Through his death, he was able to convert sinners / and he brought all those whom he intended to convert / to that very conversion. He was united with humanity through a close bond; he shared the same nature with them; he had become one body with them; and the Father / who had appointed him as Surety <term>Borg: A legal term for a guarantor who takes responsibility for another's debt</term> and Mediator / had given him those whom he had chosen. Finally, through his death, he has perfectly satisfied divine justice / and atoned for the sins of the elect / and in him, sin has been sufficiently punished.

This will become even clearer in what follows / when we examine all that Christ has done for us. For it is he / who was placed in the stead of sinners.

I have but two words to add to this.

I. It is remarkable / that those who refuse to admit that Christ died / to satisfy divine justice / because / as they claim / it is not fitting / for an innocent person to suffer for a guilty one / nevertheless maintain that he died / to give us an example of patience and virtue.

II. I further note / that our view serves greatly to make God’s perfections 

<insert>Part 1.</insert>

<column-break/>

shine forth. He teaches us to know his Holiness / for who would not call holy a Being / who cannot and will not accept a sinner into his fellowship / without satisfaction; his Justice, which demands the punishment for sin with incomprehensible severity; his Wisdom, which knew how to look after our Salvation <term>Zaligheid: Spiritual well-being or eternal life</term> so well / that his honor did not suffer by it / and which knew how to demonstrate his Mercy so well / that his justice was nevertheless satisfied; and finally / his Infinite Love / which / to spare us / did not spare his only Son / delivering the righteous for the unrighteous / the innocent for the guilty / his own Son for Slaves; there one also sees the infinite love of the Son / who did not consider it a disgrace to humble himself to the lowly form of a Servant / so that we might reign; to allow himself to be nailed to the cross / to redeem us and exalt us to his throne; to allow himself to be condemned / to set us free; and to undergo death / to obtain immortality for us.

This view also serves to increase our Piety <term>Godsvrugt: Devotion or godliness</term> / to give us an aversion to sin / to make us fear God’s justice / and to ignite in us a true love for such a holy and incomparable Benefactor.

## CHAPTER IV.

Whether it was necessary for a Divine Person to satisfy for sinners, and how that could have happened, since all the Divine Persons were equally offended.

We have seen / that it was not necessary / for the sinners themselves to satisfy divine justice for their sins.

But the question is asked: who was capable of satisfying for mankind?

We have already pointed out the qualities / with which he who would step into the place of men had to be clothed / from which it is easy to conclude / that he, above all, had to be innocent / both Man and God, etc.

# THE CHRISTIAN GOD

<meta>catchword: if</meta>

One understands without difficulty that he must be innocent; for, if he himself had committed any crime, he would have needed another to satisfy the debt for him.

We have seen, and shall consider even more closely, that he had to be human so that humanity could have fellowship with him.

But we must now investigate whether it was necessary for the **Surety** <term>Borg: A legal term for a guarantor who takes responsibility for another's debt</term> of humanity to be a **Divine Person**.

There have been ancient Teachers who did not recognize this absolute necessity of satisfying Divine justice through the incarnation of God’s Son. Among them was **Augustine** in his *Sermon on the Annunciation of the Lord* <note>original: "Serm. de Annunt. Dom."</note>, who says that those who claim God’s Wisdom could devise no other means of redemption than the incarnation are ignorant. Others include **Leo I** in his *Second Sermon on the Incarnation* <note>original: "Serm. II. de Incarn."</note>, and **Bonaventure** <note>original: "in 3. Sent. dist. XX. q. 6."</note>. However, several others have recognized this necessity, such as **Athanasius** in *On the Incarnation of the Word* <note>original: "de Verb. Incar."</note>, **Anselm** in his book *Why God Became Man* <note>original: "cur Deus hom."</note>, **Basil** on Psalm 28, **Ambrose** on Hebrews 9, and **Thomas Aquinas** in *Against the Gentiles* <note>original: "contr. Gentil."</note>.

We shall not doubt this necessity if we consider that sin deserves an infinite punishment—as we have proven elsewhere—because it is committed against an **infinite Majesty**. From this, it follows that a satisfaction of infinite value was required; and consequently, the one who would satisfy this debt had to be God, since there is nothing infinite but God.

But here a great difficulty arises: how is it possible for a Divine Person to have provided satisfaction, since all three Persons of the Trinity were equally offended? For it seems absurd to say that a Person provides satisfaction to themselves.

To this, I have two answers to give.

I. While it is indeed absurd in some cases for a person to satisfy themselves, it is not so in all. For example, if someone who was owed money by another paid themselves, or if someone who was wronged by another came to ask themselves for forgiveness, that would be absurd. But when it concerns a wrong that affects the **common good**, and a satisfaction owed to the **Authority** as Authority, nothing prevents the Authority—assuming the person of the offender—

<column-break/>

from paying on their behalf, and thus satisfying itself. <margin>Titus Livius, *History*, Book II.</margin> The history of **Menenius Agrippa** <note>A Roman consul famous for using a fable to reconcile the commoners and the nobles</note> is well known. There are other cases where one can satisfy oneself. For example, it can happen that the Authority itself breaks the Laws; in this case, if it undergoes the punishment commanded by the laws, it satisfies itself in its capacity as **Judge** and **Authority**.

Thus, a Divine Person can satisfy himself because God must not be viewed here as a private Person, but as a **public Person**: as the Lord and Judge of the World, the Governor of the universe, who is obliged to uphold the rights of the Godhead and not leave the violation of his laws unpunished.

II. One must observe that being an offended Person and being a **Mediator** are not contradictory qualities, except when the offended Person demands the total destruction of the offender. In that case, it involves a contradiction to say that a Person simultaneously demands the destruction and the preservation of someone. But when the offended party requires nothing more than satisfaction for the wrong done, they can serve the office of Mediator and even provide a means themselves by which the crime is punished and the wrong satisfied, while the guilty party remains unpunished. Now, God required nothing else than that satisfaction be made for the wrong done to the **Divine Majesty**.

It was therefore quite possible for one of the Divine Persons, though offended, to place himself between the offended Godhead and the humans who had insulted it.

Furthermore, it has been noted that in the case of the sins for which Christ acted as Mediator, the Son was offended in common with the Father and the Holy Spirit; for one cannot say that the Son was insulted specifically in contrast to the other two Persons. Now, in the **economy of our Salvation**, this common interest of the three Persons has been placed, as it were, into the hands of the Father alone. Thus, one can say that the Son here does not strictly act as an offended Person, and consequently, nothing prevents him from working as a Mediator.

The first of these observations serves to refute an objection commonly made. It is said that if...

# THEOLOGY. IX. B. V. Chapter.

if a Divine Person could satisfy himself, he would be at once angry and reconciled. I answer, that this objection seems to assume that something happens in God similar to what happens in us when we are disturbed and angry; whereas it is certain that God is not subject to **passions** <term>hertstogten: In classical theology, this refers to emotions or internal changes. God is considered "impassible," meaning He does not experience shifting moods or suffering like humans do.</term>. To solve the difficulty, one must ask whether it is possible for a Divine Person to will to punish sin, and at the same time to find the means to forgive the sinner. We see no impossibility or contradiction in that. Nothing prevents a **Ruler** <note>original: "Overheid"</note> from being offended by those who break the laws, and meanwhile providing satisfaction himself. He is angry as the Ruler, but satisfies as a private Person.

One will ask whether it was necessary that the second Divine Person satisfied for sinners.

I answer, that we do not know whether another Person could have satisfied; we know for certain that it was consistent with God's wisdom that the Son was sent by the Father, and that the Holy Spirit applied to us the salvation that the Son has earned. There are theologians who give various reasons for this, some of which are more ingenious than substantial. They say that it was fitting that He who held the middle place between the Father and the Holy Spirit should become the Mediator between God and men; that He who is Son by nature made us children of God by grace, to be His fellow heirs; that the one through whom God prepared the ages should re-create us; that He who is the **Image of the invisible God** should reshape us into God’s image; that He in whom God was well pleased should reconcile us with the Father. But it is better to remain silent than to try to fathom what God has hidden from us.

<column-break/>

### V. CHAPTER.

->How one must understand that the Father has sent His Son; by what principle He sent Him; and for what reason He did not send Him immediately after the Fall.<-

WE have seen that it was necessary for a Divine Person to satisfy for mankind, and we have stated alongside this that the second Person of the Holy Trinity placed Himself in their stead, who is therefore described to us as our **Savior**, our **Redeemer**, our **Mediator**, which we shall explain more broadly in what follows.

<margin>How one must understand that the Father sent the Son. Rom. 8:3. Gal. 4:4.</margin>
Now we have three things to consider.
I. That it is the Father who sent the Son. *God sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, condemned sin in the flesh.* Romans 8:3. *God sent forth his Son, born of a woman, born under the Law.* Galatians 4:4. If it is now true, as we have shown, that the Persons of the adorable Trinity are equal, how can one have the authority to send the other?

I answer, that these expressions do not indicate any inequality between the Persons, but only that in the work of our salvation these adorable Persons agreed among themselves that the Father would occupy the position of the first founder of the Church, of Sovereign of the world, of Protector and avenger of the Laws, and of the first director of the work of our **Redemption** <note>original: "Verlossinge"</note>. The Son that of Mediator between God and men; and the Holy Spirit that of Comforter and Sanctifier of the believers. This is what the Scripture wants to teach us when it says that the Father has sent the Son and the Spirit. Besides that, it is not always a sign of inequality to be sent, when this sending occurs by mutual consent. Finally, one must take into consideration that as soon as the Son offered Himself to the Father to serve the office of Mediator between God and men, and to die for them, He became in that respect less than the Father...

...become <note>original: "worden"</note> and that he had to receive his mission from him.

<margin>By what principle God sent his Son into the world</margin>
II. The second matter that we must investigate is by what principle God sent his Son into the world. I answer that the Scripture says that God gave his Son out of a principle of love. *John 3:16:* <note>original: "Joh. III. 16"</note> it is difficult to conceive that God loved the world when he gave his Son, since he gave him to satisfy his justice and wrath. I answer that one can easily understand that God was able to love humans as his creatures, even though they were the objects of his justice; he loved them so much that he provided them with the means to be reconciled with him and to obtain the forgiveness of the sins they had committed. This truly causes us to stand amazed at God’s infinite love, that he willed to give us a **Mediator** <term>Middelaar: A go-between or advocate; in this context, Jesus Christ acting as the bridge between humanity and God.</term> himself, while we were worthy of nothing else than to bear the righteous punishment of his wrath.

<margin>Why God did not send his Son immediately after the Fall.</margin>
III. But, it is asked, why is it that God did not send his Son immediately after the Fall?

Answer. One might be satisfied with saying that it so pleased God, and that his good pleasure sets limits to our curiosity. But one can give several reasons for this action of God.

1. It was fitting that a work of such great importance as that of our **Redemption** <term>Verlossing: The act of being saved or "bought back" from the debt of sin.</term> should be expected for a long time, to make its importance known and to warn people of it many centuries in advance.

2. It was good that humans saw for many centuries what they could do by themselves, so they might recognize the futility of their own attempts at reconciliation and be made to confess that they would never have discovered the true means to satisfy Divine justice.

3. If sin had been reconciled immediately after it was committed, it might have been viewed as a trivial matter that passes in a moment.

4. It seems it was not appropriate for the Son of God to come during the time of the "infancy" of the Church, because he had to bring with him a perfect knowledge of the secrets

<column-break/>

of the Kingdom of Heaven. Now, the church in her infancy required that she be given the first and weak principles, and that she be kept under the discipline of the law.

# CHAPTER VI.
## Concerning the Divine Oracles that foretold the coming of the Messiah.

**GOD**, who did not wish to send his Son into the world immediately after the fall, nevertheless desired to warn mankind of his coming and to foretell all the circumstances of it, so that they might know him, and so that their faith and hope might be nourished and strengthened by these predictions. It was indeed fitting that such a matter should be foretold, and that God—who has marked in his word the extraordinary purposes of his wisdom, the judgments of his justice, and other changes that occur in the world—likewise revealed this great work of grace therein.

Furthermore, all believers under the Old Testament were bound to believe in the Messiah, not only because it is a truth revealed to them, but also because it is the most important of all truths and the source of all consolation.

But, before we bring forward these **Divine Oracles** <term>Godspraaken: Literally "God-speeches," referring to the prophetic utterances or revelations found in the Bible.</term>, it is necessary to make some general observations.

The 1st is that there are Oracles that belong to no one but the Messiah; and there are those that seem to fit another subject, but which cannot be applied perfectly and in all their extent to any subject other than the Messiah.

The 2nd is that the oldest Oracles are contained in the most general terms, which were presented much more distinctly and clearly as the time approached in which the Messiah was to come into the world.

The 3rd is that the Oracles that foretold the Messiah are sometimes mixed with other things that seem to have no relation to his coming; which may have happened because...

### DIVINITY. IX. B. VI. Chapter.

...that the prophecies of one and the same Prophet are joined together, even though they were spoken at different times.

The 4th point is that most of the divine oracles concerning the Messiah are joined with other prophecies that concerned the temporal deliverance and preservation of the Jewish people, because these were the necessary means to fulfill the promise of the Messiah and to carry out God’s great purpose.

The 5th point is that, since the Messiah is described to us as one who would unite the glory of the Godhead with the weakness and humility of human nature in his Person, and would pass through various states, one must not set what the Prophets give as something great in their prophetic descriptions of the Messiah against the idea they give of his humiliation and of his suffering, as if they were contradictory things; rather, they were meant to converge in his person and in his various states.

The 6th and final observation is that some divine oracles characterize the time of his coming, and others his Person.

We shall begin with the first.

<margin>Gen. 49:10</margin>
The first divine oracle that mentions the time of the coming of the Messiah is contained in the words of the dying Jacob, Gen. 49:10. *The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the Lawgiver from between his feet (or from among his citizens, as some translate) until Shiloh comes; and to him shall the obedience of the peoples be.* <note>original: "tot dat de Scilo komt"</note> This divine oracle is applied by the Jews themselves to the Messiah, although some of them attribute it to Moses, others to David, others to Jeroboam, and others to other Kings of Judah.

<margin>See further Sanhedrin c. 11; Bereshit Rabbah; R. Bechai; R. M. Gerundensis; R. Joel Ben Sueb; Abrabanel in Manasseh’s Conciliator.</margin>
The Chaldean Paraphrast <note>The Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible.</note> named Onkelos, the Jerusalem Targum, Jonathan Uziel, and Rabbi Solomon <note>Known as Rashi, a famous medieval commentator who lived around 1100.</note> have all assigned this prophecy to the Messiah. There are even those who, through the **Kabbalah of Numbers** <term>Gematria: A Jewish system of assigning numerical values to Hebrew letters to find hidden meanings in words.</term> <note>original: "La Cabale des Nombres"</note>, have found in two words of this prophecy the same numerical value found in the word that means *Messiah*. Others bring these words of Jacob home to Moses, because the name of Moses and that of Shiloh in Hebrew both amount to 345.

<column-break/>

But what Scepter did Judah have until the coming of Moses? And how can it be said of Moses that he was the expectation of the nations and the object of their hope? What is drawn from the hidden art of numbers is ridiculous; by that method, one could also find the word *Messiah* and the name *Jesus* in these prophecies. Others apply the same to Saul because, they say, he was anointed at Shiloh. But 1. Saul was not anointed at Shiloh, but at Ramah. 2. Before Saul, the Scepter had not been in the Tribe of Judah. 3. Finally, it was during the life of Saul that the Scepter was transferred to the Tribe of Judah, far from departing from it.

Others have assigned it to David. But, far from the Scepter of Judah departing in the time of David, it can be said that this Tribe then only first began to reign; although one cannot deny that before this time it had some precedence over the other Tribes in certain cases. Others refer it to the place called Shiloh, where the Tabernacle stood in the beginning, and translate the text thus: *until the Tabernacle of Shiloh shall be destroyed.*

But this opinion is no less ridiculous than that of those who assign it to Ahijah the Shilonite. They do not deserve to be refuted. Others attribute it to Jeroboam, whom they claim was crowned at Shiloh; but he was crowned at Shechem, 1 Kings 12, and the Scepter did not then depart from Judah. Others assign it to Nebuchadnezzar; but it is clear that Jacob here foretells the advantages of the Tribe of Judah, and in no way its calamities. Now everyone knows that this godless Prince brought one of the greatest calamities to this Tribe that it ever suffered. This is enough to refute those who believe that *Shiloh* is not a person, nor a beneficial thing, but a disastrous one—namely, the destruction of the Royal Dignity and Scepter of Judah—and thus translate the Hebrew: *The scepter or the government shall not depart, until it shall end forever, whether the tribe or the government.*

One is blind if one does not see the inappropriateness of this interpretation. It is said that *Shiloh* can be derived from a Chaldean verb meaning *to cease* or *to end*; or from an Arabic one meaning *he has failed* or *he has stopped*

# THE CHRISTIAN

...to be, signifies. But a clever 
<margin>Gusset <note>James Gusset (1636–1704) was a French Hebrew scholar often cited in these theological debates.</note></margin>
man observes: 1. That one sees no reason why one would wish to make Jacob speak Chaldean <note>A term often used for Aramaic.</note> or Arabic in a Hebrew discourse. 2. That neither Daniel nor Ezra <note>original: "Esdras"</note> ever used this word to mean "to cease"; and that consequently, one has reason to doubt that the word itself—or the word it is derived from—meant "to cease" in the Old Chaldean language; although one cannot deny that it is used in the Chaldean paraphrases <note>The Targums: Aramaic translations/interpretations of the Hebrew Bible.</note> in the sense of "destruction": but there is little appearance that it was taken in that sense in the time of Jacob. 3. That one finds in no Arabic dictionary that this word means "he has failed" or "he has ceased to be." But in order not to occupy ourselves with all these bitterness-inducing details, it will be enough to observe that those who translate and expand upon this passage in such a way completely miss the objective of Jacob. To make him say that the Tribe of Judah shall not end until it ends is to make him speak an unripened language that has no meaning.

<margin>Menasseh, Question 65 on Genesis. <note>Referring to Menasseh ben Israel (1604–1657), a famous Portuguese Rabbi in Amsterdam.</note></margin>
There are those who translate: *The scepter shall never depart from Judah, even when the Messiah shall have come.* But it is certain that the Hebrew word which these interpreters translate as "never" or "eternally" does not mean that, except when it concludes a sentence entirely; and then it is usually either repeated with the same word or paired with another that signifies eternity. Now, in this place, it is joined with a word that commonly means "until." It is not true that the accent-mark <note>original: "toon-stip," referring to the Hebrew cantillation marks (trope) that guide the reading and logic of the verse.</note> which stands above this word divides the sentence. The contrary appears through the following verse.

Others say that these words amount to this sense: that when there shall be Kings in Israel, they shall all be of the Tribe of Judah. But this has not been proven; for the ten tribes had Kings from other Tribes.

In order to properly understand the oracle <note>original: "Godspraak"</note> of Jacob, one must make the following observations:

1. That the same is a prophecy for the benefit of the Tribe of Judah in particular, just as every oracle that precedes or follows this one concerns each individual Tribe.

2. That by the word "scepter" one 

<column-break/>

must understand the Royal dignity to which this Tribe would be elevated, Zechariah 10:11.

The Jews translate it as "rod," <note>Implying a rod of punishment or affliction.</note> but they are mistaken. 1. For Jacob does not present a threat to Judah here, but a promise. 2. It is untrue that the rod never departed from the back of Judah before the coming of the Messiah. 3. The Tribe of Judah has not been more chastised than the others. Finally, the fact that something is added regarding the Lawgiver shows that we are not speaking here of a rod of chastisement, but of a scepter of government. The translations of the Septuagint <note>original: "LXX," the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>, of Aquila, Symmachus, and the Chaldean paraphrases favor our interpretation. There are Jews who say that this oracle means that the Jews will never lack support in their oppressions (Menasseh, *Conciliator* Question 65 on Genesis, page 89). But 1. if this had been the meaning of Jacob, he would have expressed himself differently. 2. The root word, when stated absolutely like this, does not mean "support," unless it were paired with something else, as in Psalm 23. Furthermore, Jacob would not have limited this promise to the Tribe of Judah alone. Finally, it is ridiculous to explain these last words thus: "and to him shall be the oppression of the Heathens."

There are scholars who believe that one should translate: "and the tribe shall not depart from Judah," to say that this tribe would always remain distinct from the other tribes until the coming of the Messiah, after which they would be mixed with the others. But it seems to me that the common explanation is the most natural, although this latter one can indeed be defended. One can even say that through this explanation, one more easily solves some difficulties that are raised, and of which I shall speak in what follows.

3. That it appears through this oracle that the tribe of Judah would ascend the Throne.

The same has always had some precedence; God commanded that it should be the first to set out, Numbers 2:3, 10:14. Their leaders offered the first gifts, Numbers 7:11, 12. In the time of Joshua, this tribe took its inheritance without drawing lots. After Joshua, God commanded that Judah should hold the supreme command to take the remainder of the promised land. This tribe has given its name to the others. <note>Referring to how the term "Jew" is derived from "Judah."</note>

### THEOLOGY. IX. BOOK VI. CHAPTER.

4. That the same tribe would reign for a considerable time; indeed, there were Kings from this tribe until the taking of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar <note>The Babylonian king who destroyed the first Temple in 586 BCE.</note>.

1. There are Jews who explain Jacob's words thus: *The scepter and the lawgiver from the blood of Judah shall not depart forever, since the Shiloh <note>A title traditionally interpreted by both Jews and Christians as referring to the Messiah.</note> shall come,* and the reason they give for this is that the temporal scepter did not remain with Judah until the coming of the Messiah. But 1. We have already shown that the text cannot be translated in that way. 2. It is not true that the scepter and the Lawgiver entirely departed before the coming of the Messiah. 3. The rebellion of Jeroboam <note>The first king of the breakaway Northern Kingdom of Israel.</note> did not cause the scepter of Judah to depart. 4. This happened through the Babylonian captivity. But the Jews later obtained rulers from this tribe. If one had to translate this <term>oracle</term> <note>original: "Godspraak," referring to a divine prophecy.</note> in such a way, it would conflict with that of Daniel, who says that after the coming of the Messiah, the people of the Prince shall come, who shall destroy the City and the Temple.

5. That this tribe, in the course of time, would come to lose some of its dignity; and therefore the Lawgiver is spoken of after the Scepter.

This happened by degrees. Under David's grandson <note>Rehoboam, whose reign saw the ten northern tribes secede.</note>, ten tribes fell away, who no longer wished to subject themselves to the scepter of Judah. The kings who followed Rehoboam became tributary to neighboring Kings, whereas David had extended the borders of his kingdom to the gates of Babylon. The Babylonians brought the Jews under subjection and took from the Kings of Judah the authority they had. Then the scepter departed. But then came Lawgivers; Zerubbabel <note>The grandson of King Jehoiachin and a leader of the Jewish people returning from Babylonian exile.</note> was the head of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin. Since his time, the tribe of Judah has had heads of the Jewish Nation, although they were not always of the tribe of Judah, which was not necessary for the fulfillment of the Prophecy. For it is not always true that Kings must be of the same nation as their subjects; just as Poland has had French Kings. The Hasmoneans <note>The dynasty of the Maccabees who ruled Judea in the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE.</note> always maintained authority in this tribe, until it was stripped of it by the Romans, which also happened gradually and by degrees: 1. Under Pompey <note>The Roman general who captured Jerusalem in 63 BCE.</note>, 60 years before the birth of Christ. 2. When Judea became a province of the Roman Empire. 3. Under Titus,

<column-break/>

when the Temple and City were destroyed. Yet it appears that there were always either Kings or Lawgivers until the coming of the Messiah.

6. Finally, the prophecy indicates that the tribe of Judah would remain in possession of at least some form of government until the coming of the Messiah, so that one must conclude that this prophecy here, as a sign of the time of Christ’s coming, gives the time of the downfall of the power and authority which the tribe of Judah had still retained in some measure after the Babylonian captivity. Furthermore, one should not be surprised that the scripture teaches us that the scepter and the lawgiver shall not depart before the coming of the Messiah; for, since the Messiah had to be born from the tribe of Judah, he had to come before the Jewish commonwealth had perished and the tribes were mixed together.

The Second Prophecy, in which the coming of the Messiah is predicted, is taken not only from the 2nd Chapter of Daniel, where the Empire under which he would appear is pointed out, but specifically from the 9th Chapter of that Prophet, which marks the time of his coming and of his death.

To understand this <term>prophecy</term> <note>original: "Godspraak," referring to a divine oracle or word from God.</note>, one must observe:

1. That by the "Weeks" of which Daniel speaks, one must understand seven years <note>The "day-year principle," where each day in a prophetic week represents one calendar year.</note>, each day for a year, according to the Hebrew style, *Ezekiel 4:6, Leviticus 25:8.* Thus, 70 weeks make 490 years. For, if one spoke here of weeks properly named of 7 days, they would make only one and a half years, in which nothing of what the Angel had foretold occurred. To imagine that this refers to weeks of 10 years, as *Origen* <note>An early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 CE).</note> believed—who calculated that the 70 weeks from *Adam* made 4900 years until *Christ*—or to weeks of Jubilee years, so that 70 weeks yield 3430 years, is without the slightest basis; never is the word "Week" taken for a week of 10 years. Daniel places the coming of the *Messiah* before the destruction of the Temple. But if one had to take Daniel's weeks as weeks of 10 years or Jubilee years, the destruction of the Temple would have preceded the coming of the *Messiah*.

2. One must observe that the years of the Chaldeans <note>The Babylonians.</note> were of 360 days, from which one can deduce that 1260 days make three and a half years.

### DIVINE LEARNING. IX. B. VI. Chapter. ###

books [state] that the Prophet has determined the time that would pass from the destruction of the first Temple under **Zedekiah** <note>The last king of Judah before the Babylonian captivity.</note> until that of the second Temple by the **Romeinen** <note>The Romans, who destroyed the Temple in 70 CE.</note>; and they maintain that this calculation is correct, since exactly 490 years passed from the first to the second destruction. **Marsham** <note>Sir John Marsham (1602–1685), an English chronicler known for his work *Canon Chronicus*.</note>, who separates these two numbers and believes that the first concerns the times of **Cyrus** and the second those of **Antiochus Epiphanes**, presents his view as follows. Answer. But 1. there is no appearance that these three weeks signify 21 years: for, besides many reasons that could be brought against this opinion, **Daniel** says that he speaks of "weeks of days," <note>Daniel 10:2-3 specifically uses the Hebrew term *shabuim yamim* to distinguish them from the prophetic "weeks of years."</note> and consequently not of 21 years, but of 21 days or three weeks. **Marsham** valid. 2. If the first 7 weeks of **Daniel** end with **Cyrus**, as **Marsham** desires, and the 62 and a half weeks—that is, 444 and a half years—end with **Antiochus**, one would have to posit that 444 and a half years elapsed from **Cyrus** to **Antiochus**. Now, **Marsham** himself does not believe this. To make his calculation fit, he made other additions, according to which one would have to say that only 60 weeks were determined for the Jewish People, instead of 70, as the **Angel** testifies.

# THE CHRISTIAN GOD

...to be the foundation and the support of the Church, verse 22: *The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.* <note>original: "hooft des hoeks"</note>

<margin>
Psalm 132 and 89.

The 132nd Psalm teaches us, as well as the 89th, that the *Messiah* would spring from the house of *David*.

<margin>
Isaiah 7:14.
</margin>
The Book of *Isaiah* is full of prophecies of the *Messiah*. I will only bring up a few. According to Isaiah 7:14, he was to be born of a virgin; *behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name IMMANUEL.* To understand this oracle <note>original: "Godspraak"</note> fundamentally, one would have to bring many matters to the table; but since they would lead me too far astray, and I must still speak of it in the 18th Chapter, I will content myself for the present by making the following remarks.

I. That the Prophet presents this birth as a miracle and an unheard-of thing, which certainly would not be so highly exalted if it spoke only of an ordinary childbirth of a married woman, according to the opinion of the Jews.

<margin>
Exodus 3:12.
1 Samuel 2:34.
1 Kings 22:25.
2 Kings 8:2.
Jeremiah 44:29.
</margin>
II. That the Prophet gives this promise of the *Messiah* to *Ahaz* in order to confirm to this King, and to the Jews, the promises he made to them at that time—that they would be delivered from the violence of their enemies who were besieging *Jerusalem*. This should seem strange to no one:
1. Because as a sign of things yet to happen, one can give other things that will not occur until after the promised or predicted matter has taken place.
2. Because all the promises God made to the Jews rested upon the *Messiah*.
3. Finally, because if it were true, as *Ahaz* feared, that the entire nation was about to perish, God would not have sent the *Messiah*; thus, by assuring them that he will send them the *Messiah*, God assured them at the same time that he would provide all the deliverances he deemed necessary for that end. Furthermore, one should not be surprised that it seems the following words refer to another object than the *Messiah*; for in all appearance the Prophet gave two signs to *Ahaz*: one taken from the coming of the *Messiah*, and another of a child he had with him and pointed to with his finger. The first sign was a future matter, and the second a present one.

<column-break/>

III. That the son of the virgin, named *Immanuel*, is depicted in the following 8th Chapter as the Lord of the whole earth, verse 8.

Indeed, when this oracle was spoken, *Hezekiah* <note>King Hezekiah of Judah.</note> was nine years old. Therefore, *Isaiah*, speaking of *Hezekiah*, could not say, *behold, a virgin shall conceive.* Some say that since *Hezekiah*, no *Messiah* was to be expected. But can a greater absurdity be thought of?

<margin>
Isaiah 9:5. The Chaldean Paraphrase <note>The Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary.</note> applies this passage to the Messiah.
</margin>
The 9th Chapter also contains a glorious description of the *Messiah*, verse 5: *A child is born to us, a son is given to us, and the government is upon his shoulder, and his name is called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Father of Eternity, Prince of Peace.*

To apply this oracle to *Hezekiah* is also to blind oneself; for is there anyone of sound mind and reason who would dare to attribute to a mortal Prince all that the Prophet states here? These words also cannot be applied to God the Father, as if *Isaiah* had only meant to say that God the Father, who is the *Wonderful One*, etc., would call this child the *Prince of Peace*. For what reason would the Prophet have heaped so many titles of honor upon one another to signify God the Father, when it clearly appears that his aim is to speak of the Son, and not of the Father? Also, the name of *Counselor* <note>original: "Raad"</note> does not belong to the Father.

<margin>
Isaiah 11:1 etc.
</margin>

## CHAPTER VII.

->That the Messiah has come, and that Jesus Christ is the Messiah.<-

We have walked through the prophecies that foretold the time of the Messiah’s coming and pointed out his distinguishing marks. Now it is not difficult to know whether the Messiah has come. One cannot doubt it, if one takes note:
<margin>In Jewish Hak. p. 40. 26. from Avoda Zara chapter 1 <note>original: "In Jood. Hak... ex Avoda Sara." Reference to Johann Wagenseil's work and the Talmudic tractate on idolatry.</note></margin>

(c) They were therefore already stripped of their supreme power. It is true that they were still a people
