Even one of their most famous Rabbis acknowledges that they sit without a King or Prince of their own nation, and that they are under the power of the Gentiles. For to say that they have Kings in Babylon or elsewhere who are of the House of David, as one of their <margin>Benjamin in his Itinerary</margin> writers <note>Likely Benjamin of Tudela, a 12th-century Jewish traveler.</note> would claim, is a mere fiction, the falsehood of which the Jews themselves know; for if this were so, they would not fail to go to that place with hope, where they could be subject to their own Kings. One must not say that this is merely a temporary suspension of the acts of government, such as happened to them during the Babylonian captivity. For between that captivity, which lasted only 70 years, and the miserable state in which they have been for 1600 years, there is a great difference.

II. Moreover, it is certain that the 70 weeks of Daniel have expired, whether one begins counting them from the 2nd year of Darius Nothus, or from the 20th of Artaxerxes, or from another point in time that we have cited in the preceding chapters. The Messiah, who was to come then and be cut off after the end of 69 weeks, has come.

III. This observation is confirmed by the following. The Messiah had to come while the Second Temple stood; he has therefore come, since this Second Temple was destroyed and laid in ashes by the Romans.

To these reasons, which we draw from scripture, we can add several others that confirm the same truth.

The wretched state of the Jews, the confusion of their tribes, the futile efforts they have made to restore themselves, are proofs that place the coming of Christ beyond dispute. In the year 135, Emperor Hadrian forbade them from even turning their eyes toward Judea. <margin>Apology, chapter 21</margin> Tertullian <note>An early Christian author from Carthage, writing around 200 AD.</note> recounts how in his time they

The Emperor Honorius deprived them of the right to appoint Patriarchs and to pay them the tribute money; Julian the Apostate, having permitted them to rebuild the Temple in the year 363 and having given the management thereof to Alypius of Antioch, who had previously been the Governor in Britain, it happened, <margin>Book 23. Now everyone knows how greatly their tribes and genealogical registers are confused, and that the House of David is entirely unknown among them; who then can doubt that the Messiah has come?

The calling of the Gentiles, which was to follow the coming of the Messiah, also proves as clear as day that he has come.

According to the tradition of the House of <margin>In the Talmud, Codex Sanhedrin, chapter 11</margin> Elias, which the Jews highly extol, the Messiah was to come 4000 years after the Creation of the world.

Maimonides <note>A preeminent medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher and scholar.</note>, in the letter cited by Vossius, brings forward a tradition which says that the Messiah was to come in the year 4976.

<margin>Objections of the Jews.</margin>
I. They say that the Messiah indeed should have come at the time we specify, but that their sins have prevented his appearance, and that he awaits Israel’s conversion.

**Answer 1.** Let them tell us what this great sin is that has delayed the coming of the Messiah. They acknowledge that their first Temple was destroyed because of their idolatry, their licentiousness, and their murders. Yet, they remained in captivity in Babylon for no longer than 70 years, and they had Prophets who comforted them. How is it that God has kept them in this miserable state now for more than 1,600 years, even though during this time they have guarded themselves against all idolatry? It is true that they already had a great aversion to it under the second Temple, preferring to suffer anything rather than allow the Image of the Emperor or the Roman Eagle to be erected in the Temple. Certainly, the Jews can point to no cause for their long-lasting dispersion, unless they consider that it is because they put the Messiah to death. Therefore, the Messiah has come.

The Jews will say that the death of Christ is a crime that cannot be blamed on the Judges of that time. But 1. It was the crime of the Great Council, which represented the entire people. 2. One must well note that they cried out, *His blood be upon us and upon our children.* 3. Today’s Jews, through their stubbornness, approve the verdict of the ancients.

2. How can they prove that the coming of the Messiah is conditional? Where has God said, "if they should convert"? And how is it that we have seen, and still see, that everything which according to the Prophets was to happen after the coming of the Messiah has indeed occurred, if he has not come? There is in the <term>Talmud</term><note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah and the Gemara.</note> (Codex Sanhedrin, Chapter Helek) a dispute between two prominent Rabbis, R. siah is postponed because of their sins, and the other denies it.

II. They say that the Messiah must only come at the end of days, <term>Isaiah II. 2.</term>

**Answer.** They do not notice that the "last days" do not signify the end of the world, but the end of the old dispensation <note>original: "huishoudinge"; referring to the era of the Old Testament law.</note>. They themselves distinguish between two ages: the present and the future. They call the present the time in which the Prophets prophesied, and the future the time of the coming of the Messiah. Why then can one not say that the Messiah was to come at the end of the age which they themselves call the present age? One must not always press too hard on the word "end"; compare in this regard <term>Job XLII. 12.</term> with verse 16.

<margin>Maimonides in "The Laws of Kings," final chapter <note>original: "Maim. in Hilcot Melachim, e. ult."</note></margin>
III. They say that the mountain of the Lord has not yet been seen exalted above the other mountains, as was predicted, <term>Isaiah II. 2.</term>

**Answer.** One would have to make oneself ridiculous to take this divine oracle literally. The Jews themselves acknowledge that the Messiah was not meant to change nature. Who does not see that the aim of the Spirit in these words is to promise the Church a greater glory than she had previously possessed; but a spiritual glory, as some Jews acknowledge.

IV. They object with the following words from <term>Verses 2 and 3</term>: *And all nations shall go thither, and say, come let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, etc.* This, according to their view, indicates that when the Messiah comes, all nations will place themselves under his banner, and there will be only one faith.

**Answer.** This is not the sense of the words. They mean only that the Church shall be gathered from all nations: for the scripture teaches us that in the beginning, all things are not to be subjected to Christ. It says that he must rule in the midst of his enemies, that he would crush them with an iron scepter, and that he would be an object of offense.

That the oracles which foretold that idols would be destroyed in the time of the Messiah did not have to receive their fulfillment all at once, but by degrees; that furthermore, the Christian Religion condemns all sorts of idolatry; and that idolatry is banished from all places and communities where the true Gospel is confessed in its purity; and that if there is still a Church that gives itself the name of "Christian Church" and is nonetheless defiled with idolatry, it must be regarded as an Antichristian Church.

They say that the Gospel differs so much from the law which God has instituted, that one cannot regard the maker of the Gospel as the Messiah.

I answer that the Law contains two kinds of commandments, of which some are so consistent with God's holiness that one cannot release oneself from the obligation one has to maintain them. Others depend so much on His will that He himself could release men from them whenever He judged it good. If the Gospel opposed the first kind of commandments, there would be reason to regard it as a false doctrine, and not to recognize its giver as the Messiah; but far from opposing these commandments, it confirms them. Regarding the others, it is true that he no longer desires us to maintain them, but it is because it clearly appears through the oracles of the Old Testament that God no longer requires it, since He had only prescribed these commandments for a time, as we just said.

They say that Christ caused himself to be worshipped as God.

They say that it appears to them as something inconceivable that the Deity should unite Himself with human nature.

### VIII. CHAPTER.

->Of the Law.<-

Before God sent his Son into the world, he wished to give his Law to mankind. We shall see in the following why he acted in this manner; now we must investigate what the Law is that God has given. But, before we come to the investigation of this matter, it is necessary to make two or three observations.

1. That one must generally understand the **Law** as a standard <note>original: "rigtsnoer," meaning a rule or plumb-line</note> that binds the people to whom it is given.
2. That, from the beginning of Creation, God imprinted a natural Law in the heart of man to be a rule for his duties.
3. That all people find this Law written in their hearts, the principles of which are these: that one must worship God, that one must honor one's parents, that one must do to another what one
<sig>Part I.</sig>

<column-break/>

wishes to be done to oneself, etc.

Holy Scripture does not allow us to doubt that there is such a natural Law. Paul speaks of it expressly, Rom. II, 14, saying that the Heathens are a Law unto themselves. We have dealt with that in Book I of our work.

This is confirmed by the unanimous consent of nations, among whom one finds these first seeds of knowledge and these first principles, of which we have spoken elsewhere.

It is true that there are nations that have even established godless Laws: but it is because they misused the reason that God had given them, and took no heed of the principles of Natural Law that were within them.

The Heathens then recognized the Natural Law. Cicero, speaking of the efforts one makes to protect one's life, says that it is a Law which is not written, but born with us, which we have not learned, received, nor read, but have accepted and sucked in from nature, for which we were not fashioned or taught, but for which we were made and imbued. <note>original: "non scripta, sed nata lex" - a famous quote from Cicero’s defense of Milo, arguing that self-defense is a natural right.</note>

This Natural Law can neither be abolished nor destroyed. It is the same in Rome, in Athens, everywhere.

God has had the same Law proclaimed to mankind, and then it is called the Moral Law <term>Moral Law: "Zede-Wet," referring to the divinely revealed ethical commandments, such as the Ten Commandments, as opposed to ritual or civil laws</term>. This he has done: 1. To confirm the Natural Law which he had engraved in the hearts of all men. 2. To prevent the natural knowledge one has of good and evil from being erased by the corruption of mankind. 3. To prevent this knowledge from being taken for a mere human invention. 4. To place people’s duty more clearly before their eyes. 5. To restore the Natural Law, as it has suffered through sin, and to renew the ideas that had perished. There are other reasons to be given for this, which we shall cite in the following.

There is, then, no essential difference between the Natural and the Moral Law. Both prescribe the same duties, both toward God and toward our neighbor.

The difference is further minor. The proclaimed Law explains the duties of man more clearly than the Natural Law, not to mention that the one is written on stone, and the other on the fleshy tables of

# THE CHRISTIAN...

...had been written on the heart; that the one is common to all, and the other was made known only to those who have the Law of Moses.

<margin>Acts VII. 38.</margin>
From the sermon of Stephen, it appears that it was the Son of God who gave the Law, and that Moses received it from him. Acts VII. 38. *This is he who was in the congregation (of the people) in the wilderness with the Angel, who spoke to him on Mount Sinai, and (with) our Fathers, who received the living words to give to us.* This same Angel appeared to Moses in the burning bush, verse 35, and called himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, verse 32, which belongs to none but Christ, who is the Angel of the Covenant <note>This identifies the "Angel of the Lord" in the Old Testament as the pre-incarnate Christ.</note>.

<margin>Acts VII. 53. Gal. III. 19. Heb. II. 2.</margin>
The Angels appeared at the giving of the Law as God’s servants, as Stephen testifies in Acts VII. 53, saying that the Jews had received the Law through the "dispositions" <note>original: *bestellingen*; referring to the administrative ordering or ranks of angels</note>, or multitude of the Angels. Paul says, Gal. III. 19, that it was ordained by the hand of Angels, and calls it in Heb. II. 2 a word spoken through Angels.

Mount Sinai or Horeb, situated in the deserts of Arabia, was the place where God proclaimed his Law.

The Ancients sought many mysteries in the giving of the Law on a mountain, and particularly on Mount Sinai. Their thoughts are more ingenious than substantial, except for those based on the explanations of Paul.

They said that the Law was given on a mountain so that man might take heed of how far God is exalted above him, and that this small elevation might bring to mind the infinite distance between the Creator and the creatures. 2. To signify how far the Law that he gave his people is exalted above all human laws. 3. To teach us that, however much God might descend to us, we still have high to climb, and we shall never reach his height. They added that God chose Mount Sinai over other mountains because there is none that better represents the nature of the Law. Sinai was a barren mountain, and so full of sharp rocks that one shuddered just to look at it. Moreover, Sinai is the same as Hagar, according to Paul in Gal. IV. 24, who signifies

<column-break/>

servitude—a beautiful example of the Law, which is barren and bears no children to God, but makes slaves <note>In Galatians, Paul uses the allegory of Hagar and Sarah to contrast the "slavery" of the Law with the "freedom" of the Gospel.</note>.

The time at which God gave the Law was the fiftieth day after the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt; therefore it is called Pentecost <note>original: *Pinksterdag*; literally "fiftieth day," referring to the feast of Shavuot or Pentecost</note>, and it is Moses to whom God gave it.

When God gave the Law, the mountain was entirely in fire and flame; it lightened and thundered from all sides; and there were barriers set around the foot of the mountain to prevent the people from approaching, Heb. XII. 18, 19, 20, 21. *You are not come unto the mount that might be touched,* says Paul, *and the burning fire, and blackness, and darkness, and tempest, and the sound of a trumpet, and the voice of words; which they that heard entreated that the word should not be spoken to them any more; for they could not endure that which was commanded. And if so much as a beast touch the mountain, it shall be stoned, or thrust through with a dart; and Moses (so terrible was the sight) said, I exceedingly fear and quake.*

One must not doubt that God used this terrible display to compel the Israelites to receive his Law with fear and trembling. Through this, he also wished to signify the effects that the Law would produce.

If we read the ancient and modern commentators, they will tell us:

1. That God appeared in the midst of the fire to show that he is a consuming fire to those who transgress his commandments; and that his Law itself is a fire that shows us the thistles of man's sins but does not consume them; which burns the conscience but neither softens nor gladdens it.

2. That there was darkness to represent the darkness of the old dispensation <note>original: *Huishouding*; literally "household management," used here for the theological concept of a divine "economy" or era.</note>.

3. That there were storms and whirlwinds to signify what the Law is; it is like a whirlwind that rustles the soul, overturns it, and sometimes brings it to despair by showing it the abyss of Hell.

4. If it is said that all were spectators and witnesses of this terrible display, so amazed...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the giving of the Law on Mount Sinai, specifically examining the reaction of the Israelites and the distinction between the three types of laws given to Moses: the Moral, Ceremonial, and Civil laws. ->### DIVINITY. BOOK IX. CHAPTER VIII.<-

stood, so that they said to Moses: *You speak with us, and we will hear, but let the Lord speak no more to us!* This is to teach us: 1. That the usual effect of the Law is to strike fear into man and to disturb him. 2. That the sinner cannot hear God’s voice without trembling. 3. That God’s wrath is unbearable for the creature. 4. That the Law is a schoolmaster <note>The author uses the term "tugtmeester" (tutor or schoolmaster), referencing Galatians 3:24, where the Law leads believers to Christ.</note> who makes us seek a Mediator between God and ourselves.

5. If it is said that God had the mountain marked out with boundaries and forbade the people from approaching it on pain of death, it is to give us to understand: 1. That God drives sinners away from His presence, whereas Christ calls them to Himself through the Gospel; Matthew 11:28: <note>The original text cites Matthew 12:28, but the verse quoted is actually Matthew 11:28.</note> *Come unto me, all ye that labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.* 2. That one must not be too curious regarding holy things.

This Law was written down, and God willed to write it Himself upon stone tablets so that it would not be forgotten. Theologians give various reasons for this; those of the Jewish Masters <note>A reference to Rabbinic scholars or commentators.</note> are full of clever subtlety.

It is said that God willed to describe the Law with His own finger, that is to say, immediately and by Himself,
<margin>Exodus 31:18. 32:16.</margin>
1. To show the excellence of His Law above all human laws, and above the other laws that He subsequently gave to Moses. 2. To teach us that God alone can write His law in our hearts. That it was written on stone tablets indicated: 1. That the same should always be the rule of our deeds; that which is engraved in stone or steel is not easily erased. 2. That the heart by nature is a heart of stone. These tablets were written on both sides, so that one would neither add to nor take away from them.

Moses gave three laws to the people. The **Moral Law**, divided into two tablets, which teaches us what we owe to God and our neighbor. The **Ceremonial Law**, which deals with the rites of the Levitical Service. The **Civil Law**, which concerned the governance of Israel's State.

The **Moral Law** regards the people of Israel as a gathering of men who must be obedient to their Creator. The **Ceremonial Law**, as a

<column-break/>

church that expected the Messiah who had been promised to her. The **Civil Law**, as a people and commonwealth set apart from all others. The Ceremonial Law looks directly toward God; the Civil Law toward our fellow man; and the Moral Law toward what we owe to both.

These Laws are very different from one another. The **Moral Law** has been impressed upon the heart of man since the beginning of creation. The other two were given in the time of Moses. The Moral Law is a universal rule that obligates all men. The others obligate the Israelites alone.

The Moral Law is almost entirely grounded in <term>natural law</term> <note>Law believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason.</note>. By natural law, one understands that which rests upon God’s holy and righteous being. For example, the commandment that makes up the summary of the Law—*Thou shalt love the Lord thy God*—is grounded in God’s nature, and it is an unbreakable command; otherwise, one would have to say that God could command that one hate Him, which is a godless thought. But the other Laws are grounded in a <term>positive and arbitrary law</term> <note>Laws based on specific decrees or the will of a legislator rather than inherent nature.</note>. By positive and arbitrary law, one understands that which depends entirely upon God’s will and pleasure, such that God could have chosen not to prescribe it to men without offending any of His perfections. One of the most learned Jews who lived in recent centuries <note>Likely referring to Maimonides or a similar Sephardic scholar.</note> said that the Moral Law, if it were not written, would have to be written; but that if God had not seen fit to give the others, one could do things entirely contrary to them without sinning. The Moral Law is naturally known. The Heathens have not been ignorant of it, even though they did not have it written on stone tablets and had greatly corrupted it through their conduct of life. The Ceremonial Law does not naturally occur to man's thoughts; and regarding the Civil Law, although it rests upon sound reason in its general commands, it is nevertheless certain that, regarding its specific decrees, it depends solely upon God. The Moral Law is immutable and must last forever, although not all the commandments of this Law are equally unchangeable; for there are those which are founded absolutely upon God’s being and His holiness, so that God could not command that

one could transgress them without denying God’s own nature. Thus, God cannot command that one serve other Gods, that one use His name in vain, that one lie, etc. etc. But there are other commandments of the **Moral Law** which are grounded in the nature of things in the state wherein God has placed them. Men must never transgress these commandments on their own authority; but God has the power to command such in certain cases. For example, God can command one to kill, and to take a neighbor’s property, just as He commanded **Abraham** to offer up his son, and the **Israelites** to take the vessels of the **Egyptians** with them. <note>Referencing Genesis 22 and Exodus 11:2, where God gives specific commands that seem to contradict the general Moral Law against killing and theft.</note> Although the Law commands that we shall be obedient to our Parents, God nevertheless forbids us to obey them if they demand anything of us that runs against His will.

Regarding the determination of the **seventh day**, which we, according to the precept of the Moral Law, must hallow to God, it is clear that this commandment could be revoked and abolished by God Himself, since it rests upon a <term>positive law</term> <note>The original Dutch "willekeurig regt" refers to laws established by God's choice or decree (positive law), rather than laws inherent to His moral nature (natural law).</note>; so that God, if it had pleased Him, could have required of men the celebration of the first day of the week as well as the last. It appears, therefore, that the Moral Law, in respect of most commandments, is unchangeable, but that the **Ceremonial** and **Civil** laws could be abolished, as we shall see in the following that they have been abolished. It is more difficult for man to keep the commandments of the Moral Law than those of the Ceremonial, because he must struggle against his passions and resist his natural inclinations.

The Moral Law is called the **Ten Commandments** or Words, because it consists of ten commandments. Paul calls the Ceremonial Law, in Ephesians 2:15, the *Law consisting of ordinances*; and the Civil Law is often expressed in Scripture by the word *Judgment*.

We shall have opportunity to speak more broadly of the Moral Law when we deal with the work of **Sanctification**: for it is the perfect rule of our works and morals.

### CHAPTER IX.

->*On the Ceremonial Law.*<-

**W**E have said that the **Ceremonial Law** regarded the ceremonies of the old <term>dispensation</term> <note>The "old economy" or "old householding," referring to the religious system of the Old Testament.</note> in what concerned Religion. To clarify this, we must first note why God gave the same to His people, and secondly, examine what it generally consists of.
One can give three reasons for which God gave this Law.

The 1st was to distinguish His people from all other nations, who had their ceremonies, their customs, their religions, etc. It was fitting that the subjects of the King of kings were set apart from the other nations.

The 2nd reason was to keep the people of Israel in check, and to prevent them from giving themselves over to the superstitions of the Heathens and following their idolatry. It appears that they had begun to give themselves over to this in the land of **Egypt**.
<margin>Joshua 24:14.</margin>
Joshua 24:14: *Put away the gods,* said Joshua, *which your Fathers served on the other side of the River and in Egypt.* See Ezekiel 23:2, 3. The Israelites worshipped the golden calf in the Wilderness, and that in imitation of what they had seen done in Egypt, if one gives credit to certain Scholars.
<margin>Philo [of Alexandria], Book 3, *On the Life of Moses*, p. 677; also the Jerusalem Targum on Exodus 32:6. Lactantius, Book 4, chapter 10; on Hosea 4. Kircher, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*, vol. 1, p. 29. Bochart, *Hierozoicon* [Sacred Animals], Book 1, p. 1, Col. 346. Ephesians 1:14.</margin>
The Prophet **Amos** brings God speaking thus against His people: *But ye have borne the Tabernacle of your Moloch and Chiun your images, the star of your god, which ye made to yourselves.* Amos 5:26. To restrain a people so greatly inclined toward Idolatry, God gave them a Law that kept them occupied in constant practice.

The 3rd reason was to foreshadow the things which were to happen, and principally the **Messiah**, and all that He had to perform to accomplish the work of salvation.

# THE CHRISTIAN [DIVINITY] #

II. The Ceremonial Law concerned, among other things, the Persons who had to set themselves apart for the service of God.

There were those whom God raised up in an extraordinary way, such as the Prophets; but there were also those who were called to it in the common manner. These were:

1. **The High Priest**, of whom the scripture relates the consecration and describes the garments, qualities, and ministry of office. He alone had the privilege of entering the Holy of Holies once a year. He prefigured Christ, who is the true High Priest. <note>In Christian theology, this is known as "typology," where Old Testament figures or rituals are seen as "shadows" or symbols that point toward the life and work of Jesus.</note>

The qualities and conditions required to serve in the High-Priestly Office were: 1. That the High Priest had to be of the lineage of Aaron. 2. That there be no blemish in his birth. 3. That he did not marry an impure or frivolous woman, nor one born of a foreigner or a bastard, or from any other marriage forbidden by the Law. It was also forbidden for him to marry a widow, a prisoner, or one who had converted to Judaism. 4. He could have no other wives. <margin>Leviticus 21:5</margin> 5. There had to be no defect in any outward part of his body. 6. One must further note: 1. That there was to be only one High Priest. 2. Yet there were deputies. <note>The "deputy" or *Sagan* served as a substitute in case the High Priest became ritually "unclean" and unable to perform his duties.</note> 3. That the name of High Priest was given not only to his deputy, but also to the heads of the 24 courses or divisions of Priests who performed the Temple service; to the deposed priests; to all those of the priestly lineage from whom the High Priests were chosen; and to the President of the Sanhedrin <note>The *Sanhedrin* was the supreme judicial and religious council of the Jews.</note>, which consisted of 71 members. Thus Annas and Caiaphas were called High Priests. <margin>Acts 4:6</margin> Because one was truly the High Priest and the other presided in the Sanhedrin. 4. It is said that he had no jurisdiction in civil matters; and that if any High Priests concerned themselves with affairs of state, this happened during the minority of the Kings, or when the Queen-regents abused their power. 5. He could perform service every day and light the incense in the Holy Place. 6. He alone was anointed with the holy Oil, to the exclusion of all common priests.

Above all, one must carefully observe:

<column-break/>

1. That, according to God’s institution, there could be only one High Priest, to signify that we have only one Mediator, but that our Mediator—and at the same time High Priest—has no deputies. 2. That he was the head of the other Priests. 3. That his attire was much more precious than that of the others, and that he wore a hat on which was a plate of pure Gold, in which these words were engraved: *Holiness to the Lord.* 4. That every year he made a solemn atonement for sins and served as an intercessor for the people before God. 5. That he blessed the same. It is easy to apply all these things to Christ.

2. There were various other Priests of a lower rank.

These 1. also had to be taken from the descendants of Abraham. 2. From the tribe of Levi, and the lineage of Aaron through his sons Ithamar and Eleazar. 3. They had to have no defect or blemish on their body. <margin>Leviticus 21:17</margin> 4. They had to abstain from all strong drink. 5. They were not permitted to mourn the dead, unless it was a close relative. This was also forbidden to the High Priest. 6. They could not enter into marriage with a woman of loose living or one who had been abandoned by another.

Their duties consisted: 1. In teaching the people God’s Law. 2. In blessing them. 3. In separating the clean from the unclean according to God’s command. 4. In judging all kinds of uncleanness. 5. In the slaughter and preparation of the sacrificial animals. 6. In lighting the lamps in the Holy Place every day and maintaining the oil therein. 7. In lighting the incense before the face of the Lord every day. 8. In arranging the Showbread on the Table. It is also easy to apply all these things to Christ, the ministers of the Gospel, and the believers. The Priests were divided into 24 groups or courses, of which each group or course had its weekly service in its order and turn.

3. **The Levites** served the Priests, whether to clean the holy vessels, to slaughter the sacrificial animals, or to set the Showbread.

<margin>Numbers 3:31 etc.</margin>
There were three lineages of Levites: that of the Kohathites, who had to care for the Ark, the Table, the Lampstand, the Altars, and the vessels of the Sanctuary, as well as the hangings with their accessories. But it was not permitted for them to [touch] the—

I shall say but two words about the Gatekeepers, the Singers, and the Nethinim.

The Gatekeepers, or Overseers of the Temple doors, watched the entire day to ensure that no one caused any disorder or noise, or approached the Temple when he was forbidden by the Law to enter therein. At night they kept watch, and the Jews tell us here that there were 24 guards placed in the Second Temple, consisting of 21 Levites and 3 Priests. They made rounds the whole night and, if someone was found sleeping, it was permitted to beat him and set his clothes on fire. <note>This traditional Jewish practice of burning the clothes of a sleeping guard is often cited by commentators to explain the biblical imagery of "keeping one’s garments" so as not to walk naked.</note> Possibly this is alluded to in Revelation 16:15: *Blessed is he who watches, and keeps his clothes.* It is said that these guards were also divided into 24 groups.

The Singers were divided into 24 groups, each group consisting of twelve.

On the 1st day of the week, they sang Psalm 24; on the 2nd, Psalm 48; on the 3rd, Psalm 82; on the 4th, Psalm 94; on the 5th, Psalm 81; on the 6th, Psalm 93; on the 7th, or Sabbath day, Psalm 92, with a sixth part of the *Song of Moses*, Deuteronomy 32, in the morning service, and a sixth part of the Song from Exodus 15 in the evening service.

who were appointed to provide everything that was in the rooms of the Temple, to clean all holy things—without, however, being allowed to enter the Holy Place; they took care of the supply of wood, grain, etc., and for the garments of the Priests, etc.

These had servants under them who were called Nethinim <note>original: "Nethinim"; a Hebrew term meaning "given ones" or "dedicated ones," referring to temple assistants of non-Israelite origin.</note>, woodcutters, and water carriers. In the beginning, Joshua chose the Gibeonites for this. But David and Solomon added others to them.

4. Among the Temple servants, the Nazirites are also placed. There were two kinds of them. Some were so from their mother’s womb, like Samson (Judges 13:5); others by vow, and for a certain time. They were not permitted to consume strong drink. The Rabbis make a distinction here and say that they were indeed free to drink liquor made from dates and other fruits, but none in which wine, or that which comes from grapes, was present. Some go so far as to say that it was not permitted for them to attend gatherings where wine was drunk, or to pass by a vineyard. The razor was not allowed to pass over their head, except—say the Rabbis—in cases where the Law required it; for example, if a Nazirite had become leprous and was healed during the time of his Naziriteship, he had to allow himself to be shaved. They were not permitted to touch dead bodies, even those of their closest relatives. The Jewish Masters claim, however, that if a Nazirite found a corpse on the road and there was no one to bury it, he was obliged to do it himself; but then he was bound to begin the days and ceremonies of another Naziriteship again.

It is probable that when they entered into it, they purified themselves and shaved their heads, as is believed can be inferred from Acts 21:24 and 18:18, and from what had to be done for a Nazirite if he had touched a dead person. Finally, they had to give themselves over to the contemplation of holy things and to the strict observance of religion. The Scripture does not say how many days the Naziriteship had to last. ->THE CHRISTIAN GOD<-

did not defile himself with the dead. <note>Under Jewish law, Nazirites were forbidden from touching or being near a corpse, as it would break their vow of consecration.</note> The Nazirites are magnificent examples of Christ, the true Nazirite of the Lord, who was sanctified to God from the moment of his conception, who knew no sin, and whose life was a constant exercise in temperance, sobriety, and all virtues.

III. The Ceremonial Law also served to point out everything that had to be brought and sacrificed to God.

Two kinds of things were offered to God: inanimate and soulless things, such as bread, wine, and oil; or animate things, such as beasts.

Before we discuss this more broadly, let us first consider a few observations.

1. That the offerings were instituted by God, even though Moses does not tell us in express words that God commanded the same to the Patriarchs. We do not doubt it, however, for three reasons: 1. Because nothing in the Holy Service can be pleasing to God except that which He Himself has instituted. 2. Because it is said in **Hebrews 11:4** that Abel offered through faith. Now, faith presupposes the revelation of God’s will. 3. Because it does not naturally come to mind that, in order to serve the Deity—who is a Spirit—one must slaughter beasts.

Some, like Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople.</note> and certain Jewish scholars, have been of the opinion that the law of offering is a natural law, and that consequently the first humans sacrificed because their consciences taught them that this was a reasonable form of worship. This view has also been adopted by those who maintain the necessity of a perpetual sacrifice in the Church. But in truth, reason does not teach that one must shed the blood of animals to please the Deity. *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian; the reference is to his work *On the Truth of the Christian Religion*, Book 5.</note> (**On the Truth of the Christian Religion, Chapter 5**) was of the opinion that offerings were of human institution. But no worship belongs to God that is invented by men (**Isaiah 29:13**). One might say that no command to sacrifice is found in the text. But one also does not find many other things mentioned that were nevertheless observed.

It is said that by this explanation, one places the sacrifice of Cain on the same level as that of Abel; for thus Cain’s offering was also offered through faith—that is, by virtue of obedience to the law and institution of offerings that had been prescribed to Adam. 

<column-break/>

one adds to this, that Paul’s intention <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul’s discussion of Abel in the New Testament book of Hebrews.</note> is only to make us understand that Abel’s sacrifice was done through faith, and that of Cain was not. But this by no means follows. I admit that Paul’s intention is as it is supposed, and that Cain did not offer through faith: but I propose two things simultaneously. 1. That Cain and Abel did not sacrifice except in accordance with God’s command. 2. That Abel would not have offered through faith if he had not received a command to sacrifice. All those who offer through faith, offer by virtue of some command. But not all who obey the command to sacrifice therefore offer through faith. From Abel’s offering through faith, one can therefore certainly conclude that there was a command.

The question is asked: what offerings were sacrificed before the Law? <note>The "Law" refers to the Mosaic Law given at Mount Sinai.</note>

Answer: It is said burnt offerings (**Genesis 8:20**). Such was undoubtedly that of Abel. But it is believed that the sacrifice that Jacob offered when Laban had overtaken him was a thank offering: for it was an act of communal joy to confirm their reconciliation, and it appears that when he called his brothers to eat, it was the meat of a sacrificed animal. It is certain that Cain’s offering consisted of the fruits of the earth.

1. Regarding the beasts that were slaughtered:

The question is asked: did the distinction between clean and unclean animals exist then? It is written that Noah took of all clean animals, but one may believe that this was said by way of anticipation. <note>That is, Moses used the terms "clean" and "unclean" when writing the history of Noah to make it understandable to his contemporary readers who knew the Mosaic Law.</note> *Grotius*, writing on **Genesis 8**, is of the opinion that there was no other reason for this distinction than the aversion people have for certain animals whose meat they dare not consume.

2. One must note that in the beginning, offerings could be made by anyone. It seems to be an error to suggest that the eldest son alone had this right and that the priestly dignity belonged to him alone.

The question is asked: who were priests before the times of Moses?

Answer: According to the Jews, the eldest son was by nature clothed with this dignity; and they say that he had privileges here: 1. Authority and governance. 2. A double portion; and according to this custom, one must interpret the question of Elisha...

<meta>This page continues the catalog of Mosaic laws and religious observances from the previous page, moving from tithes and first-fruits into a detailed description of the five major Jewish feast days: Passover, Pentecost, Tabernacles, Trumpets, and the Day of Atonement.</meta>

<page-num>534</page-num>
<header>THE CHRISTIAN</header>

There were several Feast days.

1. **The Feast of the Passover** <note>original: "Paaschfeest"</note>, the institution of which can be seen in Exod. XII. 1. and XXIII 14. Lev. XXIII. 5. Deut. XVI. 15. All the male lineage was obliged to present themselves there, and it was celebrated in memory of the departure of the children of Israel out of the prison of Egypt. The same began on the 15th of the month of Nisan, which corresponds partly with our month of March and partly with April; it lasted seven days; it is also called the feast of seven days. Ezech. XLV. 21. 2 Chron. XXX. 21. We shall speak of this further when we treat of the Signs of the Covenant.

2. **The Feast of Pentecost** <note>original: "Pinxter-feest"</note>, on which the Jews held a remembrance of the Giving of the Law on Mount Sinai; the word "Pentecost" means "fiftieth," because one counted 49 days from Passover, and the 50th day was that of the Feast. It was called the Feast of Weeks or the Feast of Seven Weeks, because one counted seven weeks. Exod. XXXIV. 22. Lev. XXIII. 15. It was also called the Feast of the Harvest, or the Feast of the First-fruits, etc. One finds the institution of it in Exod. XXIII. 16. and Deut. XVI. 10. Just as one offered the first-fruits of the grains at Passover, at Pentecost one offered the first-fruits of the cakes, and two loaves were lifted up to make an offering to God, as the first-fruits of the bread by which they usually had to live. These two loaves were offered and waved around; one belonged to the High Priest, and the other to the rest of the Priests: with these loaves, two lambs were offered as a thank-offering, the meat of which also went to the Priests. On that day, the Great Hallel <note>original: "groote lofzang," referring to Psalms 113–118</note> was sung, as also at Passover: it was on this day that the Holy Spirit descended upon the Apostles in the form of divided tongues, as of fire. Acts II. 1, 2. etc.

3. **The Feast of Tabernacles** <note>original: "Loof-hutten-feest"</note>, which the Jews celebrated in memory of their fathers having lived in tents in the Wilderness, and that God had given them a Land overflowing with everything. This Feast was also called the Feast of Palms or Willow-trees, because they were accustomed to carry these during this Feast; they came into the Temple every day with a palm branch and placed their branches around the Altar, crying *Hosanna* <note>A Hebrew expression of prayer or praise, meaning "save, please"</note>, while meanwhile

<column-break/>

the Priests blew on the Trumpets; it was also called the Feast of the Ingathering, Exod. XXIII. 16. because it was celebrated after the wheat, the wine, and the other fruits had been gathered; its institution can be seen in Num. XXIX. 2. Lev. XXIII. 34. It began on the 15th of the month of Tizri <note>Tishrei</note>, which corresponds with our September and October; it lasted 8 days, the first and the last being the most solemn; they had to live in tents as long as this Feast lasted, Lev. XXIII. 42. Neh. VIII. 17. They set these up in the streets, on the roofs of their houses, in other open places, and even in the Forecourts of the Temple. Some have believed that (during this Feast) people went to draw water from the Fountain of Siloam <note>original: "Siloë"</note>, and that they performed sprinklings with it in the Temple, and that Isaiah alludes to this in the 12th Chapter, as does Christ in the 7th Chapter of John, verse 37.

4. **The Feast of Trumpets** <note>original: "Feest der Trompetten"</note>, which was celebrated on the first day of the month of Tizri, the first of the months of the Civil Year; it was the most important of the new moons; its institution can be read in Lev. XXIII. 24. Num. XXIX. 1. etc. It was called the Feast of Trumpets because of the sound of trumpets heard from all sides; Psalm LXXXI was sung in the Sanctuary. The Jews say that this was done in memory of Israel’s deliverance: but it was because it was the first day of the Civil Year.

5. **The Feast of Atonement** <note>original: "Feest der Verzoening"</note>, which was called the Day of Fasting, was held on the 10th of the month of Tizri; on that day, one was obliged to fast and to afflict one's soul; a general atonement for all sins was made then; the institution of this Feast can be read in Levit. XVI. On this day, the High Priest took two goats, which he offered to God at the door of the tent of meeting; he cast lots over them, and the one that was for God was slaughtered, and the other kept to be sent into the Wilderness: six days before this Feast, the godly and penitent made confession of the sins they had committed against their neighbor, in the presence of some witnesses, and at the same time made restitution for the harm they had done him. Six days before the day of atonement, the High Priest was placed in a chamber called the <term>Parhedrin</term> <note>A Greek term for a specific room in the Temple where the High Priest stayed for seven days prior to Yom Kippur to ensure ritual purity.</note>, and during

During these seven days, the High Priest performed the daily service himself, and a helper was given to him to perform the service should he become defiled. On the third day, the ashes of the Red Heifer <note>The Red Heifer ceremony in Numbers 19 provided water for ritual purification</note> were sprinkled upon him; some of the eldest members of the Great Council <note>the Sanhedrin, the supreme rabbinic court</note> read to him the order and the ecclesiastical solemnities of the service. On the morning of the day before, he was brought to the door of the Temple, and the sacrificial animal was shown to him. He was led into the chamber where the incense was prepared, so that he might be instructed in the manner in which one must burn incense. On the evening of the preceding day, he ate little, and the night passed in reading and explaining the Law. When the day arrived, the High Priest washed himself, put on his precious garments—called the golden garments—and offered the continual sacrifice. Thereafter, he took off his High-Priestly garments, and after having washed himself for the second time, he took the white linen garments, after which he laid his two hands upon the Bull that was to be sacrificed for himself and for his house, and he made this confession: 
> Lord, I have sinned, I and my house have acted wrongly, I pray you, cleanse me from these sins. 

Thereafter, he cast lots over the two goats with two golden pieces on which was written: *for the Lord*, *for Azazel* <note>original: "Hazazel," the "scapegoat" associated with the removal of sin</note>: these goats were placed to the right and left sides of the High Priest: the two pieces of gold were thrown into a vessel, the High Priest reached his two hands in, and took a piece of gold with each hand; the goats received the lot that came into the hand under which they stood. The Sagan <note>the deputy High Priest</note> was on the right, and the eldest of the Priests on the left; it was taken as a good omen if the lot of the goat Azazel fell into the right hand: a thread or ribbon of scarlet red was then tied between the horns of the goat Azazel; if this thread became white during the service, it was a good sign that God was appeased, and it is believed that Isaiah alludes to this. Chap. I. 18. *Though your sins be,* etc. Others believe that this ribbon became white when the goat had arrived in the wilderness; and as soon as the guide perceived this, he blew upon the horn which he had in his hand; those who stood stationed from place to place did the same, so that in an instant one could know that the re-

<column-break/>

-conciliation was accomplished, and the goat was cast away. But if the thread remained red, the horn was not blown, and the whole year the people were in mourning. I do not relate the other circumstances of these two goats, which can be read in Bochart’s *Of the Animals* <note>original: "de animalib." referring to Samuel Bochart’s 1663 work on animals in the Bible</note> and in the history of church doctrines by M. Jurieu <note>Pierre Jurieu, a prominent 17th-century Huguenot theologian</note>.

When the High Priest had slaughtered the first goat, he then went into the Holy of Holies with the incense, the blood of the cow, and of the slaughtered goat; he lit the incense, whose smoke covered the mercy seat <note>original: "verzoendekzel," the gold lid of the Ark of the Covenant where God’s presence was said to dwell</note>; subsequently, he performed the sprinkling of the shed blood seven times with his fingers.

He prayed as an intercessor before the face of God for himself and for the people.

Leaving the Holy of Holies, he cleansed the Tabernacle and the Altar, sprinkling the same seven times with blood.

Subsequently, he presented the other goat before God, which was still living and for Azazel, and he made confession of all the transgressions of the children of Israel, which he laid upon the head of the goat; he thereafter sent the same with a man into the wilderness, where he let it run free.

After this, the High Priest returned again to the Tabernacle and took off his linen garments and, after he had washed himself, he took his usual garments; thereafter he offered his burnt offering and that of the people, making atonement for himself and the people, and burning the fat of the sin offering. Finally, both the goat and the cow of the sin offering were brought outside the camp, and the hide, the flesh, and the offal were burned.

All these feasts also contain great mysteries, but one would have to write an entire book to unfold them.

6. God also willed that from seven to seven years, in the seventh year, the land should not be sown, nor harvested, nor plowed.

7. The Jubilee Year, which came every fifty years, was also remarkable. One finds the institution in Lev. XXV. 4-8. In this year 1. The land was not plowed 2. The slaves obtained their freedom 3. The lands returned again to the former owners.

To these feasts, which the church service appointed, several others were added in the following times.

1. The Jews celebrated many fast days, which are spoken of in Zechariah 7:3, 5 and 8:19. We shall deal with these in another place.

2. The Feast of Purim, mentioned in the Book of Esther, was held in memory of how God delivered the Jews from the rage of their enemies in the time of Ahasuerus. It was celebrated on the 14th and 15th of the month of Adar, which corresponds with our February. It was named Purim from a word meaning "lot," because a lot had been cast to destroy the Jews.

3. The Feast of Dedication <note>Original: "Feest van Inwying," now commonly known as Hanukkah</note>, which is spoken of in 1 Maccabees 4:59 and John 10:22, and by Josephus in *Antiquities of the Jews*, book 12, chapter 2.

This feast is also called the Feast of Lights; it was celebrated for eight days, beginning on the 25th of December. It was instituted on the occasion of the cleansing of the Temple, which had been profaned by Antiochus <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the Seleucid king</note> and was cleansed again by Judas <note>Judas Maccabeus</note>. During this feast, lights were lit in all the houses.

Josephus speaks of yet another feast that they had instituted for the time when the wood was brought into the Temple; see Book 2, chapter 17 of *The Jewish War* <note>original: "de Joodse Oorlogen"</note>.

We shall no longer dwell upon what the Ceremonial Law commanded, and we shall say nothing of the purifications which were directed toward the various uncleannesses shown by the Law in Leviticus 12, 13, 15, 18, 20; Deuteronomy 23:10; and Leviticus 5:3 and 15:5. What has been said will be enough to give us an idea of this Law.

## CHAPTER X.

->Of the Civil or Juridical Law.<-

The Civil Law was given for these four ends:

1. To show how the People of God must be led.

2. To separate them from the other nations, who also had their own laws and governments.

3. To prevent the Moral and Ecclesiastical Laws from being despised, and to ensure that they were upheld.

<column-break/>

4. To prefigure the spiritual Kingdom of Jesus Christ.

This Law appointed officials and courts of justice.

Among these officials, there were some who were instituted only for a certain time, such as the Judges, who ended with Samuel, and the Kings, of whom Zedekiah was the last. There were others who remained as long as the Jewish commonwealth lasted. Those among them who were of the highest standing were the 70 Elders who judged the people; others, who were of lesser rank, were the heads of households in the cities, and so on. There were three courts of justice among the Jews.

The 1st consisted of three Judges, and such a tribunal <note>original: "Vierschaar"</note> was in all the cities where there were fewer than 120 inhabitants. They settled all cases that arose there. These three judges were appointed either by the public authority of the Great Council <note>the Sanhedrin</note> in Jerusalem, following the command of God in Deuteronomy 16:18, or by the consent of those who were litigating together. These judges had to be wise, steadfast, and God-fearing,

<margin>Maimonides, *Sanhedrin*, ch. 11.</margin>
hating dishonest gain, loving the truth, loved by the people, and of a good reputation. These three men judged any injury done or received, and the restitution of anything that was stolen. It is said that they had the power to have someone flogged.

The 2nd consisted of 23 men, if one may believe the Rabbis, and they had their place in all large villages where there were more than 120 heads of households. There were two such courts within Jerusalem. Josephus says that each consisted of only 7 men.

<margin>*Antiquities*, book 4, ch. 8.</margin>
The 3rd was the Great Council; its institution is attributed to what God said to Moses in Numbers 11:16, 17: *Gather for me 70 men from the elders of Israel,*

<margin>Numbers 11:16, 17.</margin>
*whom you know to be the elders of the people and its officers, and you shall bring them before the Tent of Meeting, and they shall stand there with you; then I will come down and speak with you there, and I will take of the Spirit that is upon you and put it upon them, and they shall bear the burden of the people with you, so that you do not bear it alone.*

This Great Council consisted, according to some, of 72 men, and according to the—

Men were taken from every tribe, without distinction, whomever they wished to form this Great Council, but above all, many Priests were chosen.

The King was not permitted to appear there, if one may believe the famous *Maimonides* <note>Moses ben Maimon, a preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note>; but they did receive the High Priest if he possessed exemplary wisdom.

It is said that proselytes <note>Converts to Judaism</note> could be admitted there, which the Jews support with the example of Jethro <note>The father-in-law of Moses, who was a Midianite</note>.

They excluded from it: 1. Those who were burdened by great age; 2. Eunuchs <note>original: "gesnedenen"</note>; 3. Those who had no children; 4. Those who had not yet reached mature years; 5. Those who practiced no craft or art that was of benefit to human society; 6. Anyone who had a physical defect, such as blindness, a squint, etc. There were three men of great standing in this Council: 1. The President or the Prince <note>the *Nasi*</note>, 2. The Fathers of the Court <note>the *Av Beit Din*</note>, 3. The one called the Wise <note>the *Chakham*</note>, see *1 Corinthians 1:20*. Everyone was subject to the Great Council, including the High Priests and the Kings themselves.

I shall say no more of it, but I confess that I am entirely of the opinion of those who believe that the Great Council was not as the Jews describe it until they were under the power of the successors of *Alexander the Great* <note>Refers to the Hellenistic period, suggesting the Sanhedrin as described by later Rabbis was a later development</note>.

The guilty were condemned to various punishments; of those sentenced to death, some were stoned (some scholars, following the Jews, list eight different types of people who were punished with this penalty); others were burned (and they counted ten types of criminals who underwent this punishment); others were beheaded; others were strangled. If someone was stoned or killed by the sword, they tied his two hands together. They set a piece of wood upright from which a crossbar extended; they placed this crossbar between the two hands of the deceased, and they let him hang there until evening.

Of those who were not punished with death, some were condemned to a fine, *Deuteronomy 22:19*. Others to prison, others to the restitution of what they had taken or withheld, *Leviticus 5:15, 16*. Others to eq-

<column-break/>

-ual retribution <note>Original: "gelijke vergelding," referring to the *lex talionis*</note>, eye for eye, and tooth for tooth, etc. *Deuteronomy 19:21; Exodus 21*. Others were banished to the cities of refuge <note>original: "bysteden"</note>. Others were flogged, etc. *Deuteronomy 25:2, 3*.

It was not permitted to give more than forty lashes, and they usually gave only thirty-nine, *2 Corinthians 11:24*. This resulted from the form of the whip, which had three cords; everyone was subject to it, even the High Priest and the Head of the Great Council; and when he had undergone this punishment, he returned to his office, but the head of the Council descended several steps below the other councilors.

The Jews who have observed these customs add that the Kings were also subject to flogging, but they cite no example of it from the sacred Histories. *Schickard* in *The Royal Law of the Hebrews* <note>original: "Schikard. Jus Reg. c. 2. Theor. 7. p. 157"</note> cites the example of King Uzziah <note>original: "Ozias"</note>, but he also admits that God punished him directly rather than the Council.

In later times, the Jews adopted other punishments that were in use among other nations, such as Crucifixion, Sawing, being thrown into the sea or before wild beasts, Breaking on the wheel, beating with rods, Quartering, hacking into pieces, etc.

Regarding the manner of legal procedure observed in sentencing for the punishments I have mentioned, one may read those who have described the customs of the Jews.

I will add only a word regarding the Civil Law: namely, that it regulated many things concerning Religion and Church property; other things regarding household management, such as marriage, inheritance, usury <note>lending money at interest</note>, etc. Others concerned Civil matters, such as peace or war; and this shall be enough on this subject.

One can relate all the Civil Laws to the commandments of the Moral Law <note>The Ten Commandments</note>. To the first and second commandments belong what is said of Idolaters and those who deny God, *Exodus 22:20; Leviticus 20:1-5; Deuteronomy 18:9*; of idolatry, *Exodus 23:24; Numbers 33:52; Deuteronomy 7:5; 12:1-3*; Sorcerers and Witches, *Exodus 22:18; Leviticus 19:26-31; 20:6, 27; Deuteronomy 18:9, 22*; and of covenants <note>with pagans</note>, *Exodus 23:32, 33; 34:12, 16; Deuteronomy 7:1, 3*. To the third commandment belongs what is said of Blasphemers...

# CHAPTER XI.

->Why God willed to give His Law, before His Son had come.<-

It is natural to ask why God willed to give His Law before the coming of His Son.

If man had always remained in the state of righteousness, one would not have been surprised that God had given him His Law, because he was in a state to fulfill it. But it is surprising that, man having fallen into sin and no longer being able to be justified by the keeping of the Law—since he cannot fulfill it—God nevertheless gave him a Law, just as He had imprinted it in the heart of the first man. Indeed, this was even much heavier than that first Law, because it further obligated him to the keeping of an infinite number of ecclesiastical duties and civil institutions which the natural law did not require. Must not Jesus Christ (one might say) first be sent into the World to atone for the committed sin and to heal man of his corruption, before the Law was presented to him? Why then was the Law given before God's Son had come?

We have already seen why God did not judge it advisable to send His Son immediately upon the fall of the first man; nothing more remains but to examine why He gave His Law before He sent Him. But, before we investigate the reasons for this Divine economy <note>original: "Goddelyke huishouding"; the plan or management of God's dealings with humanity</note>, one must take note that as soon as man had fallen, God did not abandon him, but promised a Seed that would crush the head of the Serpent <note>A reference to the "Protoevangelium" in Genesis 3:15</note>. And not only did He grant him what was necessary for the present life, but He also gave him all the assistance he needed for the future life.

To come now to the reason why God gave His Law before

I say, firstly: That He did not give Him

II. I say that the Law was not given

One will admit this when one

between the physical blood of the beasts

and the sins of man; because sins are
actually the workings of the soul,
although the soul uses the body

The Jews object to us that (according

clearly understands that a perfect

for the sins we had committed against God.

In truth, the sacrifices of the

To grasp the matter well, one must
note that there were two kinds of
sins under the Old Testament: the
one kind which one could call symbolic,
such as the impurities which were purely
ceremonial and did not touch the conscience;
for instance, when someone, without
thinking about it, had touched a dead body.
His soul was not for that reason less pleasing
to God, and he did not deserve thereby
to be shut out of His Kingdom;
and yet he was held to be unclean;
he was banished from the Synagogue
and deprived of the sweet enjoyment of the
Holy assemblies. These were then not
true impurities, but they were symbols
of the true impurity of sin. Therefore, these
sins are called symbolic because they
were examples of true sins; and these
symbolic sins could be annulled by the
Law, and the ban on those who were
guilty of them could be lifted through
the blood of a beast sacrificed for that end.
This is what Paul wants to teach us
when he says in Hebrews 9:13:

> For if the blood of bulls and goats, and the
> ashes of a heifer, sprinkling the
> unclean, sanctifies (them) to the
> purifying of the flesh.

This does not mean "regarding
the impurities of the flesh," for the
blood and ashes are more suited to soil the
skin than to clean it; "sanctifying
according to the flesh" then means
cleansing according to the church ritual,
or cleansing from legal impurity. "The flesh"
is taken here to mean the Law,
which is called a "fleshly commandment"
in contrast to the Spiritual and
Evangelical service. But with regard to
essential sins, it is certain that all
the sacrifices could not atone for them;

All these observations must be supported by these two others.

The **1st** / that the moral Law <note>original: "redelyke Wet" (rational or moral law)</note> promises forgiveness of sins to no one / but instead threatens the sinful person with damnation and death.

The **2nd** / that the Law did not give man the power to fulfill it; that was a "letter," but one which did not give the sanctifying spirit; far from freeing man from the servitude of sin / it occasionally aroused desire <note>original: "begeerlykheid," often translated in theological contexts as concupiscence or sinful longing</note>; desire and the passions, fearing to be restrained by the Law / behaved like runaway horses / who, foaming at the mouth, gnaw at their bits / and rush forward like a flood of water / swelling up against a dike.

Why / one will then ask, did God give the Law?

I answer, that He did it / to prepare man for the coming of the Messiah.

To understand this, one must observe / that / in order to make man capable of longing with zeal for the coming of Christ / and to receive Him according to his duty / it was necessary to make him well-acquainted with these five things: 1. The infinite Majesty of God / which exalts Him far above all other beings. 2. The rightful duties / which the creature owes to the Supreme Majesty. 3. The severity of His justice / regarding those who offend Him and transgress His Law. 4. The abominableness of the sins / that one comes to commit against such a perfect being / so great and so good / and the appropriate punishment / which one deserves. 5. The impotence / in which sinful man naturally dwells / to do that which is pleasing to God / and to satisfy His justice / which He has displayed: when one has well understood these five things / one can very well comprehend the necessity / that existed /

Now the Law clearly teaches us these five things.

It was like a Mirror, which reveals to men the Majesty and the Justice of God; and sets before their eyes their sins / their deformity / their impotence / and the punishment / which they have deserved.

The Lightning / the Thunder / the Fire / the sound of the Trumpets; all that fearful apparatus / with which the Law was proclaimed / made man understand the Majesty of the Supreme Lawgiver.

The commandments of the Law showed them the duties / which they had to observe / in order to obtain life. *Do these things, and you shall live.*

> From these terrifying words / *cursed is everyone, who does not remain in all that is written in the Law,* they could judge / what they / if they had sinned / had to expect from God.

All of this helped not a little to humble the conceit of man; they also saw well / that it was impossible for them to fulfill the Law / to satisfy Divine justice / and consequently to escape damnation and death; therefore they found themselves forced / to seek a remedy for their ills:

### THEOLOGY. IX. B. XI. CHAPTER 541

one should not wonder that God, in that manner, wished to sketch out that which His Son was to do in the latter times, since this was very appropriate for the state of childhood in which the Church then existed <note>The author views the Old Testament history of Israel as the "childhood" or developmental phase of the Christian Church.</note>, and for the state of the people of Israel, who were a fickle people, naturally inclined to follow the customs of other nations.

2. These religious duties brought man to Christ, insofar as those who accepted them were made to confess that they were worthy of death, being unclean, and that they therefore had need of someone who could cleanse them and obtain life for them; now, the Messiah was the only one who could obtain these benefits for them.

3. Finally, these religious duties led man to Christ, insofar as they were a burdensome yoke under which the people of Israel groaned and from which they longed to be delivered.

The **Spirit of servitude** <note>Also translated as the "Spirit of bondage," referring to a religious state dominated by fear of the Law's demands (see Romans 8:15).</note>, with which the Law was accompanied, helped not a little to prepare men for the coming of Christ.

God had, in order to make His Law powerful, accompanied it with a certain measure of His Spirit, which did not proceed from the Law itself but went hand in hand with it. God—knowing that all that the Law contained could produce nothing if it were not accompanied by a supernatural power of the Holy Spirit, which anticipated the work that God intended to bring forth—gave to the Israelites some portions of His Spirit. This taught them the infinite greatness and majesty of God above all creatures, the obligation they had to subject themselves to His laws and judgments, their inability to obey them perfectly, the great rewards laid up for the righteous, the hideous punishments prepared for sinners, the misery of all men (who were equally punishable), and their inability to satisfy Divine justice. In this way, He prepared men to desire the Messiah: when the Israelites contemplated the awesome majesty of God, they were all terrified and looked for someone who could speak to God on their behalf. When they considered the goods that God promised to the followers of His commandments, they were moved by a powerful desire to possess them as their own

<column-break/>

property; but, recognizing themselves as unworthy of them, they were prompted to seek someone who could earn those things for them.

When they paid attention to the punishment of God's wrath, and to the severity and implacability of His justice, they found themselves in a strange state of astonishment that came very close to despair, since they recognized that they were worthy of these punishments; thus, their wish and sigh was to find someone who could make their peace with God and reconcile them with Him.

It is in this way that the Spirit of servitude accompanied the Law, brought man to Christ, and was called the "Spirit of servitude"—not only because it was given to a people who, although they were children, differed in no way from slaves, but because it held them as if in bondage through the terrors with which it struck them.

From all that I have said, it is easy to conclude that it was with great wisdom that God gave His Law before the sending of His Son.

But it also appears:

1. That God did not give His Law to give life (*Galatians 3:21*), nor to atone for our sins.

2. That God gave the same to make His people know the nature and the terribleness of sin, as the Apostle says in *Romans 3:20*: *Through the Law is the knowledge of sin.* And *Romans 7:7*: *I would not have known that lust is sin, if the Law did not say, thou shalt not covet.* <note>original: "gy zult niet begeeren" (you shall not desire/covet).</note> It is true that we have some knowledge of sin through nature, but it is very imperfect: there are movements in our nature that we consider sinless and which are nonetheless sins, such as the "lust" <note>term: <term>Begeerlijkheid</term> (concupiscence); in this theological context, it refers to the innate inclination toward sin even before an act is committed.</note> of which Paul speaks. It is, on the other hand, certain that man, by nature, does not understand the wickedness and terribleness of sin, whereas the Law teaches us very distinctly that these are things that make us worthy of damnation and plunge us into death.

3. It further appears that the Law was given to humble man. Through the excellence of its promises and the fear of its threats, it brings man to the contemplation of his duties; but then he finds that he has been powerless, not having imagined such great strengths for himself; he feels his weakness, finding himself entirely corrupted, such that he previously...

would not know—that is, to know—that it is impossible for him to lift himself up by his own power; that it is a work of God and that he must consequently seek a savior: this is what the Apostle means in Romans 10:4, saying that Christ is the end of the Law, not only because he abolishes its ceremonies and has fulfilled the Law, but also because it was given to make men understand how much we need the grace and salvation of Christ, and to lead us to this Savior.

The Law was given to somewhat restrain the outbreak of sins and to make the children of Israel observe their duty through the terror caused by the lightning-bolts of the Law; for this reason, it is called a <term>Tutor</term> <note>original: "Tugtmeester." In older translations of Galatians 3:24-25, the Law is described as a schoolmaster or guardian who disciplines children until they reach maturity.</note>: Galatians 3:25. Children are commonly given masters who, through the severity of the rod, prevent them from taking too much liberty. So it was also with the Church while it was in its infancy; not yet knowing the great mysteries that were revealed to them in the fullness of time—which contain within themselves the greatest motivations for holiness—God placed them in the hands of the Law, which, like a strict master, knew how to demand obedience with the rod.

5. Finally, it was given to serve us as a rule of conduct for our social life; I speak here of the moral law. But we shall expand upon this further in another place.

## XII. CHAPTER.

### The Various States of the Church before the Coming of Christ.

**O**ne can observe the Church in several states before the coming of the Messiah.

1. One can first observe it under the first Patriarchs up until Noah: Ten are counted, namely Adam, Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech, and Noah. The most prominent of these Fathers are: 1. Adam, the head of the human race.

The Jews recount many fables—as do the Muslims and even the

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

Christians—concerning this first man, regarding his fall, repentance, burial place, extraordinary size, and the hour in which he died; people have even trifled with the idea that he was buried in the very same place where our Savior was crucified <note>This refers to the tradition that Adam's skull was buried at Golgotha, the "Place of the Skull," symbolizing Christ's blood washing away Adam's original sin.</note>.

2. Seth, the son of Adam, born after the death of Abel, to whom many things are also attributed: it is said that he built two pillars, one of brick and the other of stone: but, one asks, where were these located, and in what letters and in what language was that which one read upon them written, etc.

3. Enosh, in whose time it is said that public worship had its beginning. Some explain the passage in Genesis 4:26 in this way, although there are teachers who interpret it differently, as if idolatry had begun in his time; <margin>Maimonides, Treatise on Idolatry.</margin> others translate it thus: "and men began to be called by the Name of God." People began to make a distinction between the children of Seth and those of Cain, by the name "children of God," which was given to the children of Seth in contrast to the children of Cain.

4. Enoch, famous for his holiness and the prophetic spirit with which he was gifted (as Jude indicates in his Letter) and further renowned for his being taken up into Heaven, which teaches us that there is another life beyond the present one, and that God is the rewarder of those who seek Him.

5. Methuselah, who became the oldest of the Patriarchs, having lived 969 years.

6. Finally, Noah, the preacher of repentance to the first world: God preserved him miraculously in an Ark when He sent the Deluge over the entire earth. One cannot doubt that men in those first times had already begun to be corrupted by idolatry, although it is not known how it began—whether through the worship of the stars or that of heroes.

Everyone knows the godlessness of Cain, the polygamy of Lamech, etc. This corruption was so great that it obliged God to wipe out the first world by the Deluge; which, according to the reckoning of the Jews, happened in the year 1656. People debate whether the Deluge was universal; those who believe it was, prove it with Genesis 7:4, 19, 23, and 2 Peter 2.

II. The Church was subsequently preserved in the house of Shem, son of Noah, and in those of the other Patriarchs until the times of Abraham, such as in the house of Eber, who—as is believed—gave his name to the Language which was used at that time and is called Hebrew, and to the Hebrew nation; it was at the birth of the son of Eber that the languages were confused while men labored on the Tower <note>original: "Toorn." This is likely a period spelling error or pun on *Toren* (Tower) and *Toorn* (Wrath).</note> of Babel; it was in the times of Serug that the Eastern savages—specifically those of Babylon—instituted the religious honoring of images and idols; idolatry was already greatly in fashion, and it was believed that there were many gods.

<margin>Gen. XXXI. 53. Josh. XXIV. 2. Job XXXI. 26. 27. Deut. IV. 19. Jerem. VIII. 2. Lev. XVII. 7. Deut. XXXII. 17.</margin>
There is much appearance that Nahor, the grandfather, and Terah, the father of Abraham, were idol-worshippers, Gen. 31:53, Josh. 24:2. Men began to worship the Sun and the Moon, Job 31:26-27. Subsequently, they worshipped the other planets and stars, Deut. 4:19, Jer. 8:2. They regarded the Earth, the Sea, and the Waters as deities; fire was the deity of the Chaldeans; they also showed religious honor to angels and to devils, Lev. 17:7, Deut. 32:17. Finally, to show the respect they had for the dead, they erected pillars and statues for them; they painted their likeness, and it is said that this occurred in the times of Serug.

III. Thereafter, the Church was seen in the houses of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and their descendants. One cannot marvel enough at the calling of Abraham, his obedience, his faith, the covenant that God made with him, the miraculous birth of Isaac, the various incidents of Jacob, his various travels; the various

<column-break/>

states that Joseph had to undergo, the imprisonment of the children of Israel in Egypt, and the wonders that God performed to deliver them.

The Jews, according to the testimony of Jerome <note>original: "Hieronimus," referring to St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin.</note>, relate many trivial things about Abraham, such as, among others, that he was allegedly thrown into a furnace by the Chaldeans because he refused to serve the idols; the Chaldeans, famous for their astronomical discoveries, held Abraham to be one of the wisest astronomers. The histories of Syria say that he was King of Damascus, although he was a stranger and had come from the area of Babylon. They add to this that he left the kingdom of Damascus to settle in the land of Canaan.

In this third interval, one must note the institution of Circumcision, and of the Passover, and of the idolatry of the surrounding nations.

The Chaldeans were like the fathers of idolatry; they worshipped the Sun and the Moon under the names of Bel, Beelsamen, Belthis, Militta or Mylitta. They also worshipped idols; the Scripture makes mention of <term>Teraphim</term> <note>Small household idols or cult objects.</note>, of Nisroch, Rimmon, Nabo or Nebo, and Bel. Those of Syria and Phoenicia were also idol-worshippers; they worshipped the Sun under the name of Molech, Adonis, El, and Il; the Moon under the name of Baaleth, Melechet, and Ashtoreth. They also worshipped the illustrious dead and their idols. The Sabines were also very famous for their idolatry, as were the Egyptians, who showed religious honor to Osiris and Isis, to the planets, to heroes, to devils, to the waters, to the Nile, to animals—such as oxen, lambs, goats, sheep, dogs, cats, birds, creeping creatures, and crocodiles, etc. Some are of the opinion that they also worshipped plants, fictional depictions of Apis and Serapis, etc. In those times, the Oracles of the Theban Jupiter among the Egyptians, of Jupiter Ammon in Libya, and of Jupiter of Delphi in Phocis were famous everywhere.
