### THE CHRISTIAN

A Jesuit named Father le Comte <note>Louis Le Comte (1637–1713) was a French Jesuit missionary to China whose writings on Chinese history sparked a major theological controversy in Europe.</note> maintained this same position and calculates that these 2,000 years first ended 300 to 400 years before the birth of Christ; however, the Sorbonne <note>The prestigious theological faculty of the University of Paris.</note> issued a sound judgment by declaring that this proposition was untrue, blasphemous, offensive, false, and slanderous toward the Christian religion. The learned Mr. du Pin has defended this judgment; he asserts that one cannot suppose these 2,000 years without openly contradicting the historical scriptures of the Old and New Testaments. If the Chinese had possessed this advantage, then God’s election of the people of Israel would be nothing more than an imagination, and the preference which the Jews so pride themselves on would be an imaginary privilege; furthermore, the distinction between Jews and Gentiles, so often repeated in the Gospel, would then have nothing essential within it.

Beyond this, it is not only in the house of Isaac and Jacob that God preserved a Church: there were several others who, as is believed, were not descended from that house, whom God honored with His covenant—such as a Melchizedek, who provides material for many questions.

<margin>Hulsius.</margin>
1. Whether he was a created human being, or whether he was the Son of God?

Everyone knows how Moses came to kill an Egyptian who was mistreating an Israelite; his flight; and his calling, which was presented to him out of a burning bush that was not consumed. IV. During this time, it appears that Moses wrote the five books that bear his name, of which I have spoken elsewhere.

In their time, there was great corruption, and the people of Israel were exposed to various calamities. VII. One can consider the Church as it was under the High Priesthood of Eli; made unfortunate by the crimes of his children; in those days, idolatry and the godlessness of the people prevailed; God also punished them by allowing the Ark <note>The Ark of the Covenant, the most sacred relic of the Israelites.</note> to be carried away.

VIII. One can subsequently consider the state in which the Church existed under Samuel, a Prophet whom God had chosen to restore the practice of religion.

IX. After that, it was under Saul, the first King over God’s people; then under David, that excellent Shepherd, conqueror of the proud Goliath and of all the enemies of Israel, a great King, a great Prophet—in a word, a man after God’s own heart. Then under Solomon, a wise, righteous, and magnanimous King who built the Temple of God, though at the end of his reign he gave himself over to the love of women and many other sins; he acknowledged the horror of these at the end of his life's journey and testified to his repentance in the Book of Ecclesiastes.

X. One must also consider the Church as it was under the Kings of Israel and Judah, from the time of the schism of the Ten Tribes under Jeroboam, son of Solomon <note>The text identifies Jeroboam as the son of Solomon, though biblical tradition names him the son of Nebat; the author may be conflating him with Rehoboam or referring to the rebellion against Solomon’s line.</note>, until the time of the Babylonian captivity. In that time, there was great corruption, especially in the Kingdom of Israel, after Jeroboam had set up the golden calves and forbidden his subjects from traveling up to Jerusalem. This corruption continued under Ahab and Jezebel, who added the godlessness of the Heathens to the idolatry of Jeroboam, and who therefore both came to a miserable end. The corruption was no less in the Kingdom of Judah under Athaliah, who brought godlessness into the house of Jehoshaphat and finally received the reward for her crimes. It continued under Joash, who had Zechariah the son of Jehoiada stoned; under Uzziah, also called Azariah, who was struck with leprosy because he dared to put his hand to the censer; and under the godless and wicked Ahaz, Manasseh, and Amon, under whom the Temple was profaned, the Majesty of God blasphemed, and a thousand abominations committed. The Church was also reformed from time to time, either by the Prophets who

<column-break/>

lived then, or by the authority of God-fearing Kings such as Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, and Josiah. One must note here that in the time of Hoshea, King of Israel, when the Israelites were carried away to Assyria, all the sins of the idolatrous nations were brought into their land, who planted there a mixed religion between God and their idols (2 Kings 17). This was the first origin of the sect of the Samaritans, of whom so much is spoken.

It is not known what became of the Ten Tribes; the Rabbis <note>original: "R. R." - refers to the Rabbinical authorities.</note> say in the discourse on the Sanhedrin that God has rejected them and that they shall never return from their exile. Josephus maintains that in his time they were on the other side of the Euphrates; Rabbi Benjamin of Tudela, in his fictionalized travels, places four of them in the cities and villages of Nisbon, near the River Gozan. These tribes are said to be those of Dan, Zebulun, Asher, and Naphtali, having as their Lord or Master R. Joseph Amarcala. Others suggest they are on the other side of the River Sabbation <note>A legendary river in Jewish mythology that flows turbulently with stones all week but stops on the Sabbath.</note>, which is unknown to geographers. Abrabanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a prominent Jewish statesman and philosopher.</note> says that he heard from some Portuguese who had been to the Indies that remnants of the Tribes of Benjamin and Judah are still found there, having remained on the other side of the Dark Mountains since their deportation by Sennacherib. R.D.K. <note>Rabbi David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), also known as Radak, a leading medieval biblical commentator.</note> says that the Prophet Elijah shall discover them.

XI. One must further consider the Church as it was during the Babylonian captivity, in which many Jews went over to the superstitions of the Chaldeans, as one may conclude from the Prophet Ezekiel; but many also preserved the purity of their religion and became famous for their zeal and adherence to the true faith, such as Daniel and his companions. One must also include here the miracles that God performed for His children under Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar, and Darius the Mede.

XII. One must consider the Church as it was after the captivity under Zerubbabel and under Joshua, in the time of Ezra the Scribe, to whom some attribute the institution of the Great Synagogue, in which were found Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi, Daniel, Nehemiah, and Simon the Just, otherwise named Jaddus, who went to meet Alexander the Great. XIII. Next, one must view the Church as it was under the Hasmoneans or the Maccabees, under whom Antiochus <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the Seleucid king who persecuted the Jews in the 2nd century BCE.</note> committed such terrible atrocities against the Jews, even causing the holy books to be burned and turning all the Laws of God’s people upside down.

They were called Hasmoneans, if we may believe Josephus in *Antiquities, Book 12, Chapter 8*, after one of the ancestors of Mattathias named *Asamoneus*; and according to others, after a Hebrew word found in *Psalm 68:32*, <note>original: "Chashmanim"</note> which signifies a Prince or a Chief Servant of holy things. They were called Maccabees after Judas Maccabeus, the third son of Mattathias; or from the four letters seen on the banners of Judah, <term>M-K-B-Y</term> <note>original: "מכבי" (Maccabi). This is an acronym for the Hebrew phrase "Mi Kamokha Ba'elim YHVH," meaning "Who is like unto thee, O Lord, among the gods?" from Exodus 15:11.</note> taken from a passage in *Exodus 15:11*. Others derive it from two Hebrew words, one of which means to subdue and the other to desire, as if to say, one who seeks to subdue or desires nothing but destruction. *1 Maccabees 2:66.*

During this time, various sects arose among the Jews.

<margin>Sects of the Asideans.</margin>
The first was that of the Asideans, <note>The Hasideans (Hasidim), meaning "pious ones."</note> spoken of in *1 Maccabees 2:42; 7:13* and *2 Maccabees 14:6*. They confessed that they held themselves to the voluntary service of the Law; it is said that they began to establish the traditions in which the religion of Moses was, as it were, submerged. It is true that it is doubted whether this was truly the specific name of a sect among the Jews, or a name given to the most pious men of this nation.

<margin>
Scaliger in *Trihaeresio*.
Casaubon, *Exercises* I, chapter 18.
</margin>
<margin>Sect of the Pharisees.</margin>
The second sect was that of the Pharisees, a name derived from a Hebrew word <note>original: "Parash"</note> meaning "separated" or "set apart," because they—imitating an extraordinary holiness—separated themselves from the rest of the people, and even distinguished themselves by their clothing. Others derive this name from two Hebrew words, one of which means to bear fruit and the other to go from place to place, as if one said: those who bear fruit by going from place to place. *Matthew 23:15.* <note>The source cites verse 19, but verse 15 refers to the Pharisees crossing sea and land to make a convert.</note> There is a dispute over the beginning of this sect: whether it should be reckoned from the time of Ezra; or from Jonathan the Maccabee, brother of Judas, who died 140 years before the coming of Christ;

<column-break/>

or from Aristobulus; or from Alexander Jannaeus, King of the Jews, around 100 years before Christ; or from Shammai or Hillel, around the time of Herod. The beliefs they held consisted of the following:

1. That one must hold not only to the written Law, but also to the unwritten Law and to the traditions; they even had many types of traditions.

2. They falsified the Law of God through their interpretations and perverse explanations. They taught, for example, that only outward murder was forbidden; that God did not forbid lust nor unchaste looking; that in speaking it was permitted to swear by Heaven, by one's head, by the earth, or by Jerusalem; to avenge oneself and repay evil with evil; to hate one's enemies; and that one could be released from the help owed to one's parents. *Matthew 15:5.*

<margin>Book II, chapter 7 of the *Jewish War*.</margin>
3. They believed that man had enough strength to do good. If we may believe Josephus, they said that it is almost always in the power of man to do good works or to leave them undone, but that fate also comes to the aid of every human purpose.

4. They justified themselves before God through their works; the witness to this is the Pharisee spoken of in the 18th chapter of Luke.

The renowned Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides, a 12th-century Jewish scholar, whose work is cited here to illustrate Jewish legalistic thought.</note> speaks thus in his treatise on repentance:
> "Each person has his merits and
> "his sins; he who has more merits, and
> "far greater merits than sins, is righteous:
> "but he who has more
> "sins than merits is evil and
> "godless."

5. Their righteousness consisted of purely outward things. They were in favor of the unmarried state and for frequent fasting during the week. They gave tithes of their goods; they washed themselves often; they spread their <term>Phylacteries</term> <note>Small leather boxes containing Torah verses, worn during prayer.</note> wide. These were certain signs by which they reminded themselves of the commandments of the Law which they had to observe, and which they tied to their hands and heads for that purpose. They slept on very narrow planks, and sometimes they laid stones upon them. They enlarged the hems of their garments, upon which they had strips of parchment hanging, whereon some proverbs of the Law were written; as they hurried, these appeared.

# DIVINITY. IX. B. XII. Chapter.

<column-break/>

they appeared in public with a sad and distraught face: they performed their prayers and alms on the corners of the cross-streets: there were some who wore long robes, which had pins like needles attached at the back, which pricked them in the lower legs and bare heels, so that blood came out, with which they bloodied the path they walked. <note>This describes extreme ascetic practices intended to demonstrate piety and penance through physical suffering.</note>

6. Some believe that the Pharisees adopted the errors of the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, known for the doctrine of metempsychosis or the transmigration of souls.</note>, who taught the passage of souls into other bodies, distinct from those they had previously animated. This is based on the words of Josephus, who, in the 7th chapter of the *Jewish Wars*, relates that the Pharisees taught that the souls of the godly alone pass into other bodies; but that those of the wicked shall be eternally tormented. There are other scholars who do not believe this, and think that this should be interpreted by what Josephus says in the 18th Book of his *Antiquities*, that the Pharisees believed that on the day of judgment God will give the souls of the godly better bodies than they had before. Indeed, the doctrine of the migration of souls conflicts with that of the resurrection; for after a soul has been drawn into many bodies, and has lived well in one and poorly in another, which body would it take up on the day of resurrection?

7. Josephus relates in the 18th Book of his *Antiquities*, chapter 2, that the Pharisees taught that when souls depart from the bodies, they are called to judgment, and that they are then sent to subterranean places, either to enjoy rest there or to be tormented.

8. The same Josephus says that, according to the opinion of the Pharisees, the souls of the wicked will not be reunited with their bodies: but this conflicts with Paul, Acts 24:15. <note>original: "Hand. XXIV. 15." refers to the Book of Acts.</note>

9. They believed, like most of the Jews, that the kingdom of Christ <note>Meaning the Messiah.</note> would be earthly, illustrious, and magnificent according to the world, and that all the institutions of Moses must remain standing until the end of the ages. There were many types of Pharisees, who also had various names.

<margin>Sect of the Sadducees.</margin>
III. After the Pharisees, we place the Sect of the Sadducees. The introducer and head of this sect was a certain Tzadok,

<column-break/>

disciple of Antigonus, who lived about 226, others say 250 years before the coming of Christ. This Antigonus gave his students this lesson: "be not like the slaves who serve their master only to draw wages, but be servants of God, like children who serve the Lord as if they were to receive no reward from it, and let the fear of Heaven rest upon you." This gave Tzadok the occasion to introduce his godless doctrines:

1. That the soul dies with the body.
2. That there is no reward nor punishment to be expected after this life.
3. That there will be no resurrection nor final judgment.

<margin>Jerome.</margin>
4. They also believed that there were no spirits nor angels, Acts 23:8. We have seen elsewhere with what thoughts they denied that there are angels.

<margin>Commentary on Matthew ch. 22:31. Josephus Antiquities Book XIII, ch. 18.</margin>
5. They are accused of having accepted only the books of Moses: but Josephus declares that they received everything that was written.

The good that they had was that they rejected the traditions; they were not in as much esteem as the Pharisees, nevertheless, there were High Priests of this Sect.

They were still in existence in the 6th century: the decree of Justinian <note>Byzantine Emperor (527–565 AD) known for his legal code.</note> condemned them to death. It is reported that some are still found in Africa. Some have confused the Karaites with the Sadducees: but they have no similarity to one another at all, unless it be in that they, like the Sadducees, also reject tradition. Some have believed that the Karaites were those who are called Teachers of the Law in the Gospel: they had famous masters in the 15th and 16th centuries; they enjoyed great freedom in the lands of the Turkish Emperor; they have synagogues in Constantinople, and they extend in the East as far as Nineveh.

<margin>The Sect of the Essenes.</margin>
IV. The Sect of the Essenes was also held in special regard; they are highly praised by Josephus and Philo the Jew.

1. They held nearly the same views as the Pharisees.

2. They led a solitary life in wild and secluded places, for which reason no mention is made of them in the New Testament.

<margin>Eusebius, Book VIII, *Preparation for the Gospel*.</margin>
3. They admitted no one into their sect except men, and those who were old.

5. They favored the celibate state.
6. They led a very strict life.
7. They practiced no arts or crafts that could cause harm to another.
8. They kept the Sabbath with great holiness; there are even curious stories told of their superstition regarding this matter: they attributed everything to fate, and nothing to human freedom. <note>In this context, "freedom" refers to free will.</note>

10. They tested their disciples for four years.
11. They punished those who did not observe their laws very severely, even letting them nearly die of hunger.
12. They avoided quarrels and disputes; it was forbidden for them to manufacture weapons.

*Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a historian of the early Christian Church.</note> in the 2nd Book of his *History*, chapters 17 and 18, says that the *Essenes* who were in *Egypt* by Lake *Maxas* <note>original: "Maxas"; this likely refers to Lake Mareotis near Alexandria.</note>, of whom the Jew *Philo* speaks in the book *On the Contemplative Life*, were Christian monks: but he is greatly mistaken, for 1. it appears that *Philo* speaks only of *Essenes* who were Jews by faith; 2. The *Essenes* Philo speaks of are the same ones *Josephus* describes in the 18th Book of the *Jewish Antiquities*, chapter 21, and in the 2nd Book of the *Jewish Wars*, chapter 7; 3. *Philo* would not have praised them so highly if they had been Christians; 4. *Philo* says that their teachings were contained in allegorical books written by ancient authors of their sect; he mentions that they leapt and danced and made various gestures with their hands, which does not suit Christians; 5. *Philo* wrote this around the time of *Gaius Caligula*, to whom he was sent as an ambassador; now, the Gospel had not yet been preached in *Egypt* at that time; 6. Finally, it seems that *Eusebius* acknowledged his mistake in the book *Evangelical Preparation*, in chapters 2 and 14, stating that *Philo* spoke of the *Essenes* who were Jews.

I cannot omit speaking here of the *Scribes*, who are so often mentioned in the Holy Scriptures: there were two kinds, Civil and Ecclesiastical.

-> DIVINE THEOLOGY. IX. B. XIII. CHAPTER. <-

Some scholars believe that the Teachers of the Law taught in the schools, while the Scribes taught in the synagogues—the former instructing the "children of the Prophets" <note>This term often refers to students or disciples in a prophetic school.</note> and the latter teaching the common people.

Finally, one can observe the Church as it was from the time of Herod the Great, under whom our Savior was born. The Church at that time was very corrupt and torn into various sects. Almost all the Jews believed that the Messiah would be a Great Conqueror who would deliver them from the servitude under which they groaned. Judea was in a sorrowful state. Pompey <note>The Roman general who captured Jerusalem in 63 BC.</note> had made the Jews tributary to the Romans sixty years prior. Gabinius the Proconsul had divided the High Council into five assemblies. M. Crassus had plundered the Temple of Jerusalem. Caesar had given the government of the land to Antipater, an Idumean <note>A person from Idumea (Edom), south of Judea; his son was Herod the Great.</note> by descent. C. Crassus had exhausted the Jews through his extortions and taxes. Mark Antony had ordered the beheading of King Antigonus, who was of the Hasmonean <note>The Hasmonean dynasty was the ruling family of Judea before the rise of Herod.</note> lineage; the state of the Jewish people was no happier under Emperor Augustus, during whose reign the King of the Angels and of men also came into the world.

## XIII. CHAPTER.

### That the Son of God has assumed human nature, and for what reason.

**W**e have seen the state in which the Church existed before the coming of the Messiah; we must now speak specifically of the manner in which he revealed himself to mankind in the fullness of time.

<margin>John 1:14. Rom. 1:3. 1 Tim. 3:16. Heb. 2:14.</margin> **S**cripture teaches us very clearly that the Son of God assumed our human nature at the time foretold by the Prophets. John says (John 1:14) that the Word became flesh. Paul says (Rom. 1:3) that our Lord Jesus Christ was of the seed of David according to the flesh; (1 Tim. 3:16) that he was revealed in the flesh; (Heb. 2:14) that he partook of the flesh and blood of the children.

<column-break/>

<margin>That Christ had a body. Heb. 10:5.</margin> **T**he Holy Pages attribute a body to Christ; besides the passage from Paul that we cited from the second chapter of Hebrews, the same Apostle speaks thus in chapter 10:5: *Coming into the world he says, sacrifice and offerings you did not desire, but you have prepared a body for me.* And Christ says of himself that he has flesh and bones (Luke 24:39). His body was like ours: material, weak, and visible, requiring food, drink, sleep, and rest, and subject to the fatigues to which our nature is liable.

<margin>That Christ had a soul. Matt. 26:38. Luke 23:46.</margin> **S**cripture also assigns to Christ a soul: an intellect, a will, and sinless passions such as joy, sorrow, fear, and love. "My soul," he said (Matt. 26:38), "is exceedingly sorrowful, even unto death." In Luke 23:46, he says: "Father, into your hands I commit my spirit."

It appears, then, that Christ was truly a man, just as we are.

<margin>That Christ had a true body.</margin> **T**herefore, we condemn: 1. The heretics who say that Christ did not have true flesh, but that he was only like a spirit <note>This refers to Docetism, a belief that Christ’s body was an illusion.</note>, as Saturninus, Basilides, Cerdon, and Marcion, etc., taught. This is refuted by the passages we have cited, as well as by several reasons derived therefrom: such as that it would have been unworthy of God and Christ to have deceived the eyes of men through the false appearance of a spirit; or that, if Christ did not have a true body, everything the Scripture tells us of his deeds—which are presented for us to imitate—as well as his death, his resurrection, and his ascension, would be a mere fiction, which one cannot say without godlessness; or that the entire work of our salvation necessarily presupposes that he was truly our Brother, partaking of one nature and subject to the same weaknesses.

<margin>Phil. 2:7.</margin> **O**ne might possibly object that Paul says (Phil. 2:7): *But emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men.*

**B**ut first, one must observe that it would be very poor reasoning to conclude from this that Christ was not a true man //

# THE CHRISTIAN

...as it would also be poor reasoning to say that Seth did not have the same nature as his father Adam, simply because Moses says that he was begotten in the likeness and image of Adam: It is clear that from this expression one can derive nothing else than that **Christ** is not the same person as other men, whose appearance he shared, just as Seth was not Adam himself. However, it does not follow from this that he did not have a nature identical to theirs. 2. One must note that the reason why the Apostle expresses himself in this way is to teach us that, in appearance, there was no distinction between **Christ** and other men; thus, it seemed he was a mere man <note>original: "bloot mensch"</note>, although he was in truth God, and as a man possessed great privileges above all others. 3. When it is subsequently said that he was "found in the form of a man," this "form" indicates the outward condition of the person. This is to say that, in outward appearance, one found nothing in him that distinguished him from other men, so that one would have taken him for an ordinary man. In the same manner, it is said of the authorities in the Book of Psalms: <margin>Psalm 82:7.</margin> Psalm 82:7. *You shall die like a man*, which is to say, like other men. It is this outward form in which **Christ** was found that caused the worldly people to ask the Bride: <margin>Song of Solomon 5:9.</margin> Song of Solomon 5:9. *What is your beloved more than another beloved?*

<margin>Around the year 373. Epiphanius, Heresies 77. Socrates, Book II, chapter 46.</margin> 2. We also condemn the heretics who believed that **Christ** did not have a rational soul, such as **Apollinaris** <note>Apollinaris of Laodicea taught that the divine Word took the place of the human mind in Jesus, a view later declared heretical.</note>, but that the Divinity served him in place of reason or soul. This not only contradicts the passages we have cited to prove that **Christ** had a soul, but also those that call him our brother—which he could not be if he did not share the most principal part of human nature with us. Add to this the passages where it is said that he was like us in everything, except for sin.

I do not consider it worthwhile to refute the extravagances of the heretics called **Origenists**, who followed the errors of **Origen** <note>An early Christian scholar whose complex views on the pre-existence of souls were later controversial.</note>. He maintained that the soul of **Christ** had been created many centuries before he came into the world, and that it was later united with his body: this foolish

<column-break/>

imagination has no foundation whatsoever.

<margin>Why the Son of God assumed our nature</margin> It will be better for us to move on to another point: to understand why **Jesus Christ** had to assume our nature.
There are several reasons for this.
The first is because Divine justice required that sin be reconciled through and in the same nature in which it was committed. The Druids, of whom <margin>Julius Caesar, The Gallic War <note>original: "De Belg. Gall."</note>, Book VI</margin> Julius Caesar speaks, said that the life of a man could not be ransomed for the gods except by the life of a man. If sin had not entered the world, it would not have been necessary for a Divine Person to take on flesh. **Origen**, in his 24th homily on Numbers, says, "that if there had been no sins, it would also not have been necessary for the Son of God to become a Lamb, and that he, being clothed in our flesh, be slaughtered; but that he would have remained the Word of God, which he was from the beginning."

<margin>Augustine, Book 1, On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, chapter 16; and Sermon 174 on the words of the Apostle. Volume 3, question 1, article 5.</margin> **Athanasius**, in his 3rd sermon against the Arians, speaks thus: "Our Lord had no cause to be the Word of God <note>meaning, to become the incarnate Word</note>, but it is our necessity that was the cause for him to clothe himself in our flesh: for without that, he would not have assumed it. He did not come into the world for himself, but for our salvation, and so that he might destroy death and condemn sin."
**Basil** in homily 29 against the Arians, **Gregory Nazianzenus** in Sermon 36, **Ambrose** in *On the Incarnation* chapter 6, **Chrysostom** in homily 31 on Matthew, **Cyril**, **Pope Leo** in Sermon III on Pentecost, **Pope Gregory** in Book IV on 1 Kings chapter 1, and **Augustine** in his *Handbook* <note>The Enchiridion</note> chapter 108, have all put forward the same reason.

Without sin, then, there would have been no need for a Mediator or an Incarnation; but, sin having entered the world, and God not willing that all men should perish entirely, but rather giving them a Mediator, it was necessary that this Mediator assume our nature.

The second reason why **Christ** assumed our nature is because Divine justice demanded the death of the sinner, or the death of the one who would be a surety for them. Now, it was only human nature that could

# DIVINITY. IX. B. XIII. Chapter.

...suffering, because a rational nature was required for it, and because the mere sacrifice of beasts could not atone for sins.

<margin>1 Tim. 6:16.</margin>
Finally, the third reason is so that man might have free access to God; for the Divine nature dwells in an inaccessible light for mortals. Thus, it was necessary that the Messiah assume our nature so that we, seeing him as like ourselves, could take our refuge in him with certainty.

It is therefore clear that it was necessary for the one who would provide satisfaction <note>The term "satisfaction" refers to the theological concept of "substitutionary atonement," where Christ pays the debt of sin owed by humanity to God's justice.</note> to have two natures, and that he was both God and Man: God, so that he would have free access to the Father; Man, so that we might approach him without fear; God, so that he would know all the secrets of the Father which were to be revealed to men; Man, so that he would proclaim them to us: God, so that he would sanctify us through his Spirit; Man, so that he would provide us an example of virtue to follow. God, so that he could satisfy Divine justice and overcome the Devil and death; Man, so that he could offer himself as a sacrifice; finally, Man, so that he could suffer; and God, so that he could impart an infinite value to his suffering.

<margin>The last works of Claude.</margin>
These two Natures are found in Christ. "In Nature, as a learned man <note>Referring to Jean Claude (1619–1687), a prominent French Protestant theologian.</note> has aptly remarked, God had found through a wondrous art the means to unite spirit and flesh together, by the breathing of the Spirit of life into a handful of earth, from which he made the body of Adam; but in Grace, he has found the secret of uniting in the union of one person the Creator with the creature, the Divine with the Human nature, the eternal Spirit with the body. So that, whereas in nature one would simply have said: 'the dust is Flesh, and the Flesh has become a living Soul,' in Grace one says: 'the Word became Flesh,' and he who was in the likeness of God, and was not ashamed to be equal to God, has taken on the form of a Servant."

The Jews and Heathens <note>A common historical term for non-Christians, particularly practitioners of polytheistic religions.</note> must not be surprised that the Son of God has clothed himself with human Nature,

<column-break/>

and appeared here below on earth in the form of a Man: the Jews can consult the Oracles of the Old Testament, which promised them that the Messiah would be a man; they can learn from the Prophet Hosea that the Man who wrestled with their father Jacob was the Almighty God; and regarding the Heathens, their books are filled with the appearances of their Gods under a human form. Those of Lycaonia also said, on the occasion of Paul and Barnabas, that the Gods, having taken the form of men, had descended to them. It is recounted that the famous Confucius said that the eternal Word would one day become Flesh, and the learned Mr. Huet, Bishop of Avranches <note>Pierre-Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French scholar and bishop known for his "Demonstratio Evangelica."</note>, says "that the Brahmins believed that God often appears in disguise, under the form of a Man, and that Vishnu <note>original: "Wisnavius," a Latinized form of the Hindu deity Vishnu.</note>, whom they say is the second Person, has nine times taken on a body, and once a human body, and that he must take it on once more."

It is said that one cannot understand how an infinite Being can unite with a finite being, because of the great distance that exists between these two beings.

I answer that this infinite distance does not prevent their union; it would be true if it were an infinite spatial distance, but it is an infinite distance of perfections. Furthermore, rather than God’s infinity preventing him from uniting with our nature, it is on the contrary this infinity that makes him capable of this union.

It has been very well noted:

1. That there is no creature that does not have some union with God, because all being created by him, all also exist through him.
2. That rational creatures, being much nobler than others, are consequently also more united with God.
3. That, God communicating himself in so many different ways to his creature, it is easy to understand that he could unite himself perfectly and personally with human nature, the salvation of his creature requiring it.

But one must not believe that the Divine nature gained any perfection through its union with the human—

# CHAPTER XIV.

## Whether the Incarnation did not create two Persons in Christ, and how the union of these Natures occurred.

<margin>Jesus Christ has assumed our Nature in the union of one Person.</margin>
Jesus Christ has assumed our Nature through the union of the person; that is to say, that his divine Nature was so united with the human that this union constituted only one Person. This is what Scripture teaches us, which always speaks of Christ as a single person. The same one who was of the seed of David according to the flesh was also named the Son of God, according to the Spirit of holiness; the same one who proceeded from the Father is named God, blessed for ever and ever; the same one who was equal to God humbled himself and assumed the form of a servant; the same one who is called the Lord of glory was crucified, and it is said there that God purchased his Church through his own blood.

<margin>Romans 1:3.</margin>
<margin>Romans 9:5.</margin>
<margin>Philippians 2:6.</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 2:8.</margin>
<margin>Acts 20:28.</margin>

<margin>Errors attributed to Nestorius.</margin>
Therefore, we condemn the opinion attributed to <term>Nestorius</term> <note>Nestorius (c. 386–450 AD) was the Archbishop of Constantinople whose views led to the "Nestorian Schism," a major division in early Christianity regarding how Christ's human and divine sides relate.</note>, Archbishop of Constantinople, who is accused of having posited two persons in Christ who cooperated in the work of our salvation: one as the principal worker, who was the Person of God's Son and the eternal Word, and the other of lower rank and acting as an instrument, namely the human Person Jesus, the Son of Mary. It was said that these two persons were united by one and the same anointing, and that they thus constitute only one Christ; that one must not say that Mary was the Mother of God <note>original: "Moeder Gods" or the Greek "Theotokos"</note>, but only the Mother of Christ; that the humanity of Christ was the Temple in which God dwelt; and that Christ-Man carried Christ-God, etc.

I do not wish to determine here whether Nestorius actually held this error; investigating this dispute would lead me too far astray; but I shall only say that the

<column-break/>

error of which he was accused was condemned by <term>Cyril of Alexandria</term> <note>A central figure in the Council of Ephesus and a fierce opponent of Nestorius.</note> in a Church assembly held in the year 430; by Pope Celestine; by the 1st Council of Ephesus, held in the year 431; by that of Chalcedon in the year 451; and by the 2nd of Constantinople in the year 553, as many learned men have believed. The second decree of the Council of Ephesus contains these words:

> If anyone does not confess that the Word of God the Father is united with the flesh according to the <term>subsistence</term> <note>original: "bestaanlykheid," referring to the Greek "hypostasis," meaning the underlying reality or "personhood" of Christ.</note> or substance, and that there is but one Christ with his own flesh, and that he is at once God and Man, let him be cursed:

One will not be surprised that we say Christ assumed a human nature, but not a human person, when one considers first, what a person is, and second, what is understood in the <term>schools</term> <note>The "schools" refers to Scholasticism, the formal system of theological and philosophical instruction used in universities during the Middle Ages and the Reformation.</note> by "personality." By the word "person," one understands a rational nature that exists of itself and is not united with another.

The word "personality" in this matter establishes nothing positive, but signifies a simple negation and shows that the rational nature of which one speaks is not united with another. I say "in this matter," because for the rest, we admit that what is called "Person" in the Trinity must be understood in another way, which we are not capable of explaining. Now it follows from this that Christ was no less a true man, even though he did not assume a human person, because "personhood" in this matter is nothing <note>The author argues that "personhood" is just a label for a nature that stands alone; since Christ's human nature stands with his divine nature, it doesn't need a separate "personhood."</note>. The human nature of Christ would have been a person if it had not been united with a Divine person, and if it had existed alone; but being united with the Divine person, one cannot call it a person, because the name of person is given only to a nature that has not been united with another.

Certainly, if there were two persons in Christ, who were only united together by the same action and set to the same work, one under the other, then one could give no reason why the Scripture speaks in the manner we have already cited, and one could not say that the one became the other, as John says,

<margin>John 1:14.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of Christ, specifically addressing the theological debate regarding the "Mother of God" title and the mechanics of how the divine and human natures are joined in one person.</meta>

# DIVINITY. IX. B. CHAPTER XIV.

...that the Word became flesh; one would not be able to say that the Son of God died and was crucified, and so on.

One asks whether one may not rightly say that the Virgin is the **Mother of God**, which <term>Nestorius</term> <note>Nestorius was an early church leader who argued that Mary should be called "Mother of Christ" rather than "Mother of God," fearing that the latter implied Mary was the source of Christ's divinity.</note> denied; I answer that this expression should give no more offense than that of the Scripture, which says that God purchased the Church through his blood, and other expressions that I have cited elsewhere; nevertheless, one must admit with many learned men that the name **Mother of God** <note>original: "Moeder Gods" / Greek: "Theotokos"</note> possibly gave occasion to the adoration that has been offered to the blessed Virgin. One has mixed the Mother with the Son, and one has given the Mother that which was owed to none but the Son.

One asks how it is possible that the human Nature of Christ makes but one **Person** with the Divine Nature, since one cannot understand how a Temple is one and the same thing as the one who dwells in the Temple.

I answer: 1. That one must not believe that the Divinity dwells in the Human Nature absolutely in the same way as God dwells in a Temple, and that there is no greater union; we shall soon see the contrary.

2. One must distinguish between a physical and a Spiritual Temple; the soul is indeed in the body as in a Temple or Tabernacle, yet it constitutes one and the same Person.

I come to another question, which is much more difficult: how the Union of the two Natures occurred in one and the same Person? It is much easier to say what it is *not* than what it is.

I. One must not understand the union of the two Natures of Christ like the union of the soul with the body; for the body and the soul, considered before they are united together, are not Persons, but from their union comes a Person who was not there before; but in Christ, the eternal Word was a Person before his assumption of the flesh, possessing a true existence, who was perfect in himself, and who had no need to be joined with humanity; and when it pleased him to unite human Nature with himself, the Person who existed before the incarnation was not destroyed:

<column-break/>

furthermore, soul and body being two imperfect Beings, preordained to be united with one another, can together constitute one human Nature; but the Divinity, possessing all kinds of perfections in itself and being unable to receive any new perfection, can indeed unite itself with another Nature to perfect it, but not to make itself more perfect: it is not for another being, but for itself. One must nonetheless admit that there is no more suitable symbol to show us the union of the two Natures in Christ than this; primarily in that all that pertains to either Nature, human and Divine, is said of the one Jesus Christ, just as one says of one and the same man what is said of his body and his soul.

II. One must not understand this union as a simple union of consent—of thoughts, desires, and inclinations—for one does not grasp how one could say that God purchased his Church through his blood if there had only been a union of consent between the Divinity and humanity; nor how one could say that *the Word became flesh*, for one does not change into his friend, whatever union there may be between him and his friend; to which one must add that this union and agreement would not have been enough to give an infinite value to the death of Christ, just as a King, by giving his consent to what his servant or slave does, does not bring to the work of the slave the same dignity it would have had if he had performed it himself.

<margin>John 8:58.</margin>
III. One must not understand that these two Natures are united in the same way as one understands a Pilot to be somewhat united with the ship he steers, or as the Holy Spirit was united with the spirit of the Prophets whom he inspired <note>The Dutch "aanblies" literally means "blew upon" or "breathed into," referring to divine inspiration.</note>; for if that were so, one could not say that *the Word became flesh*, just as one does not say that the Pilot became the ship, or the Spirit of God became the spirit of the Prophets; never would Christ have said, *Before Abraham was, I am*; for there is no Prophet who could say this and appropriate to himself what Christ said of himself.

# THE CHRISTIAN

IV. One must not understand this union as the union of the Persons of the Holy Trinity, where there is only one Essence: for here there are two natures and one Person, whereas in the Trinity there are three Persons in one and the same Essence.

V. There is also a very great difference between this union and the union of *Christ* with the Believers, as one can very easily understand.

VI. One must not view these two Natures as two parts that make up a whole: but one must note that the Divine Person has assumed a human nature. We have already noted that, in other composite things, the combined parts perfect one another, but humanity adds no perfection to the Divinity: the Divinity gives, and receives nothing.

VII. Through this union, the Natures were not mixed, but each has retained its properties, for there is no similarity between them: the human nature is finite, mortal, and changeable; the Divine nature is infinite, immeasurable, immortal, and unchangeable; one also finds in the Scripture that these two natures are set in opposition to each other:

<margin>*Rom. 1:3, 1 Pet. 3:18, Heb. 9:14, John 1:14, Phil. 2:6, 7.*</margin>
We therefore condemn the sentiment of <term>Eutyches</term> <note>Eutyches (c. 380–456) was an abbot in Constantinople who taught that after the union of the divine and human in Christ, there was only one nature—the divine—which effectively "swallowed" the human nature.</note>, who, having argued strongly against the error attributed to *Nestorius*, fell himself into another error that was no less dangerous, saying that the two natures of *Christ*, being distinct before they were united, constituted only one nature after their union: he said that *Christ* had not had flesh of the same substance as ours, but that he had assumed a heavenly body, and that he had passed through the body of the Virgin as through a pipe; he had <term>Dioscorus</term> <note>The Bishop of Alexandria who supported Eutyches and presided over the controversial Second Council of Ephesus.</note> as a follower, along with many others, who said that the human nature was swallowed up by the Divine, so that it no longer existed after the union; they used the analogy of wax being consumed by fire, and that of a drop of honey or vinegar poured into the sea.

This error was condemned by *Flavian*, Bishop of *Constantinople*,

<column-break/>

in a church assembly in the year 448: the <term>II Council of Ephesus</term> <note>Known to history as the "Robber Synod" (Latrocinium) of 449 because of the violence and intimidation used to force through Eutyches' doctrines.</note>, where *Dioscorus* presided and which consisted purely of a band of robbers, defended this error: but the same was entirely condemned in the Council of *Chalcedon* in the year 451.

We also condemn those <term>Eutychians</term> who were satisfied with saying that the human Nature was not swallowed up by the Divine until the moment of *Christ's* exaltation; that sentiment has no basis at all.

We condemn all those who believed that the two Natures did not retain all their essential qualities after their union, such as those called <term>Monothelites</term> <note>From the Greek "monos" (one) and "thelema" (will). They believed Christ had two natures but only one divine-human will.</note>, who said there was but a single will and a single operation in *Christ*; against these, the 6th general Council was held at *Constantinople* in the year 680, and this error is refuted by the passage from *Luke* which I have already

<margin>*Luke 22:42.*</margin>
cited <note>The verse reads: "Father, if you are willing, take this cup from me; yet not my will, but yours be done." This suggests a distinction between Christ's human will and the divine will.</note>, and by all the histories of the Gospel, from which it appears that the operation of the human Nature was distinct from the operation of the Divine Nature. There were, furthermore, two types of *Monothelites*: some were pure *Eutychians*, such as *Anastasius* of *Antioch*, who was the head of this Sect; others accepted the General Council of *Chalcedon* and even allowed for two wills and two Natures in some parts, but at the same time taught that the human will of *Christ* was like an instrument used by the Divine will, so that it did nothing of itself. — They said that there was but one single personal will and operation in *Christ*, and one single beginning that worked.

This Sect of *Eutychians* later had many followers under various names, such as *Acephalen*, *Severites*, *Theopaschites*, *Jacobites*, *Maronites*, *Armenians*, *Agnoetes*, *Aphthartodocetae*, *Corruptibles*, *Monothelites*, and *Fullonites* named after <term>Peter the Fuller</term> <note>Peter the Fuller was a 5th-century Bishop of Antioch who famously added the phrase "who was crucified for us" to the Trisagion (the "Thrice Holy" hymn), implying God the Trinity suffered on the cross.</note>, who added these words to the "thrice holy" hymn sung in the Church: *who was crucified for us*. Regarding these, one may consult the writers of Church Histories; yet all these errors have been condemned with great justice.

Those *Eutychians* were called <term>Acephalen</term> <note>From the Greek for "headless."</note> because, due to their many heads, they had no fixed leader...

### DIVINITY. IX. B. CHAPTER XIV.

had as their head in the year 535. **Severites**, named after a certain Severus, who was their leader. **Theopaschites**, because they believed that the Godhead suffered <note>The name "Theopaschite" comes from the Greek words for "God" and "suffering." This group was considered heretical because they suggested the eternal, divine nature of God could experience pain or death.</note>. **Jacobites**, from a certain Jacob of Syria, who lived in the 6th century.

Certainly, the properties of the two natures in Christ have never been mixed, and one nature is not changed into the other; for if that had happened, either Christ would have ceased to be God—which is the ultimate godlessness to even think, for the Divine nature is unchangeable—or he would have ceased to be Man, which completely contradicts the Scripture.

VIII. This union is so close that it never is and never can be broken, which distinguishes it from the union of Angels with the bodies they inhabit.

In a word, we agree entirely on this matter with the judgment of the General Council of **Chalcedon** in the year 451, where the Church Fathers made this confession of faith:

> "Following the holy Fathers, we all unanimously confess
> and teach one and the same Son, our Lord
> Jesus Christ, perfect in Godhead,
> and perfect in manhood, truly
> God, and truly man, having a
> rational soul and body, of one and the same
> essence and substance with the Father
> according to his Godhead, and according to his manhood
> of one and the same essence and substance
> in all things like us, except
> for sin; who was begotten by the Father
> before all ages according to
> his Godhead, but who in these last days
> was brought forth by the blessed
> Virgin and Mother of God according to the
> manhood, for our sake and for our
> salvation; one and the same Jesus
> Christ, Son of God, only Lord
> revealed in two natures, unmixed,
> unchangeable, undivided,
> inseparable (that is to say without mixing
> of the two Natures / without
> changing one into the other / and
> without them becoming divided or separated
> from one another), without the distinction
> of the natures being taken away by
> the union; but rather preserving the property
> of the two natures, which meet together
> in one person and subsistence, not that
> he should be divided or separated into
> two persons, but in such a way, that

<column-break/>

> he is the only and same Son, God,
> the Word, and our Lord Jesus Christ,
> just as the ancient prophets foretold,
> Jesus Christ himself taught, and the Confession
> of Faith of our fathers has delivered
> it to us."

One asks why these two united natures of Christ shall not be separated, since they were only united to carry out the work of our salvation.

I answer that the work of our salvation is a matter of such great importance that it suits Divine wisdom to keep an eternal memory of it.

Furthermore, one cannot marvel enough: 1. At God's wisdom, which found the secret to communicate Himself to His creature, and particularly to man, elevating flesh and blood, earth and dust, above all principalities and powers, and humbling Himself so low that He converses with us. By the Creation of the world, we know what great things God can do, but the incarnation of a God teaches us how far He has been able to humble Himself. 2. At the infinite love of God, who caused His Son to assume our nature with all its weaknesses. 3. At the infinite love of the Son, who took the despised form of a servant when He was in the form of God, and who clothed Himself with a mantel of flesh to become our Brother and Bridegroom. 4. Finally, at the power of God, who through a powerless flesh has conquered the Devil.

I end this Chapter by saying that regarding this subject, people have sometimes made use of expressions that are offensive, such as these: that Christ is composed of the Godhead and the manhood; that the Word became man; and especially this one, which the General Council of **Basel** in the 22nd session condemned: *that the human nature in Christ is the person of the word, and that she is truly the true God through the personal union.*

THE CHRISTIAN [THEOLOGY]

## CHAPTER XV.

->On the effects of the union<-
->of the two natures in<-
->Jesus Christ.<-

We have seen the union of the two natures in Christ and proven that these two natures do not constitute two persons; we must now consider the consequences of this union. There are some that concern the human nature of Christ, and others that concern his person.

<margin>First Effect of the union.</margin> The first effect of this union, regarding the human nature of Christ, is that by this very union, Christ's humanity is exalted above all creatures; this requires no proof.

2. One must not doubt that as a result of this union, the human nature of Christ was filled with all the gifts that a creature could contain. <margin>Isaiah 11:2.</margin> Isaiah says in Chapter 11, verse 2, that the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the Lord would rest upon him, which shows that the same would not only be communicated to him but would remain with him constantly. The common Latin translation <note>The author refers to the Vulgate, the standard Latin Bible of the time.</note> adds "godliness" <note>original: "pietas"</note> there as well, but it is included within the "fear of the Lord."

In another place, the Scripture says that he was anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power (Acts 10:38). That he received the Spirit without measure (John 3:34). The theologians say that in other creatures, such as Angels and Believers, there is a "fullness of capacity," because they have received as much grace as they need to be blessed, but in Christ Jesus, there is an "overflowing fullness": he not only had gifts for himself but also for others, so that we might receive from his fullness grace for grace (John 1:16). Various questions are asked here.

<margin>Whether Christ had faith and hope?</margin> I. It is asked whether Christ had faith and hope? This question is quite unnecessary; however, one can answer:
1. That one cannot say that Christ had a faith that consists in the refuge

<column-break/>

that one takes in his death <note>The author means Christ did not need "saving faith" in the way humans do, as he was the object of that faith.</note>; but one can indeed say that he had a faith consisting of the assent we give to the truths of the Gospel because of the infallible authority of God, and the trust we place in His power, wisdom, and goodness.

2. One can certainly attribute hope to him, as Paul says that for the joy that was set before him, he endured the Cross (Hebrews 12:2).

II. It is asked whether the soul of Christ, from the moment it was united with the body, or rather with his Divinity, <margin>Whether the soul of Christ was beatified in the moment of his union? Hugo of Saint Victor, Thomas [Aquinas] 1. 7. de Eustach: part II. P. 171.</margin> was filled with knowledge to such a degree that he knew everything and learned nothing?

The Scholastics <note>"Schoolgeleerden" or Scholastics were medieval theologians who used logic and philosophy to explain Christian doctrine.</note> attribute three types of knowledge to Jesus. 1. They believe that the soul of Jesus was beatified <note>State of perfect heavenly happiness and direct sight of God.</note> from the beginning of its union, and saw God in everything, and thus possessed the knowledge of the blessed even from his mother's womb; they believe that through this knowledge, the soul of Christ saw the essence of God and knew it much more clearly by virtue of its perfect union with the Word <note>The "Word" (Logos) refers to the Second Person of the Trinity.</note>. However, they do not claim that the soul of Christ completely comprehended the Divine essence, because it is infinite, but that it knew all past and future things in God. Nor do they claim that it knew all things absolutely, but all things that creatures are capable of doing. 2. They believe that Christ also had a new "infused knowledge" <note>Knowledge directly "poured" into the mind by God rather than learned through study.</note>, through which he could know all things except the Divine Essence, which he could only know through the first type of knowledge. 3. They believe that he also had an "acquired and experimental knowledge" <margin>Treatise 1 on the Incarnate Word, <note>original: "de verbo incarnato"</note> disputation 7, question 2.</margin> which could increase, whereas the other two could not grow; but they do not believe that Christ, through this knowledge, learned things he did not already know; they maintain that Christ learned through experience what he already knew through the other two types of knowledge.

Among the Reformed <note>Protestant theologians of the Calvinist tradition.</note>, Zanchius <margin>Zanchius, book 2 on the Incarnation of the Son of God, <note>original: "de Incarnatione Filii Dei"</note> Thesis 2.</margin> seems to have come very close to the opinion of the Scholastics, although with some distinction; for he maintains that the gifts of Christ did have some increase, but he also says that the infused knowledge of Christ had no increase regarding its possession, although it did have an increase regarding its actions. # DIVINE THEOLOGY. IX. B. Chapter XV.

<margin>Bellarmine, *Treatise on the Controversies against the Heretics*, regarding Christ, chapters 1, 2.</margin> note on Bellarmine, have with Zanchius accepted the three types of knowledge <note>original: "drie kennissen"</note> of the Scholastics <term>Scholastics: Medieval academic theologians who used philosophy to explain Christian doctrine</term>; but the other Reformed theologians are of the opinion that we hold: which is, that indeed Christ as Man possessed a very great knowledge; but that the same was not infinite, which we conclude from the following passages.

<margin>Luke 2:52.</margin> 1. It is said there, *Luke 2:52*, that Christ increased in Wisdom and Stature, not only before men, but also before God, so that one would not believe that he only increased according to the perception of men, to whom he revealed his wisdom more and more every day.

<margin>Mark 13:32.</margin> 2. Christ says in *Mark 13:32* that the Son of Man does not know the day of Judgment; this cannot be understood except according to his humanity.

One must not say that it is testified of Christ that he did not know the day of Judgment because he did not know it *in order to tell it to others*: that would be an answer that would not accord with Christ's dignity and would give occasion to all sorts of ambiguity. In this way, Christ could also have said that the Father does not know the day of judgment; one must not say that Christ did not know it because he did not know it in the same way as he will know it when that day arrives: For in this way, one could also say in some sense that the Father did not know the day of Judgment.

<margin>John 21:17.</margin> One can object here that it is said that Christ knows all things, *John 21:17.* But it is very easy to answer that this refers to the Divine Nature of Christ, and not to his human Nature, which is what is at issue in this matter.

<margin>Colossians 2:3.</margin> It is objected that all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ. *Colossians 2:3.* But 1. That does not mean that Christ, as man, had an infinite knowledge. 2. It is clear that the Person of Christ is spoken of there, and not the Human Nature; from the infinite knowledge that was in Christ, it does not follow that his human Nature knows everything, just as from the indwelling of the Godhead in Christ it does not follow that the man of Christ is his Godhead, and just as from the fact that in man there is a rational and immortal soul,

<column-break/>

it does not follow that the body of the man is rational and immortal.

It is said that Christ must have possessed all the gifts that were necessary for him to fulfill the Office of Mediator; Answer, 1. It was not necessary that our Mediator, as Man, had an infinite knowledge; it was enough that he possessed it as God. 2. It was not even necessary that the Godhead of Christ immediately communicated to his Humanity all the knowledge that he later imparted to her. It is said that Christ could not have been ignorant of anything without sin: Answer, one is mistaken; ignorance of things that one *must* and *can* know is punishable: but Christ, as Man, was not ignorant of those things which he, as man, was required to know.

<margin>John 3:34.</margin> It is said that it is written, *John 3:34*, That God gave the Spirit to his Son without measure; Answer, that means nothing other than that the Spirit was given to him in abundance, according to a figure of speech common among the Hebrews, *Ezra 7:22, Judith 7:12*, and that in comparison to all other believers, for to everyone else the spirit is given by measure. *Ephesians 4:7.* But the gifts, which in others are distributed in an imperfect way, are gathered in him in perfection: therefore it is said, <margin>Psalm 45:8, Hebrews 1:9, Romans 8:29</margin> *Psalm 45:8*, that he is anointed with the Oil of gladness above his companions. *Romans 8:29.* So that he might be the firstborn among many Brothers.

It is said that this is the error of the Agnoetae <note>original: "Agnoïten," a 6th-century sect that argued Christ's human nature was ignorant of some things, like the Day of Judgment.</note>, whom the ancient Church condemned: but those who know the error of these heretics know well that they attributed ignorance to Christ *as God*; also Nicephorus says, *Book XII, chapter 30*, that these erring spirits were offshoots of the Arians <note>original: "Arrianen," followers of Arius who denied Christ's full divinity.</note>.

2. It denies that this communication occurred through any infusion of Divine attributes into the Human Nature, as if the humanity of Christ possessed them separately from His Divinity.

3. It explains this communication using the analogy of a glowing iron; it is the fire and not the iron (say the authors of this Book <note>Likely referring to the *Formula of Concord*, a foundational Lutheran document</note>) that has the power to burn and to flicker. Meanwhile, the fire, united with the iron, reveals its power in the iron, with the iron, and through the iron. And the fire, burning through this union, has the power to burn and flicker without any change occurring to the nature of the iron or the fire. Similarly, they say, the *Word of God* shines forth in the *Human Nature* with all His *Majesty*, *Power*, and *Glory*, and reveals His *Power* and *Majesty*, etc., in this *Nature*, through this *Nature*, and with this *Nature*, such that one can say the *Human Nature* has a *Majesty*, a *Glory*, and a *Divine Power*, and that it can know and do everything. Today’s *Lutherans* <note>Followers of Martin Luther’s theology, particularly regarding the Real Presence in the Eucharist</note> explain this by saying that the *Divine attributes* are communicated to the *Human Nature*—not shared as a separate gift, but by virtue of the union. Thus, they claim that the *Humanity* of *Christ* is *Omnipresent*, *Almighty*, and *Omniscient*; some even go so far as to say that the *Human Nature* is *God* Himself.

<margin>Wendelin, *Christian Theology*, Book 1, Chapter 6.</margin>
4. There are *Lutherans* who believe that the *Human Nature* of *Christ* has become eternal and immeasurable, and that the body of *Christ* is infinite. However, few hold this view; others distinguish between the Divine attributes through which God acts—such as His *Omnipotence*, *Omniscience*, and *Omnipresence*—and His attributes that are not "active," such as *eternity*, *simplicity*, and *infinity*. They claim that the former are communicated, but the latter are not.

5. Finally, there are *Lutherans* who absolutely deny the [ubiquitous] presence of *Christ’s* Body, while others accept it. The Swedes

even believe that the Body of *Christ* has been everywhere from the first moment of His conception.

As for us <note>The author is writing from the Reformed/Calvinist perspective</note>, we believe that the attributes of the *Divine Nature* are not communicated to the *Human Nature*; and one will not doubt this if one considers these observations.

The first is that it is the same with the attributes of the Godhead as it is with the *Divine Essence*; for the *Divine Essence* is not essentially distinct from its attributes. Now, the *Divine Essence* cannot be communicated to the *Human Nature*, for otherwise the *Human Nature* would change into a *Divine Nature*.

The second observation is that the attributes of one subject cannot in any way be communicated to another subject, because that which is unique to one subject alone cannot be shared.

One might say that the union of the two *Natures* in *Christ* is the cause by which some attributes of the Godhead are communicated to the *Humanity*, and that this happens through grace, which otherwise would not occur. I answer that one cannot say this. 1. Because this union of natures occurred in a way where each nature preserves its own attributes. 2. Because, if the attributes of the *Divine Nature* were communicated to the *Human Nature* because of the union of the two *Natures*, one would have to say for the same reason that the attributes of the human *Nature* must also be communicated to the Divine, which is ridiculous. One might say that the human nature needed the attributes of the Divine to be communicated to it, but that the Divine *Nature* did not need the attributes of the *Human* to be communicated to it. I answer: 1. That the issue here is not whether the human *Nature* needed this communication, but whether it is true that this communication had to happen because of this union; for if that were so, our reasoning holds. 2. One disputes whether infinite attributes can be communicated to a subject that is finite.

It will be said that there is a distinction between the attributes of God; that some make themselves known through their outward workings, and that it was necessary for these to be communicated to the human Nature so that Christ might be our Mediator, but that the same is not true for others that do not work outwardly. Thus, one attribute could no more be shared than another. It is said that theologians nevertheless acknowledge that there are communicable and incommunicable attributes. I answer that theologians mean nothing more than that there are attributes in God of which one sees some signs in creatures—such as Goodness and Holiness—but they do not mean to say that these attributes are truly shared in their divine essence.

To make these truths even clearer—since those who maintain that some of the Divine attributes were communicated to the Human Nature speak of Omnipresence, Omniscience, and the Power to Give Life—let us see if this can be said in any way.

Thus, all the articles of faith would be overturned.

To say that Christ, from His birth onward, could truly be everywhere but simply did not wish to make this attribute known at that time, is to propose a matter without foundation; for how can one be prevented from being everywhere if one possesses omnipresence as an attribute?

To say that Christ left the world only in terms of His visible presence is to assume something that cannot be proven—namely, that a body can be in a place without being seen. To say that Christ obtained omnipresence through the Glory of His Resurrection is to teach something that the Scripture does not say.

To say that a glorified body does not resemble a common body is to say nothing at all. For I ask: if Glory makes it so that a body is no longer a body, then surely the nature of the Body of Christ is destroyed, neither by the union with the Godhead nor by the Glory of the resurrection. For the rest, we shall speak of the omnipresence of Christ's body in another place.

<margin>Col. II. 9.</margin>
It is objected that Colossians 2:9 says that all the fullness of the Godhead dwells in Christ. I answer: first, it is clear that this refers to the **Person** of Christ <note>The author distinguishes between the "Person" (the whole Christ) and the individual "Natures" (the specific divine or human parts)</note>.

<margin>John II. 19.</margin>
2. Even if the Humanity of Christ were the focus, it is one thing to say that the Godhead dwelt in the human Nature of Christ as in its Temple, and quite another to say that the attributes of the Divine Nature were shared with the Human; it is further said that the Godhead dwells *bodily* in Christ, which is to express that the Divine Being with all its perfections was united with the Human Nature, not in shadow or imagination—as it was formerly said God dwelt in the Ark—but truly and personally; for God is also truly present through his power in all creatures; he indeed dwells in believers, but he is personally in Christ alone.

It is objected: if Christ’s Human Nature is not everywhere, where then is the Divine Nature? The Human Nature would then be separated from the Divine; for when two things are united, where one is, the other must consequently be as well.

I answer: one is mistaken; when two things that are unequal are united, it is not necessary that where one is, the other must also be. If I had a staff that could reach from one end of the world to the other, and something were hung on one of the ends, that thing would never be separated from the staff, and yet it would not be everywhere that the staff is; thus Christ’s Human Nature is never—

<column-break/>

—separated from his Godhead, because the Godhead is infinite: but it does not follow from this that the Humanity is everywhere the Godhead is found.

It is said that Christ is seated at the right hand of his Father, and that this right hand is everywhere.

**Answer 1.** Sitting at God's right hand is a dignity <note>original: "waardigheid"</note> attributed to the **Person** of Christ, and not to one of his Natures; it belongs to him as the Christ and the Mediator of Men, and not strictly as Man; now, it is a false argument <term>sophisme: a clever but fallacious argument</term> to appropriate to one nature in particular what belongs to the whole person; it is just as if I wanted to conclude that the human body is rational, under the pretext that it is said of the whole Human.

**2.** This reasoning is based on a false interpretation of this Scripture passage; one perceives GOD as having a physical right hand, and Christ as truly sitting, instead of realizing that this is a figurative way of speaking <note>original: "bebloemde wys van spreeken"</note> which means *to reign*.

**3.** If this reasoning were sound, and one could conclude from the fact that God's right hand is everywhere that he who sits at this right hand is also everywhere, one would also have to conclude that because God's right hand is eternal, the one sitting at his right hand is also eternal—which one would not dare to say.

<margin>Eph. I. 20. Hebr. VIII. 1.</margin>

<margin>Eph. IV. 8. Eph. IV. 10.</margin>
It is objected that Paul says that Christ ascended into Heaven so that he might fill all things.

I answer that in this passage, it is not a filling of all things by his physical presence that is seen, but by the presence of his spirit and gifts.

**Answer:** this reasoning is based on the idea one has that the term *Son of Man* includes only the human Nature, whereas the Office of Mediator is included therein,

and that by allusion to Daniel VII <note>original: "Daniel VII." Refers to the vision of the 'Son of Man' receiving an everlasting dominion</note>, where the Messiah is thus named: every nature shall do its work on the day of the last judgment. Jesus Christ will then let himself be seen as man, but as God he will know what men have done, and he will have all the power that is required to pronounce the judgment.

One objects Matthew XXVIII. 18. against this, where Christ says: All <margin>Matt: XXVIII. 18.</margin> power is given to Me, in Heaven and on earth.

Answer 1. Here the focus is not on the power that Christ received according to the union of the two Natures, but on the power that was given to him after his resurrection, to be able to exercise the ministry of the head of the Church.

2. In this passage it is not about Omnipotence, which is an essential property of God, but about the authority and the right that Christ has received, and which caused him to say to his Disciples: *Go forth, teach all nations* etc.

One will say that authority presupposes omnipotence, and that consequently it is necessary that he who has this authority also has an infinite power; but it is not necessary that he who has this authority possesses this power in regards to his two Natures <note>The author argues that while Christ the Person is omnipotent, his human nature does not become "all-powerful" in itself</note>.

One objects that Christ did miracles, and consequently must have been omnipotent; but Christ did them through the power that he possessed as God, and not that which he had as man.

One objects that Christ says that his flesh gives life to the world. John VI. 51. <margin>John VI. 51.</margin>

Answer: one does not comprehend that this only means that the flesh of J. Christ, the God-Man, has acquired life for us and bestowed the Spirit, who makes alive; one must then not believe that he meant to say that his human Nature has the power of itself to produce eternal life: Christ, who is God, has earned life for us through the death which he suffered as man, which he communicates to us as Mediator.

One says that the soul communicates life to the body, and that thus, consequently, the Divine Nature can communicate its properties to the human Nature.

I answer, that one can draw no other conclusion from that than that the Divine Nature of Christ has come to communicate life to his human nature; but, just as the soul does not communicate the ability to think, which is its property, to the

<column-break/>

body, so it follows then that the Divine Nature of Christ does not communicate its properties to his human Nature.

<margin>Effects of the union of the two natures.</margin>
Hitherto we have considered the effects of the union of the two Natures of Christ with regard to his human Nature; we must now see what the effects of this union are in respect to the Person of Christ.

The first effect of this union is the **communication**, through which one attributes to the **Person** of Christ the properties of one and the other Nature, which happens in various ways.

1. Just as Christ is sometimes named with a name that only signifies his Divine Nature, so the properties of this Nature are also attributed to him, just as when it is said, John I. 1. *In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God*; likewise when Christ is sometimes named with a name that seems only to indicate his human Nature, the properties of this Nature are also attributed to him, just as when it is said that the Son of man ate and was present <note>original: "geweest heeft" - literally "has been," referring to his physical presence and human activities</note>.

2. Sometimes the properties of the human Nature are attributed to Christ although he is named with a name that indicates only his Godhead, just as when it is said that the Son of God was made from a woman, that the Lord of glory was crucified, that God has ransomed his Church through his blood; for in all these places one attributes to the Son of God that which is only said of him as man.

3. Sometimes the properties of the Divine Nature are attributed to Christ although he is named with a name that seems only to indicate his human Nature, just as when it is said that the Son of man is in Heaven, at the same time that he is still on the earth; for being in Heaven <note>referring here to omnipresence</note> belongs only to the Divine Nature; this is the communication that the Scholastics <note>original: "Schoolgeleerden" - the academic theologians of the Middle Ages and the Reformation</note> call the *communication (idiomatum)* or the communication of properties <note>original: "mededeeling (idiomatum) of der eigenschappen"</note>.

The second effect of the union with regard to the Person is that all the acts of Christ which concern our salvation and relate to his mediatorial office...
