## CHAPTER XVI.

### Of the two States of Jesus Christ.

After we have spoken of the Natures of Christ, we must treat the two States through which he passed.

The Scripture describes these to us with care; it speaks to us of his Humiliation and of his Exaltation, and of the various degrees of his Humiliation and of his Exaltation.

To make his humiliation known to us, it says:

<margin>Phil. II. 7: 8.</margin>
1. That he humbled himself, which gives an idea of the glory that Christ possessed beforehand.

2. That he annihilated <note>The Dutch *vernietigt* here refers to the theological concept of "kenosis" or the "emptying" of Christ's divine status to take on human form.</note> himself: which nevertheless does not mean that Christ brought himself to nothing, but it reveals to us the infinite distance that existed between the state in which he first found himself and the Nature that he assumed; a distance that is as great as that between being and non-being. In the original text <note>referring to the Greek text of Philippians 2:7</note> it says that he *emptied* himself, which one must understand in opposition to the fullness he possessed, which consisted in part in appearing with all the luster and all the glory that corresponded to his state.

3. It says that he took on the form of a Servant, which is to say, the human Nature with all its weaknesses and all its humiliations.

4. That he was found in the appearance of a Man, which is to say, that he became like other men, without being clothed with any splendor or greatness that distinguished him from others.

<column-break/>

5. That he was obedient unto the death of the cross, which demonstrates the depth of his obedience.

<margin>John I. 1. Tim. III. 16.</margin>
6. That the Word became flesh, and that he was manifested in the flesh, to teach us that he assumed our Nature with its weaknesses.

<margin>Heb. II. 9.</margin>
7. That he became lower than the Angels: 1. In that which he suffered, in contrast to the Angels, who do not suffer. 2. In the shame with which he was covered, whereas the Angels are always surrounded with glory. 3. In the death that he underwent, whereas the Angels are immortal. 4. Finally, in the power of God's wrath <note>original: *gramschap*</note> that he bore, in place of His Favor, which the Angels always enjoy.

<margin>Rom. VIII. 3.</margin>
8. It says that he assumed the likeness of sin, which is to say, that he assumed our nature with all the miseries and pains that are the essential and inseparable signs of sin, so that if one looked upon him, one could have believed that he had come forth from the corrupt mass <note>original: *verdorve klomp*. A common term in Calvinist theology referring to fallen humanity as a "corrupt lump."</note> of the human race.

<margin>Isa. LIII. 2.</margin>
9. It says that he grew up before His face like a tender plant <note>original: *Ryske*</note>, and like a root out of dry ground; that he had no form or glory, etc., which signifies not only the pitiable state in which the house of David was to be at the time of the Messiah, but also the humility with which Christ wished to appear.

<margin>Ps. CX. 7.</margin>
10. It says that he shall drink from the brook along the way; which can well signify the pains that Jesus would feel and the distress in which he would exist, although others apply these words to the victory that Christ would achieve over his enemies, like a conqueror who pursues his enemies with such vigor that he allows no time to gain new strength, scarcely giving himself the time to drink from a brook that he finds on his path.

There are many other expressions, yet I have kept to these, following great Divines <note>or "Theologians"</note> therein, because they are the most important.

<margin>Claude Garissoles.</margin>

GOD-GELEERDHOID <note>Divine Theology</note>. IX. B. XVI. Chapter.

<columns>
...delivered from the miseries, weaknesses, shame, and pains that he had suffered, but that he also gave him supreme power, so that all creatures should worship him and be subject to his Kingdom.

<margin>Hebrews 2:9.</margin>
2. It says that he is crowned with glory and honor, like a King and Conqueror who has overcome his enemies.

<margin>Luke 24:26.</margin>
3. That he entered into glory and sits at the right hand of God, which we shall explain in another place.

The various descriptions of the humiliation and the exaltation of the Messiah found in the Old Testament have greatly troubled the Jews. Unwilling to admit these two states [in one person], they devised two Messiahs: one poor, the other victorious; one a Son of Joseph and Ephraim, under the name of Nehemia <note>Nehemiah ben Hushiel, a figure in Jewish apocalyptic tradition who precedes the final Messiah</note>, insignificant and despised, who would lead a small number of people back from captivity and be killed in the fight against Gog and Magog by Armillus <note>A legendary figure in Jewish eschatology, often depicted as a monstrous king who opposes the Messiah</note>, the head of the children of Edom (or Christians), and who would thereafter be raised again by his successor; the other, the Son of David, to whom all the twelve tribes and all the kings of the earth would pay homage.

It was necessary that Christ pass through these two States.

<margin>On the necessity of these two States of Christ.</margin>
1. Because it was necessary that the one who would save us perform two tasks: that he satisfy Divine justice, and that he acquire and apply salvation to us, and subsequently sanctify us through his Spirit. To achieve the first of these goals, Christ had to suffer and be annihilated <note>theological "emptying" or kenosis</note>; for the second, it was necessary for him to be exalted. Through his humiliation, we have obtained the forgiveness of our sins; through his exaltation, we are cleansed of our corruption and have become new creatures.

2. We needed to have free access to him; to that end, it was necessary for him to be humbled and to have a commonality of nature, of weakness, and of pain with us. He has, says Paul, <margin>Hebrews 2:17.</margin> Hebrews 2:17, *become like his brothers in all things, so that he might be a merciful and faithful High Priest to reconcile the sins of the people;* for because he suffered, having been tempted, he is also able to help those who are being tempted. But subse-

<column-break/>

quently, we had to be convinced that he is capable of delivering us from all evil and giving us eternal goods; it was therefore necessary that he be exalted.

One will be particularly convinced of the necessity of the humiliation of Christ when one considers:
<margin>The necessity of his humiliation.</margin>
1. That Christ could not better restore what sin had corrupted than by infinitely humbling himself beneath his natural state, just as the first man had exalted himself above his lawful state.

2. That Divine justice could not be satisfied except by the death of our surety <term>surety: a person who takes legal responsibility for another's debt or conduct; here, Christ acting as the legal guarantor for humanity</term>.

3. That God could not better teach us the sorrowful consequences of sin than by making his Son descend to the utmost contempt and handing him over to death.

4. Finally, that God could not more powerfully demonstrate his wisdom and his power than by destroying the kingdom of the devil through the cross of his Son.

One will be convinced of the necessity of Christ's exaltation when one takes into account:
<margin>The necessity of his exaltation.</margin>
1. That the eternal Son of God could not remain in an annihilated state forever; that it was necessary for his supreme dignity to be finally recognized and for him to be exalted above all creatures.

2. That Divine justice could not deprive the one who had satisfied it of his righteous reward.

3. That his wisdom had to restore the natural Order, which had been overturned, and that it had to raise Christ up again into that state which was his due.

4. That the love of the Heavenly Father did not allow him to leave in humiliation the one who had so worthily upheld the rights of his Divinity.

5. That Christ had to send his Spirit, which he could not do until after he was glorified. John 7:39.

6. Finally, that the faith and the hope of the believers required that Christ be exalted.

One will have no difficulty understanding why the humiliation of Christ had to precede his exaltation if one considers:
<margin>Why the humiliation of Christ preceded the exaltation of Christ.</margin>
1. That before Heaven was opened...

DIVINITY. IX. B. CHAPTER XVII.

...parts to investigate: the first two concern the time of the Birth of Christ and his Precursor <note>The "Precursor" refers to John the Baptist.</note>. We shall handle these in this Chapter.

<margin>
Concerning the time of the Birth of Christ. Galatians 4:4.
</margin>
One cannot point out the exact time of the birth of Christ; yet four things can be stated with certainty.

1. It is certain that Christ came in the "fullness of time" as designated by the Prophets, at a time when the Heathens were submerged in a terrible idolatry, when the Jews were greatly corrupted and divided by many sects, and when darkness had stretched over the entire earth; all of which were driven away before the Sun of Righteousness.

<margin>
Luke 2:2.
</margin>
2. It is established that he was born under the Fourth Monarchy <note>In traditional biblical interpretation, the "Four Monarchies" were Babylon, Persia, Greece, and finally Rome.</note>, and under the Emperor Augustus, at the time when he ordered the census <note>original: "beschryving"</note> of all the subjects of the Roman Empire; which occurred when Cyrenius (or Quirinius), as an extraordinary envoy of the Emperor, was sent into Syria and Judea, in the place where Saturninus was the ordinary Governor, who was followed by Quintilius Varus, and thereafter by Quirinius. This census is called "The First," either in regards to Quirinius, who carried it out for the first time; or in regards to Judea, in which the Romans had not yet conducted a census; or because it was general and extraordinary.

<margin>
Ancyran Monument <note>original: "Monum. Ancyr."</note> in the additions of Lipsius. Leunclavius in the *Pandects*.
</margin>
There were three censuses under Augustus; see Suetonius in *Life of Octavius*, chapter 27; Henri Valois in Book I; Eusebius, chapter 5. If we possessed the ten-year History of Dio Cassius, which we have lost, we would without doubt find therein the census that Augustus had conducted at the time of the birth of our Savior; but one must not doubt the truth of this history. Justin Martyr (in his *Second Apology*) and Tertullian in his work *Against Marcion* (Book IV, chapter 7) would have directed the Heathens and the Heretics to the registers that were still being preserved. Opinions are very divided regarding this census: Tertullian says that it was conducted by Sentius Saturninus, who was indeed the Governor of Syria around that time, according to Josephus. (Tertullian *Against Marcion*, Book IV, chapter 19; Josephus *Antiquities*, Book XXVII, chapters 6 and 7). Henri Valois wishes for us to read "Sentius Saturninus" in place of "Quirinius" in the Gospel of Luke; but some are of the opinion that one should not give the slightest heed to Tertullian; others say that Quirinius could well have held the supreme authority in Syria as a Lieutenant of Saturni-

<column-break/>

-nus, and could have conducted the census in Judea by his order and in his name; or that he, as one of the twenty-four extraordinary commissioners who were appointed by Augustus beyond the usual practice, had Syria and Palestine for his division, which did not prevent Saturninus from remaining Governor and even having a part in the census. Ludovicus Cappellus believes that one should read "Quintilius Varus." The famous Mr. Huet <note>Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a renowned French scholar.</note> believes one should read "Quintillius" <note>original Greek: "Κυιντιλλιος"</note>. Other scholars translate it thus: *this first census occurred before Quirinius was Governor of Syria*, but we leave these disputes to the chronologers.

3. It is certain that Christ was born under Herod the Great. Matthew 2:1.

<margin>
Spanheim page 11. Spanheim the Younger, *Chronicle* page 15. *Gospels* page 8.
</margin>
4. That, in the fifteenth year of the Emperor Tiberius, Christ was about 30 years old. Luke 3:1.

This is what we know for certain, but we cannot conclude from it what the exact year of the birth of Christ was: we do not know in what year of Herod, nor in what year of Augustus, Christ was born.

The common opinions are that Christ was born in the year of the world 3950, or the year 3983, or 4000, or 4004.

<margin>
Pagi, Spanheim, Basnage, Cappellus.
</margin>
It was in the year 532 that Dionysius the Small <note>Dionysius Exiguus, the monk who invented the AD/BC dating system.</note> began to count the years since the birth of Christ: but it is believed that he was mistaken; some say he miscalculated by 8 years (like the Greeks), others by a year and some months, others by two, three, four, or six years. According to his calculation, Christ would have been born after the death of Herod, and it would not be possible for Christ to have been 30 years old in the 15th year of Tiberius.

<margin>
*Against Celsus* Book 8. Tertullian *On Modesty* chapter 14. *Stromata* Book I.
</margin>
Regarding the Month of the Year, nothing certain can be said about that either. In the first three Centuries, no fixed day was set for the Feast of Christmas-time <note>original: "Kers-tyd"</note>. Origen, who accurately records the days which the Christians were accustomed to celebrate, speaks only of Sunday and Pentecost. The writers of the first three Centuries do the same. Clement of Alexandria relates that there were people who said Christ was born on the 20th of May, others on the 20th of April; but he reproaches both for excessive curiosity. Besides that, it is established by the testimony of Chrysostom that the celebration of the Feast of

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the historical timing of the birth of Christ. The previous page established that he was born during the Roman census under Augustus; this page now examines the specific calendar date and the conflicting traditions of the early Church, before transitioning to the life of John the Baptist.</meta>

<header>THE CHRISTIAN</header>

<margin>Homily on the Nativity of the Lord <note>original: "Hom. in Nat. Dom."</note>, question 31, Vol. 5.</margin>
...time first came into use in Antioch around the year 370, and in all the churches of the Eastern Dioceses that depended on it. At the time of Epiphanius—that is to say, toward the end of the 4th Century—all the churches of Egypt and the Island of Cyprus celebrated the memory of the birth of Jesus Christ on the 6th of January, the day on which the Feast of the Three Kings <note>The Epiphany, traditionally celebrating the visit of the Magi.</note> falls. The churches of Jerusalem, Egypt, and Asia believed this as well, as many learned writers assert. Others say that he was born on the 25th of December, and this is the opinion generally adopted in the Western Churches.

<margin>
Phil. Lansberg
Apostolic Constitutions <note>original: "Const. Clem." referring to the Constitutiones Apostolicae attributed to Clement.</note> Book V, ch. 12.
</margin>
A Paschal letter from Theophilus of Caesarea is cited; but Mr. Ittigius <note>Thomas Ittig (1643–1710), a Lutheran theologian and historian.</note> demonstrates that this letter is a forgery. He refutes Andreas du Saussay, who claims that this custom was carried out by Sabinian and his companions.

<margin>Appendix to the dissertation on Heresies, Leipzig 1696.</margin>
A letter from John of Nicaea is also cited, which says that it was first under Pope Julius that the Feast of the Nativity was fixed to fall on the 25th of December. However, those who provide us with the letter of this writer, and those who have examined it, do not give us a high opinion of the author. It is certain that before the Emperor Justin in the 6th Century, the Feast of the Epiphany <note>original: "Verschining," referring to the manifestation of Christ to the Gentiles.</note> was not celebrated throughout the entire East. Others maintain that Christ was born in the month of September.

<margin>Beroaldus, Scaliger, Calvin.</margin>
Those who argue that Christ was born on the 25th of December rely on a false premise: namely, that Zacharias, the father of John the Baptist, was the High Priest; that he entered the Temple on the Day of Atonement in the month of September; and that consequently, John the Baptist was conceived in the month of October. Following this, 6 months later—that is to say, in the month of April—Christ was also conceived (Luke 1:26). In this manner, he would have come into the world in the month of December. However, Zacharias was not called the High Priest. 1. It is stated there that he was performing his office according to his "order," which pertained to the common priests who served the Altar and then returned to their homes after the passing of eight days. 2. It is stated that this fell to him by lot; now it is certain that, regardless of whatever irregularity existed among the Jews, the office of High Priest never-the-less did not depend on the lot or on the priestly 

<column-break/>

orders. It is said that he came into the Temple to burn the incense; but it is well known that every priest chosen by lot was permitted to offer incense outside the Sanctuary (Exodus 30:7, 8, 9). It is said that the Angel appeared to him on the right side of the Altar of Incense; but it was on the side of that Altar where the incense was burned in the morning and evening, and not toward the Ark.

<margin>Scaliger.</margin>
The opinion of those who want Christ to have been born in the month of September has no secure foundations. They claim that, according to the institution of David mentioned in 1 Chronicles 24 (after which the lineages of the priests were divided into 24 orders), Zacharias, who was in the 8th order, had to take his turn on the 21st of July—160 years and 192 days after the Dedication by Judas Maccabeus. They argue that Zacharias returned home at the beginning of August; that Christ was conceived in the month of January; and was born at the end of September or the beginning of October, in the Autumn, when day and night are of equal length. But one must prove that this order was never interrupted, as it is certain that many events could have disturbed it. The reason brought forward—that there were shepherds in the field—is not convincing enough, for that could well happen in Judea in the winter. There are lands where the flock is left in the open air all year round. The reason taken from the census that Augustus ordered to be made is also insufficient, for the Emperors did not take much heed of the people, and above all not of the Jews. Furthermore, there was no necessity at all for Christ to come into the world at the same time as it was created. It is best to decide nothing on this matter.

<margin>Concerning the Forerunner of Jesus Christ.</margin>
The second question presented concerns the Forerunner of Christ; this Forerunner was John, named John the Baptist.

->The Scripture testifies of him:<-

1. That an Angel from Heaven was sent to foretell his birth.
2. That he was the son of Zacharias, a priest, and of Elizabeth, who was of the lineage of Aaron and a relative of the Holy Virgin, both of them being righteous.
3. That Zacharias his father, not believing what the Angel told him of this son, lost his speech.

# THEOLOGY. IX. B. XVII. Chapter.

4. That he was conceived six months before *Christ*.

5. That when the Virgin *Mary* went to visit *Elizabeth*, her child—filled with the Holy Spirit—leaped in her womb at the greeting of *Mary*.

6. That upon his birth, *Zacharias* regained his speech, and the child was given the name *John*.

7. That he lived in the Desert of *Judea*; that is to say, in that part of *Judea* situated toward the South, which, being much more rugged than the rest of the land, was also less populated with Cities, Villages, and inhabitants.

<margin>Mark 1:6.</margin> 8. That he fed on wild honey and locusts, which the poor in *Palestine* ate and which were permitted to the Jews by the Law. I can see no necessity, following *Isidore of Seville* <note>A 7th-century scholar and bishop; his "Etymologies" was a standard reference for the Middle Ages.</note>, to say that by "locusts" one must understand the tips or tops of herbs and the branches of trees. Mr. *Morisson*, Canon of *Bar-le-Duc* and Knight of the Holy Sepulchre, in his historical account of a journey made to Mount *Sinai* and *Jerusalem*, says that locusts are found in abundance in the desert where *John* stayed; that they are as large as a fist, that the country folk cut off their legs and let them dry in the sun, and that once dried, they have a taste very close to hazelnuts. This writer also believes that the wild honey was the fruit of a tree fairly common in *Judea*, called the *Caroubier* <note>original: "Caroubier"; the Carob tree.</note> after the name of its fruit, called *Caroub* in the language of the country, which means "wild honey." He says this tree looks much like a walnut tree and its fruits like green peas growing in our gardens; that this fruit, when green, is so bitter it cannot be eaten, but when ripe and fully grown, it has the sweetness of honey.

9. The Evangelists add that the clothing of *John* was of camel hair, with a leather belt that he wore around his waist, just like *Elijah*.

10. That he made himself known to the world in the fifteenth year of *Tiberius* by the *Jordan*.

11. That he preached repentance to prepare the people for the arrival of the *Messiah*, whose Forerunner he was.

12. That he baptized those who came to him in the *Jordan*, according to the custom of the Jews, who baptized their new

<column-break/>

converts, and that he baptized *Christ* therein, as we shall see elsewhere.

13. That he pointed out the Lamb of God—that is to say, the *Messiah*—to those who came to his baptism.

14. That he strongly rebuked *Herod Antipas*, the Tetrarch <note>A ruler of a fourth part of a region; Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and Perea.</note>, because he had married *Herodias*, the wife of his brother *Philip*, saying that it was not permitted for him to have his brother's wife; but that *Herod*, unable to endure such language, had him thrown into prison.

15. That *Herod*, giving a great feast for his courtiers on his birthday, was so pleased by the daughter of *Herodias* dancing before the king that he promised her with an oath to give her whatever she might ask of him, even if it were half of his kingdom; that when this girl, on the advice of her mother, requested of *Herod* that the head of *John* the Baptist be given to her on a platter, this Prince—though saddened by this demand—had that holy man beheaded so as not to break his oath. Thus, the death of *John* was the reward for a girl's dance and the consequence of a thoughtless oath made in drunkenness and excess.

This is the *John* who is called a "burning and shining lamp," a "Prophet," and "more than a Prophet," the "Angel" <note>Used here in the sense of a messenger, following the Greek *angelos*.</note> whom God would send before *Christ*, the "*Elijah*" who was to come, the "greatest born of woman," and the "Friend of the Bridegroom."

Many stories have been told of this holy man that need not be recounted here.

It is asked whether it is true that the oracles of the Heathens ceased at the time of the birth of *Christ*?

This opinion was reasonably common, and *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, an early Christian historian.</note> contributed the most to convincing Christians of it. To prove it, he made use of the confession of *Porphyry* <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher often critical of Christianity.</note>, and confirmed it with the famous story found in *Plutarch's* dialogue regarding the oracles that had ceased: that a certain pilot named *Thamus* heard a voice in the night commanding him to cry out, "The Great *Pan* <note>The Greek god of the wild and shepherds.</note> is dead." There are also added the words which some claim the oracle at *Delphi* gave to the Em- <note>The text cuts off mid-word; likely "Emperor" (Keizer).</note>

THE CHRISTIAN

Augustus answered: "The Hebrew child forces me to return to hell again." <note>This refers to a famous medieval legend where the Oracle of Delphi told Emperor Augustus that a 'Hebrew Child' had commanded the gods to leave their temples and return to the underworld.</note>

I answer that it appears that the Oracles were consulted until after the death of the great Theodosius: this has been proven and demonstrated by Mr. van Gaalen, a Mennonite Physician in Haarlem (in his book on the *Oracles of the Pagans*, printed in the year 1673) through various passages from Plutarch, Strabo, Suetonius, Tacitus, Dio Cassius, Herodian, Philostratus, Pausanias, Dio Chrysostom, Lucian, Capitolinus, Spartianus, Trebellius Pollio, Tertullian, Zosimus, Ammianus Marcellinus, Macrobius, Theodoret, and Sozomen, and by the Laws of the Emperors in the Year 385.

## CHAPTER XVIII.

->On the Mother of Christ, and why He willed to be born of a Virgin.<-

The third question concerns the Mother of Christ.

The Scripture teaches us that it is the Virgin Mary, who was betrothed to Joseph, of the Tribe of Judah and of the Seed of David, being a daughter of Heli: Matthew and Luke prove this truth.

The renowned Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and rabbinical scholar known for using the Talmud to illustrate the New Testament.</note> cites a passage from the Talmud from which one can conclude that the Jews knew that Mary was a daughter of Heli; in the Latin and Greek Church, it has been believed that Joachim was the Father and Anna the Mother of the Virgin.

<margin>Matt. 1. Luke 3:23.</margin> There is much probability that Luke gives us the genealogy of Mary, and Matthew that of Joseph, so it is not surprising that these two genealogies are different: Matthew derives Joseph from David through Solomon, and Luke derives Mary from David through Nathan; it is true that Mary is not mentioned there, because no mention was made of women in the genealogies, but mention is made of Heli, who is called the Father of Christ because he

<column-break/>

was the Father of the Virgin. For I believe that one must read verse 23 of the 3rd chapter of Luke thus: "And Jesus began to be about 30 years old, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph and of Heli"; thus it is testified here that Jesus was in truth held to be the Son of Joseph, but that in fact he was a Son—that is to say, a grandson—of Heli: now it follows from this that Mary was truly of the lineage of David, since she was descended from David through Nathan.

<margin>Luke 2:4.</margin> The Church Fathers and the Theologians prove the same from Luke, saying that when the Jews were obliged to travel to the city from which they originated, and that Joseph for this reason also went to Bethlehem, as being of the lineage of David, the Virgin at the same time also traveled thither to be enrolled with him, as I have noted.

It is also brought forward that the Law obliged daughters to marry within their Tribe, which was nevertheless restricted to those daughters who, having no brother, inherited the property of their house either alone or with other sisters; such was the case of the five daughters of Zelophehad (Numbers 27:1), for whose sake this Law was made: it is maintained that the Virgin was also in the same situation.

I do not wish to bring up here the fables that have been told of the Father and Mother of the Virgin, of her birth, of her presentation in the Temple, of her marriage, and of her death; there is no person of understanding today who gives credit to them. Therefore, without dallying upon them, I shall content myself with noting that she <margin>Isa. 7:14.</margin> was a Virgin when she conceived Christ: Isaiah had foretold it in his Prophecy, Chapter 7:14: "Behold, a Virgin shall conceive and she shall bear a Son, and call his name Immanuel."

The Jews, who forget nothing that might serve to distort the Oracles <note>In this context, 'Oracles' refers to divine prophecies in the Bible.</note> containing the clearest proofs for Christ, say that the word we have translated as "a Virgin" <note>The Hebrew word *Almah*.</note> only signifies a young woman, whether she be a virgin or not; and consequently, that one must apply this divine prophecy to <margin>Isa. 7:3. R. Salom. Jarchi</margin> Shear-jashub, son of Isaiah, or to Hezekiah, son of Ahaz, or to some son that Ahaz would procreate from a young woman he had married.

### DIVINE THEOLOGY. IX. BOOK XVIII. CHAPTER.

it is easy to refute the Jewish arguments.

1. The word <note>The Hebrew word is *almah* (עַלְמָה).</note> that we have translated as **Virgin** was interpreted as such by the LXX <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament from the 3rd century BCE.</note> Translators.

2. The word is used in this sense in all places of the Scripture, as one will be convinced when they are examined with attention. Gen. XXIV. 3. Exod. II. 8. Ps. LXVIII. 26. Song of Sol. I. 3. VI. 7. Prov. XXX. 18. etc.

3. It is the only word in the Scripture that so clearly signifies a **Virgin** who has not known a man; it even implies a **Daughter** who keeps herself enclosed and hidden within the house, an allusion to the custom of the Jews and those of the East, who raised their **Daughters** without ever letting them leave the house until they were married off. The other expressions by which the Hebrews signify a Daughter sometimes mean a young married Daughter (Ruth IV. 12) or one who has been ravished (Deut. XXII. 19) or one who has been married and mourns for her Husband (Joel I. 8), where something else is added, as in Gen. XXIV. 16.

4. Even among foreign nations, this word has passed over with the same meaning.

5. The Hebrew language has no other expression to signify a **Virgin**.

6. God promises here something beyond the ordinary; now, it is no extraordinary thing for a young Woman to be pregnant with a Son, unless she is a **Virgin**.

7. Finally, it is probable that Shear-jashub could already walk before Isaiah proclaimed this divine oracle; Hezekiah was at least 9 years old, and one reads nowhere else that Ahaz had other children.

It is said that this sign of the Messiah was not enough to quiet the Spirit of Ahaz and of the people, who were concerned about the impending destruction of Jerusalem.

I have already answered this difficulty when speaking in another place of this divine oracle; I will further remark here:

1. That the word <note>Referring to the Hebrew *oth* (sign).</note> is not well explained, for it does not always mean a prophetic sign, but sometimes a miracle; just as when God, promising Hezekiah that he would be delivered from the hands of Sennacherib, added that they would have this sign: that for two

I. Part.

<column-break/>

years they would eat what the land produced of itself, and that in the 3rd year they would have to sow—which did not happen until after Sennacherib had broken off the siege.

2. That the promise of the **Messiah** was the great object of the faith of the Jews; thus this divine oracle had no other purpose than to lift the faith of the believers, who were of the descendants of David, toward the **Messiah**, who would earn them the favor of God, of which Ahaz had made himself unworthy.

The question is asked, why did the Son of God willed to be born from the Womb of a Virgin?

I answer, that the will of God must bring our curiosity to a standstill; but it was very fitting that the Christ should be born in this manner.

<margin>
Gen. XXI. 2.
Gen. XXX. 23.
Judges XIII. 24.
1 Sam. I. 20.
</margin>
1. Most of those by whom the Messiah was prefigured were conceived and born by way of a miracle. Isaac was born of a Mother who was barren and a Father who was very aged. Joseph was born of Rachel, who had been barren for a long time; Samson and Samuel were also born of women <note>The Dutch uses *Rigts-vrouwen*, likely referring to women of the era of the Judges or notable women of faith.</note> who had been a long time without bearing children.

2. It has very often been noted that the conception and birth of great men, who were to excel, had something special and remarkable about them.

3. It was fitting that the birth of the Savior of the world be distinguished from other men; he had to be born of a Woman so that he would be a true human; but he did not wish to be born of a Man so that it would be acknowledged that he was more than a human.

4. Just as God does not wish to multiply miracles without necessity, so he did not wish for Christ to be born like others from a Man and Woman, because he would have had to sanctify the Seed of the Man and the Woman from whom he would be born.

Adam was created immediately by God; Eve was taken from a rib of Adam; now everyone is born of Man and Woman; Christ willed to be born of a Woman without the involvement of a Man; thus he, who was without a Mother as the Son of God, was without a Father as the Son of man.

That our Lord *Jesus Christ*, having come to save the human race—which consists of Men and Women—did not despise the male sex, as he clothed himself in their form, nor that of Women, for he was born of a Woman. 2. But how, it is asked, can it be that *Christ* was born of a Virgin?

I admit that the pregnancy of a Virgin, without the involvement of a Man, has always been held as an impossible thing in nature; indeed, the *Romans* maintained that the Temple they had built for peace must last forever, because the Oracle they had consulted regarding its durability had replied that it would not be destroyed until a Virgin should bring a child into the World. <note>This refers to a medieval legend that the Temple of Peace in Rome collapsed on the night of Christ's birth.</note>

But, as the Angel says to *Mary*, nothing is impossible with God (*Luke 1:37*). It is no more difficult for Him to bring forth a body from the substance of a Virgin than it was to make that of *Adam* from the dust of the earth.

One asks, why did God will that *Mary* be betrothed to *Joseph*?

I answer: because without this, *Mary*—according to the strictness of the Law—would have had to lose her life, being unable to show how she had become pregnant; furthermore, her Son, who would have been regarded as the product of an unlawful union, could not, according to the Law, have been received into the assembly of God’s people, far from being recognized by them as the true Head and the *Messiah*. It also appears that *Christ*, being born of a betrothed Woman, willed to sanctify the state of marriage.

One asks whether the virgin *Mary* remained a virgin forever after she gave birth to *Jesus*, and whether, being married to *Joseph*, she produced no children?

I answer that the Scripture does not decide this matter:

Some Church Fathers opposed this, yet they simultaneously showed that it does not touch the foundations of the mysteries of our faith, for which it is sufficient that *Mary* remained a Virgin until the birth of our Savior.

Those who maintained that the Virgin did not keep her virginal state after she gave birth to *Christ* rely on this: 1. That *Christ* is called the firstborn of *Mary*.

It is said that the Son of the living God cannot be the Son of *Mary*.
I admit that it cannot be so in one and the same respect, but indeed, that he who is the Son of the living God, in regard to his Divine Nature, is at the same time the Son of *Mary*, in regard to his human Nature.

It was not, therefore, out of powerlessness, but because he willed it so.

Answer: The opposite was demonstrated against two Spanish Bishops, Felix and Elipandus <note>Felix of Urgell and Elipandus of Toledo were 8th-century bishops who taught "Adoptionism," the idea that Christ as a man was God's son by adoption rather than by nature.</note>, because the humanity of Christ was not raised to a mere union of grace with the Word, but to a personal union <note>Also known as the hypostatic union, where the divine and human natures are joined in one person.</note>: nevertheless, this dispute is of little importance; one must add another, made to know whether Christ, as a man, is God’s Son by grace. This expression is ambiguous; if one understands by it that the grace which God poured into his humanity makes him the Son of God, it is an error; for it is through the Person of the Word itself, who united with humanity, that Christ is the Son of God: but, if one simply wishes to say that it was a gracious act of God to raise Christ's humanity to that incomprehensible union, and thereby cause the Son of God to become man, then it is a truth.

## XX. CHAPTER.

->Why Christ was conceived by the Holy Spirit.<-

<margin>Matthew 1:18. Luke 1:35.</margin>
Christ was not born or conceived like other men, although some Heretics have dared to say that he had Joseph as a Father; instead, he was conceived of the Holy Spirit: Matthew says that Mary was found to be pregnant from the Holy Spirit, and Luke relates that when Mary asked the Angel how that which he made known to her would happen, this Heavenly Messenger answered: *The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you*; in which words one can observe two allusions: 1. To the Cloud that descended upon the Tabernacle and covered it, so that the glory of the Lord filled this Holy place; the body of Mary was like a Tabernacle; into this Tabernacle the Divinity came at the same time as the Holy Spirit came upon her; the work of the incarnation was thus accomplished, and the Divine and Human Nature

<column-break/>

are closely united. 2. To the passages where it is said that the Holy Spirit comes upon those who are predestined for a great work: *Judges 14:6*, and to that which is related in *Genesis 1:2*, that in the beginning of the world the Holy Spirit hovered over the waters to bring forth the wonders seen in the whole universe.
But, it is asked, why was it necessary for the Holy Spirit to intervene in this conception?
I answer: 1. That it was necessary to prepare the material substance from which Christ’s body was to be formed.
2. To prepare it to be united with a rational soul.
3. To prepare the human Nature to unite with the Divine Nature, although we cannot explain in what this preparation consisted.
4. To purify it from the secret poison <note>A common historical metaphor for "Original Sin," the inherited corruption believed to affect all humanity since the Fall of Adam.</note> that had spread through the entire mass of the human race since the disobedience of the first man.
It was absolutely necessary that the human Nature of Christ was pure and without sin. How could the Holy of Holies dwell in an impure dwelling? How could he have personally united himself with a tainted Nature? But above all, how could he have reconciled our transgressions through his sacrifice if he himself had not been free of sin? And how could his sacrifice have been pleasing to God if he had not been a lamb without blemish? It was therefore of the highest necessity that the Holy Spirit purified the flesh of the Virgin by his power, and that from this purified substance he fashioned the human Nature of Christ, and the eternal Tabernacle of the Holy of Holies; but it was the Holy Spirit who built the hidden Ark.
Thus the conception of Christ is for us a beautiful symbol of our sanctification: the same Spirit that brought forth the flesh of Christ in the Virgin brings forth the image of the Savior in our heart, being a new man who grows until he has attained perfect wisdom.
<margin>Justin Martyr.</margin>

<margin>
Revelation 2.
Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*.
Ambrose.
</margin>
Just as the Word is sometimes called "Spirit," as some of the Ancients <note>Early Church Fathers like Tertullian and Ambrose often used "Spirit" to refer to the divine nature of Christ before the more precise Trinitarian language was fully standardized.</note> have believed.

There is nothing harmful in this view; however, it is not necessary to depart from the common opinion that interprets what the Scripture says as referring to the third Person of the Holy Trinity; especially since Luke, in the first chapter and other places, always takes the Holy Spirit to be the third Person.

But one must not conclude from this that the Holy Spirit is the Father of Christ: for to be the Father of Christ, the human nature of Christ would have to have been generated from the substance of the Spirit, and this nature would have to have been equal to that of the Spirit; which cannot be said: except that God the Father alone is called the Father of Jesus Christ.

### CHAPTER XXI.

->Concerning what happened at the Birth of Christ, and shortly thereafter, such as his Circumcision, the Naming of Jesus, etc.<-

<margin>
Micah 5.
I.
</margin>
One must observe:
1. That Bethlehem was the place where Jesus came into the world; it was only about two miles from Jerusalem. Micah had foretold it in the fifth chapter of his revelations <note>The prophecy in Micah 5:2: "But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah... out of you will come for me one who will be ruler over Israel."</note>: people do not agree whether he was born within the town limits of Bethlehem, which is the most likely; or in the suburbs, or in the neighboring countryside: Joseph and Mary had gone into this city to register their names; thus Bethlehem—which signifies "house of bread"—became the birthplace of him who is the true bread of life.

2. Since Joseph and Mary found no place in the Inn, they were forced to move into a stable, and it was there that Mary gave birth. What a palace that was for the King of Glory!

Some ancient Church Fathers and the scholars who follow them have said that Joseph and Mary were obliged to go into a cave, which possibly served as a stable for the inn; it is said that this cave became very famous in later times. Petrus Damianus <note>An 11th-century monk and cardinal known for his strict asceticism and writings on church reform.</note> relates that the Temple of Peace in Rome collapsed

<column-break/>

on the very same night as the Virgin gave birth; but the Temple of Peace was only built later by Vespasian <note>The author is pointing out a historical anachronism: Vespasian reigned from 69–79 AD, long after the birth of Christ.</note>.

3. It was in a manger that the Savior of the world was born; this was the cradle of the King of Kings, and of the Master of angels and men, and as the Throne of the God of Israel, whom Isaiah had seen shining with a bright light.

<margin>
Baronius
in the Appendix
to the Year
12, I,
14.
</margin>
Some believe that the root word should not be translated as "manger," but these opinions are based on being overly clever. Baronius <note>Cesare Baronius (1538–1607), a Catholic cardinal and historian famous for his "Ecclesiastical Annals."</note> relates, from a sermon attributed to Chrysostom but which is actually by a Latin writer, that the manger in which Christ lay was made of earth, and that it had been taken away to put one of silver in its place. The same Cardinal brings up some Church Fathers to prove that there were an Ox and a Donkey in the stable where Christ was laid: but all these stories have no foundation <note>The author notes that the famous presence of the ox and donkey is a later tradition, not found in the Gospel accounts.</note>; one can place it among other embellishments that have been spread, such as that while the Virgin was in labor, a fountain miraculously sprang from the rock that formed the cave; that Augustus raised an Altar for the firstborn of God, and that he, having consulted the oracle of Apollo, received the answer:
> The Hebrew child, whom all the Gods obey,
> Drives me from here, and sends me back to Hell;
> Depart from this Temple without speaking.

4. The Shepherds, who grazed their cattle in the fields of Bethlehem, were the first to whom the Angel made known the birth of the Chief Shepherd and of the Lamb of God, and they also went immediately to worship him.

5. A Heavenly Host appeared in the air and made the valleys of Bethlehem echo with their songs:
> Glory to God in the highest heavens, peace on earth, and goodwill toward men.
Luke 2:14.

6. A new Star appeared, as if to announce the rising of the Sun of Righteousness: it was likely an extraordinary, new, high-flying light, the movement of which was directed by providence in such a way that it indicated the place where the Lord of Glory rested, and led the Wise Men from the East there.

# THEOLOGY. BOOK IX. CHAPTER XXI.

7. The eighth day having arrived, the Son of Mary was circumcised. It is necessary that we pause here for a moment.

Circumcision was—as we shall see in its proper place—one of the primary signs of God’s people. It was a sign of their covenant with God, indicating that whoever received it in their flesh entered into the fellowship of His people to accept His promises and to show Him all the submission He demanded from His Israel. It also distinguished God’s people from others. Circumcision signified the "pruning" <note>Original: *besnoeijing*; here used metaphorically for the cutting away or removal of sins.</note> of sins.

It seems, then, that Christ ought not to have been circumcised, his human nature being entirely holy. Circumcision, which was regarded as a remedy against sin, was altogether unnecessary for Christ; nevertheless, he desired to receive this Sacrament:

<margin>Matthew 3:15.</margin>
1. Because he had to fulfill all righteousness, as he himself said to John the Baptist; that is to say, to demonstrate a perfect obedience to the commandments of God.

2. To show that he recognized the people of Israel as the true people of God.

3. To make the Jews understand that he was no enemy of Moses <note>The author refers to the Mosaic Law, which Christ upheld rather than abolished.</note>.

4. To deliver us from the curse of the law by thus fulfilling the law himself. Galatians 4:5.

5. If Christ had not been circumcised, his person would have been hateful to the Jews. They would have considered him a godless man and outside the fellowship of God. He received circumcision to remove all offenses they might have taken if he had remained uncircumcised. This was also the reason why he wished to pay the "Holy Tribute" <note>The Temple tax or *shekel* required of Jewish males for the upkeep of the Sanctuary.</note> which was collected in all Jewish places according to the command of Moses for the use of the Temple: "The sons are free," he says, "but so that we do not offend them, go to the sea," etc. Matthew 17:26, 27.

<margin>Matthew 17:26, 27.</margin>
6. Christ, then, allowed himself to be circumcised, and thereby he: 1. demonstrated the reality of the nature he had assumed; 2. showed that he belonged to the lineage of Abraham; 3. sanctified the circumcision of the Old Patriarchs in his own body, confirming the promises made to them, and became the "minister of circumcision." Romans 15:8. Some have

<column-break/>

said that just as circumcision assured Abraham of the multiplication of his seed, so this same Sacrament was for Christ a sign of the multiplication of his "hidden seed" <note>This likely refers to the spiritual offspring or the Church, the "seed" of Christ's kingdom.</note>.

8. It was on the day Christ was circumcised that he was named **Jesus**, just as the Angel had said before he was conceived in his mother’s womb. Luke 2:21.

It was the custom to give children their names when they were circumcised, which was a very timely moment to give everyone, in their own name, a memory of their covenant with God, and to remind them through their name that they had the honor of having entered into God’s household. According to this custom, the name of **Jesus** was given to the Son of God when he was circumcised.

Regarding this name, one must note:

1. That the writers of the New Testament took this word from the ancient Greek translators <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, who used it to express the name of **Joshua**.

2. That this word is Hebrew in its origin, and that it comes from another word meaning "to save," so that it translates to the word **Savior**, just as the Angel explained it to the Virgin and the shepherds. Many have believed that the word Jesus means "The Lord Savior." Isaiah 43:11. Also, when the Angel had said that the Son of Mary would be named Jesus, Matthew adds that this would fulfill what was written: that his name would be **Emmanuel** <note>Matthew 1:23; Emmanuel translates from Hebrew as "God with us."</note>. Matthew 1:23.

3. That many have been called by this name: **Joshua**, the great successor of Moses, who led the people of Israel into the land of Canaan; **Joshua**, the great High Priest, the son of Josedek, who with Zerubbabel rebuilt the Temple at Jerusalem after their return from the Babylonian captivity; and **Jesus**, son of Sirach, the author of the Book of Wisdom <note>The deuterocanonical book *Sirach* or *Ecclesiasticus*.</note>.

4. That among the Greeks and Romans, many "Physicians" <note>The author uses *Phisicen*, referring to the Greek *Physikos*, but links it to titles like *Soter* (Savior/Preserver) often given to rulers or healers.</note> were called "preservers," as can be seen from ancient commemorative medals.

5. It is even said that a learned Rabbi stated that since the Messiah would preserve mankind, he should be called...

[THE CHRISTIAN THEOLOGY]

would name him Jeschua, but that the Gentiles <note>Original: *Heidenen*</note> would name him Jesus; and that one indeed finds the name of Jesus in the 49th Chapter of Genesis, verse 10, when one joins together the first letter of every word of this verse in Hebrew. <note>This refers to a Kabbalistic or acrostic interpretation where the initial letters of the Hebrew words in Genesis 49:10 are said to form the name of Jesus.</note>

6. One must also observe that, as high as the Heaven is above the Earth, so much difference is found between those who have borne the name of Josue or Joshua and our Jesus: their deliverance was but temporal; but that which Christ has gained for us is eternal. The Amorites, the Jebusites, the Canaanites, and the Hittites, those of Assyria and of Babylon, etc., are not to be compared to the spiritual wickednesses which our Jesus conquered and openly put to shame. No one has ever deserved the name of Jesus more than our most glorious Savior, who delivers his people from sin, has broken the doors of the Grave, and has chained the Devil with the bonds of darkness. Joshua took possession of the land of Canaan for the Israelites, but our Jesus has obtained for us the Heavenly Canaan and the delights of Paradise. Joshua <note>Original: *Jehoschua*, referring to Joshua the High Priest mentioned in Zechariah and Ezra.</note> helped in the rebuilding of the Temple of Jerusalem; our Jesus has founded the Church, which is the Temple of God, the pillar and the ground of the truth.

In the Gospel histories, the Son of God is almost always called by the name of Jesus alone, without other addition, because it was the only name that men gave him. John 9:11.

<margin>Luke 2:22, 23, 24. Leviticus 12:8.</margin>
When the forty days of the purification of Mary were fulfilled, Jesus was brought to Jerusalem to be presented there to the Lord; then Mary gave the offering of the poor, namely a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons. Sergius, Pope of Rome, instituted the feast of the purification in honor of the Mother of our Savior, desiring that in all Churches processions should be made with burning wax candles in hand. He chose the same day and time in which the Ancient Romans, every five years, performed a general procession through the City of Rome for the entire night with burning wax candles and torches in hand in honor of Februa, whom they recognized as the Mother of Mars (whom they called the God of War), so that he, taking pleasure in their church ceremonies, would grant them victories

<column-break/>

over their enemies. These same Romans sacrificed in the same month to an Idol whom they called Februus, others Pluto, as well as to the other idols of Hell for the souls of the deceased, offering to them wafers, prayers, and solemn church hymns, and spending the entire night in this service with lighted torches. On the same days, the wives of these Idol-worshippers held their "feast of lights," running hither and thither in the manner of a procession through all the streets with candles in their hands, in memory of Ceres having formerly sought her daughter Proserpina. Thus one sees that the Latin Church gives the same honor to the Virgin Mary that was given in Heathendom to the daughter of Ceres; behold there the origin of "Our Lady of Candlemas" <note>Original: *Vrouw Ligtmis*, the feast of the Presentation of Jesus at the Temple, commonly called Candlemas.</note>, as the renowned Latin writer Durandus <note>Guillaume Durand (c. 1230–1296), a prominent medieval canonist and liturgical writer.</note> has noted, and many others after him.

<margin>Luke 2:29.</margin>
It was in the Temple that the good old Simeon embraced Jesus and sang the Canticle <note>The *Nunc Dimittis* or "Song of Simeon."</note> which Luke has recorded. That Simeon was supposedly blind and regained his sight upon embracing the Child Jesus is pure fiction.

<margin>Spanheim, *Dubia Evangelica*.</margin>
Many believe that the Wise Men <note>The Magi.</note> came after Mary had returned from Jerusalem; everything that is told of their names, of their number, and of their Royal status, smacks of fabrication. There is no agreement whether they came from Arabia, or from Persia, or from Chaldea; opinions are very divided.

I do not speak of the flight of Christ to Egypt, nor of the Murder at Bethlehem. I proceed to other notable matters of the life of our Savior.

So that he might fulfill all righteousness and subject himself to all ordinances. 2. So that he might confirm the ministry of John and seal the same by his authority. 3. The fourth matter deserving our attention is that Christ, being baptized, was led by the power of the Spirit into the Wilderness, where he was with the wild beasts: it is not agreed whether it was merely an impulse or an inspiration that set the will of Jesus in motion and caused him to travel to the Wilderness, or whether that happened to him which befell Philip after he had baptized the Ethiopian; <margin>Acts 8:39.</margin> for the Scripture says that the Spirit of the Lord took him away; however it may be, there Christ fasted 40 days and 40 nights, just as Moses and Elijah had also done. It is noteworthy that all those who fasted in a miraculous way have fed others in a miraculous way: Moses made the Manna descend; Elijah multiplied the oil and the flour of the Widow; and Christ multiplied the loaves: it is upon this forty-day fast that the Roman Church builds her Lent; we shall see in another place whether this institution is well-founded.

V. In this Wilderness, Christ was tempted by the Devil, who attacked him three times and was three times overcome: thus was Satan, who had triumphed over Adam the first man, overcome by the second: There are many difficulties regarding this temptation <note>Original: *aanvegting*, implying a spiritual assault or trial</note>, but we cannot investigate them here; it is enough that we observe: 1. That this temptation was real, and not in a vision. 2. That one should no more be surprised that Christ allowed himself to be tempted by the Devil than that he exposed himself to death. 3. That Christ wished to teach us: 1. What enemy we have to deal with as soon as we have entered into his fellowship; 2. What the arrows are that the Devil shoots at us, and with what weapons he attacks us. 3. How one must resist and overcome him. 4. Finally, that no one should flatter himself that he will be free from temptation, since Christ was exposed to it.

Matthew, Luke, and John relate the glorious discourses which Christ gave before the crowds and his disciples.

VII. The miracles of Christ deserve special attention / all the more because the Jewish Teachers recognize / that the Messiah shall be greater than Moses / and his miracles greater than those of Moses. They apply to him the prophecy <term>prophecy|Dutch: *God-spraak*, literally 'God-speech' or 'oracle'</term> of Isaiah 35:5–6.

<margin>Isaiah 35:5, 6.</margin>
One must note:
<margin>John 21:25.</margin>
1. That he performed such a number of miracles (John 21:25) that / if they were all written down / the whole world could not contain them / whereas the Jews count only 150 miracles in the span of 3328 years / from the beginning of the world until the destruction of the first Temple.

2. That he performed them / at least for the most part / in the presence of many witnesses / by which he distinguished himself from the deceivers / who seek secret places to lead the weak in faith astray <note>The Dutch phrase *om den Tuin te leiden* means to lead someone up the garden path or to deceive them</note>.

3. That he performed them upon nearly all creatures / upon the Devils / Men / the Seas / the Winds / the Fish / the Loaves / the Pigs / the Water / the Fig Tree / upon all sorts of diseases / and even upon death.

4. That these miracles exceeded the powers of nature and of the Devil: for it is not possible / that the Devil can raise a dead man / or satisfy five thousand people with five loaves.

5. That these miracles were nearly all acts of favor / deliverances or benefits / except for two or three occasions / in which Christ sent the Devils into the herd of Pigs / cursed the Fig Tree / and drove the sellers from the Temple; so that the miracles of Christ are very different from the miracles of Moses / and from the other Prophets / which were commonly terrifying <note>original: *verschrikkelyk*. In this context, it refers to the awesome and fearsome nature of Old Testament signs, like plagues or fire, contrasted with Christ's healing acts</note>.

6. That the effects of these Miracles were lasting; those he had healed / remained healed / whereas the effects of the false miracles of deceivers lasted only a few moments.

7. That Christ often performed his Miracles solely by his word: *I will, be clean*, he said to the Leper / Matt. 8:3.

8. That he gave others the power / to perform Miracles in his name / Matt. 10:8, Luke 10:9.

9. That Christ never performed Miracles for his own benefit / such as when he was hungry or thirsty / although all creatures are subject to him: for / just as he had come / only for the well-being of others / so he labored not / except for the benefit of the human race.

10. That several Miracles of the Old Testament had more outward splendor / than most of the Miracles of Christ; but that those of Christ were more beneficial to mankind: giving sight to one born blind / was a deed much more beneficial than making the Sun stand still / as Joshua did.

11. The first Miracle of Christ was / changing the water into Wine; thereafter he revealed his power in the healing of the sick; finally he raised the dead.

12. Furthermore, of all the types of Miracles / that occurred in the Old Testament / Christ repeated only a few / and he gave them a greater scope / than they had previously had. Under the Old Testament, two were healed of leprosy / namely the sister of Moses <note>Miriam</note>, and Naaman the Syrian; but many lepers were healed by Christ / even ten at once (Luke 17:17). Under the Old Testament, three were raised from the dead; Christ not only raised three dead persons / of whom one had already lain four days in the grave / but also many Saints, who had been buried for a long time. Elijah <note>original: *Elias*</note> multiplied the Oil and the Flour of the Widow / to sustain her and her Son / Elisha <note>original: *Eliza*</note> multiplied the Oil of a poor Woman; the same Prophet satisfied a great multitude of people with 20 loaves; but Christ satisfied with 5 loaves and 2 small Fish 5,000 / and with 7 loaves and a few small fish 4,000 people. Further, I do not believe / that it will be necessary / to further prove the truth of Christ's Miracles / after all that we have said / to demonstrate the Divinity of the Holy Scripture...

...to show; I also do not believe it is necessary to refute the Jews who have claimed that Christ performed his miracles through Beelzebub, or through the name of JEHOVAH; those are all fantasies and impieties that deserve no refutation.

13. It is also a curious matter that has been spread abroad, that the Wedding at Cana, where Christ performed his first miracle, was the wedding of the Apostle John, and that he prevented the consummation of his marriage through this miracle. Cardinal Baronius <note>Cesare Baronius (1538–1607) was a prominent Catholic historian known for his "Annales Ecclesiastici."</note> says that it is a tale of monks from later centuries, which they drew from some unknown books; he adds that, if this had been true, Jerome would not have been ignorant of it: he would have stopped the mouth of Jovinian, who maintained against him that John had always remained in the unmarried state; likewise, the Manichaeans <note>An early dualistic religious movement that often criticized traditional Christian views on marriage.</note> would not have forgotten this story. But this Cardinal himself has no better reason for saying that it was the wedding of Simon the Canaanite; one must place this opinion alongside the thoughts of those who said that it was the wedding of a certain Anacletus to Mary Magdalene, and who made the Master of the Feast <note>The original Dutch uses "Hofmeester," referring to the steward or governor of the feast mentioned in John 2:8.</note> who served at the wedding into a "Saint Architriclinus" <note>original: "Architriclinus." This is the Greek title for the master of the feast; the author is mocking those who mistook the title for a proper name of a saint.</note>. Epiphanius (in *Against Heresies*, 51) <note>original: "in hær. 51." Epiphanius of Salamis was a 4th-century Church Father known for his catalog of heresies.</note> says that this same miracle renews itself in a village in the land of Caria by a fountain, at the same hour as it happened in Cana on the 5th of January: but none of the Ecclesiastical writers make mention of it: it is likely that the credulity of this Church Father has been taken advantage of.

VIII. The Transfiguration of Christ upon the holy Mountain, which Matthew and Luke relate, must also be taken into consideration: it has been believed that Christ was transfigured on Mount Tabor, but this tradition seems very uncertain. However that may be, it was on a mountain that Christ displayed some rays of his Glory in the presence of three Disciples: on this mountain, one saw living men who had to die, namely the three Apostles; a man who had been dead and was now alive, namely Moses; a man who had never died but had ascended bodily to Heaven, namely Elijah; and a 

<column-break/>

man who, having died, would become living again and would have to ascend to Heaven, namely Jesus Christ.

IX. One cannot wonder enough at the obedience that Christ showed to the Law, not only in his circumcision but in all other things that the Law prescribed: he was bound to this not only as a Man and as a creature of God, not only as a child of Abraham, but also as our Surety <note>The "Surety" (Dutch: *Borg*) is a theological concept where Christ acts as a legal guarantor, fulfilling the debt of the Law on behalf of sinners.</note>, for our Surety had to do two things: 1. He was required to fulfill all that the Law demands of man. 2. He had to bear the punishments that our sins deserved; we were in no state to fulfill either one or the other: Christ fulfilled it. Besides that, Christ, as Man, was not bound to keep the Law of God in the same manner as sinful men, but only as the Saints who are in Heaven; above all, as a Holy Man, he was not bound to keep the Law of God which presupposes that he who observes it is a sinner: it was then a part of the humiliation of Christ that he, being on the earth for a time, wished to keep those same Laws to which men, who are in the world and have sinned against God, are bound.

X. There would be many more things to note in the life of the Lord Christ, such as the election of the XII Apostles, of whom one betrayed him and the others forsook him; the calling of the LXXII Disciples; But I shall only note that the ministry of Christ, according to some writers, lasted 4 years, and according to others 3 years and some months, which is the most probable, so that Christ reached 33 years and some months.

<margin>
Irenaeus
Book II, *Against 
Heresies*, ch. 39.
</margin>
Irenaeus <note>An early Church Father (c. 130–202 AD) who wrote against Gnosticism.</note> seems to have believed that Jesus was 50 years old when he died, because of what the Jews said of him in John 8:57 <note>"You are not yet fifty years old," the Jews said to him, "and you have seen Abraham?"</note>. But Mr. Dodwell <note>Henry Dodwell (1641–1711), an Anglo-Irish scholar and theologian.</note> understands this passage of Irenaeus differently. One may consult his first discourse on this Church Father.

XI. It is reckoned that Jesus Christ celebrated four Passover Feasts; at the first, he cleansed the Temple and performed many miracles (John 2:13). At the 2nd, he healed a sick man on the Sabbath day by the pool of Bethesda (John 5:1 etc.). The 3rd is spoken of in John 6.

## CHAPTER XXIII.

### On the Suffering of J. Christ in General.

<margin>Hebrews 2:10.</margin>
**O**ne cannot deny that Christ was subjected to various sorrows and pains; the Scripture teaches it to us explicitly. It even says, *it became him, for whom are all things, and by whom are all things, in bringing many sons unto glory, to make the captain of their salvation perfect through sufferings.* For this reason, one cannot wonder enough that there were people in former times who dared to maintain that Christ did not suffer except in appearance.

These heretics were called <term>Aphthartodocetae</term> <note>original: "Aphartodoceten." A 6th-century sect that believed Christ’s body was incorruptible and his sufferings were not natural but voluntary and perhaps only apparent</note>, of whom Nicephorus speaks in Book XVII, Chapter 29. It seems that Hilary <note>Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367), an influential Latin bishop and theologian</note>, in Book 10 of *On the Trinity*, was of this opinion, although the <term>Master of the Sentences</term> <note>original: "Meester van de gedenk-spreuken." This refers to Peter Lombard (c. 1100–1160), whose book of 'Sentences' was the standard textbook of medieval theology</note> (Lombard, Book III, Sentences, Distinction 15) wishes to excuse him by saying that he did not want to deprive Christ of the feeling of His suffering, but only wanted to deny that Christ *deserved* to suffer. However, the words of Hilary are very emphatic: he says, "Christ felt no pain in his suffering and in his death, but he only wanted to give us the idea that he had some pain in his suffering, and that the blows brought him no more pain than an arrow piercing water or wounding the air."

The Benedictines, who published a new edition of Hilary in the year 1693, nevertheless maintain that he is being wronged by having this error attributed to him.

<column-break/>

But the question is asked whether Christ suffered only in his body. There are some who hold that the Savior did not suffer in his soul, except through the sympathetic feeling it had with the body, because of the union between the flesh and the spirit. This union makes the spirit a sharer in the pains of the body—or at least, they say, if the soul suffered, it was only in regard to its "lower part" <note>This refers to the medieval psychological distinction between the 'higher' rational soul and the 'lower' sensitive soul where emotions and passions reside</note> where the passions arise.

<margin>Matthew 26:38.</margin>
One only has to read the Scripture to be convinced that Christ suffered in his soul: for it says that before Christ was taken prisoner, he was very distressed and cried out, *my soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death.* This is a sign that it was not only the body that suffered, but also his soul. One should make no distinction here between the lower and the upper part of the soul; the soul being a spirit, it is ridiculous to suppose that it can suffer in one part and not in another.

It is said that one cannot understand how Christ could suffer in his soul, since one cannot conceive how a soul can suffer except through the remorse it has because it did not do what it was obliged to do.

Answer: It is certain that God can cause the soul to suffer in various ways.

The same Scripture says that the sorrow of Christ was then so great that he sweated drops of blood, which is a sign of the most terrible disturbances in nature that can be imagined, and a proof that the body was in suffering more through its sympathy with the soul than the soul through its sympathy with the body.

It is said that it does not befit the dignity of a God to be sorrowful: for either he knew the end of his suffering, and why then be sorrowful? Or he did not know it, and if this were so, how is he God?

I answer that he was not sorrowful except in his Human Nature, which naturally fears pain; besides, our salvation required that Christ suffer in his soul as well as in his body. We had sinned in our soul and in our body, and even our soul was the guiltiest; wherefore our <term>Surety</term> <note>original: "Borge." A legal-theological term for Christ acting as the legal guarantor who pays the debt of sin on behalf of humanity</note> as well in the...

suffered in the one [the soul] almost as much as in the other [the body]. The pains of Christ were the punishment that we had deserved. It was therefore necessary that they were paired with the feeling of God’s wrath and with the most terrible aspects of His justice. Now, everyone knows that between the justice of God and that of men, there is this distinction: that the justice of men extends over the body, while often the soul remains at rest; whereas, on the contrary, the justice and wrath of God extend primarily over the soul, and go to the

<margin>Claude <note>Jean Claude (1619–1687), a prominent French Protestant theologian known for his defenses of the Reformation.</note></margin> heart. It was the soul, says a learned man, that had been the first origin of disobedience against God, the seat of sins, where Satan and the world had erected their throne; it was more involved than the body, which had no part in the sins except in the capacity of an instrument or companion of the soul. Consequently, the satisfaction of God’s justice had to take place in the soul.

Because the Scripture attributes our salvation to the death of Christ and to His cross, one must not conclude that He suffered only in His body; for it is evident that His soul also suffered in the final hour, while He cried out: *My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?*

It is said that the sacrifices of the ancients <note>The animal sacrifices of the Old Testament.</note> could not have been examples of the suffering of Christ’s soul.

I answer that these sacrifices represented His suffering in general, and all those sufferings which human nature was capable of enduring. The fire that consumed the victim was a symbol of God’s wrath, the heat of which Christ had to feel in soul and body.

It appears then that the suffering of Christ was particularly heavy because there was nearly a total suspension of the sweet influences which the Divinity usually poured into the soul of the Savior. God made Him feel the entire weight of His wrath; there was no part of His body, nor any power of His soul, that did not endure pains.

But, it is asked, is it possible that the Person of Christ was exposed, in regard to His human nature, to the hatred and wrath of God?

I answer that Christ was never the

<column-break/>

object of the hatred of His Father, but was always the object of His love; but being viewed as the <term>Surety</term> <note>A legal term for one who takes responsibility for another's debt or obligation.</note> of men, He suffered the pains that were prepared for sinners, and which proceed from being pursued by divine wrath or justice against the sins of men. He has, says Isaiah

<margin>Isaiah 53:4, 5.</margin> 53:4, 5. *borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows, etc. But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities.*

It is asked how it could have been that Christ, at one and the same time, could be the object of the love of His Father and, nevertheless, bear all the force of His wrath and justice which was kindled against sinners.

I answer that one must distinguish between the love of God and the *feeling* of that love that is poured out into the soul. It has been very well said that the love of God in regard to Christ never wavered, and that the feeling of it was never fully extinguished in the soul of the Savior; but that the same feeling was particularly diminished and weakened at the moment of His suffering. This occurred through a wonderful wisdom to carry out the work of our redemption, which could not be accomplished except through great suffering. Now, there is nothing contradictory between this diminution of God’s love—or, if I may be permitted to speak so, between this weakening of the influence of joy and comfort in the soul of Christ—and the anguish that He endured for us.

It is absolutely necessary that one observes here:

1. That the suffering of Christ, although immeasurably great, was nonetheless not eternal. We were worthy of being punished eternally, but it was not necessary that our Surety suffered eternally, because, He being God, His suffering—though of short duration—had an infinite value, as if He had suffered eternally.

2. That His suffering, although very heavy, never brought Him to sin. The soul of our Savior has been compared to a pure and beautiful vessel in which clear water can indeed be shaken with force and violence, but with-

that this shaking makes it [the vessel] impure; on the contrary, water poured into an impure vessel becomes completely impure when it is shaken. <note>The author uses the metaphor of a vessel to show that Christ’s suffering did not create sin within Him, but rather proved His purity, whereas the suffering of the wicked only stirs up their inherent corruption.</note>

In this way, one can understand the distinction between the suffering of Christ and that of the godless, whom God punishes in His wrath.

They differ in many ways. I could say that the reprobate suffer through the hatred that God has for them, and that Christ suffered through the hatred that God had for sins; that the punishments of the godless are the sensation of the hatred that God bears toward them, and that the punishment of Christ is the sensation of the hatred that God naturally has against the sins of mankind; that the damned are entirely abandoned by God, but that Christ was not, except in certain respects that made him cry out: *My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?*; that the godless have not the slightest ray of hope, but that Christ always hoped and was certain of victory.

I must also say that the punishment of the godless is always paired with fury, curses, madness, and sin, which continually embitters Divine justice against them; and just as their spirit in the midst of pains becomes a source of new sins, so also Eternal Justice becomes a constant source of new punishments against them. But the suffering of Christ was always accompanied by a perfect innocence, a complete righteousness, a fiery devotion, and a burning love for his Father, and an unspeakable love for the Human race. The godless suffer through a necessity that Divine justice imposes on them; but Christ suffered through a voluntary obedience.

<margin>John 12:27.</margin>
One must consider the suffering that preceded the death of Christ, and that which accompanied it. Regarding the first, the Lord Christ already suffered in his soul when he said, John 12:27: *Now is my soul troubled; and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour: but for this cause came I unto this hour.* His suffering increased particularly when, a few hours before he was captured—as I have already mentioned—being on the Mount of Olives in the Garden of

<column-break/>

Gethsemane, he burst out in these words:

<margin>Matt. 26:38, 39.</margin>
> Matt. 26:38. *My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death;* and subsequently casting himself with his face upon the ground, he prayed, saying, verse 39: *O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt,* which he repeated three times.

His sadness was so great that an angel had to come and strengthen him, and his sweat became like drops of blood rolling to the ground, which we have also already noted in another place.

One asks, what caused this immoderate fear and sadness?

I answer in a word: it was death, armed with God’s curses, and paired with the suspension of the comforting influence of the Godhead. One sees daily that a thunderclap followed by lightning that makes the earth tremble, a great storm at sea, or a lion coming out of a forest terrifies the souls of the boldest men; how much more then so terrifying a death as our Savior had to suffer.

One asks why Christ feared death, since so many men are found—not only among the Martyrs, but even among the Heathens—who did not fear it? Many wise men received it with steadfastness: Socrates underwent it without agitation, and Seneca with patience. <note>Socrates and Seneca were famous ancient philosophers who met their deaths with calm; the author argues their experience was fundamentally different because they did not face the spiritual weight of human sin.</note>

I answer: it was because the death of Christ was paired with the unbearable weight of God’s wrath. The Martyrs did not carry their own sins; they enjoyed the peace of their conscience, and God showed them a reconciled face. Regarding the Heathens, there was much vanity in their deeds.

One asks whether the Godhead should not have prevented his humanity from fearing death.

I answer that it had to be so, in order that he might atone for our sins. All this requires special observations, but they would lead us too far astray.

We shall speak in another place of the suffering that accompanied his death or preceded it by a few moments; I will add no more here than these two remarks.
