I answer, that it was enough that our Mediator suffered an infinite punishment / which through its weight <note>The author uses "weight" to mean the severity or intensity of the suffering, rather than its length in time.</note> equaled an eternal punishment.

6. It is said, that Christ did not suffer an infinite punishment / since his suffering lasted so short a time.

I answer, that Christ suffered a punishment of an infinite value / although it was not infinite in duration. The merits of the one suffering / cause the punishment to become infinite.

It is said, that / if it were true / that the infinity of the Person made the punishment infinite / it would follow from this / that Divine justice would have been satisfied / even if Christ had suffered only a light punishment / and shed a single drop of his blood / as Pope Clement VI <gloss>the sixth</gloss> (Extravagantes: *Unigenitus*) <note>A papal bull issued in 1343 concerning the "Treasury of Merit."</note> and Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a Cardinal and influential defender of Catholic doctrine against the Reformation.</note> (*On Indulgences*, book 1, ch. 4) said.

I answer, that not all suffering / although borne by an infinite person / is satisfaction / but only that / which Divine justice demanded / which the Law required / and which corresponded to the greatness of the crimes committed.

It is further said / that the dignity of the Person adds nothing to the infinity of the punishment / because with God there is no acceptance of persons <term>acceptance of persons: a biblical phrase meaning partiality or favoritism based on status rather than facts</term>.

But the Scripture only means to say thereby / that God does not look at the outward qualities / which have nothing to do with the matter / at hand ; just as it is forbidden for a Judge to pardon a criminal / because he is rich / or a great Lord : but it does not follow from this / that God must pay no heed to the perfect merits of his adorable Son / in whom he has all his delight ; and that he must distinguish his counsel in an infinite manner from the suffering of all creatures / since he possesses the same Majesty / and the same perfections as his Father.

It is said, that this could take place / if Christ had suffered as God / but that his Humanity alone suffered.

I answer, that it is not necessary / for the punishment to be of an infinite power / that the Godhead suffer; it is enough / that the Person / who suffers / be Divine / although he suffers only in respect to the human nature / which he has personally united to himself.

It is said, that Christ / being God /

<column-break/>

could not bring to God that which God did not already possess.

**Answer.** I admit it / but / although everything belongs to God / nevertheless he desires that we offer him certain things / as if they belonged to us : thus he desired / that one slaughter sacrificial offerings for him ; and in this way Christ was able to sacrifice his own blood to him : for it depended on his will / whether to sacrifice the same or not. But in the same manner as we must bear the punishments / which Divine justice demands from Sinners / and the wicked suffer in hell / Christ was also able to bear the punishments / that we deserve.

It is said, that one could not sacrifice blood to God.

I answer, that this, however, does not prevent the shed blood from being able to satisfy Divine justice. Thus a Prince / who holds someone captive / can offer to release him / under the condition that he who seeks his freedom / exposes his life to his service.

7. It is said, that / if Christ had suffered the punishment / which we had deserved / and which the outcasts <note>The "reprobate" or those not chosen for salvation.</note> suffer / he would have fallen into despair / like the damned.

I answer, that despair is not the essence of the punishment / which we were bound to suffer ; and that / if the outcasts despair / such is a consequence of their corruption. Secondly, I do not know / whether one may well say / that Christ suffered the pains of the damned. One can read further what I have said about that in the treatise on Christ’s descent into hell.

8. It is objected, that it is impossible / that Christ has satisfied for men / because every Sinner / and even every sin deserving an infinite punishment / Christ would have been bound to suffer many deaths.

**Answer 1.** Those who make this objection / openly oppose the Scripture / which says / that God has caused the iniquities of us all to fall upon his Son ; Isaiah 53:4, 5, 6 <note>original: "Esa. LIII. 4. 5. 6."</note> and that he died for all, 2 Corinthians 5:15 <note>original: "2 Cor. V. 15."</note>.

**2.** One could add to this / that indeed / when several people owe a certain sum / for example a thousand rix-dollars <term>rix-dollar: a silver coin used across Northern Europe during this period</term> / one must pay a thousand rix-dollars for each person, head by head /

### DIVINITY. IX. Book. XXXVII. Chapter.

Part I. M m m m

but that the punishment of one is sometimes enough for the debts of several; that the life of a King like David, was esteemed more than that of half of his army / 2 Sam. XVIII. 3. and that consequently the death of Christ could have been sufficient for the redemption of many.

3. But one must moreover observe / that the infinity of the Person of Christ is enough to satisfy for all men / although each of them deserves several infinite punishments.

9. It is said, that the forgiveness of sins is attributed to repentance and faith.

Answer. That is true / because those are the only conditions that God demands of us; but he demands <term>satisfaction: the legal payment or reparation for a debt or sin</term> from our <term>Surety: one who takes responsibility for another's debt or obligation; in this context, Christ</term>. Secondly, faith has as its object the Messiah / who has made the satisfaction.

10. It is said, that one cannot produce any Law / by which one can demand of an innocent person / that he suffer the punishment / which another deserves to bear in his body.

I answer, that the point here is not to know / whether there is some Law regarding this matter / but whether the Scripture does not clearly say / that Christ has borne our sins; the example of our Savior is extraordinary / but it is for that reason no less certain.

11. It is objected, that / if Christ had satisfied for us / we would be more obliged to him / than to his Heavenly Father.

Answer. This reasoning has no force / for the love of the Father / who has given us his Son / was an infinite love / just as well as the love of the Son / who delivered himself for us. Therefore, we have infinite obligations to these two adorable Persons. The Scripture also praises the love of the Father to us everywhere / 1 John III. 16. IV. 9. Rom. V. 8.

12. It is objected, that / if Christ has satisfied the Law for us / we are no longer bound to fulfill it.

But one is mistaken; this conclusion must not be drawn from it / but much rather these two.

1. That those / for whom Christ has died / are no longer subject to the curse of the Law. 2. That we must not keep the

<column-break/>

Law / as if we / through the keeping of the same / could satisfy God's justice; for we cannot fulfill the Law. Far from the doctrine of satisfaction releasing us from obedience to the Law / the Gospel draws a motive from it / which incites us to sanctification. It says / that God has redeemed us / so that we might serve him in holiness and in righteousness / Luke I. 74. and that Christ has borne our sins on the wood of the cross, so that we, having died to sin, might live to righteousness, 1 Pet. II. 24. Heb. IX. 14. 1 Thess. IV. Eph. II. 10. Tit. II. 14. 1 Pet. II. 9. 1 Cor. VI. 19. 20. 2 Cor. V. 15.

13. It is objected, that / if Christ had satisfied for us / and had died for us / the believers would not be necessitated to die.

I answer, that the death of believers is no punishment / but a blessed passage to eternal life.

14. It is objected, that the doctrine of satisfaction obscures the honor of God's omnipotence / as if God did not have the power to forgive us our sins without satisfaction.

But this is to deceive oneself. 1. It is not for a lack of power / that God could not forgive sin without satisfaction / but because his justice did not allow sin to go unpunished.

2. Far from the doctrine of Satisfaction obscuring the honor of God's omnipotence / it causes the same to shine forth with all its luster. It reveals to us his justice, which preferred not to spare God's own Son / rather than leave sin unpunished; his mercy, which has spared men / whom he / without delivering his Son to death / could not make blessed: his wisdom, which has combined the wonderful means of making his justice and mercy harmonize together: his omnipotence, which conquered the Devil and sin through the cross / and has drawn life out of death.

15. It is said, that our doctrine obscures the mercy of God / who demands no satisfaction; and his justice, which desires / that sin be punished in the sinners themselves.

I answer. 1. That mercy has not been wounded; God has demanded the satisfaction not from us / but from our Surety. 2. That justice demands nothing else / than that sin be punished.

it is said that God blots out our transgressions, that he covers them with a cloud, that he casts them behind his back into the depths of the Sea, that he removes our transgressions from us as far as the East is from the West, that he does not reproach us for our sins, that he does not remember them; <note>The author is listing various biblical metaphors to emphasize that divine forgiveness is absolute and leaves no residue of guilt or punishment.</note> all the passages where it is said that Christ has blotted out and destroyed the "handwriting" of our sins <note>original: "hand-schrift onzer zonden," referring to a legal bond or debt-note.</note> which was against us: for it would not be destroyed at all if a portion of the debt—consisting of temporal punishment—were still in effect; finally, all the passages where it is said that we are justified freely. <note>original: "om niet," meaning by grace or without cost.</note>

It will be said that God forgives our debts and sins because he forgives the largest part of them; but 1. who has ever heard it said that a creditor remits the debts of his debtor if he still demands something from him? 2. Since the debt has such a connection with the punishment that there is no punishment where there is no debt, it is utterly ridiculous to say that God remits the debt but not the punishment.

<margin>Bellarmine, Book IV, *On Penance*, ch. 15.</margin>
It is said <note>referring to the arguments of Cardinal Robert Bellarmine, a leading Counter-Reformation theologian.</note> that there are things which would not happen if there were not certain causes, and which remain standing once they have happened even though the causes no longer exist; just as a building would not be completed if no one built it, yet the building remains even if the master builder is no longer present. But there is a very great difference between the analogy being brought forward and the matter in dispute: it is not necessary for a building to exist that the master who built it remains alive; but there is no man who can understand how God could demand punishment for a sin that he has already forgiven; once the builder is dead he works no more, and likewise the debt, once destroyed, can no longer bring punishments upon the sinners.

It is said that a King can forgive someone for their misdeeds, but at the same time demand that he give satisfaction to the party who was insulted; and that God can also forgive men their transgressions, yet still demand that they satisfy.

I answer that one is comparing two distinct things; a King can act in such a way because he is distinct from the insulted party, but here God is the insulted party.

3. This distinction harms the justice of God, for it suggests that God punishes that which he no longer judges to be guilty; it likewise contradicts the mercy of God as it is described to us in Scripture: for since it presents God to us as a Father of mercy, whose love far exceeds the tenderness of a Mother, how can one conceive that this merciful Father would still demand heavy satisfaction from those he has forgiven?

4. It is without basis that a distinction is made between sins committed before Baptism and sins committed after Baptism.

There are still some objections made which must necessarily be resolved.

<margin>Bellarmine, Book I, *On Indulgences*, ch. 3.</margin>

That it must be that Christ left something that still remains to be done, since there is talk of the "remnants of the afflictions of Christ," and 2. That Paul testifies that he fulfills the remnants of these afflictions.

<margin>
Thomas Aquinas on this passage.
Contarini on this.
Justinian on this passage.
</margin>
To answer this, one must only make these two observations. The first observation is that by the "afflictions of Christ" one must not understand the suffering that Christ suffered in his own person during the days of his flesh, of which his death was the final part: for Paul speaks here of a suffering that was not yet ended, whereas it is certain that Christ suffered everything on the cross, and that nothing more was left for him to suffer for the reconciliation of our sins; one must then understand by these sufferings of Christ the sufferings that Christ imposes on each of his members who are in his communion: thus this expression is taken in 2 Corinthians 1:5, *as the sufferings of Christ abound in us,* says the Apostle, *so also through Christ our consolation abounds.* He calls it in other places the "affliction of the Gospel," the "bodily torment," the "dying and marks of the Lord Jesus." # THE CHRISTIAN [THEOLOGY]

<columns>

[one] can easily give a reason for this way of speaking; it is because we endure this suffering for the love of Jesus and for the sake of his name, because there is such a close bond between Christ and his members <note>The "members" refers to the individual believers who make up the "body" of the Church.</note> that whatever the believers happen to suffer makes up a part of the sufferings of Christ, just as we name our wounds after the limbs in which we received them.

The second observation one must make is that God has assigned to every believer the share of suffering that he must endure for His name's sake, so that he might be conformed to His Son: this is what Paul wants to show us when he says that he "fills up what is lacking" of Christ’s afflictions; to teach us that he had already suffered a good portion of them, but that some still remained for him according to the counsel of God, as if he were saying: "Christ has suffered all that he had to suffer for our redemption; now I also, in my turn, am going to suffer everything to which he calls me for his glory and to advance his Kingdom, of which I have already suffered much." One can here compare the passage from 1 Peter 5:9.

2. Further, some passages are raised as objections, from which it is concluded that God, after he has forgiven the sins of believers, nevertheless chastises them in this life. For example: 1. What was said to David by Nathan, 2 Samuel 12:13, 14: *The Lord also has taken away your sin; you shall not die. Nevertheless, because by this deed you have given great occasion to the enemies of the Lord to blaspheme, the son also who is born to you shall surely die.* 2. That which one reads of David in 2 Samuel 24:10, 11, 12, who, although he had obtained mercy regarding the sin he committed in numbering the people, was nevertheless heavily punished. 3. That which is found in Exodus 32:10, 14, where it is said that although God forgave the children of Israel the sins of idolatry, he nevertheless caused a great part of them to perish in the wilderness. 4. The 14th Chapter of Numbers, verse 20, where it is shown that although God ceased to be further angry against the children of Israel who had murmured against him, he nevertheless caused almost all of them to fall in the wilderness. 5. That which one reads in Numbers 20:4, 25, and Deuteronomy 32:50, 51, of Aaron and Moses, who

<column-break/>

did not enter the promised land because of their unbelief; from all these passages it is concluded that although God forgives men their sin for the sake of the <term>satisfaction</term> <note>original: "voldoeninge." In this context, it refers to the theological belief that Christ's death paid the debt for sin.</note> of Christ, he nevertheless still demands some temporal punishment from man to give satisfaction to His justice.

But all those who make these objections here confuse fatherly chastisements with the actual punishments that God imposes to satisfy his justice. We readily grant that God often chastises his children for their improvement and conversion, but we deny that he demands "satisfactory" punishments from those whose sins he forgives. The chastisements of believers can indeed be called a "punishment" if one wishes to use this word improperly <note>In the sense of "figuratively" or "loosely."</note>: 1. either because they are, by their nature, the consequences and "stings" of sins; 2. or because they are painful to the flesh—but not everything that is painful to our nature is a punishment. When a sick person endures the iron and the fire <note>A reference to surgical tools and cauterization used in early modern medicine.</note>, he is not being punished. Because blood was drawn from a soldier who did not observe his duty among the Roman warriors, it does not follow that <term>blood-letting</term> <note>original: "aderlaaten." A common medical practice of the time; the author argues the act itself is medicinal, even if triggered by a mistake.</note> is a punishment. 3. or because believers sometimes view them as effects of God's wrath, and as if they were true punishments. 4. or because they are assigned by God just as punishments are pronounced by judges upon criminals. 

But one cannot give them this name in the same sense in which it is given to the judgments that God carries out over evildoers; and there is a very great difference between the chastisements with which God visits believers and the judgments he exercises over the godless: The one proceeds from a Father, who only chastises those whom he loves; the others are carried out by a strict Judge. The one is paired with a feeling of God's grace, and the other with a feeling of the wrath and the curse of God. The first last but a moment, and the second are forerunners of eternal punishments.

<margin>
Hebrews 12:6.
Proverbs 3:11.
Hebrews 12:8.
</margin>

When the Scripture speaks of the afflictions of believers, it says that they proceed from God's love; that those who are free from them are bastards <note>A reference to Hebrews 12:8, meaning they are not true children of God.</note>; that God sends the same for our improvement and to make us partakers of his holiness; that these are indeed trials, but that the...

# THEOLOGY. BOOK IX. CHAPTER XXXVIII.

[believers] have reason to be joyful about it.

If God wills that the child of David should die, it is not to satisfy his justice, but for the improvement of David, and to teach others not only to beware in the future of giving God's enemies cause to blaspheme the Lord, but also to strike the enemies of God with awe by letting them see that he does not leave sins unpunished. David's sin was the cause and the occasion why God caused David's child to die, but the death of the child was not the legal punishment for his sin. <note>In this context, the author distinguishes between "retributive punishment" (paying a debt of justice) and "chastisement" (a fatherly correction for the benefit of the child and others).</note>

It is said that it is clear enough that David did not view the death of his child as a remedy or a beneficial improvement, but as a very great evil and a punishment, since he wept, lamented, and fasted. This reasoning does not hold up, for everyone knows that the Saints pray to God that he might ward off all evil from them, even though they know that the evil must work together for their good; a sick person does not like bitter drinks, even though he hopes to be healed by them.

One must reason in much the same way regarding 2 Samuel 24. <note>This refers to the story where David conducts a census and God sends a plague upon Israel.</note>

What we read in Exodus 32:10, 14 does not provide a firm proof here, for although it is said there that God held back the heat of his anger so as not to utterly root out his people, it is not noted there that he forgave them; on the contrary, it is said that Moses still had to ask in verse 31 that this sin might be forgiven them. The slaughter by the Levites <note>After the incident of the Golden Calf, the Levites were ordered to kill those who had rebelled.</note> can indeed be called a true punishment regarding the evildoers who were killed; but if any believers were included in this slaughter, it was for them a chastisement that God wanted them to feel, to serve as an example to others, or for other reasons that he has not revealed to us. Moses acted then like a commander who punishes every tenth man of his regiments when they have caused a mutiny; one can say the same of Numbers 14.

Regarding Moses and Aaron, to whom God had granted forgiveness and who nonetheless died in the wilderness:

I answer, that it was not to satisfy his justice that God

<column-break/>

punished them so severely, but to give all the people a righteous terror, seeing that he did not even spare their leaders; to which one can add that the death of Moses and Aaron contained an indignation, and that God willed that they should die in the wilderness to teach us that it is not the Law—of which Moses was the servant—that gives us entrance into the heavenly Canaan, but Christ, who was prefigured by Joshua. <note>The author is using "typology," a common method of interpreting the Bible where Old Testament figures foreshadow New Testament truths. Moses represents the Law, which cannot save, while Joshua (whose name in Hebrew is the same as Jesus) represents the Savior who leads the people to the promised land.</note> One can apply the first answer to what is said in 1 Kings 13:2 <note>Likely referring to 1 Kings 13:24.</note> regarding a prophet who was torn apart by a lion.

3. It is further objected that Scripture often speaks of judgments that God exercises over his own children. Peter says in 1 Peter 4:17 that judgment begins at the House of God; now, whoever says "judgment" implies a punishment properly so called. But it is easy to answer that one should not press the word "judgment" too hard, for Paul teaches us in 1 Corinthians 11:32 that when we are judged, we are chastened by the Lord.

<margin>Oecumenius, Theophylact, Chrysostom on this passage. Claude Guillaud on this place.</margin> He does not say "we are punished," but "we are chastened," to show that these afflictions or judgments are not condemnations, but warnings; not death-penalties, but remedies; not punishments, but improvements; as a learned man of the Roman Church <note>Referring to Claude Guillaud, a 16th-century French theologian who, though Catholic, sometimes offered interpretations that Protestants found useful.</note> has noted with much discernment.

4. Other passages are also brought forward which seem to prove human "satisfactions"; Isaiah 1:16–17, where the Prophet promises the forgiveness of sins not only to those who are cleansed, but who are also practiced in works of mercy:

<margin>Bellarmin, Book 4 on Penance, chapter 3.</margin> Proverbs 16:6: *By mercy and truth iniquity is atoned for.* <note>original Latin: "Iniquitas expiatur."</note> Daniel 4:27: *Therefore, O King, let my counsel please you, and break off your sins by righteousness, and your iniquity by showing mercy to the poor.* Luke 11:41: *But give for alms those things which are within; and behold, everything is clean for you.* Matthew 3:8: *Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance.* 2 Corinthians 7:11, where mention is made of a "vengeance" that sinners exercise upon themselves. 2 Chronicles 7:14: *If my people, upon whom my name is called, shall humble themselves and pray and seek my face and turn from their evil ways, then I will hear from heaven and...*

forgiven their sin. It is clear that all these passages do not prove that kindness, faithfulness, mercy and love, humility, alms, repentance, and holiness are satisfactions <note>Theologians used the term "satisfaction" to mean a payment made to satisfy a debt of justice.</note> for sins to the justice of God; but rather that they are simply the conditions that God requires from those whose sins he forgives. This will become even clearer if one examines the passages themselves closely.

<margin>
Isaiah 1:16, 17.
2 Chronicles 7:14.
</margin>
The passage from *Isaiah* 1:16, 17 and that of 2 *Chronicles* 7:14 prove that God forgives sins to those who fulfill their religious duties; but they do not show in the least that those who perform these duties are satisfying Divine justice.

<margin>Proverbs 16:6.</margin>
The passage from *Proverbs* 16:6 is clear; it can be explained in three ways. The first amounts to this: that there is reconciliation through the mercy and truth of God, which shows that the kindness and faithfulness of God are the principles and origin of our reconciliation with him. The second, which seems more proper to me, is that God forgives the sins of those who clothe themselves with a spirit of love and sincerity, and that he is not satisfied with the outward service that hypocrites show him. The word in the original language <note>Hebrew: *kaphar* (כפר), usually translated as "atone" or "cover."</note> sometimes means to forgive, just as the Septuagint <note>original: "LXX. Overzetters," the early Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translators rendered it in *Proverbs* 22:14 and 27:9. The third is that through the practice of mercy and truth, we rid ourselves of the habits of sin, according to the meaning of the root word, which sometimes signifies taking away or removing far off; the Hebrew word *kaphar* <note>original: כפר</note> means to displace or do away with; and the Septuagint translators translated it as *to take away* <note>original: "ἀφαιρεῖν"</note>, and the common translation <margin>* Vulgate.</margin> <note>The Vulgate is the late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible.</note> as "to blot out" in *Isaiah* 28:18. This would then agree very well with what the Wise Man adds there: that through the fear of the Lord, one turns away from evil. It appears, therefore, that no "satisfaction" is intended here.

<margin>Daniel 4:27.</margin>
As for the passage in *Daniel* 4:27, it proves nothing at all.
1. There, we see a godless and idolatrous monarch <note>Nebuchadnezzar, King of Babylon.</note>; now, even those who uphold human satisfaction admit that only true believers—those to whom God has already forgiven the guilt and eternal punishment—are capable of making satisfaction.

<column-break/>

2. The meaning of these words is clear; Daniel exhorts Nebuchadnezzar to behave entirely differently than he had done, and through his righteousness, or through his alms and love, to turn away the calamities that were hanging over his head. There are those who translate this passage differently because the root word in the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> and Hebrew languages means "to break"; as in *Numbers* 1:51, *Proverbs* 17:9, 1 *Kings* 19:11, *Genesis* 27:40, *Psalms* 7:3, *136:24*, *Exodus* 32:2, 3, and *Lamentations* 5:8. It is as if the Prophet wanted to say: break off the course of your sins through works of love. It is also said that it means to ransom or preserve, but scholars have noted that it only has that meaning when applied to a person.

3. If this passage were to be pressed, one would have to say that one can atone for the guilt as well as the punishment: for it says, "redeem your sins by almsgiving." Even the Jesuit Vasquez <note>Gabriel Vasquez (1549–1604), a prominent Catholic theologian often cited in these debates.</note> does not want this passage to be used for this purpose.

<margin>Luke 11:41.</margin>
*Luke* 11:41 is very poorly cited [by opponents]. *Christ* only means to say that those who have cleansed their hearts from the stain of greed and other flaws that might defile them did not need to worry about the washing of their dishes and hands, as if those things were capable of defiling them.

<margin>Matthew 3:8.</margin>
When John the Baptist exhorted the Jews to "bring forth fruits worthy of repentance," one must be willfully blind not to see that this is not a matter of making satisfaction; rather, the Baptist wants the Jews to produce the fruits that ought to be produced by those who truly repent of their sins.

The "revenge" or "vengeance" that Paul speaks of in 2 *Corinthians* 7 is nothing other than the sentence of exclusion <note>Excommunication</note> that the Corinthians had pronounced against the incestuous man. This exclusion involves a regular and ecclesiastical punishment to remove the scandal and serve as an example, but it contains no "satisfying" punishment in the eyes of God. One calls "satisfaction" a heavy and difficult work that a sinner willingly undergoes to pay for temporary punishment; but this cannot be said of the exclusion...

Answer: Firstly, those who make

have died to whom death was not imposed
as a punishment for their sins, such as
the Virgin Mary. Secondly, they fail to notice
that God can have many purposes in
the death of believers: sometimes
he takes them out of the world so that he
might, with one stroke, subdue all the

through their deliverance from all temptations

threaten believers for some time with death,
so that he might bring them back from their errors
and cause them to think of their conscience.
However, we shall see in another

of sin and a punishment with regard to

Secondly, it is said that, since children,

children are not yet capable

I answer that God wills that

the same with them from the mother’s womb;
for if they were not born sinners,
God would not condemn them to death.
He has willed that from the time

nature would be full of the signs of

children to die, sometimes to

David was disciplined by the death

children who are in the covenant is

one must also speak of the death of

sends them. One could ask those who say
they cannot understand why
believers suffer so much: whether someone,
after having properly obtained various indulgences,
is free from tribulations and death?
For according to their faith, tribulations
and death serve him as a
satisfactory punishment, or they do not. If they
serve as a satisfactory punishment, then indulgences
are unnecessary, since they do not free
them from that for which they were
received—namely, temporal punishments.
And if they are not satisfactions, then it
can happen that visitations and
tribulations in believers have another
use than to be satisfactions to
God’s justice.

3. It is said that the sacrifices under the Old Testament were sufficient. 
That is true: but these satisfactions were exemplary satisfactions <note>The author means these were "types" or models intended to point toward a greater reality.</note> which only foreshadowed the satisfaction of Christ / and by no means the imagined satisfactions of men.

4. It is said that / since the good works of believers are meritorious / the same then come to satisfy sufficiently: 
But that is building on a foundation / which we shall overthrow in another place / namely the claim that good works are meritorious <note>The author plans to argue in a later chapter that human works cannot earn favor or "merit" with God.</note>.

5. It is said that / one must distinguish between the sins / committed before and after Baptism; that the latter are more "crying" <note>An idiom for sins so grave they "cry out" for justice.</note> and more inexcusable than the former; and that consequently one should not be surprised / that God does not forgive them without satisfaction. 
I answer that the blood of Christ cleanses us from all sins.

6. It is said, That in all the works of God one sees both mercy and justice shining out / and that consequently it appears / that at the same time as He shows grace / He nevertheless still demands / that His justice be satisfied. 
I answer, that one also sees these two virtues in the work of our Salvation; He shows grace to sinners / but He willed that their surety <term>Borg: a legal guarantor who takes on the debt of another; in this context, Jesus Christ.</term> satisfy His justice; it is not from the sinners then / that He demands satisfaction / but from Him who offered Himself as Mediator.

7. It is said, that it is right / that we be conformed to our head <note>The "head" refers to Christ.</note> / and that we satisfy as He did. 
I answer, that / although Christ has suffered so that we should follow His footsteps / and suffer with Him / it does not follow from this / that we must suffer for the same ends / for which Christ suffered; on the contrary, Christ has satisfied / so that we would not be obliged to satisfy: that was impossible for us.

8. It is said that sins still remain in us / and that in order to take them away entirely / we must still satisfy. 
One is deceived in this; it is not through "satisfaction" that we release ourselves from the unhappy remnants of sin / which 

<column-break/>

so often cause us to sigh / but through a steady pursuit of holiness and a constant exercise in good works; besides which, it is the Holy Spirit / who, completing our sanctification at the hour of death / delivers us from the corruption / that yet remains in us.

9. It is said, that it is useful for the Sinner / that he does not remain unpunished; that the thought that he must still satisfy / makes man realize the greatness of his sins / and that it serves to root out the habits of sin. 
But these reasons are far too weak. 1. I allow that it is useful for a Sinner / that he does not remain without chastisement: therefore God chastises him. 2. Yet it is not necessary to think / that one must satisfy in order to understand the greatness of one's sins / and to root out the habits thereof; the thoughts of what Christ has suffered / those of death and of the last judgment are more than enough / to bring forth these healthy effects. 3. Finally / it is certain that these pretended satisfactions are not the satisfaction of Christ / but are very harmful to piety <note>original: "Godvruzt," meaning godliness or religious devotion.</note> / and serve only to make man puffed up <note>original: "opgeblaasen," meaning arrogant or prideful.</note>.

I end this chapter with the remark of the famous Arnauld <note>Antoine Arnauld (1612–1694) was a prominent French Catholic theologian associated with Jansenism. He often criticized what he saw as "easy" or superficial religious practices.</note> in his treatise on the *Frequent use of the Holy Communion* <note>original: "H: Nagtmaal," referring to the Lord's Supper or Eucharist.</note> Part 2, chapters 24, 25, etc. 1. That it is without reason to make penitence consist of five Paternosters <note>The "Our Father" prayer.</note> and the penitential Psalms (p. 566). 2. That the fear of not saying one's Rosary <note>original: "Rooze Krans."</note> correctly / or of giving some small alms / is of no great importance in the spirit of man to turn him away from vice / which the corruption of our nature presents to us with many allurements. It appears then from what has been said / that we are not obliged / nor even able to satisfy for ourselves.

## CHAPTER XXXIX.

->### That, since Believers cannot satisfy for themselves, they also cannot satisfy for others.<-

The same reasons / which prove to us the perfection of the satisfaction of Christ and the impossibility / of men satisfying for themselves / also clearly show / that the Saints <note>In this context, "Saints" refers to exceptionally holy believers whose "excess" good works were historically claimed to form a "treasury of merit" that the Church could distribute.</note> cannot satisfy for other men; nevertheless, to set this matter in more light / it is necessary to note that one cannot accept the satisfaction of the Saints / without first establishing these three principles:

1. That man can satisfy the justice of God / and through his satisfaction be freed from the punishment / which he has to fear.
2. That the Saints can free us from some punishments / which sin has deserved.
3. That they have done and suffered much more than was necessary for the atonement of their own sins.

The first fundamental principle is false / for to satisfy the justice of God / which is infinite / one must be perfectly holy / and find oneself in a state to offer a ransom of an infinite value; therefore the Scripture speaks to us so often of the Holiness of our Mediator / *My servant the righteous*, says Isaiah, LIII. 11. *shall justify many*. *If any man sin*, says John, 1 John II. 1. *We have an advocate with the Father Jesus Christ the righteous*. *He who knew no sin, he has made sin for us*, says Paul 2 Cor. V. 21. *We are bought free by the precious blood of Christ as of a lamb without blemish and without spot*, says Peter: 1 Pet. I. 19. For the same reason / the Scripture so often teaches us that Christ is God; God has obtained the church through his own blood: Acts XX. 28. In Hebrews IX. 14. it stands / that Christ has offered himself through the eternal Spirit: From this it follows that no one but Christ [is] perfectly 

<column-break/>

Holy and God / who alone has been able to satisfy Divine justice; it also follows / that he cannot give to man the power to satisfy God through his suffering / because he cannot make his [man's] suffering infinite / nor communicate his Divine nature to him.

The second principle is likewise [false] / for one would thus make the saints on one hand Saviors / and on the other hand Mediators / because they would free us from a part of the punishment / which we have deserved / namely from the temporal punishment <note>The author is refuting the idea that Christ's death pays for eternal punishment while human "satisfaction" must pay for temporal (temporary) punishment on earth or in purgatory.</note> / and thus one would also unite them with Christ; now the Scripture nowhere speaks of various Saviors or Mediators; it says / Acts IV. 12. *For there is no other name under Heaven, given among men, by which we must be saved*, and 1 Tim. II. 5. 6. *There is one God, there is also one Mediator between God and men, the man Jesus Christ, who gave himself a ransom for all*.

One will perhaps say, following Bell. <note>original: "Bell. l. 1. c. 4." referring to Cardinal Robert Bellarmine, a leading Roman Catholic theologian of the Counter-Reformation.</note> that it is indeed not necessary / to unite the suffering of Christ with that of the Saints / as if the suffering of Christ were not sufficient enough / but that one can unite them / so that the suffering of the Saints does not remain useless / the more so because this serves the honor of Christ / who is the source of all the good / that is found in the saints.

Answer, it is easy to answer: 1. If the suffering of the Saints must be united with that of Christ / only because it would otherwise be useless / then one has much more reason / not to unite them / for fear that one might judge / that the suffering of Christ is not sufficient. 2. It is an error to believe / that / if one does not unite the suffering of the Saints with that of Christ / it [suffering] does not serve to promote the honor of God and to edify men. 3. Finally, one deceives oneself / by imagining / that the mixing of human satisfactions with those of Christ / increases the honor of the Savior / for by doing so one divides the honor of our salvation between Christ and the creatures / and one joins companions to him / which offends him in the highest degree.

The third principle is Godless / and runs against

OF THE CHRISTIAN

against the Scripture and the testimony of the Saints themselves: For the Scripture teaches us that the Saints did no more than they were duty-bound to do, and that they were unprofitable servants <note>Referring to Luke 17:10: "So likewise ye, when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do."</note>, that none of them were justified through their works or suffering, that they all needed the grace of God for the reconciliation of their sins—far from having suffered more than was required to atone for them—and that all their suffering is not to be compared with the glory with which God will crown them: from all this it appears that the Saints did not satisfy for us, and that they could not have done so; we shall be convinced of this if we take heed of the following passages:

1. Paul asks in 1 Cor. 1:13: *Is Paul crucified for you?* Now, what the Apostle says of himself can be applied to all the Saints; it is therefore clear that no saint suffered for us, and consequently gave no satisfaction <note>The term "satisfaction" refers to the legal payment or atonement required to satisfy God's justice regarding sin.</note> for us.

2. He says in Gal. 6:5 that *every man shall bear his own burden* and 1 Cor. 3:8: *Every man shall receive his own reward according to his own labor*.

Add to this: 1. That the Saints have received a reward far above what they have deserved, since their suffering is not to be valued against the glory revealed to them; and thus what they have done, for which they received such a great reward, cannot be attributed to others as a satisfaction: could a soldier, who is gloriously rewarded for his service, rightly say that he has not been paid, because, besides the reward given to him, he was not granted the lives of some evildoers?

2. Add further that the satisfactions of the Saints are of no necessity, since the satisfaction of Christ is sufficiently enough to acquire a perfect redemption for us.

However, people still come forward with some objections; let us resolve them.

1. They once again object with Col. 1:24, on which we have already given our remarks in the previous Chapter, and where Paul nevertheless assures us that he fills up the remains of the tri-

<column-break/>

bulations of Christ for his body, which is the church: as proof that the suffering of Paul was satisfying.

But this is not the conclusion one should draw from it; for the Apostle says that he suffered for the church, not only because the church was the occasion and cause of his suffering, but that he endured the same for the edification and comfort of the church: *if we are afflicted*, he said to those of Corinth, 2 Cor. 1:6, *it is for your consolation, which is effective in the enduring of the same sufferings which we also suffer*. Following this interpretation, which is natural, it appears that no satisfaction is spoken of here; and in this sense, many sensible men of the Romish Church have themselves understood this passage.

Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Catholic philosopher and theologian.</note>, explaining these words, says:
> "that the same could indeed be taken in a bad sense,
> as if the suffering of Christ were not satisfying
> for our redemption: but that would be
> heresy," he adds there.

Cardinal Contarinus <note>Gasparo Contarini (1483–1542), a Venetian diplomat and cardinal known for seeking reconciliation with Protestants.</note> says of this place that one must not explain it as if the suffering of Christ were not sufficient to blot out sins, and as if something were still lacking that we could complete: but that Paul speaks thus because we must follow Christ, and suffer for the edification of the church, just as Christ suffered.

The Jesuit Justinianus <note>Benedetto Giustiniani (1550–1622), a Jesuit scholar.</note> expressly denies that satisfaction is spoken of here.

Eckius <note>Johann Eck (1486–1543), a major Catholic opponent of Martin Luther.</note> does not find it good that one uses this passage to show that the suffering of the believers serves for the forgiveness of sin, which is called an Indulgence: see Espenæus <note>Claude d'Espence (1511–1571), a French theologian and expert on the Epistles.</note> on the second letter to Timothy.

<margin>Great Sermon.</margin>
It is in the same way that one must explain what Paul says in another place, 2 Tim. 2:10: *Therefore I endure all things for the sake of the elect*: certainly not to obtain for them forgiveness and salvation, but to bring them to his preaching, and through patience to Salvation: for, as was very well said by an Church Father, although the suffering of Christ is enough for our Salvation, yet the martyrdom of Peter and Paul serves us as an example.

<header>THEOLOGY. IX. B. CHAPTER XL.</header>

If one asks: what power could the suffering of Paul have to bring the elect to salvation? I answer that, with regard to the elect—who were mingled with the children of this age like stones still in their quarry, though already predestined for the building of a great palace—the sermons of Paul, supported by his suffering, served to draw them out of the world and bring them to Christ. With regard to the others, who were already believers, it served to strengthen them in their faith.
<margin>Ephesians 5:1, 2.</margin>
2. It is objected that we must be followers of Christ, and consequently satisfy for our brothers just as Christ satisfied for us: Ephesians 5:1, 2. Answer: by this reasoning, I could also prove that we must raise the dead and redeem the world. Who does not see that we are only obliged to follow Christ in those things where we *can* follow him, and not in things that exceed our power, such as satisfying for others? <note>The author distinguishes between imitating Christ's character (attainable) and imitating His redemptive work (impossible for humans).</note>
<margin>Galatians 6:2.</margin>
3. It is further objected against us what Paul says to the Galatians: that we must help bear one another’s burdens. Galatians 6:2.
Answer: one must be blind not to see that the Apostle's purpose is to teach us that we, through our love, must meet the needs of others. One only has to read what immediately precedes it to be convinced: *Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness.* Galatians 6:1.
In this manner, various Roman teachers <note>The author lists prominent Catholic scholars to show that even they agree with the Protestant interpretation of this verse.</note> have also explained this passage, such as Justinianus, Guillaud, Godeau, Lyranus, Cajetanus, Emanuel-Sa, Adam Sasbout, Titelmannus, Arias Montanus, etc.
The other objections do not deserve for us to dwell upon them.
It is said that the "communion of saints" obliges us to satisfy for one another: this we deny, and it will never be proven to us. One can only show from that doctrine that we must take part in the prosperity or adversity of our brothers and share with them the goods that we possess. They also object with 2 Corinthians 8:14, but

<column-break/>

it appears that Paul intended to say nothing else there than that, just as the poverty of the Saints had been relieved by the abundance of those in Corinth, it might also happen that they [the Corinthians] would at some time be relieved in their poverty by the abundance of those to whom they were now distributing aid.
They object with Romans 15:27; yet the meaning is clear: that just as the Gentiles had received the faith from the Jews, they should in turn make them sharers in their temporal goods.
They object with Psalm 119:63; but it is certain that David means nothing other than that he is in a holy communion with the believers, and that he seeks to cultivate their friendship. It is said that God sometimes punishes many for the sin of a single person, and that consequently he could very well take away the deserved punishment of some through the satisfactions of another. But one always ends up assuming that man *can* satisfy, and that is what we deny. It is said that God grants much to the Saints and to their prayers; that I admit, but it is not because they deserve it: it is solely a work of His grace. No one has yet dared to say that Abraham, who prayed for Lot, or Paul, who prayed for all those who suffered shipwreck with him, would have "satisfied" for those for whom they prayed. <note>In this context, "satisfied" means to have paid the legal penalty for another's sins.</note>

...of his desire (d); sometimes they say that one who has offended his neighbor gives satisfaction to the same when he testifies to him, whether through his deeds or through his words, the displeasure he has for having offended him, and the desire he shows to be reconciled with him again. (e) If someone had offended another, he was obliged to give satisfaction through an oath, which was taken from him to make him acknowledge that the person he had wronged did not deserve it, and that he wished he had not done it. (f) Therefore, when the Church Fathers <note>The early Christian theologians of the first few centuries.</note> say that sinners satisfy God, it is not to teach that they do everything that the justice of God demands for the reconciliation of sin; but simply to tell us that they do that which is pleasing to God, and with which his mercy is satisfied, because his justice has been satisfied through the death of his Son. One cannot doubt this when one considers:

1. That they sometimes say that those who, having left the ungodliness of the Heathens, convert and receive baptism, satisfy God (g), because they do something that is pleasing to him.

(h) And it is certain that these duties of repentance, which the Church Fathers call satisfaction, are very often expressed by the name that signifies confession (i); but it has happened that the Ecclesiastical punishments, which the Ancient Church sometimes imposed on the penitents to satisfy the Church for the restoration of the offense they had committed, have been changed into punishments through which people have imagined that one can satisfy Divine justice.

<margin>

You have miserably lost your soul; spiritually dead, you have begun to survive yourself and, walking, to carry your own corpse, and yet you do not wail bitterly, you do not groan continually? (l) See Augustine, *Enchiridion*, ch. 65. Ivo of Chartres, Epistle 228.

If the Ancient Church demanded punishment, such as when they required someone to wear sackcloth and ashes, etc., it was not because they believed that he would thereby satisfy the justice of God, but to make them understand the magnitude of their sins and to oblige them to give public signs of their regret. (k). They also imposed a long period of penance on them, to see if it was truly sincere. (l).

# THE CHRISTIAN

Ambrose calls "satisfying" asking for forgiveness.
<margin>Ambrose, *On Penance*, Book II, Ch. 10.</margin>
If the Church Fathers say that the fire of Hell <note>original: "Gehenna," a term for the place of fiery punishment</note> is extinguished by confession (m) and that sins are wiped out by the work of repentance, they intended to say nothing else than that those who have a true remorse certainly obtain forgiveness for their sins, so that they shall never come into the fire of Hell—as if they had extinguished it with their own tears—and that they, through their remorse and the mortification of the flesh, wipe out the sinful habits they had acquired through excess and intemperance.

Cyprian says with truth (*Sermon on Works and Alms*), that the faults committed before baptism have been cleansed by the blood of Christ and by his satisfaction, and that other [sins] are washed away by alms and faith; but in this he has greatly deceived himself, and there is no one in these days who would dare to say that no other sins are washed away by the blood of Christ than those committed before baptism. Thus, one must understand that these same Church Fathers have said that we atone for our sins through works of repentance—that is to say, that the goodness of God is so great toward those who have true remorse for their sins and, renouncing them, give themselves over to holiness, love, generosity, and other good works, that he forgives all their faults as if they themselves had paid the ransom for their deliverance. For if one does not grant this meaning to the words of the Fathers, they would have taught the greatest impieties in the world.

Tertullian (*On Penance*, Book IV, Ch. 9) says that the repentant works of the first disciples of Christianity are the price by which their sins were wiped out. But this is a parable taken from commerce, where no goods are had unless one gives a price for them; likewise, God gives no forgiveness of sins except to those who have faith and sorrow. This is the same parable that Christ uses in Matthew 13:46, where he speaks of a man who buys the field in which he had found a treasure. However, one must admit that the Fathers

---

<note>Footnote at bottom of column 1</note>
(m) Tertullian, *On Penance*, ch. 12: "You extinguish hell for yourself through confession." <note>original: "gehennam ſibi exomologosis extinguis." Exomologosis refers to the early Christian practice of public confession and penance.</note>

<column-break/>

used very harsh expressions regarding that matter, and particularly Origen (*Exhortation to Martyrdom*), who says that just as many were redeemed by the blood of Christ, there might also be some who will be redeemed by the blood of the Martyrs. But it is certain that if one takes the word "redeem" or "purchase" in the sense in which it is used when dealing with Christ, the Fathers then said that one brother can redeem neither another nor even himself; thus speaks Basil regarding the 48th Psalm.

For the rest, one must not imagine that the Fathers would have believed that the suffering of the Martyrs was applied to other people under the pretext that their recommendations and letters had great weight in reconciling those who had fallen <note>The "lapsed" (lapsi) were Christians who had renounced their faith under Roman persecution and sought reentry into the Church.</note> back with the Church, etc.

Cyprian complains about the errors committed regarding this; one may consult many epistles he wrote on the subject, such as 45, 46, 47, etc.

The Church Fathers did not believe that men could "satisfy" <note>In this context, "satisfy" means to pay the penalty or make full legal amends to God for sin.</note> one for the other.

1. They said that no one can appease God for their own sin, much less for those of others.
<margin>Basil on Psalm 48.</margin>

2. That no one, by their death, can free others from death, except only the Son of God.
<margin>Tertullian, *On Modesty*, Ch. 22.</margin>

3. That, although the believers died for their brothers, nevertheless no blood of any Martyr was shed for the forgiveness of sin; that no one but Christ has done such for us, and that he thereby gave us an example—not to imitate him [in atoning], but to be grateful to him.
<margin>Augustine, *Tractates on John*, 84; also Book IV *To Boniface against the two Epistles of the Pelagians*.</margin>

4. Finally, that although the death of many Saints is precious in the eyes of the Lord, nonetheless not one was capable—however innocent they might have been—of having their death be an atonement for the world; that the righteous received the crown, but did not themselves distribute any; and that from their perseverance and firmness in faith came examples of patience, not gifts of righteousness; that their death was a private death, but
<margin>Leo, Epistle 83 and Sermon 12 *On the Passion*.</margin>

## CHAPTER XLI.

->Of Indulgences.<-

**S**ince we have already made mention of Indulgences, it will not be unhelpful for us to treat this subject in a bit more detail.

It must then be observed:

1. That the Christians, who bowed under the harshness of persecution / had heavy penances imposed upon them by the Church / according to the rules of discipline.

2. That, as they were not all in a position / to be able to endure these long-lasting penances / they requested that they might be released / and accepted back into the peace of the Church.

3. To obtain this grace / they often took their recourse to the Martyrs and Confessors <note>In the early church, "Confessors" were those who had suffered and remained firm in their faith under torture or imprisonment but had not been executed.</note> / who were imprisoned for the cause of Christ.

4. These confessors wrote letters of intercession to the Bishops / to the Priests / and to the people / so that these Sinners might be accepted back into the peace and communion of the Church / without having to undergo all the severity of the discipline: the respect / that people had for them / meant that / since one could refuse them nothing / the Sinners were readmitted to the peace of the church at their request / and that was called AN INDULGENCE. Cyprian <note>St. Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258 AD), whose letters often deal with the "Lapsed" who fell away during persecution.</note> complains about this: Letters X. XI. XII. XIII. XIV. XV. etc.

<margin>Ancyra <note>The Council of Ancyra, 314 AD.</note> Canon V.</margin>
5. One calls an indulgence, then, the lessening of the severity of the discipline / which the Church allowed at the request of the Martyrs / or also for other reasons: but one never gave the name of indulgence to the forgiveness of the punishment / which one owes to God's judgment.

6. But today, in the Roman Church, this name is given to the forgiveness

<column-break/>

of the punishment for sins in God's judgment, which it is supposed / that God grants in consideration of the suffering and of the merits of the Martyrs / who / so it is said / have suffered more / than was necessary for themselves; they describe the indulgence in various ways / some call it a forgiveness of what has been committed through actual and indubitable deeds / and that through a lawful distribution of the treasury of the Church; others say that it is the acquittal from the penance / which the Priests impose based on the institutions of the Church / the forgiving of the temporal punishment / which still remains to be suffered / after the forgiveness of sins / which is granted outside the Sacrament / by those who have the spiritual jurisdiction to distribute the Heavenly treasury of the Church.

The foundation of the opinion of those of the Roman Church is:

1. That through the forgiveness of sins the eternal punishment is taken away / but not the temporal punishment; that one / consequently / must still suffer the same / either in this life / or in purgatory.

2. That there is an infinite treasury in the Church / consisting of the merits of Christ and of the blessed Virgin Mary / along with all the Saints in their satisfactions and in their suffering.

3. That the Pope has the power / to distribute this treasury: some believe that the Pope alone has this power: others that the Pope has the primary right to it / and that the Archbishops in their Provinces / and the Bishops in their Dioceses also have it / but under certain prescribed limitations by the Pope; that in regard to their Churches / even of the Cardinals / who are neither Bishops nor Abbots / they do not have this power.

There are various indulgences.

One objects using that / which Paul did regarding the guilty offender in 2 Corinthians 2:1.

<margin>Estius and Noel Alexander bring up Hebrews 10:26.</margin>

We have seen / what indulgences were in the early times: later, others were introduced / when a means was found to create a certain compensation and exchange of <term>penance</term> <note>Penance here refers to the outward discipline or punishment imposed by the church, such as fasting or prayer.</note>.

<margin>Bernhardin.</margin>
At that time, indulgences were granted at the request of the penitents / when they declared / that they were not in a position to fulfill the penance imposed on them; subsequently, indulgences were offered to the people for various things; those who collected charitable gifts for the Hospitals, in order to obtain them all the more quickly / offered indulgences to those who gave abundant alms; various errors occurred there / which were condemned in the IV. ### DIVINITY. IX. B. XLI. Chapter.

...was nothing other than to weaken Church discipline; it was said that indulgences were "pious frauds" <note>original: "Godvruztige bedriegeryen"</note>, by which people were incited to piety: others asserted that they were dangerous.

<margin>Innocent III in the Year 1215.</margin>
The Popes, however, did not cease to offer full indulgences to those who went to the war for the Holy Land <note>The Crusades.</note>, and to those who merely performed pilgrimages.

Clement VI, having proclaimed a full indulgence for those who promised to take up the cross, with the assurance that at their request three or four souls would leave <term>purgatory</term> <note>In Catholic doctrine, an intermediate state where souls are purified before entering heaven.</note>, and having given orders to the Angels to bring the souls of those who were out on pilgrimages directly into Paradise; there was a Teacher named Jan van Engel, who publicly taught that the souls in purgatory were under the jurisdiction of the Pope, and that, if the Pope only wished it, he could make the entire purgatory empty.

But without involving myself in the particulars of everything regarding indulgences, I will only say that the abuses were great, such that the King of France had great complaints made about them to Pope Sixtus IV; these were discussed in the Council of Vienne in the year 1511 <note>The author may be referring to the later sessions of the Fifth Lateran Council or a local synod, as the Great Council of Vienne took place in 1311.</note>.

All of this did not stop these abuses: Leo X had the sale of indulgences proclaimed in all the Provinces belonging to the Roman Church, and he gave the money that would come from the Provinces of Saxony, and from many places in Germany, to his sister Magdalena, who was married to Franceschetto Cibo, the natural son of Pope Innocent VIII. Arembold <note>Johannes Angelus Arcimboldi, a papal commissioner for indulgences.</note>, who had risen from a merchant of Genoa to become a Bishop, collected this tax, and Germany was refilled with indulgence-sellers: the country was greatly offended by this, and Martin Luther, an Augustinian Monk, was the first who took up the banner against them; he proclaimed and publicly maintained ninety-five theses against the doctrine of indulgences, which gave the occasion for the Reformation in Germany in the years 1517, 1518, etc.

At the same time, Zwingli did in Zurich what Luther had done in Saxony; he opposed himself to Zweder Samson, a Franciscan Monk from Milan, who had already collected 120,000 <term>Reichsthalers</term> <note>A standard silver coin used in the Holy Roman Empire.</note> through the selling of indulgences; see there the true cause of the Reformation in Switzerland.

3. Such as are given based on false representations, on false histories, which have no other foundation than private visions and revelations to which no authority has been given by any reputable writer.

5. Such as exceed the power of those who grant them, like those that Popes give for 100 or 200 years, or even for 1,000 and 2,000 years; or those which Cardinals give for more than 100 days.

# THEOLOGY. IX. B. Chapter XLII.

<margin>On the Inventors, Book VIII, ch. 1.</margin>
...every hundred years, they would obtain a full <term>indulgence</term> <note>A remission before God of the temporal punishment due to sins whose guilt has already been forgiven.</note>; it does not appear, however, that he called this great forgiveness by the name of "Jubilee Year." Polydore Vergil <note>Polydore Vergil (c. 1470–1555) was an Italian humanist scholar and historian.</note> asserts that this Pope seems to have intended to draw the Roman people away from celebrating the centennial games <note>The *Ludi Saeculares*, ancient Roman religious celebrations involving sacrifices and theatrical performances.</note>.

Clement VI, fifty years later, set the Jubilee Year at every fifty years; and the first celebrated after this new institution was in the year of our Lord 1350.

Urban VIII brought it to every 33 years; Paul II to every 25 years, which was confirmed by Pope Sixtus IV and came into use in the year 1475. It is said that Pope Gregory XIII would have set it to every 15 years, if death had not surprised him. Boniface VIII had chosen every hundred years, to—as he said—follow the old tradition, though no proof of this is found anywhere. Clement VI said that he had set the Jubilee at the 50th year to follow the Jubilee Year of the Jews. Urban VII <note>original: "Urbanus de VII," likely referring to Urban VI regarding the 33-year cycle.</note> said he set it at 33 years because our Savior was on earth for only 33 years. Paul II said he shortened the time because of the brevity of human life. Boniface VIII required nothing more than that one should visit the Churches of St. Peter and St. Paul. Clement VI added the Church of St. John Lateran; Paul II added the Church of St. Mary Major; here is how the Jubilee Year is celebrated in Rome:

1. On the day of the Feast of the Ascension preceding the Jubilee Year, after the Gospel has been read and a solemn Mass performed in the Church of St. Peter in the Vatican, the <term>Papal Bull</term> <note>An official edict or public decree issued by the Pope, named after the lead seal (bulla) appended to it.</note> is read in Latin and Italian from two different pulpits, by which he announces the Jubilee for the coming year; and this bull is posted in four different places in the city of Rome.

2. In each of the four Churches one is obliged to visit, there is a gate that is walled up, which is given the name of the "Holy Door."

3. In the Jubilee year itself, on Christmas Eve, a great procession is held,

<column-break/>

<margin>Sanctatellius on the Jubilee.</margin>
where all the ambassadors of the princes, the Council of Rome, the Grand Penitentiary <note>The head of the Vatican office dealing with the forgiveness of sins.</note> of St. Peter, the prelates, the Cardinals, and the Pope himself are present; after the midday meal, the Pope goes from the Chapel of the Palace to the Church of St. Peter, up to the Holy Door, which he finds walled up, like those of the other three churches; and while he murmurs some prayers, he knocks three times on the door with a silver hammer, which he then gives to the Grand Penitentiary, who is accompanied by two others, who also strike with the same hammer as the Pope did; thereupon the Pope sits down, but no sooner has he reached his carrying chair than the wall of the gate is broken down by stonemasons, and those present take up the stones and the cement with much devotion; then the Grand Penitentiaries come in priestly robes and sprinkle holy water on the spot where the masonry of the gate was; after this is done, the Pope enters the Church through this gate, where the evening prayers are then sung, accompanied by a choice choir. While the stonemasons tear down the wall closing the gate of St. Peter, the Pope sends three Cardinals to open the Holy Doors of the other churches with the same ceremonies.

4. When the Jubilee Year is about to end, a few days before Christmas Eve, the day is announced on which the door will be walled up again; when this day has come, a great procession is made in the afternoon; the evening prayers being ended, the Pope again appoints three Cardinals to also close the doors of the other three churches, who, as soon as they have received the Papal blessing, depart to carry out his orders; then the Pope goes through the Holy Door of St. Peter of the Vatican, gives his blessing to the company that will be used to wall it up, whereupon taking in hand a silver trowel offered to him by the head of the Grand Penitentiaries, he scatters cement three times with the trowel on the middle of the threshold of the door, and places upon it several pieces of gold and silver; then he lays three thick stones on this spot, speaking these words: "In the faith and in the power of Jesus Christ." <note>original: "in het geloove en in de kragt van Jesus Christus," translating the Latin formula "In fide et virtute Jesu Christi."</note>

<header>THE CHRISTIAN</header>

*Christ*, son of the living God, who said to the Prince of the Apostles <note>A traditional title for Saint Peter.</note>, "You are *Peter* and on this rock I will build my congregation," so we set this first stone to close the holy gate, which may not be opened again until the time of the next Jubilee Year; in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. This speech being finished—while one of the masons prepares the stones—the Chief of the <term>Penitentiaries</term> <note>original: "Biegt-vaders." These are priests, specifically the Grand Penitentiary and his assistants, who have special authority to hear confessions and grant absolution for reserved sins during the Jubilee.</note> lays another stone on top with a silver trowel, being assisted by the other Chief Penitentiaries who accompany him; and the gate having been walled up with all speed by twelve masons, the Pope gives his blessing to all who are present, along with a plenary <term>indulgence</term> <note>A "plenary" indulgence is believed to remove all temporal punishment due to sin.</note>.

It is believed that the opening of the holy gate occurs: 1. To represent that *Christ* opened the <term>Limbo of the Fathers</term> <note>original: "voorburg van de helle" (the suburb of hell). In Catholic theology, this was the place where the righteous who died before Christ’s resurrection awaited their salvation.</note> to the Fathers who were imprisoned there before his resurrection. 2. To show that the treasury of the church is opened. 3. To demonstrate with what longing those in *Rome* expect the arrival of all peoples from the East, West, South, and North, in accordance with the number of the four gates.

The Hammer, with which the Pope knocks on the gate, shows the supreme authority that God gives to him, whom they hold to be His <term>Vicar</term> <note>original: "Stedehouder." A representative or deputy acting in the place of a superior.</note> on earth; the holy water, with which the gate is sprinkled, signifies—as they believe—that only those will gain the Jubilee Year who cleanse themselves of their defilement through their confession; that by virtue of the Jubilee, sinners shall regain almost the entire purification they received in Baptism; and that all the gracious goods we receive proceed from the suffering of our Savior.

I do not speak here of the indulgences earned in the Jubilee Year, how one must visit the churches, what cases the Pope reserves for himself from which one is released during the Jubilee, what power the Penitentiaries have in the Jubilee Year, and many other things that can be found in various writers of the Roman church; as well as in the treatise on the Jubilee by the renowned Mr. *Drelincourt* <note>Charles Drelincourt (1595–1669) was a famous French Protestant author known for his critiques of Catholic doctrine.</note>, and by yet another unnamed English Writer, printed in London in the year 1700 by

->Their grounds are:<-
1. That *Christ* has freed us from the guilt and eternal punishment, but that we must still satisfy the justice of God for venial sins <note>original: "vergetelyke zonde," likely a typo for "vergeeflyke" (venial/forgiveable) sin.</note> and for temporal punishment.
2. That there are people who perform far holier works than God commands. <note>original: "Bell. de Monach. c. 13." - referring to Robert Bellarmine’s *On Monks*, chapter 13.</note>
3. That there are holy martyrs, confessors, and pilgrims who have suffered more than their sins deserved. <note>original citations from Bellarmine, Angles, and Gregory of Valencia regarding indulgences.</note>
4. That all good works, insofar as they are <term>satisfactory</term> <note>Works that "satisfy" or pay the debt of temporal punishment.</note>, can be attributed to others, and that the suffering of the saints can take away the temporal punishment we have earned because of our sins.
5. That the abundant satisfaction of *Christ* and of the saints is the material of the treasury of the churches.
6. That the Pope possesses the key to this treasure chest, from which he takes the satisfactions as it pleases him, to release the faithful from all satisfactions through indulgences.
7. That the Pope grants the riches of this church treasury to the faithful by way of payment and absolution, and to the dead by way of <term>suffrage</term> <note>original: "toestemming" (consent/support). In this context, it refers to prayers or acts offered to help souls in Purgatory.</note>. When the Pope takes some pieces from this treasure chest to give to someone on specific occasions, it is a simple indulgence: but when he opens the treasure chest in general for all kinds of people, and shows great liberality through it, then it is called the Jubilee Year.
8. That the Fathers of the Old Testament were imprisoned in the Limbo of Hell.
9. That there is a <term>purgatory</term> <note>A place of temporary suffering or purification for souls before entering heaven.</note>.
10. That Priests have the power to forgive sins.
11. That the grace of God is bound to certain churches.

### CHAPTER XLIII.

->Of the Intercession of Jesus Christ,<-
->of his blessing, and the ef-<-
->fects of his Priesthood.<-

**T**he second act of Christ’s Priesthood is his intercession, just as the High Priest of old / after he had offered the sacrifice / entered into the Holy of Holies <note>The innermost chamber of the biblical Tabernacle and Temple, which the High Priest entered only once a year on the Day of Atonement.</note> to pray for the people as an advocate.

One must not understand this intercession / as if Christ bowed his knees before his Father in Heaven / for that would not be consistent with the glorified state / to which he has been exalted / sitting at the right hand of God in the highest Heavens.

When Holy Scripture says / that Christ prays for us / it wishes to teach us:

1. That Christ appears before the Father for us / ever presenting before His face his Divine body / which he has brought into the Sanctuary / in which he suffered death for us / and showed him a perfect obedience. This presentation is / so to speak / a constant Intercession; the blood of Christ speaks for us / just as that of Abel spoke against Cain / not through the pronunciation of words / but through the effect of his shed blood / which cries out as if it had a voice. Therefore, the intercession of Christ is nothing other than his Appearance for us as High Priest before his Father / and the continuous offering of his satisfaction to His justice / and of the Suffering / that he endured in our place. Therefore he is shown in *Revelation 5:6* as a Lamb that was slain / because his blood is always living.

2. Scripture also teaches us through this / that Christ always desires / that we have a share in the fruits of his death / and that his desires are always heard; that he protects and defends us before God’s face against the accusations of Satan / and the curses of the law; and that he / just as he from the Fa-

<column-break/>

ther obtains the gifts of grace / which we need / likewise promises him in our name our obedience and faithfulness.

3. Scripture further teaches us through the Intercession of Christ / that Christ constantly presents our persons and our prayers / in which he covers the defects / through his perfect righteousness to God. Therefore he is represented in *Revelation 8:3* as an Angel with a golden censer, to whom much incense was given, etc.

I have said / that the Intercession of Christ is an act of his Priesthood / and not of his Kingly office.

Holy Scripture teaches us this; for it shows us Christ performing the work of an intercessor as Priest, and not as King *Hebrews 9:24, 25.* Where it clearly appears / that Paul alludes to that which the High Priest performed after the offering of the sacrifice, etc. This is confirmed from *Revelation 8:3* where the intercession of Christ is described by an Angel / who held a golden censer in his hand.

This Intercession was necessary: 1. So that Christ would be our perfect High Priest / for the High Priest was obligated to pray for the people as an advocate. 2. So that he would make the Salvation / which he obtained through his death / our own. 3. So that he would bring our prayers to God / and make the same acceptable to him. 4. So that he would obtain from the Father the continuation of all his gifts of grace / to lead us into his fellowship / and to protect us against the enemies of our Salvation / and in particular to stop the mouth of Satan our accuser *Zechariah 3:2.* Thus one sees that the intercession of Christ is a source of comforts. If anyone has sinned, says John *1 John 2:1* we have an advocate with the Father. *Hebrews 4:16.* Let us then go with boldness to the throne of grace, etc.

This Intercession takes place in Heaven / and therefore Christ also ascended after his resurrection. His sacrifice had to be slain and offered on earth / because it was a work of his humiliation; but his intercession had to be performed in Heaven / being the work of his exaltation.

This intercession ensures / that Christ is Priest for eternity / according to the order
