# THEOLOGY. IX. B. Chapter 50.

<margin>Acts 18:18.</margin>
6. ¶ One might object using what the Apostles at times have done to win over the Jews and to accommodate their weakness.

But it is evident from what has been said that what they did in that regard was only for a time, in order to bring the weak brothers to Christ. <note>The author refers to "weak brothers" as those early Jewish Christians who still felt bound by old customs; the Apostles accommodated them temporarily to avoid unnecessary conflict while they grew in faith.</note>

7. Finally, it is said that one must abolish all kinds of external ceremonies in the Church.

I answer that this conclusion does not follow. Some ceremonies are necessary for the sake of order, as long as one does not seek to gain merit from them, nor imagines that they are so necessary that those who do not observe them sin greatly—provided they act without despising the Church that prescribed them and without giving offense.

One must also be careful not to multiply these ceremonies so much that they become an unbearable burden.

There is a great difference between the ceremonies of the Old and those of the New Testament. The former are no longer in use because they prefigured the Messiah, who has come. The latter serve for the maintenance of good order in the Church. The former constituted the primary part of the religious service; the latter are merely aids to it.

### CHAPTER L.

->Whether the Civil Law is abolished.<-

REngarding the Civil Law, <note>In this context, "Civil Law" refers to the judicial and political laws given specifically to the nation of Israel in the Old Testament, distinct from the Ten Commandments (Moral Law).</note> one can consider it in two ways.

1. One can consider it as that which separated the people of Israel from all other nations, and as a Law that prefigured the Kingdom of Christ. In that respect, it is <margin>Gal. 2:28. Eph. 2:14.</margin> abolished; for there is no longer any distinction between Jew and Gentile in Christ. The middle wall of separation is broken down. Christ having come, we no longer need the symbols that formerly foreshadowed Him. The Jews themselves no longer constitute a commonwealth. They are subject to the powers and authorities under which they are scattered. One can also consider this Law as containing various statutes that concerned none but the 

<column-break/>

Jews in particular, or which were shadows of things that were to happen; such as, for example, the Law of divorce, the firstborn, the <term>cities of refuge</term> <note>Specified towns where someone who committed accidental manslaughter could claim asylum from blood vengeance.</note>, the jubilee years, the <term>waters of jealousy</term> <note>A ritual ordeal described in Numbers 5 used to determine if a wife had been unfaithful.</note>, the manner in which one had to sow both <note>Likely referring to the prohibition against sowing a field with two different types of seed.</note>, and the division of the Land of Canaan. In this respect, the Civil Law is also annulled.

2. But one can consider it under another respect, as containing some laws which are based on the Law of nature—sound and common to all men—which serve as explanations of the ten commandments and can be observed by all nations. In this respect, it is not abolished; thus, nothing prevents the maintenance of laws that punish the guilty, prescribe the maintenance of order, protect widows and orphans, etc. The most civilized nations have observed these, and their fulfillment is strictly recommended to us in the New Testament.

One can consider the children of Jacob <note>The Israelites.</note> either as a people in general or as the Jewish people in particular; all the Laws that suit the children of Jacob, when considered as a people in general, can be common to other nations. But all those given to them specifically as the descendants of Jacob no longer suit us any more than those of the Assyrians, Persians, and Greeks.

One might say that it were to be wished that all nations conformed to the Jewish Civil laws. But this is impossible, because the maintenance of those laws depends on certain circumstances that are not found among other nations. God, who made these laws primarily for the Jews and did not place other nations in the state in which they were, has also not subjected them to the same. If it then happens that Christians prefer certain laws of the old Roman Emperors over the Civil laws that God made for the Jews, it is only because the former better suit their state than the latter.

One might say that if Christ had wanted the Civil law to be abolished, he would have put another in its place. When he was on earth, he never wanted to involve himself in the settling of disputes. Luke 12:13, 14.
